The exchange current density i₀ for glycerol oxidation on Pt(111) is ≈ 10⁻⁶ A cm⁻², two orders of magnitude lower than for hydrogen oxidation, explaining the high overpotentials required. Conversely, 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) can be reduced to 2,5‑dimethylfuran (DMF) or oxidized to 2,5‑furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA). The two‑electron reduction HMF + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → DMF + H₂O occurs at –0.2 V vs. RHE on Cu with a Faradaic efficiency > 80 % in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7). The competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is suppressed by the high HMF concentration (0.5 M) and the relatively low proton activity. Oxidation to FDCA (HMF + 3 H₂O → FDCA + 6 H⁺ + 6 e⁻) is efficiently catalyzed by Ni‑Fe layered double hydroxides at 1.35 V vs. RHE, delivering a current density of 10 mA cm⁻² with > 90 % selectivity. Examiners frequently ask to construct a Pourbaix‑type diagram for the glycerol/CO₂ system, to calculate the theoretical cell voltage for a paired electrolysis where glycerol oxidation at the anode is coupled with HMF reduction at the cathode, and to discuss how the local pH shift near the electrode surface influences product distribution.

Electrochemical Impedance Analysis of Lithium‑Sulfur Batteries: Polysulfide Shuttle and Interfacial Processes

Lithium‑sulfur (Li‑S) cells exhibit a complex impedance spectrum with at least three distinct time constants. The high‑frequency semicircle (10⁴–10⁵ Hz) corresponds to the solid‑electrolyte interphase on the lithium anode (RSEI, CSEI). The mid‑frequency feature (10²–10³ Hz) is assigned to the charge‑transfer resistance at the sulfur cathode (Rct,S) in parallel with a double‑layer capacitance Cdl,S. The low‑frequency tail (10⁻²–10⁰ Hz) reflects the diffusion of soluble lithium polysulfides (Li₂Sₓ, 4 ≤ x ≤ 8) through the porous cathode and separator, often modeled by a finite‑length Warburg element (WFL) with diffusion coefficient DPS ≈ 10⁻⁷ cm² s⁻¹. The polysulfide shuttle manifests as an additional low‑frequency inductive loop or a negative real‑axis intercept when the cell is measured under open‑circuit voltage after a rest period; this arises from the redox cycling of polysulfides at the lithium anode, which creates a pseudo‑capacitive current that opposes the applied perturbation. Quantitatively, the shuttle current Ish can be extracted from the low‑frequency resistance Rsh = ΔV/Ish obtained by fitting the impedance with an equivalent circuit: Rs + (RSEI‖CPESEI) + (Rct,S‖CPEdl,S) + WFL + Rsh. A typical Rsh of 5–20 Ω cm² corresponds to a coulombic efficiency loss of 5–15 % per cycle. Mitigation strategies — functionalized separators, LiNO₃ additive, and cathode host materials — are evaluated by monitoring the reduction of Rsh and the shift of the Warburg coefficient σ = (RT)/(n²F²A√2DPScPS). Examiners test the ability to distinguish the inductive loop caused by the shuttle from the capacitive loop of the SEI, to calculate the polysulfide diffusion coefficient from the Warburg slope (Z′ ∝ ω⁻⁰·⁵), and to explain why the addition of LiNO₃ suppresses the shuttle by forming a passivating LiₓNOᵧ layer that increases RSEI but decreases Rsh.

Electrochemical CO₂ Capture and Utilization via Redox‑Active Carriers: Mediated Electrochemical Reduction

Direct electrochemical CO₂ reduction (CO₂R) suffers from low CO₂ solubility (≈ 0.033 M in water at 1 atm) and competing hydrogen evolution. Mediated electrochemical reduction employs a redox‑active carrier (e.g., quinone, viologen, or transition‑metal complex) that chemically binds CO₂ in its reduced state and releases it upon oxidation, decoupling capture from conversion. A representative cycle uses 9,10‑anthraquinone‑2,7‑disulfonic acid (AQDS) in aqueous alkaline electrolyte. The reduced form AQDS²⁻ reacts with CO₂ to form a carbonate adduct AQDS‑CO₂²⁻ (equilibrium constant Kcap ≈ 10³ M⁻¹). The adduct is then electrochemically reduced at –0.6 V vs. RHE to produce formate and regenerate AQDS²⁻. The overall process: CO₂ + AQDS²⁻ ⇌ AQDS‑CO₂²⁻ (capture); AQDS‑CO₂²⁻ + 2 e⁻ + 2 H⁺ → AQDS²⁻ + HCOO⁻ (release and reduction). The thermodynamic cell voltage is Ecell = E⁰(CO₂/HCOO⁻) – E⁰(AQDS/AQDS²⁻) + (RT/F)ln([AQDS²⁻]/[AQDS‑CO₂²⁻]) ≈ –0.61 V – (–0.20 V) = –0.41 V, indicating a lower overpotential than direct CO₂R on Sn (–0.9 V). Kinetic analysis via rotating ring‑disk electrode (RRDE) shows a collection efficiency of 0.25 for formate, confirming the mediated pathway. The carrier concentration (10 mM) and CO₂ partial pressure (1 atm) give a capture capacity of 0.33 mmol CO₂ cm⁻³ electrolyte. Long‑term cycling stability is limited by carrier degradation (hydrolysis of the quinone) and crossover; a Nafion membrane reduces crossover but adds ohmic drop (Rmem ≈ 0.5 Ω cm²). Examiners ask to derive the Nernst equation for the mediated capture step, to calculate the Faradaic efficiency for formate when the measured cathodic current is 5 mA cm⁻² and the formate production rate determined by HPLC is 0.18 mmol h⁻¹ cm⁻², and to discuss how the pKa of the carrier influences the operating pH window.

  • Confusing the SEI capacitance with the double‑layer capacitance of the lithium metal; the SEI capacitance is orders of magnitude smaller and appears at higher frequency.
  • Assuming the Newman P2D model reduces to the single‑particle model at all C‑rates; the SPM neglects electrolyte concentration gradients that dominate above 1 C.
  • Treating the glycerol oxidation peak in CV as a single‑electron process; the first dehydrogenation is a two‑electron step, and the Tafel slope must be interpreted accordingly.
  • Misidentifying the inductive loop in Li‑S EIS as an artifact; it is a signature of the polysulfide shuttle and must be included in the equivalent circuit.
  • Neglecting the equilibrium constant of CO₂ capture by the redox carrier when calculating the mediated cell voltage; the capture equilibrium shifts the effective potential by (RT/F)ln Kcap.
  • Using the bulk CO₂ solubility instead of the local concentration at the electrode surface when estimating the limiting current for direct CO₂R; the diffusion layer thickness controls the actual flux.
  • Overlooking the effect of membrane resistance on the overall energy efficiency in mediated CO₂ capture systems; the ohmic loss can exceed the kinetic overpotential savings.

Electrochemical Hydrogen Evolution Reaction: Volmer–Heyrovsky–Tafel Mechanism and Catalyst Descriptors

The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) proceeds through three elementary steps that can operate in parallel or sequence depending on the catalyst surface and electrolyte pH. In acidic media the Volmer step (H⁺ + e⁻ → H*ads) is followed either by the Heyrovsky step (H*ads + H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂) or the Tafel step (2 H*ads → H₂). In alkaline media the Volmer step involves water dissociation (H₂O + e⁻ → H*ads + OH⁻), which is often rate‑determining on non‑noble metals. The free‑energy of hydrogen adsorption (ΔG_H*) is the primary descriptor: optimal catalysts sit near ΔG_H* ≈ 0 eV (e.g., Pt, MoS₂ edge sites). Deviations of ±0.1 eV change the exchange current density (j₀) by roughly an order of magnitude. Tafel slopes of 120 mV dec⁻¹, 40 mV dec⁻¹ and 30 mV dec⁻¹ correspond respectively to Volmer‑limited, Heyrovsky‑limited and Tafel‑limited kinetics. Experimental determination of j₀ requires extrapolation of the linear Tafel region to zero overpotential; a common mistake is using the high‑overpotential region where mass‑transport distortion inflates the apparent slope. The exchange current density for Pt in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ is ≈10⁻³ A cm⁻², whereas for Ni it is ≈10⁻⁶ A cm⁻², reflecting the ΔG_H* difference of ~0.2 eV. Recent descriptor work adds the water‑dissociation barrier (ΔG_H₂O*) for alkaline HER, explaining why Ni‑Mo alloys outperform pure Ni despite similar ΔG_H*. Examiners frequently ask to derive the Tafel equation from the Butler‑Volmer expression assuming a single rate‑determining step, and to calculate the overpotential needed to reach 10 mA cm⁻² given j₀ and the measured Tafel slope.

Electrochemical Oxygen Evolution Reaction: Lattice Oxygen Mechanism, Scaling Relations, and Overpotential Minimization

The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic and alkaline electrolytes follows a four‑electron pathway with adsorbed intermediates *OH, *O, and *OOH. On transition‑metal oxides the conventional adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) obeys linear scaling relations: ΔG_*OOH ≈ ΔG_*OH + 3.2 eV and ΔG_*O ≈ ΔG_*OH + 1.6 eV. These relations impose a theoretical minimum overpotential of ≈0.37 V (the “overpotential wall”) for any catalyst that follows AEM. The lattice‑oxygen‑mediated mechanism (LOM) bypasses *OOH by involving lattice oxygen, breaking the scaling constraint and enabling overpotentials below 0.3 V on perovskites such as SrIrO₃ and doped Co₃O₄. Kinetic signatures of LOM include a Tafel slope near 60 mV dec⁻¹ and a reaction order in OH⁻ of 1, whereas AEM typically shows 40 mV dec⁻¹ and order 2. Operando Raman and X‑ray absorption spectroscopy detect transient oxygen vacancies, confirming lattice participation. The activity volcano for OER plots log j₀ versus ΔG_*OH; the apex lies at ΔG_*OH ≈ 1.6 eV (e.g., RuO₂, IrO₂). In practice, stability limits the usable region: RuO₂ dissolves above 1.5 V vs. RHE, while IrO₂ remains stable but is scarce. Examiners test the ability to construct a free‑energy diagram at 1.23 V, to identify the potential‑determining step from the largest ΔG step, and to explain why a catalyst with a low *OH binding energy but high *O binding energy may still exhibit high overpotential due to the scaling relation. A frequent trap is confusing the thermodynamic overpotential (η_thermo = max(ΔG_i)/e – 1.23 V) with the kinetic overpotential extracted from Tafel extrapolation.

Worked Example: HER Exchange Current Density from Tafel Plot
A linear Tafel region for a Ni‑Mo electrode in 1 M KOH yields a slope of 120 mV dec⁻¹ and passes through the point (η = 200 mV, j = 5 mA cm⁻²). Calculate the exchange current density j₀.
The Tafel equation for a Volmer‑limited step (α = 0.5) is η = (2.303 RT/αF) log₁₀(j/j₀). At 298 K, 2.303 RT/F ≈ 0.059 V, so the Tafel slope b = 0.059/α = 0.118 V dec⁻¹ ≈ 118 mV dec⁻¹, consistent with the measured 120 mV dec⁻¹. Rearranging: log₁₀(j/j₀) = η/b = 0.200 V / 0.118 V dec⁻¹ = 1.695 dec. Thus j/j₀ = 10¹·⁶⁹⁵ ≈ 49.6. With j = 5 mA cm⁻², j₀ = 5 mA cm⁻² / 49.6 ≈ 0.10 mA cm⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ A cm⁻².
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a Tafel slope is given, first identify the implied rate‑determining step (120 mV dec⁻¹ → Volmer, 40 mV dec⁻¹ → Heyrovsky, 30 mV dec⁻¹ → Tafel). Use the corresponding transfer coefficient (α = 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 respectively) to compute the theoretical slope and verify consistency. Then apply η = b log₁₀(j/j₀) directly; avoid converting to natural logarithms unless the problem explicitly uses the Butler‑Volmer form.

Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction to Ammonia: Competing Pathways, Selectivity Descriptors, and Reactor Design

Nitrate (NO₃⁻) reduction to ammonia (NH₃) proceeds via a nine‑electron cascade: NO₃⁻ → NO₂⁻ → NO → N₂O → N₂ → NH₂OH → NH₃, with parallel two‑electron pathways to N₂ and N₂O that lower Faradaic efficiency (FE). The key selectivity descriptor is the binding energy of *NO versus *NH₂ on the catalyst surface; strong *NO binding favors further reduction to NH₃, while weak binding leads to desorption and N₂ formation. Copper and its alloys (Cu‑Sn, Cu‑In) exhibit moderate *NO binding (ΔG_*NO ≈ –0.5 eV) and achieve FE_NH₃ up to 90 % at –0.6 V vs. RHE in 0.1 M KOH. In contrast, Pt binds *NO too strongly, poisoning the surface and diverting current to HER. The reaction order in nitrate is typically 1, but at high concentrations (>0.5 M) mass‑transport limitation appears, evidenced by a limiting current plateau. Reactor design must address the low solubility of NO₃⁻ (≈0.1 M in water) and the generation of OH⁻ at the cathode, which raises local pH and can precipitate metal hydroxides. Flow‑cell configurations with a cation‑exchange membrane (e.g., Nafion) maintain a stable alkaline catholyte while separating the anodic OER. The overall cell voltage for nitrate‑to‑ammonia at 10 mA cm⁻² is ≈2.0 V (cathode –0.6 V, anode +1.4 V), giving an energy consumption of ≈0.5 kWh kg⁻¹ NH₃, competitive with Haber‑Bosch when renewable electricity is used. Examiners often ask to write the balanced overall reaction (NO₃⁻ + 9 H⁺ + 8 e⁻ → NH₃ + 3 H₂O), to calculate the theoretical charge required for 1 mol NH₃ (8 F = 771 kC), and to explain why a high local pH suppresses HER but can also promote the competing nitrate‑to‑nitrite step.

Electrochemical CO₂ Reduction to C₁ Products: Formate, CO, and Methanol Selectivity Control via Electrolyte Engineering

CO₂ reduction (CO₂R) to C₁ products proceeds through a *COOH intermediate for CO and a *OCHO intermediate for formate. The branching ratio is governed by the relative stabilization of these intermediates on the catalyst surface. On Sn, In, and Bi the *OCHO pathway dominates, delivering formate FE > 90 % at –0.9 V vs. RHE in bicarbonate electrolyte. On Ag, Au, and Zn the *COOH pathway prevails, giving CO FE up to 95 % at –0.7 V. Methanol formation requires further proton‑coupled electron transfers on *CO, which is only feasible on Cu‑based catalysts where *CO binding is moderate (ΔG_*CO ≈ –0.5 eV). Electrolyte cations (K⁺, Cs⁺) and anions (HCO₃⁻, OH⁻) tune the interfacial electric field and the local CO₂ concentration. Large alkali cations compress the double layer, stabilizing *COOH and enhancing CO selectivity on Ag; conversely, high bicarbonate concentration buffers pH and favors formate on Sn by maintaining a high *OCHO coverage. The local pH at the cathode can rise to >10 under 10 mA cm⁻², shifting the equilibrium CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ and reducing dissolved CO₂. Gas‑diffusion electrodes (GDEs) with a hydrophobic PTFE layer supply CO₂ directly to the catalyst, achieving partial current densities >200 mA cm⁻² for CO. The overall cell voltage for CO production at 200 mA cm⁻² in a zero‑gap MEA is ≈2.5 V (cathode –0.7 V, anode +1.8 V), corresponding to an energy efficiency of ≈45 % based on the higher heating value of CO. Examiners test the ability to construct a microkinetic model linking *COOH and *OCHO free energies to product distribution, to calculate the CO₂ utilization efficiency from the measured CO partial current and the inlet CO₂ flow rate, and to discuss why a high cation concentration can simultaneously increase CO FE and decrease overall cell voltage by lowering the ohmic drop in the catholyte.

Electrochemical Impedance of Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductors: Transmission Line Modeling and Grain Boundary Effects

Mixed ionic–electronic conductors (MIECs) such as La₀.₆Sr₀.₄Co₀.₂Fe₀.₈O₃₋δ (LSCF) and Ce₀.₈Gd₀.₂O₂₋δ (CGO) exhibit coupled transport of oxygen ions and electrons. Their impedance spectra are described by a transmission‑line model (TLM) where each infinitesimal segment contains a parallel combination of ionic resistance (R_ion), electronic resistance (R_el), and chemical capacitance (C_chem) representing the oxygen‑vacancy concentration. The characteristic impedance of the line is Z₀ = √[(R_ion + R_el) / (jωC_chem)], and the total impedance for a finite length L with blocking electrodes is Z = Z₀ coth(γL) where γ = √[jωC_chem(R_ion + R_el)]. At high frequencies the response is dominated by the bulk (R_ion‖R_el) and appears as a depressed semicircle; at low frequencies the Warburg‑type diffusion tail (45° line) reflects the finite diffusion length of oxygen vacancies. Grain boundaries introduce an additional RC element (R_gb‖C_gb) that often manifests as a second semicircle at intermediate frequencies (10²–10⁴ Hz). The grain‑boundary resistance can exceed the bulk resistance by an order of magnitude in undoped CGO, but acceptor doping (e.g., Gd³⁺) reduces the space‑charge potential and narrows the depletion layer, lowering R_gb. Quantitative fitting yields the chemical diffusion coefficient D_chem = L²/(τ π²) where τ is the characteristic time constant from the low‑frequency knee. For LSCF at 700 °C, D_chem ≈ 10⁻⁶ cm² s⁻¹ and the surface exchange coefficient k_chem ≈ 10⁻⁴ cm s⁻¹. Examiners require the derivation of the TLM impedance expression, the identification of the grain‑boundary arc from its temperature dependence (activation energy ≈ 1.0 eV vs. 0.6 eV for bulk), and the calculation of the area‑specific resistance (ASR) contribution from the cathode in a solid‑oxide fuel cell using the fitted R_ion and R_el values.

  • Assuming the HER Tafel slope alone identifies the rate‑determining step without verifying the transfer coefficient.
  • Confusing the thermodynamic overpotential wall (0.37 V) with the kinetic overpotential measured at a given current density.
  • Neglecting the competing two‑electron nitrate‑to‑nitrite pathway when calculating Faradaic efficiency for ammonia.
  • Using bulk CO₂ solubility instead of the local concentration at a gas‑diffusion electrode for limiting‑current estimates.
  • Treating the grain‑boundary semicircle in MIEC impedance as a simple parallel RC element without accounting for the distributed transmission‑line nature.
  • Overlooking the effect of cation size on the interfacial electric field when rationalizing CO₂R product selectivity.
  • Forgetting that the chemical capacitance in a MIEC transmission line scales with the oxygen‑vacancy concentration and thus varies strongly with temperature and oxygen partial pressure.

Electrochemical Direct Methane Oxidation to Methanol: Partial Oxidation Pathways and Catalyst Design

Direct electrochemical oxidation of methane (CH₄) to methanol (CH₃OH) offers a route to valorise natural gas under mild conditions, avoiding the high‑temperature steam‑reforming step. The overall reaction CH₄ + H₂O → CH₃OH + H₂ has a standard potential of +0.03 V vs. RHE at pH 0, but the kinetic barrier for C–H bond activation (≈ 439 kJ mol⁻¹) makes selective oxidation extremely challenging. Two mechanistic families dominate the literature: (i) a *hydroxyl‑radical* pathway in which water oxidation generates •OH that abstracts hydrogen from methane in the diffusion layer, and (ii) a *surface‑mediated* pathway where methane adsorbs on a metal‑oxo site (M=O) and undergoes concerted proton‑coupled electron transfer (PCET) to form a *CH₃O* intermediate. On Pt and IrO₂ the •OH route prevails, leading to over‑oxidation to CO₂; on Cu‑exchanged zeolites and certain perovskite oxides (e.g., La₂CuO₄) the surface‑mediated route shows Faradaic efficiencies (FE) for methanol up to 12 % at 1.6 V vs. RHE in 0.5 M H₂SO₄. Key design principles include: (a) tuning the metal‑oxo bond strength to match the *CH₃O* binding energy (ΔG_*CH₃O ≈ –0.3 eV) so that methanol desorbs before further oxidation; (b) engineering hydrophobic pores to concentrate CH₄ and exclude water from the active site, thereby suppressing •OH formation; (c) operating at low overpotentials (≤ 0.3 V) and high pressures (10–30 bar) to increase dissolved CH₄ concentration (Henry’s law constant ≈ 1.4 mM bar⁻¹ at 298 K). Recent operando X‑ray absorption spectroscopy on Cu‑zeolite shows a Cu²⁺→Cu³⁺ oxidation coincident with methanol formation, confirming the metal‑oxo intermediate. Examiners often ask to derive the theoretical maximum FE from the competing 2‑electron methanol pathway versus the 6‑electron CO₂ pathway, using the measured partial current densities and the total charge passed.

Electrochemical CO₂ Reduction in Non‑Aqueous Media: Ionic Liquids, Supercritical CO₂, and Product Distribution

Non‑aqueous electrolytes circumvent the low CO₂ solubility (≈ 33 mM in water at 1 atm, 298 K) and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) that dominates in protic media. Ionic liquids (ILs) such as 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ([EMIM][BF₄]) provide CO₂ solubilities up to 0.5 M at 1 atm and exhibit wide electrochemical windows (> 4 V). In [EMIM][BF₄] with 0.1 M water as proton source, Ag and Au cathodes deliver CO FE > 90 % at –0.6 V vs. RHE, while the HER is suppressed by a factor of 10⁻³ relative to aqueous 0.1 M KHCO₃. The high viscosity (≈ 30 cP) reduces mass transport; rotating‑disk studies show Levich‑limited current densities of 5–10 mA cm⁻² at 1600 rpm, compared with 30 mA cm⁻² in water. Supercritical CO₂ (scCO₂, 31 °C, 73 bar) combined with a supporting electrolyte (e.g., 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate in acetonitrile) yields CO₂ concentrations > 1 M and diffusion coefficients ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹. Under these conditions Cu foam produces C₂ products (ethylene, ethanol) with combined FE ≈ 55 % at –1.0 V vs. RHE, attributed to the high local CO₂ activity that favours *CO dimerisation. The double‑layer structure in ILs is markedly different: the cation forms a compact layer that screens the electrode field, shifting the potential of zero charge (PZC) by +0.2 V and stabilising *COOH intermediates. Examiners test the ability to calculate the CO₂ mass‑transport limit using the Nernst‑Planck equation with activity coefficients from the Pitzer model for ILs, and to explain why the Tafel slope for CO formation on Ag in [EMIM][BF₄] remains ≈ 120 mV dec⁻¹ (first electron transfer rate‑determining) despite the altered solvation environment.

Worked Example: CO₂ Mass‑Transport Limit in an Ionic Liquid
A rotating‑disk electrode (RDE) of 5 mm diameter operates in [EMIM][BF₄] at 298 K with 0.1 M water. The CO₂ solubility is 0.45 M, diffusion coefficient D = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹, kinematic viscosity ν = 0.03 cm² s⁻¹. Calculate the Levich limiting current density for CO formation (2 e⁻ per CO₂) at 1600 rpm.
The Levich equation: j_lim = 0.62 n F D2/3 ν–1/6 ω1/2 C. n = 2, F = 96485 C mol⁻¹, D = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹, ν = 0.03 cm² s⁻¹, ω = 2π × 1600/60 = 167.6 rad s⁻¹, C = 0.45 mol cm⁻³ (since 1 M = 10⁻³ mol cm⁻³). Compute D2/3 = (1.2 × 10⁻⁵)0.667 ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻⁴, ν–1/6 = (0.03)–0.167 ≈ 2.0, ω1/2 = √167.6 ≈ 12.9. Multiply: 0.62 × 2 × 96485 × 5.3 × 10⁻⁴ × 2.0 × 12.9 × 0.45 × 10⁻³ ≈ 6.8 mA cm⁻². The predicted limiting current density is ≈ 6.8 mA cm⁻², consistent with experimental values of 5–10 mA cm⁻².
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a limiting current in a non‑aqueous electrolyte, always check whether the concentration is given in mol L⁻¹ or mol cm⁻³ and convert consistently. Remember that the Levich constant 0.62 assumes a smooth disk; for porous electrodes multiply by the roughness factor. If the viscosity is high, the ν–1/6 term changes only modestly, so the dominant effect is the reduced D. Write the full Levich expression before substituting numbers to avoid unit‑conversion slips.

Electrochemical Impedance of Composite Electrodes: Percolation Theory, Effective Medium Approximations, and Deconvolution of Charge‑Transfer Processes

Composite electrodes (e.g., LiFePO₄‑carbon, Ni‑YSZ cermets, Pt‑C catalyst layers) consist of electronically conductive, ionically conductive, and electrochemically active phases. Their impedance spectra cannot be described by a single Randles circuit; instead a transmission‑line network with distributed elements is required. Percolation theory predicts that the effective electronic conductivity σ_e follows σ_e ∝ (φ – φ_c)^t for volume fraction φ above the percolation threshold φ_c, with critical exponent t ≈ 1.6–2.0 for three‑dimensional systems. The Bruggeman effective‑medium approximation (EMA) gives a symmetric relation: (1 – φ) (σ_i – σ_eff)/(σ_i + 2σ_eff) + φ (σ_e – σ_eff)/(σ_e + 2σ_eff) = 0, where σ_i and σ_e are the ionic and electronic conductivities of the pure phases. In practice, the impedance of a porous composite of thickness L is modeled by the de Levie transmission line: each infinitesimal slice dx contains a parallel combination of ionic resistance r_ion dx, electronic resistance r_el dx, and double‑layer capacitance c_dl dx. The overall impedance Z(ω) = √[(r_ion + r_el)/(jωc_dl)] coth[√{jωc_dl(r_ion + r_el)} L]. At high frequencies the response collapses to the parallel r_ion‖r_el semicircle; at low frequencies a 45° Warburg tail appears if the ionic path is finite. Grain‑boundary resistance in the ionic phase adds a second RC element (R_gb‖C_gb) that often overlaps with the charge‑transfer arc. Deconvolution is achieved by fitting the full transmission‑line model simultaneously to the real and imaginary parts, constraining r_ion and r_el from independent four‑probe conductivity measurements. For a Ni‑YSZ anode at 800 °C, typical fitted values are r_ion ≈ 0.02 Ω cm², r_el ≈ 0.005 Ω cm², c_dl ≈ 0.1 F cm⁻³, giving a characteristic frequency f_c = 1/(2π r_ion c_dl L²) ≈ 10 Hz for L = 20 µm. Examiners require the derivation of the transmission‑line impedance, the identification of the percolation threshold from a log‑log plot of σ_eff versus φ, and the calculation of the area‑specific resistance (ASR) contribution of the charge‑transfer step using the fitted charge‑transfer resistance R_ct extracted from the mid‑frequency semicircle after subtracting the transmission‑line baseline.

Electrochemical Stability of High‑Voltage Cathode Materials: Surface Reconstruction, Electrolyte Oxidation, and Mitigation Strategies

Layered oxide cathodes such as LiNi₀.₈Mn₀.₁Co₀.₁O₂ (NMC811) and Li‑rich Li₁.₂Ni₀.₁₃Mn₀.₅₄Co₀.₁₃O₂ operate above 4.3 V vs. Li⁺/Li, where the electrolyte (typically 1 M LiPF₆ in EC/DEC) becomes thermodynamically unstable. Oxidative decomposition of carbonate solvents generates CO₂, CO, and reactive radicals that attack the cathode surface, forming a cathode‑electrolyte interphase (CEI) rich in Li₂CO₃, LiF, and organic oligomers. Simultaneously, transition‑metal (TM) ions (especially Ni⁴⁺) migrate from the bulk to the surface, triggering a layered‑to‑spinel‑to‑rock‑salt phase transformation that increases impedance and reduces capacity. Operando X‑ray diffraction shows the onset of the spinel phase at ≈ 4.5 V after 50 cycles, while differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) detects CO₂ evolution correlating with the voltage plateau at 4.6 V. Mitigation strategies include: (i) surface coatings (Al₂O₃, ZrO₂, LiNbO₃) applied by atomic‑layer deposition (ALD) at ≤ 2 nm thickness, which act as physical barriers and suppress TM dissolution; (ii) electrolyte additives such as tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphite (TMSPi) that preferentially oxidise to form a protective phosphorous‑rich CEI; (iii) single‑crystal cathode particles that eliminate grain‑boundary pathways for electrolyte penetration; (iv) high‑concentration “solvent‑in‑salt” electrolytes (e.g., 3 M LiFSI in DME) that reduce free solvent molecules and raise the oxidative stability to > 5 V. Quantitative evaluation uses the “voltage‑fade” metric: dV/dQ vs. cycle number, where a stable cathode shows < 0.5 mV cycle⁻¹. Examiners ask to construct a kinetic model coupling TM dissolution rate (k_diss ∝ exp[–E_a/RT] · a_H⁺) to the growth of the rock‑salt layer thickness (δ ∝ √(D_TM t)), and to calculate the resulting increase in charge‑transfer resistance R_ct = ρ δ/A, where ρ is the resistivity of the rock‑salt phase (≈ 10⁴ Ω cm).

Electrochemical Nitrogen Oxidation to Nitrate: Mechanisms, Catalysts, and Environmental Implications

The anodic oxidation of ammonia (NH₃) or dissolved N₂ to nitrate (NO₃⁻) is relevant for wastewater treatment and for closing the nitrogen cycle in electrochemical synthesis. In alkaline media (1 M KOH) the overall reaction NH₃ + 3 H₂O → NO₃⁻ + 9 H⁺ + 8 e⁻ has a thermodynamic potential of +0.77 V vs. RHE, but the kinetic pathway proceeds through adsorbed *NH₂, *NH, *N, *NO, *NO₂ intermediates. On Pt(100) the rate‑determining step is the *NO → *NO₂ oxidation (ΔG ≈ 0.85 eV), giving a Tafel slope of ≈ 120 mV dec⁻¹ and a Faradaic efficiency for nitrate of 60 % at 1.2 V vs. RHE; the remainder forms N₂ via *N–*N coupling. Transition‑metal oxides such as NiFe‑oxyhydroxide and Co₃O₄ exhibit lower overpotentials (≈ 0.35 V at 10 mA cm⁻²) because the lattice oxygen participates in a Mars‑van‑Krevelen mechanism: *NH₃ + O_lattice → *NH₂ + OH⁻ + e⁻, regenerating the oxygen vacancy by water oxidation. In situ Raman shows the formation of surface Ni⁴⁺=O species that correlate with nitrate selectivity > 85 %. Competing oxygen evolution reaction (OER) becomes dominant above 1.5 V vs. RHE, limiting the practical voltage window. Reactor design for continuous flow uses a porous NiFe anode with a cation‑exchange membrane to separate the anolyte (NH₃‑rich) from the catholyte (H₂ evolution), achieving nitrate production rates of 2 mmol h⁻¹ cm⁻² at 80 % current efficiency. Environmental analysis must account for the formation of nitrite (NO₂⁻) as a transient intermediate; its disproportionation 3 NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ + 2 NO + H₂O can release NO gas, a regulated pollutant. Examiners test the ability to write the full eight‑electron balanced equation, to derive the Nernst potential for the NH₃/NO₃⁻ couple at pH 14 (E = 0.77 – 0.059 × pH ≈ –0.05 V vs. SHE), and to discuss how the Pourbaix diagram of the Ni‑Fe‑O‑H system predicts the stable Ni⁴⁺=O phase under operating conditions.

  • Using bulk CO₂ solubility instead of the local concentration at a gas‑diffusion electrode for limiting‑current estimates.
  • Treating the grain‑boundary semicircle in MIEC impedance as a simple parallel RC element without accounting for the distributed transmission‑line nature.
  • Overlooking the effect of cation size on the interfacial electric field when rationalising CO₂R product selectivity.
  • Forgetting that the chemical capacitance in a MIEC transmission line scales with the oxygen‑vacancy concentration and thus varies strongly with temperature and oxygen partial pressure.

Electrochemical Phase Transitions in Intercalation Electrodes: Thermodynamics of Miscibility Gaps, Voltage Plateaus, and Phase-Field Modeling

Intercalation electrodes such as LixFePO4, LixCoO2, and NaxMnO2 exhibit two fundamentally distinct thermodynamic behaviors during (de)intercalation: solid-solution reactions with continuously varying voltage, and two-phase reactions with a flat voltage plateau. The distinction arises from the shape of the molar Gibbs free energy curve G(x) versus composition x. When G(x) is convex everywhere, the system forms a single-phase solid solution; the equilibrium voltage E(x) = −(1/F) dG/dx varies smoothly with x. When G(x) develops a concave region (∂2G/∂x2 < 0), the system lowers its energy by separating into two coexisting phases of compositions x1 and x2 determined by the common-tangent construction. The voltage remains constant at Eplateau = −(1/F)(G(x2) − G(x1))/(x2 − x1) until the phase transformation completes. LiFePO4 is the canonical two-phase system (orthorhombic LiFePO4 olivine FePO4) with a 3.45 V plateau; LiCoO2 shows a series of two-phase regions (hexagonal monoclinic hexagonal) between 3.9–4.2 V; graphite exhibits multiple staging transitions (stage 4, 3, 2, 1) with distinct plateaus.

The kinetics of phase-boundary motion control rate capability in two-phase systems. The Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂c/∂t = ∇·(M∇μ) with chemical potential μ = δF/δc and mobility M describes spinodal decomposition and nucleation-and-growth. In LiFePO4, the phase boundary is atomically sharp (≈ 1 nm) and moves by a “domino-cascade” mechanism where Li+ insertion at the interface triggers cooperative lattice distortion. Operando X-ray diffraction shows that at high rates (> 5 C) the transformation becomes heterogeneous: some particles fully transform while others remain unchanged, leading to “phase-separation” voltage hysteresis. Phase-field models couple the Cahn–Hilliard equation with linear elasticity (stress-dependent chemical potential μ = μchem + Ωσh, where Ω is partial molar volume and σh hydrostatic stress) to predict fracture in particles > 200 nm. The miscibility gap shrinks with temperature; above the critical temperature Tc (≈ 300 K for LiFePO4) the system becomes a solid solution. Cation doping (Mg, Ti) or nanosizing (< 50 nm) suppresses the two-phase behavior by increasing interfacial energy penalty, yielding sloping voltage profiles beneficial for state-of-charge estimation.

Examiners test the ability to: (i) sketch G(x) curves for solid-solution vs two-phase systems and derive the common-tangent construction; (ii) calculate the plateau voltage from DFT-computed formation energies of end-members; (iii) explain why nanosizing eliminates the voltage plateau (surface energy contribution γA/V shifts the common tangent); (iv) distinguish between nucleation-limited (low overpotential, sharp phase boundary) and spinodal (high overpotential, diffuse interface) transformation kinetics using the dimensionless Cahn number Cn = κ/L2 (gradient energy coefficient κ, system size L). A frequent trap is assuming all flat plateaus indicate two-phase reactions; some arise from highly non-ideal solid solutions with near-zero ∂2G/∂x2 over a composition range (e.g., LixNi0.5Mn1.5O4 at 4.7 V).

Electrolyte Stability Windows and Decomposition Pathways: From Thermodynamic Limits to Kinetic Stabilization Strategies

The electrochemical stability window (ESW) of an electrolyte is defined by the potentials at which its components undergo reductive or oxidative decomposition. Thermodynamically, the reductive limit is set by the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy of the solvent/anion relative to the Fermi level of the anode, and the oxidative limit by the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy relative to the cathode Fermi level. For 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DEC (1:1 v/v), DFT calculations place the reductive limit at ≈ 0.8 V vs. Li+/Li (EC reduction to Li2CO3 + C2H4) and the oxidative limit at ≈ 4.3 V vs. Li+/Li (EC oxidation to CO2 + radical cations). However, kinetic barriers allow practical operation beyond these limits: graphite anodes operate at 0.1 V because EC reduction forms a passivating solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) that electronically insulates the surface while remaining Li+-conductive. Similarly, NMC811 cathodes charge to 4.4 V because oxidative decomposition is sluggish and forms a cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI).

Decomposition pathways are highly specific. At the anode, EC undergoes a two-electron reduction: EC + 2 e− + 2 Li+ → Li2CO3 + C2H4 (g). Linear carbonates (DEC, EMC) reduce via one-electron steps to radical anions that oligomerize into polycarbonates (ROCO2Li)n. PF6− reduces to LiF + PF5; the Lewis acidic PF5 catalyzes further solvent decomposition and attacks transition-metal oxides. At the cathode, oxidative decomposition of EC proceeds via a radical cation EC•+ that deprotonates to form vinylene carbonate (VC) or attacks lattice oxygen to release CO2. High-voltage cathodes (> 4.5 V) require electrolytes with higher HOMO levels: fluorinated carbonates (FEC, TFEC) raise the oxidative limit to 5.0 V; sulfones (TMS, DMS) and nitriles (AN, PN) reach 5.5 V but suffer from poor reductive stability and high viscosity. “Solvent-in-salt” electrolytes (e.g., 3 M LiFSI in DME) shift both limits by coordinating all solvent molecules to Li+, reducing free EC available for oxidation and lowering the LUMO of the anion-derived SEI. Ionic liquids (PYR14FSI, PIP14FSI) offer ESWs > 6 V but exhibit high viscosity and interfacial resistance.

Quantitative ESW measurement uses linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) on inert electrodes (Pt, GC, Au) at 0.1 mV s−1; the onset potential is defined at 0.1 mA cm−2. However, LSV overestimates practical stability because it lacks the catalytic surfaces of real electrodes. Operando differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) detects gaseous products (CO2, CO, C2H4, H2) with faradaic efficiency. The “voltage-fade” metric dV/dQ vs. cycle number correlates with cumulative electrolyte oxidation. Examiners expect: (i) balanced half-reactions for EC/DEC reduction and oxidation; (ii) explanation of why LiF in the SEI is beneficial (wide bandgap ≈ 14 eV, high Li+ conductivity via defects); (iii) analysis of how salt concentration affects ESW via activity coefficients (concentrated solution theory); (iv) critique of LSV vs. DEMS for stability assessment.

Worked Example: Thermodynamic ESW Calculation
Given DFT-computed HOMO = −8.2 eV and LUMO = −1.5 eV for EC relative to vacuum, and the Li/Li+ Fermi level at −3.0 eV vs. vacuum, calculate the thermodynamic oxidative and reductive limits vs. Li/Li+. Explain why practical cells exceed these limits.
Oxidative limit: Eox = −(EHOMO − EF,Li)/e = −(−8.2 + 3.0) = 5.2 V vs. Li/Li+. Reductive limit: Ered = −(ELUMO − EF,Li)/e = −(−1.5 + 3.0) = −1.5 V vs. Li/Li+. Thermodynamic ESW = 6.7 V. Practical cells exceed reductive limit (graphite at 0.1 V) because EC reduction forms a passivating SEI that kinetically blocks further electron transfer. They exceed oxidative limit (NMC at 4.4 V) because oxidative decomposition is slow and forms a protective CEI; the measured onset in LSV (≈ 4.3 V) is kinetic, not thermodynamic.
Exam-Day Strategy
When asked to “write the reduction half-reaction of EC at the anode,” always include Li+ and electrons explicitly: C3H4O3 + 2 Li+ + 2 e− → Li2CO3 + C2H4. For oxidative decomposition, show the radical cation intermediate: EC → EC•+ + e− followed by deprotonation or nucleophilic attack. Memorize the key SEI components (Li2CO3, LiF, ROCO2Li, (CH2OCO2Li)2) and their origin (EC, PF6−, linear carbonates, VC additive). Distinguish thermodynamic ESW (HOMO/LUMO) from practical ESW (kinetic onset with passivation).

Conducting Polymer Electrochemistry: Redox Doping Mechanisms, Ion Transport, and Pseudocapacitive Charge Storage

Conducting polymers (CPs) such as poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT), polypyrrole (PPy), and polyaniline (PANI) store charge through reversible redox doping/dedoping accompanied by ion and solvent exchange with the electrolyte. Unlike battery intercalation hosts, CPs undergo large volumetric changes (10–30 %) and their conductivity spans 10 orders of magnitude (10−10 to 103 S cm−1) between dedoped (insulating) and doped (metallic) states. PEDOT:PSS, the commercial standard, is a polyelectrolyte complex where PSS− provides charge balance for oxidized PEDOT+; electrochemical dedoping expels PSS− and inserts electrolyte cations (M+) to maintain electroneutrality. The doping level y in PEDOT+y(A−)y (A− = PSS−, ClO4−, TFSI−) is controlled by potential: y = 0 (fully dedoped, neutral) to y ≈ 0.33 (fully doped, one hole per three thiophene rings).

The charge-storage mechanism is classified by the mobile ionic species: (i) anion-exchange (p-doping): polymer0 + yA− ⇌ polymer+yAy + ye− (e.g., PPy/ClO4−); (ii) cation-exchange (n-doping or p-dedoping): polymer+yAy + yM+ + ye− ⇌ polymer0 + yMA (e.g., PEDOT:PSS in Na+ electrolyte); (iii) dual-ion: both cations and anions move (e.g., PANI in H2SO4). EQCM measurements reveal the mass change Δm per charge Q: for anion-exchange Δm/ΔQ = MA/F (positive); for cation-exchange Δm/ΔQ = −MM/F (negative). PEDOT:PSS in 1 M NaCl shows Δm/ΔQ ≈ −23 g mol−1 (Na+ insertion, 23 g mol−1), confirming cation-driven dedoping.

Ion transport in CPs is governed by the morphology: crystalline domains (π–π stacking distance ≈ 3.5 Å) provide electronic conduction; amorphous regions with swollen polymer chains facilitate ion diffusion. The apparent diffusion coefficient Dapp from GITT or CV peak separation scales with electrolyte concentration and ion size: DNa+ ≈ 10−10 cm2 s−1 in PEDOT:PSS vs. DLi+ ≈ 10−12 cm2 s−1 in PPy. Pseudocapacitive behavior (linear CV response, i ∝ v) arises when ion diffusion is fast relative to the timescale (τdiff = L2/D < τCV = ΔE/v). For a 1 μm thick PEDOT film at v = 10 mV s−1, τCV ≈ 100 s, τdiff ≈ 10 s → pseudocapacitive. At v = 1 V s−1, τCV ≈ 1 s → diffusion-limited (battery-like). The specific capacitance Csp = Q/ΔV reaches 200–400 F g−1 for PEDOT, 500–800 F g−1 for PPy, and 600–1000 F g−1 for PANI (in acidic media). Examiners test: (i) writing balanced doping/dedoping reactions for p-type and n-type CPs; (ii) interpreting EQCM frequency shifts (Sauerbrey equation Δf = −CfΔm) to identify mobile ion; (iii) calculating Dapp from CV peak current ip = 0.446 nFAC√(nFvD/RT) for surface-confined redox; (iv) explaining why PEDOT:PSS is stable in air (PSS− immobilizes counterions) while PPy/ClO4 degrades (ClO4− expulsion causes structural collapse).

Microbial Electrochemical Systems: Extracellular Electron Transfer Pathways, Biofilm Kinetics, and Reactor Design

Microbial electrochemical systems (MXS) exploit microorganisms that transfer electrons to or from solid electrodes, enabling microbial fuel cells (MFCs), microbial electrolysis cells (MECs), and microbial electrosynthesis (MES). The central challenge is extracellular electron transfer (EET) across the cell envelope. Three pathways are established: (i) direct electron transfer (DET) via outer-membrane c-type cytochromes (e.g., OmcA/OmcB in Shewanella oneidensis, OmcS/OmcZ in Geobacter sulfurreducens) that form conductive “nanowires” (pili with metallic-like conductivity ≈ 5 mS cm−1); (ii) mediated electron transfer (MET) via secreted redox shuttles (flavins, phenazines, humic acids) that diffuse between cell and electrode; (iii) conductive biofilm matrix where cytochromes and pili create a redox gradient enabling long-range (> 50 μm) electron hopping. Geobacter biofilms on graphite anodes achieve current densities > 10 A m−2 at 0.2 V vs. SHE; the biofilm acts as a living catalyst with a formal potential Ef ≈ −0.1 V vs. SHE for the cytochrome network.

Biofilm kinetics follow a modified Butler–Volmer–Monod framework. The anodic current density j = jmax (S/(KS + S)) (exp(αaFη/RT) − exp(−αcFη/RT)), where S is substrate (acetate) concentration, KS half-saturation constant (≈ 10–50 mg L−1), jmax maximum current density, and η overpotential relative to Ef. At low overpotentials (< 50 mV), the current is activation-limited (Tafel slope ≈ 120 mV dec−1); at high overpotentials, substrate diffusion through the biofilm (thickness L ≈ 50–200 μm) limits current to jlim = nFDSSbulk/L. The coulombic efficiency (CE) = Qrecovered/Qtheoretical typically ranges 60–90 %; losses arise from methanogenesis, sulfate reduction, and biomass growth. In MECs, a small applied voltage (0.2–0.8 V) drives hydrogen evolution at the cathode: 2 H+ + 2 e− → H2; the overall reaction CH3COO− + 2 H2O → 2 CO2 + 4 H2 has ΔG° = +104 kJ mol−1, requiring electrical energy input. MES uses cathodic biofilms (e.g., Sporomusa ovata) to reduce CO2 to acetate (2 CO2 + 4 H2 + 8 e− → CH3COO− + H+ + 2 H2O) at −0.6 V vs. SHE with Faradaic efficiency > 85 %.

Reactor design optimizes power density and scalability. Single-chamber air-cathode MFCs eliminate the need for catholyte circulation; the cathode (Pt/C or Fe–N–C on carbon cloth) faces air, while the anode chamber is anaerobic. Power densities reach 2–3 W m−2 (projected anode area) with domestic wastewater. Stacked MFCs in series/parallel face voltage reversal and microbial competition; individual potentiostatic control of each unit cell is essential. For MECs, membrane-free designs with biocathodes reduce cost but allow O2 crossover that inhibits anaerobes. Examiners test: (i) distinguishing DET vs. MET via cyclic voltammetry (DET shows surface-confined redox peaks at Ef; MET shows diffusion-limited waves); (ii) calculating the theoretical maximum voltage from acetate oxidation (CH3COO− + 2 H2O → 2 CO2 + 7 H+ + 8 e−, E° = −0.28 V vs. SHE) coupled to O2 reduction (E° = +0.82 V) giving Ecell° = 1.10 V; (iii) explaining why CE < 100 % even with pure cultures (maintenance energy, biomass synthesis); (iv) analyzing polarization curves to separate activation, ohmic, and concentration losses in bioanodes.

Electrochemical Impedance of Conversion and Alloying Anodes: Volume Expansion, SEI Dynamics, and Reaction Heterogeneity

Conversion (e.g., Fe2O3, Co3O4, NiO) and alloying (Si, Sn, Sb, Ge) anodes offer high theoretical capacities (Fe2O3: 1007 mAh g−1; Si: 3579 mAh g−1) but suffer from massive volume expansion (Fe2O3 → 2 Fe + 3 Li2O: ≈ 100 %; Si → Li15Si4: ≈ 280 %). This mechanical degradation pulverizes particles, exposes fresh surfaces, and triggers continuous SEI reformation, leading to rapid capacity fade and distinctive impedance signatures. The impedance spectrum of a conversion anode (e.g., Fe2O3 nanoparticles in carbon matrix) typically shows three features: (i) a high-frequency semicircle (RSEI–CPESEI) representing Li+ transport through the SEI; (ii) a mid-frequency semicircle (Rct–CPEdl) for charge transfer at the active-material/electrolyte interface; (iii) a low-frequency 45° Warburg tail (finite-length diffusion in solid Li2O or metallic Fe). During cycling, RSEI increases monotonically as the SEI thickens; Rct shows a minimum at intermediate states of charge where both reactant (Fe2O3) and product (Fe, Li2O) phases coexist, maximizing interfacial area.

For Si anodes, the impedance evolution is more complex due to the amorphous-to-crystalline transition (a-Si → c-Li15Si4) at ≈ 0.05 V vs. Li/Li+. Operando EIS reveals a “breathing” SEI: during lithiation, the expanding Si particle cracks the SEI, causing a transient drop in RSEI as fresh electrolyte penetrates; during delithiation, the contracting particle leaves voids, and the SEI partially heals, increasing RSEI. The charge-transfer resistance Rct is potential-dependent with a minimum near the two-phase plateau. The chemical capacitance Cchem = dQ/dV shows sharp peaks at phase transitions (a-Si/LixSi, LixSi/Li15Si4), which appear as additional semicircles or distortions in the Nyquist plot. Distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis deconvolutes these overlapping processes: peak at τ ≈ 10−3 s (SEI), τ ≈ 10−1 s (charge transfer), τ ≈ 101 s (solid-state diffusion in Li15Si4), τ ≈ 103 s (particle-level diffusion in porous electrode).

Binders and electrode architecture critically influence impedance. Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) + styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) binders accommodate strain better than PVDF, reducing particle isolation. The “self-healing” binder (polyacrylic acid with dynamic hydrogen bonds) maintains electrical contact during cycling, keeping Rct low. Porous Si nanowires or yolk-shell structures (Si@void@C) provide internal void space for expansion, eliminating SEI fracture; their EIS shows stable RSEI and a single charge-transfer semicircle. Examiners test: (i) sketching the equivalent circuit for a conversion anode (Rs + (RSEICPESEI) + (RctCPEdl) + Wfinite); (ii) explaining why Rct decreases then increases during lithiation of Fe2O3 (interfacial area maximized at two-phase coexistence); (iii) calculating the diffusion coefficient from the Warburg coefficient σ = RT/(n2F2A√2 C√D) for finite-length diffusion; (iv) discussing how DRT separates SEI growth (increasing τSEI magnitude) from contact loss (new low-frequency peak). A common trap is attributing all low-frequency impedance to solid-state diffusion; in conversion/alloying anodes, the dominant low-frequency process is often SEI rearrangement or particle isolation, not bulk diffusion.

  • Confusing the thermodynamic miscibility gap (concave G(x)) with kinetic phase separation (spinodal vs. nucleation) when interpreting voltage plateaus.
  • Assuming the LSV onset potential equals the thermodynamic stability limit of an electrolyte, ignoring kinetic passivation (SEI/CEI) that enables practical operation beyond it.
  • Writing the doping reaction for PEDOT:PSS as anion insertion instead of cation-driven dedoping (PEDOT+PSS− + M+ + e− → PEDOT0 + M+PSS−).
  • Neglecting the sign of the EQCM mass change: positive Δf (mass loss) for cation expulsion, negative Δf (mass gain) for anion insertion.
  • Treating microbial anode kinetics as simple Butler–Volmer without the Monod substrate-dependence term (S/(KS + S)).
  • Assuming 100 % coulombic efficiency in MFCs/MECs; forgetting competing metabolisms (methanogenesis, biomass growth) consume substrate without current.
  • Attributing the low-frequency Warburg tail in Si anodes solely to Li diffusion in Li15Si4; the dominant process is often SEI restructuring or electrical disconnection of particles.

Electrochemical Ammonia Oxidation: Thermodynamics, Kinetics, and Catalyst Design

The oxidation of ammonia (NH₃ → N₂ + 6 H⁺ + 6 e⁻) offers a carbon‑free route to hydrogen production and direct ammonia fuel cells. The standard equilibrium potential at pH 0 is 0.06 V vs. RHE, but practical anodes operate at 0.4–0.6 V vs. RHE because of large kinetic overpotentials. In alkaline media the reaction proceeds via adsorbed *NH₂, *NH, *N intermediates; the rate‑determining step is often the N–N coupling of two *N species to form *N₂, which then desorbs. Platinum group metals (Pt, Ir, Rh) show the highest activity, yet they suffer from poisoning by strongly adsorbed *NHₓ species and from oxidative dissolution at high potentials. Alloying Pt with Ru or Ni weakens *NH binding and shifts the d‑band centre, lowering the onset potential by 50–80 mV. Non‑precious catalysts such as NiFe layered double hydroxides (LDH) and Co₃O₄ nanowires achieve current densities of 10 mA cm⁻² at ≈0.55 V vs. RHE in 1 M KOH, but their long‑term stability is limited by phase transformation to inactive oxides. The Tafel slope for the N–N coupling step on Pt(100) is ≈120 mV dec⁻¹, consistent with a one‑electron pre‑equilibrium followed by a chemical recombination. In situ surface‑enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) reveals a *NH₂ band at 1120 cm⁻¹ that disappears as the potential exceeds 0.45 V, confirming its role as a reactive intermediate. For practical ammonia fuel cells, the anode must tolerate 0.5–2 M NH₃, operate at 60–80 °C, and deliver >200 mA cm⁻² with <50 mV degradation over 1000 h. Recent membrane‑electrode assemblies using a PtRu/C anode and a Pt/C cathode with a Nafion 212 membrane have demonstrated peak power densities of 120 mW cm⁻² at 0.6 V, highlighting the importance of catalyst‑ionomer interface engineering to mitigate NH₃ crossover and carbonate formation.

Electrochemical Hydrogen Oxidation Reaction in Alkaline Media: Mechanism and Catalyst Requirements

The hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) in alkaline electrolyte (H₂ + 2 OH⁻ → 2 H₂O + 2 e⁻) is the anodic counterpart of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and is central to alkaline fuel cells and electrolyzers. Unlike the acidic HOR, which follows a simple Volmer–Tafel or Volmer–Heyrovsky pathway with exchange current densities >10⁻³ A cm⁻² on Pt, the alkaline HOR is 2–3 orders of magnitude slower (j₀ ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶ A cm⁻²). The kinetic bottleneck is the water‑mediated Volmer step (H₂ + 2 * + 2 OH⁻ ⇌ 2 H* + 2 OH⁻) where the hydroxide ion must donate a proton to the adsorbed hydrogen. Density‑functional theory shows that the binding energy of H* on Pt(111) is near‑optimal, but the activation barrier for OH⁻ adsorption and subsequent proton transfer is high because of strong solvation of OH⁻. Alloying Pt with Ru, Ni, or Co introduces oxophilic sites that bind OH⁻ more strongly, facilitating the bifunctional mechanism: OH⁻ adsorbs on the oxophilic metal, while H₂ dissociates on Pt; the adjacent sites enable rapid H* + OH* → H₂O + 2 *. Experimental rotating‑disk electrode (RDE) data on PtRu/C (1:1 atomic) in 0.1 M KOH give a Tafel slope of 60 mV dec⁻¹ at low overpotentials, shifting to 120 mV dec⁻¹ when OH⁻ coverage saturates. Non‑precious catalysts such as NiMoN nanosheets and CoP nanowires achieve j₀ values within a factor of 5 of Pt in 1 M KOH, but their stability under potential cycling is limited by phosphorus leaching or nitride oxidation. The HOR exchange current density scales linearly with the hydroxide concentration (j₀ ∝ [OH⁻]⁰·⁵) up to 5 M KOH, after which viscosity effects dominate. In anion‑exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs), the anode overpotential at 1 A cm⁻² is typically 50–80 mV, contributing significantly to the overall voltage loss. Mitigation strategies include (i) increasing the Pt loading to >0.2 mg cm⁻², (ii) engineering a gradient ionomer distribution to maintain high OH⁻ activity at the catalyst surface, and (iii) operating at elevated temperature (80 °C) to accelerate OH⁻ mobility and reduce the activation barrier.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Calculate the exchange current density for the alkaline HOR on a PtRu/C catalyst given a measured current of 0.5 mA at an overpotential of 30 mV in 0.1 M KOH, assuming a Tafel slope of 60 mV dec⁻¹ and a geometric electrode area of 0.196 cm²."
Using the Tafel equation η = b log₁₀(j/j₀) with b = 60 mV dec⁻¹, η = 30 mV, and j = 0.5 mA / 0.196 cm² = 2.55 mA cm⁻². Rearranging: log₁₀(j/j₀) = η/b = 30/60 = 0.5 → j/j₀ = 10⁰·⁵ ≈ 3.16 → j₀ = j / 3.16 = 2.55 / 3.16 ≈ 0.81 mA cm⁻² = 8.1×10⁻⁴ A cm⁻². The trap is forgetting to convert the measured current to current density before applying the Tafel equation; using the raw current would give an erroneously low j₀ by a factor of the electrode area.
Exam‑day strategy
When a problem provides a Tafel slope and a single (η, j) point, always convert the measured current to current density using the geometric area before solving for j₀. Remember that the Tafel slope in alkaline HOR is often quoted per decade of current density, not per natural log; use base‑10 logarithm unless the problem explicitly states a natural‑log form.

Gas Diffusion Electrodes for CO₂ Reduction: Mass Transport, Flooding, and Performance Metrics

Gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) enable high‑rate CO₂ electrolysis by supplying gaseous CO₂ directly to the catalyst layer through a porous hydrophobic backing (typically PTFE‑treated carbon paper). The three‑phase boundary (gas, electrolyte, catalyst) must remain stable; flooding occurs when liquid electrolyte penetrates the gas pores, blocking CO₂ access and causing a sharp drop in partial current density for CO or C₂ products. The capillary pressure that resists flooding is given by P_c = (2γ cosθ)/r_pore, where γ is the surface tension of the electrolyte (≈72 mN m⁻¹ for water), θ the contact angle (>120° for PTFE), and r_pore the pore radius (≈1–5 µm). Operating at a gas‑flow rate of 10–30 sccm cm⁻² and a differential pressure of 10–30 kPa maintains a stable gas‑phase saturation >80 %. The CO₂ limiting current density under diffusion control is j_lim = nF D_CO₂ C_CO₂ / δ, where D_CO₂ ≈ 1.9×10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹ in 0.5 M KHCO₃, C_CO₂ ≈ 0.033 M at 1 atm, and δ the diffusion layer thickness (≈10 µm in a well‑designed GDE). This yields j_lim ≈ 300 mA cm⁻² for CO (n=2) and ≈ 150 mA cm⁻² for ethylene (n=12). In practice, the achievable partial current density for C₂H₄ on Cu‑based GDEs is 200–400 mA cm⁻² at cell voltages of 3.0–3.5 V, with Faradaic efficiencies of 50–70 %. The single‑pass CO₂ conversion is limited to 20–30 % to avoid local pH rise and carbonate formation; higher conversion requires recirculation or a membrane‑electrode assembly with an anion‑exchange membrane. Performance metrics reported in literature include (i) partial current density (mA cm⁻²), (ii) Faradaic efficiency (%), (iii) energy efficiency (EE = (ΔG° × FE) / (E_cell × nF) × 100 %), and (iv) stability (hours at constant current). A common degradation mode is catalyst detachment caused by gas‑bubble evolution at the catalyst‑ionomer interface; incorporating a thin (≈5 µm) microporous layer of carbon black and PTFE between the catalyst and the gas diffusion layer reduces this effect and improves durability to >1000 h at 200 mA cm⁻².

Redox Flow Battery Membrane Impedance: Ion Selectivity, Crossover, and Equivalent Circuit Modeling

In vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) and emerging organic redox flow batteries, the ion‑exchange membrane separates the positive and negative electrolytes while allowing charge‑balancing ion transport. The membrane contributes a distinct impedance signature that can be deconvoluted by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). A typical equivalent circuit for a Nafion 117 membrane in 2 M H₂SO₄ consists of a high‑frequency ohmic resistance R_Ω (electrolyte + contacts), a mid‑frequency resistance R_m (proton conduction through the hydrated channels) in parallel with a constant‑phase element CPE_m (non‑ideal capacitance of the water‑filled pores), and a low‑frequency Warburg element W_c representing vanadium ion crossover diffusion through the membrane. The proton conductivity σ_H⁺ follows the empirical relation σ_H⁺ = 0.0055 × λ × exp(1268(1/303 – 1/T)) S cm⁻¹, where λ is the water uptake (mol H₂O per mol SO₃⁻). For Nafion 117 at 25 °C, λ ≈ 14, giving σ_H⁺ ≈ 0.1 S cm⁻¹ and an area‑specific resistance of ≈0.15 Ω cm² for a 180 µm thick membrane. Vanadium crossover is quantified by the permeability P_V = D_V × K_V, where D_V is the diffusion coefficient of VO²⁺/VO₂⁺ in the membrane (≈10⁻⁷ cm² s⁻¹) and K_V the partition coefficient (≈0.1). The resulting capacity fade per cycle is ΔQ/Q ≈ (P_V × A × ΔC × t) / (V × C₀), typically 0.5–1 % per cycle for Nafion. Alternative membranes such as sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone) (SPEEK) or porous polymer membranes functionalized with charged groups show lower vanadium permeability (P_V reduced by 5–10×) but higher area resistance (0.3–0.5 Ω cm²). The trade‑off is captured by the figure of merit FOM = σ_H⁺ / P_V; state‑of‑the‑art membranes achieve FOM > 10⁶ S s cm⁻³. In EIS, the crossover Warburg appears as a 45° line at frequencies <0.1 Hz; its coefficient σ_W = RT/(n²F²A√2 C √D) can be used to extract D_V. A common modelling error is assigning the mid‑frequency semicircle solely to charge transfer at the electrode; in flow batteries the membrane resistance often dominates this feature, especially at low states of charge where electrolyte conductivity drops.

In situ surface‑enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) reveals a *NH₂ band at 1120 cm⁻¹ that disappears as the potential exceeds 0.45 V, confirming its role as a reactive intermediate. For practical ammonia fuel cells, the anode must tolerate 0.5–2 M NH₃, operate at 60–80 °C, and deliver >200 mA cm⁻² with <50 mV degradation over 1000 h. Recent membrane‑electrode assemblies using a PtRu/C anode and a Pt/C cathode with a Nafion 212 membrane have demonstrated peak power densities of 120 mW cm⁻² at 0.6 V, highlighting the importance of catalyst‑ionomer interface engineering to mitigate NH₃ crossover and carbonate formation.

Electrochemical CO₂ Reduction to Oxalate and Glyoxylate: Two‑Electron Pathways and Catalyst Design

Thermodynamics and Reaction Stoichiometry

The two‑electron reduction of carbon dioxide to oxalate (C₂O₄²⁻) proceeds via the overall reaction 2 CO₂ + 2 e⁻ → C₂O₄²⁻. The standard potential for this couple at pH 0 is –0.49 V vs. SHE (–0.49 V vs. RHE). In alkaline media the reaction is written 2 CO₂ + 2 e⁻ + 2 OH⁻ → C₂O₄²⁻ + H₂O, shifting the equilibrium potential by –0.059 V per pH unit. Glyoxylate (OCHCOO⁻) formation follows a parallel 2 e⁻ pathway: CO₂ + HCOO⁻ + 2 e⁻ + H⁺ → OCHCOO⁻ + H₂O, with a standard potential near –0.61 V vs. RHE. Both processes are thermodynamically more favorable than the 8‑electron reduction to methane (–0.24 V vs. RHE) but suffer from kinetic barriers associated with C–C bond formation.

Mechanistic Insights

On copper electrodes the first electron transfer generates a surface‑bound *CO₂⁻ radical anion that dimerises to *C₂O₄²⁻ before protonation. In situ surface‑enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) shows a transient band at 1650 cm⁻¹ assigned to the *CO₂⁻ intermediate, disappearing within 100 ms at –0.6 V vs. RHE. On tin and bismuth the *CO₂⁻ is stabilized by the metal‑oxide surface, favouring formate rather than C–C coupling. Molecular catalysts based on cobalt‑phthalocyanine (CoPc) immobilised on carbon nanotubes display a well‑defined Co(I)/Co(0) redox couple at –0.55 V vs. RHE that mediates the two‑electron reduction with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) for oxalate up to 68 % at –0.8 V vs. RHE in 0.5 M KHCO₃.

Catalyst Design Strategies

Key design principles include (i) tuning the metal‑center redox potential to match the CO₂/oxalate couple, (ii) providing adjacent active sites for *CO₂⁻ dimerisation, and (iii) suppressing the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) by operating at pH > 7 where HER kinetics are slower. Recent work on Cu‑Ag alloy nanoparticles shows that a 10 % Ag surface enrichment raises the oxalate FE from 45 % to 72 % at –0.75 V vs. RHE by weakening *H adsorption while preserving *CO₂⁻ binding. Electrolyte engineering with 0.1 M Cs⁺ cations further stabilises the *C₂O₄²⁻ intermediate through non‑covalent interactions, lowering the overpotential by 80 mV.

Performance Metrics and Stability

State‑of‑the‑art gas‑diffusion electrodes (GDEs) using CoPc/CNT achieve a partial current density for oxalate of 120 mA cm⁻² at –0.85 V vs. RHE with a cell voltage of 2.9 V (including anodic OER at 1.6 V vs. RHE). Long‑term chronoamperometry for 50 h shows <5 % decay in FE, attributed to gradual catalyst leaching mitigated by covalent anchoring via diazonium grafting. The energy efficiency (EE) for oxalate production, defined as (ΔG⁰ × FE)/(cell voltage × total charge), reaches 42 % under these conditions, surpassing the 30 % EE typical for CO production on Ag.

Electrochemical Water Oxidation in Neutral pH: Catalyst Stability, Mechanistic Insights, and Membrane Electrode Assembly Integration

Thermodynamic Baseline and Overpotential Requirements

The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in neutral solution (pH 7) has a thermodynamic potential of 0.82 V vs. RHE (1.23 V – 0.059 × 7). Practical catalysts require overpotentials (η) of 300–450 mV to deliver 10 mA cm⁻². The benchmark Co‑Pi (cobalt‑phosphate) catalyst operates at η ≈ 350 mV at 10 mA cm⁻² in 0.1 M phosphate buffer, while NiFe layered double hydroxides (LDH) reach η ≈ 280 mV under identical conditions. The lower overpotential of NiFe LDH originates from a favourable *OOH binding energy (ΔG_*OOH ≈ 3.2 eV) that aligns with the theoretical optimum of 3.2 eV for the four‑electron OER pathway.

Mechanistic Pathways and Rate‑Determining Steps

Operando X‑ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) on NiFe LDH reveals a Ni³⁺/Ni⁴⁺ redox transition at 1.35 V vs. RHE preceding O₂ evolution. The Tafel slope of 60 mV dec⁻¹ indicates a one‑electron pre‑equilibrium (Ni³⁺ → Ni⁴⁺) followed by a chemical O–O bond formation step as the rate‑determining step (RDS). In contrast, Co‑Pi exhibits a 120 mV dec⁻¹ slope, consistent with a concerted proton‑electron transfer (CPET) RDS. Isotope labelling with H₂¹⁸O confirms that lattice oxygen participates in O₂ formation for Co‑Pi (lattice‑oxygen‑mediated mechanism, LOM) but not for NiFe LDH, which follows the conventional adsorbate‑evolution mechanism (AEM).

Stability Challenges in Neutral Media

Phosphate buffers accelerate Co dissolution via formation of soluble Co‑phosphate complexes; after 100 h at 10 mA cm⁻² Co‑Pi loses 30 % of its initial activity. NiFe LDH shows superior stability (<5 % loss) because Fe incorporation suppresses Ni dissolution and the layered structure accommodates volume changes during redox cycling. Accelerated stress tests (potential cycling 1.0–1.6 V vs. RHE, 50 mV s⁻¹) reveal that the charge‑transfer resistance (R_ct) of NiFe LDH increases only 12 % after 5000 cycles, whereas Co‑Pi R_ct doubles.

Integration into Membrane Electrode Assemblies (MEAs)

For neutral‑pH water electrolysis, anion‑exchange membranes (AEMs) such as Sustainion X37‑50 are paired with NiFe LDH anodes and Pt/C cathodes. The MEA operates at 1.85 V cell voltage to achieve 500 mA cm⁻² at 60 °C with 0.5 M K₂CO₃ feed. The area‑specific resistance (ASR) of the membrane (0.12 Ω cm²) contributes <10 % of the total overpotential. Catalyst loading of 0.5 mg cm⁻² NiFe LDH on a porous Ti current collector yields a mass activity of 1.2 A mg⁻¹ at 1.55 V vs. RHE, meeting the DOE 2025 target for low‑temperature electrolysis.

Worked Example: Estimating OER Overpotential from Tafel Data
A NiFe LDH catalyst shows a Tafel slope of 60 mV dec⁻¹ and a current density of 0.5 mA cm⁻² at 1.40 V vs. RHE in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7). Calculate the overpotential required to reach 10 mA cm⁻².
The Tafel equation: η = b log₁₀(j/j₀), where b = 60 mV dec⁻¹. First find the exchange current density j₀ using the known point (j = 0.5 mA cm⁻², η = 1.40 V – 0.82 V = 0.58 V). 0.58 V = 0.060 V × log₁₀(0.5/j₀) → log₁₀(0.5/j₀) = 9.67 → 0.5/j₀ = 10⁹·⁶⁷ ≈ 4.68 × 10⁹ → j₀ ≈ 1.07 × 10⁻¹⁰ mA cm⁻². Now for j = 10 mA cm⁻²: η = 0.060 × log₁₀(10 / 1.07 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 0.060 × log₁₀(9.35 × 10¹⁰) = 0.060 × 10.97 ≈ 0.658 V. The required potential = 0.82 V + 0.658 V = 1.48 V vs. RHE. Thus the overpotential at 10 mA cm⁻² is ≈ 660 mV.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question provides a Tafel slope and a single (j, η) data point, always compute j₀ first; then use the same slope to extrapolate to the target current density. Remember that the thermodynamic OER potential shifts –0.059 V per pH unit, so at pH 7 the equilibrium is 0.82 V vs. RHE, not 1.23 V.

Electrochemical Nitrogen Reduction to Hydrazine: Alternative Pathways, Competing HER, and Catalyst Strategies

Thermodynamics of the N₂/N₂H₄ Couple

The four‑electron reduction of dinitrogen to hydrazine, N₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → N₂H₄, has a standard potential of –0.23 V vs. RHE at pH 0. In alkaline media the reaction is N₂ + 4 H₂O + 4 e⁻ → N₂H₄ + 4 OH⁻, shifting the equilibrium by –0.059 V per pH unit (–0.65 V vs. RHE at pH 14). The competing hydrogen evolution reaction (2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → H₂) is thermodynamically favoured (0 V vs. RHE), making selective N₂ reduction to hydrazine kinetically demanding.

Mechanistic Pathways

Two principal pathways are recognised: (i) the distal pathway, where the first protonation occurs on the terminal nitrogen to give *N₂H, followed by successive proton‑electron transfers to *N₂H₂, *N₂H₃, and finally *N₂H₄; (ii) the alternating pathway, where protonation alternates between the two nitrogen atoms, generating *N₂H, *N₂H₂ (diazene), *N₂H₃, and *N₂H₄. Density‑functional theory (DFT) on Fe‑N₄ single‑atom catalysts shows the distal pathway has a lower free‑energy barrier for the *N₂H → *N₂H₂ step (ΔG ≈ 0.45 eV) compared with the alternating route (ΔG ≈ 0.78 eV). However, the *N₂H₃ → *N₂H₄ step is endergonic by 0.32 eV on Fe‑N₄, indicating that product desorption is rate‑limiting.

Catalyst Design for Hydrazine Selectivity

Effective catalysts must (a) bind *N₂ strongly enough to activate the N≡N bond, (b) stabilise *N₂Hₓ intermediates without over‑stabilising *H, and (c) facilitate *N₂H₄ release. Molybdenum‑based complexes such as Mo(N₂)₂(PPh₃)₂ achieve a Faradaic efficiency (FE) for hydrazine of 45 % at –0.4 V vs. RHE in 0.1 M HClO₄/MeCN, with a partial current density of 2.3 mA cm⁻². Heterogeneous analogues – MoS₂ edge sites doped with Co – show FE ≈ 38 % at –0.55 V vs. RHE in 0.5 M H₂SO₄, but suffer from rapid degradation due to Mo leaching. Recent work on Cu‑N₄ single‑atom catalysts in a gas‑diffusion electrode (GDE) configuration reports FE = 62 % at –0.35 V vs. RHE with a hydrazine production rate of 1.8 mmol h⁻¹ cm⁻², attributed to a favourable *N₂H₃ binding energy (–0.68 eV) that lowers the desorption barrier.

Suppressing the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction

Operating in neutral or slightly alkaline electrolytes (pH 7–9) reduces HER kinetics by two orders of magnitude relative to acidic media, while the N₂/H₂O reduction potential moves only modestly. Adding 0.1 M Cs⁺ cations creates a local electric field that stabilises the *N₂Hₓ dipoles and raises the HER overpotential by ~120 mV. Pulsed electrolysis (10 ms on, 90 ms off) further improves selectivity by allowing surface *H to recombine and desorb during the off‑time, decreasing the average HER current by 35 % without affecting the N₂ reduction rate.

Stability and Product Separation

Hydrazine is chemically unstable in the presence of O₂ and metal oxides, disproportionating to N₂ and NH₃. In‑situ product extraction using a bipolar membrane (BPM) that separates the catholyte (pH 7) from an anolyte (pH 1) enables immediate acidification of the product stream, forming stable N₂H₄·H₂SO₄ salts. Long‑term operation (200 h) of a Cu‑N₄/GDE/BPM cell shows <8 % decay in FE, with the main degradation mode being Cu nanoparticle agglomeration observed by post‑mortem TEM.

Electrochemical Hydrogen Peroxide Synthesis via Two‑Electron Water Oxidation: Reactor Design, Selectivity, and Energy Efficiency

Thermodynamics and Competing Pathways

The two‑electron water oxidation to hydrogen peroxide, 2 H₂O → H₂O₂ + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻, has a standard potential of 1.77 V vs. RHE (pH 0). The four‑electron OER (2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻) is thermodynamically more favourable at 1.23 V vs. RHE, so selective H₂O₂ production requires catalysts that kinetically suppress the O–O bond cleavage step. The selectivity descriptor ΔG_*OOH – ΔG_*OH is used: a value near 3.2 eV favours H₂O₂ release, whereas lower values promote further oxidation to O₂.

Catalyst Materials and Performance

Bismuth vanadate (BiVO₄) modified with a thin Co‑Pi overlayer achieves a H₂O₂ Faradaic efficiency of 85 % at 1.85 V vs. RHE in 0.1 M Na₂SO₄ (pH 7), delivering a partial current density of 12 mA cm⁻². The Co‑Pi layer acts as a hole‑transfer mediator that accelerates the *OH → *OOH step while the underlying BiVO₄ stabilises the *OOH intermediate. In contrast, pristine TiO₂ shows <10 % FE because the *OOH binding is too weak, leading to rapid O₂ evolution. Molecular catalysts such as [Ru(bda)(pic)₂] (bda = 2,2′‑bipyridine‑6,6′‑dicarboxylate) immobilised on carbon nanotubes reach 92 % FE at 1.70 V vs. RHE in 0.5 M H₂SO₄, with a turnover frequency (TOF) of 0.8 s⁻¹ per Ru site.

Reactor Configurations

Two main reactor architectures are employed: (i) a divided H‑cell with a cation‑exchange membrane (Nafion 117) separating anode and cathode, where the cathode reduces O₂ to H₂O₂ (two‑electron ORR) and the anode performs water oxidation; (ii) a single‑compartment flow cell using a gas‑diffusion electrode (GDE) anode that directly oxidises water to H₂O₂, with the product continuously extracted by the flowing electrolyte. The flow cell achieves a space‑time yield of 0.45 mol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 200 mA cm⁻², corresponding to an energy consumption of 12 kWh kg⁻¹ H₂O₂ (based on cell voltage 2.1 V). The divided H‑cell, while simpler, suffers from crossover of H₂O₂ to the cathode where it is reduced, lowering overall FE to 60 %.

Energy Efficiency and Techno‑Economic Metrics

The theoretical minimum energy for H₂O₂ synthesis via water oxidation is 1.77 eV per electron (≈ 171 kJ mol⁻¹). Practical cells operate at 2.0–2.3 V, giving an electrical energy efficiency (EEE) of 77–88 % relative to the thermodynamic limit. Including the energy for product separation (distillation of 30 wt % H₂O₂) raises the total specific energy to 18–22 kWh kg⁻¹, competitive with the anthraquinone process (≈ 25 kWh kg⁻¹). Catalyst durability remains the key cost driver; accelerated stress tests (1.6–2.0 V, 100 mV s⁻¹, 10 000 cycles) show BiVO₄/Co‑Pi retains 78 % of initial activity, whereas molecular Ru complexes degrade to 45 % due to ligand oxidation.

Electrochemical Impedance of Sodium‑Ion Battery Cathodes: Phase Transitions, Na⁺ Diffusion, and Equivalent‑Circuit Deconvolution

Typical Cathode Materials and Phase Behaviour

Layered oxide cathodes such as NaNi₁/₃Mn₁/₃Co₁/₃O₂ (NMC) and P2‑type Na₂/₃[Ni₁/₃Mn₂/₃]O₂ exhibit multiple phase transitions during (de)sodiation. Operando X‑ray diffraction shows a P2 → O2 transition at ~3.9 V vs. Na/Na⁺ for the latter, accompanied by a 12 % volume collapse that generates micro‑cracks. The voltage profile displays plateaus at 3.3 V (P2 → P2′) and 3.9 V (P2′ → O2), each associated with distinct Na⁺ ordering patterns. These transitions manifest as separate semicircles in the Nyquist plot, reflecting changes in charge‑transfer resistance (R_ct) and Na⁺ diffusion coefficient (D_Na).

Impedance Signatures and Equivalent‑Circuit Model

A robust equivalent circuit for a porous NMC cathode includes: (1) high‑frequency ohmic resistance R_Ω (electrolyte + current collector), (2) a constant‑phase element CPE_dl in parallel with R_ct for the charge‑transfer process at the active‑material/electrolyte interface, (3) a finite‑length Warburg element W_FL representing Na⁺ diffusion in the secondary particles (radius ~300 nm), and (4) an additional R_ct2‖CPE2 branch capturing the interfacial resistance of the surface‑reconstructed rock‑salt layer that forms above 4.2 V. Fitting of EIS data at 50 % state of charge (SOC) yields R_ct = 45 Ω cm², D_Na = 1.2 × 10⁻¹¹ cm² s⁻¹ (from W_FL parameter σ = R_ct √(D_Na)⁻¹), and R_ct2 = 120 Ω cm². At 90 % SOC, R_ct2 drops to 30 Ω cm² as the rock‑salt layer becomes more conductive, while D_Na decreases to 3 × 10⁻¹² cm² s⁻¹ due to Na⁺ site ordering.

Deconvolution of Overlapping Processes

Distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis separates the overlapping time constants: a peak at 10⁻³ s corresponds to charge transfer at the pristine layered surface, a peak at 10⁻¹ s to Na⁺ solid‑state diffusion, and a broad feature at 10¹ s to the rock‑salt interphase. The DRT amplitude of the diffusion peak scales linearly with the inverse of the particle radius, confirming the finite‑length Warburg assignment. Machine‑learning‑assisted DRT (using a Gaussian process regression) reduces the fitting uncertainty of D_Na from ±30 % to ±12 % across the full SOC range.

Impact of Electrolyte and Binder on Interfacial Impedance

Switching from 1 M NaPF₆ in EC:DEC (1:1) to 1 M NaFSI in diglyme lowers R_ct by 35 % because the fluorinated anion forms a thinner, more ion‑conductive solid‑electrolyte interphase (SEI). Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder contributes an additional 15 Ω cm² interfacial resistance due to its poor Na⁺ affinity; replacing it with sodium alginate reduces this contribution to <3 Ω cm². The combined electrolyte/binder optimisation yields a total cell impedance at 1 kHz of 12 Ω cm² for a 2 mAh cm⁻² cathode loading, enabling >90 % capacity retention at 5 C rate.

Electrochemical Water Splitting in Seawater: Chloride Oxidation Competition, Catalyst Selectivity, and Membrane-Free Designs

Seawater electrolysis avoids the energy and cost of desalination but introduces a formidable selectivity challenge: the thermodynamic potential for chloride oxidation to chlorine (Cl₂/Cl⁻ = 1.36 V vs. RHE) lies 0.87 V below the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) potential (1.23 V vs. RHE at pH 0, 0.40 V at pH 14). In practice, kinetic overpotentials shift the effective crossover; at pH 8 (typical seawater), the Nernst-corrected Cl₂/Cl⁻ potential is 1.05 V vs. RHE, while OER on state-of-the-art catalysts (IrO₂, RuO₂, NiFe LDH) requires 1.45–1.55 V at 10 mA cm⁻². The 400–500 mV window is narrow enough that local pH shifts, mass-transport limitations, and catalyst surface reconstruction can tip selectivity toward chlorine. Chlorine evolution reaction (CER) follows a Volmer–Heyrovsky pathway: Cl⁻ adsorption (*Cl), electrochemical desorption to Cl₂, or chemical recombination. The *Cl binding energy is the primary descriptor; metals binding *Cl too strongly (Pt, Pd) poison the surface, while weak binders (Au, carbon) favour OER. Optimal catalysts (RuO₂, Co₃O₄, MnO₂) sit near the top of a *Cl vs. *OH volcano plot. Membrane-free designs exploit this by using cation-exchange layers (Nafion, sulfonated polyether ether ketone) that repel Cl⁻ via Donnan exclusion, or by operating at high current density (>500 mA cm⁻²) where the diffusion-limited Cl⁻ flux to the anode surface is exceeded, forcing water oxidation. A 2023 demonstration of a NiFe LDH anode on a porous Ti substrate with a 50 μm Nafion coating achieved 99 % Faradaic efficiency for O₂ at 1 A cm⁻² in artificial seawater (0.5 M NaCl) for 1000 h, with cell voltage 1.85 V. The cathode (Pt/C) produces H₂ at −0.1 V vs. RHE; the overall stack efficiency reaches 78 % LHV. Critical failure modes include Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺ precipitation on the cathode (mitigated by periodic polarity reversal) and hypochlorite crossover oxidising the membrane (addressed by radical-scavenging cerium-doped Nafion).

Electrochemical Impedance of Three-Phase Boundaries in Solid Oxide Electrolysis Cells: Gas Diffusion, Surface Diffusion, and Charge Transfer

Solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) operating at 700–850 °C convert steam and CO₂ to H₂ and syngas with near-100 % electrical efficiency (ΔH/ΔG ≈ 1.25). The anode (oxygen electrode) and cathode (fuel electrode) are porous mixed ionic–electronic conductors (MIECs) such as La₀.₆Sr₀.₄Co₀.₂Fe₀.₈O₃₋δ (LSCF) or Ni-YSZ cermets. The electrochemical reaction occurs at the three-phase boundary (TPB) where gas pore, electronic conductor, and ionic conductor meet. Impedance spectra typically show three arcs: a high-frequency (HF) arc (10⁴–10⁵ Hz) assigned to oxygen-ion transfer across the electrolyte/electrode interface (R_ion), a mid-frequency (MF) arc (10²–10³ Hz) to charge transfer at the TPB (R_ct), and a low-frequency (LF) arc (0.1–10 Hz) to gas diffusion in the porous electrode (R_diff) coupled with surface diffusion of adsorbed intermediates (O_ad, H_ad). The MF arc resistance follows R_ct ∝ exp(E_a/RT) pO₂⁻ⁿ with n ≈ 0.25 for LSCF, indicating a rate-determining step of oxygen incorporation via a surface peroxide intermediate. The LF arc is modelled by a Gerischer element (Z_G = R_G / √(1 + jωτ_G)) where τ_G = L²/D_eff combines pore diffusion length L and effective surface diffusivity D_eff. For a 20 μm thick LSCF electrode at 800 °C, typical values are R_ion = 0.05 Ω cm², R_ct = 0.15 Ω cm², R_G = 0.3 Ω cm², τ_G = 0.5 s. Degradation manifests as a growing HF arc (Cr poisoning from interconnects forming SrCrO₄ insulating layers) and a shifting MF arc (Ni coarsening in Ni-YSZ reducing TPB density). Operando EIS during co-electrolysis of H₂O/CO₂ (70/30) reveals an additional arc at 1 Hz attributed to CO₂ adsorption and carbonate formation on LSCF, which suppresses R_ct by 40 % at 1.5 V. Equivalent-circuit fitting must constrain the constant-phase element (CPE) exponent α_HF > 0.9 for the electrolyte interface to avoid non-physical capacitance values (>100 μF cm⁻²). Distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis cleanly separates the TPB charge-transfer peak (τ ≈ 10⁻³ s) from the gas-diffusion peak (τ ≈ 1 s), enabling targeted electrode microstructure optimisation: increasing porosity from 30 % to 45 % reduces R_G by 35 % but raises R_ct by 20 % due to lower electronic percolation.

Worked Problem: TPB Length and Polarisation Resistance
A Ni-YSZ cathode has 35 % porosity, 40 % Ni, 25 % YSZ by volume. The average particle radius is 0.5 μm. Assuming spherical particles and random packing, estimate the TPB length per unit volume (μm⁻²). If the specific charge-transfer resistance per unit TPB length is 50 Ω μm, calculate the area-specific R_ct (Ω cm²) for a 15 μm thick electrode. How does R_ct change if the particle radius is halved while keeping volume fractions constant?
For a binary mixture of equal-sized spheres, the TPB length density Λ = (3/2) × (φ_Ni φ_YSZ / r) × (1 − φ_pore) where φ are volume fractions of the solid phases and r is particle radius. φ_Ni = 0.40, φ_YSZ = 0.25, φ_pore = 0.35, r = 0.5 μm. Λ = 1.5 × (0.40 × 0.25 / 0.5) × 0.65 = 0.195 μm⁻². Total TPB length in 1 cm² electrode area = Λ × thickness = 0.195 μm⁻² × 15 × 10⁴ μm = 2.925 × 10⁴ μm. R_ct = (50 Ω μm) / (2.925 × 10⁴ μm) = 1.71 × 10⁻³ Ω cm². If r → 0.25 μm, Λ doubles to 0.39 μm⁻², so R_ct halves to 8.5 × 10⁻⁴ Ω cm². This illustrates the strong microstructural leverage: finer particles exponentially increase TPB density but accelerate coarsening degradation.
Exam-Day Strategy: Deconvoluting SOEC Impedance Arcs
When presented with a Nyquist plot showing three overlapping arcs, assign them by frequency decade and physical origin: HF (>10 kHz) = electrolyte/electrode interface (ohmic + interfacial capacitance), MF (100 Hz–10 kHz) = charge transfer at TPB (strong pO₂ dependence, Arrhenius E_a ≈ 1–1.5 eV), LF (<100 Hz) = gas diffusion/surface diffusion (Warburg/Gerischer, pO₂⁻⁰·⁵ dependence).
