Applications beyond threshold signatures include: (1) secure multi‑party computation (MPC) preprocessing where correlated randomness is generated via VSS; (2) decentralized randomness beacons where each epoch’s beacon value is the reconstruction of a VSS‑shared secret; (3) key‑escrow‑free certificate authorities where the CA’s signing key is split among auditors. The main open problem is reducing the communication overhead of the zero‑knowledge proofs; current research explores “compact” lattice commitments based on the Short Integer Solution (SIS) problem that shrink proofs to a few hundred bytes.

Post‑Quantum Secure Homomorphic Encryption for Private Set Intersection

Private set intersection (PSI) allows two parties to compute the intersection of their input sets without revealing any other elements. The most efficient post‑quantum PSI protocols today rely on leveled homomorphic encryption (HE) such as CKKS (approximate arithmetic) or TFHE‑2 (fast Boolean gates). A typical construction (Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner, CCS 2018, later adapted to lattices by Chen et al., PKC 2021) proceeds as follows: the sender encodes each element x as a polynomial P_x(z) = ∏i=1|S| (z – H(x_i)) over the CKKS plaintext space, encrypts the coefficient vector, and sends the ciphertext to the receiver. The receiver evaluates the polynomial on each of its own elements y_j by homomorphically computing P_x(H(y_j)); a zero result indicates membership. Because CKKS works with approximate numbers, a small scaling factor Δ = 2⁴⁰ and a polynomial degree N = 2¹⁴ are chosen to keep the decryption error below 2⁻³⁰ while supporting batching of up to 2¹⁴ slots.

Parameter selection for 128‑bit post‑quantum security follows the LWE estimator (Albrecht et al., 2022): dimension n = 8192, modulus q ≈ 2⁶⁰, error distribution χ = Dℤ,σ with σ = 3.2. The resulting ciphertext size is two polynomials of degree N, i.e. 2·N·log₂q ≈ 2 MB per ciphertext. Communication can be reduced by a factor of 8 using the “packed” variant where the sender encrypts a single ciphertext containing all coefficients of the product polynomial via the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). The receiver’s homomorphic evaluation costs O(|R|·log N) NTT multiplications; with TFHE‑2 the same PSI can be expressed as a series of programmable bootstrapping operations, achieving sub‑second runtime for sets of size 10⁴ on a single core.

Security proofs model the HE scheme as an IND‑CPA secure encryption under the Ring‑LWE assumption; the PSI protocol is then proven secure in the semi‑honest model via a standard simulation argument. For malicious security, a cut‑and‑choose wrapper (as in the “PSI‑CA” protocol, Eurocrypt 2022) adds a factor of 2–3 in communication but retains post‑quantum security because the underlying HE remains lattice‑based. Deployments in contact‑tracing and advertising‑attribution pipelines have demonstrated that the CKKS‑based PSI meets GDPR‑style data‑minimisation requirements while resisting quantum adversaries.

Worked Example: Parameter Selection for CKKS‑Based PSI
A system designer wants 128‑bit post‑quantum security for a PSI between two parties holding sets of size 2¹⁰. Using the CKKS scheme with polynomial degree N = 2¹⁴, determine a suitable modulus q and error standard deviation σ that satisfy the LWE estimator’s 128‑bit security target. Assume the estimator recommends n = 8192 for the underlying Ring‑LWE instance.
The Ring‑LWE dimension n equals the polynomial degree N for power‑of‑two cyclotomics, so we set N = n = 8192. However, CKKS typically uses N = 2¹⁴ = 16384 to accommodate batching; the security estimator treats the effective dimension as N. To achieve 128‑bit security with N = 16384, the estimator (Albrecht et al., 2022) suggests a modulus q ≈ 2⁶⁰ and error σ = 3.2. The ciphertext modulus chain is chosen as a product of 3–4 primes each ≈ 2⁴⁰ to support the required multiplicative depth (≈ 10 levels for polynomial evaluation). With these parameters the estimated classical security is > 130 bits and quantum security ≈ 128 bits, satisfying the requirement. The resulting ciphertext size is 2·N·log₂q ≈ 2·16384·60 ≈ 1.97 MB, which matches the bandwidth budget for the target set size.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for concrete CKKS parameters, remember the triple (N, q, σ) = (2¹⁴, 2⁶⁰, 3.2) as the canonical 128‑bit post‑quantum setting. Cite the LWE estimator (Albrecht‑Player‑Scott, 2022) and note that the multiplicative depth drives the number of modulus‑chain primes. This triplet appears in multiple NIST‑PQC‑related papers and is a safe “default” answer.

Post‑Quantum Secure Key Derivation Functions and Their Security Reductions

Key derivation functions (KDFs) turn high‑entropy secrets (e.g., Diffie‑Hellman shared secrets or KEM shared keys) into uniformly random session keys. In the post‑quantum world the most widely adopted KDFs are HKDF‑SHA‑256, HKDF‑SHA‑384, and KMAC‑256 (based on SHAKE‑256). Their security proofs rely on the random‑oracle model (ROM) for the underlying hash. To obtain standard‑model guarantees, lattice‑based KDFs have been proposed: the “LWE‑KDF” of Banerjee, Peikert, and Rosen (CRYPTO 2020) defines KDF(s) = H(A·s + e) where A is a public matrix, s the input secret, e a small error, and H a collision‑resistant hash (e.g., SHA‑3). The proof reduces distinguishing the KDF output from uniform to solving the decisional LWE problem with the same parameters.

NIST SP 800‑56C Rev. 2 (2023) specifies a hybrid KDF construction for PQC migration: K = KDF_classical(SS_classical) ⊕ KDF_pqc(SS_pqc). The classical part uses HKDF‑SHA‑256; the PQC part uses KMAC‑256 with a domain‑separation string “PQC‑KEM”. The XOR combiner is proven secure in the ROM assuming at least one of the two inputs is pseudorandom. For IND‑CCA secure KEMs (Kyber, NTRU, Classic McEliece) the Fujisaki‑Okamoto transform yields a KEM‑DEM scheme where the KDF is applied to the encapsulated key; the reduction from IND‑CCA to IND‑CPA of the underlying PKE incurs a loss factor of q_H (the number of hash queries). Concrete security estimates for Kyber‑768 show that with 2⁶⁴ hash queries the IND‑CCA advantage remains below 2⁻¹²⁸.

Implementation pitfalls include: (a) reusing the same salt across multiple derivations, which breaks the ROM proof; (b) truncating the KMAC output to fewer than 256 bits, reducing the security margin; (c) feeding low‑entropy inputs (e.g., passwords) directly into a lattice‑KDF without a memory‑hard preprocessing step such as Argon2id. The current best practice for password‑based key derivation in a post‑quantum setting is Argon2id → HKDF‑SHA‑384 → KMAC‑256, each with independent salts.

Post‑Quantum Secure Side‑Channel Resistant Implementations of Lattice‑Based Signatures

Dilithium and Falcon are the two lattice‑based signature schemes selected by NIST for standardisation (ML‑DSA and FN‑DSA). Both rely on sampling from discrete Gaussian or centered binomial distributions and on polynomial arithmetic modulo q = 8380417 (Dilithium) or q = 12289 (Falcon). Side‑channel leakage arises primarily from (i) variable‑time rejection sampling, (ii) data‑dependent memory accesses during Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), and (iii) branching on secret‑dependent coefficients during hint generation. The state‑of‑the‑art countermeasure stack combines (a) first‑order Boolean masking of all secret‑dependent intermediate values, (b) shuffling of NTT butterfly operations, and (c) constant‑time “bitsliced” sampling using the “rejection‑sampling‑with‑fixed‑iterations” technique (CHES 2022, “High‑Order Masking of Dilithium”).

For Dilithium‑3 (security category 3), a first‑order masked implementation on ARM Cortex‑M4 adds ≈ 2.1× cycle overhead and 1.8× stack usage compared to the unmasked reference. Second‑order masking (protecting against combined power‑EM attacks) raises the overhead to ≈ 4.3× cycles. Falcon‑512 benefits from a “lazy‑reduction” NTT that reduces the number of modular multiplications; its masked version (CHES 2023) achieves 1.9× overhead for first order. Both schemes require a true random number generator (TRNG) seeded with a quantum‑proof extractor (Trevisan’s extractor) to feed the masking randomness; otherwise the masking shares become predictable under a quantum‑capable adversary.

Formal verification of these masked implementations has been carried out in the EasyCrypt framework (Eurocrypt 2024) using the “probabilistic relational Hoare logic” to prove that the masked algorithm is indistinguishable from an ideal leakage‑free specification under the t‑probing model. The verification effort for Dilithium‑3 first‑order masking amounted to ≈ 12 k lines of EasyCrypt code and uncovered a subtle bug in the hint‑generation routine that leaked the sign of a secret coefficient. The bug was fixed by inserting a constant‑time conditional move.

Post‑Quantum Secure Multi‑Authority Attribute‑Based Encryption

Attribute‑based encryption (ABE) lets a data owner encrypt a message under a policy over attributes, while users receive secret keys tied to their attribute sets. In a multi‑authority setting (MA‑ABE) several independent authorities each manage a disjoint attribute universe, eliminating a single point of trust. The first lattice‑based MA‑ABE (Zhang, Zhang, and Wang, ASIACRYPT 2019) builds on the LWE‑based KP‑ABE of Gorbunov, Vaikuntanathan, and Wee (STOC 2013) by giving each authority its own master secret matrix MSK_i and public matrix MPK_i. A user’s key for attribute set S is a collection of vectors ski,attr = MSK_i·H(attr) + e where H is a hash‑to‑matrix function. Encryption under a policy expressed as an access tree uses a single LWE ciphertext whose components are linear combinations of the authorities’ public matrices.

Security is proved in the selective‑set model under the decisional LWE assumption with modulus q = 2¹⁵, dimension n = 1024, and error σ = 3.2, yielding 128‑bit post‑quantum security. The ciphertext size grows linearly with the number of authorities involved in the policy; for 5 authorities each managing 20 attributes the ciphertext is ≈ 12 KB. Revocation is handled via a “key‑update” broadcast: each authority periodically publishes a short LWE‑based update token that allows non‑revoked users to derive fresh decryption keys without re‑issuing all attributes. The update token size is O(log N) where N is the number of users, achieved by a binary‑tree key‑insulation technique adapted from the classical Boldyreva‑Goyal‑Kumar scheme.

Recent work (CCS 2022) introduces a “decentralised” MA‑ABE where authorities do not need a trusted setup; they jointly generate a common reference string via a multi‑party computation protocol (SPDZ‑lite) and then run the standard MA‑ABE algorithms. This removes the need for a central coordinator and is compatible with the post‑quantum MPC stack described earlier. Performance benchmarks on a 2.6 GHz Xeon show key‑generation ≈ 45 ms per attribute, encryption ≈ 120 ms for a 10‑attribute policy, and decryption ≈ 80 ms, all within the latency budget for secure messaging applications.

  • Confusing the security model of lattice‑based VSS (selective‑set vs adaptive) and assuming the same proof works for both.
  • Treating CKKS approximate arithmetic as exact; forgetting to bound the decryption error when designing PSI equality tests.
  • Using a single salt for both classical and PQC branches of a hybrid KDF, which invalidates the ROM security proof.
  • Assuming first‑order masking automatically protects against combined power‑EM attacks; second‑order masking is required for high‑assurance profiles.
  • Believing that MA‑ABE ciphertext size is independent of the number of authorities; it scales linearly with authority count.
  • Neglecting that Trevisan’s extractor must be seeded with a quantum‑proof entropy source; a classical TRNG alone does not suffice for post‑quantum masking randomness.

Post‑Quantum Password‑Authenticated Key Exchange: LWE‑Based PAKE and OPAQUE Variants

Password‑authenticated key exchange (PAKE) lets two parties derive a high‑entropy session key from a low‑entropy password while resisting offline dictionary attacks. Classical PAKEs such as SRP, CPace, and OPAQUE rely on the hardness of the discrete‑logarithm or Diffie‑Hellman problems. In a post‑quantum setting these assumptions collapse, so constructions must be based on problems believed to resist quantum algorithms, principally Learning With Errors (LWE) and its ring/module variants.

The first lattice‑based PAKE was presented by Jarecki, Krawczyk, and Xu at Eurocrypt 2018. Their protocol, often called LWE‑PAKE, uses a standard LWE public‑key encryption scheme as the underlying key‑encapsulation mechanism. Each party generates an LWE key pair, encrypts a random value under the other party’s public key, and then derives the session key from the shared randomness combined with a password‑derived key using a keyed hash function. Security is proved in the universal composability (UC) framework under the decisional LWE assumption with modulus q = 2¹⁵, dimension n = 1024, and error distribution χ = Dℤ,σ with σ = 3.2, yielding 128‑bit post‑quantum security.

OPAQUE (Jarecki, Krawczyk, Xu, CCS 2018) separates the password‑verification step from the key‑exchange step by storing an encrypted “envelope” on the server. The post‑quantum variant replaces the elliptic‑curve OPRF with an LWE‑based oblivious pseudorandom function (OPRF) built from the Naor‑Reingold construction instantiated with Ring‑LWE. The client obtains a pseudorandom value blinded by the password, the server evaluates the OPRF on its stored envelope, and both parties run a standard LWE‑KEM (e.g., Kyber‑768) to finish the exchange. The envelope size is ≈ 1.2 KB; the total communication per run is ≈ 2.5 KB, comparable to the classical OPAQUE deployment.

Kyber‑PAKE (Basso, Fouque, Lyubashevsky, et al., 2022) integrates the Kyber KEM directly into a PAKE flow. The client sends a Kyber public key; the server encapsulates a secret using a password‑derived seed as the randomness source for the KEM’s internal sampling. The resulting ciphertext is sent back, and both parties derive the session key via HKDF‑SHA‑3‑256 with a domain‑separation tag “KyberPAKE”. The construction achieves forward secrecy because the password‑derived seed is never reused, and the KEM’s IND‑CCA security lifts to the PAKE security model.

Implementation considerations: constant‑time sampling of the LWE error distribution is mandatory; rejection sampling with a fixed iteration bound (e.g., 64 iterations) prevents timing leakage. Masking the secret key shares at first order adds ≈ 2× cycle overhead on Cortex‑M4, matching the overhead reported for masked Kyber KEM. A true random number generator seeded with a quantum‑proof extractor (Trevisan’s extractor) must feed the masking randomness; otherwise a quantum‑capable adversary could predict the masks.

Hybrid Key Derivation Functions: Domain Separation, HKDF, and Quantum‑Random‑Oracle Proofs

Key derivation functions (KDFs) turn shared secrets of varying length and entropy into uniformly random keys suitable for symmetric primitives. In hybrid deployments a single KDF must combine a classical secret (e.g., an ECDH shared secret) with a post‑quantum secret (e.g., a Kyber‑768 shared secret) without weakening either branch. The standard construction is HKDF (RFC 5869) instantiated with SHA‑3‑256 or SHA‑256, applied to the concatenation of the two secrets preceded by a domain‑separation tag.

Domain separation is essential: the tag “Hybrid‑KEM‑v1” is prefixed to the input keying material (IKM) before the HKDF‑extract step. If the same salt were used for both the classical and post‑quantum branches, the random‑oracle proof would fail because the adversary could query the oracle on the classical branch and learn information about the post‑quantum branch. The hybrid KDF therefore uses distinct salts: salt₁ = “Classical‑Salt” for the ECDH secret, salt₂ = “PQC‑Salt” for the Kyber secret, and a final salt₃ = “Hybrid‑Combine” for the concatenated output of the two extracts.

Security in the quantum random‑oracle model (QROM) was established by Bindel, Hamburg, Hövelmanns, and Persichetti (Eurocrypt 2019) for the Fujisaki‑Okamoto transform applied to Kyber. Their proof shows that HKDF‑SHA‑3‑256 with independent salts yields an IND‑CCA secure KEM combiner assuming the underlying KEMs are IND‑CPA secure and the hash function is a quantum‑accessible random oracle. The reduction loss is quadratic in the number of hash queries, which is acceptable for the query bounds in TLS 1.3 (≤ 2⁶⁴).

Concrete parameters: the IKM length is 32 bytes (ECDH) + 32 bytes (Kyber‑768) = 64 bytes. HKDF‑extract with SHA‑3‑256 produces a 32‑byte pseudorandom key (PRK). HKDF‑expand with label “tls13‑derived” and length 48 bytes yields the traffic keys. The total hash calls per handshake are two extracts plus one expand, well within the performance budget of modern servers (≈ 0.3 ms on a 2.6 GHz Xeon).

Implementation pitfalls: using a single salt for both branches invalidates the QROM proof; reusing the same PRK for multiple labels without proper context binding leads to key‑reuse attacks; and feeding a low‑entropy password directly into HKDF‑extract without a prior PAKE step defeats the purpose of the hybrid construction.

Worked Example: Hybrid KDF Input Construction
A TLS 1.3 implementation uses ECDH‑P‑256 (shared secret Z₁) and Kyber‑768 (shared secret Z₂). Show the exact byte sequence fed to HKDF‑extract for the classical branch, the post‑quantum branch, and the final combine step, assuming the domain‑separation tags “Classical‑Salt”, “PQC‑Salt”, and “Hybrid‑Combine”.
The HKDF‑extract input for each branch is salt ∥ IKM. For the classical branch: salt₁ = ASCII “Classical‑Salt” (13 bytes), IKM₁ = Z₁ (32 bytes). Input₁ = 0x43 0x6C 0x61 0x73 0x73 0x69 0x63 0x61 0x6C 0x2D 0x53 0x61 0x6C 0x74 ∥ Z₁. For the post‑quantum branch: salt₂ = ASCII “PQC‑Salt” (8 bytes), IKM₂ = Z₂ (32 bytes). Input₂ = 0x50 0x51 0x43 0x2D 0x53 0x61 0x6C 0x74 ∥ Z₂. The combine step takes PRK₁ ∥ PRK₂ (64 bytes) as IKM₃ with salt₃ = ASCII “Hybrid‑Combine” (13 bytes). Input₃ = 0x48 0x79 0x62 0x72 0x69 0x64 0x2D 0x43 0x6F 0x6D 0x62 0x69 0x6E 0x65 ∥ PRK₁ ∥ PRK₂. Each input is then hashed with SHA‑3‑256 to produce the respective PRKs.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the hybrid KDF construction, write the three distinct salts explicitly and note that the QROM proof requires independent salts. Mention the Bindel‑et‑al. Eurocrypt 2019 reduction and the quadratic loss factor; this distinguishes a passing answer from a top‑tier answer.

Lattice‑Based Verifiable Secret Sharing and Distributed Key Generation

Verifiable secret sharing (VSS) lets a dealer distribute shares of a secret among n parties such that any subset of size t can reconstruct the secret, while any subset of size < t learns nothing, and every party can verify that its share is consistent with a unique secret. Lattice‑based VSS replaces the classical Shamir polynomial with a linear secret‑sharing scheme over a module R_q = ℤ_q[x]/(xⁿ+1). The dealer samples a secret vector s ∈ R_q^k, encodes it as a degree‑(t‑1) polynomial f(x) with coefficients in R_q^k, and sends each party i the share f(α_i) where α_i are distinct public evaluation points.

Verification uses a commitment to the polynomial coefficients via a lattice‑based commitment scheme such as the one from Baum, Damgård, and Orlandi (CRYPTO 2020). The commitment is a vector c = A·f + e where A ∈ R_qm×k is a public matrix and e is a small error vector. Each party checks that its share satisfies the commitment by recomputing A·share + e_i and comparing to the public commitment. Soundness follows from the binding property of the commitment, which reduces to the Module‑SIS assumption with parameters n = 1024, q ≈ 2²³, and β = 2¹⁰.

Distributed key generation (DKG) builds on VSS: each party acts as a dealer for its own secret share, and the final public key is the sum of all committed polynomials evaluated at zero. The protocol of Gennaro, Jarecki, Krawczyk, and Rabin (J. Cryptology 2007) was adapted to lattices by Baum, Cozzo, and Smart (PKC 2021). The resulting DKG produces a joint public key for a threshold version of the Kyber KEM. Communication complexity is O(n²·k·log q) bits; for n = 10, k = 3, q ≈ 2²³ this is ≈ 1.2 MB total, feasible for a one‑time setup.

Security model: the DKG is proven secure in the adaptive corruption model under the Module‑LWE assumption. The simulator extracts the adversary’s shares by rewinding the commitment openings, a technique that carries over to the quantum setting because the commitment is statistically binding. The threshold decryption protocol then uses the reconstructed secret to perform the Kyber decapsulation in a distributed manner, with each party contributing a partial decryption share that is combined via Lagrange interpolation over R_q.

Performance: a 10‑party DKG with threshold t = 6 completes in ≈ 350 ms on a 2.6 GHz Xeon (single‑threaded). The dominant cost is the NTT‑based polynomial multiplication for commitment verification. First‑order masking of the NTT adds ≈ 2.1× overhead, matching the masked Kyber figures reported in CHES 2022.

Covert‑Security Multi‑Party Computation and Publicly Verifiable MPC in the Post‑Quantum Setting

Covert security (Aumann and Lindell, TCC 2007) relaxes full malicious security by guaranteeing that a cheating party is caught with probability at least ε (the deterrence factor). In the post‑quantum world, covert‑secure MPC protocols are built from lattice‑based oblivious transfer (OT) extensions. The base OT uses the Peikert‑Vaikuntanathan‑Waters (PVW) LWE‑based OT (STOC 2008), and the extension follows the IKNP framework instantiated with a lattice‑based pseudorandom generator (e.g., the AES‑based PRG replaced by a SHA‑3‑based PRG).

The SPDZ‑lite preprocessing model (Dalskov, Escudero, Keller, et al., CCS 2020) provides a covert‑secure MPC with ε = 1/2. The offline phase generates authenticated multiplication triples using a lattice‑based homomorphic commitment (the same Module‑SIS commitment as in VSS). The online phase evaluates the arithmetic circuit with a single round of communication per multiplication gate. The total communication for a circuit with 10⁶ multiplication gates is ≈ 200 MB, dominated by the triple size (≈ 200 bytes each).

Publicly verifiable MPC (PV‑MPC) adds a non‑interactive proof that the output is correct, verifiable by any third party. Baum, Damgård, and Orlandi (CRYPTO 2021) constructed a lattice‑based PV‑MPC using a succinct non‑interactive argument of knowledge (SNARK) built from the lattice‑based commitment and the Fiat‑Shamir transform in the QROM. The proof size is O(log C) group elements where C is the circuit size; for C = 10⁶ the proof is ≈ 2 KB. Verification requires a single pairing‑free lattice‑based verification algorithm, making it suitable for blockchain smart contracts.

Security reductions: covert security reduces to the hardness of Module‑LWE with the same parameters as Kyber‑768. Public verifiability reduces to the soundness of the underlying SNARK, which in turn relies on the Module‑SIS assumption and the QROM security of Fiat‑Shamir (Don, Fehr, Majenz, Schaffner, Eurocrypt 2020). The combined protocol achieves a deterrence factor ε = 1/2 with a soundness error of 2⁻⁸⁰.

Implementation notes: the offline triple generation can be parallelised across cores; a 16‑core server reduces the offline time to ≈ 1.2 s for 10⁶ triples. Constant‑time sampling of the error vectors in the commitment is mandatory; the same rejection‑sampling‑with‑fixed‑iterations technique used for masked Kyber applies. A quantum‑proof TRNG seeded with Trevisan’s extractor feeds the randomness for both the OT extension and the commitment errors.

Secure Computation in the Quantum Random Oracle Model: Fiat‑Shamir, QROM Reductions, and Post‑Quantum Signatures

The Fiat‑Shamir transform converts a public‑coin interactive proof into a non‑interactive signature by hashing the transcript. In the classical random‑oracle model (ROM) the transform is sound; in the quantum random‑oracle model (QROM) the adversary can query the hash function in superposition, breaking many classical proofs. Boneh, Dagdelen, Fischlin, et al. (ASIACRYPT 2011) showed that Fiat‑Shamir remains sound for Σ‑protocols with a special “lossy” property, but the reduction loss is quadratic in the number of quantum queries.

Don, Fehr, Majenz, and Schaffner (Eurocrypt 2020) gave a tight QROM security proof for the Fiat‑Shamir transform applied to the lattice‑based identification scheme of Lyubashevsky (EUROCRYPT 2012). Their proof uses the “measure‑and‑reprogram” technique: the simulator measures the adversary’s query register, reprograms the oracle at the measured point, and bounds the distinguishing advantage by O(q²/2ⁿ) where q is the number of quantum queries and n is the output length of the hash (256 bits for SHA‑3‑256). For q ≤ 2⁶⁴ the loss is negligible.

This result underpins the security of Dilithium and Falcon signatures, both of which are Fiat‑Shamir transforms of lattice‑based identification protocols. Dilithium‑3 uses the “lossy” mode of the underlying Module‑LWE instance (q = 2²³, n = 256, k = 4, ℓ = 4) to achieve a tight reduction. Falcon‑512 uses the NTRU‑based identification scheme with a Gaussian sampler; its QROM proof follows the same measure‑and‑reprogram framework but requires a bound on the sampler’s statistical distance (≤ 2⁻¹²⁸).

Concrete parameter selection: the hash output length must be at least 256 bits to keep the QROM loss below 2⁻⁸⁰ for q = 2⁶⁴. The signature size for Dilithium‑3 is 2 420 bytes; for Falcon‑512 it is 666 bytes. Verification time on a 2.6 GHz Xeon is ≈ 0.12 ms for Dilithium‑3 and ≈ 0.08 ms for Falcon‑512. Both schemes are included in the NIST PQC standardisation round 3 finalists.

Open problems: extending the tight QROM proof to multi‑party Fiat‑Shamir (e.g., threshold signatures) and to the “hash‑then‑sign” paradigm used in hash‑based signatures (LMS, XMSS). Recent work (CCS 2023) proposes a “dual‑mode” hash function that is both collision‑resistant and lossy, enabling a unified proof for both lattice and hash‑based signatures.

  • Assuming a single salt for both classical and post‑quantum branches of a hybrid KDF invalidates the QROM security proof.
  • Confusing the deterrence factor ε in covert security with the soundness error of a publicly verifiable MPC; they are independent parameters.
  • Treating the Fiat‑Shamir transform as automatically secure in the QROM without citing the measure‑and‑reprogram bound.
  • Believing that lattice‑based VSS commitments are statistically hiding; they are only computationally hiding under Module‑LWE.
  • Neglecting that the quantum‑proof TRNG must feed both masking randomness and the error vectors in commitments; a classical TRNG alone is insufficient.
  • Overlooking the quadratic loss in the QROM reduction for Fiat‑Shamir when estimating concrete security levels.
  • Assuming that the communication cost of a lattice‑based DKG is independent of the number of parties; it scales quadratically.

Post‑Quantum Secure Multi‑Party Computation in the Honest‑Majority Setting with Preprocessing

Honest‑majority MPC protocols such as BGW (Ben‑Or, Goldwasser, Wigderson) and its modern variants rely on Shamir secret sharing over a prime field 𝔽ₚ with p > n, where n is the number of parties. In the preprocessing model the parties first generate correlated randomness — typically Beaver multiplication triples (a, b, c = a·b) — using a lightweight semi‑honest protocol such as the SPDZ‑offline phase or a dedicated OT‑extension. The online phase then evaluates an arithmetic circuit with only O(1) rounds per multiplication gate, because each party locally computes its share of the product using the pre‑distributed triple and a single broadcast of the masked values. Communication per multiplication is 2·(n‑1) field elements, which for n = 5 and a 61‑bit prime amounts to roughly 120 bytes per gate. The offline phase can be parallelised across cores; a 16‑core server produces 10⁶ triples in ≈ 1.2 s using the same constant‑time sampling routine employed for masked Kyber. Security reduces to the hardness of Module‑LWE with the same parameters as Kyber‑768 when the triples are generated from a lattice‑based PRG, giving a concrete 128‑bit post‑quantum security level.

Compared with dishonest‑majority SPDZ‑Lite, the honest‑majority setting avoids the heavy MAC‑checking overhead and achieves a lower round complexity (one round per layer of the circuit). However, it requires a trusted dealer or a distributed key generation (DKG) for the initial sharing of the secret‑sharing polynomial. Recent work (CCS 2023) shows that a lattice‑based DKG with Feldman VSS can be instantiated with Module‑SIS parameters (n = 256, q = 2²³) and incurs O(n²) communication, which is acceptable for n ≤ 10. The protocol also supports reactive computation: parties can input new values after the offline phase by re‑sharing them using the same secret‑sharing scheme, preserving the same security guarantees.

Implementation notes: the field 𝔽ₚ must be chosen so that p ≡ 3 (mod 4) to enable fast square‑root extraction for the Gaussian sampler used in the lattice PRG. Constant‑time rejection sampling with a fixed iteration bound (e.g., 16 iterations) eliminates timing leakage. The same quantum‑proof TRNG seeded with Trevisan’s extractor feeds both the OT‑extension randomness and the error vectors in the lattice PRG, ensuring that a classical TRNG alone does not become a side‑channel. Benchmarks on a 2.6 GHz Xeon show an online throughput of ≈ 3 × 10⁶ multiplication gates per second for a 5‑party deployment with 10⁶ pre‑generated triples.

Lattice‑Based Multi‑Authority Attribute‑Based Encryption with Dynamic Revocation

Multi‑authority attribute‑based encryption (MA‑ABE) allows several independent attribute authorities to issue secret keys for disjoint attribute sets while a single encryptor can enforce a policy that spans all authorities. The lattice construction of Agrawal, Freeman, and Vaikuntanathan (EUROCRYPT 2011) builds on the dual‑Regev encryption scheme: each authority holds a master secret key (MSK) consisting of a short basis for a Module‑LWE lattice, and derives user secret keys by sampling short vectors from the corresponding coset. The ciphertext contains a vector 𝐜 = A·𝐬 + 𝐞 + μ·⌊q/2⌋ where A is the public matrix common to all authorities, 𝐬 is the encryption randomness, and μ is the message bit. Policy enforcement is achieved by embedding a linear secret‑sharing scheme (LSSS) matrix into the ciphertext; each row corresponds to an attribute and is bound to the authority that controls it.

Dynamic revocation is handled by a key‑update mechanism: the authority periodically publishes a short update key 𝐮ₜ derived from a hierarchical identity‑based encryption (HIBE) tree over time epochs. A non‑revoked user combines his long‑term secret key with the current update key to obtain a valid decryption key for epoch t. The update key size is O(log T) lattice vectors, where T is the total number of epochs; for T = 2¹⁶ the update key is ≈ 1.2 KB. Revoked users cannot compute the update key because they lack the leaf secret in the HIBE tree. Security reduces to the hardness of Module‑LWE and Module‑SIS with the same parameters as Kyber‑768 (n = 256, q = 2²³, k = 4). The ciphertext size grows linearly with the number of attributes in the policy; a policy with 20 attributes yields a ciphertext of ≈ 4.5 KB.

Performance figures from the reference implementation (C + AVX2) on a 3.0 GHz Core i7: key generation per authority ≈ 2.3 ms, encryption for a 20‑attribute policy ≈ 3.1 ms, decryption ≈ 2.8 ms. The scheme supports attribute addition without re‑encrypting existing data by issuing a new authority key pair and updating the public matrix A via a trapdoor‑preserving extension (using the Micciancio‑Peikert trapdoor). This property is essential for large‑scale deployments such as healthcare record sharing where new attributes (e.g., “COVID‑19‑vaccinated”) appear over time.

Worked Example: Revocation Update Key Size
An MA‑ABE system uses a binary HIBE tree with 2¹⁶ epochs. Each node stores a Module‑LWE secret vector of length n = 256 over ℤ_q with q = 2²³. Compute the size in bytes of the update key for a non‑revoked user at epoch t = 2¹⁵, assuming each coefficient is stored in 32 bits.
The update key consists of the secret vectors on the path from the root to the leaf representing epoch t. A binary tree of height 16 has 16 nodes on this path. Each vector has 256 coefficients × 4 bytes = 1024 bytes. Total size = 16 × 1024 bytes = 16384 bytes = 16 KB.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for concrete sizes, always identify the lattice dimension, modulus bit‑length, and number of vectors. Multiply dimension × (modulus bits / 8) × vector count. Keep a small table of standard parameters (Kyber‑768: n=256, q≈2²³) to avoid recomputing during the exam.

Post‑Quantum Secure Threshold Encryption for Distributed Key Management

Threshold encryption enables a group of n parties to jointly decrypt a ciphertext only when at least t parties cooperate, while any subset of fewer than t parties learns nothing about the plaintext. A lattice‑based construction uses the Kyber KEM as the underlying public‑key encryption: the public key is a Module‑LWE matrix A ∈ ℤ_qk×k and a vector 𝐛 = A·𝐬 + 𝐞. The secret key 𝐬 is shared among the n parties using Shamir secret sharing over ℤ_q with threshold t. To encrypt, the sender runs Kyber.Encaps to obtain a shared secret K and a ciphertext (𝐜₁, 𝐜₂). Decryption requires each party to compute a partial decryption share 𝐝ᵢ = 𝐜₁·𝐬ᵢ (where 𝐬ᵢ is the party’s share) and broadcast it. The combiner reconstructs 𝐬 = Σ λᵢ·𝐬ᵢ using Lagrange coefficients λᵢ and recovers K = KDF(𝐜₂ ⊕ 𝐝). Security reduces to the IND‑CCA security of Kyber (Module‑LWE) and the secrecy of Shamir sharing, which is information‑theoretic.

The distributed key generation (DKG) for the shared secret 𝐬 can be instantiated with a lattice‑based Feldman VSS: each party commits to its polynomial coefficients using a Module‑SIS commitment (A·𝐟 + 𝐠) and broadcasts the commitments. The verification equations are linear, allowing each party to check consistency in O(k²) operations. The DKG communication cost is O(n²·k) field elements; for n = 7, k = 4 this is ≈ 2 KB total. The resulting threshold decryption latency is dominated by the partial decryption step: each party performs a matrix‑vector multiplication of size k×k, taking ≈ 0.04 ms on a modern CPU. The combiner’s reconstruction adds another ≈ 0.02 ms.

Forward secrecy is achieved by periodically refreshing the shared secret via a proactive secret sharing (PSS) protocol: each party generates a fresh random polynomial of degree t‑1 with zero constant term, distributes shares, and adds them to the existing shares. The refresh requires one broadcast round and O(n·k) communication. If the refresh interval is 24 hours, the total bandwidth per party per day is < 10 KB. The scheme is compatible with hybrid KEM combiners: the Kyber ciphertext can be combined with a classical ECIES ciphertext, and the threshold decryption proceeds independently on each component, preserving security even if one assumption fails.

Post‑Quantum Secure Verifiable Secret Sharing with Public Verifiability

Verifiable secret sharing (VSS) ensures that a dealer’s shared secret can be publicly verified without revealing the secret. The lattice‑based VSS of Baum, Damgård, and Orlandi (CRYPTO 2018) uses a Module‑SIS commitment scheme: the dealer samples a random polynomial f(x) = Σ a_j x^j of degree t‑1 over ℤ_q, where the constant term a₀ is the secret. For each coefficient a_j the dealer computes a commitment C_j = A·a_j + e_j with a short error vector e_j. The commitments are published; any verifier can check that the shares s_i = f(i) are consistent by evaluating the polynomial at the public points and confirming that A·s_i + Σ e_j·i^j equals the corresponding linear combination of commitments. The verification is public because it only uses the public matrix A and the commitments.

The scheme achieves computational hiding under Module‑LWE (the commitments are indistinguishable from uniform) and statistical binding under Module‑SIS (finding two distinct polynomials with the same commitments solves SIS). The soundness error is 2⁻⁸⁰ when the challenge space is 256 bits. The dealer’s communication is (t·k) lattice vectors for the commitments plus n shares; for t = 5, k = 4, n = 10 this is ≈ 3 KB. The verification cost per party is O(t·k²) matrix‑vector multiplications, ≈ 0.06 ms on a 2.6 GHz Xeon. The protocol integrates naturally with the honest‑majority MPC preprocessing: the VSS commitments become the correlated randomness for Beaver triples, and the public verifiability eliminates the need for a trusted dealer.

Recent optimisations (ASIACRYPT 2022) replace the Module‑SIS commitments with a lattice‑based Pedersen commitment using a second independent matrix B, reducing the commitment size by a factor of two while preserving the same security reduction. The trade‑off is an additional matrix‑vector multiplication during verification. For applications such as threshold signing (FROST) the VSS can be used to distribute the signing key with public auditability, enabling any observer to verify that the key shares are well‑formed without learning the key.

Post‑Quantum Secure Zero‑Knowledge Proofs for Regulatory Compliance

Regulatory compliance often requires proving that a confidential computation (e.g., a risk model) satisfies certain constraints without revealing the model parameters. Lattice‑based zk‑SNARKs such as Aurora (EUROCRYPT 2019) and its successor Ligero‑Lattice (CCS 2021) provide succinct non‑interactive arguments for arithmetic circuits over ℤ_q with proof size O(log C) group elements, where C is the number of multiplication gates. The prover commits to the witness using a Module‑SIS commitment, then runs a sum‑check protocol over the circuit’s polynomial encoding. The Fiat‑Shamir transform in the QROM (measure‑and‑reprogram technique) yields a non‑interactive proof with soundness error 2⁻⁸⁰ for a 256‑bit hash output. For a circuit with C = 10⁶ gates the proof is ≈ 2 KB and verification requires a single pairing‑free lattice verification (≈ 0.12 ms on a 2.6 GHz Xeon).

The compliance circuit typically encodes linear constraints (e.g., capital adequacy ratios) and range checks (e.g., non‑negative exposures). Range checks are implemented via a binary decomposition gadget that adds O(log M) multiplication gates per bounded variable, where M is the maximum value. For 32‑bit integers this adds ≈ 32 gates per variable. The overall circuit size for a Basel III‑style stress test with 500 variables is ≈ 2 × 10⁵ gates, yielding a proof of ≈ 1.5 KB. The prover’s runtime is dominated by the commitment and the sum‑check; with AVX2‑optimised NTT it completes in ≈ 0.8 s on a 16‑core server.

Integration with existing audit pipelines is straightforward: the verifier runs the same verification algorithm on the submitted proof and the public circuit description. Because the proof is publicly verifiable, regulators can archive proofs for future re‑audit without storing the confidential data. The security reduction relies on Module‑LWE for the commitment hiding and Module‑SIS for the binding, both instantiated with Kyber‑768 parameters. A common pitfall is to reuse the same randomness for the commitment and the Fiat‑Shamir hash; this breaks the QROM proof and must be avoided by deriving independent seeds from a quantum‑proof TRNG.

  • Confusing the honest‑majority threshold t with the number of parties n; security only holds when t > n/2.
  • Assuming that the update key in MA‑ABE can be derived from the public parameters alone; it requires the HIBE leaf secret.
  • Treating the lattice‑based DKG communication as O(n) instead of O(n²); the quadratic term dominates for n > 5.
  • Believing that VSS commitments are statistically hiding; they are only computationally hiding under Module‑LWE.
  • Reusing the same salt for the classical and post‑quantum branches of a hybrid KDF, which invalidates the QROM security proof.
  • Neglecting the quadratic loss in the QROM reduction for Fiat‑Shamir when estimating concrete security levels for zk‑SNARKs.
  • Overlooking that proactive secret sharing refreshes require a broadcast round; omitting it breaks forward secrecy.

Indistinguishability Obfuscation: From Multilinear Maps to Lattice-Based Candidates

Indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) is a cryptographic primitive that transforms any two functionally equivalent circuits into computationally indistinguishable obfuscated programs. Formally, a uniform PPT algorithm iO satisfies: for all circuits C₁, C₂ of the same size with C₁(x) = C₂(x) for all inputs x, the distributions iO(C₁) and iO(C₂) are computationally indistinguishable. The first candidate construction by Garg, Gentry, Halevi, Raykova, Sahai, and Waters (FOCS 2013) relied on multilinear maps, specifically the GGH13 graded encoding scheme. Subsequent work replaced multilinear maps with simpler assumptions: the Lin (2016) construction uses only constant-degree multilinear maps, while the Jain, Lin, and Sahai (STOC 2021) breakthrough achieves iO from well-founded assumptions including the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) assumption over large fields, the Decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH) assumption, and the existence of a pseudorandom generator in NC⁰. The most recent lattice-based candidate by Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta (EUROCRYPT 2020) builds iO from the Learning With Errors (LWE) assumption with subexponential modulus-to-noise ratio, combined with a circular-security assumption for LWE. All known constructions follow a common template: (1) a bootstrapping step that converts a weak obfuscator for NC¹ circuits into a strong obfuscator for all polynomial-size circuits using fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), and (2) a weak obfuscator built from the underlying algebraic assumption. The FHE step requires a circular-secure FHE scheme, which is known from LWE. The weak obfuscator for NC¹ is the core differentiator: multilinear-map-based constructions encode the circuit as a matrix branching program and use the graded encoding to evaluate it, while LPN-based constructions use a variant of the Goldreich PRG. Concrete efficiency remains a major barrier: the Jain-Lin-Sahai construction incurs a polynomial blowup of degree ≈ 10⁶, making it purely theoretical. For exam purposes, the critical distinctions are: (a) iO implies witness encryption, deniable encryption, and functional encryption for all circuits; (b) iO does not imply virtual black-box obfuscation, which is impossible for general circuits (Barak et al., CRYPTO 2001); (c) post-quantum iO candidates rely on LWE or LPN, not on isogenies or codes; (d) the circular-security assumption for FHE is a non-standard but widely accepted assumption in the lattice setting.

Witness Encryption and Its Applications to Time-Lock Puzzles and One-Time Programs

Witness encryption (WE), introduced by Garg, Gentry, Sahai, and Waters (STOC 2013), allows encrypting a message m under an NP statement x such that anyone holding a witness w for x ∈ L can decrypt, while the ciphertext reveals nothing about m if x ∉ L. Formally, a WE scheme for an NP language L with relation R consists of algorithms Enc(1λ, x, m) and Dec(w, ct) satisfying correctness: if R(x, w) = 1 then Dec(w, Enc(x, m)) = m; and security: for any x ∉ L, the distributions Enc(x, m₀) and Enc(x, m₁) are computationally indistinguishable. The original construction uses iO and a one-way function. A direct construction from multilinear maps was given by Garg et al., but it inherits the same security concerns. Post-quantum WE can be built from iO based on LWE/LPN, or more directly from the hardness of approximating the shortest vector problem (GapSVP) on lattices combined with a hash function modeled as a random oracle. The most efficient lattice-based WE (Zhandry, CRYPTO 2016) uses a lossy trapdoor function derived from LWE. Applications: Time-lock puzzles — encrypt a message under the statement "there exists a sequential computation of length T that outputs y." The witness is the computation trace. Using a verifiable delay function (VDF) as the sequential computation yields a time-lock puzzle where decryption requires T sequential steps. One-time programs (OTP) — Goldwasser, Kalai, and Rothblum (CRYPTO 2008) showed how to compile any circuit into a one-time program using a hardware token that self-destructs after one use. WE provides a software-only alternative: the program is encrypted under the statement "there exists a valid signature on input x under the user's public key." The user provides the signature as witness to decrypt and evaluate. The program can only be evaluated once because the signature scheme is one-time (e.g., Lamport signatures). Extractable witness encryption (EWE) strengthens WE by requiring that any successful decryptor must "know" a witness; this is formalized via an extractor that outputs a witness given the decryptor's code. EWE is equivalent to iO for NP languages with unique witnesses. For exams, remember: WE does not require the encryptor to know a witness; the statement x can be false. This distinguishes WE from attribute-based encryption where the encryptor chooses attributes. The security definition is only meaningful for x ∉ L; if x ∈ L, the ciphertext may leak m to an unbounded adversary who can find a witness.

Worked Example: Distinguishing WE from ABE
A protocol designer wants to encrypt a message m such that any party who can produce a valid solution to a specific Sudoku puzzle can decrypt. The puzzle instance is public. The designer does not know a solution. Which primitive should be used: witness encryption (WE) or ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption (CP-ABE)? Justify your answer and explain what happens if the puzzle has no solution.
Use witness encryption. In WE, the encryptor only needs the NP statement x (the Sudoku instance) and the message m; no witness is required. The ciphertext is Enc(x, m). Any party holding a solution w (a witness for x ∈ L) can decrypt via Dec(w, ct). In CP-ABE, the encryptor must specify an access policy and encrypt under attributes; the decryptor's key is issued by an authority based on attributes. There is no mechanism for "any solution to this puzzle" without a trusted authority. If the puzzle has no solution (x ∉ L), WE security guarantees that the ciphertext hides m computationally — no PPT adversary can distinguish Enc(x, m₀) from Enc(x, m₁). However, an unbounded adversary could eventually determine that no solution exists, but this does not break the computational security definition.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks for "encryption under an NP statement without a trusted setup," the answer is witness encryption. If the question adds "and the encryptor knows a witness," it could be WE or functional encryption. If it says "the authority issues keys based on attributes," it is ABE. Memorise the three-way distinction: WE (no setup, no witness needed to encrypt), FE (setup, function key derived from master secret), ABE (setup, attribute keys from authority).

Proof-Carrying Data: Recursive Proof Composition and Incrementally Verifiable Computation

Proof-carrying data (PCD), introduced by Chiesa and Tromer (TCC 2010), generalises incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) to distributed computations represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of messages. Each node in the DAG produces a message z along with a proof π that z was correctly computed from its predecessors' messages according to a local compliance predicate Φ. The proof π is verified by any party receiving z without needing the entire history. PCD is constructed from a succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (SNARK) that supports recursive composition: the verifier circuit of the SNARK is itself expressed as an arithmetic circuit, and the SNARK proves that the previous proof verified correctly. The first PCD construction used the Micali CS-proofs (random oracle model). The breakthrough by Ben-Sasson, Chiesa, Tromer, and Virza (CRYPTO 2014) achieved PCD from a knowledge-of-exponent assumption (KEA) on elliptic curves, yielding the Pinocchio SNARK with a universal trusted setup. Subsequent work removed the trusted setup: Sonic (CCS 2019), Marlin (EUROCRYPT 2020), and Plonk (EUROCRYPT 2020) provide universal and updatable structured reference strings (SRS). The most efficient recursive SNARK for PCD is Halo (S&P 2020) and its successor Halo2, which use a cycle of elliptic curves (Pasta curves: Pallas and Vesta) to avoid a trusted setup entirely. The recursion works by having the verifier circuit compute the pairing check inside the circuit using the other curve's arithmetic. For post-quantum PCD, lattice-based SNARKs such as Ligero-Lattice (CCS 2021) and the more recent LaBRADOR (EUROCRYPT 2023) can be used, but recursive composition is harder because lattice verifiers involve matrix-vector multiplications and norm checks that are not easily expressed as low-degree arithmetic circuits. A practical approach uses a hybrid: a lattice-based outer SNARK for the compliance predicate and an inner elliptic-curve SNARK for the recursion, with a trusted setup for the inner curve. IVC is the special case where the DAG is a linear chain: each step proves that the current state si+1 = F(si) for a transition function F. Applications include: (1) blockchain light clients that verify the entire chain history with a single proof (e.g., Mina protocol uses Kimchi, a Plonk variant); (2) verifiable delay functions where the proof of sequential work is itself a PCD proof; (3) secure hardware attestation where a chain of measurements is compressed into a constant-size proof. Concrete parameters: for a compliance predicate with 10⁴ R1CS constraints, a Plonk-based PCD proof is ≈ 2 KB and verification takes ≈ 5 ms on a modern CPU. The trusted setup for the universal SRS requires a multi-party ceremony; if all participants are corrupted, soundness fails. For exams, distinguish PCD (distributed, DAG, arbitrary compliance predicate) from IVC (linear chain, fixed transition function) and from recursive SNARKs (the cryptographic tool enabling both).

Constrained Pseudorandom Functions: Prefix-Constrained PRFs, Key-Homomorphic PRFs, and Applications

A constrained pseudorandom function (CPRF) allows the holder of a master key k to derive a constrained key kC that evaluates the PRF on inputs satisfying a constraint C, while revealing nothing about the PRF outputs on inputs outside C. Formally, a CPRF for a constraint family C consists of algorithms KeyGen(1λ), Constrain(k, C), and Eval(k, x) with the property that Eval(kC, x) = Eval(k, x) for all x ∈ C, and for any PPT adversary, the outputs on x ∉ C are indistinguishable from random even given kC. The first CPRFs were built by Boneh and Waters (ASIACRYPT 2013) for prefix constraints (bit-fixing) using multilinear maps. Subsequent work achieved CPRFs for circuits from iO (Boyle, Goldwasser, and Ivan, PKC 2014) and for inner-product predicates from standard lattice assumptions (Boneh, Lewi, Montgomery, and Raghunathan, CRYPTO 2017). Prefix-constrained PRFs are the most practical: the constraint Cp = {x : x starts with prefix p}. The Boneh-Waters construction uses a binary tree of PRF keys; the constrained key for prefix p consists of the keys on the path to p. This yields a key-homomorphic PRF: Eval(k₁ + k₂, x) = Eval(k₁, x) ⊕ Eval(k₂, x). Key-homomorphic PRFs (KH-PRFs) were formalised by Banerjee, Peikert, and Rosen (EUROCRYPT 2012) and are implied by the Learning With Rounding (LWR) assumption. The Banerjee-Peikert-Rosen KH-PRF is Eval(k, x) = ⌊Ax · k⌉p where Ax is a matrix derived from x via a hash function, and rounding is modulo p. This PRF is post-quantum secure under LWR. Applications: Broadcast encryption — the master key encrypts to a set of users; each user gets a constrained key for their identity prefix. Key rotation — a constrained key for time period t allows decryption only for that period. Watermarking PRFs — a constrained key embeds a mark that is detectable in the output distribution. Policy-based key distribution — in a hierarchical organisation, a manager derives constrained keys for subordinates' access patterns. For exams, the critical comparison is: CPRFs from iO support arbitrary circuit constraints but are inefficient; CPRFs from lattices support inner-product and prefix constraints with concrete efficiency; KH-PRFs are a special case where the constraint is a linear subspace (the set of keys that evaluate to zero on a given input). The security definition for CPRFs is selective (adversary commits to challenge inputs before seeing the constrained key) or adaptive (adversary chooses after). Adaptive security is stronger and harder to achieve; the Boneh-Waters prefix CPRF is selectively secure under multilinear maps, while the lattice-based inner-product CPRF achieves adaptive security under LWE.

Post-Quantum Secure Searchable Encryption: Forward Privacy, Volume-Hiding, and Leakage-Abuse Attacks

Searchable symmetric encryption (SSE) allows a client to outsource an encrypted document collection to a server while retaining the ability to search for keywords. The server learns the search pattern (which queries are repeated) and the access pattern (which documents match each query). Forward privacy, introduced by Bost (CCS 2016), ensures that adding a new document does not reveal its keywords to the server, even if the server later obtains the search token for those keywords. Formally, an SSE scheme is forward-private if for any two sequences of updates that result in the same final database, the server's view is indistinguishable. The most efficient forward-private SSE is the Sophos construction (Bost, Minaud, and Ohrimenko, CCS 2017) which uses a puncturable PRF to derive per-keyword state. The client maintains a counter ctrw for each keyword w; the search token for w is PRF(k, w || ctrw). When a document with keyword w is added, the client increments ctrw and sends an encrypted index entry keyed by the new token. The server cannot link the new entry to previous searches for w because the token changes. Volume-hiding SSE (Kamara and Moataz, EUROCRYPT 2019) additionally hides the number of documents matching each keyword (the volume). This is achieved by padding each keyword's index to a fixed size or using an oblivious RAM (ORAM) to access the index. The trade-off is significant: volume-hiding SSE incurs O(log N) or O(√N) overhead per search. Leakage-abuse attacks (Cash, Grubbs, Perry, and Ristenpart, CCS 2015) demonstrate that even "secure" SSE schemes leak enough information for an adversary with auxiliary data (e.g., a known subset of documents) to recover keywords and documents. The attack exploits the access pattern and search pattern leakage. Defences include: (1) suppressing the search pattern by using a fresh token for each query (requires stateful client); (2) suppressing the access pattern via ORAM or padding; (3) differential privacy on the access pattern. Post-quantum SSE replaces the underlying PRF and symmetric encryption with quantum-resistant primitives: AES-256 for encryption (Grover's algorithm gives √2²⁵⁶ = 2¹²⁸ security, acceptable), and a lattice-based PRF such as the Banerjee-Peikert-Rosen KH-PRF for token generation. The puncturable PRF for forward privacy can be built from the GGM tree using a lattice-based PRG. Concrete parameters: for a database of 10⁶ documents with 10⁴ unique keywords, a forward-private SSE index is ≈ 500 MB; search time is ≈ 10 ms per keyword on the server. Volume-hiding adds a 10-100× overhead. For exams, remember the leakage profile hierarchy: basic SSE leaks search pattern + access pattern; forward-private SSE leaks only search pattern (access pattern for updates is hidden); volume-hiding SSE leaks only search pattern and total volume; fully leakage-free SSE requires ORAM and leaks nothing. No practical scheme achieves full leakage-freeness without ORAM overhead.

  • Confusing witness encryption (encryptor needs no witness) with functional encryption (key generation needs master secret) or attribute-based encryption (authority issues keys).
  • Assuming indistinguishability obfuscation implies virtual black-box obfuscation; Barak et al. proved VBB is impossible for general circuits, while iO is plausible.
  • Treating proof-carrying data as merely "recursive SNARKs" without distinguishing the DAG compliance predicate from the linear-chain IVC special case.
  • Believing constrained PRFs from lattices support arbitrary circuit constraints; they are limited to inner-product, prefix, and bit-fixing constraints unless combined with iO.
  • Overlooking that forward privacy in SSE only hides update keywords, not the search pattern; volume-hiding requires separate padding or ORAM.
  • Assuming post-quantum SSE only requires replacing AES with a lattice-based cipher; the PRF for token generation must also be post-quantum, and puncturable PRFs need quantum-secure PRGs.
  • Confusing the trusted setup in universal SNARKs (one-time ceremony for all circuits) with the per-circuit setup in Groth16; universal setups are updatable, per-circuit setups are not.

Post‑Quantum Secure Password‑Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) Protocols

Password‑authenticated key exchange allows two parties who share a low‑entropy secret to derive a high‑entropy session key while resisting offline dictionary attacks. Classical PAKEs such as SPAKE2+, CPace and OPAQUE rely on the hardness of the Diffie‑Hellman problem in cyclic groups. A quantum adversary can solve discrete logarithms in polynomial time, so these constructions lose their security guarantees. Post‑quantum PAKEs replace the group‑based Diffie‑Hellman exchange with a key‑encapsulation mechanism (KEM) that is believed to resist quantum attacks, typically a lattice‑based or code‑based KEM.

The most studied design pattern is the KEM‑based PAKE: each party runs the KEM encapsulation algorithm using a public key derived from the password (via a password‑to‑public‑key map such as a hash‑to‑curve or a lattice‑based trapdoor generation). The encapsulated ciphertext is sent to the peer, who decapsulates using the corresponding secret key derived from the same password. Because the KEM is IND‑CCA secure, an active adversary who intercepts the ciphertext cannot test password guesses without interacting with an honest party, preserving the online‑only dictionary‑attack property.

Concrete proposals include KyberPAKE (built on the Kyber KEM), FrodoPAKE (built on FrodoKEM), and SIDH‑PAKE (now broken by the Castryck‑Decru attack). KyberPAKE inherits Kyber’s IND‑CCA security under the Module‑LWE assumption and achieves a communication cost of roughly 2 KB per flow for NIST Level 3 parameters. FrodoPAKE uses the plain LWE‑based FrodoKEM, offering a more conservative security reduction at the cost of larger ciphertexts (≈ 10 KB). Both protocols have been analysed in the Universal Composability (UC) framework with a programmable random oracle, showing that they realise the ideal PAKE functionality assuming the underlying KEM is UC‑secure.

Implementation considerations: the password‑to‑public‑key map must be constant‑time and side‑channel resistant; a common choice is to derive a seed from the password using a memory‑hard KDF (e.g., Argon2id) and then run the KEM key‑generation algorithm deterministically from that seed. The KEM encapsulation and decapsulation must also be constant‑time. Standards bodies (IETF CFRG, ISO/IEC 11770‑4) are currently evaluating post‑quantum PAKE candidates for inclusion in future TLS‑PAKE and messaging‑layer security extensions.

Post‑Quantum Secure Identity‑Based Encryption and Hierarchical IBE

Identity‑based encryption (IBE) lets any string (e‑mail address, user ID) serve as a public key, with a trusted Private Key Generator (PKG) issuing the corresponding private key. The original Boneh‑Franklin IBE uses bilinear pairings on elliptic curves, which are vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm. Post‑quantum IBE constructions rely on the Learning With Errors (LWE) or Ring‑LWE assumptions. The seminal GPV IBE (Gentry‑Peikert‑Vaikuntanathan, 2008) builds a trapdoor for a random lattice matrix and uses the GPV pre‑image sampling algorithm to extract private keys for arbitrary identities. Security reduces to the hardness of LWE in the random‑oracle model.

Hierarchical IBE (HIBE) extends IBE by allowing a PKG to delegate key‑generation authority to lower‑level authorities, forming a tree of identities. Lattice‑based HIBE schemes (e.g., ABB10, Cash‑Hofheinz‑Kiltz‑Peikert 2010) use a sequence of trapdoor delegations: each level samples a short basis for a lattice that extends the parent’s basis. The delegation algorithm preserves the Gaussian distribution of the secret keys, ensuring that the resulting keys are statistically close to those generated directly by the root PKG. Parameter sizes grow linearly with the hierarchy depth; for a depth of 5 and 128‑bit post‑quantum security, public parameters are on the order of a few megabytes.

Recent NIST PQC submissions include FrodoIBE (derived from FrodoKEM) and SABER‑IBE (derived from SABER). Both avoid the Gaussian sampling of GPV by using the “dual‑Regev” encryption paradigm, which only requires uniform sampling and a simple rounding step. This simplifies constant‑time implementations and reduces the trusted code base. However, dual‑Regev IBE typically yields larger ciphertexts (≈ 2×) compared to GPV‑style schemes.

Key management challenges: the PKG holds a master secret that can decrypt all traffic, so compromise is catastrophic. Threshold PKG constructions (distributed key generation using Shamir secret sharing over lattices) mitigate this risk and are compatible with the same LWE assumptions. Revocation in IBE/HIBE is usually handled by appending a time‑period to the identity (e.g., “alice@example.com‖2025‑Q3”) and issuing short‑lived keys, or by using a revocation list combined with a broadcast encryption layer.

Technique
Explain why a lattice‑based IBE such as GPV remains secure against a quantum adversary, whereas the pairing‑based Boneh‑Franklin IBE does not. Include the underlying hardness assumptions and the role of the random oracle.
Boneh‑Franklin IBE security reduces to the Bilinear Diffie‑Hellman (BDH) problem in groups equipped with an efficiently computable pairing. Shor’s algorithm solves the discrete logarithm problem in those groups in polynomial time on a quantum computer, which also breaks BDH. Consequently the pairing‑based assumption collapses. GPV IBE security reduces to the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem: given (A, A·s + e) with small error e, recover s. No known quantum algorithm solves LWE substantially faster than the best classical lattice‑reduction attacks; the best known quantum speed‑up is a square‑root improvement via Grover on the search space, which is accounted for by choosing parameters with a 2× security margin. The GPV proof works in the random‑oracle model, where the hash function mapping identities to lattice vectors is modelled as a truly random function. This model is standard for IBE and does not introduce additional quantum‑specific weaknesses.
Exam Day Strategy
When a question asks to compare classical and post‑quantum IBE, structure the answer in three rows: (1) underlying hard problem, (2) quantum algorithm impact, (3) parameter‑size consequences. Cite GPV (LWE) vs Boneh‑Franklin (BDH) and note that lattice‑based schemes need larger public parameters but avoid pairings. This tabular comparison scores full marks for clarity.

Post‑Quantum Secure Commitment Schemes: Lattice‑Based and Hash‑Based Constructions

A commitment scheme allows a sender to bind to a value while keeping it hidden, later revealing the value and proving it matches the commitment. The two core properties are binding (the sender cannot open to two different values) and hiding (the receiver learns nothing before opening). Classical constructions include Pedersen commitments (based on discrete logarithms) and hash‑based commitments (e.g., SHA‑256). Quantum attacks break Pedersen commitments because the binding property relies on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem.

Hash‑based commitments remain secure in the quantum random‑oracle model: a commitment is C = H(m ‖ r) where H is a collision‑resistant hash function (SHA‑3‑256 or SHAKE‑256) and r is a random nonce. Binding reduces to collision resistance; Grover’s algorithm gives a quadratic speed‑up for finding collisions, so a 256‑bit hash provides 128‑bit post‑quantum security. Hiding is information‑theoretic if r is uniformly random and never reused. This construction is simple, constant‑time, and widely used in post‑quantum protocols such as SPHINCS+ signatures and the Merkle‑tree based commitments in lattice‑based zero‑knowledge proofs.

Lattice‑based commitments offer statistically hiding and computationally binding (or vice‑versa) under the Short Integer Solution (SIS) or LWE assumptions. The Kawachi‑Tanaka‑Xagawa (KTX) commitment uses a random matrix A ∈ ℤ_qn×m and commits to a message vector μ by computing C = A·s + G·μ + e, where s is a short random vector, G is a gadget matrix, and e is a small error vector. Binding follows from the hardness of finding two distinct (μ, s, e) that give the same C, which is an SIS instance. Hiding follows from the LWE‑style indistinguishability of A·s + e from uniform. Parameters for 128‑bit post‑quantum security: n = 512, q ≈ 215, m = 1024, yielding commitments of ≈ 2 KB.

Another important lattice commitment is the Lyubashevsky commitment used in the Dilithium signature scheme: C = A·y + H(μ) where y is a short random vector and H is a hash to the lattice. This commitment is computationally binding (via SIS) and statistically hiding because y masks the message. It integrates naturally with the Fiat‑Shamir transform for lattice‑based zero‑knowledge proofs.

Choice guidelines: use hash‑based commitments when simplicity and minimal bandwidth are paramount (e.g., in Merkle trees, blockchain headers). Use lattice‑based commitments when the protocol already operates in a lattice setting and needs algebraic homomorphic properties (e.g., adding commitments corresponds to adding messages). Both families are compatible with the NIST PQC standardisation timeline and have constant‑time reference implementations.

Post‑Quantum Secure Time‑Lock Puzzles and Their Applications

A time‑lock puzzle forces a solver to spend a prescribed amount of sequential computation to recover a secret, with no known parallel speed‑up. Rivest, Shamir and Wagner (1996) proposed the classic construction: choose an RSA modulus N = p·q, a random base a ∈ ℤ_N^*, and a time parameter T. The puzzle is (N, a, T) and the solution is a2^T mod N. The creator, knowing φ(N), can compute the solution quickly using Euler’s theorem, while any solver must perform T sequential squarings. This construction is broken by a quantum computer because factoring N reveals φ(N).

Post‑quantum time‑lock puzzles replace the RSA group with a structure where repeated application of a function is inherently sequential and quantum‑resistant. Two main approaches exist:

  • Iterated hash‑based puzzles: define f(x) = H(x) for a quantum‑secure hash H (e.g., SHA‑3‑256). The puzzle is (x0, T) and the solution is x_T = f^T(x0). Because each evaluation of H is a black‑box query, Grover’s algorithm does not reduce the sequential depth; the best quantum attack still requires T sequential hash evaluations. The creator can compute x_T quickly only if a trapdoor exists (e.g., a pre‑image oracle), which is not available for standard hashes. Therefore this design is a verifiable delay function (VDF) rather than a traditional time‑lock puzzle with a fast‑forward trapdoor.
  • Lattice‑based puzzles with a trapdoor: Boneh, Bünz and Fisch (2020) construct a puzzle from the LWE assumption. The creator samples a secret s and publishes a matrix A and a vector b = A·s + e. The puzzle asks to compute s after T sequential applications of a “repeated‑sampling” function that uses the LWE trapdoor to accelerate. The trapdoor allows the creator to compute the solution in polylog(T) time, while any quantum adversary without the trapdoor must perform T sequential LWE‑sample steps. Security reduces to the hardness of LWE even with quantum queries.

Applications include sealed‑bid auctions (bids committed via a time‑lock puzzle that opens after the bidding period), randomness beacons (the puzzle solution serves as unpredictable entropy), and blockchain consensus (proof‑of‑elapsed‑time). In all cases the puzzle parameters must be calibrated so that the expected wall‑clock time matches the desired delay on the target hardware, accounting for possible ASIC or FPGA acceleration. A common rule of thumb: choose T such that a single core at 3 GHz needs ≈ 1 second per 106 iterations of SHA‑3‑256; for a one‑hour delay set T ≈ 3.6·109.

Post‑Quantum Secure Honest‑Majority Multi‑Party Computation Using Shamir Secret Sharing

Honest‑majority MPC protocols tolerate up to t < n/2 corrupted parties among n participants. The classic BGW protocol (Ben‑Or, Goldwasser, Wigderson, 1988) uses Shamir secret sharing over a finite field: a secret s is encoded as a degree‑t polynomial f with f(0)=s, and each party receives a share f(i). Addition of shared values is local; multiplication requires a degree‑reduction step where parties exchange shares of the product polynomial and reconstruct a fresh degree‑t sharing via a linear recombination vector. Security is information‑theoretic against a passive adversary; active security is achieved by adding zero‑knowledge proofs of correct sharing (e.g., using Feldman VSS).

To obtain post‑quantum security, the underlying field arithmetic must be instantiated with a quantum‑resistant algebraic structure. The most direct approach is to keep the field (e.g., a 256‑bit prime field) because field operations are not broken by quantum algorithms; the only quantum‑sensitive component is the verifiable secret sharing (VSS) and any commitment scheme used to enforce honest behaviour. Replacing Pedersen commitments with hash‑based or lattice‑based commitments (as described in the previous section) yields a fully post‑quantum BGW variant. The communication complexity remains O(n2) field elements per multiplication gate.

An alternative is the SPDZ‑lite family, which uses an offline preprocessing phase to generate multiplication triples (a, b, c = a·b) shared among parties. In the honest‑majority setting the preprocessing can be done with a simple distributed key generation (DKG) for a threshold Paillier‑style encryption, but Paillier is not post‑quantum. Recent work (e.g., “MPC from LWE” by Döttling et al., 2021) builds multiplication triples directly from LWE‑based somewhat homomorphic encryption, eliminating the need for number‑theoretic assumptions. The resulting protocol retains the honest‑majority threshold and achieves active security with a modest constant‑factor overhead.

Practical deployments: the MP‑SPDZ framework now includes a “Shamir‑LWE” backend that compiles arithmetic circuits into a post‑quantum honest‑majority protocol. Benchmarks on a 10‑party LAN show ≈ 5 ms per multiplication gate for 128‑bit security, comparable to classical BGW over a 64‑bit field. The main engineering challenge is the size of LWE‑based ciphertexts (several kilobytes), which increases network traffic; compression techniques (seed‑expansion for public matrices) mitigate this.

  • Assuming a post‑quantum PAKE only needs a quantum‑secure KEM; the password‑to‑public‑key derivation must also be quantum‑resistant and constant‑time.
  • Confusing the master secret in IBE with a threshold‑shared master key; the former is a single point of failure, the latter requires a distributed key generation protocol.
  • Treating hash‑based commitments as computationally hiding; they are only computationally binding, hiding is information‑theoretic provided the nonce is uniform and never reused.
  • Believing Rivest‑Shamir‑Wagner time‑lock puzzles survive quantum attacks because they use repeated squaring; factoring the modulus breaks the trapdoor.
  • Thinking honest‑majority MPC automatically becomes post‑quantum by changing the field size; the commitment and VSS layers must also be instantiated with quantum‑secure primitives.
  • Overlooking that lattice‑based time‑lock puzzles with a trapdoor require a trusted setup for the trapdoor; loss of the trapdoor makes the puzzle unsolvable even for the creator.
  • Assuming all post‑quantum IBE schemes have comparable ciphertext sizes; dual‑Regev variants are typically twice as large as GPV‑style schemes.

Post‑Quantum Secure Verifiable Secret Sharing and Distributed Key Generation

Verifiable secret sharing (VSS) lets a dealer distribute a secret among n parties so that any subset of size t+1 can reconstruct it, while any subset of size ≤ t learns nothing. Classical VSS (e.g., Feldman or Pedersen) relies on discrete‑log or pairing assumptions that are broken by Shor’s algorithm. A post‑quantum VSS replaces the commitment layer with a lattice‑based commitment scheme such as the Module‑LWE commitment used in the Dilithium signature framework. The dealer samples a secret polynomial s(x) over the ring Rq=ℤq[x]/(xn+1) and publishes commitments Ci=Ai·s+ei for each share index i, where Ai are public matrices derived from a seed and ei are small error vectors. Verification uses the homomorphic property of the commitment: each party checks that its share si satisfies Ci−Ai·si is a short vector, which can be tested with a lattice‑norm bound. Because the commitment is statistically binding and computationally hiding under Module‑LWE, the VSS inherits post‑quantum security.

Distributed key generation (DKG) builds on VSS to let parties jointly generate a public key without any single party learning the secret key. The Gennaro‑Jarecki‑Krawczyk‑Rabin (GJKR) DKG protocol, originally proven secure under the Decisional Diffie‑Hellman assumption, can be instantiated with the lattice VSS above. Each party acts as a dealer for its own secret share, runs the VSS, and the final public key is the sum of the individual commitment polynomials. The resulting threshold public key supports threshold decryption or threshold signing (e.g., a lattice‑based variant of FROST). Security proofs follow the same simulation paradigm: a simulator extracts the adversary’s shares from the VSS commitments using the trapdoor of the underlying Module‑LWE instance, which exists only in the security reduction. Concrete parameters for 128‑bit post‑quantum security typically use n=256, q≈223, and error distribution χ with standard deviation σ≈3.2. Communication per party is O(n·log q) ≈ 2 KB per share, and the total round complexity remains three broadcast rounds, matching the classical GJKR efficiency.

Implementation considerations include constant‑time polynomial multiplication (NTT) and rejection sampling for the error vectors to avoid side‑channel leakage. The MP‑SPDZ framework now ships a “Shamir‑ModuleLWE” backend that compiles arithmetic circuits into this DKG‑enabled VSS, reporting ≈ 6 ms per multiplication gate on a 10‑party LAN. The main engineering challenge is the size of the public matrices Ai; seed‑expansion from a 256‑bit seed reduces the transmitted data by a factor of 8 without affecting security.

Post‑Quantum Secure Private Set Intersection Using Lattice‑Based Oblivious Transfer

Private set intersection (PSI) allows two parties, each holding a set of identifiers, to compute the intersection without revealing any other elements. The most communication‑efficient PSI constructions use oblivious transfer (OT) as a building block: the sender encodes its set as a polynomial, the receiver obtains evaluations on its own elements via OT, and both parties locally compute the intersection. In a post‑quantum setting the OT must be instantiated with a quantum‑secure primitive. The Kyber KEM (Module‑LWE, NIST‑selected) provides a natural 1‑out‑of‑2 OT via the “dual‑mode” technique: the sender generates a Kyber key pair (pk, sk), the receiver chooses a random bit b and sends a Kyber ciphertext c that encrypts a random string kb under pk; the sender decapsulates both possible messages using sk and returns the two strings masked with the receiver’s choice. Because Kyber’s IND‑CCA security reduces to Module‑LWE, the resulting OT is secure against quantum adversaries.

The PSI protocol proceeds as follows. Party A (sender) holds set SA of size N. It builds a polynomial f(x)=∏a∈SA(x−a) over a prime field Fp with p≈261−1 (a Mersenne prime enabling fast reduction). Party B (receiver) holds set SB of size M. For each element b∈SB, B engages in a 1‑out‑of‑2 OT where the two messages are f(b) and a random field element. B receives f(b) for its own elements and random values for dummy queries, preventing A from learning which elements B queried. After the OT phase, B evaluates f(b) locally for all b∈SB and sends the list of evaluations to A. A checks which evaluations equal zero; those correspond to the intersection. The communication cost is O((N+M)·log p) field elements plus O(M) Kyber ciphertexts (≈ 1 KB each). For N=M=105 the total bandwidth is ≈ 150 MB, comparable to the best classical OT‑based PSI.

Security proof follows the standard simulation paradigm: a simulator for a corrupt sender extracts the receiver’s set by programming the Kyber public key in the random‑oracle model; a simulator for a corrupt receiver extracts the sender’s polynomial by rewinding the OT. Both reductions rely on the IND‑CCA security of Kyber, which is proven under Module‑LWE with a tight loss factor of O(qH) where qH is the number of hash queries. Side‑channel resistance is achieved by constant‑time NTT and rejection sampling in Kyber, and by masking the polynomial coefficients during evaluation. The open‑source library “psi‑lattice” implements this protocol and reports 2.3 s runtime for 105 elements on a single core at 3.2 GHz.

Worked Example: Parameter Selection for Lattice‑Based PSI
A deployment targets 128‑bit post‑quantum security with sets of size 217 (≈ 131 k) elements each. Choose Kyber‑768 (Module‑LWE dimension k=3, n=256, q=3329) for OT. Determine the prime field size p for the polynomial representation and estimate the total communication in megabytes.
Step 1 – Field size. The polynomial degree equals the sender’s set size N=131 072. To avoid wrap‑around, p must be > N. A 61‑bit Mersenne prime p=261−1 ≈ 2.3·1018 satisfies this and allows fast reduction. Step 2 – Kyber ciphertext size. Kyber‑768 ciphertext is 1088 bytes. For M=131 072 OT instances the OT traffic is 1088 × 131 072 ≈ 142.6 MB. Step 3 – Polynomial coefficient traffic. The sender transmits the polynomial coefficients (N+1 field elements). Each element is 8 bytes (61 bits rounded up). That is (131 073 × 8) ≈ 1.0 MB. The receiver sends back M evaluations (8 bytes each) ≈ 1.0 MB. Step 4 – Total. 142.6 + 1.0 + 1.0 ≈ 144.6 MB. Rounding up for protocol overhead gives ≈ 150 MB, matching the library benchmark.
Exam‑Day Strategy
