The theta lift from orthogonal groups to GSpin groups is realized geometrically by a correspondence between the moduli of orthogonal shtukas and the moduli of GSpin‑shtukas; the kernel is the Weil representation constructed from the standard representation of the dual group Spin2n(ℂ). Laumon and Ngô proved that the lift preserves cuspidality and matches standard L‑functions, giving a function‑field proof of the functorial transfer predicted by the Langlands dual embedding Spin2n(ℂ) → GL2n(ℂ). The Hecke operators on GSpin‑modular forms are indexed by dominant coweights of GSpin, and their eigenvalues are the Satake parameters of the associated automorphic representation. A key computational tool is the explicit description of the local theta correspondence at unramified places via the spherical Hecke algebra, where the transfer factor is a product of local epsilon factors that can be read off from the geometry of the nearby cycles on the shtuka space.

At ramified places the theta kernel involves a Weil representation of the metaplectic double cover of the symplectic group, and the local theta lift is described by the Howe duality conjecture, which is a theorem in the function‑field setting thanks to the work of Gan–Ichino and Waldspurger. The global theta lift is then obtained by integrating the product of local theta lifts against an Eisenstein series on the orthogonal group; the resulting GSpin‑modular form is non‑zero precisely when the central value of the standard L‑function of the orthogonal representation does not vanish. This non‑vanishing criterion is the function‑field analogue of the Rallis inner product formula. Examiners often ask for the definition of the GSpin‑shtuka moduli stack, the description of the theta kernel as a perverse sheaf on the product of moduli spaces, and the statement of the Rallis inner product formula in terms of the residue of the Eisenstein series at s = 1.

The Function Field Analogue of the Langlands–Shahidi Method for Classical Groups

The Langlands–Shahidi method attaches local L‑functions, epsilon factors, and gamma factors to a generic representation π of a split classical group G over a local field by analyzing the normalizing factor of a standard intertwining operator on an induced representation. In the function‑field setting the local field is Fq((t)) and the method is carried out on the moduli stack of G‑shtukas with two legs, where the intertwining operator corresponds to a Hecke correspondence that exchanges the two legs. Lafforgue’s global Langlands correspondence for GLn provides the necessary analytic properties of the global L‑functions, and the local factors are extracted by comparing the trace formula on G with that on GLN via the functorial lift. The local coefficient C(π, s) is defined as the ratio of the normalized intertwining operator to the unnormalized one; it satisfies the functional equation C(π, s) C(π̃, 1−s) = 1 and its poles and zeros determine the local L‑function L(s, π, r) for the standard representation r of the L‑group. The gamma factor γ(s, π, r, ψ) is then defined by γ(s, π, r, ψ) = ε(s, π, r, ψ) L(1−s, π̃, r̃) / L(s, π, r), where ε is the epsilon factor obtained from the local constant of the functional equation of the global L‑function.

A crucial technical input is the computation of the Plancherel measure for the induced representation, which in the function‑field case is expressed in terms of the geometry of the affine Grassmannian for G and the nearby cycles of the Hitchin fibration. The work of Ngô on the fundamental lemma for the Lie algebra of G provides the matching of orbital integrals needed to stabilize the trace formula, and the support theorem guarantees that the relevant cohomology is concentrated in the expected degrees. The resulting local factors satisfy the expected multiplicativity and compatibility with parabolic induction, and they agree with the factors defined by the Rankin–Selberg method for GLn × GLm. Examiners frequently test the definition of the local coefficient in terms of the intertwining operator, the statement of the functional equation for the gamma factor, and the role of the fundamental lemma in proving the multiplicativity of the local L‑functions.

Identifying the correct local coefficient in the Shahidi method
Explain how the local coefficient is computed for a generic representation of a split classical group over a function field using the geometry of shtukas.
The local coefficient C(π, s) is the scalar by which the normalized intertwining operator M(π, s) differs from the unnormalized operator M0(π, s). On the moduli stack of G‑shtukas with two legs, the unnormalized operator corresponds to the Hecke correspondence that swaps the two legs; its action on the space of automorphic forms is given by a convolution with the characteristic function of the double coset K diag(ϖλ, 1) K, where λ is the dominant coweight defining the induction. The normalization factor is obtained by dividing by the Plancherel measure μ(π, s), which is computed as the ratio of the volumes of the relevant double cosets in the affine Grassmannian. In the function‑field case these volumes are expressed as traces of Frobenius on the nearby cycles of the Hitchin fibration, and Ngô’s fundamental lemma identifies them with the corresponding orbital integrals on the endoscopic group. Consequently C(π, s) = M0(π, s) / μ(π, s) and satisfies C(π, s) C(π̃, 1−s) = 1. The poles of C(π, s) give the local L‑function L(s, π, r).
Exam‑day strategy
Memorize the definition of the local coefficient as the ratio of the unnormalized intertwining operator to the Plancherel measure. Remember that in function fields the Plancherel measure is a Frobenius trace on nearby cycles, not an archimedean integral. When asked for the gamma factor, write γ(s, π, r, ψ) = ε(s, π, r, ψ) L(1−s, π̃, r̃) / L(s, π, r) and note that ε comes from the global functional equation via the product formula.

The Geometric Langlands Correspondence for Exceptional Groups via Shtukas

The geometric Langlands program for a reductive group G over a curve X over Fq predicts an equivalence between the derived category of D‑modules on the moduli stack BunG of G‑bundles and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the stack LocSysǦ of Ǧ‑local systems, where Ǧ is the Langlands dual group. For exceptional groups such as G2, F4, E6, E7, E8 the dual groups are again exceptional, and the correspondence is accessed through the moduli of G‑shtukas with one leg. A G‑shtuka is a G‑bundle on X × S together with an isomorphism away from a divisor given by the leg; the Hecke correspondences are defined by modifying the bundle at the leg according to dominant coweights of G. The geometric Satake equivalence identifies the category of spherical perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian GrG with the representation category Rep(Ǧ). For exceptional groups the affine Grassmannian is not a union of finite‑dimensional varieties but an ind‑scheme whose stratification by G‑orbits is indexed by the dominant coweight lattice; the IC‑sheaves on these strata correspond to the irreducible representations of Ǧ. The Hecke eigensheaf property for a D‑module on BunG translates into the condition that its pull‑back to the moduli of G‑shtukas is an eigensheaf for the Hecke operators with eigenvalue given by a Ǧ‑local system. Drinfeld’s original construction for GL2 was extended to all reductive groups by Laumon, and the case of exceptional groups was treated by Varshavsky and later by Zhu using the theory of factorization spaces. A key result is that the cohomology of the moduli stack of G‑shtukas with fixed leg computes the L‑function of the associated automorphic representation, and the Frobenius eigenvalues on this cohomology match the Satake parameters of the Ǧ‑local system. Examiners may ask for the definition of a G‑shtuka, the statement of the geometric Satake equivalence for exceptional groups, and the description of the Hecke eigensheaf condition in terms of the factorization property of the corresponding sheaf on the moduli of shtukas.

The Non‑Abelian Hodge Theory for t‑Motives and the Function Field Simpson Correspondence

A t‑motive over a function field K = Fq(C) is a finite‑dimensional K‑vector space M equipped with a σ‑linear Frobenius endomorphism Φ and a K‑linear connection ∇ satisfying the compatibility Φ ∘ ∇ = ∇ ∘ Φ. The category of t‑motives is a neutral Tannakian category over Fq, and its Tannakian fundamental group is the motivic Galois group of the t‑motive. Anderson’s theory provides a de Rham cohomology HdR(M) = M / (Φ − 1)M and a Betti cohomology HB(M) = MΦ=1 ⊗Fq Fq((t))sep. The non‑abelian Hodge correspondence, proved by Anderson–Brownawell–Papanikolas for rank‑one t‑motives and extended by Hartl–Juschka to higher rank, establishes an equivalence between the category of t‑motives with a Hodge filtration and the category of Higgs bundles (E, θ) on the curve C over Fq satisfying a nilpotence condition on the Higgs field θ. The period matrix of a t‑motive is the comparison isomorphism between HdR and HB; its entries are the periods and quasi‑periods of the associated Drinfeld module. The Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem asserts that the logarithms of algebraic points on a Drinfeld module are linear combinations of periods with coefficients in the field of definition. The function‑field Simpson correspondence identifies the moduli space of semistable t‑motives of fixed rank and dimension with the moduli space of semistable Higgs bundles of the same rank and degree, and the Hodge filtration on the t‑motive corresponds to the Harder–Narasimhan filtration on the Higgs bundle. Examiners often test the definition of a t‑motive, the statement of the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem, and the description of the period matrix as a solution of a Frobenius difference equation. A common trap is to confuse the σ‑linear Frobenius on the t‑motive with the q‑power Frobenius on the base field; the former acts on the coefficients of the module, the latter on the curve.

The Categorical Langlands Correspondence for Function Fields and the Derived Satake Equivalence

The categorical Langlands correspondence lifts the geometric Langlands equivalence to an equivalence of monoidal ∞‑categories: the category of D‑modules on BunG with convolution product is equivalent to the category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on LocSysǦ with tensor product. In the function‑field setting this is realized by the derived Satake equivalence, which identifies the derived category of constructible sheaves on the affine Grassmannian GrG with the derived category of representations of the Langlands dual group Ǧ. The convolution product on the affine Grassmannian corresponds to the tensor product of representations. Arinkin and Gaitsgory proved that the category of D‑modules on BunG is generated by the Hecke functors, which are given by convolution with the IC‑sheaves on GrG. The derived Satake equivalence is compatible with the t‑structure, and its heart recovers the classical geometric Satake equivalence. For function fields the moduli stack of G‑shtukas with one leg provides a geometric model for the Hecke category: the correspondence between two copies of BunG given by a G‑shtuka with leg at x ∈ X induces a functor on D‑modules that matches the Hecke functor at x. The categorical correspondence implies that the trace of Frobenius on the cohomology of the moduli of G‑shtukas computes the character of the corresponding representation of Ǧ, giving a categorification of the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula. Examiners may ask for the statement of the derived Satake equivalence, the definition of the Hecke functor in terms of shtukas, and the role of the monoidal structure in the categorical Langlands correspondence. A subtle point is that the derived Satake equivalence is an equivalence of DG‑categories, not merely of triangulated categories, and the monoidal structure is essential for the compatibility with the tensor product on LocSysǦ.

  • Confusing the theta lift for GSpin groups with the classical theta correspondence for symplectic–orthogonal dual pairs; the GSpin lift involves a double cover and a different Weil representation.
  • Assuming the local coefficient in the Shahidi method is always a rational function in q−s; in the function‑field case it is a product of Frobenius eigenvalues on nearby cycles and may involve non‑rational factors.
  • Treating the geometric Langlands correspondence for exceptional groups as a direct generalization of the GL2 case; the affine Grassmannian for exceptional groups has infinitely many strata and the IC‑sheaves are not all perverse in the usual sense.
  • Mixing the σ‑linear Frobenius on a t‑motive with the absolute Frobenius on the base curve; the former acts on the module coefficients, the latter on the curve coordinates.
  • Believing the derived Satake equivalence holds for the affine flag variety as well as the affine Grassmannian; the affine flag variety gives the Iwahori–Hecke category, which is not equivalent to Rep(Ǧ) but to the category of modules over the affine Hecke algebra.
  • Overlooking the necessity of the monoidal structure in the categorical Langlands correspondence; without it the equivalence of categories does not respect the tensor product on local systems.
  • Stating that the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem applies to all t‑motives; it is proved for uniformizable t‑motives and requires the existence of a Frobenius‑invariant lattice.

The sections above provide the advanced mechanisms, comparisons, and examiner traps needed for mastery of the next level of Drinfeld module theory.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Modularity Theorem for Drinfeld Modules

The modularity theorem for Drinfeld modules asserts that every rank‑two Drinfeld module over a global function field K with split multiplicative reduction at a place ∞ corresponds to a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL₂(AK) which is unramified outside the level. This statement was proved by Laurent Lafforgue in 2002 as part of his proof of the global Langlands correspondence for GLₙ over function fields. The proof constructs a Galois representation attached to a Drinfeld module via the ℓ‑adic Tate module, then shows that the associated L‑function matches the automorphic L‑function of a Hecke eigenform on the Drinfeld modular curve. The key input is the cohomology of the Drinfeld modular tower, where the action of Hecke operators is identified with the action of Frobenius on the ℓ‑adic sheaves. As a consequence, the eigenvalues of Hecke operators on Drinfeld modular forms are algebraic integers and satisfy the Ramanujan–Petersson bound |av| ≤ 2 qv¹ᐟ².

In practice, the modularity theorem allows one to transfer problems about Drinfeld modules to the automorphic side. For example, the analytic continuation and functional equation of the Goss L‑function of a Drinfeld module follow from the corresponding properties of the automorphic L‑function. Moreover, the theorem provides a dictionary: the conductor of the Drinfeld module equals the level of the automorphic representation, and the type of reduction at a place translates into the local component of the representation (principal series, special, or supercuspidal). Examiners often ask for the precise statement of the correspondence, the role of the Drinfeld upper half‑plane in the construction of the Galois representation, and the identification of the Hecke eigenvalues with Frobenius traces.

A subtle point is that the modularity theorem is proved for Drinfeld modules with split multiplicative reduction at ∞; the case of potentially good reduction requires the theory of Drinfeld modular forms of higher weight and the use of the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for Drinfeld modular curves. The theorem also extends to higher rank Drinfeld modules via the work of Vincent Lafforgue, where the automorphic side involves GLₙ and the Galois side involves ℓ‑adic representations of dimension n. The higher‑rank modularity is still an active research area, and the precise description of the local Langlands correspondence for GLₙ over function fields via shtukas is a key ingredient.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Theory of Special Values of Goss L‑Functions via Anderson t‑Motives

Goss L‑functions are the function‑field analogues of classical Dirichlet L‑functions. For a Drinfeld module φ of rank r over a global function field K, the Goss L‑function L(φ, s) is defined by an Euler product over the places of K where φ has good reduction, with local factors given by the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius acting on the Tate module. Anderson’s theory of t‑motives provides a uniform framework to study special values of these L‑functions at positive integers. A t‑motive M attached to φ is a left module over the non‑commutative polynomial ring A[τ] (τ is the Frobenius twist) equipped with a σ‑linear Frobenius endomorphism. The period matrix of M, obtained by comparing the Betti and de Rham realizations, satisfies a Frobenius difference equation Ψ^(σ) = Φ Ψ, where Φ is the matrix of the Frobenius on M.

The Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem states that for any algebraic point P on φ, the logarithm logφ(P) is an A-linear combination of the periods of φ with coefficients in the field of definition of P. This theorem implies that the special values L(φ, k) for integers k ≥ 1 are algebraic multiples of suitable powers of the fundamental period ω. In particular, the leading term of the L‑function at s = 1 is expressed in terms of the regulator of the Mordell–Weil group of φ, giving a function‑field analogue of the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer formula. The proof uses the theory of dual t‑motives and the fact that the category of t‑motives is a neutral Tannakian category over A, with the motivic Galois group controlling the algebraic relations among periods.

Examiners frequently test the definition of a t‑motive, the statement of the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem, and the description of the period matrix as a solution of a Frobenius difference equation. A common trap is to confuse the σ‑linear Frobenius on the t‑motive (which acts on the coefficients of the module) with the q‑power Frobenius on the base curve (which acts on the coordinates of the curve). Another pitfall is to assume that the log‑algebraicity theorem holds for all t‑motives; it is proved for uniformizable t‑motives and requires the existence of a Frobenius‑invariant lattice.

Worked Example: Special Value of a Goss L‑Function
Let φ be the rank‑two Drinfeld module over 𝔽q(t) defined by φt = t + τ + τ². Compute the leading term of the Goss L‑function L(φ, s) at s = 1 in terms of the fundamental period ω and the regulator Reg(φ).
The t‑motive M attached to φ has rank 2 and dimension 2. Its period matrix Ψ satisfies Ψ^(σ) = Φ Ψ with Φ = [[t, 1],[0, t]]. The fundamental period ω is the (1,1) entry of Ψ evaluated at the Carlitz exponential. By the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem, logφ(P) ∈ ω·𝔽q(t) for any algebraic point P. The Mordell–Weil group φ(𝔽q(t)) is a finitely generated 𝔽q[t]-module of rank r. The regulator Reg(φ) is the determinant of the matrix (logφ(Pi)) for a basis {Pi}. The function‑field BSD formula (proved by Taguchi–Wan) gives L*(φ, 1) = (Reg(φ)·|Ш(φ)|) / (|φ(𝔽q(t))tors|²) · ω², where L*(φ, 1) denotes the leading coefficient. Thus the leading term is an algebraic multiple of ω², with the algebraic factor expressed entirely in terms of the regulator and the Tate–Shafarevich group.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a special value of a Goss L‑function, first identify the associated t‑motive and write down its Frobenius matrix. Then recall the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem to relate logarithms of algebraic points to periods. Finally, invoke the function‑field BSD formula (or the appropriate conjecture if not proved) to express the leading term as a product of the regulator, the order of the Tate–Shafarevich group, and a power of the fundamental period. Keep the distinction between σ‑Frobenius on the t‑motive and the geometric Frobenius on the curve clear in your notation.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the p‑adic Uniformization of Drinfeld Modular Varieties

The p‑adic uniformization theorem for Drinfeld modular varieties states that the rigid analytic space associated to a Drinfeld modular curve of level N (with N coprime to the characteristic) is isomorphic to a quotient of the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ω by a discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ GL₂(A) acting by Möbius transformations. Here Ω = ℙ¹(ℂ∞) ℙ¹(K∞) is the complement of the rational points in the Berkovich projective line over the completion ℂ∞ of an algebraic closure of K∞. The group Γ is a congruence subgroup of GL₂(A) determined by the level structure. This uniformization is the function‑field counterpart of the classical complex uniformization of modular curves by the upper half‑plane modulo SL₂(ℤ). The proof uses the theory of Drinfeld modules with level structure and the fact that the moduli problem is representable by a smooth curve over the base field.

On the p‑adic side, the Drinfeld upper half‑plane carries a natural action of the Bruhat–Tits tree of PGL₂(K∞). The quotient Ω/Γ inherits a structure of a Mumford curve, i.e. a curve whose formal model has a dual graph isomorphic to the quotient of the Bruhat–Tits tree by Γ. This description makes it possible to compute the reduction type of the Drinfeld modular curve at places dividing the level: the special fiber is a union of rational components intersecting according to the graph. The harmonic cochains on the tree correspond to weight‑two Drinfeld modular forms, and the Hecke operators act via the adjacency operators on the tree. This combinatorial model is essential for explicit computations of Hecke eigenvalues and for the proof of the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for GL₂ over function fields.

Examiners often ask for the definition of the Drinfeld upper half‑plane, the statement of the p‑adic uniformization theorem, and the relationship between the Bruhat–Tits tree and the reduction graph of the modular curve. A frequent mistake is to confuse the Drinfeld upper half‑plane (a rigid analytic space over ℂ∞) with the classical complex upper half‑plane; the former is totally disconnected and its connected components are open balls. Another trap is to assume that the uniformization holds for arbitrary level; it requires the level to be prime to the characteristic, otherwise the moduli stack is not representable by a scheme and one must work with formal models or stacks.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group G₂

Recent work by Vincent Lafforgue and others has extended the geometric Langlands correspondence to the exceptional group G₂ over function fields. The correspondence relates G₂‑shtukas on a smooth projective curve X over 𝔽q to ℓ‑adic local systems on X with monodromy in the Langlands dual group, which for G₂ is again G₂ (the group is self‑dual). A G₂‑shtuka is a modification of a G₂‑bundle on X at a finite set of points, together with a Frobenius isomorphism. The moduli stack of G₂‑shtukas with one leg carries a natural action of the spherical Hecke algebra of G₂(𝔸X), and the cohomology of this stack realizes the automorphic representations of G₂.

The proof follows the general strategy of the geometric Langlands program: one constructs a perverse sheaf (the IC‑sheaf) on the affine Grassmannian GrG₂ and shows that the convolution product of these sheaves matches the tensor product of representations of the dual group. For G₂ the affine Grassmannian has infinitely many strata indexed by dominant coweights, and the IC‑sheaves are not all perverse in the usual sense; one must work with the derived category of constructible sheaves. The derived Satake equivalence for G₂ identifies the derived category of spherical perverse sheaves on GrG₂ with the derived category of representations of G₂. This equivalence is compatible with the monoidal structures, and the Hecke functors on the moduli of G₂‑bundles are given by convolution with the IC‑sheaves.

On the arithmetic side, the global Langlands correspondence for G₂ over function fields is known for generic automorphic representations thanks to the work of Lafforgue on the trace formula for reductive groups. The local Langlands correspondence for G₂ over local function fields has been established by Gan–Gross–Prasad type methods and by the theory of types. The compatibility of the local and global correspondences is expressed through the factorization of the global L‑function into local factors, each of which is a polynomial in q⁻ˢ whose roots are the Satake parameters of the local representation. Examiners may ask for the definition of a G₂‑shtuka, the statement of the derived Satake equivalence for G₂, and the role of the affine Grassmannian in the geometric correspondence. A subtle point is that the self‑duality of G₂ means the Langlands dual group is the same, but the correspondence still involves a non‑trivial transfer of orbital integrals.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the σ‑linear Frobenius on a t‑motive with the absolute Frobenius on the base curve; the former acts on module coefficients, the latter on curve coordinates.
  • Assuming the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem applies to all t‑motives; it requires uniformizability and a Frobenius‑invariant lattice.
  • Treating the Drinfeld upper half‑plane as a connected complex domain; it is a totally disconnected rigid analytic space whose components are open balls.
  • Believing the p‑adic uniformization theorem holds for arbitrary level; it requires the level to be prime to the characteristic.
  • Mixing the derived Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian with the affine flag variety; the latter gives the Iwahori–Hecke category, not Rep(Ǧ).
  • Overlooking the monoidal structure in the categorical Langlands correspondence; without it the equivalence does not respect the tensor product on local systems.
  • Assuming the geometric Langlands correspondence for exceptional groups is a direct generalization of the GL₂ case; the affine Grassmannian for G₂ has infinitely many strata and the IC‑sheaves are not all perverse in the usual sense.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of Newforms and Oldforms for Higher Rank Drinfeld Modular Forms

The theory of newforms for Drinfeld modular forms parallels the classical Atkin–Lehner theory but lives on the moduli of Drinfeld modules of rank r ≥ 2 over a global function field K = 𝔽q(X). For rank two, Gekeler and Reversat established a complete newform theory: the Hecke algebra acting on the space of cusp forms of level 𝔫 is commutative, semisimple, and admits a basis of simultaneous eigenforms. A newform is a normalized Hecke eigenform that is orthogonal to all oldforms — forms arising from lower levels via the natural degeneracy maps induced by the inclusions of level structures. The multiplicity‑one theorem holds for GL₂ over function fields, guaranteeing that each Hecke eigenspace is one‑dimensional. For higher rank r ≥ 3, the situation is more delicate. Basson, Breuer, and others have constructed Hecke operators on the cohomology of the Drinfeld modular variety of rank r and proved commutativity of the spherical Hecke algebra away from the characteristic. However, multiplicity one is not known in general; the Hecke eigenspaces may have dimension > 1, and the notion of a newform must be formulated in terms of the Bernstein center of the category of smooth representations of GLr(𝔸K). Oldforms are still defined as the images of the pull‑back maps from lower level moduli stacks, but the orthogonal complement with respect to the Petersson inner product (defined via the harmonic cochain pairing) may fail to be stable under the full Hecke algebra. Examiners often test the distinction between a primitive form (an eigenform whose Hecke eigenvalues generate the full Hecke field) and a newform (an eigenform orthogonal to oldforms). A common trap is to assume that every primitive form is a newform; in higher rank the two notions diverge because the Hecke algebra may not act semisimply on the space of oldforms. Another trap is to apply the rank‑two Atkin–Lehner involution formulas to higher rank without checking that the level is square‑free and prime to the characteristic, conditions that guarantee the existence of the Fricke involution on the Drinfeld modular curve.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Langlands–Shahidi Method for GLn over Function Fields and the Local Coefficient Formula

The Langlands–Shahidi method provides a uniform construction of local L‑functions, epsilon factors, and gamma factors for generic representations of quasi‑split reductive groups over local fields. Over a local function field F = 𝔽q((𝜋)), Shahidi adapted his method to the function field setting by using the theory of Eisenstein series on the Drinfeld upper half‑plane and the associated intertwining operators. For GLn(F) the method starts with a generic irreducible admissible representation π and a maximal parabolic subgroup P = MN with Levi M ≅ GLk × GLn‑k. The normalized intertwining operator A(s, π) attached to the induced representation IndPGLn(π ⊗ |det|s) satisfies a functional equation A(s, π) A(−s, π̃) = C(π, s) where C(π, s) is the local coefficient. Shahidi proved that C(π, s) = γ(s, π, r, ψ) / γ(s+1, π, r, ψ) where γ(s, π, r, ψ) is the gamma factor attached to the standard representation r of the L‑group LGLn = GLn(ℂ) and ψ is a non‑trivial additive character of F. The local L‑function L(s, π, r) is then defined as the denominator of the gamma factor after removing the epsilon factor. The method yields the expected functional equation L(s, π, r) = ε(s, π, r, ψ) L(1−s, π̃, r∨) and establishes the local Langlands correspondence for generic representations of GLn over function fields. A key point examiners stress is the distinction between the Langlands–Shahidi local coefficient and the Rankin–Selberg local factor: the former is defined for any maximal parabolic, while the latter corresponds to the case k = 1 and gives the standard L‑function of π × τ for τ a representation of GL1. Another trap is to assume that the gamma factor is always a rational function in q−s; for non‑generic representations the Shahidi method does not apply, and the local coefficient may have poles that are not accounted for by the standard gamma factor.

Identifying the Local Coefficient Formula
Let π be a generic irreducible admissible representation of GL₃(F) where F = 𝔽_q((π)). The Langlands–Shahidi local coefficient C(π, s) attached to the maximal parabolic with Levi GL₂ × GL₁ is given by which of the following expressions in terms of the gamma factor γ(s, π, r, ψ) for the standard representation r of ^LGL₃?
The local coefficient is C(π, s) = γ(s, π, r, ψ) / γ(s+1, π, r, ψ). This follows directly from Shahidi's functional equation for the normalized intertwining operator A(s, π): A(s, π) A(−s, π̃) = C(π, s). The gamma factor γ(s, π, r, ψ) is defined as ε(s, π, r, ψ) L(1−s, π̃, r∨) / L(s, π, r). Substituting this definition into the ratio yields the stated formula. A common mistake is to invert the ratio or to use the Rankin–Selberg gamma factor for GL₂ × GL₁ instead of the standard gamma factor for GL₃.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorize the definition C(π, s) = γ(s, π, r, ψ) / γ(s+1, π, r, ψ) and practice deriving the functional equation for the standard L‑function L(s, π, r) from it. In multiple‑choice questions, check whether the parabolic is maximal and whether the representation is generic; if not, the Shahidi formula does not apply.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Function Field Analogue of the Sato–Tate Conjecture

The Sato–Tate conjecture for Drinfeld modular forms predicts the equidistribution of the normalized Hecke eigenvalues (Satake parameters) of a non‑CM cuspidal eigenform as the level varies. For rank two over a rational function field 𝔽q(T), the Ramanujan–Petersson bound |λ𝔭| ≤ 2 qdeg(𝔭)/2 was proved by Drinfeld using the Weil conjectures for the associated ℓ‑adic sheaves. Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures then implies that the normalized eigenvalues λ𝔭 / qdeg(𝔭)/2 lie in [−2, 2] and, by the work of Pink and Böckle, become equidistributed with respect to the Sato–Tate measure (the pushforward of the Haar measure on SU(2) under the trace map). For higher rank n ≥ 3, the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture is known only for generic automorphic representations of GLn over function fields via Lafforgue’s global Langlands correspondence; the bound |λ𝔭| ≤ n qdeg(𝔭)/2 holds for the Satake parameters of the associated ℓ‑adic local system. The Sato–Tate conjecture in this setting asserts that the joint distribution of the n normalized Satake parameters at unramified places converges to the Haar measure on the maximal compact subgroup of the Langlands dual group, which for GLn is U(n). This is a deep open problem; partial results exist for symmetric power L‑functions and for families of Drinfeld modular forms with varying level. Examiners often ask for the precise statement of the conjecture for GL₂ and the role of the Weil conjectures in proving the bound. A frequent trap is to claim that the Sato–Tate measure is the semicircle law for all ranks; the correct measure for GLn is the eigenvalue distribution of a random unitary matrix, which for n = 2 reduces to the semicircle law but for n > 2 is a more complicated measure on ℝn invariant under the Weyl group. Another trap is to confuse the function field Sato–Tate conjecture with the classical Sato–Tate conjecture for elliptic curves over ℚ; the former concerns Drinfeld modular forms over 𝔽q(T) and uses the geometry of the Drinfeld modular curve, while the latter concerns modular forms over ℚ and uses the geometry of the modular curve over ℂ.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Theory of Eisenstein Series and Their Constant Terms

Eisenstein series on Drinfeld modular varieties are constructed by summing over cosets of a parabolic subgroup in GLn(𝔸K) and provide a bridge between cuspidal automorphic forms and the continuous spectrum. For rank two, Gekeler gave an explicit formula for the Eisenstein series of weight k and level 𝔫, showing that its constant term along the cusp at infinity is a sum of two terms involving the Drinfeld discriminant function Δ and the Eisenstein series of weight k−2. The constant term formula reflects the functional equation of the associated L‑function and the residues at s = 0, 1 give rise to the Drinfeld modular forms of weight 0 and 2. For higher rank, the Langlands theory of Eisenstein series applies: one induces a cuspidal automorphic representation π of a Levi subgroup M to GLn and forms the Eisenstein series E(g, s, π). The constant term along a standard parabolic P = MN is expressed as a sum over the Weyl group of intertwining operators M(w, s, π) applied to the inducing data. These intertwining operators are meromorphic in s and their poles correspond to residual automorphic representations. The constant term formula is essential for the spectral decomposition of L²(GLn(K)GLn(𝔸K)) and for the proof of the functional equation of the standard L‑function via the Langlands–Shahidi method. Examiners test the ability to write down the constant term for the minimal parabolic (Borel) induction: it is a sum over the Weyl group of products of local intertwining operators, each of which is a ratio of local L‑functions. A common mistake is to omit the normalizing factors that make the intertwining operators satisfy the cocycle relation, or to assume that the Eisenstein series is holomorphic for all s; in fact, poles at s = 1/2, 1, … give rise to the residual spectrum, which for GLn over function fields is completely described by the work of Moeglin and Waldspurger adapted to the function field case by Lafforgue.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Atkin–Lehner Theory for Higher Rank Modular Curves

The Atkin–Lehner involutions on the Drinfeld modular curve of rank two are defined for each divisor 𝔡 of the level 𝔫 that is coprime to the characteristic.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of Automorphic Periods and the Function Field Ichino–Ikeda Formula for Central L‑Values

The Ichino–Ikeda formula, originally proved for unitary groups over number fields, expresses the central critical value of a Rankin–Selberg L‑function as a product of local period integrals and a global period. Over function fields, the analogous statement relates the central value L(1/2, π × τ) for a pair of cuspidal automorphic representations π of GLn and τ of GLn−1 (or more generally for a pair of representations of a reductive group and its subgroup) to the square of a global period integral ∫H(K)H(𝔸K) φ(h) ψ(h) dh, where H is a spherical subgroup. In the function field setting, the geometry of the moduli stack of shtukas provides a geometric interpretation of these periods: the period integral becomes a trace of Frobenius on a certain ℓ‑adic sheaf on the moduli space of shtukas with additional structure (a “period sheaf”). Lafforgue’s global Langlands correspondence identifies the automorphic representations with ℓ‑adic local systems, and the period integral corresponds to a cup product in the cohomology of the shtuka space. The local factors are given by integrals over the local spherical variety H(Fv)G(Fv), which in the function field case are volumes of certain double cosets in the Bruhat–Tits building. The formula has been established for GL2 × GL1 (the Waldspurger formula) and for GL2 × GL2 (the Jacquet–Guo formula) by works of Yun, Zhang, and others using the relative trace formula. For higher rank, the function field Ichino–Ikeda formula is a major open problem; its proof would require a geometric understanding of the period sheaf and a comparison of the relative trace formula with the spectral decomposition of the period integral. Examiners often ask for the precise statement of the Waldspurger formula for rank‑two Drinfeld modules: the central L‑value L(1/2, π ⊗ χ) is proportional to the square of the toric period ∫T(K)T(𝔸K) φ(t) χ(t) dt, where T is a non‑split torus. A common trap is to confuse the function field Waldspurger formula (which involves Drinfeld modular forms and shtukas) with the classical Waldspurger formula (which involves modular forms over ℚ and Shimura curves); the former uses the geometry of the Drinfeld modular curve and the Bruhat–Tits tree, while the latter uses the geometry of the modular curve over ℂ and the upper half‑plane.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of p‑adic Eigenvarieties and Families of Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLₙ

Just as Coleman–Mazur eigencurves parametrize p‑adic families of classical modular forms, one can construct eigenvarieties for Drinfeld modular forms over function fields. Let K = 𝔽q(T) and fix a place ∞ of K. A Drinfeld modular form of weight k and level 𝔫 is a rigid analytic function on the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ωr satisfying a transformation law under a congruence subgroup of GLr(A), where A = 𝔽q[T]. The Hecke operators T𝔭 for primes 𝔭 ∤ 𝔫∞ act on the space of such forms. To build a p‑adic family, one fixes a finite place v of K (the “p” in p‑adic) and considers the action of the Hecke operator Uv (the analogue of the classical Up) on the space of overconvergent Drinfeld modular forms — rigid analytic functions on a strict neighbourhood of the ordinary locus in the Drinfeld modular curve. The ordinary locus is the set of points where the Drinfeld module has ordinary reduction at v; its structure is governed by the theory of canonical subgroups for Drinfeld modules, developed by Gekeler and others. The eigenvariety ℰ is a rigid analytic space equipped with a finite flat map to weight space 𝒲 (a rigid analytic space parametrizing continuous characters of the group of units of the completion of A at v) and a universal Hecke eigensystem. The construction follows the Buzzard–Kilford method: one takes the Fredholm series of Uv acting on the space of overconvergent forms, and the eigenvariety is the rigid analytic subspace of 𝒲 × 𝔸1 cut out by the characteristic power series. The points of ℰ correspond to finite‑slope eigenforms, and the classical eigenforms of weight k are exactly the points lying over the classical weight k ∈ 𝒲. The geometry of ℰ encodes deep arithmetic information: its irreducible components correspond to p‑adic families of automorphic representations, and the tangent space at a classical point is related to the Selmer group of the associated Galois representation. For GL2, the eigenvariety has been studied by Boeckle, Pink, and others; for higher rank GLn, the theory is less developed but the framework of overconvergent cohomology on the Bruhat–Tits building (work of Emerton, Hansen, and others adapted to function fields) provides a path. Examiners test the definition of the Uv operator: for a Drinfeld modular form f of level Γ0(𝔫v), (Uvf)(z) = ∑i f(γiz) where the γi are coset representatives for Γ0(𝔫v)\Γ0(𝔫)∩GL2(Kv). A frequent trap is to assume that the eigenvariety is always equidimensional; in fact, the dimension can jump at points corresponding to non‑classical weights or to forms with non‑trivial nebentypus, and the “halo” phenomenon (families passing through classical points of different weights) is a subtle feature that appears in the function field setting just as in the classical case.

Worked Example: Computing a Toric Period for a Rank‑Two Drinfeld Module
Let K = 𝔽3(T), and let φ be the rank‑two Drinfeld module over K defined by φT = T + τ + τ2. Let χ be the quadratic character associated to the extension K(√T)/K. Compute the toric period P(φ, χ) = ∫T(K)T(𝔸K) φ(t) χ(t) dt, where φ is the automorphic form on GL2(𝔸K) corresponding to φ via the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence, and T is the non‑split torus isomorphic to K(√T)×.
Step 1: Identify the automorphic form. The Drinfeld module φ corresponds to a cuspidal automorphic representation π of GL2(𝔸K) with conductor 𝔫 = (T). The newform φ ∈ π is spherical at all places v ∤ T∞. Step 2: Choose a factorizable test vector. At the infinite place ∞, take the spherical vector. At the finite place v = (T), take the newvector. At all other places, take the spherical vector. Step 3: The toric period factorizes as a product of local integrals Pv(φv, χv). For v ∤ T∞, the local integral is the local L‑factor L(1/2, πv ⊗ χv) by the unramified computation. For v = (T), the local integral is a normalized local period which can be computed explicitly using the Kirillov model; it equals ε(1/2, πT ⊗ χT) L(1/2, πT ⊗ χT) where ε is the local epsilon factor. For v = ∞, the local integral is a volume factor. Step 4: By the Waldspurger formula (proved for function fields by Yun and Zhang), the global period squared is proportional to the central L‑value: |P(φ, χ)|2 = C · L(1/2, π ⊗ χ) / L(1, π, Ad), where C is an explicit constant involving Tamagawa numbers and local epsilon factors. Step 5: The L‑function L(s, π ⊗ χ) is the Goss L‑function of the twisted Drinfeld module. Its central value can be computed via the functional equation and the known value at s = 1. The final answer is an explicit algebraic number in the coefficient field of φ, which in this case is 𝔽3.
Exam Strategy: Distinguishing Function Field and Classical Period Formulas
When a question asks for a period formula, first identify the field: function field (𝔽q(T)) or number field (ℚ). For function fields, the geometric input is the moduli of shtukas and the Bruhat–Tits building; for number fields, it is Shimura varieties and the upper half‑plane. The Waldspurger formula in function fields uses the Drinfeld modular curve and the tree; the classical version uses the modular curve and the upper half‑plane. The Ichino–Ikeda formula in function fields is proved for GL2 × GL1 and GL2 × GL2 via the relative trace formula on the moduli stack of shtukas; the classical version uses the relative trace formula on Shimura varieties. Always state the geometric object (shtuka space vs. Shimura variety) and the analytic object (Goss L‑function vs. classical L‑function).

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of Arthur's Endoscopic Classification for Classical Groups

Arthur’s endoscopic classification of the discrete automorphic spectrum for classical groups (symplectic, orthogonal, unitary) over number fields is a cornerstone of the Langlands program. Its function field analogue classifies the discrete spectrum of classical groups over a global function field K = 𝔽q(C) in terms of endoscopic data: pairs (H, s) where H is an endoscopic group (a quasi‑split reductive group whose dual group is the centralizer of a semisimple element s in the dual group of G) and s ∈ LG. The classification asserts that the discrete automorphic representations of G(𝔸K) are partitioned into packets Πψ indexed by global Arthur parameters ψ : LK × SL2(ℂ) → LG, where LK is the conjectural Langlands group of K (in the function field case, LK is replaced by the Weil group WK because the Langlands group is known to be WK × SL2(ℂ) by work of Lafforgue and others). Each packet Πψ is a finite set of irreducible representations of G(𝔸K) that are locally equivalent at almost all places, and the multiplicity of each representation in the discrete spectrum is given by a formula involving the component group Sψ = π0(ZLG(Im ψ)). The proof in the function field setting uses the geometric Langlands correspondence for the group G and its endoscopic groups, together with the trace formula for the moduli stack of G‑shtukas. The key input is the fundamental lemma for the Lie algebras of G and its endoscopic groups, proved by Ngô Bào Châu for all reductive groups over function fields (and later extended to number fields). The geometric side of the trace formula involves the cohomology of the moduli stack of G‑shtukas, which by the geometric Langlands correspondence carries an action of the dual group LG. The endoscopic transfer of orbital integrals corresponds to a morphism between the moduli stacks of G‑shtukas and H‑shtukas, which is constructed using the theory of “endoscopic shtukas” — shtukas with a reduction of structure group to the endoscopic group H. The classification has been completed for unitary groups (work of Lafforgue, Shin, and others) and for symplectic and odd orthogonal groups (work of Arthur adapted to function fields by Kaletha, Minguez, and others). For even orthogonal groups, the classification involves the additional complication of the non‑connectedness of the dual group. Examiners often ask for the definition of an Arthur parameter in the function field context: it is a homomorphism ψ : WK × SL2(ℂ) → LG that is Frobenius‑semisimple and satisfies certain boundedness conditions. A common trap is to confuse the Arthur parameter (which includes an SL2 factor encoding the unipotent part) with the Langlands parameter (which is a homomorphism WK → LG); the Arthur parameter refines the Langlands parameter by adding the SL2 data, and the packet Πψ contains representations whose Langlands parameters are obtained by restricting ψ to WK × {diag(t, t−1)}.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Local Langlands Correspondence for Reductive Groups over Function Fields via the Fargues–Scholze Geometrization

The Fargues–Scholze geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence, developed for p‑adic fields, has a function field analogue that replaces the Fargues–Fontaine curve with the “Fargues–Fontaine curve for function fields” — a scheme over 𝔽q whose points correspond to untilts of a perfectoid field of characteristic p. Let F be a local field of characteristic p (i.e., F = 𝔽q((t))). The Fargues–Scholze construction associates to a reductive group G over F a category of G‑bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve XF, and the local Langlands correspondence is realized as a correspondence between the category of smooth representations of G(F) and the category of L‑parameters (continuous homomorphisms WF → LG) via the cohomology of the moduli stack of G‑bundles on XF. In the function field setting, the curve XF is the “curve of untilts” of a perfectoid field; its geometry is simpler than in the p‑adic case because the untilt is unique up to Frobenius. The moduli stack BunG of G‑bundles on XF is a locally spatial diamond, and its étale cohomology with coefficients in ℓ‑adic sheaves carries an action of G(F) × LG. The local Langlands correspondence is then the statement that the derived category of smooth representations of G(F) is equivalent to the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the stack of L‑parameters, and this equivalence is induced by a Hecke eigensheaf on BunG. For GLn, this recovers the local Langlands correspondence of Lafforgue (for global fields) and of Harris–Taylor / Henniart (for p‑adic fields) adapted to function fields. For general reductive groups, the Fargues–Scholze approach provides a geometric construction of the correspondence that is independent of the global Langlands correspondence. The key technical tool is the “spectral action” of the category of representations of LG on the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on BunG, which is constructed using the geometry of the Hecke stack. The function field version of the Fargues–Scholze conjecture (now a theorem in many cases) has been worked out by Fargues, Scholze, and others, and it provides a uniform framework for the local Langlands correspondence for all reductive groups over local function fields. Examiners test the definition of the Fargues–Fontaine curve in characteristic p: it is the quotient of the perfectoid space Spa(F♭)[1/t] by the Frobenius action, where F♭ is the tilt of F. A frequent trap is to assume that the Fargues–Scholze correspondence for function fields is identical to the p‑adic case; the characteristic p setting simplifies the perfectoid geometry (no need for the “untilt” construction because the tilt is the field itself) but introduces new complications in the definition of the spectral action because the curve is not proper.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Gan–Gross–Prasad Conjecture for Special Orthogonal and Symplectic Groups

The Gan–Gross–Prasad (GGP) conjecture relates the non‑vanishing of a period integral of an automorphic form on a classical group to the non‑vanishing of a central L‑value. For function fields, the conjecture has been formulated and proved in many cases by works of Yun, Zhang, and others using the relative trace formula on the moduli stack of shtukas. Let G = SO2n+1 or Sp2n over a global function field K, and let H = SO2n or Sp2n−2 be the subgroup stabilizing a non‑isotropic vector. For a cuspidal automorphic representation π of G(𝔸K) and a cuspidal automorphic representation σ of H(𝔸K), the GGP period is the integral P(φ, ψ) = ∫H(K)H(𝔸K) φ(h) ψ(h) dh. The conjecture asserts that P(φ, ψ) ≠ 0 for some choice of φ ∈ π, ψ ∈ σ if and only if the central L‑value L(1/2, π × σ) ≠ 0 and the local Hom spaces HomH(Kv)(πv, σv) are non‑zero for all places v. In the function field setting, the global Langlands correspondence of Lafforgue identifies π and σ with ℓ‑adic local systems on the curve C, and the period integral becomes a trace of Frobenius on a certain sheaf on the moduli space of (G, H)‑shtukas — shtukas with a reduction of structure group to H. The local Hom spaces are computed using the geometry of the affine Grassmannian for G and H. The proof for SO2n+1 × SO2n and Sp2n × Sp2n−2 uses the relative trace formula for the spherical variety G/H, which is a symmetric space. The geometric side of the trace formula involves the cohomology of the moduli stack of (G, H)‑shtukas, and the spectral side involves the sum over automorphic representations of the period integrals. The fundamental lemma for the spherical variety (proved by Ngô and others) allows the comparison of the geometric side with the spectral side. The function field GGP conjecture for unitary groups was proved earlier (by Yun and Zhang) and is included in the existing lesson; the extension to special orthogonal and symplectic groups requires the additional input of the endoscopic classification for these groups (the previous section) to handle the non‑generic representations that appear in the discrete spectrum. Examiners often ask for the precise statement of the local GGP conjecture: for a local field F of characteristic p, and for tempered representations π of G(F) and σ of H(F), the dimension of HomH(F)(π, σ) is at most 1, and it is 1 if and only if the local root number ε(1/2, π × σ) = 1. A common trap is to confuse the GGP period (which integrates over a subgroup H) with the Waldspurger period (which integrates over a torus); the GGP period involves a larger subgroup and the L‑function is a Rankin–Selberg product, while the Waldspurger period involves a torus and the L‑function is a twist by a character.

  • Trap 1: Confusing the function field Ichino–Ikeda formula (which involves periods on spherical varieties and central L‑values of Rankin–Selberg L‑functions) with the classical Ichino–Ikeda formula (which involves periods on unitary groups and central L‑values of standard L‑functions). The geometric input is shtukas vs. Shimura varieties.
  • Trap 2: Assuming the p‑adic eigenvariety for Drinfeld modular forms is always equidimensional; dimension jumps occur at non‑classical weights and at points with non‑trivial nebentypus, and the “halo” phenomenon must be accounted for.
  • Trap 3: Conflating the Arthur parameter (WK × SL2(ℂ) → LG) with the Langlands parameter (WK → LG); the Arthur parameter refines the Langlands parameter by adding unipotent data via the SL2 factor.
  • Trap 4: Treating the Fargues–Fontaine curve in characteristic p as identical to the p‑adic case; in characteristic p the tilt is the field itself, simplifying perfectoid geometry but complicating the spectral action because the curve is not proper.
  • Trap 5: Mixing up the GGP period (integration over a classical subgroup H ⊂ G, L‑function is Rankin–Selberg) with the Waldspurger period (integration over a torus, L‑function is a twist); the subgroups, L‑functions, and geometric moduli spaces are different.
  • Trap 6: Claiming the function field endoscopic classification is complete for all classical groups; even orthogonal groups require extra care due to the non‑connectedness of the dual group, and the full classification for all inner forms is still being written up.
  • Trap 7: Stating that the local Langlands correspondence for function fields via Fargues–Scholze is proved for all reductive groups; it is established for GLn and many classical groups, but the full generality (including non‑quasi‑split groups and the compatibility with the global correspondence) remains an active area of research.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn

The Drinfeld modular forms for GLn over a global function field admit a Fourier expansion along the unipotent radical of the standard Borel subgroup. The coefficients of this expansion are indexed by effective divisors on the underlying curve and satisfy Hecke multiplicativity relations that mirror the classical case. The Hecke algebra generated by the spherical double cosets at unramified places acts semisimply on the space of cusp forms, and the eigenvalues of the Hecke operators correspond under the global Langlands correspondence of Lafforgue to the Frobenius traces of an ℓ‑adic local system of rank n on the curve. The Eisenstein series constructed from cuspidal data on Levi subgroups provide the continuous spectrum; their constant terms are expressed as products of local intertwining operators, and the functional equation follows from the meromorphic continuation of the associated Rankin–Selberg L‑functions. The cohomology of the Drinfeld modular varieties, computed via the Lefschetz trace formula for shtukas, yields a geometric realization of the automorphic spectrum and furnishes the compatibility of the local and global correspondences.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn

The Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for Drinfeld modular curves identifies the first ℓ‑adic cohomology group of the compactified modular curve with the direct sum of the space of cusp forms of weight two and its dual, twisted by the Tate module of the Jacobian. This isomorphism is equivariant for the action of the Hecke algebra and the Galois group of the function field. The Jacobian of the modular curve decomposes up to isogeny into abelian varieties attached to newforms, and the endomorphism algebra of each factor contains the Hecke field generated by the eigenvalues. The period lattice of the Drinfeld module associated to a newform is recovered from the de Rham cohomology of the corresponding t‑motive, and the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem relates special values of Goss L‑functions to logarithms of algebraic points on the Jacobian. These structures provide the function field analogue of the classical modularity theorem and underpin the proof of the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture for rank‑two Drinfeld modules in many cases.

Worked Example
Let C be a smooth projective curve over 𝔽q and let π be a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL2(𝔸K) corresponding to a rank‑two Drinfeld module φ over K. Show that the central L‑value L(1/2, π) is non‑zero if and only if the Mordell–Weil rank of the associated Drinfeld modular Jacobian J0(N) is zero.
By the function field Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer theorem for Drinfeld modules (proved by Gekeler, Reversat, and others), the order of vanishing of L(s, π) at s = 1/2 equals the rank of the Mordell–Weil group of the abelian variety Aπ attached to π inside J0(N). The central value L(1/2, π) is therefore non‑zero precisely when the rank is zero. The proof uses the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism to identify the π‑isotypic component of H1(J0(N), ℚℓ) with the Galois representation attached to π, and the Tate conjecture for Drinfeld modules (known in this setting) to relate the L‑function to the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius on the Tate module. The non‑vanishing of the central value forces the Frobenius eigenvalues to avoid 1, which implies the Tate module has no invariant vectors, i.e. the Mordell–Weil group is finite.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the relationship between a central L‑value and a Mordell–Weil rank in the function field setting, recall the exact statement of the Drinfeld‑module BSD theorem: the order of vanishing equals the rank, and the leading coefficient is expressed via the regulator, Tamagawa numbers, and the order of the Tate–Shafarevich group. Do not confuse this with the classical BSD conjecture over number fields, where the formula is still conjectural. Cite the theorem by name (Gekeler–Reversat) and note that the proof uses the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism and the Tate conjecture for Drinfeld modules, both of which are theorems in characteristic p.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn

The theory of p‑adic families of Drinfeld modular forms is built on the eigenvariety constructed by Buzzard–Kilford techniques adapted to the rigid analytic Drinfeld upper half‑plane. The weight space is the rigid analytic space parametrizing continuous characters of the group of units of the endomorphism ring of the Carlitz module. Classical points correspond to Drinfeld modular forms of integral weight, and the eigenvariety is equidimensional of dimension one at classical points of non‑critical slope. At critical slope points the dimension may jump, producing the so‑called halo phenomenon; this is controlled by the geometry of the associated (φ, Γ)‑modules over the Robba ring. The spectral halo reflects the failure of the classicality theorem for overconvergent forms of critical slope, and its study requires the theory of trianguline (φ, Γ)‑modules developed by Colmez and Kedlaya in the function field context. The eigenvariety carries a natural Hecke action, and its irreducible components correspond to p‑adic families of automorphic representations of GLn over the function field.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GLn

The geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn over a curve C over 𝔽q is realized via the moduli stack of n‑shtukas with one leg. The Hecke eigensheaf property for a perverse sheaf on Bunn is equivalent to the condition that its Frobenius trace function on the set of ℱq‑points of the moduli stack of shtukas satisfies the Hecke eigenvalue equations. Lafforgue’s proof of the global Langlands correspondence for GLn constructs the required Hecke eigensheaves as the intermediate extension of the ℓ‑adic local system attached to a cuspidal automorphic representation, using the cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas with level structure. The categorical formulation, due to Gaitsgory and Lurie, replaces perverse sheaves by D‑modules on the de Rham stack and identifies the category of Hecke eigensheaves with the category of ind‑coherent sheaves on the stack of local systems. The function field analogue of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula is obtained by applying the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula to the correspondence on the moduli stack of shtukas defined by Hecke modifications, and the spectral side decomposes according to the automorphic spectrum.

  • Trap 1: Assuming the eigenvariety for Drinfeld modular forms is always smooth; dimension jumps at critical slope create singularities that must be accounted for in deformation problems.
  • Trap 2: Confusing the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for Drinfeld modular curves (which involves the Jacobian of the modular curve) with the classical Eichler–Shimura isomorphism (which involves the cohomology of modular curves over ℂ). The function field version is a theorem, not a conjecture.
  • Trap 3: Stating that the central L‑value L(1/2, π) vanishes exactly when the Mordell–Weil rank is positive; the correct equivalence is non‑vanishing ⇔ rank zero, but the order of vanishing equals the rank, not merely positivity.
  • Trap 4: Treating the geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn as a direct translation of the classical geometric Langlands over ℂ; the function field version uses ℓ‑adic sheaves and Frobenius trace functions, while the classical version uses D‑modules and the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence.
  • Trap 5: Claiming that the Arthur–Selberg trace formula for GLn over function fields is proved for all test functions; the formula is established for spherical Hecke functions, but the full generality with arbitrary compactly supported functions requires the fundamental lemma for all endoscopic groups, which is known only in special cases.
  • Trap 6: Mixing up the halo phenomenon in p‑adic families of Drinfeld modular forms with the classical halo in Coleman families; the function field halo is governed by (φ, Γ)‑modules over the Robba ring in characteristic p, which have a simpler tilt but a non‑proper Fargues–Fontaine curve.
  • Trap 7: Asserting that the categorical Langlands correspondence for function fields is fully proved for all reductive groups; it is established for GLn and some classical groups, but the general case remains open.

These advanced topics illustrate the depth of the Drinfeld module theory and its central role in the function field Langlands program.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GL n and the Theory of the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group GL n

The function field Langlands program for GL n over a global function field F = 𝔽 q (C) attaches to each cuspidal automorphic representation π of GL n (𝔸 F ) an n‑dimensional ℓ‑adic Galois representation ρ π : Gal(F̄ /F) → GL n (ℚ̄ ℓ ). The construction proceeds via the cohomology of the moduli stack Sht n of n‑shtukas with one leg, following Lafforgue’s proof. The Hecke eigensheaf property is encoded in the Frobenius trace function on the ℱ q ‑points of Sht n . For each place v of F, the local component π v corresponds under the local Langlands correspondence to a Weil–Deligne representation of the Weil group W F v . The global compatibility is expressed by the equality of L‑functions L(s, π) = L(s, ρ π ). The proof uses the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula on Sht n with level structure, together with the fundamental lemma for the spherical Hecke algebra. The resulting Galois representation is pure of weight zero and satisfies the expected local‑global compatibility at all places, including the ramified ones. The method also yields the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for GL n over function fields, since the eigenvalues of Frobenius on the ℓ‑adic cohomology have absolute value q (w/2) for the appropriate weight w.

The spectral side of the trace formula is realized by the cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas with multiple legs, and the spectral decomposition follows from the decomposition of the Hecke algebra action. The geometric Langlands correspondence for GL n thus provides a geometric incarnation of the automorphic‑to‑Galois direction of the classical Langlands program.

Worked Example: Hecke Eigensheaf Condition
Let F be a Hecke eigensheaf on Bun n corresponding to a local system E. Show that the Frobenius trace function f F on the ℱ q ‑points of the moduli stack Sht n satisfies the Hecke eigenvalue equation T v f F = λ v f F for each place v, where λ v is the trace of Frobenius on the stalk of E at v.
The Hecke correspondence at v gives a diagram Sht n ← H v → Sht n . The Hecke operator T v acts on functions by pull‑push along this correspondence. By the definition of a Hecke eigensheaf, the pullback of F to H v is isomorphic to the pushforward of F twisted by the stalk E v . Taking Frobenius trace functions, the pull‑push formula yields T v f F = Tr(Frob v , E v ) f F = λ v f F . This equality holds pointwise on the ℱ q ‑points of Sht n , establishing the eigenvalue equation.

The Fundamental Lemma for Function Fields and Its Role in the Trace Formula

The fundamental lemma is a combinatorial identity between orbital integrals on a reductive group and its endoscopic groups. Over function fields, it was proved in full generality by Ngô Bao Châu in 2008, building on the geometric interpretation of the lemma as a statement about the cohomology of the Hitchin fibration. Ngô's proof uses the decomposition theorem for perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base and the purity of the intersection cohomology of the affine Springer fibers. The result applies to all reductive groups over a global function field F = Fq(C) and is a crucial input for the stabilization of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula in the function field setting.

In the trace formula, the geometric side is expressed as a sum over conjugacy classes of orbital integrals. To isolate the contribution of automorphic representations that transfer to a given endoscopic group, one must match orbital integrals on the group with stable orbital integrals on its endoscopic groups. The fundamental lemma provides precisely this matching for the unit elements of the spherical Hecke algebras at almost all places. With the lemma established, the stabilized trace formula yields a decomposition of the discrete automorphic spectrum into packets associated to endoscopic data, enabling the proof of functoriality for classical groups over function fields.

The function field case is technically simpler than the number field case because the Hitchin fibration is a proper map over a finite field, allowing the use of ℓ‑adic cohomology and the Weil conjectures. Ngô's work also introduced the notion of the "Hitchin fibration for the Lie algebra" and proved the "support theorem" which controls the support of the perverse sheaves appearing in the decomposition. These geometric insights have since been adapted to the number field setting via the work of Waldspurger and others, but the function field proof remains the geometric heart of the argument.

For exam purposes, it is essential to distinguish the fundamental lemma (a local statement about orbital integrals) from the global stabilization of the trace formula. The lemma is a local identity at each unramified place; the global argument assembles these local identities using the product formula for the trace formula. A common mistake is to claim that the fundamental lemma alone proves the Langlands correspondence; it is a necessary but not sufficient ingredient.

The Hitchin Fibration and the Geometric Langlands Correspondence for GLn over Function Fields

The Hitchin fibration is a completely integrable system on the moduli space of Higgs bundles over a smooth projective curve X over a finite field Fq. For GLn, the moduli space MHiggs parametrizes pairs (E, φ) where E is a rank‑n vector bundle and φ ∈ H⁰(X, End(E) ⊗ ΩX). The Hitchin map h : MHiggs → A sends (E, φ) to the characteristic polynomial coefficients of φ, which lie in an affine space A = ⊕i=1n H⁰(X, ΩX⊗i). The generic fiber is an abelian variety — the Prym variety of the spectral curve — and the singular fibers encode the geometry of the nilpotent cone.

In the function field setting, the Hitchin fibration plays a dual role. First, it provides the geometric framework for Ngô's proof of the fundamental lemma: the orbital integrals are expressed as traces of Frobenius on the cohomology of the Hitchin fibers, and the fundamental lemma follows from a comparison of the perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base for the group and its endoscopic groups. Second, the Hitchin fibration is the natural home for the geometric Langlands correspondence over Fq. The correspondence predicts an equivalence between the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on the moduli stack of G‑bundles and the derived category of coherent sheaves on the moduli stack of LG‑local systems. For GLn, the Hitchin fibration intertwines the two sides via the Fourier–Mukai transform on the abelian fibers, a construction due to Laumon and Rothstein.

The function field geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn was proved by Lafforgue using the moduli of shtukas, not directly via the Hitchin fibration. However, the Hitchin fibration provides a complementary perspective: the Hecke eigensheaves constructed by Lafforgue can be realized as the pushforward of certain perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base. Recent work by Yun and others has shown that the categorical geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn over function fields can be approached by studying the singular support of Hecke eigensheaves, which is contained in the global nilpotent cone — the zero fiber of the Hitchin map. This links the automorphic side (shtukas) to the spectral side (local systems) through the geometry of the Hitchin fibration.

Key points for examination: the Hitchin base A is an affine space of dimension n²(g−1)+1; the generic fiber is a torsor for the Prym variety; the fundamental lemma is proved by comparing the decomposition theorem for the Hitchin map for G and its endoscopic group H; the geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn over function fields is a theorem (Lafforgue), while the categorical version remains a conjecture in higher genus.

Applying the Fundamental Lemma to Stabilize the Trace Formula
Explain how the fundamental lemma for function fields enters the stabilization of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula for GLn.
The Arthur–Selberg trace formula expresses the trace of a test function on the automorphic spectrum as a sum of geometric terms (orbital integrals). To separate the contribution of representations that are functorial lifts from an endoscopic group H, one must rewrite the geometric side in terms of stable orbital integrals on H. The fundamental lemma provides the matching of orbital integrals for the unit element of the spherical Hecke algebra at almost all unramified places. With this matching, the global trace formula can be stabilized: the sum over conjugacy classes in G is reorganized into a sum over stable conjugacy classes in H, weighted by transfer factors. The stabilized formula then yields a decomposition of the discrete spectrum into L-packets attached to endoscopic data, which is the key step in proving functoriality for classical groups over function fields.
