When a question asks for the local L‑factor of an unramified representation, write down the Satake parameters immediately and apply the determinant formula for the relevant representation of the dual group. Do not re‑derive the Satake isomorphism unless explicitly required.

The Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group F4 via Shtukas

The exceptional group F4 is a simply‑connected simple algebraic group of rank 4 with trivial center. Its Langlands dual group is again F4(ℂ). Vincent Lafforgue’s global correspondence applies to F4 because the theorem holds for every reductive group. The moduli stack of F4‑shtukas is constructed by considering F4‑torsors on a smooth projective curve X over 𝔽_q together with Frobenius‑equivariant modifications at a finite set of points. The geometric Satake equivalence for F4 identifies the category of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian GrF4 with the representation category of F4(ℂ). The fundamental representations of F4(ℂ) have dimensions 26, 52, 273, and 324; the corresponding Hecke operators generate the spherical Hecke algebra.

An automorphic representation π of F4(𝔸_F) that occurs in the cohomology of the F4‑shtuka moduli gives rise to a continuous Galois representation ρ_π : Gal(F^sep/F) → F4(ℚ_ℓ). The excursion operators attached to the four fundamental representations cut out the π‑isotypic component and their eigenvalues are the traces of ρ_π(Frob_v) in those representations. Because F4 has no non‑trivial central characters, the global L‑parameter is determined entirely by these traces. The compatibility with the unramified local Langlands correspondence follows from the Satake isomorphism for F4, which identifies the spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of F4(ℂ).

Explicit computation of automorphic forms on F4 is considerably harder than for classical groups. There is no known analogue of the Drinfeld upper half‑plane for F4, so the analytic theory of automorphic forms relies entirely on the cohomology of the shtuka moduli. Recent work of Zhu and others on the geometric Satake for exceptional groups provides the necessary perverse sheaves, but the description of the cuspidal spectrum and the analytic properties of the associated L‑functions remain active research areas.

The Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group E6 via Shtukas

The group E6 exists in two isogenous forms: the simply‑connected form E6sc with center μ3, and the adjoint form E6ad with trivial center. Their Langlands dual groups are E6ad(ℂ) and E6sc(ℂ) respectively. Lafforgue’s theorem covers both forms because it is stated for arbitrary reductive groups. The moduli of E6‑shtukas are built from E6‑torsors with Frobenius modifications. The geometric Satake equivalence for E6 identifies perverse sheaves on GrE6 with representations of the dual group. The fundamental representations of E6(ℂ) have dimensions 27, 78, 351, 2925, and 3003; the 27‑dimensional representation is minuscule and plays a role analogous to the standard representation for GL_n.

For an automorphic representation π of E6(𝔸_F) appearing in the cohomology, the associated Galois representation ρ_π lands in the dual group E6ad(ℚ_ℓ) or E6sc(ℚ_ℓ) depending on the central character of π. The excursion operators attached to the fundamental representations produce the traces of ρ_π(Frob_v) in those representations. Because the center of E6sc is μ3, the central character of π determines a cubic character of the Galois group, which appears as the determinant of ρ_π in the 27‑dimensional representation. This interplay between the center and the Galois side is a distinctive feature of the E6 correspondence.

As with F4, there is no known Drinfeld‑type symmetric domain for E6, so the entire analytic theory is encoded in the geometry of the shtuka moduli. The work of Lafforgue guarantees the existence of the global L‑parameter, but explicit construction of cuspidal automorphic forms, computation of their Hecke eigenvalues, and verification of functorial lifts to classical groups are still largely open. The function field setting provides a unique laboratory where these questions can be approached via the geometry of moduli stacks and the categorical Langlands program.

  • Confusing the role of excursion operators with ordinary Hecke operators; excursion operators are specific linear combinations that isolate the L‑parameter, while Hecke operators generate the full spherical Hecke algebra.
  • Assuming the unramified local Langlands correspondence for GL_n implies the full local correspondence for all reductive groups; the ramified case for exceptional groups is not known.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the simply‑connected and adjoint forms of E6; the center μ3 affects the Galois representation and the central character of automorphic forms.
  • Thinking that the Drinfeld upper half‑plane uniformizes shtuka moduli for groups beyond GL_n; it exists only for GL_n and its inner forms.
  • Neglecting that the geometric Satake equivalence for exceptional groups requires the full machinery of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian, not just the classical Satake isomorphism.
  • Treating the global L‑parameter as a homomorphism into the dual group over ℂ instead of ℚ_ℓ; Lafforgue’s construction yields ℓ‑adic representations.
  • Believing that the existence of the global correspondence for F4 and E6 automatically gives explicit formulas for their automorphic L‑functions; analytic properties such as meromorphic continuation are known, but explicit Euler product expansions beyond the unramified places are not generally available.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group E7 via Shtukas

The global Langlands correspondence for split exceptional groups over function fields is a direct consequence of the geometric Langlands program developed by Vincent Lafforgue. For the simply‑connected group of type E7, the Langlands dual is the adjoint group E7ad(ℂ). Lafforgue’s theorem constructs, for every automorphic representation π of E7(𝔸F) occurring in the cohomology of the moduli stack of E7‑shtukas, a continuous ℓ‑adic Galois representation ρπ : Gal(Fsep/F) → E7ad(ℚℓ). The construction uses excursion operators attached to the fundamental representations of the dual group; the dimensions of these representations are 56, 133, 912, 8645, 365750, and 27664. The 56‑dimensional representation is minuscule and plays a role analogous to the standard representation for GLn. Because the center of the simply‑connected E7 is trivial, the central character of π does not impose an extra determinant condition on ρπ. The compatibility with the unramified local Langlands correspondence follows from the geometric Satake equivalence for E7, which identifies the spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of E7ad(ℂ). Explicit computation of automorphic forms on E7 remains out of reach because there is no Drinfeld‑type symmetric domain for this group; the entire analytic theory is encoded in the geometry of the shtuka moduli. Recent advances in the categorical Langlands program provide perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian GrE7, but the description of the cuspidal spectrum and the analytic properties of the associated L‑functions are still active research areas.

A key technical point is the construction of the moduli stack of E7‑shtukas. An E7‑shtuka over a scheme S is an E7‑torsor ℰ on the curve X × S together with an isomorphism between the Frobenius pullback of ℰ and ℰ away from a finite set of points (the legs). The legs are equipped with reductions to a Borel subgroup, and the modifications at the legs are governed by dominant coweights of E7. The cohomology of this stack carries an action of the spherical Hecke algebra via Hecke correspondences, and the excursion operators are defined as certain linear combinations of Hecke operators that isolate the L‑parameter. The proof that these operators satisfy the required commutation relations uses the geometric Satake equivalence and the theory of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian. The resulting Galois representation is characterized by the property that for every unramified place v, the characteristic polynomial of ρπ(Frobv) in each fundamental representation matches the eigenvalue of the corresponding excursion operator.

One of the main open problems is the extension of this correspondence to ramified places. For GLn the local Langlands correspondence is known in full generality, but for exceptional groups the ramified case is largely unexplored. The function field setting offers a unique laboratory because the geometry of the affine flag variety for E7 can be studied using the theory of shtukas with parahoric level structure. Recent work of Zhu and others on the geometric Satake for exceptional groups with parahoric level provides a framework, but a complete classification of irreducible smooth representations of E7(Fv) in terms of Langlands parameters is still missing. Another direction is the study of functorial lifts from E7 to classical groups, which would allow the transfer of automorphic forms and the comparison of L‑functions. The trace formula for E7, which would be the function field analogue of Arthur’s endoscopic classification, has not yet been developed.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Local Langlands Correspondence for the Group G2 via the Bruhat–Tits Building

The split exceptional group G2 over a local function field Fv has a Bruhat–Tits building that is a two‑dimensional simplicial complex. The local Langlands correspondence for G2(Fv) has been established by combining the geometric Langlands program with the theory of types and covers developed by Bushnell–Kutzko and extended to exceptional groups by Gan–Gross–Prasad. The correspondence assigns to each irreducible smooth representation π of G2(Fv) a Langlands parameter φπ : WFv × SL2(ℂ) → G2(ℂ), where WFv is the Weil group. The parameter is uniquely determined by the character of π on the spherical Hecke algebra and by the restriction of π to a maximal compact subgroup, which can be described using the Moy–Prasad filtration on the Bruhat–Tits building. The building for G2 has vertices corresponding to parahoric subgroups of types G2, A2, and A1 × A1. The depth‑zero representations are parametrized by Deligne–Lusztig representations of the finite reductive quotients, while positive‑depth representations are constructed via compact induction from characters of Moy–Prasad subgroups.

The function field analogue of the local Langlands correspondence for G2 is compatible with the global correspondence via the theory of shtukas with parahoric level structure. A G2‑shtuka with parahoric level at a place v is a G2‑torsor on the curve together with a Frobenius isomorphism and a reduction to a chosen parahoric subgroup at v. The moduli stack of such shtukas carries an action of the local Hecke algebra at v, and the cohomology realizes the local Langlands correspondence. The geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian of G2 identifies the spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of G2(ℂ). For ramified representations, one uses the affine flag variety and the theory of perverse sheaves on it. The work of Zhu on the geometric Satake for parahoric groups provides the necessary categorical framework. The resulting local parameters satisfy the expected properties: they preserve L‑functions, ε‑factors, and the local Langlands correspondence for the Levi subgroups of G2.

An important application is the explicit construction of supercuspidal representations of G2(Fv) via the theory of types. A type for a supercuspidal representation is a pair (J, λ) where J is a compact open subgroup and λ is an irreducible representation of J such that compact induction of λ yields the supercuspidal. For G2, the types are built from characters of Moy–Prasad subgroups attached to points in the building. The Langlands parameter of such a representation can be read off from the character λ and the embedding of the corresponding torus into G2. This explicit description allows one to verify the local Langlands correspondence in many cases and to compute local L‑functions and ε‑factors. The function field setting simplifies some aspects because the residue field is finite, but the combinatorics of the building and the structure of the Weyl group of G2 (of order 12) still make the classification intricate.

Examiner's technique: identifying the minuscule representation
In the global Langlands correspondence for E7 over a function field, the excursion operator attached to the 56‑dimensional fundamental representation isolates the L‑parameter. Explain why the 56‑dimensional representation is called minuscule and how this property is used to define the excursion operator.
A representation of a reductive group is minuscule if its weights form a single orbit under the Weyl group. For E7, the 56‑dimensional representation is minuscule because its highest weight is a fundamental weight that is minuscule in the sense of Bourbaki. This implies that the corresponding coweight is also minuscule, so the associated Schubert variety in the affine Grassmannian is smooth and its intersection cohomology sheaf is the constant sheaf shifted by the dimension. The geometric Satake equivalence then identifies the spherical Hecke operator attached to this coweight with the action of the representation on the cohomology. The excursion operator is defined as the trace of this Hecke operator composed with the Frobenius correspondence on the shtuka moduli. Because the representation is minuscule, the Hecke operator is a simple correspondence (not a combination), and its trace directly gives the eigenvalue of ρπ(Frobv) in the 56‑dimensional representation. This eigenvalue determines the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius in that representation, which is a key piece of the global L‑parameter.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks about the role of a specific fundamental representation in the Langlands correspondence for an exceptional group, first recall whether that representation is minuscule. Minuscule representations give rise to simple Hecke operators and excursion operators that are easier to describe. For E7, the 56‑dimensional representation is the only minuscule one; for E6 the 27‑dimensional is minuscule; for G2 the 7‑dimensional is minuscule. Knowing this list allows you to quickly identify which excursion operator corresponds to a simple Hecke correspondence and which require linear combinations.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group Spin(8) and Triality

The split group Spin(8) over a global function field F exhibits the phenomenon of triality: its outer automorphism group is the symmetric group S3, permuting the three eight‑dimensional fundamental representations (the vector representation and the two half‑spin representations). The Langlands dual of Spin(8) is the adjoint group SO(8)(ℂ), which also has triality. The global Langlands correspondence for Spin(8) has been established by Lafforgue’s method using excursion operators attached to the three eight‑dimensional representations. Because these representations are permuted by triality, the corresponding excursion operators satisfy the same permutation relations. This symmetry is reflected in the Galois side: the associated Galois representation ρπ : Gal(Fsep/F) → SO(8)(ℚℓ) has the property that its composition with the three eight‑dimensional representations of SO(8)(ℂ) are permuted by the action of the outer automorphisms of the L‑group. The central character of an automorphic representation π of Spin(8)(𝔸F) is a character of the center μ2 × μ2, and it determines which of the two isogenous forms (Spin(8) or SO(8)) the Galois representation lands in.

The moduli stack of Spin(8)‑shtukas is built from Spin(8)‑torsors with Frobenius modifications. The geometric Satake equivalence for Spin(8) identifies perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian with representations of SO(8)(ℂ). The three minuscule coweights corresponding to the eight‑dimensional representations give rise to three families of Hecke operators. The excursion operators are defined as the traces of these Hecke operators on the cohomology of the shtuka moduli. Because the three representations are minuscule, each Hecke operator is a simple correspondence, and the excursion operators are directly the eigenvalues of Frobenius in the three representations. The triality symmetry implies that the three families of excursion operators are permuted by the outer automorphisms of the moduli stack induced by the triality automorphisms of Spin(8). This provides a geometric realization of triality on the automorphic side.

An important application is the study of functorial lifts from Spin(8) to GL8 via the three eight‑dimensional representations. The global Langlands correspondence for Spin(8) predicts that for each automorphic representation π of Spin(8), there are three automorphic representations of GL8 obtained by composing ρπ with the three eight‑dimensional representations of SO(8)(ℂ). These lifts are expected to be cuspidal or residual depending on the image of ρπ. The function field setting allows one to construct these lifts explicitly using the trace formula for Spin(8) and the comparison of Hecke eigenvalues. The work of Lafforgue and others on the trace formula for classical groups over function fields provides the necessary analytic tools. The triality symmetry also predicts relations among the L‑functions of the three lifts, which can be verified using the properties of excursion operators.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: Automorphic Distributions on the Bruhat–Tits Building for GLn

The theory of automorphic distributions on the Bruhat–Tits building provides a local counterpart to the global theory of Drinfeld modular forms. For GLn over a local function field Fv, the Bruhat–Tits building is a simplicial complex of dimension n−1 whose vertices correspond to homothety classes of lattices in Fvn. An automorphic distribution is a linear functional on the space of locally constant compactly supported functions on GLn(Fv) that is invariant under the action of a compact open subgroup and satisfies certain transformation properties under the center. Schneider and Teitelbaum developed the theory of harmonic cocycles on the building, which are alternating sums of values of a function on the vertices of an apartment. These cocycles correspond to automorphic distributions and provide a concrete realization of the local Langlands correspondence for GLn(Fv) in terms of the cohomology of the building.

The Schneider–Teitelbaum transform establishes an isomorphism between the space of harmonic cocycles of a given weight and the space of locally analytic vectors in the corresponding smooth representation of GLn(Fv). This transform is the function field analogue of the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GLn(ℚp). In the function field case, the target category is the category of smooth representations over ℚℓ (or ℂ), and the transform is easier to describe because the building is a tree for n=2 and a higher‑dimensional complex for n>2. The harmonic cocycles are computed using the action of Hecke operators on the building, and the eigenvalues of these operators give the local L‑parameters. The theory has been extended to inner forms of GLn, such as division algebras, where the building is replaced by the Bruhat–Tits building of the inner form.

A key application is the explicit construction of the local Langlands correspondence for supercuspidal representations of GLn(Fv) via the theory of types. A type for a supercuspidal representation is a pair (J, λ) where J is a compact open subgroup (a maximal compact subgroup of a Levi subgroup) and λ is an irreducible representation of J. The compact induction of λ yields the supercuspidal representation. The corresponding harmonic cocycle is supported on the fixed point set of J in the building, and its values are given by the character of λ. The Schneider–Teitelbaum transform then recovers the representation from the cocycle. This explicit description allows one to compute local L‑functions, ε‑factors, and the local Langlands correspondence in concrete terms. The function field setting simplifies the analysis because the residue field is finite, but the combinatorics of the building and the structure of the types remain rich.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Function Field Analogue of the Arthur–Selberg Trace Formula for Classical Groups

The Arthur–Selberg trace formula is a fundamental tool for studying the automorphic spectrum of reductive groups over number fields. Over function fields, an analogous trace formula has been developed by Lafforgue and others for GLn, and extended to classical groups (symplectic, orthogonal, unitary) by the work of Yun, Zhang, and others. The trace formula expresses the trace of a Hecke operator on the space of automorphic forms as a sum of geometric terms (orbital integrals) and spectral terms (contributions from automorphic representations). In the function field setting, the geometric side is computed using the cohomology of moduli stacks of shtukas with level structure, while the spectral side involves the decomposition of the cohomology into irreducible representations of the Hecke algebra. The trace formula for classical groups requires a careful treatment of the endoscopic groups, which are products of smaller classical groups and general linear groups. The stabilization of the trace formula, which separates the contributions of different endoscopic groups, is achieved using the theory of twisted endoscopy and the fundamental lemma for function fields, proved by Ngô Bảo Châu.

The function field trace formula for classical groups has several important applications. First, it provides a proof of the global Langlands correspondence for these groups by comparing the trace formula for a classical group with that of its endoscopic groups. The comparison yields a transfer of automorphic representations, which is the function field analogue of Langlands functoriality. Second, it allows the computation of the multiplicities of automorphic representations in the cohomology of shtuka moduli, which is essential for the construction of Galois representations via excursion operators. Third, it gives a geometric interpretation of the local Langlands correspondence for classical groups via the local trace formula, which relates orbital integrals on the group to stable orbital integrals on its endoscopic groups. The local trace formula for function fields has been developed by Waldspurger and others, and it plays a crucial role in the proof of the fundamental lemma.

An outstanding problem is the extension of the trace formula to non‑quasi‑split classical groups and to groups with non‑trivial center. The quasi‑split case is well understood, but the non‑quasi‑split case requires the theory of twisted endoscopy and the stabilization of the trace formula for non‑connected groups. Another direction is the development of a relative trace formula for classical groups, which would allow the study of periods of automorphic forms and the function field analogue of the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjectures. The relative trace formula for function fields has been initiated by Yun and Zhang for unitary groups, and it is expected to generalize to other classical groups. The function field setting provides a unique advantage: the moduli stacks of shtukas are algebraic stacks over finite fields, so the trace formula can be proved using the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula and the theory of ℓ‑adic sheaves, avoiding the analytic difficulties of the number field case.

  • Confusing the minuscule representations for different exceptional groups; only the 56‑dimensional for E7, 27‑dimensional for E6, and 7‑dimensional for G2 are minuscule.
  • Assuming the local Langlands correspondence for GLn implies the full correspondence for all classical groups; the ramified case for classical groups requires separate treatment.
  • Overlooking the role of the center in the global correspondence for Spin(8); the center μ2 × μ2 determines whether the Galois representation lands in Spin(8) or SO(8).
  • Thinking that the Bruhat–Tits building for GLn is a tree for all n; it is a tree only for n=2, and a higher‑dimensional complex for n>2.
  • Believing that the Arthur–Selberg trace formula for classical groups over function fields is identical to the number field version; the geometric proof uses ℓ‑adic cohomology of shtuka moduli, not harmonic analysis on adelic groups.
  • Neglecting that the fundamental lemma for function fields was proved by Ngô Bảo Châu using the Hitchin fibration, not by direct computation of orbital integrals.
  • The function field Langlands program for exceptional groups relies entirely on the geometry of shtuka moduli because no Drinfeld upper half‑plane exists for these groups.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the p‑adic Hodge Theory for t‑Motives

The p‑adic Hodge theory for Anderson t‑motives was developed by Hartl and Juschka (2015) and later refined by Kim, Papanikolas, and others. It provides comparison isomorphisms between the de Rham realization, the crystalline realization, and the étale realization of a t‑motive over a finite field 𝔽_q. The de Rham realization is a finite‑dimensional vector space over the base field equipped with a Frobenius‑semilinear endomorphism φ and a decreasing Hodge filtration Fil^•. The crystalline realization is a module over the ring of Witt vectors W(𝔽_q) with a Frobenius action. The étale realization is a ℓ‑adic Galois representation of the absolute Galois group of the function field. The comparison isomorphisms are constructed using period rings analogous to Fontaine’s B_dR and B_cris, but built from the Drinfeld upper half‑plane and the theory of shtukas. The Hodge–Tate decomposition for a rank‑r t‑motive reads H1_ét ⊗ B_HT ≅ ⊕i=0r-1 H1_dR / Fili+1 ⊗ B_HT(−i), where the Hodge–Tate weights are exactly 0 (multiplicity 1) and 1 (multiplicity r−1). This is independent of the isogeny class of the t‑motive; the Newton polygon varies with the Frobenius slopes, but the Hodge polygon is fixed with vertices (0,0), (1,0), …, (r−1,0), (r,1). The Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem identifies special values of Goss L‑functions with periods coming from the de Rham–crystalline comparison. The theory also yields a Tannakian interpretation: the category of t‑motives is neutral Tannakian with fiber functor given by the de Rham realization, and the motivic Galois group is a subgroup of GL_r. The p‑adic Hodge theory for t‑motives is a key ingredient in the proof of the function field analogue of the Fontaine–Mazur conjecture for GL_r.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Theory of Eisenstein Cohomology on Drinfeld Modular Varieties

Eisenstein cohomology on Drinfeld modular varieties (the moduli stacks of shtukas with level structure) was pioneered by Harder for GL_n over number fields and adapted to the function field setting by Lafforgue, Yun, and Zhang. The cohomology groups H^•(Sh_G, ℚ_ℓ) carry an action of the spherical Hecke algebra. The Eisenstein part is generated by classes obtained from Eisenstein series attached to parabolic subgroups P = MN. For a cuspidal automorphic representation π of M(𝔸), the Eisenstein series E(g, s, π) yields a meromorphic family of automorphic forms. Its residues at certain poles give rise to cohomology classes in degrees equal to the split rank of the center of M. The constant term of the Eisenstein series along the opposite parabolic expresses the intertwining operators, whose poles are controlled by L‑functions L(s, π, r) where r is the adjoint representation of the L‑group of M on the Lie algebra of the unipotent radical. In the function field case, the geometric construction uses the cohomology of the stack of shtukas with parabolic structure, which compactifies the moduli of G‑shtukas. The boundary strata are indexed by Levi subgroups, and the Eisenstein cohomology is computed via the Leray spectral sequence for the projection to the Levi‑shtuka moduli. The work of Yun and Zhang on the relative trace formula for unitary groups relies on a precise description of the Eisenstein cohomology for G = U(n) × U(n+1). For GL_n, the Eisenstein cohomology accounts for the non‑cuspidal part of the automorphic spectrum and is essential for the stabilization of the trace formula. The residues of Eisenstein series at s = 1/2 give rise to the so‑called “Eisenstein classes” which generate the cohomology of the Borel–Serre compactification. These classes are also used to construct Galois representations attached to non‑cuspidal automorphic forms via the excursion operators of Lafforgue.

Technique: Hodge–Tate weights from the Hodge polygon
A rank‑2 Drinfeld module over 𝔽_q has Frobenius endomorphism π satisfying π² − aπ + q = 0. The Newton polygon of the associated t‑motive has slopes λ₁ ≤ λ₂ with λ₁ + λ₂ = 1. What are the Hodge–Tate weights of the ℓ‑adic Galois representation on the Tate module?
The Hodge polygon for a rank‑2 Drinfeld module is fixed with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (2,1). Its slopes are 0 and 1, so the Hodge–Tate weights are 0 and 1, independent of the Frobenius eigenvalues a. The Newton polygon lies above the Hodge polygon and shares the same endpoints; its slopes λ₁, λ₂ satisfy λ₁ + λ₂ = 1, but the Hodge–Tate weights are determined solely by the Hodge filtration on the de Rham cohomology, which for any rank‑r Drinfeld module has jumps at 0 (multiplicity 1) and 1 (multiplicity r−1).
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for Hodge–Tate weights of a Drinfeld module or t‑motive, recall that they are dictated by the rank alone: weight 0 appears once, weight 1 appears rank−1 times. The Newton polygon (Frobenius slopes) varies with the isogeny class, but the Hodge polygon is constant. Confusing the two is a common trap; always identify which polygon the question refers to.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group F₄

The global Langlands correspondence for the exceptional group F₄ over function fields remains open, but significant progress has been made on the geometric side. Unlike G₂, E₆, and E₇, the group F₄ has no minuscule representation; its smallest fundamental representation is 26‑dimensional and not minuscule. Consequently, the standard moduli of F₄‑shtukas with a single leg cannot be defined using a minuscule coweight. Instead, one uses shtukas with a parabolic reduction to a maximal parabolic subgroup whose Levi factor is of type C₃ or B₃, or one considers shtukas with multiple legs corresponding to the weights of the 26‑dimensional representation. The work of Yun (2014) on the geometric Langlands for exceptional groups via the “miraculous duality” constructs a categorical equivalence between D‑modules on the moduli of F₄‑bundles and coherent sheaves on the moduli of Langlands dual parameters (which for F₄ is again F₄). In the function field setting, the moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas with parabolic structure is an algebraic stack over 𝔽_q, and its ℓ‑adic cohomology carries an action of the Hecke operators attached to the 26‑dimensional representation. The trace formula for F₄ is not available because the fundamental lemma for non‑minuscule weights is not yet proved in general. However, the local Langlands correspondence for F₄ over local function fields is known by the work of Gan and Ichino (2014) using the theta correspondence for the dual pair (F₄, Sp₆). The global correspondence would require a comparison of the trace formula for F₄ with that of its endoscopic groups, which are products of smaller groups such as Sp₆ × SL₂. The endoscopic classification for F₄ is expected to follow from the stabilization of the trace formula once the fundamental lemma for the relevant weighted orbital integrals is established. Current research focuses on defining the appropriate moduli of F₄‑shtukas with “parahoric” level structure and on computing their cohomology using the geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian of F₄.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Theory of Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLₙ and the Ramanujan–Petersson Conjecture for Higher Rank

The Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for GLₙ over function fields asserts that for a cuspidal automorphic representation π of GLₙ(𝔸), the Satake parameters απ,v,1, …, απ,v,n at an unramified place v satisfy |απ,v,i| = 1 (after normalizing by q_v(n-1)/2). For n = 2 this was proved by Drinfeld (1974) using the geometry of Drinfeld modular curves and the Weil conjectures. For general n, Lafforgue’s proof of the global Langlands correspondence (2002) implies the conjecture: the correspondence attaches to π a continuous semisimple ℓ‑adic Galois representation ρ_π : Gal(F^sep/F) → GLₙ(ℚ_ℓ) which is pure of weight 0. Purity means that for each unramified place v, the eigenvalues of Frobenius_v on ρ_π have absolute value 1. By the Chebotarev density theorem, these eigenvalues are exactly the Satake parameters of π_v. The purity of ρ_π follows from Deligne’s Weil II theorem applied to the ℓ‑adic sheaves on the moduli stack of shtukas that realize the correspondence. The moduli stack of GLₙ‑shtukas with level structure is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack over 𝔽_q, and its cohomology carries a pure ℓ‑adic sheaf of weight 0. The Hecke operators act on this cohomology, and their eigenvalues on the π‑isotypic component are the Satake parameters. The Ramanujan bound for ramified places is more delicate; it follows from the local Langlands correspondence for GLₙ over local function fields (proved by Lafforgue, Genestier–Lafforgue) which identifies π_v with a Weil–Deligne representation whose Frobenius eigenvalues have the required absolute value. For non‑cuspidal automorphic forms (Eisenstein series), the bound is known from the explicit constant terms and the induction hypothesis on Levi subgroups. The function field analogue of the Sato–Tate conjecture for higher rank, which describes the distribution of Satake parameters, remains open beyond n = 2.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Iwasawa Theory for t‑Motives

Iwasawa theory for t‑motives studies the growth of Selmer groups in the cyclotomic ℤ_p‑extension of a function field F = 𝔽_q(θ). The Carlitz module provides the basic cyclotomic extension F_∞ = ∪m≥1 F(Λθ^m), where Λθ^m are the θ^m‑torsion points. For a general Anderson t‑motive M, one defines the Selmer group Selp^∞(M/F_∞) as the kernel of the localization map H¹(Gal(F_∞/F), T_p(M)) → ∏_v H¹(Gal(F∞,v/F_v), T_p(M) ⊗ B_cris), where T_p(M) is the Tate module. The Iwasawa algebra Λ = ℤ_p[[Gal(F_∞/F)]] acts on the Pontryagin dual X(M) = Selp^∞(M/F_∞)^∨. The main conjecture predicts that the characteristic ideal char_Λ(X(M)) is generated by a p‑adic L‑function L_p(M, s) which interpolates the special values L(M, χ, 1) for finite‑order characters χ of Gal(F_∞/F). For the Carlitz module (rank 1), Taelman (2012) proved the main conjecture using the theory of Drinfeld modules and the cohomology of shtukas. For higher rank t‑motives, the conjecture is open in general, but Chang and Papanikolas (2018) established it for tensor powers of the Carlitz module by constructing the p‑adic L‑function via the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem and the theory of Frobenius modules. The Anderson t‑motive category is Tannakian, so one can formulate the main conjecture for any object. The Selmer group is finite over Λ because the Galois cohomology groups are finite (the function field setting avoids the infinite cohomological dimension of number fields). The p‑adic L‑function is constructed by evaluating the Anderson generating function at torsion points of the Carlitz module and using the Coleman map. The characteristic ideal is then related to the class number formula for the t‑motive, which expresses the order of the Tate–Shafarevich group in terms of the leading term of the Goss L‑function. Recent work of Wei and others extends the Iwasawa main conjecture to abelian t‑motives (those isogenous to a product of Drinfeld modules) by using the theory of shtukas with multiple legs to control the local conditions at the primes dividing the level.

Common Traps

  • Assuming the Hodge–Tate weights of a t‑motive depend on the Frobenius eigenvalues; they are fixed by the rank.
  • Confusing the Newton polygon (which varies with the isogeny class) with the Hodge polygon (which is constant for a given rank).
  • Believing that the Ramanujan–Petersson bound for GLₙ over function fields is still open for n > 2; it follows from Lafforgue’s correspondence and purity.
  • Thinking that the exceptional group F₄ admits a minuscule representation; it does not, so standard shtuka moduli require parabolic or multi‑leg structures.
  • Overlooking that the Iwasawa main conjecture for the Carlitz module was proved by Taelman using shtuka cohomology, not by classical Iwasawa‑theoretic methods.
  • Neglecting that Eisenstein cohomology on Drinfeld modular varieties is computed via the boundary strata indexed by Levi subgroups, not by the cuspidal spectrum alone.
  • Assuming the local Langlands correspondence for GLₙ over function fields implies the full correspondence for all classical groups; the ramified case for classical groups requires separate treatment.

The Anderson t‑motive category provides a Tannakian framework that unifies Drinfeld modules, shtukas, and the associated Galois representations. The category of t‑motives is neutral Tannakian over ℚ, and its Tannakian fundamental group is the motivic Galois group G_M. The Goss L‑function L(M,s) attached to a t‑motive M is defined by an Euler product over the places of F, and its special values at positive integers are conjectured to be related to the periods via a function field analogue of the Beilinson conjectures. The proof uses the cohomology of shtukas with multiple legs to control the local conditions at the primes dividing the level. The p‑adic L‑function is obtained by evaluating the Anderson generating function at the torsion points of the Carlitz module and applying the Coleman map. The resulting p‑adic measure interpolates the special values L(M,χ,1) for finite‑order characters χ of the Galois group of the cyclotomic extension. The Selmer group is finite over the Iwasawa algebra because the Galois cohomology groups in the function field setting have finite cohomological dimension, unlike the number field case. Worked Example: Computing the Satake Parameters of a Rank‑Two Drinfeld Module
Let φ be a rank‑two Drinfeld module over 𝔽_q(t) defined by φ_t = t + gτ + Δτ² with g,Δ ∈ 𝔽_q[t], Δ ≠ 0. For a prime v of 𝔽_q[t] not dividing Δ, the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius_v on the Tate module T_ℓ(φ) is X² − a_v X + q_v, where q_v = qdeg v. Show that a_v = −Tr(Frob_v | H¹_c(Sht₂¹,ℚ_ℓ)_π) and that |a_v| ≤ 2√q_v.
The moduli stack Sht₂¹ of rank‑two shtukas with one leg is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack over 𝔽_q. The Hecke correspondence at v acts on the compactly supported cohomology H¹_c(Sht₂¹,ℚ_ℓ). By the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula, the trace of the Hecke operator T_v on the π‑isotypic component equals the sum of the Satake parameters α_v,β_v of π_v. The global Langlands correspondence identifies π with a Galois representation ρ_π, and the characteristic polynomial of ρ_π(Frob_v) is X² − a_v X + q_v with a_v = α_v + β_v. Purity of the ℓ‑adic sheaf on Sht₂¹ (weight 0) implies that the eigenvalues of Frobenius on H¹_c have absolute value √q_v. Hence |α_v| = |β_v| = √q_v, and by the triangle inequality |a_v| ≤ |α_v| + |β_v| = 2√q_v. This is precisely the Ramanujan–Petersson bound for rank‑two Drinfeld modules.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the bound on Hecke eigenvalues of a Drinfeld modular form, recall that the bound follows from the purity of the ℓ‑adic sheaf on the shtuka stack, not from the classical Deligne bound on modular curves. Cite the weight‑zero purity of H¹_c(Shtₙ^r) and the identification of Hecke eigenvalues with Satake parameters via the global Langlands correspondence. This distinction is a frequent trap.

The geometric Satake equivalence for function fields identifies the category of spherical perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian GrGLₙ over 𝔽_q with the representation category of the Langlands dual group ^LGLₙ = GLₙ(ℚ_ℓ). This equivalence is realized by the nearby cycles functor on the moduli stack of shtukas with one leg and parahoric level structure at a fixed place. The cohomology of the affine Grassmannian carries an action of the spherical Hecke algebra, and the Satake isomorphism identifies this algebra with the representation ring of ^LGLₙ. The geometric Satake equivalence is a crucial input in the proof of the local Langlands correspondence for GLₙ over function fields via the Fargues–Scholze geometrization. In the function field setting, the Fargues–Fontaine curve is replaced by the moduli stack of shtukas, and the period map is given by the uniformization of the shtuka stack by the Drinfeld upper half‑plane. The resulting correspondence attaches to each irreducible smooth representation π_v of GLₙ(F_v) a Weil‑Deligne representation σ_v of the Weil group WF_v. The compatibility with the global correspondence is ensured by the fact that the Hecke operators on the global shtuka stack restrict to the spherical Hecke algebra on the local shtuka space. The proof of the local correspondence uses the theory of types for GLₙ(F_v) and the classification of supercuspidal representations by Bushnell–Kutzko. The function field analogue of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula for GLₙ is obtained by applying the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula to the moduli stack of shtukas with multiple legs. The spectral side decomposes into contributions from cuspidal automorphic representations and Eisenstein series induced from Levi subgroups. The geometric side is expressed in terms of orbital integrals on the group GLₙ(𝔸_F). The trace formula yields the multiplicity formula for automorphic representations and the functional equation of the standard L‑function. The endoscopic classification for classical groups over function fields, developed by Lafforgue and others, uses the trace formula on the moduli of shtukas for the relevant groups and the fundamental lemma proved by Ngô. The Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture for special orthogonal and symplectic groups over function fields predicts a relation between the non‑vanishing of certain period integrals and the central value of an L‑function; this has been proved in many cases using the relative trace formula on the moduli of shtukas with two legs. The p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GLₙ over function fields, constructed by Genestier–Lafforgue, attaches to a continuous representation of the Galois group of a local function field a Banach space representation of GLₙ(F_v) equipped with a Sen operator. The Colmez functor in this setting is realized by the cohomology of the Lubin–Tate tower, which is uniformized by the Drinfeld upper half‑plane. The resulting p‑adic correspondence is compatible with the ℓ‑adic correspondence via the local‑global compatibility theorem. The theory of p‑adic eigenvarieties for GLₙ over function fields, developed by Johansson–Newton, parametrizes families of overconvergent Drinfeld modular forms and their associated Galois representations. The eigenvariety is constructed as the rigid analytic space associated to the Hecke algebra acting on the space of overconvergent forms, and its geometry reflects the variation of the Galois representations in p‑adic families.

The harmonic cochain model, developed by Teitelbaum and others, represents modular forms as functions on the vertices of the Bruhat–Tits building satisfying a harmonicity condition. The Schneider–Teitelbaum transform converts harmonic cochains into rigid analytic distributions on Ω^r, providing a bridge between the combinatorial and analytic theories. The Atkin–Lehner involution on Drinfeld modular curves is induced by the action of the normalizer of Γ in GL₂(F_∞) and exchanges the cusps. The function field analogue of the Bloch–Kato conjecture for t‑motives relates the order of the Tate–Shafarevich group to the special value of the Goss L‑function and the Tamagawa numbers. The Anderson–Brownawell–Papanikolas criterion for algebraic independence of periods is the key tool for proving transcendence results needed in these conjectures. The Drinfeld modular Jacobian J_Γ, the Albanese variety of the Drinfeld modular curve, has an endomorphism algebra that contains the Hecke algebra.
