The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group E6

The exceptional group E6 over a global function field F_q(t) admits a minuscule fundamental representation of dimension 27, which makes it possible to construct a moduli stack of E6‑shtukas with a single leg. Drinfeld’s original construction for GL_n uses vector bundles with a Frobenius‑linear endomorphism; for E6 one replaces the vector bundle by a principal E6‑bundle equipped with a Frobenius‑invariant reduction to the minuscule parabolic. The resulting moduli space is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack of dimension 27·(g−1) where g is the genus of the curve. The cohomology of this stack carries an action of the Hecke algebra for E6 and of the absolute Galois group of F_q(t). Lafforgue’s method of excision and the Weil‑type bounds for the Frobenius eigenvalues extend to this setting because the minuscule condition guarantees that the Hecke correspondences are finite étale. Consequently one obtains a global Langlands correspondence for E6: to each cuspidal automorphic representation π of E6(A_F) one attaches a continuous semisimple ℓ‑adic representation ρ_π of Gal(F^sep/F) of dimension 27, pure of weight zero, whose local L‑factors match those of π at all unramified places. The proof uses the same geometric ingredients as for GL_n — the Lefschetz trace formula on the shtuka stack, the purity theorem of Deligne for the ℓ‑adic sheaves arising from the minuscule representation, and the Chebotarev density argument to identify the Galois representation. A crucial new feature is the appearance of the dual group ^L E6 = E6(C) and the need to verify that the local Langlands correspondence for the unramified principal series of E6(F_v) matches the Satake isomorphism for the spherical Hecke algebra. This verification was carried out by L. Lafforgue and later refined by V. Ginzburg using the geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian of E6. The correspondence predicts, in particular, that the Ramanujan–Petersson bound for Hecke eigenvalues of π holds with the optimal constant 271/2·q_v1/2. The E6 case also provides a testing ground for functoriality: the 27‑dimensional representation of ^L E6 yields a lift to GL27, and the compatibility of the two correspondences is a theorem of D. Kazhdan and G. Lusztig via the theory of perverse sheaves on the affine flag variety.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Theory of Drinfeld Modular Forms for GL_n and the Theory of Congruences between Modular Forms and Galois Representations

Let φ be a Drinfeld module of rank r over a global function field K with ring of integers A. The associated Drinfeld modular forms are rigid analytic functions on the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ω^r satisfying a transformation law under a congruence subgroup Γ ⊂ GL_r(A). For each prime ℓ ≠ char(K) one can attach a compatible system of ℓ‑adic Galois representations ρφ,ℓ: Gal(K^sep/K) → GL_r(ℚ_ℓ) coming from the ℓ‑adic Tate module of φ. The Fourier coefficients a_𝔭 of a normalized Hecke eigenform f of weight k and level Γ are algebraic integers in a number field E. A congruence between two eigenforms f and g modulo a prime 𝔩 of E means that a_𝔭(f) ≡ a_𝔭(g) (mod 𝔩) for almost all primes 𝔭. By the work of G. Böckle, M. Harris, and R. Taylor adapted to the function field setting, such a congruence forces an isomorphism between the residual Galois representations ρ̄f,𝔩 and ρ̄g,𝔩 after semisimplification. The proof proceeds by constructing a Galois deformation ring R_f parametrising lifts of ρ̄f,𝔩 with prescribed local conditions (crystalline at places dividing ℓ, unramified outside a finite set) and a Hecke algebra 𝕋_f acting on the space of modular forms of the given level and weight. One then shows that the natural map R_f → 𝕋_f is an isomorphism after localisation at the maximal ideal corresponding to f. This “R = 𝕋” theorem is the function field analogue of the modularity lifting theorems of Wiles and Taylor–Wiles. The key input is the existence of a suitable Taylor–Wiles system of auxiliary primes, which in the function field case is provided by the Chebotarev density theorem for the constant field extension and the fact that the deformation problem is unobstructed because the cohomological dimension of Gal(K^sep/K) is two. As a consequence, any congruence between eigenforms yields a congruence between the associated Galois representations, and conversely, a congruence between residual representations lifts to a congruence of eigenforms provided the deformation ring is formally smooth. This principle underlies the proof of the function field analogue of Serre’s conjecture for GL2, established by V. Drinfeld and later by L. Lafforgue for GL_n, and it also provides a method to produce new Galois representations from known ones by varying the level or the weight in a p‑adic family.

Worked Example: Congruence Lifting
Let f be a weight‑2 Drinfeld modular form of level Γ0(𝔭) over F_q(t) with Fourier coefficients in ℤ_ℓ. Suppose the residual representation ρ̄_f is absolutely irreducible and unramified outside 𝔭 and ℓ. Show that any eigenform g congruent to f modulo ℓ gives rise to a Galois representation ρ_g whose residual representation is isomorphic to ρ̄_f.
By the R = 𝕋 theorem for the deformation problem with fixed determinant and prescribed local conditions at 𝔭 and ℓ, the Hecke algebra 𝕋_f localized at the maximal ideal m_f corresponding to f is isomorphic to the universal deformation ring R_f. The eigenform g defines a homomorphism 𝕋_f → ℤ_ℓ whose kernel contains m_f^N for some N because the Fourier coefficients of g are congruent to those of f modulo ℓ. This homomorphism factors through R_f, yielding a lift ρ_g of ρ̄_f. Since the residual representation is uniquely determined by the maximal ideal, ρ̄_g ≅ ρ̄_f. The absolute irreducibility of ρ̄_f guarantees that the deformation functor is representable and that the map R_f → 𝕋_f is an isomorphism, so the lift is unique up to strict equivalence.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks about congruences between Drinfeld modular forms, first identify the residual Galois representation and the deformation conditions (determinant, local behaviour at ℓ and at the level primes). Then invoke the R = 𝕋 isomorphism: the Hecke algebra at the relevant maximal ideal is the universal deformation ring. Any congruence of Fourier coefficients modulo a prime 𝔩 corresponds to a homomorphism from this Hecke algebra to the residue field, which by the isomorphism gives a deformation of the residual representation. The key points to mention are absolute irreducibility of the residual representation, the Taylor–Wiles method adapted to function fields, and the fact that the deformation problem is unobstructed because the Galois group has cohomological dimension two.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Iwasawa Main Conjecture for Higher Rank t‑Motives

For a Drinfeld module φ of rank r over a global function field K, the Anderson t‑motive M(φ) is a finitely generated module over the non‑commutative polynomial ring K[t]{τ} equipped with a Frobenius‑semilinear endomorphism. The Iwasawa main conjecture in this setting predicts a precise relationship between the characteristic ideal of the Selmer group of the dual t‑motive M(φ)^∨ over the cyclotomic ℤ_p‑extension K_∞/K and the p‑adic L‑function L_p(φ,s) constructed by Goss and Taelman. The Selmer group is defined as the kernel of the global-to-local map in Galois cohomology H1(K_∞, M(φ)^∨) → ∏_v H1(K∞,v, M(φ)^∨) where the product runs over all places of K_∞. The p‑adic L‑function interpolates the special values L(φ, χ, 1) for finite order characters χ of Gal(K_∞/K). The conjecture asserts that the characteristic ideal of the Pontryagin dual of the Selmer group, viewed as a module over the Iwasawa algebra Λ = ℤ_p[[Gal(K_∞/K)]], is generated by L_p(φ,s). This was proved by L. Taelman for the Carlitz module (rank 1) using the theory of Drinfeld modular forms and the explicit class field theory of Hayes. For higher rank, the conjecture remains open in general, but significant progress has been made by D. Brownawell and M. Papanikolas using the Anderson–Brownawell–Papanikolas criterion for algebraic independence of periods to control the μ‑invariant of the Selmer group. Their work shows that the μ‑invariant vanishes for a large class of t‑motives arising from Drinfeld modules with complex multiplication, and that the λ‑invariant equals the order of vanishing of the Goss L‑function at s = 1, in agreement with the function field Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture. The proof strategy adapts the Euler system method of Kato to the function field setting: one constructs an Euler system from the torsion points of the Drinfeld module over the tower of cyclotomic extensions, and then uses the explicit reciprocity law of Anderson to relate the Euler system to the p‑adic L‑function. The main technical obstacle for higher rank is the lack of a general theory of p‑adic Hodge theory for t‑motives, which is needed to define the local conditions at places dividing p in the Selmer group. Recent work of A. Genestier and V. Lafforgue on the Fargues–Fontaine curve for function fields provides a framework that may eventually supply the missing p‑adic Hodge theory.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Theory of p‑adic L‑functions for Higher Rank Drinfeld Modules

Let φ be a Drinfeld module of rank r ≥ 2 over a global function field K with constant field F_q. For each prime ℓ ≠ char(K) one can construct a p‑adic L‑function L_p(φ,s) on the weight space W = Homcont(Gal(K_∞/K), ℂ_p^×) by interpolating the critical values L(φ, χ, 1) for finite order characters χ of the Galois group of the cyclotomic ℤ_p‑extension K_∞/K. The construction follows the method of Goss: one first defines a measure μ_φ on the profinite group Gal(K_∞/K) using the Anderson generating function of φ evaluated at torsion points of the Carlitz module. The measure satisfies a distribution relation reflecting the action of the Hecke operators on the space of Drinfeld modular forms. The p‑adic L‑function is then the Mellin transform of μ_φ. For rank 1 (the Carlitz module) this yields the classical p‑adic L‑function of Goss, which satisfies a functional equation relating s 1−s and whose zeros encode the Iwasawa invariants of the cyclotomic extension. For higher rank, the existence of a p‑adic L‑function with the expected interpolation property was established by M. Papanikolas and D. Thakur using the theory of Anderson t‑motives and the de Rham cohomology of the associated shtuka. The key new ingredient is the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem, which expresses the special values L(φ, χ, 1) as ℚ‑linear combinations of logarithms of algebraic points on the Drinfeld module. These logarithms are periods of the t‑motive M(φ) and can be p‑adically interpolated because the Frobenius endomorphism on the crystalline realization of M(φ) acts with eigenvalues that are p‑adic units. The resulting p‑adic L‑function is expected to satisfy a functional equation whose sign is given by the Atkin–Lehner eigenvalue of the associated Drinfeld modular form. Moreover, the order of vanishing of L_p(φ,s) at the trivial character should equal the rank of the Mordell–Weil group φ(K) (the function field Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture), and the leading coefficient should be expressed in terms of the p‑adic regulator built from the p‑adic heights of a basis of φ(K). Recent work of G. Böckle and R. Pink on the p‑adic uniformization of Drinfeld modular varieties provides a geometric interpretation of the p‑adic L‑function as the p‑adic avatar of the ℓ‑adic L‑function arising from the cohomology of the shtuka stack.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Local Langlands Correspondence for GL_n via the Theory of Diamonds

The Fargues–Scholze geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence for GL_n over a p‑adic field has a function field counterpart where the p‑adic field is replaced by the completed local field F_q((t)) and the role of perfectoid spaces is played by the theory of diamonds over F_q((t)). A diamond is a sheaf on the pro‑étale site of perfectoid spaces that satisfies a representability condition; in the function field setting the basic diamond is the adic space associated to the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ω^n = ℙn−1 ∖ ∪H H(F_q((t))) where H runs over all F_q((t))‑rational hyperplanes. The group GL_n(F_q((t))) acts on Ω^n, and the quotient stack [Ω^n / GL_n(F_q((t)))] is a diamond that classifies shtukas with one leg and a trivialization at the leg. The cohomology of this diamond with coefficients in ℓ‑adic sheaves carries a smooth action of GL_n(F_q((t))) × WF_q((t)) where W is the Weil group. The local Langlands correspondence for GL_n over F_q((t)) is then realized as an equivalence between the category of smooth irreducible representations of GL_n(F_q((t))) on ℚ_ℓ‑vector spaces and the category of Frobenius‑semisimple Weil‑Deligne representations of dimension n. The construction proceeds by first establishing a geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian of GL_n over F_q((t)), which identifies the category of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian with the representation category of the dual group GL_n(ℚ_ℓ). Then one uses the Hecke operators on the moduli stack of shtukas to produce a correspondence between the cohomology of the diamond and the category of representations of GL_n(F_q((t))). The crucial input is the purity of the ℓ‑adic sheaves on the shtuka stack, proved by V. Lafforgue using the theory of weights for ℓ‑adic sheaves on stacks over finite fields. The resulting correspondence matches the one constructed by L. Lafforgue via the global Langlands correspondence and the local‑global compatibility theorem. An important consequence is the explicit description of the local L‑ and ε‑factors in terms of the geometry of the diamond: the L‑factor is the determinant of the Frobenius acting on the stalk of the nearby cycles sheaf, and the ε‑factor is given by the monodromy operator on the vanishing cycles. This geometric realization also provides a natural framework for the local Langlands correspondence for inner forms of GL_n, such as division algebras, by replacing the Drinfeld upper half‑plane with the corresponding Rapoport–Zink space for the inner form.

  • Confusing the minuscule representation of E6 (dimension 27) with the adjoint representation (dimension 78) when computing Hecke eigenvalues.
  • Assuming the R = 𝕋 theorem holds without verifying absolute irreducibility of the residual Galois representation.
  • Neglecting that the Iwasawa main conjecture for higher rank t‑motives requires a p‑adic Hodge theory that is still under development.
  • Thinking that the p‑adic L‑function for rank ≥ 2 automatically satisfies a functional equation; the sign depends on the Atkin–Lehner eigenvalue which must be computed.
  • Believing that the diamond [Ω^n / GL_n(F_q((t)))] is a scheme; it is only a diamond, and its cohomology must be taken in the pro‑étale topology.
  • Overlooking that the local Langlands correspondence for GL_n over function fields is a theorem of Lafforgue, not a conjecture, and that the geometric realization via diamonds is a recent reinterpretation.

These advanced sections complete the required coverage for the next level of study.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Function Field Analogue of the Local Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group F₄ via Shtukas

The exceptional group F₄ has rank four and dimension 52. Over a global function field K = 𝔽q(C) the Langlands dual group is again F₄, so the local correspondence at a place v of K should match irreducible smooth representations of F₄(Kv) with Frobenius‑semisimple Weil‑Deligne representations of the Weil group WKv of dimension 52. The geometric realization uses the moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas with one leg at v and a level structure away from v. V. Lafforgue’s proof of the global Langlands correspondence for reductive groups over function fields (2018) provides the necessary compatibility: the Hecke operators at v act on the cohomology of the shtuka stack and generate a commutative algebra isomorphic to the spherical Hecke algebra of F₄(Kv). The Satake isomorphism identifies this algebra with the representation ring of the dual group F₄(ℚℓ). By extracting the ℓ‑adic local systems on the shtuka stack that correspond to cuspidal automorphic representations of F₄(𝔸K), one obtains the local Langlands parameters. The key technical input is the purity of the ℓ‑adic sheaves on the F₄‑shtuka stack, proved by adapting Lafforgue’s weight arguments to the non‑simply‑connected case. The resulting correspondence respects L‑ and ε‑factors: the local L‑factor is the determinant of Frobenius on the stalk of the nearby cycles sheaf, and the ε‑factor is given by the monodromy operator on the vanishing cycles. An important consequence is the explicit description of the supercuspidal representations of F₄(Kv) in terms of the geometry of the affine Grassmannian for F₄. Examiners often test the distinction between the simply‑connected and adjoint forms of F₄; the former has trivial center while the latter has center of order two, which affects the normalization of the Satake isomorphism and the precise statement of the local correspondence.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Function Field Analogue of the Geometric Langlands Correspondence for the Loop Group of GLn

The geometric Langlands program over a complex curve X replaces the Weil group by the fundamental group of X and studies D‑modules on the moduli stack BunG(X) of G‑bundles. In the function field setting the curve is defined over 𝔽q and the role of D‑modules is played by ℓ‑adic perverse sheaves on the moduli stack of G‑shtukas. For G = GLn the loop group LG = GLn(𝔽q((t))) acts on the affine Grassmannian GrGLn. The geometric Satake equivalence identifies the category of perverse sheaves on GrGLn with the representation category of the dual group GLn(ℚℓ). The Hecke operators on the shtuka stack are constructed by modifying the shtuka at a point using the affine Grassmannian. The categorical geometric Langlands correspondence predicts an equivalence between the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on BunGLn and the derived category of coherent sheaves on the stack of local systems LocSysGLn(X). In the function field case this equivalence is realized by the Fourier–Mukai transform with kernel given by the universal shtuka. The work of Gaitsgory, Lurie, and others on the categorical trace formula provides a proof for GLn over 𝔽q using the theory of ind‑coherent sheaves and the theory of factorization algebras. A crucial point is the compatibility with the classical (non‑categorical) correspondence: taking the trace of Frobenius on both sides recovers the equality of L‑functions proved by L. Lafforgue. Examiners frequently ask for the difference between the “spectral” side (coherent sheaves on LocSys) and the “automorphic” side (sheaves on Bun) and for the role of the Whittaker normalization in fixing the equivalence. The loop group perspective also clarifies the appearance of the affine Weyl group and the alcove geometry in the description of Hecke eigenvalues.

Technique: Identifying the Correct Satake Parameter for a Supercuspidal Representation of F₄(Kv)
Let π be an irreducible supercuspidal representation of F₄(Kv) obtained from the cohomology of the F₄‑shtuka stack with one leg at v. Explain how the Satake isomorphism for the spherical Hecke algebra of F₄(Kv) determines the Langlands parameter of π, and why the center of the adjoint form of F₄ forces a quadratic twist of the parameter.
The spherical Hecke algebra ℋ(F₄(Kv)//F₄(𝒪v)) is commutative and, via the Satake isomorphism, canonically isomorphic to the representation ring Rep(F₄(ℚℓ)). The action of ℋ on the F₄‑shtuka cohomology yields a character χ: ℋ → ℚℓ. By the Satake isomorphism χ corresponds to a semisimple conjugacy class s(π) in F₄(ℚℓ), which is the Satake parameter. For a supercuspidal π the parameter is discrete, i.e. its centralizer in F₄(ℚℓ) is finite. The adjoint form F₄ad has center Z ≅ μ₂. The simply‑connected cover F₄sc maps onto F₄ad with kernel Z. The Langlands dual of F₄ad is F₄sc, so the parameter naturally lives in F₄sc(ℚℓ). The projection F₄sc → F₄ad identifies parameters that differ by the non‑trivial element of Z. Consequently the parameter attached to π is well‑defined only up to the quadratic twist by the unique non‑trivial character of Z. This twist is exactly the ambiguity coming from the choice of a central character for π, and it must be fixed by specifying the central character of π (which is trivial for supercuspidals of the adjoint group). The examiner expects the candidate to mention the Satake isomorphism, the role of the center, and the distinction between simply‑connected and adjoint forms.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “local Langlands correspondence for an exceptional group”, first state the group, its dual, and the relevant moduli stack (shtukas with one leg). Then outline the three pillars: (1) geometric Satake for the affine Grassmannian, (2) Hecke operators on the shtuka stack, (3) purity of ℓ‑adic sheaves. Finally, note any subtlety coming from the center (simply‑connected vs adjoint) and the resulting quadratic twist. This structured answer covers all marking points.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Function Field Analogue of the p‑adic Langlands Correspondence for GLn via (φ,Γ)‑modules over Function Fields

The p‑adic Langlands correspondence for GL2(ℚp) relates continuous p‑adic representations of the absolute Galois group of ℚp to unitary Banach space representations of GL2(ℚp). Over a function field K = 𝔽q(C) the role of ℚp is played by the completed local field Fq((t)). The analogue of (φ,Γ)‑modules is provided by the theory of étale (φ,∇)‑modules over the Robba ring ℛKv, where φ is the Frobenius and ∇ is a connection encoding the action of the Galois group. For GLn the correspondence should match continuous ℚp‑representations of the local Galois group Gal(Fq((t))sep/Fq((t))) of dimension n with admissible locally analytic representations of GLn(Fq((t))) on p‑adic Banach spaces. The construction proceeds by first establishing a p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GL2 using the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ω² and its p‑adic uniformization by the Lubin–Tate tower. The Colmez functor is replaced by the functor that sends a (φ,∇)‑module to the locally analytic vectors in the completed cohomology of the Drinfeld modular tower. For higher rank n ≥ 3 the theory is still conjectural; the main obstacle is the lack of a p‑adic Hodge theory for (φ,∇)‑modules over Fq((t)) that satisfies the required comparison isomorphisms. Recent work of G. Böckle and R. Pink on the p‑adic uniformization of Drinfeld modular varieties provides a geometric interpretation of the p‑adic L‑function as the p‑adic avatar of the ℓ‑adic L‑function arising from the cohomology of the shtuka stack. The expected functional equation of the p‑adic L‑function involves the Atkin–Lehner eigenvalue of the associated Drinfeld modular form. Examiners often test the distinction between the ℓ‑adic and p‑adic settings: in the ℓ‑adic case the correspondence is a theorem (Lafforgue), while in the p‑adic case it remains a conjecture for n ≥ 3, and the role of the Robba ring and the (φ,∇)‑module category must be clearly explained.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Function Field Analogue of the Arthur–Selberg Trace Formula for Inner Forms of Classical Groups

The Arthur–Selberg trace formula for a reductive group G over a global field expresses the spectral side (automorphic representations) in terms of the geometric side (orbital integrals). For inner forms of classical groups over function fields, such as unitary groups U(n) or symplectic groups Sp(2n) that are not split, the trace formula must incorporate the endoscopic transfer of orbital integrals. The function field analogue was developed by L. Lafforgue for GLn and extended by V. Lafforgue to all reductive groups using the geometry of shtukas. For an inner form H of a classical group G, the moduli stack of H‑shtukas is a twisted form of the G‑shtuka stack. The trace formula for H is obtained by applying the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula to the cohomology of the H‑shtuka stack with coefficients in a suitable Hecke sheaf. The geometric side involves sums over conjugacy classes in H(K) of orbital integrals of the test function, while the spectral side is a sum over automorphic representations of H(𝔸K) of their traces. The endoscopic transfer matches orbital integrals on H with stable orbital integrals on the endoscopic groups, which are products of smaller classical groups. The fundamental lemma for function fields, proved by Ngô Bảo Châu (2008) using the Hitchin fibration, guarantees the equality of the transferred orbital integrals. A key point for examiners is the distinction between the stable trace formula (which sums over stable conjugacy classes) and the ordinary trace formula; the former is needed to state the endoscopic classification. The Arthur multiplicity formula for inner forms predicts that the multiplicity of an automorphic representation in the discrete spectrum equals the size of a certain centralizer in the dual group, up to a sign given by the Arthur parameter. This formula has been verified for many inner forms of classical groups over function fields using the geometric trace formula and the theory of endoscopy.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence: The Theory of the Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Group Spin(8) and Triality

The group Spin(8) is the simply‑connected double cover of SO(8) and possesses an outer automorphism group isomorphic to the symmetric group S₃, known as triality. This automorphism permutes the three 8‑dimensional irreducible representations: the vector representation and the two half‑spin representations. Over a global function field K the Langlands dual of Spin(8) is the adjoint group SO(8) (or PGO(8)). The local Langlands correspondence for Spin(8)(Kv) should match irreducible representations of Spin(8)(Kv) with Langlands parameters valued in SO(8)(ℚℓ) up to the action of the outer automorphisms. The geometric realization uses the moduli stack of Spin(8)‑shtukas. Because of triality, the Hecke operators at a place v come in three families, each associated to one of the three 8‑dimensional representations. The Satake isomorphism identifies the spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of SO(8)(ℚℓ), but the outer automorphisms act on this ring by permuting the fundamental weights corresponding to the three 8‑dimensional representations. Consequently, an automorphic representation of Spin(8)(𝔸K) gives rise to three (possibly distinct) Langlands parameters related by triality. The global correspondence, proved by V. Lafforgue for all reductive groups, ensures that these three parameters are conjugate under the outer automorphism group. A subtle point is the distinction between the simply‑connected group Spin(8) and the adjoint group PGO(8): the center of Spin(8) is (ℤ/2ℤ)², and the three non‑trivial central characters correspond exactly to the three 8‑dimensional representations. Examiners often ask how triality manifests in the functional equation of the standard L‑function of an automorphic representation of Spin(8); the answer is that the three L‑functions attached to the three 8‑dimensional representations are equal, reflecting the symmetry of the parameter under S₃. Another common trap is to confuse the dual group of Spin(8) (which is SO(8)) with the dual group of SO(8) (which is Spin(8)); the direction of the duality reverses the simply‑connected/adjoint distinction.

  • Confusing the simply‑connected and adjoint forms of exceptional groups when stating the Satake isomorphism.
  • Assuming the p‑adic Langlands correspondence for GLn over function fields is a theorem for n ≥ 3; it remains conjectural.
  • Neglecting the quadratic twist arising from the center of the adjoint form of F₄ in the local correspondence.
  • Mixing up the stable trace formula with the ordinary trace formula when discussing endoscopic transfer for inner forms.
  • Overlooking the role of triality in permuting the three 8‑dimensional representations of Spin(8) and its effect on L‑functions.
  • Treating the loop group LG as a finite‑dimensional algebraic group; it is an ind‑scheme and its affine Grassmannian is an ind‑projective ind‑scheme.
  • Believing that the geometric Langlands equivalence for GLn over function fields is proved without using the theory of factorization algebras and ind‑coherent sheaves.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group F4

The exceptional group F₄ is the simply‑connected simple algebraic group of type F₄ over a global function field K. Its Langlands dual is the adjoint group of type F₄, which coincides with the simply‑connected form because the center of F₄ is trivial. The local Langlands correspondence for F₄(Kv) matches irreducible smooth representations of F₄(Kv) with Langlands parameters valued in the dual group F₄(ℚℓ) up to conjugacy. V. Lafforgue’s global correspondence for all reductive groups over function fields provides the global parameter for automorphic representations of F₄(𝔸K). The geometric realization uses the moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas with one leg at a place v and possibly level structure at other places. The Hecke operators at v are indexed by dominant coweights of F₄, and the Satake isomorphism identifies the spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of the dual group F₄(ℚℓ). A subtle point for examiners is the absence of a non‑trivial center: unlike Spin groups, there is no quadratic twist ambiguity in the local correspondence. The fundamental lemma for F₄, proved by Ngô Bảo Châu as part of the general proof for all reductive groups, guarantees the equality of orbital integrals needed for endoscopic transfer. Endoscopic groups for F₄ are products of smaller groups such as Spin(9) and Sp(6) × SL(2); the stable trace formula for F₄ involves sums over stable conjugacy classes in these endoscopic groups. The Arthur multiplicity formula predicts that the multiplicity of an automorphic representation in the discrete spectrum equals the size of a certain centralizer in the dual group, which for F₄ is always 1 because the center is trivial. The geometric side of the trace formula for F₄‑shtukas involves the cohomology of the moduli stack with coefficients in Hecke sheaves; the Lefschetz trace formula expresses the trace of Frobenius as a sum over fixed points, which correspond to F₄‑shtukas with prescribed Frobenius action. The Drinfeld upper half‑plane for F₄ does not exist in the same way as for GLn, but the Bruhat–Tits building for F₄ provides a combinatorial model for the local uniformization of the moduli of F₄‑shtukas. The theory of harmonic cochains on the building yields a description of the space of automorphic forms for F₄, analogous to the theory of harmonic cochains on the Bruhat–Tits tree for GL₂. The function field analogue of the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for F₄ asserts that the Satake parameters of cuspidal automorphic representations are bounded by 1; this follows from Lafforgue’s proof of the global Langlands correspondence and the purity of the associated ℓ‑adic Galois representations. The Drinfeld modular forms for F₄ are sections of line bundles on the compactified moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas; their Fourier expansions involve Whittaker functions on the Bruhat–Tits building. The Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for F₄ relates the cohomology of the moduli stack to the space of cuspidal automorphic forms, and the Hecke operators act compatibly on both sides. The theory of periods for F₄‑shtukas, developed by Anderson and others, connects special values of L‑functions to algebraic periods arising from the de Rham cohomology of the associated t‑motives.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Groups E6, E7, E8

The simply‑connected exceptional groups E₆, E₇, and E₈ have non‑trivial centers: the center of E₆ is μ₃, of E₇ is μ₂, and E₈ is adjoint (center trivial). Their Langlands duals are the adjoint forms E₆ad, E₇ad, and E₈ respectively. The global Langlands correspondence for these groups over a function field K is a consequence of V. Lafforgue’s theorem for all reductive groups. The local correspondence at a place v matches irreducible representations of the simply‑connected group with Langlands parameters valued in the dual adjoint group, up to the action of the outer automorphism group (which for E₆ is of order 2, for E₇ and E₈ trivial). The moduli stack of G‑shtukas for G = E₆, E₇, E₈ provides the geometric setting; the Hecke operators are indexed by dominant coweights, and the Satake isomorphism identifies the spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of the dual group. A key examiner trap is the distinction between the simply‑connected and adjoint forms: the center of the simply‑connected group gives rise to central characters that must be specified to obtain a bijection in the local correspondence. For E₆, the three central characters correspond to the three 27‑dimensional representations permuted by the outer automorphism; the stable trace formula for E₆ involves endoscopic groups such as Spin(10) × U(1) and F₄. The fundamental lemma for these endoscopic groups was proved by Ngô as part of the general proof. The Arthur multiplicity formula for inner forms of E₆, E₇, E₈ predicts multiplicities in terms of centralizers in the dual group; for E₈ the center is trivial so multiplicities are 1. The geometric side of the trace formula involves the cohomology of the moduli stack of G‑shtukas with coefficients in Hecke sheaves; the Lefschetz trace formula expresses the trace of Frobenius as a sum over fixed points. The Bruhat–Tits buildings for these groups are high‑dimensional simplicial complexes; harmonic cochains on these buildings give a combinatorial model for automorphic forms. The function field analogue of the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture holds for all three groups by Lafforgue’s purity theorem. Drinfeld modular forms for E₆, E₇, E₈ are sections of automorphic line bundles on the compactified moduli stacks; their Fourier coefficients are given by Whittaker functions on the Bruhat–Tits building. The Eichler–Shimura isomorphism relates the cohomology of the moduli stack to the space of cuspidal automorphic forms. The theory of periods for t‑motives associated to these groups, developed by Anderson, Brownawell, and Papanikolas, connects special values of L‑functions to algebraic periods. The Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem gives explicit formulas for logarithms of algebraic points on the associated uniformized varieties. The geometric Langlands correspondence for these exceptional groups, proved by Gaitsgory and Lurie in the geometric setting, uses the moduli stack of G‑bundles on a curve and the category of D‑modules; the function field analogue is realized via the cohomology of the moduli stack of G‑shtukas.

Examiner's trap: dual group versus simply‑connected group for E₆
A question asks: “State the Langlands dual group of the simply‑connected exceptional group E₆ over a function field and explain how the outer automorphism of order 2 acts on its irreducible representations.”
The Langlands dual of the simply‑connected group E₆ is the adjoint group E₆ad (type E₆ with trivial center). The outer automorphism of order 2 of E₆ corresponds to the diagram automorphism of the Dynkin diagram; it permutes the two 27‑dimensional fundamental representations (the minuscule representations) and fixes the adjoint representation. In the local Langlands correspondence, an irreducible representation of E₆(Kv) with a given central character corresponds to a Langlands parameter valued in E₆ad(ℚℓ) up to conjugacy; the outer automorphism acts on the parameter by composing with the diagram automorphism of the dual group. The three central characters of the simply‑connected E₆ correspond exactly to the three orbits of the outer automorphism on the set of 27‑dimensional representations. Therefore, the stable trace formula for E₆ must sum over stable conjugacy classes in the endoscopic groups, which are invariant under this outer automorphism.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions an exceptional group, first identify whether it is simply‑connected or adjoint. Write down the center and the dual group immediately; this earns easy marks. Then recall the role of the outer automorphism group (only E₆ has a non‑trivial one). For trace formula questions, distinguish stable conjugacy classes (endoscopic) from ordinary conjugacy classes. Memorise the list of endoscopic groups for each exceptional type: F₄ → Spin(9), Sp(6)×SL(2); E₆ → Spin(10)×U(1), F₄; E₇ → E₆×U(1), Spin(12)×SU(2); E₈ has no proper endoscopic groups. This checklist prevents confusion under time pressure.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the p‑adic Langlands Correspondence for GLn over Function Fields (n ≥ 3)

The p‑adic Langlands correspondence over a p‑adic field relates continuous representations of the absolute Galois group to admissible unitary Banach space representations of a p‑adic reductive group. Over a global function field K of characteristic p, the analogue replaces the p‑adic field by the completion Kv at a place v of characteristic p. For GL₂, the correspondence was constructed by V. Lafforgue using the moduli of shtukas and the Fargues–Fontaine curve; the resulting functor (the Colmez functor) attaches to a continuous ℓ‑adic Galois representation a locally analytic representation of GL₂(Kv). For GLn with n ≥ 3, the correspondence remains conjectural. The main obstacle is the lack of a suitable p‑adic period domain for higher rank; the Drinfeld upper half‑plane uniformizes only GL₂‑shtukas. The Fargues–Scholze geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence provides a candidate framework: the moduli stack of local shtukas for GLn over the Fargues–Fontaine curve is expected to carry a sheaf of categories whose cohomology realizes the correspondence. The theory of (φ,Γ)‑modules over the Robba ring for function fields, developed by Kedlaya and Liu, gives a classification of p‑adic Galois representations in terms of Frobenius modules; this is the function field analogue of Fontaine’s theory. The Colmez functor for GL₂ uses the cohomology of the Drinfeld upper half‑plane; for higher rank one would need a higher‑dimensional rigid analytic variety uniformizing GLn‑shtukas, which is not known. The work of Fargues and Scholze on the geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence for all reductive groups over p‑adic fields suggests that the moduli stack of local shtukas for GLn over the Fargues–Fontaine curve should play the role of the period domain. The categorical Langlands correspondence for function fields, proved by Gaitsgory and Lurie in the geometric setting, provides a geometric incarnation of the correspondence for GLn over the curve; the p‑adic analogue would require a p‑adic version of the geometric Satake equivalence. The function field analogue of the Breuil–Mézard conjecture, relating deformation rings of Galois representations to cycles on the moduli of local shtukas, is open for n ≥ 3. The theory of p‑adic eigenvarieties for GLn over function fields, constructed by Andreatta, Iovita, and Pilloni using overconvergent cohomology of the moduli of shtukas, gives families of p‑adic automorphic forms; the correspondence would match these families with families of Galois representations. The local‑global compatibility for GLn (n ≥ 3) is known only in the ℓ‑adic setting (Lafforgue); the p‑adic compatibility is a major open problem. Examiners often test the distinction between the ℓ‑adic global Langlands correspondence (a theorem for all n) and the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence (a theorem only for GL₂). They also ask for the role of the Fargues–Fontaine curve: it replaces the Drinfeld upper half‑plane in the p‑adic setting and provides a geometric object whose vector bundles are classified by the Harder–Narasimhan filtration, mirroring the classification of p‑adic Galois representations.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Iwasawa Main Conjecture for Higher Rank Drinfeld Modules

The classical Iwasawa main conjecture relates the characteristic ideal of the Selmer group of an elliptic curve over a cyclotomic ℤp-extension to the p‑adic L‑function. In the function field setting, the cyclotomic extension is replaced by the constant field extension K∞/K obtained by adjoining all p-power roots of unity (which are just the constant field extensions). For rank‑one Drinfeld modules (the Carlitz module), the Iwasawa main conjecture was proved by Goss and later by Taelman using the theory of t‑motives and the Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem. For higher rank Drinfeld modules, the conjecture predicts an equality between the characteristic ideal of the Selmer group of the associated t‑motive over the constant field ℤp-extension and the Goss L‑function evaluated at the trivial character. The Selmer group is defined using the Galois cohomology of the Tate module of the Drinfeld module; the t‑motive provides a Frobenius module whose rigid analytic trivialization yields the p‑adic L‑function via the Anderson–Brownawell–Papanikolas criterion. The main conjecture for higher rank has been proved in several cases by Maurischat and others using the theory of Anderson dual t‑motives and the Euler system of Drinfeld module torsion points. The Euler system is constructed from the norm‑compatible system of torsion points of the Drinfeld module over the constant field extension; its non‑vanishing is equivalent to the non‑vanishing of the L‑function at the central point. The characteristic ideal lives in the Iwasawa algebra Λ = 𝔽q[[Γ]] where Γ ≅ ℤp is the Galois group of the constant field extension. The p‑adic L‑function is an element of Λ constructed by interpolating special values of the Goss L‑function at characters of finite order. The main conjecture asserts that the characteristic ideal of the Pontryagin dual of the Selmer group equals the principal ideal generated by the p‑adic L‑function. The proof uses the control theorem for Selmer groups over the constant field extension, the explicit reciprocity law for Drinfeld modules (the Drinfeld reciprocity law), and the theory of syntomic cohomology for t‑motives. A key examiner point is the distinction between the constant field ℤp-extension and the cyclotomic ℤp-extension in number fields: in function fields the constant field extension is unramified outside the infinite place, while the cyclotomic extension in number fields is ramified at p. The function field Iwasawa theory is therefore simpler in terms of ramification but requires the theory of t‑motives to handle the Frobenius action. The Anderson log‑algebraicity theorem gives an explicit formula for the logarithm of algebraic points on the uniformized Drinfeld module, which is used to compute the p‑adic L‑function. The function field analogue of the Greenberg conjecture (vanishing of the μ‑invariant) is known for the Carlitz module and for many higher rank Drinfeld modules; the μ‑invariant measures the growth of the p‑part of the class group in the constant field extension. The main conjecture for higher rank Drinfeld modules with complex multiplication has been proved by using the theory of complex multiplication for Drinfeld modules (Hayes) and the explicit class field theory for the constant field extension.

The Drinfeld Modules and the Function Field Analogue of the Geometric Langlands Correspondence for the Exceptional Group F4 via Shtukas

The geometric Langlands correspondence for a reductive group G over a curve X over a finite field relates the derived category of D‑modules on the moduli stack BunG of G‑bundles on X to the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSysLG of local systems for the Langlands dual group LG. For the exceptional group F₄, the dual group is again F₄ (adjoint). The function field analogue replaces D‑modules by ℓ‑adic sheaves and local systems by ℓ‑adic local systems; the correspondence is realized via the cohomology of the moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas. The moduli stack ShtF₄ of F₄‑shtukas with one leg at a point x ∈ X and possibly level structure at other points carries Hecke correspondences indexed by dominant coweights of F₄. The geometric Satake equivalence identifies the spherical Hecke category with the category of representations of the dual group F₄(ℚℓ). The categorical Langlands correspondence, proved by Gaitsgory and Lurie for all reductive groups, constructs a functor from the category of ind‑coherent sheaves on LocSysF₄ to the category of D‑modules on BunF₄ which is an equivalence after suitable completions. In the function field setting, the cohomology of the moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas with coefficients in Hecke sheaves provides a geometric realization of the automorphic spectral decomposition. The trace of Frobenius on this cohomology computes the automorphic L‑functions for F₄. The endoscopic classification for F₄, proved by Ngô using the Hitchin fibration, ensures that the stable trace formula for F₄ matches the stable trace formula for its endoscopic groups (Spin(9) and Sp(6)×SL(2)). The geometric Langlands correspondence for F₄ predicts that the Hecke eigensheaves on BunF₄ correspond to F₄‑local systems on X. The construction of Hecke eigensheaves for F₄ uses the geometric Satake equivalence and the factorization property of the Hecke category. The moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas with parabolic structure at a divisor provides a compactification that allows the definition of Eisenstein sheaves; the constant term of these Eisenstein sheaves is computed by the geometric Langlands correspondence for the Levi subgroups (which are products of GLn and smaller exceptional groups). The function field analogue of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula for F₄ is obtained by applying the Lefschetz trace formula to the moduli stack of F₄‑shtukas; the geometric side involves sums over conjugacy classes in F₄(K) of orbital integrals, while the spectral side involves sums over automorphic representations. The fundamental lemma for F₄, proved by Ngô, guarantees the equality of orbital integrals needed for endoscopic transfer. The geometric Langlands correspondence for F₄ also implies the function field analogue of the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture: the Satake parameters of cuspidal automorphic representations are bounded by 1, which follows from the purity of the associated ℓ‑adic local systems (Deligne’s Weil II). The theory of periods for F₄‑shtukas, developed via the Anderson t‑motive framework, connects special values of L‑functions to algebraic periods arising from the de Rham cohomology of the associated t‑motives.

  • Confusing the simply‑connected and adjoint forms of exceptional groups when stating the Satake isomorphism.
  • Assuming the p‑adic Langlands correspondence for GLn over function fields is a theorem for n ≥ 3; it remains conjectural.
  • Neglecting the quadratic twist arising from the center of the adjoint form of F₄ in the local correspondence.
  • Mixing up the stable trace formula with the ordinary trace formula when discussing endoscopic transfer for inner forms.
  • Overlooking the role of triality in permuting the three 8‑dimensional representations of Spin(8) and its effect on L‑functions.
  • Treating the loop group LG as a finite‑dimensional algebraic group; it is an ind‑scheme and its affine Grassmannian is an ind‑projective ind‑scheme.
  • Believing that the geometric Langlands equivalence for GLn over function fields is proved without using the theory of factorization algebras and ind‑coherent sheaves.

The Drinfeld Modular Forms for GLn and the Theory of Eisenstein Cohomology

The Eisenstein cohomology of Drinfeld modular varieties provides a bridge between the cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas and the spectral decomposition of automorphic forms for GLn over a global function field K. For a split reductive group G = GLn, the Borel–Serre compactification of the Drinfeld symmetric space yields a space whose cohomology carries an action of the Hecke algebra. The Eisenstein classes are constructed by inducing cuspidal automorphic representations from proper Levi subgroups M ⊂ G and integrating over the corresponding boundary strata. In the function field setting, the boundary strata are indexed by parabolic subgroups and are isomorphic to products of lower‑rank Drinfeld modular varieties. The resulting Eisenstein cohomology classes lie in the cohomology of the locally symmetric space with coefficients in the local system attached to a finite‑dimensional representation of G. A fundamental theorem of Harder, extended by Lafforgue and later by Vincent Lafforgue, shows that the Eisenstein cohomology accounts for the non‑cuspidal part of the automorphic spectrum and that the Hecke eigenvalues on Eisenstein classes match the Langlands parameters of the induced representations. The constant terms of Eisenstein series are expressed as sums over the Weyl group of intertwining operators; their meromorphic continuation and functional equations are proved using the theory of L‑functions for GLn over function fields, which are rational functions in q−s. The Eisenstein cohomology also controls the contribution of the continuous spectrum to the trace formula, and its explicit description is essential for the proof of the global Langlands correspondence for GLn via the comparison of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula with the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula on the moduli of shtukas. In particular, the residues of Eisenstein series at poles corresponding to the trivial representation give rise to the one‑dimensional automorphic representations that appear in the cohomology of the boundary. The theory of Eisenstein cohomology for Drinfeld modular varieties has been developed in the works of G. Harder, J. Heinloth, and B. C. Ngô, and it plays a central role in the geometric Langlands program for GLn because the Hecke eigensheaves on the moduli stack Bunn are constructed from the perverse sheaves that realize the Eisenstein cohomology classes under the function‑field analogue of the Matsushima formula.

The Function Field Analogue of the Local Langlands Correspondence for Non‑Split Groups via Shtukas

For a non‑split reductive group G over a local function field F = 𝔽q((t)), the local Langlands correspondence predicts a bijection between irreducible smooth representations of G(F) and Langlands parameters, i.e. homomorphisms from the Weil–Deligne group W'F to the L‑group LG. In the function field setting, this correspondence can be realized geometrically using the moduli space of G‑shtukas with one leg at a point of a curve X over 𝔽q and with prescribed level structure at other points. The key idea, due to V. Lafforgue and later refined by Zhu, is to consider the affine Grassmannian GrG for the loop group LG and the convolution action of the spherical Hecke category on the derived category of constructible sheaves on GrG. The geometric Satake equivalence identifies the spherical Hecke category with the category of finite‑dimensional representations of the dual group ˇG. For non‑split groups, the dual group is a semi‑direct product of the complex dual group with the Galois group of the splitting field. The moduli stack of G‑shtukas with one leg carries a natural action of the local Langlands group via the monodromy of the Frobenius at the leg. The cohomology of this moduli stack, equipped with the Hecke action, decomposes into a direct sum of tensor products of irreducible representations of G(F) and the corresponding Langlands parameters. The proof of the correspondence for non‑split groups uses the theory of K‑types and the classification of supercuspidal representations via Yu’s construction, together with the fact that the local Langlands correspondence for GLn over function fields is already known (Lafforgue). By endoscopic transfer and the fundamental lemma (proved by Ngô for all groups), the correspondence for a general non‑split group is reduced to the split case. The resulting bijection respects L‑functions, epsilon factors, and the local functional equation. Moreover, the geometric construction yields a canonical normalization of the local factors, which is essential for the global Langlands correspondence and for the definition of the automorphic L‑functions attached to G. The method also extends to inner forms of GLn and to classical groups, where the moduli of shtukas with parahoric level structure provides a uniform framework for the local correspondence.

Worked Example: Eisenstein Cohomology Class for GL2
Let K = 𝔽q(t) and consider the Drinfeld modular curve Y(Γ) of level Γ ⊂ GL2(𝔽q[t]). Describe the Eisenstein cohomology class in H1(Y(Γ), ℚℓ) attached to the trivial character of the Borel subgroup, and compute its Hecke eigenvalues at a prime 𝔭 not dividing the level.
The Eisenstein class is obtained by inducing the trivial representation from the Borel B to GL2. On the modular curve, the boundary consists of cusps indexed by GL2(K) / B(K) Γ. The Eisenstein series E(z, s) = Σγ∈BGL2 Im(γz)s converges for Re(s) > 1 and has a simple pole at s = 1 with residue a constant function. The associated cohomology class is the Poincaré dual of the divisor given by the sum of all cusps. The Hecke operator T𝔭 acts on this class by multiplication by qdeg 𝔭 + 1, which are the Satake parameters of the induced representation IndBGL2(1). This matches the Langlands parameter of the trivial representation of the Weil group, confirming the local‑global compatibility at 𝔭.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Hecke eigenvalue on an Eisenstein class, first identify the inducing data (character of the Levi). The eigenvalue is the value of the corresponding Satake polynomial at the Frobenius conjugacy class. For GL2 the polynomial is X2 − (qdeg+1)X + qdeg; the Eisenstein class corresponds to the root qdeg+1. Memorise this pattern for rank‑two and generalise to GLn by using the elementary symmetric functions of the Satake parameters.

The Theory of Drinfeld Modules over Global Function Fields with Infinite Places

Classical Drinfeld modules are defined over a global function field K with a fixed place ∞, and they provide an analogue of elliptic curves over number fields. When one allows the base field to have several places at infinity, the theory extends to S‑Drinfeld modules, where S is a finite set of places containing ∞. An S‑Drinfeld module of rank r over a ring A = 𝒪K(S) is a homomorphism φ : A → End𝔾a(R) such that for each a ∈ A the endomorphism φa is a polynomial in the Frobenius endomorphism τ with leading coefficient a and degree r·deg(a). The presence of several infinite places changes the analytic uniformization: the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ωr is replaced by a product of r‑dimensional Drinfeld symmetric spaces associated to each place in S {∞}. The uniformization theorem of Drinfeld and later of Kapranov and Reversat states that the moduli space of S‑Drinfeld modules with level structure is isomorphic to a quotient of this product by a discrete subgroup of the product of the corresponding GLr(Kv). The cohomology of these Shimura‑type varieties carries an action of the Hecke algebra away from S and realizes the automorphic forms for GLr over K that are unramified outside S. The theory of S‑Drinfeld modules also provides a natural framework for the function field analogue of the Stark conjectures: the special values of the Goss L‑functions at s = 1 are expressed in terms of logarithms of S‑units in the torsion fields of the S‑Drinfeld module. Hayes’ explicit class field theory for the Carlitz module (rank one, S = {∞}) generalises to higher rank S‑Drinfeld modules via the work of Gekeler, Reversat, and others, yielding explicit generators of abelian extensions of K ramified only at places in S. The period lattice of an S‑Drinfeld module is a discrete A‑submodule of the product of the completions Kv for v ∈ S, and its rank equals r·|S|. The Anderson–Brownawell–Papanikolas criterion for transcendence of periods extends to this setting, giving algebraic independence results for the periods of S‑Drinfeld modules. Finally, the moduli of S‑Drinfeld modules with parabolic level structure at the places in S provides a compactification whose boundary strata are indexed by Levi subgroups of GLr, enabling the study of Eisenstein cohomology and the trace formula for the group GLr over K with prescribed ramification.

The Drinfeld Modular Curves and Their Integral Models over the Ring of Integers

The integral models of Drinfeld modular curves over the ring of integers 𝒪K at a prime 𝔭 not dividing the level are constructed by extending the moduli problem of Drinfeld modules with level structure to schemes over 𝒪K. The key input is the theory of canonical subgroups for Drinfeld modules, developed by Gekeler and later by Vincent Lafforgue, which provides a finite flat subgroup scheme of rank qdeg 𝔭 inside the 𝔭‑torsion of a Drinfeld module with good reduction. Using this canonical subgroup, one defines a moduli stack over 𝒪K that classifies Drinfeld modules together with a Drinfeld level structure away from 𝔭 and a canonical subgroup at 𝔭. The resulting stack is proper and flat over 𝒪K, and its generic fibre is the usual Drinfeld modular curve. The special fibre at 𝔭 is a union of irreducible components isomorphic to projective lines, intersecting transversally at supersingular points. The dual graph of the special fibre is the Bruhat–Tits tree of GL2(K𝔭), and the action of the Hecke operators on the special fibre corresponds to the action of the Hecke algebra on the tree. This description yields a precise formula for the reduction of Drinfeld modular forms modulo 𝔭: a modular form of weight k reduces to a section of the k‑th power of the Hodge bundle on the special fibre, and its restriction to each component is a polynomial in the coordinate on the projective line. The Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for Drinfeld modular curves identifies the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the generic fibre with the space of cuspidal automorphic forms for GL2(K) and shows that the Frobenius eigenvalues on the special fibre match the Hecke eigenvalues. The integral model also allows one to define the 𝔭‑adic uniformization of the Drinfeld modular curve via the Drinfeld upper half‑plane Ω2 over K𝔭, and to construct 𝔭‑adic L‑functions by integrating modular forms against measures on the boundary of Ω2. The theory of bad reduction at primes dividing the level is more subtle; the special fibre acquires non‑reduced structure and the monodromy operator on the nearby cycles is described by the weight‑monodromy conjecture, which is known in this setting thanks to the work of Laumon, Rapoport, and Stuhler. The integral models are essential for the proof of the local Langlands correspondence for GL2 over function fields via the realization of the correspondence in the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the Lubin–Tate tower, which is the 𝔭‑adic analogue of the Drinfeld modular curve.

  • Confusing the role of the canonical subgroup with the full 𝔭‑torsion when describing the integral model.
  • Assuming the special fibre of a Drinfeld modular curve is always a union of smooth rational curves; at primes dividing the level it can be non‑reduced.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the Drinfeld upper half‑plane and the Bruhat–Tits tree when discussing 𝔭‑adic uniformization.
  • Overlooking the fact that the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for Drinfeld modular curves involves the cohomology of the generic fibre, not the special fibre.
  • Treating the Hecke action on the dual graph as the same as the Hecke action on the space of harmonic cochains without the twist by the determinant character.
  • Believing that the period lattice of an S‑Drinfeld module is a free A‑module of rank r; its rank is r·|S|.
  • Mixing up the Satake parameters of an Eisenstein class with those of a cuspidal representation; the Eisenstein parameters are induced from the Levi and are not tempered in general.

These traps highlight the subtle points that often appear in advanced examinations.
