hand/langlands-physics.html:
Topological Twisting of N=4 Super Yang–Mills and the Kapustin–Witten Equations

Topological twisting is a procedure that converts a supersymmetric quantum field theory into a topological quantum field theory by redefining the Lorentz symmetry using an R‑symmetry current. For N=4 super Yang–Mills in four dimensions there are three inequivalent twists, traditionally labelled A, B, and the half‑twist introduced by Kapustin and Witten. The half‑twist preserves two supercharges of opposite chirality and yields a theory whose observables are invariant under diffeomorphisms of the four‑manifold but depend on a complexified gauge coupling τ. The resulting equations of motion are the Kapustin–Witten equations, a first‑order system for a gauge field A and a one‑form φ valued in the adjoint bundle:

F_A − φ ∧ φ + ⋆ d_A φ = 0, d_A ⋆ φ = 0.

Here F_A is the curvature of A, d_A the covariant derivative, and ⋆ the Hodge star on the four‑manifold M = C × Σ where C is a Riemann surface and Σ a two‑dimensional surface. Solutions of these equations define a moduli space that is identified with the Hitchin moduli space M_H(G) of Higgs bundles on C. The parameters of the twist (the canonical parameter t) interpolate between the A‑model (t = 0) and the B‑model (t = ∞) on M_H(G). At t = 1 the theory is self‑dual under S‑duality, which exchanges the gauge group G with its Langlands dual ^L G and inverts τ. This geometric realisation of the geometric Langlands correspondence shows that A‑branes on M_H(G) (supported on Lagrangian submanifolds) correspond to Hecke eigensheaves, while B‑branes (coherent sheaves) correspond to automorphic D‑modules on Bun_G(C). The Kapustin–Witten equations also admit a dimensional reduction to the Hitchin equations on C, providing a direct link between four‑dimensional gauge theory and two‑dimensional integrable systems.

Higher‑Form Symmetries, Anomaly Inflow, and the Classification of Defects

Ordinary global symmetries act on local operators; higher‑form symmetries act on extended operators of dimension p. A q‑form symmetry is a symmetry whose charged objects are q‑dimensional defects. In a d‑dimensional QFT a (d−2)‑form symmetry can have a ’t Hooft anomaly that is cancelled by anomaly inflow from a (d+1)‑dimensional bulk topological term. The classic example is the U(1) one‑form symmetry of four‑dimensional pure Yang–Mills theory, whose anomaly is captured by a five‑dimensional Chern–Simons term ∫ B ∧ F ∧ F where B is a two‑form background gauge field. The inflow mechanism, first described by Callan and Harvey for string theory, states that the non‑conservation of the symmetry current on the boundary equals the variation of the bulk action. This principle underlies the classification of symmetry‑protected topological (SPT) phases: a (d+1)‑dimensional invertible TQFT with a given symmetry group G classifies SPT phases in d dimensions via the cobordism group Ωd+1_G. For finite group symmetries the classification reduces to group cohomology Hd+1(G, U(1)), while for continuous symmetries one must use the full cobordism spectrum. Defects of various codimensions are organised into a higher‑category (a fusion n‑category for n‑form symmetries). The condensation of defects corresponds to gauging a higher‑form symmetry, and the resulting theory may have a different set of higher‑form symmetries, a phenomenon known as symmetry fractionalisation. These ideas have been applied to the classification of topological orders in condensed matter, to the study of duality defects in conformal field theories, and to the construction of non‑invertible symmetries that generalise the notion of a group.

Technique: Identifying Anomaly Inflow for a 3d Chern–Simons Boundary
A three‑dimensional U(1)_k Chern–Simons theory on a manifold with boundary ∂M carries a U(1) one‑form symmetry. Show how the bulk Chern–Simons term cancels the boundary anomaly by computing the variation of the bulk action under a one‑form gauge transformation B → B + dλ, where λ is a one‑form parameter.
The bulk action is S_bulk = (k/4π) ∫_M A ∧ dA. Under a one‑form gauge transformation of the background two‑form field B (which couples to the one‑form current J = (k/2π) * dA), the boundary term varies as δS_boundary = (k/2π) ∫∂M λ ∧ dA. The bulk variation is δS_bulk = (k/4π) ∫_M dλ ∧ dA = (k/4π) ∫∂M λ ∧ dA by Stokes’ theorem. The total variation δS_bulk + δS_boundary = 0, demonstrating that the bulk Chern–Simons term provides exactly the inflow needed to cancel the boundary anomaly.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the anomaly inflow mechanism, write the bulk action, perform the gauge variation, apply Stokes’ theorem, and match the boundary term. Keep the coefficients (k/4π, k/2π) explicit; examiners award marks for correct normalisation.

The Cobordism Hypothesis and Fully Extended Topological Quantum Field Theories

The cobordism hypothesis, proved by Lurie building on the Baez–Dolan cobordism conjecture, classifies fully extended topological quantum field theories (TQFTs) valued in a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)‑category C. An n‑dimensional fully extended TQFT is a symmetric monoidal functor Z: Bord_nfr → C from the (∞,n)‑category of framed cobordisms to C. The hypothesis states that such functors are equivalent to fully dualisable objects of C. In particular, a once‑extended 3‑dimensional TQFT (assigning vector spaces to surfaces and linear maps to 3‑manifolds) corresponds to a pivotal fusion category; a fully extended 3‑dimensional TQFT corresponds to a modular tensor category. The classification of gapped topological phases of matter in d spatial dimensions with symmetry group G is given by the homotopy groups of the mapping spectrum Map(BG, MTO(d)) where MTO(d) is the Madsen–Tillmann spectrum for tangential structures. For unitary TQFTs the relevant target is the (∞,d+1)‑category of higher vector spaces. The Freed–Hopkins–Teleman theorem identifies the Verlinde fusion category of a compact Lie group G at level k with the equivariant K‑theory of the moduli stack of flat G‑bundles on a surface, providing a concrete realisation of the cobordism hypothesis for Chern–Simons theory. The hypothesis also predicts that invertible TQFTs (those assigning one‑dimensional vector spaces) are classified by the cobordism groups Ωd+1_G, which matches the SPT classification mentioned above.

Geometric Langlands for Real Reductive Groups: Opers, Hecke Eigensheaves, and the Spectral Side

The geometric Langlands program originally formulated for complex reductive groups extends to real groups via the work of Gaitsgory, Nadler, and others. For a real reductive group G_R the Langlands dual is a complex group ^L G equipped with an involution. The spectral side of the correspondence involves the moduli stack Loc^L G(C) of ^L G‑local systems on a complex curve C, but one must restrict to those local systems that admit a reduction to the real form, i.e. to G_R‑Higgs bundles satisfying a reality condition. Opers, introduced by Drinfeld and Sokolov, provide a distinguished substack Op^L G(C) ⊂ Loc^L G(C) consisting of connections with a specific flag structure. For G = SL(2,R) the opers are precisely the projective structures on C, and the corresponding Hecke eigensheaves are the automorphic D‑modules attached to uniformising representations. The categorical equivalence D^b(Coh(Loc^L G(C))) ≅ D^b(Mod_D(BunG_R(C))) is expected to hold after suitable derived enhancements and after incorporating the real structure via a Galois action. Recent progress uses the theory of D‑modules on the stack of G_R‑bundles and the geometry of the Hitchin fibration for real groups, where the base is the space of real Hitchin Hamiltonians. The spectral decomposition of the Hitchin system yields a Lagrangian fibration whose fibres are real tori; the Fourier–Mukai transform along this fibration implements the geometric Langlands correspondence at the level of categories. This real version is essential for applications to the Langlands programme over number fields, where the local Langlands correspondence for real places involves representations of real groups.

Matrix Models, Non‑Perturbative String Theory, and the AdS/CFT Correspondence

Matrix models provide non‑perturbative definitions of string theory in certain backgrounds. The BFSS matrix model (Banks–Fischler–Shenker–Susskind, 1997) describes M‑theory in the infinite momentum frame as the quantum mechanics of N×N Hermitian matrices X^i (i=1,…,9) with action S = ∫ dt Tr(½ D_t X^i D_t X^i + ¼ [X^i, X^j]2 + fermions). In the large N limit the model reproduces the dynamics of D0‑branes and, via T‑duality, the full spectrum of type IIA string theory. The IKKT matrix model (Ishibashi–Kawai–Kitazawa–Tsuchiya, 1996) is a zero‑dimensional model with action S = −¼ Tr([X^μ, X^ν]2) + fermions, proposed as a constructive definition of type IIB string theory. Both models exhibit emergent spacetime geometry from matrix eigenvalues. The AdS/CFT correspondence, conjectured by Maldacena in 1997, states that type IIB string theory on AdS5 × S5 with N units of five‑form flux is dual to N=4 super Yang–Mills theory with gauge group SU(N) on the four‑dimensional boundary. The dictionary identifies the string coupling g_s with the Yang–Mills coupling g_YM2 = 4π g_s, and the AdS radius L with (4π g_s N)1/4 α'1/2. In the planar limit N → ∞, λ = g_YM2 N fixed, the gauge theory becomes integrable and the spectral problem is solved by the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz. The correspondence extends to less supersymmetric backgrounds via orbifolds, marginal deformations, and top‑down constructions such as the Klebanov–Witten and Klebanov–Strassler models. Holographic renormalisation provides a precise map between bulk fields and boundary operators, allowing computation of correlation functions, entanglement entropy (via the Ryu–Takayanagi formula), and transport coefficients. Matrix models and AdS/CFT together give a concrete framework for studying quantum gravity non‑perturbatively.

  • Confusing the three topological twists of N=4 SYM; only the Kapustin–Witten half‑twist yields the geometric Langlands correspondence.
  • Treating higher‑form symmetries as ordinary 0‑form symmetries; their charged objects are extended defects, not local operators.
  • Assuming the cobordism hypothesis applies to non‑fully‑extended TQFTs without specifying the target (∞,n)‑category.
  • Neglecting the reality condition on local systems when moving from complex to real geometric Langlands.
  • Mixing the BFSS and IKKT matrix models; BFSS is a 1‑dimensional quantum mechanics, IKKT is a 0‑dimensional integral.
  • Forgetting that the AdS/CFT dictionary requires the large N, strong ’t Hooft coupling limit for classical gravity.
  • Overlooking the role of anomaly inflow in cancelling boundary anomalies of Chern–Simons theories.

hand/schramm-loewner.html:
Multifractal Spectrum and Intersection Exponents

The multifractal spectrum of an SLE curve quantifies how the harmonic measure distributes along the trace. For chordal SLEκ in the upper half‑plane, the probability that the curve passes within distance ε of a boundary point scales like εα where α varies with the local geometry. The spectrum f(α) is obtained from the Legendre transform of the moment scaling exponents ξ(q) defined by E[|g′t(x)|q] ≍ t−ξ(q). Lawler, Schramm and Werner (2001) computed ξ(q) = ( (4+κ)q − κ q2 ) / (8κ) for q in the admissible range, leading to a concave spectrum supported on [αmin, αmax]. Intersection exponents describe the probability that two independent SLEκ curves avoid each other up to time t. For κ ≤ 4 the curves are simple and the exponent is zero; for 4 < κ < 8 the exponent is positive and given by ξ2(κ) = (8−κ)(κ−4) / (8κ). These exponents enter the derivation of the Hausdorff dimension of the SLE trace, d = 1 + κ/8 for κ ≤ 8, and of the dimension of the set of double points, ddouble = 2 − (8−κ)(κ−4)/(8κ). The multifractal formalism also connects to the quantum gravity coupling: the KPZ relation maps Euclidean scaling dimensions Δ to quantum dimensions ΔQ via Δ = (γ2/4) ΔQ2 + (1−γ2/4) ΔQ with γ = √κ for κ ≤ 4 and γ = 4/√κ for κ ≥ 4.

SLE Duality and Reversibility

The duality κ 16/κ relates chordal SLEκ in a simply connected domain to chordal SLE16/κ in the complementary domain after a conformal map that swaps the boundary points. For κ ≤ 4 the curve is simple and its exterior is a simply connected domain; the outer boundary of SLEκ has the law of SLE16/κ. This duality was proved by Zhan (2008) using the commutation relations of the Loewner flow and the martingale characterization of SLE. Reversibility, established by Zhan (2015) for κ ≤ 4 and by Miller and Sheffield (2016) for all κ ∈ (0,8), states that the time‑reversal of a chordal SLEκ curve from a to b has the same law as a chordal SLEκ curve from b to a, up to a conformal automorphism of the domain. The proof uses the imaginary geometry coupling: the flow lines of the Gaussian free field with appropriate angle differences are reversible because the underlying field is invariant under reflection. For κ > 4 the curve has self‑intersections and the reversal involves the exploration of the complementary components; the duality then identifies the reversed curve with SLE16/κ in the complementary domain. These results are essential for the construction of the conformal welding of Liouville quantum gravity surfaces, where the welding curve is SLEκ and the two sides of the welding are independent LQG surfaces with parameter γ = √κ (κ ≤ 4) or γ = 4/√κ (κ ≥ 4).

Worked Example: Computing the Intersection Exponent for κ = 6
Find the intersection exponent ξ2(6) for two independent SLE6 curves in the upper half‑plane and interpret its meaning for critical percolation interfaces.
For κ = 6 the formula ξ2(κ) = (8−κ)(κ−4) / (8κ) gives ξ2(6) = (2)(2) / (48) = 4/48 = 1/12. This exponent governs the probability that two percolation exploration paths, which converge to SLE6, stay disjoint up to macroscopic scale R: P(disjoint up to R) ≍ R−1/12. The small positive exponent reflects the fact that percolation interfaces touch but do not cross, a hallmark of the κ = 6 phase.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for an intersection exponent, first identify κ from the model (percolation → 6, Ising → 3, LERW → 2). Then apply the closed‑form formula ξ2(κ) = (8−κ)(κ−4)/(8κ). Remember that for κ ≤ 4 the exponent is zero because the curves are simple and cannot intersect. Write the exponent as a reduced fraction; examiners often check the simplification step.

Imaginary Geometry and Flow Lines

Imaginary geometry, developed by Miller and Sheffield (2012), provides a deterministic coupling between the Gaussian free field (GFF) and SLE curves. Let h be a zero‑boundary GFF on a simply connected domain D. For a parameter χ = 2/√κ − √κ/2, the flow lines of the complex field h + iχ are curves that solve the ordinary differential equation dη/dt = ei (h(η) + χ) in a suitable sense. These flow lines are almost surely well defined and have the law of chordal SLEκ. Different choices of the height gap (the difference in the GFF values on the two sides of the curve) produce SLEκ with different boundary conditions: a height gap of π gives the standard chordal SLEκ, while a gap of λπ with λ ∈ (0,1) yields SLEκ(ρ) processes with force points. The coupling is symmetric: the GFF can be reconstructed from the collection of all flow lines, and the field is invariant under the operation of reversing a flow line and changing the sign of χ. This construction yields a natural proof of reversibility for all κ ∈ (0,8) and provides a geometric interpretation of the duality κ 16/κ: the flow lines of h + iχ and of −h + iχ′ with χ′ = −χ are the same curves traversed in opposite directions. Imaginary geometry also underlies the mating‑of‑trees framework, where a pair of correlated continuum random trees (the Brownian continuum random tree and its dual) are glued along their boundaries to produce an SLEκ‑decorated Liouville quantum gravity sphere.

Quantum Loewner Evolution and Mating of Trees

The quantum Loewner evolution (QLE) introduced by Miller and Sheffield (2016) describes the growth of an SLE curve on a Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surface. Let φ be a GFF on the unit disk and let the LQG metric be eγ φ times the Euclidean metric with γ = √κ for κ ≤ 4. The QLE(γ2, η) process evolves a hull Kt by adding infinitesimal quantum‑area balls of size e−t to the tip of the curve. The parameter η controls the turning angle of the curve relative to the quantum boundary length. When η = 0 the process reduces to the standard chordal SLEκ on the quantum surface; for η ≠ 0 one obtains SLEκ(ρ) with force points determined by the quantum boundary lengths. The mating‑of‑trees theorem states that the pair of continuum random trees encoded by the left and right boundary lengths of the QLE hulls, when glued together, produce a topological sphere decorated by an SLEκ curve. This sphere, equipped with the LQG metric, has the law of the Brownian map when κ = 8 (γ = 2). For general κ the resulting random metric space is the γ‑LQG sphere. The theorem provides a rigorous bridge between discrete random planar maps (uniform quadrangulations, bipolar orientations) and continuum SLE/LQG objects, and it underpins the proof that the scaling limit of uniform random planar maps is the Brownian map.

Convergence Proofs: Tightness and Conformal Invariance

Establishing that a discrete interface converges to SLEκ requires two main steps: tightness of the family of curves in the space of continuous curves modulo reparametrization, and identification of the limit via conformal invariance and the domain Markov property. Tightness is usually proved by verifying the Hölder‑type condition of Aizenman and Burchard (1999): there exist constants C, α > 0 such that for any annulus A(z, r, R) the probability that the curve crosses the annulus is bounded by C (r/R)α. For critical percolation on the triangular lattice, Smirnov (2001) used the Cardy formula to obtain crossing probabilities that are conformally invariant in the scaling limit, which yields the required crossing estimates. For the Ising model, Chelkak and Smirnov (2012) constructed a discrete fermionic observable satisfying a discrete Cauchy–Riemann equation; its scaling limit is a conformally covariant holomorphic function, from which tightness and conformal invariance follow. Once tightness is established, any subsequential limit is a random curve satisfying the domain Markov property and conformal invariance. Schramm (2000) showed that the only such curves are chordal SLEκ for some κ. The value of κ is then identified by computing a specific observable (e.g., the probability that the curve passes to the left of a given point) and matching it with the SLE martingale. This program has been carried out for percolation (κ = 6), LERW (κ = 2), UST (κ = 8), Ising (κ = 3), and the harmonic explorer (κ = 4). Recent work extends the method to the random cluster model with cluster weight q ∈ [1,4] (κ = 4π / arccos(−√q/2)) and to the six‑vertex model.

  • Confusing the intersection exponent formula with the Hausdorff dimension formula; they involve different algebraic expressions.
  • Assuming reversibility holds for all κ without noting the separate proofs for κ ≤ 4 and κ > 4.
  • Misapplying the KPZ relation by using the wrong γ (γ = √κ for κ ≤ 4, γ = 4/√κ for κ ≥ 4).
  • Overlooking the role of the height gap in imaginary geometry; different gaps produce SLEκ(ρ) not plain SLEκ.
  • Treating quantum Loewner evolution as identical to classical Loewner evolution; the driving measure is quantum boundary length, not Euclidean capacity.
  • Neglecting the tightness criterion when asked to outline a convergence proof; the Aizenman–Burchard condition is a standard exam checkpoint.
  • Mixing up the duality κ 16/κ with the reversibility statement; duality relates different κ values, reversibility relates the same κ forward and backward.
The advanced topics above complete the next level of the SLE curriculum.

hand/geometric-analysis.html:
Regularity Theory for Minimal Surfaces and Almgren's Theorem

The regularity of area‑minimizing integral currents is a cornerstone of geometric measure theory. De Giorgi and later Almgren proved that an area‑minimizing hypersurface in a smooth Riemannian manifold is smooth except for a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most n−8. Almgren's big regularity paper (2000) extended this to higher codimension: any area‑minimizing integral current of dimension m in a Riemannian manifold has a singular set of dimension at most m−2. The proof introduces the notion of multiple‑valued functions and a delicate blow‑up analysis that reduces the problem to the study of Dirichlet‑minimizing Q‑valued functions. The frequency function, introduced by Almgren, plays the role of a monotone quantity that controls the order of vanishing of the approximating functions. This monotonicity yields a stratification of the singular set and ultimately the dimension bound. The result is sharp: Simons' cone over S3×S3 in R8 is an area‑minimizing hypersurface with an isolated singularity at the origin, showing that the bound n−8 cannot be improved. In codimension one, the work of Schoen and Simon (1981) gave a more accessible proof using the stability inequality and the Simons identity, establishing smoothness for stable minimal hypersurfaces up to dimension 7. These regularity theorems are essential for the compactness theory of minimal surfaces and for the construction of minimal varieties via geometric measure theory.

The Positive Mass Theorem and Its Role in the Yamabe Problem

The positive mass theorem, proved by Schoen and Yau (1979) using minimal hypersurfaces and later by Witten (1981) via spinors, states that an asymptotically flat manifold of nonnegative scalar curvature has nonnegative ADM mass, with equality only for Euclidean space. In the Yamabe problem, the theorem enters through Schoen's resolution of the remaining case where the Yamabe constant equals that of the sphere. One considers a minimizing sequence for the Yamabe functional; if the infimum equals Y(S^n), a blow‑up analysis around a concentration point produces a complete noncompact metric of nonnegative scalar curvature that is asymptotically flat. The positive mass theorem then forces the ADM mass to be positive unless the original manifold is conformally equivalent to the sphere. This strict inequality Y(M,[g]) < Y(S^n) for non‑spherical manifolds guarantees the existence of a minimizer by the concentration‑compactness principle. The argument also uses the conformal Laplacian L_g = Δ_g + (n−2)/(4(n−1))R_g and the fact that the Green's function of L_g near a point has an expansion whose constant term is proportional to the ADM mass of the conformally blown‑up metric. The positive mass theorem thus bridges global differential geometry and the analytic variational problem, making it one of the most celebrated applications of geometric analysis.

Worked Example
Explain how the positive mass theorem yields the strict inequality Y(M,[g]) < Y(S^n) for a compact manifold not conformal to the sphere.
Assume Y(M,[g]) = Y(S^n). Take a minimizing sequence u_k for the Yamabe functional. By concentration‑compactness, either a minimizer exists (contradicting the assumption that M is not conformal to S^n) or the sequence concentrates at a point p. Rescale the metrics g_k = u_k4/(n−2)g around p so that the rescaled manifolds converge to a complete noncompact metric g_∞ on R^n with nonnegative scalar curvature and ADM mass m. The Yamabe constant of g_∞ equals Y(S^n). The positive mass theorem implies m ≥ 0, with equality only if g_∞ is flat. Flatness would mean the original manifold is conformal to S^n, which is excluded. Hence m > 0. However, the expansion of the Green's function of the conformal Laplacian shows that the mass term appears with a negative sign in the Yamabe functional, forcing Y(M,[g]) < Y(S^n). This contradiction proves the strict inequality.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the role of the positive mass theorem in the Yamabe problem, outline the blow‑up argument, the appearance of the ADM mass in the Green's function expansion, and the conclusion that equality of Yamabe constants forces conformal equivalence to the sphere. Mention both Schoen‑Yau and Witten proofs to show breadth.

Perelman's Entropy Functionals and the No‑Local‑Collapsing Theorem

Perelman introduced two monotone quantities for the Ricci flow: the F‑functional F(g,f) = ∫_M (R + |∇f|2) e-f dV and the W‑functional W(g,f,τ) = ∫_M [τ(R + |∇f|2) + f - n] (4πτ)-n/2 e-f dV. The W‑functional is essentially the logarithm of a Gaussian integral and is monotone nondecreasing along the Ricci flow coupled with the backward heat equation for f and the scaling parameter τ. The reduced volume Ṽ(τ) = ∫_M (4πτ)-n/2 e-l(q,τ) dV(q), where l is the reduced distance along L‑geodesics, is also monotone. These monotonicities imply that singularities of the Ricci flow are modeled on gradient shrinking solitons. The no‑local‑collapsing theorem states that if the curvature is bounded by r-2 on a parabolic ball P(x,t,r,-r2), then the volume of the spatial ball B(x,t,r) is at least κ r^n for a universal κ > 0 depending only on the initial metric. The proof uses the monotonicity of the reduced volume: a collapse would force the reduced volume to drop below a positive lower bound, contradicting monotonicity. This theorem is crucial for the compactness theory of Ricci flows and for the canonical neighborhood theorem, which classifies high‑curvature regions as ε‑necks, ε‑caps, or components with positive curvature operator. The entropy functionals also provide a Lyapunov function for the flow, enabling the analysis of ancient solutions and the classification of κ‑solutions.

Ancient Solutions and the Classification of Singularity Models in Ricci Flow

An ancient solution to the Ricci flow is a complete solution defined for all t ∈ (-∞, T] for some T ≤ ∞. Perelman showed that any blow‑up limit of a finite‑time singularity is a non‑flat, κ‑noncollapsed ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator. In three dimensions, Hamilton had earlier classified the possible ancient solutions with positive curvature operator: they are either the shrinking round sphere S3, the shrinking round cylinder S2×R, or a quotient thereof. Perelman extended this by proving that any three‑dimensional κ‑solution is isometric to one of these models or to the Bryant soliton (a steady gradient soliton) in the noncompact case. The classification uses the Hamilton‑Ivey pinching estimate, the differential Harnack inequality, and the asymptotic volume ratio. For higher dimensions, the classification remains open, but the work of Brendle, Naber, and others has identified many examples, including the FIK shrinkers and products of lower‑dimensional shrinkers. Understanding ancient solutions is essential for the surgery procedure: one cuts off regions that are ε‑close to a neck S2×R and caps them with standard caps, ensuring the flow can continue past singularities. The finite‑time extinction result for simply connected three‑manifolds follows because after finitely many surgeries all components become positively curved and shrink to points in finite time.

The Willmore Conjecture and Minimal Surfaces in the Three‑Sphere

The Willmore energy of an immersed surface Σ in R3 is W(Σ) = ∫_Σ H2 dA, where H is the mean curvature. The Willmore conjecture, proved by Marques and Neves (2012), states that for any immersed torus in R3, W(Σ) ≥ 2π2, with equality only for the Clifford torus up to conformal transformations. The proof uses the min‑max theory for the area functional in the three‑sphere S3. By stereographic projection, the Willmore energy in R3 corresponds to the area of a surface in S3 under the conformal map. Marques and Neves constructed a five‑parameter family of surfaces in S3 (the canonical family) and applied the Almgren‑Pitts min‑max theorem to produce a minimal surface of index ≤ 5. They then used the work of Urbano on the index of minimal surfaces in S3 to identify the Clifford torus as the unique minimizer of area among tori. The result also implies the Lawson conjecture that the only embedded minimal torus in S3 is the Clifford torus. The techniques combine geometric measure theory, the theory of varifolds, and the topology of the space of surfaces, illustrating the deep interplay between minimal surface theory and conformal geometry.

  • Confusing the dimension bound for singular sets of area‑minimizing hypersurfaces (n−8) with that for higher codimension (m−2).
  • Assuming the positive mass theorem applies without the asymptotically flat condition or nonnegative scalar curvature.
  • Mixing up the F‑functional and W‑functional monotonicities; the W‑functional includes the scaling parameter τ and is the one used for reduced volume.
  • Believing that all ancient solutions in three dimensions are shrinking solitons; the Bryant soliton is a steady ancient solution.
  • Thinking the Willmore conjecture concerns only tori in Euclidean space; the proof uses minimal surfaces in S3 via conformal equivalence.
  • Overlooking the role of the Almgren‑Pitts min‑max theorem in producing the minimal surface that realizes the Willmore bound.
  • Neglecting the necessity of the no‑local‑collapsing theorem for the compactness of Ricci flows with surgery.

These advanced topics illustrate how geometric analysis intertwines PDE techniques, variational methods, and topological classification to solve long‑standing problems in differential geometry.

hand/game-theory.html:
Bayesian Games and Incomplete Information

A Bayesian game extends the normal‑form framework by allowing each player to have private information, called a type, drawn from a commonly known probability distribution. Formally, a Bayesian game consists of a set of players N, a set of actions Ai for each player, a set of types Ti, a prior probability distribution p over the type profile space T = ×i Ti, and payoff functions ui(a, t) that depend on both the action profile a and the realized type profile t. Each player observes his own type but not the types of others, and forms beliefs about opponents’ types using Bayes’ rule wherever possible.

The solution concept is Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE): a strategy profile σ = (σi) where each σi : Ti → Δ(Ai) maximizes player i’s expected payoff given the strategies of others and the prior. Harsanyi’s transformation shows that any Bayesian game can be represented as an extensive‑form game with an initial move by Nature that draws types, turning incomplete information into imperfect information. This guarantees existence of a BNE in finite games by Nash’s theorem applied to the transformed game.

Key applications include auctions with private values (first‑price and second‑price sealed‑bid auctions), signaling games (Spence’s education model), and mechanism design where the revelation principle holds: any BNE outcome can be implemented by a direct mechanism in which truthful type reporting is a BNE. The interim individual rationality and incentive compatibility constraints are the building blocks of optimal auction design (Myerson 1981) and of the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism in Bayesian settings.

Common pitfalls: confusing ex‑ante, interim, and ex‑post stages of reasoning; forgetting that beliefs must be updated on the equilibrium path; and assuming that a dominant‑strategy equilibrium in a complete‑information game remains dominant when types are introduced.

Correlated Equilibrium and Communication Devices

Introduced by Aumann (1974), a correlated equilibrium generalizes mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium by allowing a correlation device — a public random signal — to recommend action profiles to players. A probability distribution μ over the set of pure action profiles A is a correlated equilibrium if, for every player i and every recommended action ai with μ(ai) > 0, the conditional expected payoff from following the recommendation is at least as high as the payoff from any unilateral deviation, given the conditional distribution over opponents’ actions induced by μ.

The set of correlated equilibria is a convex polytope described by linear inequalities, making it computable in polynomial time via linear programming. Every mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium is a correlated equilibrium (product distribution), but the converse is false: correlated equilibria can yield higher total welfare. Classic examples include the traffic‑light game, where a signal “green for row, red for column” and its symmetric counterpart produce a correlated equilibrium with payoff (1,1) that Pareto‑dominates the mixed Nash equilibrium (½,½). In the Battle of the Sexes, a device that recommends (Opera, Opera) with probability ½ and (Football, Football) with probability ½ gives each player 2, whereas the mixed Nash gives ⅔.

Communication equilibria extend the idea by allowing cheap‑talk messages before the device’s recommendation. Myerson (1982) showed that any communication equilibrium outcome can be replicated by a correlated equilibrium with an appropriately expanded signal space, so the correlated equilibrium polytope already captures the full power of pre‑play communication without binding commitments.

Technique: Computing a Correlated Equilibrium by Linear Programming
In the following two-player game, each player chooses between actions A and B. Payoffs are given as (row player, column player).
Payoff matrix:
A,A : (4,4)
A,B : (0,5)
B,A : (5,0)
B,B : (1,1)
Find a correlated equilibrium that gives each player an expected payoff of at least 3.5.
Let the correlation device recommend action profiles with probabilities p1 for (A,A), p2 for (A,B), p3 for (B,A), p4 for (B,B). The constraints for a correlated equilibrium are:
For row player when recommended A: 4 p1 + 0 p2 ≥ 5 p1 + 1 p2 → -p1 - p2 ≥ 0 → p1 + p2 ≤ 0, so p1 = p2 = 0.
When recommended B: 5 p3 + 1 p4 ≥ 4 p3 + 0 p4 → p3 + p4 ≥ 0 (always true).
For column player symmetric constraints give p1 = p3 = 0.
Thus only (B,B) can be recommended with positive probability. But (B,B) yields payoff 1 each, not 3.5. Hence no correlated equilibrium achieves 3.5 in this game. The maximum symmetric payoff in any correlated equilibrium is 1. The mixed Nash equilibrium gives each player 2.5, which is higher than any correlated equilibrium here. This illustrates that correlated equilibrium does not always improve on Nash equilibrium.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks for a correlated equilibrium, first write the linear-programming constraints for each player's recommended action. Check feasibility before attempting to compute payoffs; many exam problems are designed so that the only feasible correlated equilibria are the Nash equilibria themselves.

Coalitional Game Theory: Core, Shapley Value, and the Bondareva–Shapley Theorem

Coalitional (or cooperative) game theory studies situations where groups of players can form binding agreements. A transferable‑utility (TU) game is a pair (N, v) where N is the player set and v : 2N → ℝ with v(∅)=0 assigns a worth to each coalition. An allocation x ∈ ℝN is efficient if ∑i∈N xi = v(N). The core is the set of efficient allocations that no coalition can improve upon: x ∈ Core iff ∑i∈S xi ≥ v(S) for all S ⊆ N. The core may be empty; the Bondareva–Shapley theorem (1963, 1967) characterizes non‑emptiness: the core is non‑empty iff the game is balanced, i.e., for every balanced collection of weights λS ≥ 0 with ∑S∋i λS = 1 for all i, we have ∑S λS v(S) ≤ v(N).

The Shapley value φ(v) is the unique allocation satisfying four axioms: efficiency, symmetry, dummy player, and additivity. It can be computed as the average marginal contribution over all permutations of players: φi(v) = ∑S⊆N{i} (|S|! (n-|S|-1)! / n!) [v(S∪{i}) - v(S)]. For convex games (where marginal contributions are increasing), the Shapley value lies in the core. In voting games (simple games with v(S) ∈ {0,1}), the Shapley–Shubik index measures a player’s power as the probability of being pivotal in a random ordering.

Applications include cost‑sharing problems (airport runway, telephone network), bankruptcy allocation, and the assignment of seats in proportional representation systems. The nucleolus, another solution concept, lexicographically minimizes the vector of excesses e(S,x) = v(S) - ∑i∈S xi and always belongs to the core when the core is non‑empty.

Algorithmic Game Theory: Price of Anarchy and Equilibrium Computation

Algorithmic game theory analyses the efficiency of equilibria and the computational complexity of finding them. The price of anarchy (PoA) of a game is the ratio between the worst‑case social welfare at a Nash equilibrium (or correlated equilibrium) and the optimal social welfare: PoA = maxequilibrium SW(opt) / SW(eq). The price of stability (PoS) uses the best equilibrium instead of the worst. In congestion games (Rosenthal 1973), where players choose paths in a network and edge costs are non‑decreasing functions of load, the PoA for pure Nash equilibria with affine cost functions is 5/2 (Roughgarden & Tardos 2002). The smoothness framework (Roughgarden 2009) provides a unified method to bound PoA for a wide class of games, including auctions and routing.

Computational results: finding a mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium in a two‑player normal‑form game is PPAD‑complete (Chen & Deng 2006), implying no polynomial‑time algorithm unless PPAD = P. However, a correlated equilibrium can be found in polynomial time via linear programming, and a coarse correlated equilibrium (where players cannot condition on the signal) is even easier — it is the solution of a linear program with only O(|A|) variables. For congestion games, best‑response dynamics converge to a pure Nash equilibrium in polynomial time because they are potential games (Monderer & Shapley 1996). In contrast, computing the Shapley value for a general TU game is #P‑complete, but for weighted voting games it can be approximated efficiently.

These results guide mechanism designers: if a mechanism’s equilibria are hard to compute, participants may not play them, undermining the mechanism’s guarantees. Hence there is a growing emphasis on designing mechanisms with simple, efficiently computable equilibria (e.g., dominant‑strategy mechanisms).

Dynamic Games with Incomplete Information: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium

Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) refines Nash equilibrium for extensive‑form games where players have private information that evolves over time. A PBE consists of a strategy profile σ and a belief system μ (a probability distribution over decision nodes within each information set) satisfying two conditions: sequential rationality — at every information set, the player’s strategy maximizes expected payoff given beliefs and continuation strategies; and consistency — beliefs are derived from strategies via Bayes’ rule wherever possible (on the equilibrium path). Off the equilibrium path, beliefs are unrestricted but must be specified.

Signaling games are the canonical application: an informed sender chooses a message, an uninformed receiver observes the message and takes an action. A pooling equilibrium occurs when all sender types choose the same message; a separating equilibrium occurs when different types choose different messages, fully revealing the type. The Beer‑Quiche game (Cho & Kreps 1987) illustrates how intuitive criteria (e.g., the Intuitive Criterion) can eliminate unreasonable PBEs by restricting off‑path beliefs.

In multi‑stage games with observed actions, the concept of sequential equilibrium (Kreps & Wilson 1982) imposes a stronger consistency requirement: beliefs must be limits of completely mixed strategy profiles. Every sequential equilibrium is a PBE, but not vice versa. Applications include reputation models (Kreps, Milgrom, Roberts, Wilson 1982), where a long‑run player may mimic a commitment type to influence short‑run opponents, and dynamic mechanism design, where the revelation principle extends to dynamic settings under appropriate conditions (Pavan, Segal, Toikka 2014).

  • Confusing Bayesian Nash equilibrium with perfect Bayesian equilibrium — the former applies to static incomplete‑information games, the latter to dynamic ones.
  • Assuming the core is always non‑empty; the Bondareva–Shapley theorem gives the exact balancedness condition.
  • Treating correlated equilibrium as a subset of mixed Nash equilibrium; it is a superset.
  • Neglecting off‑path belief restrictions when applying the Intuitive Criterion or other refinements.
  • Misapplying the price of anarchy formula by using the optimal welfare in the denominator instead of the numerator.
  • Believing that every finite game has a pure‑strategy Nash equilibrium; only potential games and certain supermodular games guarantee it.
  • Overlooking that the Shapley value may lie outside the core for non‑convex games.

Mastery of these advanced concepts separates top scorers from the rest.

hand/calc-variations.html:
Second Variation and Sufficient Conditions for Minima

The Euler‑Lagrange equation gives a necessary condition for a stationary point of a functional, but it does not distinguish minima from maxima or saddle points. To decide whether a stationary function y₀(x) actually minimises the functional J[y] = ∫ₐᵇ L(x, y, y') dx one examines the second variation δ²J. For a variation η(x) with η(a)=η(b)=0 the second variation reads

δ²J = ∫ₐᵇ [ Lyy η² + 2 Lyy' η η' + Ly'y' η'² ] dx.

If δ²J > 0 for all non‑zero admissible η, the stationary point is a strict local minimum. The classical sufficient conditions are the Legendre condition and the Jacobi condition. The strengthened Legendre condition requires Ly'y'(x, y₀, y₀') > 0 on [a, b]; it guarantees that the quadratic form in η' is positive definite. The Jacobi condition demands that the accessory equation (the linearised Euler‑Lagrange equation for η) has no conjugate points in (a, b]. A conjugate point is a point c ∈ (a, b] where a non‑trivial solution of the accessory equation vanishes at both a and c. If a conjugate point exists, one can construct a variation that makes δ²J negative, so y₀ cannot be a minimum. Together, the strengthened Legendre condition and the absence of conjugate points are sufficient for a weak local minimum. For strong minima one also needs the Weierstrass excess function E(x, y, y', p) = L(x, y, p) − L(x, y, y') − (p − y') Ly'(x, y, y') to be non‑negative for all p, which is the Weierstrass condition.

These criteria are not merely theoretical; they appear in optimal control as the second‑order conditions for the Pontryagin maximum principle and in numerical analysis as checks for the convergence of discretisation schemes. In practice, verifying the Jacobi condition often reduces to solving a Sturm‑Liouville eigenvalue problem for the accessory equation, and the smallest eigenvalue being positive is equivalent to the absence of conjugate points.

Broken Extremals and Weierstrass‑Erdmann Corner Conditions

Classical derivations of the Euler‑Lagrange equation assume the extremal y(x) is continuously differentiable. Many physical problems, however, admit optimal curves with corners — points where y' has a jump discontinuity. A broken extremal is a piecewise C¹ curve that satisfies the Euler‑Lagrange equation on each smooth segment and meets certain matching conditions at the corners. The Weierstrass‑Erdmann corner conditions state that at a corner x = c the quantities ∂L/∂y' and L − y' ∂L/∂y' must be continuous:

∂L/∂y'|c⁻ = ∂L/∂y'|c⁺, L − y' ∂L/∂y'|c⁻ = L − y' ∂L/∂y'|c⁺.

These are the analogues of momentum and energy conservation across a discontinuity. They follow from requiring the first variation to vanish for variations that are allowed to move the corner point. If the Lagrangian does not depend explicitly on x, the second condition reduces to the continuity of the Hamiltonian H = y' ∂L/∂y' − L. If L is independent of y, the first condition gives continuity of the canonical momentum p = ∂L/∂y'.

A classic example is the refraction of light (Fermat's principle) where the optical Lagrangian L = n(x, y) √(1 + y'²) changes abruptly across an interface. The corner conditions yield Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. In mechanics, a particle moving in a piecewise constant potential exhibits corners in its trajectory; the corner conditions enforce conservation of momentum and energy across the potential step. The theory of broken extremals extends to fields with higher‑order derivatives, where the corner conditions involve continuity of higher‑order momenta. Modern treatments place these conditions in the framework of functions of bounded variation (BV), where the jump set of the derivative is rectifiable and the Weierstrass‑Erdmann conditions hold almost everywhere on that set.

Worked Example: Corner Conditions for a Piecewise Lagrangian
Consider the functional J[y] = ∫₀¹ L(x, y, y') dx with L = (y')² for 0 ≤ x < ½ and L = 2(y')² for ½ < x ≤ 1. Find the broken extremal satisfying y(0)=0, y(1)=1 and the Weierstrass‑Erdmann conditions at x = ½.
On each subinterval the Euler‑Lagrange equation gives d/dx (∂L/∂y') = 0, so ∂L/∂y' is constant on each piece. For 0 ≤ x < ½, ∂L/∂y' = 2 y' = C₁ ⇒ y' = C₁/2. For ½ < x ≤ 1, ∂L/∂y' = 4 y' = C₂ ⇒ y' = C₂/4. The first corner condition requires continuity of ∂L/∂y': C₁ = C₂ = C. The second corner condition requires continuity of L − y' ∂L/∂y'. On the left: L − y' ∂L/∂y' = (y')² − y'(2 y') = −(y')² = −C²/4. On the right: 2(y')² − y'(4 y') = −2(y')² = −2(C/4)² = −C²/8. Equating gives −C²/4 = −C²/8 ⇒ C = 0. Hence y' = 0 on both pieces, so y is constant. The boundary conditions y(0)=0, y(1)=1 cannot be satisfied simultaneously, therefore no broken extremal exists for this problem. The functional has no minimiser in the class of piecewise C¹ functions; the infimum is approached by a sequence of steep slopes near x = ½, illustrating the Lavrentiev phenomenon.
Exam Strategy: Recognising Corner Problems
When a problem statement mentions a piecewise defined Lagrangian, a change of medium, or a potential with a jump, immediately write down the two Weierstrass‑Erdmann conditions. Check whether the Lagrangian depends explicitly on x or y; if not, the corresponding conserved quantity (Hamiltonian or momentum) must be continuous. A quick way to earn partial credit is to state the conditions even if you cannot solve the resulting algebraic system completely.

Variational Problems with Constraints and Lagrange Multipliers

Many optimisation problems in physics and engineering involve constraints. An isoperimetric constraint fixes the value of another functional, e.g. ∫ₐᵇ M(x, y, y') dx = constant. A holonomic constraint restricts the admissible functions to a submanifold, e.g. g(x, y) = 0. The method of Lagrange multipliers extends to functionals: one forms the augmented Lagrangian L̃ = L + λ(x) M for an isoperimetric constraint with a constant multiplier λ, or L̃ = L + μ(x) g(x, y) for a holonomic constraint where μ(x) is a function multiplier. The Euler‑Lagrange equations for L̃ together with the constraint determine the extremal and the multiplier(s). For an isoperimetric problem the multiplier is a constant because the constraint is a single scalar equation; for a holonomic constraint the multiplier is a function because the constraint must hold pointwise.

A celebrated example is the catenary of given length hanging between two points: minimise potential energy ∫ y √(1 + y'²) dx subject to fixed length ∫ √(1 + y'²) dx = L₀. The augmented Lagrangian is (y + λ) √(1 + y'²). Since L̃ does not depend explicitly on x, the Beltrami identity gives (y + λ) / √(1 + y'²) = constant, leading to the standard catenary y = a cosh((x − b)/a) − λ with a = 1/constant. The multiplier λ adjusts the vertical shift to meet the length constraint. In optimal control, the Pontryagin maximum principle can be derived by adjoining the dynamics constraints with time‑dependent multipliers (costates), yielding a Hamiltonian system on an extended phase space. The multiplier functions satisfy adjoint equations that are precisely the costate equations.

When the constraint is an inequality, e.g. y(x) ≥ 0, the problem becomes a variational inequality. The Kuhn‑Tucker conditions in infinite dimensions state that there exists a non‑negative multiplier measure μ such that the Euler‑Lagrange equation holds with an extra term μ, and μ is supported on the contact set where y = 0. This framework underlies obstacle problems and free‑boundary problems such as the American option pricing model in finance.

Geometric Variational Problems: Minimal Surfaces and Plateau's Problem

When the unknown is a surface rather than a curve, the functional is the area integral A[S] = ∫_S dA. For a graph z = u(x, y) over a domain Ω ⊂ ℝ² the area functional becomes ∫_Ω √(1 + u_x² + u_y²) dx dy. The Euler‑Lagrange equation is the minimal surface equation div( ∇u / √(1 + |∇u|²) ) = 0, which expresses zero mean curvature. Classical solutions include the catenoid, helicoid, and Scherk's surfaces. The Plateau problem asks for a surface of least area spanning a given closed contour. Douglas and Radó independently solved it in the 1930s by minimising the Dirichlet integral ∫_Ω |∇u|² dx dy over a suitable class of parametrisations, earning the Fields Medal in 1936. Their method uses the direct method of the calculus of variations: a minimising sequence is bounded in the Sobolev space W1,2, a weakly convergent subsequence exists, and lower semicontinuity of the Dirichlet integral yields a minimiser. The solution is a conformal harmonic parametrisation, and the resulting surface has branch points only at the boundary.

Modern geometric measure theory extends the notion of surface to rectifiable currents, allowing solutions with singularities. Almgren's regularity theorem (1983) shows that area‑minimising integral currents of codimension one are smooth except on a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most n−8. In codimension one this means minimal hypersurfaces are smooth in dimensions ≤ 7; the Simons cone provides a singular minimiser in ℝ⁸. The theory of varifolds, developed by Allard, provides a compactness theorem for sequences of surfaces with bounded area and mean curvature, leading to existence results for the Plateau problem in arbitrary Riemannian manifolds. Applications range from soap films and capillary surfaces to the study of event horizons in general relativity, where the area of a black‑hole horizon satisfies a variational principle.

  • Confusing the Legendre condition (positivity of Ly'y') with the Weierstrass condition (non‑negativity of the excess function) — they are distinct and both are needed for strong minima.
  • Forgetting that the Jacobi condition requires the absence of conjugate points in the open interval (a, b], not just at the endpoints.
  • Applying the standard Euler‑Lagrange equation across a corner without enforcing the Weierstrass‑Erdmann continuity conditions.
  • Treating an isoperimetric multiplier as a function of x instead of a constant, or vice‑versa for a holonomic constraint.
  • Assuming that a solution of the minimal surface equation automatically minimises area; it is only a stationary point and may be unstable.
  • Neglecting the Lavrentiev phenomenon: the infimum over smooth functions can be strictly larger than the infimum over piecewise smooth or BV functions.
  • Overlooking the role of lower semicontinuity in the direct method; convexity of L in y' is sufficient but not necessary, and quasiconvexity is the correct condition for vector‑valued problems.

hand/thin-groups.html:
The Bourgain–Gamburd Expansion Machine and Sum‑Product Estimates in SL₂(𝔽_p)

The Bourgain–Gamburd expansion machine, introduced in their 2005 Annals paper and refined in 2008, provides a general framework to prove that Cayley graphs of finite simple groups of Lie type form expander families. The machine reduces the problem to three ingredients: (1) a non‑concentration estimate showing that random walks on the group do not concentrate on proper subgroups; (2) a product theorem (also called a growth theorem) stating that any subset A ⊂ G not too close to a subgroup satisfies |A³| ≥ |A|1+ε; and (3) an initial flattening (or early‑mixing) lemma that gives a power‑saving bound on the L² norm of the random walk after O(log |G|) steps. For G = SL₂(𝔽_p), the product theorem is supplied by Helfgott’s 2008 result: any generating subset A ⊂ SL₂(𝔽_p) either is very large (|A| ≥ |G|1−δ) or satisfies |A³| ≥ |A|1+ε. The non‑concentration estimate relies on the sum‑product phenomenon in 𝔽_p: for any subset A ⊂ 𝔽_p not too close to a subfield, either A+A or A·A is significantly larger than A. Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak used this to show that the eigenvalues of the generators of a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) are real (a condition later removed by Varju and others) and that the random walk on Γ mod p equidistributes rapidly. The machine has since been extended to SL_n and other Chevalley groups by Breuillard–Green–Tao (2011) and Pyber–Szabó (2010), using the classification of approximate subgroups. The key technical step is the flattening lemma: if μ is a probability measure on G with ‖μ‖₂ ≤ |G|-1/2+δ, then ‖μ*k‖₂ ≤ |G|-1/2+δ/2 for some k = O(log |G|). This iterative improvement of the L² norm, combined with the product theorem, yields a uniform spectral gap for the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ_q, S_q) as q ranges over square‑free integers.

The Affine Sieve, the Beta‑Sieve, and the Level of Distribution

The affine sieve developed by Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2006) adapts classical sieve methods to orbits of thin groups. Let Γ ⊂ GL_n(ℚ) be a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup, x₀ ∈ ℤ^n a base point, and f : ℤ^n → ℤ a polynomial. The goal is to show that f takes almost‑prime values (integers with a bounded number of prime factors) on the orbit O = Γ·x₀. The sieve requires a level of distribution θ > 0: for any square‑free q, the number of orbit points v with |v| ≤ X and f(v) ≡ 0 (mod q) is approximated by a main term ρ(q) X^δ / q + error, where δ is the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set of Γ. The expander property of the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ_q, S_q) gives a power‑saving error term O(Xδ−η) uniformly in q ≤ X^θ, which is exactly the level of distribution needed for the beta‑sieve (Rosser–Iwaniec). The beta‑sieve then produces a lower bound for the number of v ∈ O with f(v) having at most r prime factors, where r depends on θ and the sieve dimension κ (the average number of prime factors of f(v)). For the Apollonian packing, f is the curvature polynomial, κ = 1, and the expander gap gives θ = 1/2 − ε, yielding r = 2 (i.e., almost‑primes with at most two prime factors). Later work by Salehi‑Golsefidy and Sarnak (2013) improved the level of distribution using the spectral gap for the Laplacian on ℍ²/Γ and the theory of automorphic forms, pushing r closer to the optimal value. The saturation problem asks for the minimal r such that f takes values with at most r prime factors infinitely often; for many thin orbits this remains open, but the affine sieve provides the only general method to obtain finite r.

Worked Example: Level of Distribution from Spectral Gap
Let Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense Schottky group with limit set dimension δ = 0.7. Suppose the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ_q, S_q) form an expander family with uniform spectral gap ε = 0.1. Explain how this yields a level of distribution θ for the affine sieve applied to a polynomial f of sieve dimension κ = 1.
The expander property implies that the random walk on Γ_q mixes in O(log q) steps. By the expander mixing lemma, for any subset A ⊂ Γ_q, the number of steps needed to equidistribute is bounded by C log q / ε. This translates into an error term in the orbit counting modulo q: |{v ∈ O : |v| ≤ X, f(v) ≡ 0 (mod q)} − ρ(q) X^δ / q| ≤ C Xδ−η for some η > 0 depending on ε and the geometry of Γ. The uniformity in q holds for q ≤ X^θ with θ = η / (δ + η). For δ = 0.7 and a typical η ≈ 0.05 (derived from the spectral gap), we get θ ≈ 0.05 / 0.75 ≈ 0.066. The beta‑sieve with κ = 1 then gives r = ⌈1/θ⌉ ≈ 16 prime factors. Improved spectral gaps (e.g., Selberg’s 3/16 theorem for congruence subgroups) increase η and thus θ, reducing r. In practice, for Apollonian packings, the best known θ is close to 1/2, giving r = 2.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the connection between expanders and the affine sieve, state the chain: expander family → uniform spectral gap → rapid mixing of random walk → power‑saving error in orbit counting modulo q → level of distribution θ → beta‑sieve parameter r. Memorise the formula θ = η/(δ+η) and the role of the Hausdorff dimension δ. Examiners often test whether you know that the expander property is used to obtain uniformity in q, not just a pointwise bound.

Thin Subgroups and the Local–Global Principle for Integral Quadratic Forms

The local–global principle (Hasse principle) for integral quadratic forms asks whether an integer represented locally everywhere (i.e., modulo every prime power and over ℝ) is represented globally by the form. For thin orbits arising from the action of a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ O_Q(ℤ) on a vector x₀, the set of values Q(γ·x₀) is a subset of the integers represented by the quadratic form Q. The local–global conjecture for thin orbits, formulated by Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak, predicts that every integer satisfying the necessary congruence conditions appears in the orbit, provided the orbit is not contained in a proper subvariety. This is known for the Apollonian packing (Bourgain–Kontorovich, 2010) and for certain Pythagorean quadruples (Bourgain–Kontorovich, 2014). The proof uses the circle method combined with the expander property to control the minor arcs. The key is to show that the number of representations of an integer n by the orbit is asymptotically given by a product of local densities, with an error term that is smaller than the main term for all sufficiently large n satisfying the congruence conditions. The expander property provides the required equidistribution of the orbit modulo q, which translates into bounds for the exponential sums on the minor arcs. For general thin groups, the local–global principle remains open, but the affine sieve gives a weaker result: the set of integers represented by the orbit has positive density in the set of locally admissible integers. The work of Oh and Shah (2012) on the equidistribution of expanding horospheres on homogeneous spaces provides a dynamical approach to the local–global problem for orbits of thin groups on quadric hypersurfaces.

Superstrong Approximation for Perfect Groups and the Work of Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varju

The original superstrong approximation theorem of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak required the generators of Γ to have real eigenvalues, a technical condition that was later removed. In 2012, Salehi‑Golsefidy and Varju proved superstrong approximation for any Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ of a perfect group (i.e., a group equal to its own commutator subgroup) under the sole assumption that Γ is not virtually solvable. Their proof uses the product theorem for perfect groups (Breuillard–Green–Tao) and a non‑concentration estimate derived from the classification of approximate subgroups. The result states: if G is a connected semisimple algebraic group over ℚ, Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) is a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup, and the projection of Γ to each simple factor is infinite, then the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ_q, S_q) form an expander family as q ranges over square‑free integers. This covers all thin subgroups of SL_n(ℤ), Sp2n(ℤ), and other Chevalley groups. The proof avoids the sum‑product phenomenon by using the escape from subvarieties lemma: a random walk on Γ does not concentrate on any proper algebraic subvariety of G. This lemma, combined with the product theorem, yields the initial flattening needed for the Bourgain–Gamburd machine. The Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varju theorem is the most general form of superstrong approximation to date and has applications to the Zaremba conjecture on continued fractions (Bourgain–Kontorovich, 2014) and to the spectral gap for the Laplacian on locally symmetric spaces associated to thin groups.

Applications to the Zaremba Conjecture and Continued Fractions

The Zaremba conjecture (1972) asserts that every integer q ≥ 2 appears as the denominator of a finite continued fraction [0; a₁, a₂, …, a_k] with all partial quotients a_i bounded by an absolute constant (e.g., 5). This is equivalent to the statement that the set of matrices in SL₂(ℤ) with bounded entries generates a subgroup whose congruence quotients cover all of SL₂(ℤ/qℤ). Bourgain and Kontorovich (2014) used superstrong approximation for the thin subgroup Γ_A generated by the matrices (1 A; 0 1) and (1 0; A 1) with A = 5 to show that the set of denominators q for which the continued fraction expansion has all partial quotients ≤ 5 has positive density. Later, Huang (2015) improved the bound to A = 50, and the current record is A = 5 (Bourgain–Kontorovich, 2019) using the full strength of the Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varju theorem. The connection is as follows: the continued fraction algorithm corresponds to the action of SL₂(ℤ) on the upper half‑plane, and the set of matrices with bounded entries forms a thin subgroup. The expander property of the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ_q, S_q) implies that the random walk on Γ_q equidistributes, which in turn implies that the set of reachable denominators modulo q is large. By a sieving argument, one shows that a positive proportion of integers q are denominators of continued fractions with bounded partial quotients. The Zaremba conjecture remains open in full generality, but the expander machinery has brought it within reach of a complete solution.

  • Trap 1: Confusing the Selberg 3/16 theorem (which applies only to congruence subgroups of SL₂(ℤ)) with the spectral gap for thin groups (which is given by the Patterson–Sullivan exponent δ(1−δ)).
  • Trap 2: Assuming the affine sieve gives primes directly; it only gives almost‑primes (bounded number of prime factors). The jump to primes requires additional input (e.g., the parity problem).
  • Trap 3: Thinking the Bourgain–Gamburd machine works for any generating set; it requires the product theorem and non‑concentration, which fail for solvable groups.
  • Trap 4: Overlooking the role of the Hausdorff dimension δ in the level of distribution θ = η/(δ+η); a larger δ actually makes it harder to get a good θ.
  • Trap 5: Believing the local–global principle is proved for all thin orbits; it is only known for Apollonian packings and a few other cases.
  • Trap 6: Confusing superstrong approximation (expander family for all square‑free q) with strong approximation (surjectivity onto the profinite completion).
  • Trap 7: Misstating the Zaremba conjecture as "every integer is a denominator of a continued fraction with partial quotients ≤ 5" without the positive density nuance; the conjecture is exactly that every integer appears, which is stronger than positive density.

These advanced topics illustrate the deep interplay between algebraic groups, spectral theory, and combinatorial number theory that defines the modern theory of thin groups.
