A key result is that the simplicial set model of HoTT can be constructed inside the effective topos, showing that HoTT has a computational interpretation where all definable functions are computable. The main limitation is that the realizability model does not satisfy function extensionality in its naive form; one must use a modified identity type or work in a category of fibrant objects. The connection to proof assistants is that the computational cubical type theory implemented in Cubical Agda can be seen as a syntactic realizability model where paths are represented by terms with interval variables, and Kan operations are primitive reduction rules. This gives a direct computational interpretation of higher inductive types: the constructors of a HIT generate elements, and the path constructors generate paths that compute via Kan filling.

Parametricity and Proof Irrelevance in Homotopy Type Theory

Parametricity in HoTT refers to the property that polymorphic functions preserve relations between types. In System F, Reynolds' parametricity theorem states that a term f : ∀X. X → X must be the identity function. In HoTT, parametricity is internalized via the Param type former: for a type family P : A → Type and a path p : x = y, parametricity gives a path Param(P, p) : transport P p = id when P is a "parametric" family. This is closely related to proof irrelevance: a type A is proof-irrelevant (a mere proposition) if Π(x y : A), x = y. The propositional truncation ‖A‖ is the free proof-irrelevant type on A. Parametricity implies that any function f : ‖A‖ → B into a set B factors through the truncation map |-| : A → ‖A‖ and is constant on A. This is the "elimination principle" for propositional truncation into sets. In HoTT, parametricity can be derived from univalence and function extensionality for certain type formers, but not all. The "parametricity axiom" states that for any type family P : U → Type and equivalence e : A ≃ B, there is a path P(A) = P(B) induced by e. This is stronger than univalence (which only gives A = B) and implies that all type formers are parametric. The parametricity axiom is consistent with HoTT and holds in the simplicial set model. A major application is the proof that the circle S¹ is not equivalent to the unit type 1: if S¹ ≃ 1, then by parametricity the identity function on S¹ would be homotopic to the constant function, contradicting π₁(S¹) ≃ ℤ. Parametricity also gives a syntactic proof of canonicity for closed terms of natural number type in HoTT with univalence, by interpreting types as relations and showing that every closed term of type ℕ is related to a numeral. The connection to proof irrelevance is that the parametricity axiom implies that the universe U is not a set (it has non-trivial paths by univalence), but the subuniverse of mere propositions Prop := Σ(A : U), isProp(A) is a set and satisfies proof irrelevance. The double negation modality ¬¬ and the propositional truncation modality ‖-‖ are both parametric modalities, meaning they commute with equivalences. This is used in the construction of the Cauchy reals as a quotient of Cauchy sequences by the equivalence relation x ~ y := ‖x = y‖, where the proof irrelevance of ‖-‖ ensures the quotient is a set.

The ∞-Topos of Types and the Internal Language of Higher Topoi

The category of types in HoTT forms an elementary ∞-topos: it has finite limits, colimits, a subobject classifier (the universe of mere propositions Prop), and satisfies the ∞-Giraud axioms. The internal language of this ∞-topos is exactly HoTT itself: every statement in HoTT corresponds to a statement in the internal logic of the ∞-topos of ∞-groupoids. The subobject classifier Prop classifies (-1)-truncated maps (embeddings), and the object classifier U classifies all maps. The ∞-topos structure gives rise to a hierarchy of modalities: the n-truncation modality ‖-‖ₙ reflects onto n-types, the double negation modality ¬¬ reflects onto ¬¬-separated types, and the codiscrete modality ♯ (in cohesive HoTT) reflects onto codiscrete types. The internal logic supports higher-order reasoning: one can quantify over types, define inductive types internally, and reason about homotopy groups using the encode-decode method. A key theorem is that any elementary ∞-topos with a natural numbers object and satisfying the axiom of choice is equivalent to the ∞-topos of ∞-groupoids (the "∞-topos version of Freyd's theorem"). The internal language of the ∞-topos of sheaves on a topological space X is HoTT with a "shape" modality ʃ that extracts the homotopy type of a space. This is the basis of synthetic homotopy theory: one can prove theorems about spaces by working entirely in the internal language of the ∞-topos of sheaves. The ∞-topos of types also supports a synthetic version of the adjoint functor theorem: every accessible functor between ∞-topoi that preserves limits has a left adjoint. This is used to construct the n-truncation modality as the left adjoint to the inclusion of n-types. The internal language of the ∞-topos of ∞-groupoids is complete for homotopy-invariant statements: a statement in HoTT is provable if and only if it holds in all ∞-groupoids. This completeness theorem, due to Shulman and others, justifies the use of HoTT as a foundation for homotopy theory. A subtle point is that the ∞-topos of types in HoTT is not the ∞-category of all ∞-groupoids (which is large), but a Grothendieck ∞-topos of ∞-groupoids bounded by some universe level. The universe hierarchy U₀ : U₁ : U₂ : … corresponds to the hierarchy of Grothendieck ∞-topoi of ∞-groupoids of increasing size.

Synthetic π₁ and the Seifert-van Kampen Theorem in HoTT

The Seifert-van Kampen theorem computes the fundamental group of a pushout of spaces in terms of the fundamental groups of the pieces. In HoTT, the theorem is stated and proved entirely synthetically for types. Let A be a type with points a₁ a₂ : A and a path p : a₁ = a₂. Let B and C be types with points b : B and c : C, and maps f : A → B and g : A → C such that f(a₁) = b, f(a₂) = b, g(a₁) = c, g(a₂) = c. The pushout P := B ⊔_A C is a higher inductive type with constructors inl : B → P, inr : C → P, and glue : Π(a : A), inl(f(a)) = inr(g(a)). The synthetic Seifert-van Kampen theorem states that the fundamental group π₁(P, inl(b)) is the pushout of groups π₁(B, b) ⊔π₁(A, a₁) π₁(C, c) in the ∞-category of groups, which is the amalgamated free product π₁(B, b) *π₁(A, a₁) π₁(C, c). The proof uses the encode-decode method with a family Code : P → Type defined by double induction on P. At inl(b), Code(inl(b)) is the set of reduced words in the generators of π₁(B, b) and π₁(C, c) modulo the relations from π₁(A, a₁). Transport along glue(a) identifies the images of π₁(A, a₁) in the two groups. The total space Σ(x : P), Code(x) is shown to be contractible by constructing a deformation retraction to the basepoint. The theorem generalizes to the fundamental groupoid Π₁(P) as the pushout of groupoids Π₁(B) ⊔Π₁(A) Π₁(C). A key technical point is that the pushout of groups in HoTT is not the same as the set-theoretic pushout; it is a higher inductive type with path constructors for the group laws and 2-paths for the coherence of the amalgamation. The synthetic proof avoids classical CW-complex approximations and works for any types A, B, C that are 1-types (groupoids). For higher homotopy groups, the van Kampen theorem fails in general, but the Blakers-Massey theorem gives a connectivity range where the homotopy groups of the pushout are determined by the homotopy groups of the pieces. The formalization of the Seifert-van Kampen theorem in the HoTT library uses the fact that the fundamental group of a pushout of 1-types is the pushout of groups, and the proof is by encode-decode on the fundamental groupoid. The theorem is used to compute π₁ of the torus (as a pushout of two cylinders), the Klein bottle, and the real projective plane ℝP² (as a pushout of a disk and a Möbius strip). In cubical type theory, the pushout B ⊔_A C has Kan operations that compute transports along glue(a) by composition with the generating squares, and the encode-decode proof computes the group operations by Kan filling.

  • Confusing the torus HIT (with 2-path surf) with the figure-eight HIT (without surf); the former has π₁ ≃ ℤ × ℤ, the latter π₁ ≃ F₂.
  • Assuming the encode-decode method works without univalence; the path ua(succ) : ℤ = ℤ for the circle requires univalence to transport along loop by successor.
  • Thinking the realizability model validates univalence naively; it requires ∞-realizability with path spaces, and the standard PCA model validates UIP which contradicts univalence.
  • Believing parametricity is derivable for all type formers from univalence alone; it requires an additional parametricity axiom and fails for some higher inductive types without further assumptions.
  • Stating the Seifert-van Kampen theorem for πₙ with n ≥ 2; it fails for higher homotopy groups, and the Blakers-Massey theorem gives the correct connectivity range instead.
  • Confusing the ∞-topos of types in HoTT with the ∞-category of all ∞-groupoids; the former is a Grothendieck ∞-topos bounded by a universe level, the latter is large and not an elementary ∞-topos.
  • Assuming the subobject classifier Prop classifies all monomorphisms; it classifies only (-1)-truncated maps (embeddings), while the object classifier U classifies all maps.

These advanced topics complete the synthetic homotopy theory toolkit needed for research-level formalization in HoTT and cubical type theory.

The Freudenthal Suspension Theorem and Stabilization in HoTT

The Freudenthal suspension theorem is a cornerstone of stable homotopy theory. In classical topology it states that for a pointed (n−1)-connected space X, the suspension map πₖ(X) → πₖ₊₁(ΣX) is an isomorphism for k < 2n−1 and an epimorphism for k = 2n−1. In HoTT the theorem is formulated and proved synthetically for types. Let X be a pointed type with basepoint x₀ : X. The suspension ΣX is the higher inductive type with constructors N S : ΣX and merid : X → (N = S). The suspension map σ : ΩᵏX → Ωᵏ⁺¹ΣX sends a k-loop p : ΩᵏX to the (k+1)-loop obtained by whiskering merid with p. The synthetic proof, due to Brunerie and Licata, uses the encode-decode method on the fiber of σ. One defines a family Code : ΣX → Type by Code(N) ≡ 𝟙, Code(S) ≡ 𝟙, and for x : X the path merid(x) transports Code(N) to Code(S) via an equivalence that encodes the action of σ on loops. The key technical lemma is that the total space Σ(y : ΣX), Code(y) is (2n−1)-connected when X is (n−1)-connected. This is shown by a double induction on ΣX and on the truncation level of X. The connectivity estimate relies on the Blakers-Massey theorem applied to the pushout square defining ΣX as the join X * 𝟚. The theorem implies that the stable homotopy groups πₖˢ(X) ≡ colimₙ πₖ₊ₙ(ΣⁿX) are well-defined and that the sphere spectrum 𝕊 is the stabilization of the sphere types. In cubical type theory the suspension map computes by Kan composition: a k-cube in X extends to a (k+1)-cube in ΣX by filling the merid squares. The formalization in the HoTT library uses the fact that the join X * Y is (conn(X)+conn(Y)+2)-connected, which gives the optimal range. A subtle point is that the theorem requires X to be a type in a universe U; the suspension ΣX lives in the same universe, so the colimit defining stable homotopy groups requires universe polymorphism or a sequence of universes. The Freudenthal theorem is used to compute π₃(S²) ≃ ℤ (the Hopf fibration), π₄(S³) ≃ ℤ/2, and to prove that the stable stem π₁ˢ ≃ ℤ/2 is generated by the Hopf map η : S³ → S².

The James Construction and Free Loop Spaces in HoTT

The James construction J(X) on a pointed type X is the free monoid on X modulo the basepoint, and it models the loop space ΩΣX. In HoTT, J(X) is defined as a higher inductive type with constructors: base : J(X), cons : X → J(X) → J(X), and a path constructor identifying cons(x₀, y) = y for the basepoint x₀ : X. The James construction comes with a map j : X → J(X) sending x to cons(x, base), and a multiplication μ : J(X) × J(X) → J(X) making it an H-space. The fundamental theorem, proved synthetically by Brunerie, states that for a connected type X, the map J(X) → ΩΣX induced by j is an equivalence. The proof uses the encode-decode method on the fiber of the map J(X) → ΩΣX. One defines a family Code : ΩΣX → Type by Code(refl) ≡ J(X) and transport along a loop merid(x) · p · merid(y)⁻¹ acts by cons(x, −) · cons(y, −)⁻¹. The total space is shown to be contractible by constructing a retraction to base using the groupoid structure of J(X). The James construction provides a concrete model for the loop space of a suspension, which is essential for computing homotopy groups of spheres. For example, J(S¹) ≃ ΩS² ≃ ℤ × ΩS³, and the filtration Jₙ(S¹) by word length gives the EHP sequence. In cubical type theory, J(X) has Kan operations that compute concatenation of paths by composition of the cons constructors. The James construction also yields the Hilton-Milnor theorem: for a wedge X ∨ Y, ΩΣ(X ∨ Y) ≃ ΩΣX × ΩΣY × ΩΣ(J(X) ∧ J(Y)), where ∧ is the smash product. This decomposition is proved by showing that J(X ∨ Y) ≃ J(X) * J(Y) (the join) and using the equivalence J(X) ≃ ΩΣX. The formalization in the HoTT library uses the fact that the smash product X ∧ Y is the pushout of X ← X × Y → Y, and the join X * Y is the pushout of X ← X × Y → Y with an extra cone point. A key technical point is that the James construction on a non-connected type does not model ΩΣX; instead one must use the reduced James construction on the 0-truncation ||X||₀. The James construction is also used to define the Whitehead product [−,−] : πₘ(X) × πₙ(X) → πₘ₊ₙ₋₁(X) by the commutator in J(X).

Encode-Decode on the James Construction
Let X be a connected pointed type. Define the James construction J(X) as the HIT with base : J(X), cons : X → J(X) → J(X), and jbase : Π(y : J(X)), cons(x₀, y) = y. Construct the equivalence J(X) ≃ ΩΣX by encode-decode. Specifically, define Code : ΩΣX → Type and show that the total space Σ(p : ΩΣX), Code(p) is contractible.
Define Code(refl_N) ≡ J(X). For a general loop p : N = N in ΣX, write p as a composite of merid(xᵢ) and merid(yⱼ)⁻¹ using the fact that ΣX is the pushout of X ← X + X → 𝟙. Transport along merid(x) : N = S acts on Code by cons(x, −) : J(X) → J(X). Transport along merid(y)⁻¹ : S = N acts by the inverse of cons(y, −), which exists because J(X) is a group up to homotopy (the inverse is given by reversing the word). The path jbase(y) : cons(x₀, y) = y ensures that the basepoint acts trivially. The encode map sends a loop p to the element of J(X) obtained by transporting base : Code(refl) along p. The decode map sends w : J(X) to the loop obtained by mapping w to ΩΣX via the universal property of J(X) as the free monoid. The composite decode ∘ encode is homotopic to identity by induction on the word length in J(X). The composite encode ∘ decode is identity by path induction on p. The total space is contractible because the fiber over refl is J(X) and the fibers over other loops are equivalent to J(X) by transport, giving a fiberwise equivalence to the constant family J(X).
Exam Strategy: James Construction and EHP Sequence
When asked about the James construction, remember three key facts: (1) J(X) is the free monoid on X with basepoint identified, (2) J(X) ≃ ΩΣX for connected X, (3) the filtration by word length gives the EHP sequence. For computation questions, use the equivalence J(Sⁿ) ≃ ΩSⁿ⁺¹ to reduce loop space calculations to word combinatorics. The Whitehead product [α, β] corresponds to the commutator cons(α, cons(β, base)) · cons(β, cons(α, base))⁻¹ in J(X). In cubical type theory, the Kan operations for J(X) compute concatenation by filling squares whose sides are cons constructors; this makes the group structure computable.

Whitehead Products and the Hilton-Milnor Theorem in HoTT

The Whitehead product is a bilinear operation [−,−] : πₘ(X) × πₙ(X) → πₘ₊ₙ₋₁(X) that measures the failure of the H-space structure on ΩX to be strictly commutative. In HoTT, for a pointed type X and loops α : ΩᵐX, β : ΩⁿX, the Whitehead product [α, β] is defined as the (m+n−1)-loop obtained by the commutator of the corresponding elements in the James construction J(X). Concretely, using the equivalence J(X) ≃ ΩΣX, the inclusion X → J(X) induces a map πₖ(X) → πₖ(J(X)) ≃ πₖ₊₁(ΣX). The Whitehead product [α, β] is the image of the commutator [j(α), j(β)] in πₘ₊ₙ(J(X)) under the projection to πₘ₊ₙ₋₁(X) via the EHP sequence. The Hilton-Milnor theorem describes the homotopy groups of a wedge of spheres. In HoTT, for pointed types X and Y, there is an equivalence ΩΣ(X ∨ Y) ≃ ΩΣX × ΩΣY × ΩΣ(J(X) ∧ J(Y)). The proof uses the decomposition J(X ∨ Y) ≃ J(X) * J(Y) (the join) and the equivalence J(Z) ≃ ΩΣZ. The join J(X) * J(Y) is equivalent to Σ(J(X) ∧ J(Y)), giving the third factor. Iterating this decomposition yields a splitting of ΩΣ(∨ᵢ Sⁿⁱ) into a product of loop spaces of suspensions of smash products of the J(Sⁿⁱ). The Whitehead products among the generators correspond to the projections onto the smash product factors. For example, π₃(S² ∨ S²) ≃ ℤ² ⊕ ℤ, where the ℤ summand is generated by the Whitehead product [ι₁, ι₂] of the two inclusions. In cubical type theory, the Whitehead product computes by Kan filling: given cubes representing α and β, the commutator cube is filled by composing the cons squares. The formalization in the HoTT library uses the fact that the smash product X ∧ Y is the pushout of X ← X × Y → Y, and the join X * Y is the pushout of X ← X × Y → Y with an extra cone point. A subtle point is that the Hilton-Milnor splitting is not natural in the category of types; it requires a choice of equivalence J(X ∨ Y) ≃ J(X) * J(Y), which is not unique. The Whitehead product satisfies the graded Jacobi identity and the graded antisymmetry [α, β] = −(−1)ᵐⁿ[β, α], which are proved by manipulating the corresponding words in J(X). The Samelson product ⟨−,−⟩ : πₘ(ΩX) × πₙ(ΩX) → πₘ₊ₙ(ΩX) is the loop space analogue, defined by the commutator in the loop space H-space structure, and it corresponds to the Whitehead product under the suspension isomorphism.

Two-Level Type Theory and Strict Equality in HoTT

Two-level type theory (2LTT) extends HoTT with a strict equality type =ₛ alongside the homotopical identity type =. The strict layer satisfies UIP (uniqueness of identity proofs) and function extensionality definitionally, while the fibrant layer is the full HoTT with univalence and higher inductive types. The theory was developed by Voevodsky, Shulman, and others to formalize the metatheory of HoTT and to provide a framework for strictification results. In 2LTT, types are divided into fibrant types (the HoTT types) and strict types (the UIP types). The strict equality a =ₛ b is a proposition in the strict layer, and there is a coercion from strict equality to path equality: (a =ₛ b) → (a = b). The strict layer supports a strict version of the natural numbers, lists, and other inductive types with definitional computation rules. The fibrant layer supports higher inductive types like the circle, suspension, and pushouts. A key result is the strictification theorem: every ∞-groupoid is equivalent to a strict ∞-groupoid (a globular set with strict composition). In 2LTT this is expressed by showing that for any fibrant type X, there is a strict type Xₛ and an equivalence X ≃ Xₛ. The proof uses the Reedy fibrant replacement in the category of semi-simplicial types, which can be constructed in the strict layer because it only requires strict equality. Another application is the formalization of the simplicial set model of HoTT inside 2LTT: the strict layer provides the meta-language for defining the category of simplicial sets, while the fibrant layer interprets the object language. The cubical type theory with strict equality (CTTₛ) adds a strict interval 𝕀ₛ with endpoints 0ₛ, 1ₛ and a strict path type Pathₛ(A, a, b) satisfying UIP. The strict interval is used to define the strict face lattice and the strict composition operations. A practical use of 2LTT is in the proof of canonicity for cubical type theory: the strict layer is used to define the syntactic model and the computability predicates, while the fibrant layer provides the semantic types. The formalization of 2LTT in Coq (by Shulman) and in Agda (by Cavallo and Harper) uses a universe hierarchy for both layers, with cumulativity between them. A subtle point is that the strict layer cannot eliminate into fibrant types using strict equality; the elimination principle for =ₛ only targets strict types. This restriction preserves the homotopical nature of the fibrant layer. The strict layer also supports a strict version of the univalence axiom, which states that the canonical map (A =ₛ B) → (A ≃ B) is an equivalence of strict types; this is used to transport strict structures along equivalences.

The Rezk Completion and Univalent Categories in HoTT

In HoTT, a category is a precategory where the type of objects is a 1-type (a groupoid) and the identity type of objects is equivalent to the type of isomorphisms. This is the univalence condition for categories, also called the Rezk completeness condition. A precategory C consists of a type C₀ of objects, a family of hom-sets C₁(a, b) : Set, identities, and composition satisfying the category laws up to propositional equality. The Rezk completion of a precategory C is a category Ĉ with a fully faithful functor C → Ĉ that is essentially surjective. In HoTT, the Rezk completion is constructed as a higher inductive type: the objects of Ĉ are the same as C₀, but the identity type is replaced by the type of isomorphisms Iso_C(a, b). Concretely, Ĉ is the HIT with constructors: obj : C₀ → Ĉ, and for each isomorphism f : a ≅ b in C, a path iso(f) : obj(a) = obj(b), together with coherence paths making iso a functor from the core groupoid of C to the core groupoid of Ĉ. The hom-sets of Ĉ are defined as Ĉ₁(obj(a), obj(b)) ≡ C₁(a, b), and transport along iso(f) acts by composition with f. The Rezk completion satisfies the universal property: for any category D, the type of functors Ĉ → D is equivalent to the type of functors C → D. The proof uses the encode-decode method on the identity types of Ĉ. The Rezk completion is used to define the category of types in a universe: the precategory Type_U has objects U and hom-sets (A ≃ B)₀ (the 0-truncation of equivalences). Its Rezk completion is the category of U-small types, where the identity type is exactly the type of equivalences A ≃ B, and univalence for this category is exactly the univalence axiom for U. A key technical point is that the Rezk completion of a precategory that is already a category is equivalent to the original precategory. The construction generalizes to (∞,1)-categories: a Segal type is a simplicial type satisfying the Segal conditions, and it is complete if the map from the 0-simplices to the core of the 1-simplices is an equivalence. The Rezk completion of a Segal type is obtained by replacing the 0-simplices with the core of the 1-simplices. In cubical type theory, the Rezk completion has Kan operations that compute transport along iso(f) by composition with f. The formalization in the HoTT library (by Ahrens, Kapulkin, and Shulman) uses the fact that the core of a precategory is a groupoid, and the HIT for Ĉ adds exactly the missing paths to make the object type a 1-type. A common mistake is to confuse the Rezk completion with the Cauchy completion (idempotent splitting); they are different constructions, though both are instances of a general completion under a class of morphisms. The Rezk completion is also used to define the univalent category of sets: the precategory Set_U has objects the 0-types in U and hom-sets the function types; its Rezk completion is the category of U-small sets, where equality of sets is bijection.

  • Confusing the Freudenthal suspension range: the map πₖ(X) → πₖ₊₁(ΣX) is an isomorphism for k < 2n−1 when X is (n−1)-connected, not k ≤ 2n−1; the boundary case k = 2n−1 is only an epimorphism.
  • Assuming the James construction J(X) models ΩΣX for non-connected X; it only works for connected types, otherwise one must use the reduced James construction on ||X||₀.
  • Thinking the Whitehead product [α, β] is always zero when α or β is zero; the Whitehead product is bilinear but not strictly zero on zero elements in the sense of pointed maps — the basepoint of πₘ(X) is the constant map, and [const, β] = 0 holds, but the product is defined on homotopy groups, not on representatives.
  • Believing the Hilton-Milnor splitting ΩΣ(X ∨ Y) ≃ ΩΣX × ΩΣY × ΩΣ(J(X) ∧ J(Y)) is natural in X and Y; it requires a choice of equivalence J(X ∨ Y) ≃ J(X) * J(Y) which is not functorial.
  • Confusing the Rezk completion (making a precategory univalent) with the Cauchy completion (splitting idempotents); the former replaces identity types with isomorphism types, the latter adds objects for retracts.
  • Assuming two-level type theory allows eliminating strict equality into fibrant types; the strict layer only eliminates into strict types, preserving the homotopical character of the fibrant layer.
  • Thinking the stable homotopy groups πₖˢ(X) are defined without universe polymorphism; the colimit colimₙ πₖ₊ₙ(ΣⁿX) requires a sequence of universes or universe polymorphism because each suspension stays in the same universe.

The EHP Sequence and the Computation of Homotopy Groups of Spheres in HoTT

The EHP sequence is a classical tool in algebraic topology that relates the homotopy groups of spheres of different dimensions. In Homotopy Type Theory it appears as a long exact sequence of types constructed from the fiber sequences of the suspension map Σ : ΩⁿSⁿ → Ωⁿ⁺¹Sⁿ⁺¹, the Hopf construction H : Ωⁿ⁺¹Sⁿ⁺¹ → Ω²ⁿ⁺¹S²ⁿ⁺¹, and the Whitehead product P : Ω²ⁿ⁺¹S²ⁿ⁺¹ → ΩⁿSⁿ. The synthetic proof in HoTT uses the encode‑decode method on the higher inductive definitions of the spheres Sⁿ. The suspension constructor gives a map Σ : Sⁿ → Sⁿ⁺¹, and the loop space ΩSⁿ⁺¹ is equivalent to the join Sⁿ * Sⁿ. The Hopf construction is obtained from the equivalence Ω(Sⁿ * Sⁿ) ≃ ΩS²ⁿ⁺¹, while the Whitehead product arises from the commutator in the loop space. The resulting exact sequence of homotopy groups πₖ(Sⁿ) → πₖ₊₁(Sⁿ⁺¹) → πₖ₊₁(S²ⁿ⁺¹) → πₖ₋₁(Sⁿ) matches the classical EHP sequence. In the HoTT library the sequence has been formalized up to the range where the Freudenthal suspension theorem guarantees isomorphisms, and it has been used to compute π₄(S³) ≃ ℤ/2 and π₅(S³) ≃ ℤ/2. The synthetic argument avoids the classical Serre spectral sequence and instead relies on the higher inductive structure of the spheres and the fact that the join of two n‑types is (2n+1)‑connected. A key technical point is that the Hopf construction in HoTT is defined using the universal property of the pushout that defines the join, and its fiber is shown to be equivalent to the loop space of the lower sphere by a direct encode‑decode argument. This yields a fully constructive proof that the EHP sequence is exact at each stage, and it provides a computational interpretation of the boundary maps as transport along paths in the higher inductive types.

Universe Polymorphism, Cumulativity, and the Consistency of HoTT

Homotopy Type Theory is usually presented with a cumulative hierarchy of universes U₀ : U₁ : U₂ : … where each universe is closed under the type formers of Martin‑Löf type theory and under the univalence axiom. Universe polymorphism allows definitions to be written once and instantiated at any universe level, which is essential for formalizing mathematics that involves large structures such as the category of all types in a given universe. In cubical type theory the universes are equipped with Kan composition operations that respect the cumulative inclusions, and the glue constructor provides the computational content of univalence at each level. Consistency of HoTT with univalence and higher inductive types is established by constructing a model in the category of cubical sets, where each universe Uᵢ is interpreted as a fibrant universe of Kan cubical sets of a fixed size. The cumulativity maps are interpreted as the obvious inclusions of smaller Kan cubical sets into larger ones. The model validates the univalence axiom because the glue type computes transport along equivalences by composition with the given equivalence, and it validates higher inductive types because the cubical set model supports the required Kan filling conditions for the constructors. A subtle point is that the model requires a Grothendieck universe in the meta‑theory to interpret the cumulative hierarchy; this is usually assumed in the ambient set theory (e.g. ZFC with inaccessible cardinals). The consistency proof also shows that adding the propositional resizing axiom (which identifies propositions across universes) does not increase proof‑theoretic strength beyond that of the base theory. In practice, proof assistants such as Agda and Cubical Agda implement universe polymorphism by allowing level variables that are solved by the type checker, and they enforce cumulativity by implicit coercions. The combination of universe polymorphism, cumulativity, and univalence makes it possible to formalize the Rezk completion of a precategory at any universe level without manually lifting definitions.

Encode‑Decode for the EHP Boundary Map
Given the higher inductive definition of the 2‑sphere S² with constructors base : S² and surf : base = base, sketch how the encode‑decode method proves that the boundary map ∂ : π₃(S²) → π₂(S¹) in the EHP sequence corresponds to the Hopf invariant.
Define a family Code : S² → U by Code(base) ≡ ℤ and transport along surf as the identity on ℤ. The encode function sends a loop p : base = base to the integer obtained by transporting 0 along p. The decode function sends an integer n to the n‑fold concatenation of surf. One shows that encode and decode are inverses up to homotopy, establishing π₂(S²) ≃ ℤ. For the boundary map, consider the fiber sequence ΩS² → ΩS³ → ΩS⁵ induced by the Hopf construction. The encode‑decode equivalence for ΩS³ identifies π₃(S²) with the kernel of the map π₃(S³) → π₃(S⁵). The Hopf invariant is then the integer obtained by applying the encode function to the image of a generator of π₃(S²) under the inclusion ΩS² → ΩS³. The computation reduces to showing that the composite ΩS² → ΩS³ → ΩS⁵ is null‑homotopic, which follows from the fact that the join S² * S² is 5‑connected. Hence the boundary map extracts the Hopf invariant.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a synthetic proof of an exact sequence, first identify the higher inductive types that generate the spaces involved (spheres, joins, suspensions). Then write down the fiber sequences that give the maps, and apply the encode‑decode method to each loop space. Remember that the Hopf construction in HoTT is defined via the universal property of the pushout, not by an explicit formula. Cite the Freudenthal suspension theorem for the range where the suspension map is an equivalence.

Modalities in Cohesive HoTT: Shape, Flat, and Sharp and Their Interaction with Higher Inductive Types

Cohesive Homotopy Type Theory extends HoTT with three idempotent modalities: the shape modality ʃ (also written ♯), the flat modality ♭, and the sharp modality ♯. The shape modality ʃ reflects a type into its underlying ∞‑groupoid of paths, effectively forgetting cohesive structure such as topology or smoothness. The flat modality ♭ extracts the discrete underlying type, while the sharp modality ♯ produces the codiscrete type where all points are identified. These modalities satisfy the adjoint string ʃ ⊣ ♭ ⊣ ♯ and the cohesion axioms: ʃ preserves finite products, ♭ preserves all limits, and the unit of ʃ is a monomorphism. In the presence of higher inductive types, the modalities interact with constructors in a predictable way. For a higher inductive type defined by point constructors and path constructors, applying ʃ yields a higher inductive type whose point constructors are the images of the original points and whose path constructors are the images of the original paths, but all higher paths become trivial because ʃ lands in the subcategory of ∞‑groupoids. Applying ♭ to a higher inductive type yields a higher inductive type with the same point constructors but with all path constructors replaced by reflexivity, effectively discretizing the type. The sharp modality ♯ turns a higher inductive type into a codiscrete one where any two points are equal by a unique path. These interactions are crucial for synthetic differential geometry in HoTT: the infinitesimal shape modality ℑ (a variant of ʃ) applied to the higher inductive type of the real line yields the formal disk bundle, and the flat modality applied to the higher inductive type of differential forms recovers the de Rham complex. In the formalization of the Blakers‑Massey theorem, the shape modality is used to reduce the connectivity estimates to statements about ∞‑groupoids, where the classical proof applies. A common mistake is to assume that ʃ commutes with all higher inductive types; it only commutes with those whose constructors are purely propositional, because ʃ does not preserve higher path constructors that carry non‑trivial homotopical information.

The Internal Yoneda Lemma and (∞,1)-Category Theory in HoTT

The internal language of an (∞,1)-topos can be expressed in HoTT by using the Rezk completion to obtain univalent categories and then defining (∞,1)-categories as complete Segal types. The Yoneda lemma states that for any (∞,1)-category C and any object c : C, the functor represented by c is fully faithful. In HoTT this is proved by constructing an equivalence between the hom‑type C(c, d) and the type of natural transformations from the representable functor y(c) to y(d). The proof uses the encode‑decode method on the identity types of the Rezk completion of the precategory of presheaves. A key step is to show that the type of natural transformations between two presheaves is equivalent to the limit of the corresponding diagram, which in HoTT is expressed as a dependent product over the objects of C. The internal Yoneda embedding y : C → PSh(C) is then a fully faithful functor into the (∞,1)-category of presheaves, which is itself an (∞,1)-topos. This embedding preserves all limits that exist in C and exhibits C as a reflective subcategory of PSh(C) when C is an (∞,1)-topos. In the formalization of the (∞,1)-category of types in a universe U, the Yoneda lemma yields an equivalence between the type of equivalences A ≃ B and the type of natural isomorphisms between the representable presheaves. This equivalence is exactly the univalence axiom for the universe of types. The internal Yoneda lemma also underlies the construction of the (∞,1)-category of spectra in HoTT, where the stabilization adjunction Σ^∞ ⊣ Ω^∞ is obtained by applying the Yoneda embedding to the (∞,1)-category of pointed types. A subtle point is that the internal Yoneda lemma requires the ambient (∞,1)-category to be locally small, which in HoTT translates to the requirement that the hom‑types are small relative to the universe in which the presheaf category lives.

The Synthetic Adams Spectral Sequence and Its Formalization Prospects

The Adams spectral sequence is a classical tool for computing stable homotopy groups of spheres by filtering a spectrum by its mod‑p homology. In synthetic homotopy theory, the Adams spectral sequence can be constructed entirely inside HoTT using the tower of cofibers of the map Σ^∞S⁰ → Hℤ/p, where Hℤ/p is the Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum. The E₂‑page is given by Ext groups over the Steenrod algebra, which in HoTT are defined as the homotopy groups of the function spectrum F(Hℤ/p, Hℤ/p). The synthetic construction proceeds by defining the Adams tower as a sequence of higher inductive types Aₙ with maps Aₙ₊₁ → Aₙ whose fibers are wedges of suspensions of Hℤ/p. The spectral sequence then arises from the exact couple associated to this tower. The differentials are induced by the boundary maps in the long exact sequences of homotopy groups. A major advantage of the synthetic approach is that the convergence of the spectral sequence follows from the fact that the limit of the Adams tower is the p‑completion of the sphere spectrum, which in HoTT is expressed as the sequential limit of the tower. Formalizing the Adams spectral sequence in a proof assistant requires a developed theory of spectra in HoTT, including the smash product, function spectra, and the Steenrod operations. Recent work in the HoTT library has formalized the Eilenberg–MacLane spectra Hℤ/p and the Steenrod squares up to degree 2, and has constructed the first few stages of the Adams tower for the 2‑primary sphere. The remaining challenges are the formalization of the full Steenrod algebra and the proof that the synthetic Ext groups agree with the classical algebraic Ext groups. If completed, this would provide a fully verified computation of πₖˢ(S⁰) for a range of k, and would demonstrate the power of synthetic homotopy theory for classical problems.

  • Confusing the EHP sequence with the Freudenthal suspension theorem; the EHP sequence is a long exact sequence valid in a range, while Freudenthal gives an isomorphism in a stable range.
  • Assuming universe polymorphism eliminates the need for cumulativity; polymorphism only allows level variables, but cumulativity provides the actual inclusion maps between universes.
  • Thinking the shape modality ʃ preserves all higher inductive types; it only preserves those whose higher constructors are propositional.
  • Believing the internal Yoneda lemma holds for any precategory; it requires the Rezk completion to obtain a univalent category.
  • Assuming the synthetic Adams spectral sequence converges without proving the limit of the Adams tower is the p‑completion; convergence is a theorem, not a definition.
  • Mixing up the flat modality ♭ with the discrete reflection; ♭ is a modality, while the discrete reflection is a left adjoint to the inclusion of discrete types.
  • Overlooking that the Steenrod operations in HoTT are defined on Eilenberg–MacLane spectra, not on arbitrary types.

These advanced topics illustrate the depth and breadth of current research in Homotopy Type Theory.

The Homotopy Hypothesis: Types as ∞-Groupoids and the Grothendieck Construction

The homotopy hypothesis asserts that ∞-groupoids — higher categories in which every morphism is invertible up to coherent higher equivalence — are equivalent to topological spaces up to weak homotopy equivalence. In Homotopy Type Theory, this hypothesis becomes a theorem: the identity types of a type A carry the structure of an ∞-groupoid, where objects are terms a : A, 1-morphisms are paths p : a = b, 2-morphisms are paths between paths h : p = q, and so on. The Grothendieck construction provides the bridge: given a type family P : A → Type, its total space Σ (a : A), P a corresponds to the Grothendieck construction of the corresponding ∞-groupoid fibration. The fundamental result, formalized in the simplicial set model and in cubical type theory, is that the ∞-category of types in a universe U is equivalent to the ∞-category of Kan complexes (or cubical sets with Kan filling). This equivalence is mediated by the singular complex functor Sing : Top → sSet and its left adjoint geometric realization |−| : sSet → Top, which form a Quillen equivalence. In HoTT, the univalence axiom ensures that the universe U itself is an ∞-groupoid, and the identity type A = B in U is equivalent to the type of equivalences A ≃ B. The Grothendieck construction for type families P : A → U yields a type Σ (a : A), P a whose projection to A is a fibration in the sense of model categories, and the long exact sequence of homotopy groups for this fibration is derivable using the encode-decode method. A critical subtlety is that the homotopy hypothesis in HoTT is not a single statement but a hierarchy: for each n, the n-truncated types correspond to n-groupoids, and the full hypothesis requires the coherence data for all higher morphisms, which is automatically provided by the inductive structure of identity types.

Cubical Agda: Computational Higher Inductive Types and Canonicity

Cubical Agda implements Cubical Type Theory with a primitive interval type I and Kan composition operations, providing computational content to univalence and higher inductive types. Unlike the axiomatic approach in Coq or Lean where univalence is postulated, Cubical Agda defines Path A a b as I → A with p i0 = a and p i1 = b, and the univalence axiom becomes a theorem: ua : (A ≃ B) → Path U A B computes by transporting along the equivalence. Higher inductive types are defined with point constructors and path constructors that directly manipulate the interval. For example, the circle S¹ has base : S¹ and loop : Path S¹ base base, where loop i reduces to base at endpoints. The Kan composition operations hcomp and transp ensure that all types satisfy the Kan filling condition, making every type a cubical Kan complex. Canonicity — the property that every closed term of type Nat reduces to a numeral — holds for Cubical Agda because the interval I is a De Morgan algebra with no closed terms other than i0 and i1, and the composition operations are defined by cases on the type formers. The computational behavior of higher inductive types is governed by the hcomp equations: for a HIT H with constructors c : Γ → H and path constructors p : Γ → Path H (c γ) (c' γ), the composition hcomp on H reduces by analyzing the boundary constraints. A key implementation detail is that Cubical Agda uses a glue type Glue B [ φ ↦ (A, e) ] to internalize univalence, where φ is a face formula and e : A ≃ B. The unglue operation extracts the underlying B, and glue packages an A with a proof that it matches B on φ. This mechanism allows ua to compute, and the transp operation along ua e reduces to the forward direction of e. The canonicity proof for Cubical Agda relies on a logical relations argument showing that every closed term is related to a canonical form, and the interval variables are treated as neutral elements that cannot appear in closed normal forms.

Worked Example: Transport Along Univalence in Cubical Agda
Given an equivalence e : Bool ≃ Bool that swaps true and false, compute transp (λ i → ua e i) i0 true in Cubical Agda and explain the reduction steps.
The equivalence e consists of a function f : Bool → Bool with f true = false, f false = true, and a proof that f is an equivalence (it is its own inverse). The univalence term ua e : Path U Bool Bool is definitionally λ i → Glue Bool [ (i = i0) ↦ (Bool, e) , (i = i1) ↦ (Bool, idEquiv) ]. Transport along this path at i0 is defined as transp (λ i → ua e i) i0 true = unglue (hcomp (λ j → ∂ (ua e j)) (glue (f true) (λ { (i = i0) → equivToPath e true ; (i = i1) → refl })). Since we transport at i0, the face (i = i0) is true, so the hcomp reduces using the Glue composition structure. The glue term provides f true = false on the face (i = i0), and the hcomp fills the open box with this boundary. The unglue then projects to the underlying Bool, yielding false. Thus transp (λ i → ua e i) i0 true reduces to false, exactly the action of f on true. This demonstrates that univalence computes as the forward direction of the equivalence.
Exam Strategy: Cubical Reduction Rules
When asked about computational behavior of univalence or HITs in cubical type theory, focus on the Glue type and the hcomp/transp equations. Remember: transp (ua e) i0 x reduces to e.1 x (the forward function), and transp (ua e) i1 x reduces to x. For HITs, path constructors p : Path H a b compute by cases on the interval: p i0 = a, p i1 = b. The Kan composition hcomp on a HIT analyzes which constructors are on the boundary and fills using the path constructors. Write out the Glue boundary conditions explicitly — examiners check whether you understand that φ is a face formula (cofibration) and the equivalence is only required on that face.

Univalence Implies Function Extensionality: The Proof and Its Computational Behavior

Function extensionality — the principle that pointwise equal functions are equal — is a consequence of the univalence axiom. The proof proceeds by showing that for any types A and B, the type of functions A → B is equivalent to the type of sections of the projection Σ (a : A), B → A, and then using univalence to transport the equality of sections to equality of functions. More directly, given f g : A → B and h : Π (a : A), f a = g a, one constructs a path p : f = g by defining p i a = h a i where h a : Path B (f a) (g a). This uses the fact that Path (A → B) f g is equivalent to Π (a : A), Path B (f a) (g a), which is itself a consequence of univalence applied to the equivalence between A → B and the type of graphs of functions. The computational content of this proof depends on the type theory: in axiomatic HoTT (Coq, Lean), function extensionality is a postulated axiom with no computational content; in Cubical Type Theory, it computes by η-expansion on the interval. Specifically, the path p : f = g defined as λ i a → h a i satisfies p i0 = f and p i1 = g definitionally, and transport along p reduces to applying h pointwise. The equivalence between Path (A → B) f g and Π a, Path B (f a) (g a) is given by λ p a → ap (λ f → f a) p in one direction and λ h → λ i a → h a i in the other. In Cubical Agda, this equivalence is a definitional isomorphism because Path (A → B) f g is I → (A → B), which is definitionally equal to A → (I → B) by currying, and I → B is Path B. The proof that univalence implies function extensionality in Martin-Löf type theory with univalence uses the fact that the type of equivalences A ≃ B is a subtype of A → B, and univalence gives a path ua e : A = B for each equivalence. Applying ap (λ X → X → X) to ua e yields a path between function types, and transporting the identity function along this path gives the equivalence action on functions. The computational behavior of this transport is exactly the conjugation by e, which in cubical type theory reduces to the forward and backward functions of e.

The Generalized Van Kampen Theorem for Higher Homotopy Groupoids

The classical Seifert-van Kampen theorem computes the fundamental group π₁ of a pushout of spaces from the fundamental groups of the pieces. In HoTT, this generalizes to a theorem about the fundamental ∞-groupoid of a pushout of types. Given a span of types C ← A → B and its pushout P = C ⊔_A B, the fundamental ∞-groupoid Π_∞(P) is the pushout of ∞-groupoids Π_∞(C) ← Π_∞(A) → Π_∞(B) in the ∞-category of ∞-groupoids. Since types in HoTT are already ∞-groupoids, this states that the pushout of types computes the homotopy pushout of their ∞-groupoid structures. The proof uses the encode-decode method on the identity types of the pushout higher inductive type. The pushout P has constructors inl : C → P, inr : B → P, and glue : Π (a : A), inl (f a) = inr (g a). The identity type x =_P y is characterized by a code type Code x y defined by induction on x and y, and one proves (x = y) ≃ Code x y. For the fundamental groupoid Π₁(P), the code type yields the free product with amalgamation π₁(C) *π₁(A) π₁(B). For higher homotopy groups, the generalized Van Kampen theorem states that the homotopy groups π_n(P) for n ≥ 2 fit into a long exact sequence involving the homotopy groups of A, B, C, and the homotopy fiber of the map A → C × B. This is the Blakers-Massey theorem, which gives the connectivity of the pushout square. The synthetic proof in HoTT uses the encode-decode method on the higher inductive type of the pushout, combined with the Freudenthal suspension theorem to stabilize the homotopy groups. A key insight is that the pushout in HoTT is a homotopy pushout, so the theorem holds without any cofibration assumptions on the maps A → C and A → B. The formalization in the HoTT library (Lean, Coq, Agda) uses the pushout HIT and the encode_decode tactic to compute π₁ of the circle, torus, and higher spheres. The generalized theorem for n ≥ 2 requires the n-truncated version of the pushout and the Blakers-Massey connectivity estimates.

Stable Homotopy Theory in HoTT: Spectra, Suspension Spectra, and the Stable Homotopy Category

Stable homotopy theory studies the category of spectra, which are sequences of pointed types X₀, X₁, X₂, … with equivalences X_n ≃ Ω Xn+1. In HoTT, a spectrum is a type family X : ℕ → Type_* equipped with structure maps σ_n : X_n → Ω Xn+1 that are equivalences. The suspension spectrum functor Σ^∞ : Type_* → Spectra sends a pointed type A to the spectrum with (Σ^∞ A)_n = Σ^n A and the canonical equivalences Σ^n A ≃ Ω Σn+1 A. Its right adjoint is the infinite loop space functor Ω^∞ : Spectra → Type_*, which takes a spectrum to its 0-th space X0. The stable homotopy groups of a spectrum X are defined as π_k(X) = πk+n(X_n) for sufficiently large n, which is independent of n by the equivalence structure. The sphere spectrum S is Σ^∞ S⁰, and its stable homotopy groups π_k^s = π_k(S) are the classical stable stems. In HoTT, the Freudenthal suspension theorem gives the stabilization range: the suspension map π_k(X) → πk+1(Σ X) is an isomorphism for k < 2n - 1 when X is n-connected. This implies that the stable homotopy groups of spheres can be computed by suspending sufficiently many times. The EHP sequence — a long exact sequence relating π_k(S^n), πk+1(Sn+1), and π_k(S2n+1) — is formalized in HoTT using the fiber sequence S^n → Ω Sn+1 → Ω S2n+1 derived from the James construction. The smash product of spectra X ∧ Y makes the stable homotopy category a symmetric monoidal ∞-category, and the function spectrum F(X, Y) provides the internal hom. The Eilenberg-MacLane spectra H A for an abelian group A represent ordinary cohomology: π-k(F(X, H A)) = H^k(X; A). The Steenrod operations are endomorphisms of H ℤ/p in the stable homotopy category, and their formalization in HoTT uses the fact that H ℤ/p is a ring spectrum. The Adams spectral sequence, which computes π_*^s from ExtA_*(H_*(S), H_*(S)) where A_* is the dual Steenrod algebra, is constructed synthetically as the spectral sequence of the Adams tower … → A2 → A1 → A0 = S where each fiber is a wedge of H ℤ/p. The convergence of this spectral sequence to the p-completion of the sphere spectrum is a theorem in HoTT, proved by showing that the limit of the Adams tower is the p-completion.

  • Confusing the homotopy hypothesis (types as ∞-groupoids) with the statement that all ∞-groupoids arise from spaces; in HoTT, types are ∞-groupoids by definition, and the hypothesis is the equivalence with topological spaces via the simplicial set model.
  • Assuming that Cubical Agda's canonicity for Nat implies canonicity for all types; canonicity fails for higher inductive types because path constructors introduce non-canonical forms that do not reduce further.
  • Believing that function extensionality is equivalent to univalence; univalence implies function extensionality, but the converse does not hold — there are models of type theory with function extensionality but not univalence.
  • Thinking the generalized Van Kampen theorem computes all higher homotopy groups of a pushout directly; it only gives π₁ as a pushout of groupoids, while higher groups require the Blakers-Massey theorem and the EHP sequence.
  • Confusing the suspension spectrum Σ^∞ X with the infinite suspension colim_n Σ^n X; the former is a spectrum (a sequence of types), the latter is a single type (the colimit in spaces).
  • Assuming the stable homotopy category in HoTT is equivalent to the classical stable homotopy category without specifying the model; the equivalence holds in the simplicial set model and in cubical sets, but requires the axiom of choice for the construction of the stable homotopy category as a triangulated category.
  • Overlooking that the Blakers-Massey theorem in HoTT gives a connectivity estimate for the pushout square, not an exact computation of homotopy groups; the exact computation requires additional input such as the EHP sequence or the Serre spectral sequence.

The Synthetic Whitehead Tower and Postnikov Tower in HoTT

The Whitehead tower and Postnikov tower are dual constructions that decompose a type into layers of increasing connectivity or truncation. In HoTT, the Postnikov tower of a type X is a sequence of types X⟨n⟩ with maps X → X⟨n⟩ where X⟨n⟩ is n-truncated and the map is (n+1)-connected. The fiber of X⟨n⟩ → X⟨n-1⟩ is an Eilenberg-MacLane space K(πₙ(X), n). Synthetically, X⟨n⟩ is constructed as the n-truncation ‖X‖ₙ, and the tower arises from the universal property of truncation. The Whitehead tower is the dual: a sequence of types X⟨n⟩ with maps X⟨n⟩ → X where X⟨n⟩ is n-connected and the map is n-truncated. The fiber of X⟨n⟩ → X⟨n-1⟩ is a K(πₙ(X), n-1). In HoTT, X⟨n⟩ is constructed as the homotopy fiber of X → ‖X‖ₙ₋₁, or equivalently as the n-connected cover obtained by killing homotopy groups below n. The two towers are related by the fact that the Postnikov tower of X is the Whitehead tower of the ∞-groupoid of maps from spheres into X. Formalization in the HoTT library (Agda, Lean) uses the truncation HIT and the encode-decode method to compute the homotopy groups of the fibers. A key theorem is that for a connected type X, the Postnikov tower converges to X in the sense that X ≃ limₙ X⟨n⟩, where the limit is taken in the ∞-category of types. The Whitehead tower converges to the universal cover when X is connected. The k-invariants of the Postnikov tower are maps X⟨n⟩ → K(πₙ₊₁(X), n+2) that classify the extension; in HoTT these are constructed using the universal property of Eilenberg-MacLane spaces and the fact that πₙ₊₁(X) ≃ πₙ(ΩX). The synthetic approach avoids the technicalities of Postnikov systems in classical homotopy theory (cofibrations, CW approximations) because truncation and connected covers are primitive HITs with universal properties.

The Synthetic J-Homomorphism and the Image of J in HoTT

The J-homomorphism is a map J : πₖ(O(n)) → πₖ₊ₙ(Sⁿ) from the homotopy groups of the orthogonal group to the stable homotopy groups of spheres, constructed by associating to a map Sᵏ → O(n) the fiberwise suspension of the trivial bundle. In HoTT, the orthogonal group O(n) is defined as the type of self-equivalences of ℝⁿ preserving the standard inner product, or synthetically as the automorphism group of the standard n-sphere in the ∞-category of types. The stable orthogonal group O = colimₙ O(n) is equivalent to the infinite loop space of the sphere spectrum. The J-homomorphism is then the map on homotopy groups induced by the unit of the sphere spectrum S → KO, where KO is the real K-theory spectrum. In HoTT, KO is constructed as the group completion of the type of finite-dimensional real vector spaces with direct sum, or as the K-theory of the type of finite sets with the discrete topology. The image of J is the subgroup of πₖ^s generated by the image of J. Adams proved that the image of J is cyclic of order equal to the denominator of Bₖ/4k for k ≡ 0,1 mod 8, and order 2 for k ≡ 3,7 mod 8, where Bₖ are Bernoulli numbers. In HoTT, the computation of the image of J uses the Adams spectral sequence for the sphere spectrum at the prime 2, together with the fact that the fiber of S → KO is the connective cover of the real K-theory spectrum. The synthetic construction of the Adams spectral sequence (as a spectral sequence of the Adams tower) allows the computation of the E₂-page as Ext over the Steenrod algebra, and the differentials are analyzed using the action of the Steenrod operations on the cohomology of KO. The formalization of the image of J in HoTT (by Brunerie, Hou, and others) uses the synthetic Adams spectral sequence and the computation of the cohomology of KO as a module over the Steenrod algebra. A key insight is that the J-homomorphism in HoTT is not just a map on homotopy groups but a map of spectra S → KO, and its fiber is the connective cover of the Anderson dual of the sphere spectrum. The order of the image of J is then computed by analyzing the homotopy groups of this fiber using the long exact sequence and the known homotopy groups of KO (which are periodic by Bott periodicity).

Encode-Decode for the J-Homomorphism
Explain how the encode-decode method is adapted to compute the image of the J-homomorphism in HoTT, and why the synthetic Adams spectral sequence is necessary rather than a direct encode-decode on the map J : O → Ω^∞ S.
The encode-decode method computes πₙ(X) by constructing an equivalence between ΩⁿX and a known type (e.g., ℤ for S¹). For the J-homomorphism J : O → Ω^∞ S, the domain O = colimₙ O(n) has homotopy groups πₖ(O) that are 8-periodic by Bott periodicity (π₀=ℤ/2, π₁=ℤ/2, π₂=0, π₃=ℤ, π₄=0, π₅=0, π₆=0, π₇=ℤ). A direct encode-decode on J would require characterizing the fiber of J, which is the connective cover of the Anderson dual of S — a type whose homotopy groups are the stable stems not in the image of J. This fiber is not a simple Eilenberg-MacLane space, so encode-decode fails. The synthetic Adams spectral sequence constructs a tower … → A₂ → A₁ → A₀ = S where each fiber is a wedge of Hℤ/2, and computes πₖ(S) as the limit of the spectral sequence. The map J induces a map of towers to the Adams tower for KO, whose E₂-page is computable because H*(KO; ℤ/2) is a free module over the Steenrod algebra. The image of J is then the subgroup of πₖ^s that survives to the E_∞-page and maps nontrivially to πₖ(KO). This spectral sequence approach is necessary because the fiber of J has nontrivial k-invariants and is not a product of Eilenberg-MacLane spaces.
Exam Strategy: J-Homomorphism and Adams Spectral Sequence
When asked about the image of J in HoTT, emphasize three layers: (1) J as a map of spectra S → KO induced by the unit of real K-theory; (2) the synthetic Adams spectral sequence as the computational tool, with E₂ = Ext_A(H*(S), H*(S)) converging to π_*^s; (3) the computation of H*(KO) as a free A-module implying the E₂-page for KO is trivial in positive degrees, so π_*(KO) is detected at E₂. The order of the image of J follows from the long exact sequence of the fiber and the known 8-periodic homotopy groups of KO. Memorize the 8-periodic pattern of πₖ(O) and the denominator formula for the image order.

The Synthetic Goodwillie Calculus in HoTT

Goodwillie calculus is a method for approximating homotopy functors by polynomial functors, analogous to Taylor series in analysis. In HoTT, a homotopy functor is a type family F : Type → Type that preserves equivalences. The n-excisive approximation PₙF is the universal n-excisive functor under F, where n-excisive means F sends strongly cocartesian (n+1)-cubes to cartesian cubes. The Taylor tower of F is the sequence … → P₂F → P₁F → P₀F, where P₀F is the constant functor at F(1). The layers DₙF = fib(PₙF → Pₙ₋₁F) are homogeneous degree-n functors, classified by spectra with Σₙ-action (the n-th derivative ∂ⁿF). In HoTT, the construction of PₙF uses the n-excisive approximation as a higher inductive type: for each X, PₙF(X) is the colimit of the diagram of F applied to the punctured (n+1)-cube on X. The derivative ∂ⁿF is a spectrum with Σₙ-action, constructed as the value of DₙF on the n-sphere Sⁿ. The chain rule, product rule, and composition formulas for derivatives are formalized using the universal properties of the approximations. A key result is the convergence of the Taylor tower for analytic functors: if F is analytic (a condition on the connectivity of the maps F(X) → PₙF(X)), then F(X) ≃ limₙ PₙF(X). In HoTT, the identity functor Id : Type_* → Type_* has Taylor tower where PₙId(X) is the n-truncation of X, and the layers are the Eilenberg-MacLane spaces K(πₙ(X), n). The functor Ω^∞Σ^∞ (the free infinite loop space) has Taylor tower where Pₙ(Ω^∞Σ^∞)(X) is the n-th stage of the free E_∞-algebra on X, and the layers are the extended powers. The formalization of Goodwillie calculus in HoTT (by Christensen, Opie, and others) uses the synthetic ∞-category theory developed in the HoTT library, particularly the theory of (∞,1)-categories as Rezk-complete Segal types. The n-excisive approximation is constructed as a left adjoint to the inclusion of n-excisive functors into all functors, using the adjoint functor theorem for ∞-categories. The classification of homogeneous functors by spectra with Σₙ-action uses the fact that the ∞-category of homogeneous degree-n functors is equivalent to the ∞-category of spectra with Σₙ-action, via the evaluation at Sⁿ and the extended power construction.

The Synthetic Pontryagin-Thom Construction and Cobordism in HoTT

The Pontryagin-Thom construction establishes an equivalence between the stable homotopy groups of spheres and the framed cobordism groups of manifolds. In HoTT, a framed manifold of dimension n is a type M equipped with a map M → BO(n) classifying the stable normal bundle, together with a trivialization of this bundle (a lift to the fiber of BO(n) → BO). The cobordism group Ωₙ^fr is the group of framed cobordism classes of closed n-manifolds, with disjoint union as addition. The Pontryagin-Thom map PT : πₖ^s → Ωₖ^fr sends a stable map Sⁿ⁺ᵏ → Sⁿ to the framed manifold given by the preimage of a regular value. In HoTT, the construction is synthetic: the sphere spectrum S is the suspension spectrum of S⁰, and the Thom spectrum MFr of the trivial bundle over BO is equivalent to S. The Thom isomorphism in HoTT states that for a vector bundle E → X classified by f : X → BO(n), the Thom space Th(E) is equivalent to the pushout of X ← E → *. The Pontryagin-Thom equivalence is then the statement that the map of spectra S → MFr induced by the trivial bundle is an equivalence. This is formalized by showing that the Thom spectrum functor Th : Type/BO → Spectra is symmetric monoidal and sends the trivial bundle to the sphere spectrum. The cobordism hypothesis in HoTT (the Baez-Dolan-Lurie theorem) states that the ∞-category of fully dualizable objects in an (∞,n)-category C is equivalent to the ∞-category of symmetric monoidal functors from the (∞,n)-category of cobordisms to C. In HoTT, the (∞,n)-category of cobordisms is constructed as a higher inductive type whose objects are closed (n-1)-manifolds, 1-morphisms are n-dimensional cobordisms, and higher morphisms are diffeomorphisms and isotopies. The fully dualizable objects in an (∞,n)-category are those with adjoints at all levels. The formalization of the cobordism hypothesis in HoTT (by various authors) uses the synthetic (∞,n)-category theory and the fact that the (∞,n)-category of cobordisms is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object. The Pontryagin-Thom construction for unoriented cobordism gives an equivalence between the unoriented cobordism spectrum MO and the Thom spectrum of the universal bundle over BO, and the homotopy groups πₖ(MO) are the unoriented cobordism groups, which are polynomial algebras over ℤ/2 on generators in degrees not of the form 2ⁱ-1 (Thom's theorem). In HoTT, this is proved by computing the cohomology of MO as a module over the Steenrod algebra and using the Adams spectral sequence.

The Synthetic String Group and Higher Connected Covers in HoTT

The String group String(n) is the 3-connected cover of Spin(n), obtained by killing π₃(Spin(n)) ≃ ℤ. In HoTT, Spin(n) is the 1-connected cover of SO(n), which is itself the 0-connected cover of O(n). The Whitehead tower of O(n) is … → String(n) → Spin(n) → SO(n) → O(n), where each stage kills the next homotopy group. The String group is defined as the homotopy fiber of the map ½p₁ : BSpin(n) → K(ℤ, 4), where ½p₁ is the fractional first Pontryagin class. In HoTT, BSpin(n) is the classifying type of Spin(n)-bundles, constructed as the type of Spin(n)-principal bundles over a variable base. The class ½p₁ is a map BSpin(n) → K(ℤ, 4) constructed using the synthetic Chern-Weil theory: the curvature of a Spin(n)-connection is a 2-form with values in the Lie algebra, and the invariant polynomial tr(F∧F) gives a 4-form whose integral is the Pontryagin number. The String group is then the type of Spin(n)-bundles with a trivialization of ½p₁, i.e., the homotopy fiber of ½p₁. The Fivebrane group Fivebrane(n) is the 7-connected cover of String(n), obtained by killing π₇(String(n)) ≃ ℤ, and is the homotopy fiber of a map BString(n) → K(ℤ, 8) classifying the fractional second Pontryagin class. In HoTT, these higher connected covers are constructed iteratively using the Whitehead tower HIT: for a connected type X, the n-connected cover X⟨n⟩ is the homotopy fiber of X → ‖X‖ₙ₋₁. The homotopy groups of String(n) are πₖ(String(n)) = πₖ(Spin(n)) for k ≠ 3, and π₃(String(n)) = 0. The cohomology of BString(n) is computed using the Serre spectral sequence of the fibration K(ℤ, 3) → BString(n) → BSpin(n), which in HoTT is the synthetic Serre spectral sequence of the fiber sequence. The String group appears in the Green-Schwarz anomaly cancellation in string theory, where the condition is that the class ½p₁ - ½c₂ vanishes. In HoTT, this is formalized by constructing the type of String structures on a manifold as the fiber of the map ½p₁ - ½c₂ : BSpin(n) × BSU(m) → K(ℤ, 4). The formalization of the String group and higher covers in HoTT (by various authors) uses the synthetic cohomology theory and the construction of characteristic classes as maps to Eilenberg-MacLane spaces.

  • Confusing the Postnikov tower (truncation tower) with the Whitehead tower (connected cover tower); the former kills higher homotopy groups, the latter kills lower ones.
  • Assuming the J-homomorphism in HoTT is only a map on homotopy groups; it is fundamentally a map of spectra S → KO, and its fiber is the connective cover of the Anderson dual of S.
  • Believing the synthetic Adams spectral sequence computes the image of J directly; it computes π_*^s, and the image of J is identified as the subgroup mapping nontrivially to π_*(KO) under the map induced by S → KO.
  • Thinking Goodwillie calculus in HoTT only applies to functors Type → Type; it applies to functors between any (∞,1)-categories with finite limits and colimits, and the n-excisive approximation is a left adjoint in the ∞-category of functors.
  • Confusing the Pontryagin-Thom construction (equivalence between framed cobordism and stable stems) with the cobordism hypothesis (classification of TQFTs); the former is a theorem about π_*^s, the latter is a theorem about symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-categories.
  • Assuming the String group is just the 3-connected cover of Spin(n) without the characteristic class data; in HoTT, String(n) is explicitly the homotopy fiber of ½p₁ : BSpin(n) → K(ℤ, 4), and this fiber sequence is essential for computing its cohomology.
  • Overlooking that the synthetic Serre spectral sequence for the String group fibration K(ℤ, 3) → BString(n) → BSpin(n) has a nontrivial differential d₄ that kills the generator of H³(K(ℤ, 3)) and hits ½p₁ in H⁴(BSpin(n)).

The Synthetic Hurewicz Theorem in Homotopy Type Theory

The synthetic Hurewicz theorem is the HoTT counterpart of the classical result that relates homotopy groups to homology groups. In HoTT, homology is defined via the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(G,n) and the Hurewicz map is a function πₙ(X) → Hₙ(X) constructed by mapping a pointed n-loop to its class in the n-th homology group, which is defined as πₙ(‖X‖ₙ) where ‖-‖ₙ denotes the n-truncation. The theorem states that for a pointed, (n-1)-connected type X, the Hurewicz map is an isomorphism for k ≤ n and a surjection for k = n+1. The proof proceeds by induction on n, using the encode‑decode method to characterize the path spaces of truncations and the fact that the n-truncation of an (n-1)-connected type is an Eilenberg–MacLane space K(πₙ(X), n). The base case n = 1 reduces to the statement that the fundamental group of a connected type coincides with the first homology group, which is proved by constructing an explicit equivalence between π₁(X) and H₁(X) via the abelianization of the fundamental groupoid. The inductive step uses the fiber sequence ΩⁿX → ‖X‖ₙ → ‖X‖ₙ₋₁ and the long exact sequence of homotopy groups, together with the fact that the Hurewicz map commutes with the boundary maps. This synthetic proof avoids any reference to simplicial sets or singular chains, staying entirely within the internal language of HoTT.

Formalization in the HoTT Library

The theorem has been formalized in the HoTT‑Agda library (file Hurewicz.agda) and in the Coq HoTT library. The formalization defines homology groups as Hₙ(X) := πₙ(‖X‖ₙ), constructs the Hurewicz map using the universal property of truncation, and proves the isomorphism and surjectivity statements by induction on n. The proof relies on the encode‑decode lemmas for truncations, which are themselves proved using higher inductive types for the n-truncation. The formalization also includes a version for non‑pointed types by working with the based loop space ΩX.

Applications

The synthetic Hurewicz theorem is used to compute low‑dimensional homotopy groups of higher inductive types such as spheres, real projective spaces, and the torus. For example, it gives an immediate proof that π₂(S²) ≃ ℤ because S² is 1‑connected and its second homology is ℤ. It also underlies the synthetic proof of the Freudenthal suspension theorem, where the Hurewicz map for the suspension is compared with the homology suspension isomorphism.

The Relative Hurewicz Theorem and Its Synthetic Proof

The relative Hurewicz theorem compares the homotopy groups of a pair (X,A) with the relative homology groups. In HoTT, a pair is represented by a map f : A → X and the relative homotopy groups are defined as πₙ(X,A) := πₙ₋₁(hofib(f)), where hofib(f) is the homotopy fiber of f. Relative homology groups are defined as Hₙ(X,A) := πₙ(‖hofib(f)‖ₙ). The theorem states that if A is (n-2)-connected and X is (n-1)-connected, then the relative Hurewicz map πₙ(X,A) → Hₙ(X,A) is an isomorphism for k ≤ n and a surjection for k = n+1. The synthetic proof mirrors the absolute case: one considers the fiber sequence hofib(f) → A → X, applies the absolute Hurewicz theorem to the homotopy fiber, and uses the long exact sequences of homotopy and homology groups associated to the pair. The key technical ingredient is the compatibility of the Hurewicz map with the boundary maps in the long exact sequences, which is proved by a diagram chase internal to HoTT using the universal property of truncation and the fact that truncation preserves fiber sequences up to equivalence.

Formalization Challenges

Formalizing the relative theorem requires a careful treatment of pointed versus unpointed maps. In the HoTT‑Agda library, the relative Hurewicz map is defined for a pointed map f : (A,a₀) → (X,x₀) and the proof uses the pointed homotopy fiber. The library also provides a version for unpointed maps by first replacing the map with its pointed replacement via the mapping cylinder construction, which is itself a higher inductive type. The formalization of the long exact sequence of a pair uses the fiber sequence ΩX → hofib(f) → A → X and the fact that truncation commutes with loop spaces up to equivalence.

Use in Computing Homotopy Groups of Cofibers

The relative Hurewicz theorem is particularly useful for computing the homotopy groups of cofibers of maps between highly connected types. For instance, the cofiber of the Hopf map η : S³ → S² is the complex projective plane ℂP². Applying the relative theorem to the pair (ℂP², S²) yields the isomorphism π₃(ℂP²) ≃ H₃(ℂP²) ≃ 0 and the surjection π₄(ℂP²) ↠ H₄(ℂP²) ≃ ℤ, which matches the classical calculation.

Worked Example: Relative Hurewicz for the Hopf Fibration
Let η : S³ → S² be the Hopf map and let Cη be its cofiber. Using the relative Hurewicz theorem, compute π₃(Cη) and π₄(Cη).
The cofiber sequence S³ → S² → Cη gives a pair (Cη, S²). The map S² → Cη is 2‑connected because S² is 1‑connected and the cofiber of a map from a 3‑sphere is 2‑connected. The homotopy fiber of S² → Cη is equivalent to ΩCη, which is 1‑connected. Applying the relative Hurewicz theorem with n = 3 (since the pair is 2‑connected) yields an isomorphism π₃(Cη, S²) ≃ H₃(Cη, S²). The relative homology group H₃(Cη, S²) is zero because the cellular chain complex of Cη has no 3‑cells. Hence π₃(Cη, S²) = 0. The long exact sequence of the pair gives π₃(S²) → π₃(Cη) → π₃(Cη, S²) = 0, so π₃(Cη) ≃ π₃(S²) ≃ ℤ (generated by the Hopf map). For π₄, the theorem gives a surjection π₄(Cη, S²) ↠ H₄(Cη, S²) ≃ ℤ. The relative group π₄(Cη, S²) fits into π₄(S²) → π₄(Cη) → π₄(Cη, S²) → π₃(S²). Since π₄(S²) ≃ ℤ/2 and the boundary map is the Whitehead product [ι,ι] which is non‑trivial, one obtains π₄(Cη) ≃ ℤ. Thus π₃(Cη) ≃ ℤ and π₄(Cη) ≃ ℤ.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a homotopy group computation via the Hurewicz theorem, first identify the connectivity of the type or pair. Write down the relevant absolute or relative Hurewicz statement, then compute the corresponding homology groups using cellular or synthetic homology (often just the truncation levels). Remember that the theorem gives an isomorphism up to the connectivity degree and a surjection one degree higher; do not claim an isomorphism beyond that without additional hypotheses (e.g., simple connectivity for the absolute case).

The Hurewicz Map for Higher Inductive Types: Spheres and Projective Spaces

Higher inductive types (HITs) provide direct constructions of classical spaces such as spheres Sⁿ, real projective spaces ℝPⁿ, and complex projective spaces ℂPⁿ. The Hurewicz map for these types can be described explicitly using the constructors of the HIT. For the sphere Sⁿ, defined as the suspension of Sⁿ⁻¹ with base point base, the n-th homotopy group πₙ(Sⁿ) is generated by the n-fold loop obtained by iterating the suspension constructor. The Hurewicz map sends this generator to the fundamental class in Hₙ(Sⁿ) ≃ ℤ, which is defined as the image of the generator under the truncation map Sⁿ → ‖Sⁿ‖ₙ. The proof that this map is an isomorphism uses the synthetic Hurewicz theorem together with the fact that Sⁿ is (n-1)-connected, which is proved by induction on n using the suspension connectivity lemma.

Real Projective Spaces

The real projective space ℝPⁿ can be defined as a HIT with a point constructor base, a 1‑loop loop : base = base satisfying loop² = refl, and higher constructors that enforce the appropriate truncation level. Its homotopy groups are known classically: π₁(ℝPⁿ) ≃ ℤ/2 for n ≥ 2, and πₖ(ℝPⁿ) ≃ πₖ(Sⁿ) for k ≥ 2. The synthetic Hurewicz map for ℝPⁿ sends the non‑trivial element of π₁ to the generator of H₁(ℝPⁿ) ≃ ℤ/2. For k ≥ 2, the map factors through the covering map Sⁿ → ℝPⁿ and the Hurewicz isomorphism for the sphere. The formalization in the HoTT library uses the encode‑decode method to compute π₁(ℝPⁿ) and then applies the absolute Hurewicz theorem to the universal cover.

Complex Projective Spaces

ℂPⁿ is defined as a HIT with a point, a 2‑loop generating π₂ ≃ ℤ, and higher constructors. Its homology is concentrated in even degrees. The Hurewicz map π₂(ℂPⁿ) → H₂(ℂPⁿ) is an isomorphism ℤ ≃ ℤ. For k = 3, the Hurewicz map is a surjection onto H₃(ℂPⁿ) = 0, giving π₃(ℂPⁿ) ≃ ℤ (the Hopf map). The synthetic proof uses the relative Hurewicz theorem for the pair (ℂPⁿ, ℂPⁿ⁻¹) and the cell attachment description of ℂPⁿ as a HIT.

The Hurewicz Isomorphism for n-Connected Types and n-Types

An n-connected type is one whose homotopy groups vanish up to degree n. An n-type (or n-truncated type) has no non‑trivial homotopy groups above degree n. The Hurewicz theorem takes a particularly clean form for these extremes. If X is n-connected, then the Hurewicz map πₖ(X) → Hₖ(X) is an isomorphism for all k ≤ n+1 and a surjection for k = n+2. This follows by applying the absolute theorem to the (n+1)-connected cover of X. Conversely, if X is an n-type, then Hₖ(X) = 0 for k > n, and the Hurewicz map is an isomorphism for k = n (both sides are πₙ(X)) and trivial for k > n. The synthetic proof uses the fact that the n-truncation of an n-type is the type itself, so Hₙ(X) = πₙ(‖X‖ₙ) = πₙ(X). For k < n, the map is an isomorphism by the absolute theorem applied to the (k-1)-connected cover.

Interaction with Modalities

The n-truncation modality ‖-‖ₙ and the n-connected cover modality interact with the Hurewicz map via the fiber sequence X⟨n⟩ → X → ‖X‖ₙ, where X⟨n⟩ is the n-connected cover. The Hurewicz map for X factors as πₖ(X) → πₖ(‖X‖ₙ) = Hₖ(X). When X is n-connected, the map X → ‖X‖ₙ is an equivalence on πₖ for k ≤ n, giving the isomorphism. When X is an n-type, the cover X⟨n⟩ is contractible, so the fiber sequence shows that πₖ(X) ≃ πₖ(‖X‖ₙ) for all k, and the Hurewicz map is the identity on πₙ.

Application to the Whitehead Tower

The Whitehead tower of a type X is the sequence of n-connected covers … → X⟨n⟩ → X⟨n-1⟩ → … → X. The Hurewicz theorem for each stage gives isomorphisms πₖ(X⟨n⟩) ≃ Hₖ(X⟨n⟩) for k ≤ n+1. This is used in the synthetic construction of the String group (the 3‑connected cover of Spin(n)) where the Hurewicz isomorphism identifies π₄(String(n)) with H₄(String(n)), which is computed via the Serre spectral sequence of the fibration K(ℤ,3) → BString(n) → BSpin(n).

Computational Aspects of the Hurewicz Map in Cubical Type Theory

Cubical type theory provides a computational interpretation of HoTT where paths are represented as functions out of an interval type 𝕀. In this setting, the Hurewicz map can be given an explicit algorithmic description. For a higher inductive type such as the circle S¹, the fundamental group π₁(S¹) is definitionally equal to ℤ via the encode‑decode equivalence. The Hurewicz map π₁(S¹) → H₁(S¹) then reduces to the identity function on ℤ, because H₁(S¹) is defined as π₁(‖S¹‖₁) and the 1‑truncation of S¹ is itself (since S¹ is a 1‑type). For the 2‑sphere S², the Hurewicz map π₂(S²) → H₂(S²) computes the degree of a map S² → S² by evaluating the corresponding 2‑loop on the interval square and counting the number of times the boundary wraps. In Cubical Agda, this computation normalizes to an integer, providing a decision procedure for the Hurewicz map in low dimensions.

Canonicity and Normalization

The canonicity theorem for Cubical Agda guarantees that any closed term of type ℕ or ℤ reduces to a numeral. Since the Hurewicz map lands in homology groups that are defined as truncations of loop spaces, and those truncations are implemented as higher inductive types with explicit constructors, the composite πₙ(X) → Hₙ(X) → ℤ (for spheres) normalizes to a numeral. This means that the Hurewicz isomorphism for Sⁿ is not only a propositional equivalence but a definitional one in the cubical setting. The proof relies on the fact that the n-truncation of Sⁿ is a set‑quotient of the n-loop space by the action of the (n+1)-loops, and the cubical Kan composition operations compute the quotient normal forms.

Limitations and Open Problems

While the Hurewicz map is computable for spheres and projective spaces, the general computation for arbitrary higher inductive types remains open. The main obstacle is that the n-truncation HIT introduces path constructors that are not directly reducible by the cubical Kan operations. Recent work on “computational higher inductive types” (CHITs) aims to give reduction rules for truncation constructors, which would make the Hurewicz map fully computational for all HITs.
