Another direction is the use of the synthetic spectral sequences (e.g., the Serre spectral sequence) to compute homology groups algorithmically, which would then feed into the Hurewicz map via the isomorphism theorem.

  • Confusing the absolute Hurewicz theorem (which requires simple connectivity for the isomorphism at π₂) with the relative version (which requires connectivity of the pair).
  • Assuming the Hurewicz map is always an isomorphism; it is only an isomorphism up to the connectivity degree and a surjection one degree higher.
  • Neglecting the pointedness conditions: the theorem is stated for pointed types or pointed maps, and the base point must be preserved throughout the proof.
  • Thinking that the synthetic Hurewicz theorem computes all homotopy groups; it only relates them to homology, which itself may be unknown.
  • Believing that the cubical computational interpretation gives a decision procedure for arbitrary types; canonicity holds only for types with decidable equality and explicit reduction rules for truncations.
  • Mixing up the n-connected cover (Whitehead tower) with the n-truncation (Postnikov tower); the Hurewicz theorem applies to the former for isomorphism, the latter for homology definition.
  • Overlooking that the relative Hurewicz theorem requires the domain A to be (n-2)-connected and the codomain X to be (n-1)-connected; dropping either hypothesis invalidates the isomorphism claim.
The synthetic Hurewicz theorem and its variants form a cornerstone of computational homotopy theory in HoTT, linking higher inductive constructions to algebraic invariants that can be reasoned about internally.

The Synthetic Steenrod Algebra and Cohomology Operations in HoTT

The Steenrod algebra A is the graded algebra of stable cohomology operations for mod p cohomology. In classical algebraic topology, it is generated by the Steenrod squares Sqi (for p = 2) or the Steenrod powers Pi and the Bockstein β (for odd p), subject to the Adem relations. In synthetic homotopy theory, the Steenrod algebra arises internally as the algebra of natural transformations of the cohomology functor H*(−; 𝔽p) on the ∞-topos of types. The synthetic construction proceeds by defining the cohomology groups Hn(X; 𝔽p) as the set of pointed maps X → K(𝔽p, n) in the homotopy category, where K(𝔽p, n) is the Eilenberg–MacLane space constructed as a higher inductive type. A stable cohomology operation of degree d is then a family of maps θX : Hn(X; 𝔽p) → Hn+d(X; 𝔽p) natural in X. The Yoneda lemma identifies the representing object for the functor X ↦ Hn(X; 𝔽p) as Σ∞K(𝔽p, n), and the Steenrod algebra is the ring of stable self-maps of the mod p Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum H𝔽p.

The synthetic Adem relations are proved by analyzing the action of the Steenrod operations on the cohomology of the classifying space BΣp+1 or, more synthetically, by using the internal logic of the ∞-topos to construct the operations via the extended power construction. For a type X, the p-th extended power is the homotopy quotient (Xp)hΣp = (EΣp × Xp)/Σp. The diagonal map X → Xp induces a map X → (Xp)hΣp, and applying the suspension spectrum functor and smashing with H𝔽p yields the Steenrod operations. The Adem relations follow from the equivariant homotopy theory of the symmetric groups Σp and the structure of the Steenrod algebra as the cohomology of the infinite symmetric group. In HoTT, this is formalized by constructing the extended power as a higher inductive type with constructors for the Σp-action and the diagonal, then proving the relations by path induction on the resulting higher paths. The synthetic approach has the advantage that the Adem relations become definitional equalities in the presence of a suitable cubical structure, because the extended power construction computes the operations directly on the cubical chains.

The action of the Steenrod algebra on the cohomology of spheres and projective spaces is a key computational tool. For the sphere Sn, H*(Sn; 𝔽p) is an exterior algebra on one generator in degree n, and the Steenrod operations act trivially except for Sqn (or Pn/2 for even n at odd p) which maps the generator to itself. For real projective space ℝP∞, H*(ℝP∞; 𝔽2) = 𝔽2[x] with |x| = 1, and Sqi(xj) = (j choose i) xi+j. For complex projective space ℂP∞, H*(ℂP∞; 𝔽p) = 𝔽p[y] with |y| = 2, and the operations are determined by the Cartan formula and P1(y) = yp. These computations are formalized in the HoTT library by constructing the cell structures of these spaces as higher inductive types and using the encode-decode method to compute their cohomology rings with Steenrod action. The synthetic Steenrod algebra also provides a framework for the synthetic Adams spectral sequence, where the E2-page is ExtA(H*(X; 𝔽p), 𝔽p) and the differentials are induced by the action of the Steenrod algebra on the cohomology of the fibers in the Adams resolution.

The Synthetic Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer Theorem and p-Primary Exponents

The Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer (CMN) theorem is a landmark result in stable homotopy theory stating that for an odd prime p, the p-primary component of the stable homotopy groups of spheres π*(S0)(p) has exponent p2. More precisely, for any element x ∈ πn(S0)(p), we have p2·x = 0. For p = 2, the exponent is 4 (i.e., 22 = 4). The theorem was originally proved using the theory of unstable homotopy groups and the EHP sequence, combined with a deep analysis of the p-primary torsion in the homotopy groups of Moore spaces. In synthetic homotopy theory, the CMN theorem is approached by constructing the Moore space M(ℤ/pr, n) as a higher inductive type with a single n-cell and an (n+1)-cell attached by the map pr : Sn → Sn. The synthetic proof then proceeds by analyzing the fiber sequence ΩM(ℤ/pr, n+1) → Sn → M(ℤ/pr, n+1) and using the synthetic EHP sequence to relate the homotopy groups of spheres to those of Moore spaces.

The key synthetic ingredient is the construction of the p-primary exponent map. For a type X, the p-power map p : ΩnX → ΩnX induces a map on homotopy groups πk(ΩnX) → πk(ΩnX). The CMN theorem asserts that the composite πn+k(Sn) → πk(ΩnSn) → πk(ΩnSn) given by the p2-power map is zero. In HoTT, this is formalized by constructing the p-power map as a higher inductive type with a path constructor expressing the group structure, and then proving that the p2-power map factors through a contractible type. The proof uses the synthetic Blakers-Massey theorem to analyze the connectivity of the map Sn → M(ℤ/p2, n+1), and the synthetic Freudenthal suspension theorem to stabilize the result. The exponent p2 is sharp: there exist elements of order exactly p2 in π2p-3(S0)(p) for p ≥ 5, detected by the image of the J-homomorphism. In the synthetic setting, these elements are constructed as the image of the generator of π2p-3(SO) under the synthetic J-homomorphism, which is defined using the clutching construction on vector bundles over spheres.

The CMN theorem has profound implications for the computation of homotopy groups. It implies that the p-primary part of the stable stems is a bounded p-torsion module, which in turn means that the Adams spectral sequence converges strongly and the p-completion of the sphere spectrum is a finite type spectrum. In HoTT, the synthetic CMN theorem is used to prove that the p-completion of the sphere spectrum Σ∞S0p∧ is a compact object in the synthetic stable homotopy category, and that the synthetic Adams-Novikov spectral sequence for the sphere has a horizontal vanishing line at E2s,w = 0 for s > w + 1. The formalization of the CMN theorem in Cubical Agda is an ongoing project; the main challenge is the construction of the Moore space M(ℤ/p2, n) with the correct higher coherence data for the p2-power map, which requires a careful treatment of the truncation levels and the interaction with the synthetic EHP sequence.

Synthetic Exponent Calculation
In synthetic homotopy theory, let M(ℤ/p², n) be the Moore space constructed as a HIT with a base point, an n-loop l : ΩⁿM, and an (n+1)-loop p²·l = refl. Prove that the p²-power map on πₙ(Sⁿ) factors through πₙ(M(ℤ/p², n+1)) and deduce that p² annihilates the p-primary component of πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ) for k ≥ 0.
The Moore space M(ℤ/p², n+1) fits in a fiber sequence ΩM(ℤ/p², n+1) → Sⁿ → M(ℤ/p², n+1) where the map Sⁿ → M(ℤ/p², n+1) is the attaching map of the (n+1)-cell, which is p² : Sⁿ → Sⁿ. The long exact sequence of homotopy groups gives πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ) → πₙ₊ₖ(M(ℤ/p², n+1)) → πₙ₊ₖ₋₁(ΩM(ℤ/p², n+1)). The p²-power map on πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ) is induced by the composite Sⁿ → M(ℤ/p², n+1) → Sⁿ where the second map is the projection. Since the composite Sⁿ → M(ℤ/p², n+1) → Sⁿ is p², the p²-power map factors through πₙ₊ₖ(M(ℤ/p², n+1)). But M(ℤ/p², n+1) is (n+1)-connected, so πₙ₊ₖ(M(ℤ/p², n+1)) = 0 for k ≤ 0. For k > 0, the synthetic Blakers-Massey theorem shows the map πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ) → πₙ₊ₖ(M(ℤ/p², n+1)) is (2n+1)-connected, and the p-primary part of πₙ₊ₖ(M(ℤ/p², n+1)) is annihilated by p² by construction of the Moore space. Hence p²·x = 0 for all x in the p-primary component.
Exam Strategy: Synthetic Exponent Theorems
When asked about exponent theorems in HoTT, distinguish between the unstable exponent (CMN: p² for odd p, 4 for p=2) and the stable exponent (which may be lower). Remember that the synthetic proof uses the Moore space M(ℤ/p², n) as a HIT, the fiber sequence with Sⁿ, and the Blakers-Massey connectivity estimate. The key step is showing the p²-power map factors through a type whose p-primary homotopy groups are p²-torsion by construction. For p=2, the exponent 4 comes from the fact that M(ℤ/4, n) has a 2-torsion Bockstein that squares to zero.

The Synthetic Chromatic Homotopy Theory: Morava K-Theories and the Telescope Conjecture

Chromatic homotopy theory organizes the stable homotopy category by the height of formal groups associated to complex-oriented cohomology theories. The n-th Morava K-theory K(n) at a prime p is a field theory with coefficient ring K(n)* = 𝔽p[vn±1], |vn| = 2(pn−1). The telescope conjecture, formulated by Ravenel, states that the Bousfield localization with respect to K(n) is equivalent to the localization with respect to the telescope of a vn-self-map of a finite type n spectrum. In synthetic homotopy theory, the Morava K-theories are constructed as higher inductive types representing the cohomology theories with the specified coefficients. The synthetic construction begins with the Lubin-Tate formal group law of height n over the ring W(𝔽pn)[[u1, …, un-1]], and then constructs the Morava E-theory En as an E∞-ring spectrum whose homotopy groups are π*En = W(𝔽pn)[[u1, …, un-1]][u±1], |u| = −2. The Morava K-theory K(n) is then the quotient En/(p, u1, …, un-1).

In HoTT, the construction of En and K(n) uses the synthetic version of the Goerss-Hopkins obstruction theory. The Lubin-Tate space is represented as a higher inductive type whose points are deformations of the Honda formal group law of height n over 𝔽pn. The universal deformation gives a map from the Lubin-Tate space to the moduli stack of formal groups Mfg, and the Morava E-theory is the pullback of the universal elliptic cohomology theory (or more directly, the universal complex-oriented theory) along this map. The synthetic telescope conjecture is then the statement that for any finite type n spectrum X (i.e., a spectrum with K(m)*X = 0 for m ≠ n and K(n)*X finite), the localization LK(n)X is equivalent to the homotopy colimit of the sequence X → Σ−dX → Σ−2dX → … where the maps are given by a vn-self-map. A vn-self-map is a map v : ΣdX → X such that K(m)*v is an isomorphism for m = n and zero otherwise.

The telescope conjecture is known to be true for n = 1 (by the work of Mahowald) and n = 2 (by the work of Behrens, Hill, Hopkins, and Mahowald), but false for n ≥ 2 at large primes (by the work of Ravenel, and later counterexamples by Behrens et al.). In synthetic homotopy theory, the status of the telescope conjecture is an open problem. The synthetic approach offers a new perspective: the telescope localization can be constructed as a higher inductive type with a constructor for the vn-self-map, and the K(n)-localization as a modality (a reflective subuniverse). The conjecture then becomes the statement that these two modalities are equivalent on the subuniverse of finite type n spectra. This formulation allows the use of the synthetic Blakers-Massey theorem and the synthetic nilpotence theorem to analyze the difference between the two localizations. The synthetic nilpotence theorem states that a map of finite spectra is zero in the K(n)-local category if and only if it is nilpotent in the sense that some smash power is zero. This is formalized in HoTT by defining the nilpotence modality and proving its equivalence to the K(n)-local modality on finite spectra.

The Synthetic Kervaire Invariant Problem and the Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel Theorem in HoTT

The Kervaire invariant problem asks for which dimensions n there exists a framed manifold of dimension n with Kervaire invariant 1. The Kervaire invariant is a ℤ/2-valued invariant of a framed manifold defined by the Arf invariant of the quadratic form on the middle homology. The problem was solved by Hill, Hopkins, and Ravenel (2009) who proved that such manifolds exist only in dimensions 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, and possibly 126. The proof uses the theory of the spectrum Ω (the "Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel spectrum") which detects the Kervaire invariant via a map from the sphere spectrum to Ω. In synthetic homotopy theory, the Kervaire invariant is approached by constructing the quadratic refinement of the intersection form on the middle homology of a framed manifold. For a framed manifold M of dimension 2k, the middle homology Hk(M; 𝔽2) carries a symmetric bilinear form given by the intersection pairing, and the framing provides a quadratic refinement q : Hk(M; 𝔽2) → 𝔽2 satisfying q(x+y) = q(x) + q(y) + ⟨x, y⟩. The Arf invariant of q is the Kervaire invariant.

In HoTT, a framed manifold is represented as a type M with a trivialization of its tangent bundle, which in the synthetic setting means a trivialization of the loop space ΩM as a type with a group structure. The middle homology is the homotopy group πk(M) (for a simply connected M), and the intersection pairing is the Whitehead product [−, −] : πk(M) × πk(M) → π2k-1(M). The framing gives a map π2k-1(M) → π2k-1(S0) = π2k-1s, and the Kervaire invariant is the composition of the quadratic refinement with the Arf invariant map. The Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel spectrum Ω is constructed synthetically as the cofiber of a map between certain Thom spectra, specifically the map MSpin → MSpin induced by the inclusion of the 2-typical part of the spin cobordism ring. The key synthetic theorem is that the map S0 → Ω induces an isomorphism on π2k-1 for k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (corresponding to dimensions 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, 126) and is zero otherwise. This is proved by analyzing the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence for Ω, which in the synthetic setting is constructed as a spectral sequence of types converging to the homotopy groups of Ω.

The synthetic proof of the non-existence of Kervaire invariant one manifolds in dimensions > 126 uses the synthetic version of the "slice spectral sequence" for the spectrum Ω. The slice filtration is a filtration of Ω by types Ωn such that the slices Ωn/Ωn-1 are equivalent to suspensions of the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum H𝔽2. The differentials in the slice spectral sequence are computed using the synthetic Steenrod algebra action on the cohomology of the slices. The crucial differential is a d22 differential that kills the potential Kervaire invariant element in dimension 254. In HoTT, this differential is constructed by analyzing the action of the Steenrod square Sq2 on the cohomology of the slice cells, which are built as higher inductive types. The formalization of the Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel theorem in Cubical Agda would require a full synthetic construction of the slice spectral sequence and the computation of the d22 differential, which is currently beyond the state of the art but provides a clear roadmap for future formalization efforts.

The Synthetic Lambda Algebra and the May Spectral Sequence in HoTT

The lambda algebra Λ is a differential graded algebra over 𝔽2 whose cohomology computes the E2-page of the Adams spectral sequence for the sphere spectrum at the prime 2. It is generated by symbols λi for i ≥ 1, with differential d(λi) = Σj=0i-1 (i−j−1 choose j) λjλi-j-1. The May spectral sequence is a spectral sequence converging to the cohomology of the lambda algebra, with E1-page given by the polynomial algebra 𝔽2[hi,j] where hi,j corresponds to the class of λ2i(2j+1)−1. In synthetic homotopy theory, the lambda algebra arises as the cobar construction on the dual Steenrod algebra A* = 𝔽2[ξ1, ξ2, …], where ξi are the Milnor generators. The synthetic construction of the lambda algebra uses the fact that the Steenrod algebra A is the Hopf algebra of stable cohomology operations, and its dual A* is the homology of the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum H𝔽2. The cobar construction ΩA* is a differential graded coalgebra whose cohomology is ExtA(𝔽2, 𝔽2).

In HoTT, the dual Steenrod algebra is constructed as the homology of the synthetic H𝔽2, which is a higher inductive type representing the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum. The homology groups H*(H𝔽2; 𝔽2) are computed as the homotopy groups of the smash product H𝔽2 ∧ H𝔽2, which is equivalent to a wedge of suspensions of H𝔽2 indexed by the Milnor basis. The lambda algebra is then the cobar construction on this coalgebra, which can be implemented as a higher inductive type with generators λi and differential given by the coproduct on A*. The May spectral sequence is constructed by filtering the lambda algebra by the "May weight" which assigns weight i to λ2i(2j+1)−1. The E1-page is the associated graded algebra, which is a polynomial algebra on the classes hi,j. The differentials in the May spectral sequence are computed by the synthetic version of the May differential formula, which involves the action of the Steenrod algebra on the cohomology of the Eilenberg-MacLane spaces.

The synthetic lambda algebra and May spectral sequence provide a computational framework for the Adams spectral sequence in HoTT. The E2-page of the Adams spectral sequence for a type X is ExtA(H*(X; 𝔽2), 𝔽2), which is computed as the cohomology of the cobar construction on the A-comodule H*(X; 𝔽2). For X = S0, this is the cohomology of the lambda algebra. The synthetic May spectral sequence then gives a method to compute this Ext group by successive approximations. The first few differentials in the May spectral sequence are known to produce the classes h0, h1, h2, h3 on the E∞-page, corresponding to the elements 2, η, ν, σ in the stable stems. The synthetic formalization of the May spectral sequence in Cubical Agda would allow the computation of the Adams E2-page for any finite type X by reducing it to polynomial algebra computations. The main challenge is the construction of the higher differentials, which require the synthetic Steenrod algebra action on the cohomology of the lambda algebra itself. This is an active area of research in synthetic homotopy theory, with connections to the synthetic Adams-Novikov spectral sequence and the synthetic chromatic spectral sequence.

  • Confusing the synthetic Steenrod algebra (natural transformations of cohomology) with the classical algebraic definition (generators and Adem relations); in HoTT the operations are defined by the extended power construction, and the Adem relations are theorems, not axioms.
  • Assuming the Cohen-Moore-Neisendorfer exponent p² holds for all primes including p=2 without the modification (exponent 4 for p=2); the synthetic proof uses the Moore space M(ℤ/4, n) for p=2, not M(ℤ/2², n).
  • Thinking the telescope conjecture is true for all n; it is known false for n ≥ 2 at large primes, and the synthetic formulation as equivalence of modalities on finite type n spectra makes the counterexamples visible as types where the two localizations differ.
  • Believing the Kervaire invariant one problem is solved for all dimensions in HoTT; the synthetic Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel theorem only covers the known dimensions, and the case of dimension 126 remains open even synthetically.
  • Mixing up the lambda algebra (cobar construction on dual Steenrod algebra at p=2) with the May spectral sequence (a spectral sequence converging to its cohomology); the lambda algebra is the chain complex, the May spectral sequence is a computational tool for its homology.
  • Overlooking that the synthetic Morava K-theories K(n) are field theories (their module categories are equivalent to graded vector spaces); this is a theorem in HoTT, not a definition, and follows from the fact that the synthetic Lubin-Tate space is a formal group of height n.
  • Assuming the synthetic Adams spectral sequence converges for all types; strong convergence requires the type to be a finite spectrum (or more generally, a type with finite homotopy groups in each degree), and the synthetic CMN theorem provides the nilpotence condition needed for convergence.

Synthetic Elliptic Cohomology and Topological Modular Forms in HoTT

Elliptic cohomology and topological modular forms (TMF) represent a profound synthesis of algebraic geometry, modular forms, and stable homotopy theory. In classical homotopy theory, TMF is a ring spectrum constructed from the moduli stack of elliptic curves Mell and a sheaf of E∞-ring spectra Otop over it. The synthetic approach in HoTT internalizes this construction by treating the moduli stack as a higher inductive-inductive type and the sheaf as a type family satisfying descent. The key insight is that the compactified moduli stack M̄ell can be presented as a quotient of the upper half-plane by SL2(ℤ), which in HoTT becomes a higher inductive type with constructors for the SL2(ℤ)-action and path constructors encoding the group relations. The sheaf Otop assigns to each elliptic curve E the even periodic cohomology theory EllE whose formal group is the completion of E at the identity. Synthetically, this is a family of E∞-ring types over Mell constructed via the Goerss-Hopkins obstruction theory, which itself has a synthetic formulation using the cotangent complex in HoTT. The global sections TMF = Γ(M̄ell, Otop) are then computed as the limit of a cosimplicial diagram arising from a hypercover of M̄ell. The homotopy groups π*TMF are known to detect the image of the J-homomorphism, the Greek letter elements, and the β-family. In HoTT, the synthetic TMF spectrum is a higher inductive type with constructors for the modular forms c4, c6, Δ−1 and the E∞-ring structure, together with coherence paths ensuring the q-expansion principle. The synthetic qE∞-ring types whose fiber is the connective cover of TMF. The computational power of synthetic TMF lies in the fact that the descent spectral sequence for the cover of M̄ell by the affine line and the cusp becomes a spectral sequence of types in HoTT, whose E2-page is the cohomology of Mell with coefficients in the homotopy groups of Otop. This spectral sequence has been partially formalized in Cubical Agda for low weights, revealing that the synthetic approach makes the differentials computable as higher inductive type eliminations. The main open problem is the synthetic construction of the full Goerss-Hopkins obstruction theory for E∞-ring structures on the presheaf of formal groups, which requires a synthetic theory of André-Quillen cohomology for E∞-rings in HoTT.

Synthetic Equivariant Homotopy Theory in HoTT

Equivariant homotopy theory studies spaces with group actions, and its synthetic formulation in HoTT requires a type-theoretic account of G-spaces for a group G. The central object is the ∞-category of G-spaces, which classically is the presheaf ∞-category on the orbit category OG. In HoTT, this is internalized by defining a G-type as a type X equipped with an action of a group type G, i.e., a map G × X → X satisfying the action axioms up to coherent homotopy. The orbit category OG becomes a higher inductive type whose objects are the homogeneous spaces G/H for subgroups H ≤ G, and whose morphisms are G-maps. The fixed-point functor (−)H is then a modality on the ∞-topos of G-types, and the family of fixed-point modalities for all subgroups forms a G-equivariant modality structure. The tom Dieck splitting theorem, which expresses the equivariant suspension spectrum of a G-space as a wedge of non-equivariant suspension spectra of fixed-point spaces, becomes a synthetic equivalence of types: Σ∞G X ≃ ⋁(H) Σ∞ (XH)hWGH, where the wedge is over conjugacy classes of subgroups and WGH = NG(H)/H is the Weyl group. In HoTT, this equivalence is constructed by analyzing the G-equivariant stable homotopy category as the stabilization of the ∞-topos of G-types, and using the fact that the suspension spectrum functor preserves colimits. The Burnside ring A(G) appears as the endomorphism ring of the sphere spectrum in the equivariant stable homotopy category, and synthetically it is the initial E∞-ring type in G-spectra. The Segal conjecture (now the Carlsson theorem) states that the completion of the Burnside ring at the augmentation ideal is isomorphic to the stable cohomotopy of the classifying space BG. In HoTT, this becomes a statement about the completion of the synthetic Burnside ring type at the augmentation modality, and its proof uses the synthetic version of the tom Dieck splitting together with the synthetic Adams spectral sequence for G-spectra. The main computational tool is the equivariant Adams spectral sequence, whose E2-page is Ext over the equivariant Steenrod algebra. The synthetic equivariant Steenrod algebra is constructed as the endomorphism algebra of the equivariant Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum Hℤ in G-spectra, and its structure is determined by the G-equivariant extended power construction. A major open problem is the synthetic formulation of the equivariant Adams-Novikov spectral sequence and the equivariant version of the chromatic filtration, which would require a synthetic theory of G-equivariant formal groups and Lubin-Tate theory.

Examiner's Trap: Confusing Equivariant and Non-Equivariant Fixed Points
A student claims: "In synthetic equivariant HoTT, the fixed-point modality (−)H for a subgroup H ≤ G is just the ordinary fixed-point type XH = {x : X | ∀ h : H, h·x = x}, so it commutes with all limits and colimits." Identify the error and explain the correct behavior of the fixed-point modality in the ∞-topos of G-types.
The error is treating the fixed-point construction as a strict 1-categorical limit. In the ∞-topos of G-types, the fixed-point modality (−)H is a right adjoint to the induction functor IndHG, hence it preserves all limits (including homotopy limits) but does not preserve colimits. The correct fixed-point type is the homotopy fixed points XhH = MapG(EG, X)H, which in HoTT is the type of H-equivariant maps from the universal H-space EH (a contractible type with free H-action) to X. For a discrete group H, this is equivalent to the type of sections of the Borel construction XhH → BH. The strict fixed points XH only agree with homotopy fixed points when X is a fibrant G-space in the classical sense, or in HoTT when X is a truncated type (e.g., a set). The tom Dieck splitting Σ∞G X ≃ ⋁(H) Σ∞ (XhH)hWGH uses homotopy fixed points, not strict fixed points. Confusing these leads to incorrect computations of equivariant homotopy groups and the Burnside ring.
Exam-Day Strategy: Equivariant Modalities
When a question asks about fixed points in equivariant HoTT, always check whether the context is the ∞-topos of G-types (where fixed points are a modality/right adjoint) or the 1-category of G-sets (where they are strict). The phrase "modality" or "∞-topos" signals homotopy fixed points. Remember: (−)H preserves limits, not colimits; the left adjoint is induction IndHG. The tom Dieck splitting is an equivalence of spectra, not spaces — it lives in the stabilization of the ∞-topos.

Synthetic Motivic Homotopy Theory and A¹-Homotopy in HoTT

Motivic homotopy theory, developed by Morel and Voevodsky, constructs a homotopy theory of schemes by localizing the category of simplicial sheaves on the Nisnevich site with respect to the affine line 𝔸1. In HoTT, this is internalized by working in the ∞-topos of sheaves of types on the Nisnevich site of smooth schemes over a base field k, and then imposing 𝔸1-invariance as a modality. The key synthetic object is the 𝔸1-localization modality L𝔸1, which sends a type X to its 𝔸1-localization L𝔸1X. A type is 𝔸1-local if the projection X × 𝔸1 → X is an equivalence. The 𝔸1-homotopy category is then the full subcategory of 𝔸1-local types. The motivic sphere spectrum is the suspension spectrum of the Nisnevich sheaf represented by the pointed scheme (𝔸1/{0}, 1), which in HoTT is a higher inductive type with a basepoint and a path constructor identifying 0 with 1 after 𝔸1-localization. The motivic stable homotopy category is the stabilization of the 𝔸1-local ∞-topos. The motivic cohomology of a smooth scheme X is represented by the motivic Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum Hℤ, which in HoTT is a higher inductive type constructed from the Bloch complex. The Beilinson-Lichtenbaum conjecture (now a theorem of Voevodsky, Rost, and others) states that motivic cohomology with finite coefficients agrees with étale cohomology in a range. Synthetically, this becomes an equivalence between the 𝔸1-localization of the étale sheaf ℤ/n and the motivic Eilenberg-MacLane type Hℤ/n after 𝔸1-localization. The motivic Steenrod algebra is the algebra of stable cohomology operations on motivic cohomology, and its synthetic construction uses the motivic extended power construction on the motivic Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum. The motivic Adams spectral sequence has E2-page Ext over the motivic Steenrod algebra, and it converges to the motivic stable homotopy groups of spheres. A major computational result is the computation of the motivic stable stems over ℂ by Isaksen, which in HoTT would be a computation of the homotopy groups of the motivic sphere spectrum in the 𝔸1-local ∞-topos over ℂ. The synthetic approach makes the motivic weight filtration visible as a tower of modalities, where the n-th layer corresponds to the n-th motivic cohomology group. The main open problem is the synthetic construction of the motivic Adams-Novikov spectral sequence using motivic Brown-Peterson theory, which requires a synthetic theory of formal groups over the motivic sphere spectrum and the motivic version of the Landweber exact functor theorem.

The Synthetic Adams-Novikov Spectral Sequence and BP-Theory in HoTT

The Adams-Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) is a powerful computational tool in stable homotopy theory that uses complex cobordism MU or Brown-Peterson theory BP instead of mod-p cohomology. In HoTT, the synthetic ANSS is constructed by internalizing the MU-based or BP-based Adams resolution. The spectrum MU is the Thom spectrum of the universal complex vector bundle over BU, and in HoTT it is a higher inductive type built from the synthetic BU (the classifying type for complex vector bundles) and the Thom isomorphism. The homotopy ring π*MU is the Lazard ring, which classifies formal group laws. Synthetically, the Lazard ring is the initial object in the category of formal group laws in HoTT, and the map L → π*MU is an equivalence by Quillen's theorem. The MU-Adams resolution of a type X is a tower X → M0 → M1 → ⋯ where each Ms is a wedge of suspensions of MU, and the fiber of Ms → Ms−1 is a wedge of suspensions of MU ∧ X. The E2-page of the ANSS is ExtΓ(MU*, MU*X) where Γ = MU*MU is the Hopf algebroid of the formal group. In HoTT, Γ is the synthetic Hopf algebroid whose underlying type is the homotopy type of the moduli stack of formal groups Mfg. The synthetic ANSS is then the spectral sequence of types associated to the cosimplicial type MU•+1 ∧ X. The BP-theory version uses the p-typical formal group law, and the Hopf algebroid is (π*BP, π*BP ∧ BP). The synthetic BP spectrum is constructed as a summand of MU(p) using the idempotent corresponding to the p-typical formal group law. The E2-page of the BP-ANSS is Ext over the p-typical Hopf algebroid, which is computable using the synthetic cobar construction. The chromatic filtration appears synthetically as a tower of localizations Ln of the stable homotopy category with respect to the Morava K-theories K(n). The synthetic Morava K-theories are field theories, meaning their module categories are equivalent to graded vector spaces, and this is a theorem in HoTT following from the fact that the synthetic Lubin-Tate space is a formal group of height n. The synthetic ANSS converges strongly for finite spectra, and the synthetic nilpotence theorem (Devinatz-Hopkins-Smith) provides the necessary condition. The main computational advantage of the synthetic ANSS is that the differentials can be expressed as higher inductive type eliminations on the cobar construction, and the vn-periodic families are detected by the synthetic chromatic spectral sequence. A major open problem is the synthetic formulation of the tmf-based Adams-Novikov spectral sequence, which would require a synthetic theory of elliptic curves and their formal groups internal to HoTT.

Synthetic Factorization Homology and the Cobordism Hypothesis in HoTT

Factorization homology, developed by Lurie and Ayala-Francis, is a topological field theory that assigns to a manifold M and an En-algebra A a value ∫M A by integrating A over M. The cobordism hypothesis classifies fully extended topological field theories as the ∞-category of fully dualizable objects in a symmetric monoidal ∞-category. In HoTT, factorization homology is internalized by working in the ∞-topos of types and using the synthetic theory of En-algebras. An En-algebra in HoTT is a type A equipped with an action of the little n-disks operad, which is a higher inductive type whose k-ary operations are the configuration space of k disjoint n-disks in the unit n-disk. The factorization homology ∫M A for a framed n-manifold M is then the colimit of a diagram indexed by the ∞-category of embeddings of disjoint unions of n-disks into M. In HoTT, this colimit is a higher inductive type with constructors for each embedding and path constructors for isotopies. The cobordism hypothesis states that the ∞-category of fully extended framed topological field theories Bordnfr → C is equivalent to the ∞-groupoid of fully dualizable objects in C. In HoTT, the bordism ∞-category Bordnfr is a higher inductive-inductive type whose objects are closed framed (n−1)-manifolds, 1-morphisms are framed n-cobordisms, and higher morphisms are diffeomorphisms and isotopies. A fully dualizable object in a symmetric monoidal ∞-category C is an object X such that the evaluation and coevaluation maps exhibit X as its own dual up to coherent equivalence. The synthetic proof of the cobordism hypothesis uses the fact that the free symmetric monoidal ∞-category with duals on one object is equivalent to Bordnfr. This is constructed by showing that the ∞-category of framed n-manifolds with embeddings is the free En-algebra on one generator in the ∞-category of ∞-categories. The application to topological quantum field theory is that a fully extended TQFT is determined by its value on the point, which must be a fully dualizable object. In HoTT, this means that a TQFT is a map of higher inductive-inductive types from Bordnfr to C, and such maps are classified by the type of fully dualizable objects in C. The main computational tool is the factorization homology of En-algebras on manifolds, which in HoTT can be computed using the synthetic version of the excision theorem: for a decomposition M = M1 ∪N M2, there is a pushout square of types ∫M A ≃ ∫M1 A ×∫N A ∫M2 A. The main open problem is the synthetic formulation of the cobordism hypothesis for non-framed structures (oriented, spin, string, etc.), which requires a synthetic theory of tangential structures and the ∞-category of manifolds with such structures.

  • Confusing the synthetic 𝔸¹-localization modality with Nisnevich sheafification; in motivic HoTT, 𝔸¹-localization is a modality on the Nisnevich ∞-topos, not the sheafification itself. The motivic homotopy category is the subcategory of 𝔸¹-local objects, not the Nisnevich ∞-topos.
  • Assuming the motivic Steenrod algebra is the classical Steenrod algebra with weights added; the motivic Steenrod algebra has a richer structure with Milnor basis elements τ, ρ, and the action of the motivic Galois group, and the Adem relations are modified by weight.
  • Thinking the Adams-Novikov E₂-page is Ext over the classical Hopf algebroid (MU*, MU*MU) without the synthetic topology; in HoTT the Hopf algebroid is a type-theoretic object whose cohomology is computed by a synthetic cobar construction, and the differentials are higher inductive eliminations.
  • Believing the synthetic cobordism hypothesis is proved for all tangential structures; the synthetic proof currently covers only the framed case. The oriented, spin, and string versions require synthetic tangential structures and are open problems.
  • Mixing up factorization homology (a colimit over embeddings of disks) with Hochschild homology (a colimit over the cyclic category); factorization homology of an En-algebra on an n-manifold generalizes Hochschild homology (which is the n=1 case on S¹), but the indexing categories are different.
  • Assuming TMF is just "elliptic cohomology with a compactification"; TMF is the global sections of a sheaf of E∞-ring spectra on the compactified moduli stack, and the compactification at the cusp is essential for the q-expansion principle and the map to KO[[q]]. The synthetic construction must include the cusp as a higher inductive constructor.
  • Overlooking that the equivariant fixed-point modality (−)H is a right adjoint, not a left adjoint; it preserves limits (homotopy fixed points) but not colimits. The left adjoint is induction IndHG, and the tom Dieck splitting uses homotopy fixed points, not strict fixed points.

Higher Inductive‑Recursive Types and the Construction of Universes

Higher inductive‑recursive types extend the ordinary higher inductive types by allowing a recursive function to be defined simultaneously with the type itself. The seminal work of Dybjer and Setzer (1999) introduced inductive‑recursive definitions as a way to build universes à la Tarski: a type U of codes together with a decoding function El : U → Type such that the codes are closed under the type formers of the theory. In homotopy type theory this pattern is essential for constructing a universe that is closed under the higher inductive types themselves, because the constructors of a higher inductive type may refer to the universe being defined. The Mahlo universe, the universe of propositional truncations, and the universe of higher inductive‑inductive types are all instances of this scheme.

Formally, an inductive‑recursive definition consists of a mutual specification of a type D and a function f : D → C where the constructors of D may refer to f applied to previously constructed elements. The elimination principle provides a dependent function out of D that respects both the point constructors and the recursive calls. In the presence of univalence, the decoding function El can be shown to preserve equivalences, making the universe univalent. Recent work by Altenkirch, Kaposi, and others has formalised such universes in Agda and Cubical Agda, demonstrating that the computational behaviour of the recursive component is compatible with canonicity for the higher inductive constructors.

A key technical point is the strict positivity condition for the recursive occurrence of f in the constructors of D. This condition guarantees that the simultaneous definition is well‑founded and that the resulting type supports a strong induction principle. In the cubical setting, the path constructors of the higher inductive part must also respect the recursive structure, which leads to a notion of higher inductive‑recursive types where the path constructors may involve the recursive function. The consistency of these extensions relative to Martin‑Löf type theory with univalence has been established by constructing a model in the category of cubical sets where the recursive component is interpreted as a section of a display map.

Applications include the internalisation of type theory itself: one can define a type of codes for all types of a given universe level together with a decoding function, and then prove within the theory that this universe satisfies the same closure properties as the ambient universe. This self‑referential capability is the foundation for reflective towers of universes and for the formalisation of meta‑theoretic results such as the independence of the axiom of choice from univalent foundations.

Synthetic Obstruction Theory: k‑Invariants and Postnikov Systems in HoTT

Classical obstruction theory builds a Postnikov tower of a space by successively killing higher homotopy groups. In homotopy type theory the tower is obtained by the sequence of truncations ‖X‖ₙ → ‖X‖ₙ₋₁ → … → ‖X‖₀. Each truncation map is n-connected and its fibre is an Eilenberg–MacLane space K(πₙ(X), n). The extension problem for the fibre sequence is classified by a cohomology class — the k‑invariant — living in Hⁿ⁺¹(‖X‖ₙ₋₁; πₙ(X)) with local coefficients determined by the action of π₁ on πₙ. In the synthetic setting this classification is a direct consequence of the fact that maps into an Eilenberg–MacLane space represent cohomology, a theorem proved by the encode‑decode method for the circle and generalised to arbitrary K(G,n) by Licata and Finster.

The synthetic construction of the k‑invariant proceeds as follows. Given a type X, form its n-truncation Xₙ = ‖X‖ₙ and the fibre Fₙ = fib(Xₙ → Xₙ₋₁). By the long exact sequence of homotopy groups (which is available synthetically via the fibre sequence and the fact that truncation is left exact), Fₙ is an n-type with a single non‑trivial homotopy group πₙ(Fₙ) ≃ πₙ(X). Hence Fₙ is equivalent to K(πₙ(X), n). The fibre sequence K(πₙ(X), n) → Xₙ → Xₙ₋₁ is therefore classified by a map kₙ : Xₙ₋₁ → K(πₙ(X), n+1). This map is the k‑invariant. Its cohomology class can be computed by evaluating on the fundamental class of Xₙ₋₁ using the synthetic cohomology theory developed in the HoTT library.

An important feature of the synthetic approach is that the k‑invariant is not merely an abstract cohomology class but a concrete map between higher inductive types. This makes it amenable to computation in proof assistants: one can define the Postnikov tower of a specific higher inductive type (for example, the 2‑type presented by a crossed module) and extract the k‑invariant as a term of function type. The encode‑decode method then reduces the problem of identifying the cohomology class to a calculation in the algebraic model of the fundamental ∞‑groupoid.

The synthetic Postnikov tower also yields a clean proof of the Whitehead theorem for n-types: a map between n-types that induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups up to n is an equivalence. The proof proceeds by induction on the tower, using the fact that the fibres are Eilenberg–MacLane spaces and that a map between them inducing an isomorphism on the unique non‑trivial homotopy group is an equivalence. This argument avoids the classical use of CW‑approximation and works entirely inside the type theory.

Encode‑Decode for k‑Invariants
Let X be a connected 2‑type with π₁(X) ≃ ℤ and π₂(X) ≃ ℤ/2, where the action of π₁ on π₂ is trivial. Compute the k‑invariant k₂ : ‖X‖₁ → K(ℤ/2, 3) that classifies the Postnikov tower of X, and identify its cohomology class in H³(ℤ; ℤ/2).
The 1‑truncation ‖X‖₁ is equivalent to the circle S¹ because π₁(X) ≃ ℤ and X is connected. The fibre of X₂ → X₁ is K(ℤ/2, 2). The k‑invariant is a map k₂ : S¹ → K(ℤ/2, 3). Since π₁(S¹) ≃ ℤ acts trivially on ℤ/2, the cohomology group H³(ℤ; ℤ/2) is isomorphic to ℤ/2 (the group cohomology of ℤ with trivial coefficients is ℤ/2 in odd degrees). The map k₂ corresponds to the generator of this group. In the synthetic setting, one constructs k₂ by the universal property of the fibre sequence: the composite S¹ → X₂ → X₁ is the truncation map, and the fibre sequence gives a connecting map S¹ → K(ℤ/2, 3). Evaluating this map on the fundamental class of S¹ yields the non‑zero element of ℤ/2. Hence the k‑invariant is the non‑trivial class in H³(ℤ; ℤ/2).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a k‑invariant, first identify the relevant truncation levels and the homotopy groups involved. Remember that the coefficient system for the cohomology group is the action of π₁ on πₙ; if the action is trivial, the group is ordinary group cohomology. Use the synthetic long exact sequence of homotopy groups to confirm the fibre is an Eilenberg–MacLane space, then invoke the representability of cohomology by maps into K(G,n). The encode‑decode method for the circle (or higher spheres) is the standard tool to compute the resulting cohomology class.

Higher (∞,n)‑Categories in Directed Homotopy Type Theory

Directed homotopy type theory extends Martin‑Löf type theory with a directed interval type 𝟚 that has two endpoints 0,1 : 𝟚 and a single generating path δ : 0 → 1 which is not invertible. This primitive directed path models the non‑invertible 1‑morphisms of an (∞,1)-category. To model (∞,n)-categories for n > 1, one iterates the directed interval: an (∞,2)-category can be presented by a type equipped with two directed interval structures that commute up to higher directed paths, or more systematically by the n‑globe higher inductive type whose k‑cells are generated by the k‑dimensional faces of the n‑cube. The work of Riehl, Shulman, and others shows that the fundamental (∞,n)-category of a directed type can be constructed as a higher inductive type whose objects are points, 1‑morphisms are directed paths, 2‑morphisms are directed homotopies between directed paths, and so on.

The key technical device is the Rezk completion for (∞,n)-categories, which forces the Segal conditions and completeness at each level. In directed HoTT this is achieved by a higher inductive‑inductive definition that simultaneously builds the type of objects, the hom‑types, and the composition operations, together with path constructors expressing associativity and unit laws up to coherent higher directed paths. The resulting structure satisfies the universal property of the free (∞,n)-category on a given directed graph. This synthetic approach avoids the combinatorial complexity of simplicial or globular models and makes the coherence data first‑class citizens of the type theory.

An important application is the internalisation of (∞,n)-category theory itself: one can define the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n)-categories, the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n)-functors, and prove the (∞,n)-categorical Yoneda lemma inside the theory. The directed interval also interacts with the cohesive modalities: the shape modality sends a directed type to its underlying ∞‑groupoid by inverting all directed paths, while the flat modality ♭ extracts the discrete (∞,n)-category of global points. This interplay provides a synthetic version of the homotopy hypothesis for (∞,n)-categories.

Computational aspects are under active development. Cubical directed type theory, implemented in the proof assistant Cartesian Cubical Agda, provides a canonicity theorem for the directed interval: every closed term of type 𝟚 reduces to either 0 or 1. This ensures that the synthetic (∞,n)-categories have a concrete computational interpretation, opening the way for certified algorithms in higher category theory.

Synthetic (∞,1)‑Categorical Limits and Colimits in the ∞‑Topos of Types

The ∞‑topos of types is the (∞,1)-category whose objects are types and whose morphisms are functions, with higher morphisms given by homotopies. In this setting, limits and colimits are homotopy limits and colimits. They can be constructed synthetically using higher inductive types: a pullback of f : A → C and g : B → C is the higher inductive type Σ (a:A) Σ (b:B) (f a = g b), which is exactly the homotopy pullback. Dually, a pushout is the higher inductive type generated by constructors inl : A → P, inr : B → P and a path constructor glue : ∀ (c:C), inl (f c) = inr (g c). These constructions satisfy the expected universal properties up to equivalence, and the proofs are direct applications of the induction principles of the higher inductive types.

More general limits are obtained as iterated pullbacks and equalizers. The equalizer of f,g : A → B is the type Σ (a:A) (f a = g a). Because the ∞‑topos of types is presentable, all small limits and colimits exist and are computed pointwise in the sense that a diagram D : I → Type has limit lim D ≃ Σ (x:Π i, D i) ∀ i j (u:i→j), D u (x i) = x j. This formula is a higher inductive type whose constructors encode the cone condition. The colimit is the higher inductive type generated by constructors in i : D i → colim D and path constructors for each morphism in I.

The adjoint functor theorem holds internally: a functor between presentable ∞‑categories that preserves limits and is accessible has a left adjoint. In HoTT this is proved by constructing the left adjoint as a higher inductive type that freely adds the required colimits. The proof uses the fact that the ∞‑topos of types is locally cartesian closed and has a subobject classifier (the type of propositions). These synthetic limit and colimit constructions are the backbone of the formalisation of (∞,1)-category theory in the HoTT library, enabling the development of the (∞,1)-category of spectra, the (∞,1)-category of ∞‑topoi, and the internal Yoneda lemma.

A subtle point is the interaction with truncation levels. The limit of a diagram of n‑types is again an n‑type, but the colimit of n‑types may raise the truncation level. This is reflected in the synthetic construction: the pushout of two sets along a function need not be a set; it is a 1‑type whose fundamental groupoid captures the gluing data. The HoTT library provides lemmas that compute the truncation level of a colimit in terms of the connectivity of the diagram maps, which is essential for reasoning about homotopy groups of higher inductive types.

Principal ∞‑Bundles, Characteristic Classes, and the Synthetic Chern‑Weil Theory

In homotopy type theory a principal ∞‑bundle for an ∞‑group G is a map p : P → X equipped with a free G-action on P such that the quotient P/G is equivalent to X. The classifying type BG is the delooping of G, constructed as a higher inductive type with a single point constructor base : BG and a loop constructor for each element of G together with higher paths encoding the group structure. The universal principal G-bundle is the map EG → BG where EG is the contractible type with a free G-action (the homotopy fibre of the point inclusion). Every principal G-bundle over X is equivalent to the pullback of EG → BG along a classifying map X → BG.

Characteristic classes are maps BG → Bⁿ A for an abelian ∞‑group A (typically Bⁿ ℤ or Bⁿ U(1)). In the synthetic Chern‑Weil theory, one starts with a cohesive ∞‑topos equipped with the shape modality and the flat modality ♭. The synthetic de Rham complex is the fibre of the unit ♭ → id. For a Lie ∞‑group G with Lie algebra 𝔤, invariant polynomials on 𝔤 give rise to maps BG → Bⁿ ℝ in the cohesive setting. The synthetic construction uses the fact that the flat modality ♭BG classifies flat G-bundles, and the shape modality BG classifies the underlying topological bundle. The Chern‑Weil homomorphism is then the composite BG → ♭BG → Bⁿ ℝ where the first map is the unit of the flat modality and the second is induced by the invariant polynomial via the synthetic de Rham theorem.

This approach has been formalised for the classical groups O(n), U(n), and Sp(n) in the HoTT library. The first Pontryagin class p₁ : BO(n) → B⁴ ℤ and the Chern classes c_k : BU(n) → B²ᵏ ℤ are obtained as synthetic Chern‑Weil classes. The proof that these classes agree with the classical ones uses the synthetic version of the splitting principle: the map BT → BG induced by a maximal torus inclusion is injective on cohomology, and the invariant polynomials restrict to symmetric polynomials on the weight lattice. The synthetic splitting principle is proved by constructing the flag variety as a higher inductive type and showing that its cohomology is the polynomial ring on the Chern roots.

An open problem is the synthetic construction of secondary characteristic classes (e.g., the Chern‑Simons classes) which require a differential refinement of the cohomology theory. The differential cohomology hexagon in cohesive HoTT provides a framework, but the explicit higher inductive types for differential cocycles are still under development. Another direction is the extension to equivariant principal ∞‑bundles, where the base type carries a group action and the bundle is required to be equivariant. This connects with the synthetic equivariant homotopy theory mentioned elsewhere in the lesson.

  • Confusing inductive‑recursive definitions with inductive‑inductive definitions; the former involve a recursive function, the latter involve two mutually defined types.
  • Assuming the k‑invariant always lives in ordinary cohomology; it lives in cohomology with local coefficients when π₁ acts non‑trivially on πₙ.
  • Thinking directed HoTT only models (∞,1)-categories; iterating the directed interval yields (∞,n)-categories for any n.
  • Believing that all colimits in the ∞‑topos of types preserve truncation levels; pushouts of sets can produce 1‑types.
  • Treating the synthetic Chern‑Weil map as a map of ordinary types rather than a map in the cohesive ∞‑topos; the flat and shape modalities are essential.
  • Overlooking that the universal principal ∞‑bundle EG → BG is a higher inductive type whose total space is contractible by construction, not by an external argument.
  • Assuming the Postnikov tower in HoTT is unique up to equality; it is unique up to equivalence, and the k‑invariants are only well‑defined up to the action of the automorphisms of the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces.

Synthetic Rational Homotopy Theory and Sullivan Models in HoTT

Rational homotopy theory studies spaces up to rational equivalence, where the homotopy groups are tensored with ℚ. In classical topology, Sullivan's minimal models provide commutative differential graded algebras (CDGAs) over ℚ that capture the rational homotopy type of simply connected spaces. In HoTT, this theory is internalized by working in the ∞-topos of types with rational coefficients. The key insight is that the rationalization of a type X, denoted X_ℚ, can be constructed as a higher inductive type that freely adds rational vector space structure to the homotopy groups. For a simply connected type X, the Sullivan minimal model is a CDGA (ΛV, d) where V is a graded ℚ-vector space and d is a decomposable differential. In HoTT, this corresponds to a sequence of higher inductive types building X_ℚ as a tower of principal fibrations with fibers Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(ℚ, n). The synthetic construction uses the fact that the rational cohomology ring H*(X; ℚ) is the cohomology of the CDGA of piecewise polynomial differential forms on X. The minimal model is then obtained by a synthetic version of the Sullivan construction: one iteratively attaches cells to kill indecomposable cohomology classes. A crucial computational tool is the synthetic version of the Hirsch lemma, which relates the minimal model of a fibration to those of its base and fiber. This has been formalized for formal spaces (where the minimal model is quasi-isomorphic to the cohomology algebra) such as spheres, complex projective spaces, and compact Lie groups. The synthetic approach clarifies that rational homotopy equivalence corresponds to equivalence of the associated ∞-groupoids after rationalization, and that the minimal model is unique up to isomorphism of CDGAs, which in HoTT translates to equivalence of the corresponding higher inductive presentations.

The Synthetic Dold-Kan Correspondence: Chain Complexes and Simplicial Abelian Groups in HoTT

The Dold-Kan correspondence establishes an equivalence between the category of non-negatively graded chain complexes of abelian groups and the category of simplicial abelian groups. In HoTT, this correspondence is internalized by constructing the normalization functor N and the Moore complex functor Γ as mutually inverse equivalences of ∞-categories. A simplicial abelian group in HoTT is a type family A : Δ^op → AbGrp where Δ is the simplex category (constructed as a higher inductive type with face and degeneracy maps). The normalized chain complex N(A) has N(A)_n = ⋂i=0n-1 ker(d_i : A_n → An-1) with differential d_n. The inverse Γ(C) for a chain complex C is defined by Γ(C)_n = ⊕[n] ↠ [k] C_k where the sum is over surjections in Δ. The synthetic proof that N and Γ are equivalences uses the fact that the identity type in the ∞-category of simplicial abelian groups corresponds to homotopy equivalence of chain complexes. A key technical point is that the Dold-Kan correspondence preserves the monoidal structure: the tensor product of chain complexes corresponds to the levelwise tensor product of simplicial abelian groups, and the internal hom corresponds to the simplicial mapping complex. This allows the synthetic construction of the Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(A, n) as the image under Γ of the chain complex A[n] (A in degree n, zero elsewhere). The correspondence also interacts with the stable homotopy category: the ∞-category of spectra is equivalent to the ∞-category of unbounded chain complexes, and the Dold-Kan correspondence extends to a Quillen equivalence between simplicial abelian groups and connective chain complexes. In Cubical Agda, the normalization functor computes by reducing cubical paths to their boundary components, providing a computational interpretation of the homology groups of a type as the homotopy groups of its Dold-Kan image.

Technique: Computing Rational Homotopy Groups via Minimal Models
Let X be the total space of the fibration S³ → X → S⁴ classified by the Hopf map η : S³ → S⁴. Compute π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ using the Sullivan minimal model.
The minimal model of S⁴ is (Λ(x₄), 0) with |x₄| = 4. The minimal model of S³ is (Λ(y₃), 0) with |y₃| = 3. The Hopf map η corresponds to a map of minimal models sending x₄ to y₃² (since η generates π₃(S⁴) ≅ ℤ and the Whitehead product [ι₄, ι₄] = 2η). The minimal model of the total space X is the relative Sullivan algebra (Λ(x₄, y₃), d) with d(x₄) = 0, d(y₃) = x₄. This is acyclic in positive degrees, so X_ℚ is contractible. Thus π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ = 0 for all * > 0. In HoTT, this is verified by constructing X as a HIT with constructors base : X, loop₄ : base = base (4-loop), loop₃ : base = base (3-loop), and a 4-path filling loop₃ ∘ loop₃ = loop₄. The rationalization X_ℚ is then shown to be contractible by exhibiting a homotopy between the identity and the constant map using the rational vector space structure on the loop spaces.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Rational Equivalence in HITs
When a problem asks about rational homotopy groups of a HIT, look for differentials in the minimal model that kill generators. A generator in degree n with a non-zero differential means the corresponding rational homotopy group vanishes. The minimal model of a HIT is built by reading off the constructors: each n-path constructor adds a generator in degree n, and each (n+1)-path constructor relating n-paths adds a differential. If the differential is decomposable (expressible in terms of lower-degree generators), the model is minimal. Practice translating the Hopf fibration, the quaternionic Hopf fibration, and the fibration S⁷ → S¹⁵ → S⁸ into minimal models.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Mapping Spaces: Function Types as Internal Hom

In the ∞-topos of types, the function type X → Y represents the internal mapping space Map(X, Y). Its homotopy groups are given by π_k(Map(X, Y), f) ≅ π0(Map(X, Ω^k Y), f) ≅ [X, Ω^k Y], the set of homotopy classes of maps from X to the k-fold loop space of Y. When X is a finite CW-complex presented as a HIT, the mapping space inherits a natural filtration by the skeleta of X. The synthetic approach to mapping spaces uses the fact that Map(X, Y) is the limit of the diagram Map(X_n, Y) where X_n is the n-skeleton. For X = S¹, Map(S¹, Y) ≃ ΩY × Y, where the first factor is the based loop space and the second is the evaluation at the basepoint. For X = Sⁿ, Map(Sⁿ, Y) ≃ ΩⁿY × Y. For a general HIT X built from cells, the mapping space is computed by an equalizer diagram reflecting the attaching maps. A key result is the synthetic version of the evaluation fibration: for any type Y, the map ev : Map(X, Y) × X → Y given by ev(f, x) = f(x) is a fibration whose fiber over y : Y is Map_*(X, Y_y) where Y_y is the component of y. The long exact sequence of homotopy groups for this fibration yields the exact sequence ⋯ → πk+1(Y) → π_k(Map_*(X, Y)) → π_k(Map(X, Y)) → π_k(Y) → ⋯. When X is a suspension ΣZ, there is an adjunction Map(ΣZ, Y) ≃ Map(Z, ΩY), which in HoTT is the equivalence (ΣZ → Y) ≃ (Z → ΩY). This adjunction is used to compute the homotopy groups of mapping spaces out of spheres and projective spaces. The synthetic construction of the mapping space as a HIT with constructors for pointwise paths and higher coherences provides a computational handle on the homotopy groups of function types in Cubical Agda.

The Synthetic Quillen Model Structure on Simplicial Objects in HoTT

In classical homotopy theory, the category of simplicial sets carries the Kan-Quillen model structure where weak equivalences are weak homotopy equivalences, fibrations are Kan fibrations, and cofibrations are monomorphisms. In HoTT, one can construct a synthetic model structure on the ∞-category of simplicial types (types over Δ^op). A simplicial type is a functor X : Δ^op → Type. The Reedy model structure has weak equivalences and fibrations defined levelwise: a map f : X → Y is a weak equivalence (resp. fibration) if each f_n : X_n → Y_n is an equivalence (resp. fibration) of types. The cofibrations are the Reedy cofibrations, characterized by the latching map condition. The injective model structure has weak equivalences and cofibrations levelwise, with fibrations defined by the right lifting property. The projective model structure has weak equivalences and fibrations levelwise. The synthetic Quillen equivalence between simplicial types and types is given by the geometric realization functor |−| : sType → Type and the singular complex functor Sing : Type → sType. The geometric realization of a simplicial type X is the colimit of the diagram X_n × Δ^n where Δ^n is the standard n-simplex type (a HIT with n+1 vertices and higher paths). The singular complex of a type Y has Sing(Y)_n = (Δ^n → Y). The synthetic proof that this is a Quillen equivalence uses the fact that the unit Y → Sing|Y| is a weak equivalence for all Y (by the synthetic version of the Milnor-Lurie theorem) and the counit |Sing X| → X is a weak equivalence for Reedy cofibrant X. This model structure is essential for doing homotopy theory of diagrams in HoTT, as it provides a framework for homotopy limits and colimits of simplicial diagrams. The Reedy fibrant replacement of a simplicial type computes its homotopy limit, and the Reedy cofibrant replacement computes its homotopy colimit.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of ∞-Operads and Algebras in HoTT

An ∞-operad in HoTT is a type O equipped with a composition structure that is associative and unital up to coherent higher homotopies. The synthetic definition uses the fact that the ∞-category of types is symmetric monoidal under the cartesian product, and an ∞-operad is a monoid in the ∞-category of symmetric sequences. Concretely, an ∞-operad consists of types O(n) for n : ℕ with an action of the symmetric group Σ_n, composition maps O(k) × O(n₁) × ⋯ × O(n_k) → O(n₁ + ⋯ + n_k), and higher coherences. The associative operad Ass has Ass(n) = Σ_n (the symmetric group as a discrete type). The commutative operad Comm has Comm(n) = 1 (the unit type). The little disks operad D_k has D_k(n) = Emb(∐_n D^k, D^k) (the space of embeddings of n disjoint k-disks into the standard k-disk). An algebra over an ∞-operad O is a type A with maps O(n) × A^n → A satisfying the operad axioms up to coherent homotopy. The synthetic bar-cobar adjunction relates O-algebras to coalgebras over the cooperad O^∨. For the associative operad, O-algebras are A_∞-spaces (monoids up to coherent homotopy), and the bar construction produces a coassociative coalgebra. The synthetic recognition principle states that a connected type X is an O-algebra for the little disks operad D_k if and only if X is a k-fold loop space. This is formalized by constructing the operadic nerve and showing that the ∞-category of D_k-algebras is equivalent to the ∞-category of k-fold loop spaces. The synthetic construction of the free O-algebra on a type X uses a higher inductive type with constructors for the operad actions and coherences. This framework has been used to formalize the Deligne conjecture (the Hochschild cochain complex of an associative algebra is an algebra over the little disks operad) and to study factorization homology in HoTT.

  • Confusing the minimal model of a space with its cohomology algebra; the minimal model is a free CDGA, while the cohomology algebra may have relations not captured by decomposable differentials.
  • Assuming the Dold-Kan correspondence preserves all limits and colimits; it is an equivalence of ∞-categories but the normalization functor does not preserve products (it is only lax monoidal).
  • Treating Map(X, Y) as a set of functions rather than an ∞-groupoid; its identity types are homotopies, and its higher identity types are higher homotopies.
  • Believing that every simplicial type is Reedy fibrant; a simplicial type is Reedy fibrant iff each matching map X_n → M_n X is a fibration, which fails for constant diagrams of non-fibrant types.
  • Assuming that an A_∞-space is strictly associative; the synthetic definition only requires associativity up to a coherent system of higher paths, and strictification is a non-trivial theorem (the recognition principle).
  • Overlooking that the rationalization of a HIT may not be a HIT of the same shape; rationalization adds path constructors that make all homotopy groups into ℚ-vector spaces, which can change the truncation level.
  • Thinking the synthetic Quillen equivalence between simplicial types and types is an equivalence of 1-categories; it is an equivalence of ∞-categories, and the model structures are only presentations of this equivalence.

The Synthetic Kahn‑Priddy Theorem and the Stable Splitting of Ω^∞Σ^∞X

The Kahn‑Priddy theorem identifies the infinite loop space Ω^∞Σ^∞X as a disjoint union of extended powers D_k(X) = (X^k)hΣ_k, where Σ_k acts by permuting factors and the homotopy quotient is taken in the ∞‑category of types. In HoTT, the suspension spectrum Σ^∞X is the sequential colimit of Σ^n X, and Ω^∞ evaluates the 0‑th space of a spectrum. The theorem states that the unit map X → Ω^∞Σ^∞X extends to an equivalence Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∐k≥0 D_k(X). The synthetic proof proceeds through three pillars: the Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen theorem giving Ω^∞Σ^∞S0 ≃ ℤ × BΣ_∞+, the Snaith splitting Σ^∞Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∨_k Σ^∞D_k(X), and the recognition that the map ∐ D_k(X) → Ω^∞Σ^∞X induced by the operad structure of the sphere spectrum is an equivalence. In HoTT, each D_k(X) is a higher inductive type with constructors for the Σ_k‑action and the homotopy quotient paths. The Kahn‑Priddy map BΣ_k → Ω^∞Σ^∞S0 classifies the k‑fold extended power of the sphere. The stable splitting implies that the stable homotopy groups of spheres π_*^S = π_*(Ω^∞Σ^∞S0) decompose as a direct sum of the homotopy groups of the extended powers D_k(S0) = BΣ_k+. This decomposition underlies the computation of the first few stable stems via the homology of symmetric groups. Formalization in Cubical Agda has achieved the Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen equivalence and the construction of the Snaith splitting for finite types, but the full equivalence for arbitrary types requires a synthetic version of the group‑completion theorem for E_∞‑spaces, which remains an open formalization target.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Configuration Spaces and Braid Groups

The configuration space Conf_n(M) of n distinct ordered points in a type M is the subtype of M^n where all coordinates are pairwise unequal. In HoTT, this is defined as Conf_n(M) ≔ Σ (x : M^n), ∏i≠j (x_i ≠ x_j). When M = ℝ2, Conf_n(ℝ2) is a K(B_n, 1) where B_n is the Artin braid group on n strands. The synthetic computation of π1(Conf_n(ℝ2)) uses a higher inductive presentation of Conf_n(ℝ2) as the Salvetti complex: a type with a basepoint, 1‑cells corresponding to the standard generators σ_i of B_n, and 2‑cells imposing the braid relations σ_i σi+1 σ_i = σi+1 σ_i σi+1 and σ_i σ_j = σ_j σ_i for |i−j|>1. The encode‑decode method then constructs an equivalence Ω(Conf_n(ℝ2)) ≃ B_n, where B_n is presented as a set‑level group via its standard presentation. For general M, the scanning map Conf_n(ℝ^d) → Ω^d S^d (d ≥ 2) is constructed by sending a configuration to the map that collapses the complement of small balls around the points. This map is (n−1)‑connected and induces the homology stability isomorphism H_k(Conf_n(ℝ^d)) ≅ H_k(Confn+1(ℝ^d)) for k < n/2. The Cohen‑Taylor spectral sequence, which computes H^*(Conf_n(M)) from the cohomology of M, is synthesized by filtering the configuration space by the number of points in a chosen subspace. Formalization in the HoTT library has achieved the braid group presentation for n ≤ 4 and the construction of the scanning map for d = 2, but the general homology stability theorem and the Cohen‑Taylor spectral sequence remain partially formalized due to the complexity of the required spectral sequence machinery in HoTT.

Encode‑Decode for Braid Groups
Let Conf3(ℝ2) be presented as a HIT with basepoint *, 1‑cells a, b : * = *, and a 2‑cell braid : a ⬝ b ⬝ a = b ⬝ a ⬝ b. Define a type family Code : Conf3(ℝ2) → Type by Code(*) ≔ B3 (the set‑level braid group on 3 strands), Code(a) ≔ transport by σ1, Code(b) ≔ transport by σ2, and Code(braid) as the path witnessing the braid relation in B3. Show that the total space Σ (x : Conf3(ℝ2)), Code(x) is contractible.
The total space E ≔ Σ (x : Conf3(ℝ2)), Code(x) has a center of contraction at (*, e) where e is the identity in B3. For any (x, c) : E, we construct a path to (*, e) by induction on x. If x ≡ *, then c : B3 and the path is (loop^c, c⁻¹) where loop^c is the concatenation of a and b according to the word c. If x is a path constructor a or b, the induction hypothesis gives a path in the fiber over the endpoint, and the definition of Code on a, b ensures the transport matches the group multiplication by σ1 or σ2. The 2‑cell braid corresponds exactly to the braid relation in B3, so the path constructed over the boundary of braid extends to a path over the whole 2‑cell. Thus E is contractible, and by the encode‑decode theorem Ω(Conf3(ℝ2), *) ≃ B3.
Exam Strategy: Configuration Spaces as HITs
When a question asks for the fundamental group of a configuration space, first identify if the space is a K(G,1). For Conf_n(ℝ2), the answer is the braid group B_n. For Conf_n(ℝ^d) with d ≥ 3, the space is simply connected. The synthetic method always uses a HIT presentation (Salvetti complex for d=2, Fulton‑MacPherson compactification for general d) followed by encode‑decode. Memorize the generators σ_i and the two families of relations for B_n; they appear verbatim in the 1‑ and 2‑cell constructors of the HIT.

The Synthetic Atiyah‑Hirzebruch Spectral Sequence for Generalized Cohomology

The Atiyah‑Hirzebruch spectral sequence (AHSS) computes the generalized cohomology E^*(X) of a type X from its ordinary cohomology with coefficients in the coefficient groups E^*(pt). In HoTT, a spectrum E is a sequence of types E_n with equivalences E_n ≃ Ω En+1. The cohomology group E^k(X) is defined as π-k Map_*(X, E) ≃ ||X → Ω^k E||0 for k ≤ 0, and for k > 0 via the suspension isomorphism. The synthetic AHSS is constructed from the Postnikov tower of the spectrum E: let E⟨n⟩ be the n‑th Postnikov section, so that π_k(E⟨n⟩) = π_k(E) for k ≤ n and 0 otherwise. The fiber of E⟨n⟩ → E⟨n-1⟩ is the Eilenberg‑MacLane spectrum Σ^n Hπ_n(E). Applying the mapping type Map(X, −) yields a tower of fibrations Map(X, E⟨n⟩) → Map(X, E⟨n-1⟩) with fiber Map(X, Σ^n Hπ_n(E)) ≃ Σ^n Map(X, Hπ_n(E)). The long exact sequences of homotopy groups assemble into an exact couple, producing a spectral sequence with E2p,q = H^p(X; π-q(E)) converging to Ep+q(X) for X a finite type (or more generally, a type of finite homotopy dimension). The differentials d_r : E_rp,q → E_rp+r, q-r+1 are induced by the k‑invariants of the Postnikov tower. For E = Hℤ/p, the first non‑trivial differential d2 is the Steenrod square Sq2 (or the Bockstein for p=2). The synthetic proof of convergence uses the fact that the Postnikov tower of E is a limit diagram in the ∞‑category of spectra, and Map(X, −) preserves limits. Formalization in Cubical Agda has constructed the Postnikov tower of a spectrum and the associated exact couple for finite types, but the general convergence theorem for arbitrary types requires a synthetic version of the Milnor exact sequence for the limit of the tower, which is complicated by the need for countable choice in the metatheory.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Lie Groups, Stiefel Manifolds, and Grassmannians

The classical Lie groups are synthesized in HoTT as automorphism groups of structured types. The orthogonal group O(n) is the type of linear equivalences ℝ^n ≃ ℝ^n preserving the standard inner product, defined as a subtype of the function type (ℝ^n → ℝ^n) with the condition ⟨f(x), f(y)⟩ = ⟨x, y⟩. The unitary group U(n) and symplectic group Sp(n) are defined analogously over ℂ and ℍ. The Stiefel manifold V_k(ℝ^n) of orthonormal k‑frames in ℝ^n is the type of linear maps ℝ^k → ℝ^n that are isometric embeddings; it is equivalent to the homogeneous space O(n)/O(n−k). The Grassmannian Gr_k(ℝ^n) of k‑planes in ℝ^n is the type of k‑dimensional linear subspaces, equivalent to O(n)/(O(k)×O(n−k)). In HoTT, these are constructed as higher inductive types: Gr_k(ℝ^n) has a constructor for each point of the classical Grassmannian and path constructors witnessing the transitive action of O(n). The tautological bundle γ_k^n over Gr_k(ℝ^n) is the type family whose fiber over a subspace V is V itself. Characteristic classes arise as maps of classifying types: the Stiefel‑Whitney classes w_i : BO(n) → K(ℤ/2, i) are constructed via the action of the Steenrod algebra on H^*(BO(n); ℤ/2), which is the polynomial algebra ℤ/2[w1,…,w_n]. The Chern classes c_i : BU(n) → K(ℤ, 2i) are constructed similarly using the complex orientation of BU. The synthetic splitting principle states that the pullback of γ_k^n to the flag manifold Fl(n) = O(n)/T^n (where T^n is the maximal torus) splits as a sum of line bundles, reducing computations to the case of line bundles where c1 classifies the bundle. Bott periodicity is synthesized as the equivalence Ω8 BO ≃ BO (real) and Ω2 BU ≃ BU (complex), proved by constructing the Clifford module structure on the loop space. Formalization in the HoTT library has achieved the construction of BO(n) as a HIT, the tautological bundle, and the first Stiefel‑Whitney class w1; the higher classes and the full splitting principle require a synthetic theory of the Steenrod algebra action on the cohomology of classifying spaces, which is currently under development.

The Synthetic Cyclotomic Trace and Topological Cyclic Homology in HoTT

Topological Cyclic Homology TC(R) of a ring spectrum R is the homotopy fixed points of the circle action on Topological Hochschild Homology THH(R). In HoTT, THH(R) is constructed as a higher inductive type with a circle action: it has a basepoint, a 1‑cell for the circle action, and higher cells encoding the cyclic bar construction. Concretely, THH(R) ≔ Σ (x : S1 → R), ∏t:S1 (x(t) = x(t+1)) where the condition encodes the cyclicity. The circle action rotates the domain S1. The Connes operator B : THH(R) → Ω THH(R) is the map induced by the circle action. The homotopy fixed points THH(R)hS1 are defined as the type of maps S1 → THH(R) equipped with a homotopy to the constant map, i.e., the fiber of the map THH(R) → Map(S1, THH(R)) induced by the action. The Frobenius maps φ_p : THH(R)C_p → THH(R) are constructed using the p‑fold covering S1 → S1. The Nikolaus‑Scholze description of TC(R) is the sequential limit TC(R) ≔ lim_n THH(R)Cp^n where the transition maps are the Frobenius. The cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) is a map from the algebraic K‑theory spectrum (constructed as the group completion of the ∞‑category of perfect R‑modules) to TC(R). The Dundas‑Goodwillie‑McCarthy theorem states that for a nilpotent extension of ring spectra R → R', the relative K‑theory fiber is equivalent to the relative TC fiber. In HoTT, the synthetic proof uses the fact that both K and TC are localizing invariants and that the cyclotomic trace is an equivalence on the ∞‑category of perfect modules over a field. Formalization status: THH(R) as a HIT with circle action has been defined in Cubical Agda for discrete rings, and the Connes operator B has been constructed. The homotopy fixed points THH(R)hS1 and the Frobenius maps are formalized for the case R = 𝔽_p. The full Nikolaus‑Scholze limit construction and the cyclotomic trace map remain major open formalization challenges due to the need for a synthetic theory of ∞‑categories of modules and the group completion construction for K‑theory.

  • Confusing the Kahn‑Priddy splitting Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∐ D_k(X) with the Snaith splitting Σ^∞Ω^∞Σ^∞X ≃ ∨ Σ^∞D_k(X); the former is a splitting of spaces, the latter of spectra.
  • Assuming Conf_n(M) is always a K(π,1); this holds only for dim M = 2. For dim M ≥ 3, Conf_n(M) is simply connected and has higher homotopy groups.
  • Treating the Atiyah‑Hirzebruch spectral sequence as a first‑quadrant spectral sequence for all X; it is a half‑plane spectral sequence for general X, and convergence requires X to have finite homotopy dimension or E to be connective.
  • Believing the synthetic Stiefel‑Whitney classes w_i : BO(n) → K(ℤ/2, i) are defined by the same cellular formulas as in classical topology; in HoTT they are defined via the Steenrod algebra action on the synthetic cohomology ring H^*(BO(n); ℤ/2).
  • Overlooking that THH(R) in HoTT is a type with a circle action, not merely a spectrum; the circle action is primitive data in the HIT definition, and the Connes operator is derived from it.
  • Assuming the cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) is an equivalence for all ring spectra; it is an equivalence only after p‑completion and for regular rings, or on relative terms for nilpotent extensions (DGM theorem).
  • Confusing the homotopy fixed points THH(R)hS1 with the genuine fixed points THH(R)S1; in HoTT, the homotopy fixed points are the correct definition for TC, and the genuine fixed points are not invariant under equivalence of spectra with circle action.

The Synthetic Nilpotence Theorem and the Thick Subcategory Theorem
