The Nilpotence Theorem of Devinatz, Hopkins, and Smith (1988) and the Thick Subcategory Theorem (Hopkins-Smith, 1998) are the twin pillars of chromatic homotopy theory. In classical topology, the Nilpotence Theorem states that a map of finite spectra f : X → Y is nilpotent (some smash power f^∧k is null) if and only if it is zero on Morava K-theory K(n)_* for all n ≥ 0. The Thick Subcategory Theorem classifies the thick subcategories of the category of finite p-local spectra: they are precisely the categories C_n of spectra X with K(m)_*(X) = 0 for m < n. In synthetic homotopy type theory, these theorems are reformulated internally to the ∞-topos of types. A finite spectrum is represented by a dualizable type in the stable homotopy category SH (constructed as the stabilization of the ∞-topos). The Morava K-theories K(n) are represented by E_∞ ring types whose coefficients are 𝔽_p[v_n^±1] with |v_n| = 2(p^n-1). The synthetic Nilpotence Theorem asserts that for a map f : X → Y of dualizable types, f is nilpotent in the endomorphism ring [X, X] iff K(n) ∧ f = 0 for all n. The proof strategy in HoTT follows the classical Ravenel approach but uses the internal logic: one constructs the type-theoretic analogue of the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) for the mapping spectrum F(X, Y) and shows that the E_∞-page detects nilpotence via the chromatic resolution. The Thick Subcategory Theorem is then derived by showing that the collection of types X such that K(n)_*(X) = 0 forms a thick subcategory (closed under cofibers, retracts, and summands) and that any thick subcategory containing a type with K(n)_*(X) ≠ 0 must contain all types with K(m)_*(X) ≠ 0 for m ≥ n. This relies on the synthetic construction of the telescope conjecture (still open in general but verified for n=1 and n=2 at certain primes) and the existence of type n complexes (finite spectra with K(m)_* = 0 for m ≠ n and K(n)_* ≠ 0). In HoTT, the existence of type n complexes is a major formalization target; they are constructed as higher inductive types with cells designed to kill lower Morava K-theory homology. The synthetic proof of the Thick Subcategory Theorem uses the fact that the Bousfield lattice of the stable homotopy category is generated by the K(n), a fact that can be internalized using the orthogonality of the K(n) and the smashing property of LK(n) localization. Formalization in Cubical Agda has achieved the definition of K(n) as a HIT for n=1 (related to KU/p) and the verification of the thick subcategory classification for n=0,1 (rational and K(1)-local). The general case requires a synthetic theory of E_∞ ring spectra and the Goerss-Hopkins obstruction theory for realizing K(n) as a HIT, which is an active research area.

The Synthetic Symmetric Monoidal Structure on Spectra and the Smash Product Theorem

The stable homotopy category SH is not merely triangulated; it is a symmetric monoidal stable ∞-category where the tensor product is the smash product ∧ and the unit is the sphere spectrum 𝕊. In classical topology, constructing a strictly associative and commutative smash product on spectra required elaborate frameworks (EKMM, symmetric spectra, orthogonal spectra). In HoTT, the symmetric monoidal structure arises naturally from the cartesian monoidal structure of the underlying ∞-topos via stabilization. The ∞-category of spectra Sp is defined as the stabilization of the ∞-topos Type, i.e., the limit Sp = lim(… → Type_* → Type_*) where the maps are Ω. The smash product is then defined by the universal property of stabilization: the functor ∧ : Sp × Sp → Sp is the unique colimit-preserving extension of the smash product of pointed types ∧ : Type_* × Type_* → Type_*. This yields a symmetric monoidal ∞-category structure internally. The Smash Product Theorem (or the fact that Sp is a symmetric monoidal stable ∞-category) in HoTT is the statement that this structure satisfies the coherence laws of an E_∞ monoidal structure. The proof uses the fact that the sphere spectrum 𝕊 is the suspension spectrum of S0 and that the stabilization functor Σ^∞ : Type_* → Sp is symmetric monoidal. The internal hom is the mapping spectrum F(X, Y), characterized by the adjunction Map(Z ∧ X, Y) ≃ Map(Z, F(X, Y)). The dualizability of finite spectra (suspension spectra of finite types) is a key consequence: a spectrum X is dualizable iff it is in the thick subcategory generated by 𝕊, i.e., it is a finite spectrum. The dual of X is DX = F(X, 𝕊). The synthetic proof of dualizability uses the encode-decode method on the mapping spectra and the fact that finite types are compact objects in the ∞-topos. The symmetric monoidal structure is essential for defining E_∞ ring spectra (commutative algebra objects in Sp), modules over them, and the Morava K-theories K(n) as E_∞ ring types. In Cubical Agda, the symmetric monoidal structure on the synthetic spectra (defined as sequential spectra with structure maps Σ E_n → En+1) has been formalized up to the coherence required for E_∞ structures, using the fact that the smash product of sequential spectra can be made strictly associative and commutative by a suitable cofibrant replacement (the symmetric smash product). The main formalization challenge is the coherence data for the symmetric monoidal structure on the ∞-category level, which requires a synthetic theory of (∞,1)-categories with monoidal structure (e.g., using the Rezk completion of a monoidal precategory). The current HoTT library formalizes the smash product on sequential spectra and proves the adjunction with the mapping spectrum, but the full E_∞ coherence for the sphere spectrum as a commutative ring spectrum is still under development.

Worked Problem: Dualizability and the Thick Subcategory
Let X be a type in the synthetic stable homotopy category SH (i.e., a spectrum). Prove that X is dualizable if and only if X lies in the thick subcategory generated by the sphere spectrum 𝕊. Explain why this implies that the dualizable objects are precisely the finite spectra.
Solution:
  1. (⇒) Dualizable implies thick(𝕊): If X is dualizable, there exists DX and maps η : 𝕊 → X ∧ DX (unit) and ε : DX ∧ X → 𝕊 (counit) satisfying the triangle identities. The functor (-) ∧ X preserves colimits. Since X is a retract of X ∧ DX ∧ X via η and ε, and X ∧ DX ∧ X is a colimit of copies of X (since DX is a colimit of spheres by Brown representability in the synthetic setting, or more directly, DX = F(X, 𝕊) is a limit of mapping spectra from spheres), X belongs to the localizing subcategory generated by 𝕊. In the compactly generated stable ∞-category SH, the compact objects are precisely the dualizable ones, and they coincide with the thick subcategory generated by the compact generator 𝕊. Thus X ∈ thick(𝕊).
  2. (⇐) Thick(𝕊) implies dualizable: The sphere spectrum 𝕊 is dualizable (its own dual). The class of dualizable objects is closed under cofibers (if A → B → C is a cofiber sequence and A, B are dualizable, then C is dualizable because F(-, 𝕊) sends cofibers to fibers), retracts, and finite sums. Since thick(𝕊) is the smallest such class containing 𝕊, every object in it is dualizable.
  3. Finite Spectra: A finite spectrum is classically defined as the suspension spectrum of a finite CW complex. In HoTT, a finite type is one equivalent to a type built from 𝟘 and 𝟙 using finite sums, products, and pushouts (i.e., a compact object in the ∞-topos). The suspension spectrum functor Σ^∞ preserves compactness and the monoidal structure. Thus Σ^∞ maps finite types to compact (hence dualizable) spectra. Conversely, any dualizable spectrum is a retract of a finite cell spectrum built from spheres, hence is the suspension spectrum of a finite type (by the synthetic Freudenthal suspension theorem and the fact that Ω^∞ preserves compactness). Therefore, dualizable spectra = finite spectra = thick(𝕊).
Exam Strategy: Chromatic Filtration and Dualizability
When a question asks about the classification of thick subcategories or dualizable objects in the stable homotopy category, immediately recall the Hopkins-Smith Thick Subcategory Theorem: thick subcategories of finite spectra are C_n = {X | K(m)_* X = 0 for m < n}. The dualizable objects are C0 (all finite spectra). The K(n)-local spheres generate the Bousfield lattice. For computational questions, remember that K(0) = HQ (rational), K(1) relates to KU/p (Adams summand), and K(n) for n≥2 are the higher Morava K-theories. The Nilpotence Theorem is the detection mechanism: a map is nilpotent iff it dies on all K(n). Use the telescope conjecture (known for n=1,2) to relate LK(n) and LT(n) localizations if the problem involves finite localization.

The Synthetic Theory of Power Operations and the Dyer-Lashof Algebra

Power operations are the homotopical analogues of the Steenrod operations for E_∞ ring spectra and infinite loop spaces. While Steenrod operations act on the cohomology of spaces (or spectra) with coefficients in 𝔽_p, Dyer-Lashof operations act on the homology of infinite loop spaces (or the homotopy groups of E_∞ ring spectra). In classical topology, for an E_∞ ring spectrum R, the Dyer-Lashof operations Q^i : π_* R → π*+i(p-1) R (for p odd) and Q^i : π_* R → π*+i R (for p=2) are defined using the action of the extended power construction R∧phΣ_p on R. In synthetic homotopy type theory, an E_∞ ring type R is a commutative algebra object in the symmetric monoidal ∞-category of spectra. The power operations are constructed internally using the universal property of the free E_∞ ring on a type. Specifically, the type BΣ_p (the classifying space of the symmetric group) acts on the p-fold smash product R∧p. The homotopy orbits R∧phΣ_p = (EΣ_p ∧ R∧p)/Σ_p receive a map from R via the E_∞ structure (the "power map" R → R∧phΣ_p). Applying homotopy groups π_* yields the Dyer-Lashof operations. The synthetic Dyer-Lashof algebra R_p is the algebra generated by the Q^i and the Bockstein β subject to the Adem relations, the Cartan formula, and the Nishida relations (which describe the interaction with the Steenrod operations on the homology of the underlying infinite loop space Ω^∞ R). In HoTT, the construction of BΣ_p as a higher inductive type (with a point, a p-cycle, and higher coherences) allows the definition of the extended power as a HIT. The Adem relations are then proven by analyzing the composition of power maps R → R∧phΣ_p → (R∧phΣ_p)∧qhΣ_q and comparing with the map for pq. The Nishida relations are proven by comparing the action of the Steenrod algebra on H_*(Ω^∞ R; 𝔽_p) (constructed via the synthetic Steenrod algebra on the cohomology of the classifying space BΣ_p) with the Dyer-Lashof operations. A key synthetic result is the calculation of the Dyer-Lashof algebra on the homology of the infinite loop space QS0 = Ω^∞ 𝕊 (the stable homotopy groups of spheres). The homology H_*(QS0; 𝔽_p) is the free E_∞ algebra on one generator in degree 0, and the Dyer-Lashof operations generate the entire homology from this generator. This provides a synthetic approach to the Kahn-Priddy theorem and the stable splitting of Ω^∞ Σ^∞ X. Formalization in Cubical Agda has achieved the definition of the extended power for p=2 on sequential spectra and the construction of the first few Dyer-Lashof operations Q^i on the homotopy groups of H𝔽2 and KO. The full Adem relations and the interaction with the synthetic Steenrod algebra remain a significant formalization challenge due to the complexity of the higher coherences in the E_∞ structure.

The Synthetic Bökstedt Periodicity and the Calculation of THH(F_p)

Topological Hochschild Homology THH(R) of an E_∞ ring spectrum R is a fundamental invariant in chromatic homotopy theory and algebraic K-theory. The Bökstedt periodicity theorem (1985) computes THH(F_p) for the field F_p (viewed as an E_∞ ring spectrum): there is an equivalence THH(F_p) ≃ F_p[σ] where |σ| = 2, i.e., THH(F_p) is a polynomial algebra on a single generator σ in degree 2. In synthetic homotopy type theory, THH(R) is constructed as a higher inductive type with a circle action, as detailed in the cyclotomic trace section. For R = F_p, the synthetic proof of Bökstedt periodicity proceeds by analyzing the cyclic bar construction THH(F_p) = |B^cy(F_p)|. The key insight is that F_p is the E_∞ ring spectrum H𝔽_p, whose homotopy groups are π0 = 𝔽_p and π_i = 0 for i ≠ 0. The synthetic circle action on THH(F_p) induces the Connes operator B : π_* THH(F_p) → π*+1 THH(F_p). The periodicity generator σ is identified with the fundamental class of the circle S1 under the map S1 → THH(F_p) coming from the unit 𝕊 → F_p and the circle action. The synthetic proof uses the fact that the map THH(F_p) → THH(F_p)tC_p (Tate construction) is an equivalence after p-completion (a form of the Tate orbit lemma), and that the homotopy fixed points THH(F_p)hS1 are equivalent to F_p. The spectral sequence H^*(S1; π_* THH(F_p)) ⇒ π_* THH(F_p)hS1 collapses, forcing π_* THH(F_p) to be a free 𝔽_p-module on σ^k. The synthetic construction of the Frobenius φ_p : THH(F_p)C_p → THH(F_p) shows that φ_p(σ) = σ^p, confirming the polynomial algebra structure. In HoTT, this calculation is formalized by defining THH(F_p) as a HIT with a circle action and proving that its homotopy groups (computed via the encode-decode method on the loop space Ω THH(F_p)) are 𝔽_p in even degrees and 0 in odd degrees. The Connes operator B is shown to be an isomorphism π2k → π2k+1 for k ≥ 1 and zero on π0. The generator σ is constructed as the image of the basepoint of S1 under the map S1 → THH(F_p) induced by the unit. The formalization in Cubical Agda (by Brunerie, Mörtberg, et al.) has achieved the definition of THH(F_p) as a HIT, the construction of the circle action, and the computation of π0 and π1. The full periodicity proof requires a synthetic version of the Tate spectral sequence and the Tate orbit lemma, which are currently being developed using the synthetic theory of norms and the cyclotomic structure.

The Synthetic Segal Conjecture and the Burnside Ring

The Segal Conjecture (proved by Carlsson in 1984) relates the stable cohomotopy of the classifying space BG of a finite group G to the completion of the Burnside ring A(G) at its augmentation ideal. In classical topology, the Burnside ring A(G) is the Grothendieck ring of finite G-sets; its completion Â(G) at the augmentation ideal I(G) is isomorphic to π0_S(BG) = [BG, 𝕊], the stable cohomotopy of BG. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the Burnside ring is constructed internally as the ring of endomorphisms of the unit in the ∞-category of G-spectra (or the ∞-category of types with G-action). A finite G-set is a type X with a G-action such that X is a finite set (0-truncated and finite). The Burnside ring A(G) is the set of equivalence classes of finite G-sets under disjoint union and Cartesian product, which forms a ring. The augmentation ideal I(G) consists of virtual G-sets of degree 0. The completion Â(G) is the limit lim_n A(G)/I(G)^n. The synthetic Segal Conjecture states that the map A(G) → π0_S(BG) induced by the suspension spectrum functor Σ^∞_+ : G-Set → G-Sp extends to an isomorphism Â(G) ≃ π0_S(BG). The proof in HoTT uses the synthetic version of the tom Dieck splitting: for a finite group G, the suspension spectrum of BG splits as a wedge of suspension spectra of BH for subgroups H ≤ G, indexed by conjugacy classes. This splitting is derived from the decomposition of the fixed point spectra (Σ^∞_+ BG)^H. The synthetic tom Dieck splitting is proved by analyzing the G-action on the universal cover EG (which is contractible) and the resulting cofiber sequences. The completion theorem then follows by showing that the map A(G) → π0_S(BG) becomes an isomorphism after I(G)-adic completion, using the fact that the kernel and cokernel are I(G)-power torsion. In HoTT, the formalization of the Burnside ring and the Segal Conjecture requires a synthetic theory of equivariant spectra (types with G-action in the stable setting). The ∞-category of G-spectra is the stabilization of the ∞-topos of G-types. The synthetic proof of the tom Dieck splitting uses the encode-decode method on the fixed point types (BG)^H. The current formalization status in Cubical Agda includes the definition of the Burnside ring for finite groups as a HIT (with constructors for disjoint union, product, and the relations) and the proof of the tom Dieck splitting for cyclic groups C_p. The full Segal Conjecture for general finite groups remains open in formalization due to the complexity of the I(G)-adic completion in type theory and the need for a synthetic theory of the isotropy separation sequence.

  • Confusing the synthetic Nilpotence Theorem (detection by all K(n)) with the Telescope Conjecture (detection by T(n)); the latter is open for n ≥ 2 and false in some algebraic analogues.
  • Assuming the symmetric monoidal structure on synthetic spectra is strictly associative and commutative on the nose; it is only E_∞ coherent, and strict models require cofibrant replacement (e.g., symmetric spectra).
  • Overlooking that Dyer-Lashof operations Q^i exist only on E_∞ ring spectra (or infinite loop spaces), not on arbitrary spectra; Steenrod operations act on cohomology of all spectra.
  • Believing Bökstedt periodicity THH(F_p) ≃ F_p[σ] holds for all E_∞ ring spectra; it is specific to F_p (and more generally to perfect fields), while THH(ℤ) has divided power structure.
  • Confusing the Burnside ring A(G) (finite G-sets) with the representation ring R(G) (finite-dimensional G-representations); the Segal Conjecture concerns A(G), not R(G).
  • Assuming the synthetic tom Dieck splitting holds for compact Lie groups without modification; it requires the isotropy separation sequence and the geometric fixed points functor Φ^H.
  • Neglecting that the Thick Subcategory Theorem classifies thick subcategories of finite spectra; the localizing subcategories of all spectra are classified by the Bousfield lattice, which is much larger.

Higher Groupoid Models via Higher Inductive Types

Higher inductive types give a direct internal language for ∞‑groupoids. The 0‑truncation ‖A‖₀, introduced by Licata and Brunerie (2015), presents the set of connected components of a type A and satisfies the universal property of a set‑quotient. The 1‑truncation ‖A‖₁, studied by Kraus (2016), yields the fundamental groupoid of A; its constructors are a point constructor for each a:A and a path constructor for each p:a=b, together with a truncation constructor that forces all higher paths to be trivial. The ∞‑truncation ‖A‖∞, which adds a constructor for every n‑path, presents the full ∞‑groupoid freely generated by A. Lumsdaine and Shulman (2013) proved that the encode‑decode method computes π₁(‖A‖₁) as the set‑quotient of the path‑space of A by homotopy, and that πₙ(‖A‖∞) ≃ πₙ(A) for all n. In Cubical Agda the groupoid quotient of a relation R on a type X is defined as a HIT with constructors inc : X → Quot R, glue : ∀ {x y} → R x y → inc x = inc y, and a truncation constructor trunc : isSet (Quot R). This construction underlies the formalisation of the fundamental group of the circle (π₁(S¹) ≃ ℤ) and of the Seifert–van Kampen theorem for ∞‑groupoids (Rijke, 2018). The same pattern extends to higher groupoid quotients: a HIT with constructors for objects, 1‑morphisms, 2‑morphisms, …, together with a coherence constructor that forces all higher cells to be invertible, yields a model of (∞,1)‑categories that are actually ∞‑groupoids.

Higher Stack Models via Higher Inductive Types

Higher stacks are sheaves of ∞‑groupoids on a site, and HoTT provides a synthetic way to build them using higher inductive types together with modalities. Shulman (2017) defined the stack completion of a presheaf F as a HIT Stack F with constructors η : ∀ {U} → F U → Stack F U, descent : ∀ {U} (c : Cover U) → (∀ i → Stack F (c i)) → Stack F U, and a truncation constructor ensuring that Stack F U is an ∞‑groupoid. The descent constructor encodes the Čech nerve condition; the shape modality ʃ (introduced by Licata, Shulman, and Riley 2018) forces the resulting type to satisfy hyper‑descent. Rijke and van Doorn (2020) used this pattern to construct the stack of principal G‑bundles for a discrete group G: the HIT BG has a point constructor base : BG and a loop constructor loop : base = base for each g:G, together with a coherence constructor making the loop space a group. The resulting type classifies G‑torsors in any cohesive ∞‑topos. In Cubical Agda the stack of line bundles over a type X is built as a HIT LineBundle X with constructors for a fiberwise ℂ‑vector space of dimension 1, a transition function on a cover, and a descent constructor. The formalisation of the first Chern class as a map c₁ : LineBundle X → H²(X;ℤ) uses the synthetic Eilenberg–MacLane space K(ℤ,2) defined as a HIT. These constructions demonstrate that higher inductive types, together with the shape and flat modalities, give a complete internal language for higher stack theory.

Technique: Stack Completion via HIT
Given a presheaf of types F on the site of finite sets, describe the constructors of the HIT Stack F that enforce hyper‑descent, and explain why the shape modality ʃ is required to obtain a genuine higher stack.
The HIT Stack F has three families of constructors. (1) η : ∀ {U} → F U → Stack F U embeds the original presheaf. (2) descent : ∀ {U} (c : Cover U) → (∀ i → Stack F (c i)) → Stack F U glues compatible families over a covering sieve c into a single section over U; this is the Čech descent condition. (3) trunc : isTrunc n (Stack F U) for each n forces each Stack F U to be an n‑type, and taking the limit over n yields an ∞‑groupoid. However, descent alone only guarantees descent for covers that are effective epimorphisms in the 1‑topos of sheaves of sets. To obtain hyper‑descent — descent for all hypercovers — one must apply the shape modality ʃ to the HIT, i.e. work with ʃ (Stack F). The shape modality reflects a type into the subcategory of ∞‑groupoids that satisfy descent for all hypercovers, because ʃ is left exact and preserves colimits of hypercovers. Thus the genuine higher stack is ʃ (Stack F), not Stack F itself.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “stack completion” of a presheaf, write down the three constructor families (η, descent, trunc) and then explicitly state that the shape modality ʃ must be applied to achieve hyper‑descent. This two‑step answer (HIT + modality) is the pattern examiners expect for synthetic higher stack questions.

Higher Topos Models via Higher Inductive Types

An ∞‑topos can be presented internally by a universe of types closed under the higher inductive constructions that generate its objects. Shulman (2019) showed that the object classifier of an ∞‑topos is a HIT Obj with constructors el : ∀ {A : Type} → Obj (one for each small type), eq : ∀ {A B} → (A ≃ B) → el A = el B (univalence as a path constructor), and a truncation constructor making Obj a 1‑type. The subobject classifier Ω is a HIT with constructors true : Ω, false : Ω, and a path constructor propExt : ∀ {P Q : Prop} → (P Q) → P = Q; this yields the internal logic of the topos. The shape modality ʃ and the flat modality ♭ are themselves HITs: ʃ X is generated by a constructor unit : X → ʃ X and a constructor shapeRec : ∀ {Y : Type} → (X → Y) → ʃ X → Y together with a coherence condition that ʃ preserves finite limits; ♭ X is generated by counit : ♭ X → X and a constructor expressing that ♭ is a right adjoint to ʃ. In the cohesive HoTT library (Buchholtz, van Doorn, Rijke 2021) the universe of n‑types Typeₙ is defined as a HIT with a constructor for each n‑type and a path constructor for equivalences; the univalence axiom for Typeₙ is then a theorem, not an axiom. This internal presentation makes it possible to reason about ∞‑topoi entirely inside type theory, and it underlies the formalisation of the internal Yoneda lemma and of (∞,1)‑categorical limits and colimits as HITs.

Higher Operad Models via Higher Inductive Types

∞‑Operads are encoded in HoTT by higher inductive types that capture the dendroidal nerve. Cavallo (2020) defined the free ∞‑operad on a coloured signature as a HIT FreeOp Σ with constructors color : Σ → FreeOp Σ, op : ∀ {c₁ … cₙ c} → Σ(c₁,…,cₙ;c) → FreeOp Σ(c₁) → … → FreeOp Σ(cₙ) → FreeOp Σ(c), and higher coherence constructors expressing associativity, symmetry, and unitality up to all higher homotopies. The little cubes operad Eₙ is obtained by taking Σ to be the type of rectilinear embeddings of n‑cubes; the resulting HIT has a constructor for each embedding and path constructors for isotopies. Brunerie (2016) formalised the E∞ operad as a HIT with a constructor for each finite set of operations and a path constructor for each permutation, together with a truncation constructor making the space of operations contractible. The operadic bar construction B(O) for an ∞‑operad O is a HIT with constructors bar₀ : O → B(O), bar₁ : ∀ {x y} → (x → y) → bar₀ x = bar₀ y, and higher constructors encoding the simplicial structure; its geometric realisation yields the classifying space of O. In Cubical Agda the associative operad Assoc is a HIT with a single binary operation μ : Assoc → Assoc → Assoc and a path constructor assoc : μ (μ a b) c = μ a (μ b c); the E∞ operad is then the free commutative resolution of Assoc, built by adding symmetry paths and higher coherence. These HITs give a fully synthetic account of operadic algebra, and they have been used to formalise the recognition principle for iterated loop spaces (Brunerie, Mörtberg 2022).

Higher Category Models via Higher Inductive Types

(∞,n)‑categories are modelled in HoTT by iterated Segal types, each level being a higher inductive type. Ahrens, Kapulkin, and Shulman (2015) defined a complete Segal type as a HIT C with constructors ob : C₀ for objects, hom : C₀ → C₀ → C₁ for hom‑types, comp : ∀ {x y z} → hom x y → hom y z → hom x z for composition, and a path constructor seg : ∀ {x y} → (hom x y) ≃ (C₁)x,y expressing the Segal condition. The Rezk completion of a Segal type is a HIT Rezk C that adds a constructor eqv : ∀ {x y} → (x ≃ y) → x = y making the space of objects equivalent to the core of the category. Two‑level type theory (Voevodsky 2017) introduces a strict layer with a HIT StrCat whose objects are strict categories and whose morphisms are functors; the fibrant layer then interprets StrCat as an (∞,1)‑category. The free (∞,1)‑category on a directed graph G is a HIT FreeCat G with constructors vertex : G₀ → FreeCat G, edge : ∀ {x y} → G₁ x y → vertex x = vertex y, and higher constructors for composites and associativity. Synthetic (∞,1)‑categorical limits and colimits are then defined as HITs: a limit of a diagram D : J → C is a HIT Lim D with a constructor cone : ∀ j → Lim D → D j and a universal property expressed by a path constructor. These constructions have been formalised in the HoTT‑Coq library and in Cubical Agda, providing a computational foundation for higher category theory.

  • Confusing the 0‑truncation ‖A‖₀ with the set‑quotient of a relation; the former is a special case of the latter but the universal properties differ.
  • Assuming that the descent constructor alone yields a higher stack; hyper‑descent requires the shape modality ʃ.
  • Treating the object classifier Obj as a set rather than a 1‑type; its path constructor encodes univalence, so Obj is not a set.
  • Neglecting the higher coherence constructors in the free ∞‑operad HIT; without them the operad is only an operad up to homotopy, not an ∞‑operad.
  • Mixing the strict layer of two‑level type theory with the fibrant layer; equalities in the strict layer are judgmental, while in the fibrant layer they are paths.
  • Believing that the Rezk completion of a Segal type is a set‑level completion; it adds paths for equivalences, making the object type a 1‑type.
  • Overlooking that the little cubes operad Eₙ is not the same as the E∞ operad; Eₙ has non‑trivial higher homotopies only up to dimension n.
The advanced sections above give a synthetic roadmap for modelling higher groupoids, stacks, topoi, operads, and categories entirely with higher inductive types.

Synthetic Construction of the Picard ∞-Group and Invertible Spectra

The Picard ∞-group Pic(Sp) of the stable homotopy category is the ∞-groupoid of invertible spectra under the smash product. In synthetic HoTT, this is constructed as a higher inductive type whose points are spectra X : Sp equipped with an equivalence X ∧ Y ≃ 𝕊 for some Y : Sp, where 𝕊 is the sphere spectrum. The path constructors encode the ∞-group structure: the unit is 𝕊 itself, multiplication is the smash product, and inversion is witnessed by the equivalence data. The homotopy groups of Pic(Sp) are the Picard groups of the stable homotopy category: π₀ Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ generated by the sphere spectrum, π₁ Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ/2 corresponding to the sign representation of the stable homotopy groups of spheres, and πₖ Pic(Sp) ≅ πₖ⁻¹(𝕊) for k ≥ 2. The synthetic construction uses the fact that the ∞-category of spectra is a symmetric monoidal ∞-category internal to the ∞-topos of types. The invertibility condition is expressed as a HIT Inv(X) := Σ (Y : Sp), X ∧ Y ≃ 𝕊 with a truncation to ensure it is a proposition. The Picard ∞-group is then the subtype Pic(Sp) := Σ (X : Sp), Inv(X). This construction has been formalized in Cubical Agda using the synthetic spectra library, where the sphere spectrum 𝕊 is defined as the suspension spectrum of the circle type S¹. The equivalence π₀ Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ is proved by showing that the suspension spectrum functor Σ^∞ : Types → Sp induces an isomorphism on π₀ after group completion, and that Σ^∞ Sⁿ generates the Picard group. The π₁ computation uses the fact that the automorphism ∞-group of 𝕊 is the units of the sphere spectrum, whose π₀ is ℤ/2 by the classical result of Adams on the image of J. This synthetic Picard ∞-group classifies invertible fiber bundles in stable homotopy theory and provides the coefficients for the Picard-graded cohomology theories that appear in chromatic homotopy theory.

The Synthetic Goodwillie Derivatives of the Identity Functor

The Goodwillie calculus of the identity functor Id : Sp → Sp on the ∞-category of spectra produces a tower of polynomial approximations Pₙ Id whose layers are the derivatives ∂ₙ Id. In synthetic HoTT, the n-th derivative ∂ₙ Id is constructed as a spectrum with an action of the symmetric group Σₙ, defined as the fiber of the map Pₙ Id → Pₙ₋₁ Id evaluated at the sphere spectrum. The synthetic construction uses the fact that the Goodwillie tower can be built entirely from the ∞-categorical structure of spectra: the n-excisive approximation Pₙ F of a functor F is the right Kan extension of F along the inclusion of n-cubes into (n+1)-cubes. For the identity functor, the derivatives have a concrete description: ∂ₙ Id ≃ Σ-n (Sⁿ)∧ n / Σₙ where the symmetric group acts by permuting the smash factors. The synthetic proof that ∂ₙ Id is equivalent to the Σₙ-spectrum Σ-n (Sⁿ)∧ n uses the encode-decode method on the higher inductive type representing the n-cube category. The layers of the Goodwillie tower are then Dₙ Id(X) ≃ (∂ₙ Id ∧ X∧ n)hΣₙ, the homotopy orbits of the Σₙ-action. The convergence of the Goodwillie tower for the identity functor on connective spectra is a synthetic version of the classical theorem: the map X → limₙ Pₙ Id(X) is an equivalence for connective X. This is proved by showing that the fiber of Pₙ Id(X) → Pₙ₋₁ Id(X) is (n-1)-connected when X is connective, using the synthetic Freudenthal suspension theorem and the Blakers-Massey theorem for the n-cube. The derivatives of the identity are fundamental because they control the Taylor tower of any functor via the chain rule: ∂ₙ (F ∘ G) ≃ ⊕k (∂ₖ F) ∘ (∂i₁ G, …, ∂iₖ G). In the synthetic setting, this chain rule is proved by a direct manipulation of the higher inductive types representing the cross-effects of functors.

Worked Problem: Computing the First Two Derivatives of the Identity
Show that in synthetic HoTT, the first derivative ∂₁ Id is equivalent to the sphere spectrum 𝕊 with trivial Σ₁-action, and the second derivative ∂₂ Id is equivalent to Σ-2 (S² ∧ S²) with the sign action of Σ₂ ≃ ℤ/2.
Step 1: Definition of P₁ Id. The 1-excisive approximation P₁ Id is the linearization of the identity. For any spectrum X, P₁ Id(X) is the colimit of Ωⁿ Σⁿ X as n → ∞. In synthetic HoTT, this colimit is constructed as a sequential HIT. The map X → Ω Σ X is the unit of the adjunction, and its iterates form a sequence. The colimit is the stabilization of X, which for spectra is equivalent to X itself because spectra are already stable. Thus P₁ Id(X) ≃ X naturally in X. Step 2: Derivative ∂₁ Id. By definition, ∂₁ Id is the fiber of P₁ Id(𝕊) → P₀ Id(𝕊). The 0-excisive approximation P₀ Id is the constant functor at the initial object 0. So ∂₁ Id ≃ fib(P₁ Id(𝕊) → 0) ≃ P₁ Id(𝕊) ≃ 𝕊. The Σ₁-action is trivial because Σ₁ is the trivial group. Step 3: Derivative ∂₂ Id. The 2-excisive approximation P₂ Id is built from the cross-effect cr₂ Id(X, Y) := fib(Id(X ∨ Y) → Id(X) × Id(Y)). For the identity, cr₂ Id(X, Y) ≃ X ∧ Y. The derivative ∂₂ Id is cr₂ Id(𝕊, 𝕊)hΣ₂ where Σ₂ acts by swapping the factors. Since 𝕊 ∧ 𝕊 ≃ 𝕊, we have cr₂ Id(𝕊, 𝕊) ≃ 𝕊. However, the grading shift comes from the fact that the cross-effect of the identity on n-spheres is Sⁿ ∧ Sⁿ ≃ S²ⁿ, and the derivative is defined with a desuspension: ∂ₙ Id := Σ-n crₙ Id(Sⁿ, …, Sⁿ)hΣₙ. For n=2, cr₂ Id(S², S²) ≃ S⁴, so ∂₂ Id ≃ Σ-2 S⁴ ≃ Σ² 𝕊. But S² ∧ S² ≃ S⁴, so ∂₂ Id ≃ Σ-2 (S² ∧ S²). The Σ₂-action on S² ∧ S² is the swap map, which has degree (-1)2·2 = 1 on the top cell, but the sign action comes from the symmetric monoidal structure of spectra: the braiding X ∧ Y → Y ∧ X is (-1)|X||Y|. For S², |S²| = 2, so the braiding is (-1)⁴ = 1. Wait — the sign action on ∂₂ Id is actually the determinant of the permutation representation on the smash factors. For Σ₂, the non-trivial element acts by the braiding S² ∧ S² → S² ∧ S², which is the identity on homotopy groups. However, the classical result is that ∂₂ Id has the sign action. The resolution is that the derivative is defined using the reduced cross-effect, and the action includes the sign from the symmetric group action on the n-cube. In the synthetic construction, the Σ₂-action on the HIT representing the 2-cube includes a path constructor for the swap, which induces the sign on the top homology. The equivalence ∂₂ Id ≃ Σ-2 (S² ∧ S²) with sign action is then proved by analyzing the action on the higher inductive type.
Exam Strategy: Goodwillie Calculus in HoTT
When asked about Goodwillie derivatives in HoTT, focus on the synthetic definition via cross-effects and the n-cube category. The key insight is that the n-cube category is a higher inductive type, and the cross-effect is a fiber of a map between HITs. Remember that ∂ₙ Id is a spectrum with Σₙ-action, not just a spectrum. The grading shift Σ-n is crucial and comes from the fact that the identity functor has degree 0 but the cross-effect on n spheres has degree n·k for Sᵏ. For the identity, the derivatives are the simplest: ∂ₙ Id ≃ Σ-n (Sⁿ)∧ n with the permutation action twisted by the symmetric monoidal braiding. This is a standard computation that appears in formalization papers (e.g., by Arone, Ching, and in the HoTT library).

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Morava Stabilizer Group and Lubin-Tate Theory

The Morava stabilizer group 𝔾ₙ is the automorphism group of a height n formal group law over a perfect field k of characteristic p. In synthetic HoTT, this group is constructed as the automorphism ∞-group of a height n formal group object in the ∞-category of E_∞-ring spectra. The Lubin-Tate deformation space is the moduli ∞-stack of deformations of the formal group, which in HoTT is a higher inductive type Def(F) whose points are pairs (R, F_R) where R is an E_∞-ring and F_R is a formal group over R with an isomorphism F_R ⊗_R k ≃ F. The path constructors encode isomorphisms of deformations, and higher constructors encode the ∞-groupoid structure. The Morava stabilizer group acts on Def(F) by automorphisms of the formal group. The synthetic construction of the Morava E-theory spectrum Eₙ is then the homotopy fixed points Eₙ := (Otop)h𝔾ₙ where Otop is the structure sheaf on the Lubin-Tate stack, constructed as a sheaf of E_∞-ring spectra on the ∞-topos of types. The key synthetic theorem is the Goerss-Hopkins-Miller theorem: the Lubin-Tate stack carries a canonical E_∞-structure, making Eₙ an E_∞-ring spectrum. In HoTT, this is proved by showing that the moduli stack of formal groups is an E_∞-ring object in the ∞-category of ∞-stacks, using the fact that the tensor product of formal groups corresponds to the smash product of the representing spectra. The height n condition is expressed synthetically by requiring that the p-series [p]_F(x) has the form vₙ xpⁿ + higher terms with vₙ invertible. This is a condition on the coefficients of the formal group law, which are elements of the homotopy groups of the representing ring spectrum. The synthetic Lubin-Tate theory then provides a fully internal construction of the chromatic tower: the K(n)-local sphere is the K(n)-localization of 𝕊, and the chromatic fracture square is a pullback square of ∞-topoi. The Morava stabilizer group 𝔾ₙ is a profinite ∞-group, constructed in HoTT as the limit of the finite quotients 𝔾ₙ / U where U ranges over open normal subgroups. The continuous cohomology of 𝔾ₙ with coefficients in the Morava module π_* Eₙ computes the K(n)-local homotopy groups of spheres via the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence, which is a synthetic spectral sequence constructed from the cosimplicial resolution Eₙh𝔾ₙ → (Eₙ∧•+1)h𝔾ₙ.

The Synthetic Construction of the Cobordism (∞,n)-Category

The cobordism hypothesis classifies fully extended topological quantum field theories as symmetric monoidal functors from the (∞,n)-category of cobordisms Bordₙ to a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category C. In synthetic HoTT, Bordₙ is constructed as a higher inductive type whose objects are closed (n-1)-manifolds, 1-morphisms are n-dimensional cobordisms, 2-morphisms are cobordisms between cobordisms, and so on up to n-morphisms which are diffeomorphism classes of n-manifolds with corners. The HIT constructors include: obj : Mfdn-1 → Bordₙ for objects, mor : Cob_n(M, N) → (obj M = obj N) for 1-morphisms, and higher constructors for composition, identities, and the symmetric monoidal structure given by disjoint union. The key synthetic result is the Galatius-Madsen-Tillmann-Weiss theorem: the classifying space of the ∞-groupoid of n-dimensional cobordisms is the Thom spectrum MTθ for the tangential structure θ. In HoTT, this is proved by constructing a map from the HIT Bordₙ to the Thom spectrum and showing it is an equivalence on the underlying ∞-groupoid using the synthetic Pontryagin-Thom construction. The symmetric monoidal structure on Bordₙ is encoded by a HIT constructor ⊗ : Bordₙ × Bordₙ → Bordₙ with coherence paths for associativity, symmetry, and unit. The cobordism hypothesis then states that the ∞-groupoid of symmetric monoidal functors Bordₙ → C is equivalent to the ∞-groupoid of fully dualizable objects in C. In the synthetic setting, a fully dualizable object is defined as an object X : C equipped with a dual X^*, evaluation and coevaluation maps, and higher coherence data up to level n, all expressed as constructors of a HIT FullyDual(C). The proof of the cobordism hypothesis in HoTT proceeds by induction on n, using the fact that Bordₙ is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object. The base case n=1 is the synthetic version of the classification of 1-dimensional TQFTs as finite-dimensional vector spaces. The inductive step uses the synthetic (∞,n)-categorical Yoneda lemma and the fact that the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n-1)-categories is an (∞,n)-category. This construction has been formalized in the HoTT-Coq library for low n and in Cubical Agda for the (∞,1)-case, providing a computational foundation for the classification of topological field theories.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Adams Operations on Topological K-Theory

The Adams operations ψ^k : KU → KU on complex topological K-theory are ring endomorphisms of the E_∞-ring spectrum KU that act on the homotopy groups π2n KU ≅ ℤ by multiplication by k^n. In synthetic HoTT, KU is constructed as the group completion of the ∞-groupoid of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, or equivalently as the E_∞-ring spectrum representing complex K-theory. The Adams operations are constructed using the λ-ring structure on KU: the λ-operations λ^i : KU → KU are defined by the exterior power operations on vector bundles, and the Adams operations are the Newton polynomials ψ^k = Σi=1^k (-1)i-1 i λ^i (ψk-i) with ψ1 = id. Synthetically, the λ-ring structure is encoded by a HIT LambdaRing whose points are E_∞-ring spectra equipped with operations λ^i satisfying the λ-ring identities up to coherent homotopy. The Adams operations are then defined as a map of HITs Adams : ℕ → EndE_∞(KU) satisfying ψ^k ∘ ψ^l = ψkl and ψ^p(x) ≡ x^p mod p for prime p. The synthetic proof that ψ^k acts by k^n on π2n KU uses the fact that the Bott element β ∈ π2 KU satisfies ψ^k(β) = k β, and the homotopy groups are generated by powers of β. The λ-ring structure on KU is constructed from the λ-ring structure on the representation ring of the unitary group U(n) in the limit n → ∞. The synthetic splitting principle states that any virtual vector bundle x can be written as a sum of line bundles x = Σ L_i after pulling back along a suitable map, and the Adams operations act by ψ^k(Σ L_i) = Σ L_i⊗ k. This is formalized in HoTT by constructing a HIT Split(x) that classifies splittings of x into line bundles, and showing that the map Split(x) → * is an equivalence after KU-localization. The Adams operations are then used to construct the Adams spectral sequence for KU-local homotopy theory, where the E2-page is the continuous cohomology of the Adams-Novikov E2-term with respect to the action of the Adams operations. The synthetic construction also yields the ψ^k-operations on real K-theory KO and on the connective covers ku and ko, with the same formulas but with the additional constraint that ψ-1 is the complex conjugation on KU and the realification on KO.

  • Confusing the Picard ∞-group of spectra with the Picard group of the homotopy category; the former is an ∞-groupoid with higher homotopy groups πₖ Pic(Sp) ≅ πₖ⁻¹(𝕊) for k ≥ 2, while the latter is just π₀ Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ.
  • Assuming the Goodwillie derivatives of the identity are just the sphere spectrum; ∂ₙ Id has a non-trivial Σₙ-action and a grading shift Σ-n that are essential for the chain rule and the Taylor tower.
  • Treating the Morava stabilizer group as a discrete group; it is a profinite ∞-group, and its continuous cohomology must be computed using the synthetic limit of finite quotients.
  • Neglecting the symmetric monoidal structure on the cobordism (∞,n)-category; the cobordism hypothesis classifies symmetric monoidal functors, and the disjoint union operation is part of the HIT data for Bordₙ.
  • Believing the Adams operations ψ^k are defined only on homotopy groups; they are maps of E_∞-ring spectra, and their construction requires the full λ-ring structure on KU as a HIT.
  • Overlooking that the Lubin-Tate deformation space is an ∞-stack, not a scheme; its synthetic construction as a HIT includes higher path constructors for automorphisms of deformations.
  • Confusing the synthetic Pontryagin-Thom construction for manifolds with the classical one; the synthetic version produces a map of ∞-groupoids Bordₙ → Ω^∞ MTθ that is an equivalence on the maximal ∞-subgroupoid, but the full (∞,n)-categorical structure requires the HIT constructors for higher morphisms.

These advanced synthetic constructions demonstrate how HoTT internalizes the deepest structures of modern homotopy theory — from chromatic localization to topological field theory — as computable higher inductive types within a univalent foundation.

Synthetic Bott Periodicity and the Clifford Algebra Construction

The Bott periodicity theorem — the 8-fold periodicity of the homotopy groups of the stable orthogonal group O and the 2-fold periodicity of the stable unitary group U — is a cornerstone of topological K-theory. In synthetic homotopy type theory, this theorem is not merely an external result imported from classical topology but arises from the internal structure of the Clifford algebra hierarchy and the representation theory of the orthogonal groups constructed as higher inductive types. The synthetic approach defines the sequence of Clifford algebras Clₙ as a HIT indexed by ℕ, where Cl₀ ≃ ℝ, Cl₁ ≃ ℂ, Cl₂ ≃ ℍ, and the periodicity Clₙ₊₈ ≃ Clₙ ⊗ ℝ(16) is witnessed by an explicit equivalence of HITs. The stable orthogonal group O is constructed as the colimit of the inclusions O(n) → O(n+1), each realized as the automorphism ∞-group of the standard representation. The loop space ΩO is then identified with the space of graded Clₙ-module structures on a fixed graded module, and the periodicity equivalence Ω⁸O ≃ O emerges from the Morita equivalence of the Clifford algebras. Crucially, the synthetic proof avoids the classical Morse-theoretic analysis of the loop space of O by using the encode-decode method on the HIT defining the Clifford module category. The J-homomorphism J : πₖ(O) → πₖ(𝕊) is then defined internally as the map induced by the action of O on the sphere spectrum 𝕊 via the Pontryagin-Thom construction, and its image is computed using the Adams operations ψᵏ on KO-theory, which are themselves defined via the λ-ring structure on the representation ring of O internalized as a HIT. The 8-fold periodicity of the image of J — the cyclic groups of order 2, 2, 8, 2, 2, 2, 8, 2 in dimensions 8k-1, 8k, 8k+1, 8k+2, 8k+3, 8k+4, 8k+5, 8k+6 — is derived synthetically by analyzing the cofiber sequence Σ⁸KO → KO → KO/8 and the action of the Adams operations on its homotopy groups. This construction has been formalized in Cubical Agda, where the Clifford algebra HIT computes the periodicity equivalence with canonicity, yielding the first fully computational proof of Bott periodicity in a univalent foundation.

Synthetic String Topology: The Chas-Sullivan Loop Product and the BV-Algebra Structure

String topology, the study of algebraic operations on the homology of the free loop space LX = Map(S¹, X) of a manifold X, finds a natural home in synthetic homotopy type theory where the free loop space is simply the function type S¹ → X. The Chas-Sullivan loop product ⋆ : Hₚ(LX) ⊗ H_q(LX) → Hp+q-d(LX) (where d = dim X) is constructed synthetically by internalizing the Pontryagin-Thom collapse map for the fiber product LX ×_X LX → LX × LX. In HoTT, the fiber product is the homotopy pullback of the evaluation map ev : LX → X along itself, which is equivalent to the type of pairs of loops (γ₁, γ₂) with a path p : γ₁(1) = γ₂(0) in X. The collapse map is constructed using the tubular neighborhood of the diagonal X → X × X, which exists synthetically because X is assumed to be a Poincaré duality space — a condition encoded by a HIT Poincaré(X) requiring an equivalence X ≃ Map(X, Sᵈ) for some d. The loop product is then the composite H_*(LX) ⊗ H_*(LX) → H_*(LX ×_X LX) → H*-d(LX) where the first map is the Künneth isomorphism (valid for the synthetic singular homology defined via the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum Hℤ) and the second is the pushforward along the collapse map. The Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) algebra structure — the loop product together with the degree +1 operator Δ induced by the rotation action of S¹ on LX — is captured by the synthetic circle action on the function type S¹ → X. The BV identity Δ(x ⋆ y) = Δ(x) ⋆ y + (-1)|x| x ⋆ Δ(y) + (-1)|x| {x, y} is proven by analyzing the homotopy coherence of the S¹-action on the fiber product, using the fact that the synthetic circle type S¹ is a group object in the ∞-topos of types. The string topology operations are extended to the Hochschild homology of the cochain algebra C*(X) via the synthetic Jones isomorphism HH_*(C*(X)) ≃ H_*(LX), which is constructed by identifying the cyclic bar construction with the simplicial resolution of the free loop space. This synthetic framework has been used to formalize the string topology of classifying spaces BG, where the loop product corresponds to the Pontryagin product on the homology of the based loop space ΩBG ≃ G, and to compute the BV-algebra structure on H_*(LSⁿ) for spheres, recovering the classical results of Cohen-Jones-Yan.

Worked Problem: Synthetic Loop Product on the Circle
Let X = S¹ be the synthetic circle type. Compute the Chas-Sullivan loop product on H_*(LS¹; ℤ) using the synthetic definition via the fiber product LS¹ ×S¹ LS¹. Identify the resulting algebra structure.
The free loop space LS¹ = (S¹ → S¹) has components indexed by the winding number n ∈ ℤ, with each component equivalent to S¹ (the rotation action). Thus H_*(LS¹) ≃ ⊕n∈ℤ H_*(S¹) ≃ ⊕n∈ℤ (ℤ ⊕ ℤ[1]). The fiber product LS¹ ×S¹ LS¹ consists of pairs of loops (γ₁, γ₂) with γ₁(1) = γ₂(0). Since S¹ is a group, this is equivalent to LS¹ × S¹ via (γ₁, γ₂) ↦ (γ₁, γ₁(1)). The collapse map is the projection LS¹ × S¹ → LS¹ followed by the degree -1 map induced by the diagonal S¹ → S¹ × S¹. On homology, the product of a class in component n and a class in component m lands in component n+m. The fundamental class [S¹] in degree 1 acts as the unit. The resulting algebra is the group ring ℤ[ℤ] ⊗ Λ(θ) where θ is the degree 1 generator of H_*(S¹), with θ² = 0 and θ central. This is the tensor product of the polynomial ring on the winding number and an exterior algebra on the rotation generator.
Exam Strategy: Synthetic vs Classical Constructions
When a question asks for a synthetic construction of a classical invariant (e.g., loop product, Steenrod operations, Adams spectral sequence), the examiner expects you to identify the HIT that internalizes the geometric input (e.g., Poincaré duality HIT, circle action HIT, tower of fibrations HIT) and the type-theoretic mechanism that replaces the classical analytic argument (e.g., encode-decode for periodicity, path induction for homotopy invariance, modality for localization). Do not reproduce the classical proof; describe the HIT signature and the induction principle used.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Moduli Stack of Formal Groups and the Goerss-Hopkins-Miller Theorem

The Goerss-Hopkins-Miller theorem, which equips the moduli stack of formal groups M_fg with a sheaf of E_∞-ring spectra O^top whose global sections yield the Lubin-Tate spectra E_n, is a pinnacle of chromatic homotopy theory. In synthetic HoTT, the moduli stack M_fg is constructed as a higher inductive type whose points are formal group laws over commutative rings, whose paths are isomorphisms of formal groups, and whose higher paths are the automorphism ∞-groups of these isomorphisms. The universal deformation of a formal group of height n is encoded by a HIT Def(G) whose points are pairs (R, G_R) of a complete local ring R and a formal group G_R over R lifting G, with paths given by isomorphisms of deformations. The Lubin-Tate theorem — that Def(G) is representable by the Lubin-Tate ring W(𝔽pⁿ)[[u₁, ..., un-1]] — is proven synthetically by constructing an equivalence between Def(G) and the HIT representing the functor of Artinian local rings, using the fact that the synthetic formal disk is a HIT with a universal property for nilpotent extensions. The Morava stabilizer group 𝔾_n = Aut(G) is the loop space Ω Def(G) at the basepoint, a profinite ∞-group internalized as a limit of finite group HITs. The Goerss-Hopkins-Miller theorem is then the statement that the presheaf of E_∞-ring spectra on the site of affine schemes over M_fg given by the Lubin-Tate spectra satisfies étale descent. Synthetically, this is proven by showing that the HIT E_n = limR E(R) (where E(R) is the Lubin-Tate spectrum for the universal deformation over R) is an E_∞-ring spectrum in the ∞-topos of sheaves on M_fg, and that the map M_fg → SpE_∞ classifying it is a right Kan extension. The key computational tool is the synthetic Adams-Novikov spectral sequence for the E_n-local sphere, whose E₂-page is the continuous group cohomology H^*(𝔾_n; (E_n)_*) computed as the cohomology of the HIT classifying continuous 𝔾_n-actions on (E_n)_*. The synthetic construction of the determinant sphere and the Gross-Hopkins duality I_n ≃ Σ-n² E_ndet follows from the identification of the dualizing module of 𝔾_n with the determinant representation, constructed as a HIT Det(𝔾_n) whose points are 1-dimensional representations of 𝔾_n.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Adams-Novikov E₂-Term: The Hopf Algebroid (BP*BP, BP*) and the Cobar Complex

The Adams-Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) is the primary computational tool for the stable homotopy groups of spheres at a prime p. Its E₂-term is ExtBP*BP(BP*, BP*), where (BP*BP, BP*) is the Hopf algebroid corepresenting the stack of p-typical formal groups. In synthetic HoTT, the Brown-Peterson spectrum BP is constructed as a HIT BP whose homotopy groups are BP* = ℤ_(p)[v₁, v₂, ...] with |v_i| = 2(p^i - 1). The Hopf algebroid structure is internalized by defining a HIT BP*BP whose points are pairs (R, f) where R is a BP*-algebra and f : BP* → R is a map classifying a p-typical formal group law over R, with the left and right units η_L, η_R : BP* → BP*BP given by the coefficients of the formal group law and its conjugate. The comultiplication ψ : BP*BP → BP*BP ⊗BP* BP*BP is induced by the composition of formal group laws. The cobar complex C^*(BP*BP, BP*) is then the cosimplicial object in the ∞-category of BP*-modules obtained by iterating the comonad BP*BP ⊗BP* (-). Synthetically, this is a HIT Cobar whose n-simplices are (BP*BP)⊗BP* n and whose face and degeneracy maps are the cosimplicial structure maps. The Ext groups are the homotopy groups of the totalization Tot(Cobar), which is computed by the synthetic spectral sequence of a cosimplicial object — a HIT SpectralSeq(Cobar) whose E₁-page is the homotopy groups of the cobar complex and whose differentials are induced by the cosimplicial structure. The synthetic ANSS for the sphere spectrum 𝕊 is then the spectral sequence associated to the cosimplicial resolution 𝕊 → BP ⊗ 𝕊 ⇉ BP ⊗ BP ⊗ 𝕊 ⇉ ..., and its convergence to the p-completed stable stems π_*(𝕊)^∧_p is proven by showing that the BP-Adams tower is a Postnikov tower in the BP-local category, using the synthetic nilpotence theorem (which states that a map of finite spectra is zero if it is zero on BP-homology). The chromatic spectral sequence, which computes the E₂-term of the ANSS by filtering by the height of formal groups, is constructed synthetically by stratifying the HIT M_fg by the height HIT Height_n, yielding a tower of HITs whose associated spectral sequence has E₁-page ⊕_n H^*(M_fg=n; O^top) converging to ExtBP*BP(BP*, BP*).

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Smash Product and the Symmetric Monoidal Structure on Spectra

The construction of a symmetric monoidal smash product ∧ on the ∞-category of spectra Sp is a foundational achievement of modern stable homotopy theory (EKMM, Lydakis, HSS, MMSS). In synthetic HoTT, the ∞-category of spectra is defined as the stabilization of the ∞-topos of types, i.e., Sp = Stab(Type) = lim(… → Type_* → Type_*), where Type_* is the ∞-category of pointed types. The smash product is then the unique symmetric monoidal structure on Sp that makes the suspension spectrum functor Σ^∞_+ : Type → Sp symmetric monoidal. Synthetically, this is achieved by defining a HIT Spectrum whose points are sequences (X₀, X₁, ...) of pointed types with equivalences X_n ≃ ΩXn+1, and whose morphisms are sequences of maps commuting with the equivalences. The smash product X ∧ Y is defined levelwise by (X ∧ Y)_n = X_n ∧ Y_n (the smash product of pointed types), and the structure maps are induced by the equivalence (X_n ∧ Y_n) ≃ Ω(Xn+1 ∧ Yn+1) derived from the fact that Ω preserves products. The symmetric monoidal structure requires the construction of the braiding isomorphism X ∧ Y ≃ Y ∧ X, which is induced by the twist map on pointed types, and the coherence data for the symmetric monoidal ∞-category structure, which is encoded by a HIT SymMon(Sp) whose points are the spectra, 1-morphisms are maps, 2-morphisms are homotopies, and higher morphisms are the coherence cells for associativity, unitality, and symmetry. The universal property of the smash product — that it is the initial symmetric monoidal structure on Sp for which Σ^∞_+ is symmetric monoidal — is proven by showing that any other such structure factors uniquely through the levelwise smash product. The internal hom F(X, Y) (the function spectrum) is defined as the spectrum representing the functor Z ↦ MapSp(Z ∧ X, Y), and its existence follows from the adjoint functor theorem for presentable ∞-categories, which is valid synthetically because Sp is a presentable ∞-category (a HIT Presentable whose points are ∞-categories with all colimits and a small generating set). The monoidal Bousfield localization L_E Sp for a ring spectrum E is then the symmetric monoidal reflection onto the subcategory of E-local spectra, constructed as a HIT Local_E whose points are E-local spectra and whose inclusion has a left adjoint L_E that is symmetric monoidal. This synthetic framework recovers the classical symmetric monoidal model categories and provides a computational interpretation of the smash product in Cubical Agda, where the levelwise definition computes directly on the representing sequences of types.

  • Assuming the Chas-Sullivan product requires a smooth manifold structure; in synthetic HoTT it only requires a Poincaré duality HIT, which applies to any dualizable type including classifying spaces and singular spaces.
  • Treating the moduli stack M_fg as a 1-truncated stack; it is an ∞-stack with non-trivial π_k for k ≥ 2 coming from the automorphisms of formal group isomorphisms, and the synthetic HIT must include these higher constructors.
  • Believing the Hopf algebroid (BP*BP, BP*) is just a commutative Hopf algebra; it is a Hopf algebroid over a non-commutative base (in the sense of a non-trivial left/right unit), and the synthetic cobar complex must respect the two module structures.
  • Overlooking that the synthetic smash product on spectra is defined levelwise on the representing sequences, not by a Day convolution on the ∞-category of spectra; the levelwise definition is the computational content, while the Day convolution is the universal property.
  • Confusing the synthetic Adams-Novikov spectral sequence (a spectral sequence of a cosimplicial resolution) with the classical one (a spectral sequence of a tower of fibrations); they are equivalent but the synthetic version is constructed as a HIT SpectralSeq(Cobar) with explicit differentials.
  • Neglecting the role of the synthetic nilpotence theorem in the convergence of the ANSS; it is the statement that the BP-Adams tower is a Postnikov tower in the BP-local category, and its proof uses the thick subcategory theorem internalized as a HIT.
The synthetic approach thus unifies the algebraic, geometric, and categorical structures of modern homotopy theory into a single computational framework based on higher inductive types and univalence.

The Wirthmüller isomorphism f_! ≃ f_* holds precisely when f is a proper map (i.e., its fibers are compact types), a condition detected internally by the truncation level of the fibers. The synthetic construction of the trace map S_B → X ∧ DX and the coevaluation DX ∧ X → S_B uses the encode-decode method on the fiberwise mapping types.
