The Internal Logic of (∞,1)-Topoi: From Dependent Types to Categorical Constructions

Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) is often described as the internal language of an (∞,1)-topos. This profound connection means that the syntactic constructs of HoTT directly correspond to semantic structures within such a higher categorical setting. Understanding this correspondence is crucial for grasping why HoTT behaves the way it does and how it provides a synthetic framework for higher category theory.

In classical category theory, type theory is often interpreted in a category with finite products and exponentials, known as a Cartesian Closed Category (CCC). Dependent type theory, specifically Martin-Löf Type Theory (MLTT), is interpreted in a more general structure called a Locally Cartesian Closed Category (LCCC). An LCCC is a category where every slice category C/A (objects over A) is also Cartesian Closed. This structure naturally models dependent types: a type family A → Type corresponds to a fibration p: E → C, where E is the total category and C is the base category. The fibers p-1(c) for c ∈ C are the types dependent on c.

In HoTT, this interpretation is elevated to the (∞,1)-categorical level. An (∞,1)-topos is an (∞,1)-category that satisfies certain properties analogous to those of a 1-topos (like having finite limits and colimits, and a subobject classifier). The "internal language" aspect means that every valid statement or construction in HoTT has a direct interpretation as an object, morphism, or higher cell within an (∞,1)-topos. Conversely, many constructions in (∞,1)-topoi can be expressed elegantly and synthetically within HoTT.

Key correspondences include:

  • Types as Objects: Each type A in HoTT corresponds to an object in the (∞,1)-topos.
  • Terms as Global Elements: A term x : A corresponds to a global element 1 → A, where 1 is the terminal object.
  • Functions as Morphisms: A function f : A → B corresponds to a morphism A → B in the (∞,1)-topos.
  • Dependent Types as Fibrations: A type family B : A → Type corresponds to a fibration p : E → A, where E is the total space of the family. The fibers of this fibration are the types B(a) for a : A.
  • Dependent Sums (Σ-types) as Total Spaces: The dependent sum Σ (a : A) B(a) corresponds to the total space E of the fibration p : E → A. This is the categorical coproduct or "sum" over the family.
  • Dependent Products (Π-types) as Sections: The dependent product Π (a : A) B(a) corresponds to the space of sections of the fibration p : E → A. A section is a map s : A → E such that p ∘ s = id_A. These represent functions whose codomain depends on their input.
  • Identity Types as Path Objects: The identity type a =_A b corresponds to the space of paths between objects a and b in the (∞,1)-topos. This is a fundamental aspect of the "homotopy" interpretation.
  • Universes as Object Classifiers: The universe U corresponds to an object classifier in the (∞,1)-topos, which is an object that classifies fibrations. This allows us to talk about types as objects within the type theory itself.
  • Univalence Axiom as Equivalence of Fibrations: The univalence axiom states that equivalent types are identical. Categorically, this means that the space of equivalences between two objects A and B is equivalent to the space of paths between A and B in the object classifier. This ensures that the internal logic respects the notion of equivalence in the higher category.

This internal logic provides a powerful framework for developing higher category theory synthetically. Instead of constructing complicated models of higher categories using simplicial sets, cubical sets, or other combinatorial structures, HoTT allows mathematicians to reason directly about higher categories using type-theoretic language, where the coherence conditions are handled implicitly by the identity types and the univalence axiom.

Coherence and the Synthetic Approach to Higher Categories

The concept of "coherence" is central to higher category theory. In a strict n-category, compositions are strictly associative and identity elements are strict units. However, in most naturally occurring examples, compositions are only associative and unital up to isomorphism, and these isomorphisms themselves satisfy further coherence conditions (e.g., the pentagon identity for associativity). As one goes to higher dimensions, the number and complexity of these coherence conditions grow exponentially, leading to the infamous "coherence problem."

Traditional approaches to higher categories, such as those based on operads, strict n-categories, or various model categories (e.g., simplicial sets, cubical sets), often involve explicit combinatorial data to manage these coherence conditions. This can be cumbersome and difficult to work with in practice, requiring intricate diagrams and proofs of "all diagrams commute."

Homotopy Type Theory offers a synthetic solution to the coherence problem. Instead of explicitly encoding coherence data, HoTT leverages its fundamental interpretation of types as spaces and identity types as path spaces. The key insight is that in a space, paths compose associatively and have identity paths, but these compositions and identities are only unique up to higher paths. For example, if p : x = y and q : y = z are paths, then p · q : x = z is a composite path. The associativity of composition means that (p · q) · r is "the same as" p · (q · r), but this "sameness" is itself a path of paths (a 2-dimensional path or a higher identity). This continues indefinitely, with paths of paths of paths, and so on.

In HoTT, these higher paths are precisely the higher identity types. For instance, if p, q, r are paths, then the associativity of path composition is witnessed by a term of type (p · q) · r = p · (q · r). This term itself can be compared to other terms of the same type via a higher identity type, and so forth. The univalence axiom further reinforces this by identifying equivalent types with identical types, meaning that isomorphisms are treated as equalities, and the coherence of isomorphisms is automatically handled by the identity type structure.

This synthetic approach has several advantages:

  • Implicit Coherence: Coherence conditions are not explicitly stated or proven; they are an inherent property of the identity type structure. This significantly simplifies definitions and proofs.
  • Direct Reasoning: Mathematicians can reason directly about higher categorical structures (like (∞,1)-categories, ∞-groupoids, or ∞-functors) using the familiar language of types, functions, and equalities, without needing to delve into the combinatorial complexities of a specific model.
  • Computational Content: In proof assistants like Cubical Agda, the proofs of coherence (which are terms in identity types) can often be computed, providing a concrete realization of the abstract coherence.
  • Universality: The synthetic approach provides a universal language for higher category theory, independent of any specific model. Any model of HoTT (e.g., simplicial sets, cubical sets) will automatically satisfy the coherence properties implied by the type theory.

For example, defining an (∞,1)-category in HoTT involves defining a type of objects, a type of morphisms between any two objects, and then higher identity types to capture the composition and coherence. The "category of types" itself, often denoted Type, is the archetypal (∞,1)-category in HoTT, where objects are types, morphisms are functions, and higher cells are higher identities between functions. This internal perspective makes HoTT a powerful tool for formalizing and reasoning about the most abstract structures in modern mathematics.

Understanding the Coherence of Associativity in HoTT

Consider three paths p : x = y, q : y = z, and r : z = w in a type A. In HoTT, path composition is associative up to a canonical higher path. Explain how this "associativity up to path" is represented in HoTT's type theory, and what it implies for the structure of higher identity types.

In HoTT, path composition is defined such that if p : x = y and q : y = z, then p · q : x = z is a path. The associativity of this composition is not a strict equality, but rather an equivalence witnessed by a higher path. Specifically, there exists a canonical term, often denoted assoc, with the type:

assoc : (p · q) · r = p · (q · r)

This means that the two ways of composing three paths (first p and q, then r; or first q and r, then p) are not definitionally equal, but are connected by a specific path of paths. This assoc term is itself a path, living in the 2-identity type. Its existence implies that the structure of paths forms an ∞-groupoid, where every path is invertible and all compositions are coherent up to higher paths.

The implication for higher identity types is that this assoc term is not unique up to strict equality. Instead, any two terms of type (p · q) · r = p · (q · r) are themselves connected by a 3-identity. This continues indefinitely: there are paths between paths, paths between paths of paths, and so on. This hierarchy of identity types precisely captures the infinite coherence conditions required for an ∞-groupoid (or, more generally, an (∞,1)-category). The synthetic approach of HoTT handles this by providing canonical constructors for these higher paths (like assoc), which are then treated as "definitional" coherences, simplifying the reasoning process significantly compared to explicit combinatorial models.

Navigating Abstract Concepts
When encountering highly abstract concepts like "internal language of an (∞,1)-topos" or "coherence problem," focus on the core intuition and the direct correspondences. For the internal language, remember that HoTT's syntax is a direct mirror of higher categorical structures. For coherence, understand that HoTT's identity types implicitly handle the complex "sameness up to higher sameness" that is central to higher categories. Avoid getting bogged down in the full technical definitions of (∞,1)-categories unless explicitly required; instead, concentrate on how HoTT simplifies reasoning about them.

Advanced Quotient Constructions and Their Univalent Properties

Higher Inductive Types (HITs) are a cornerstone of HoTT, allowing the construction of types with specified points and paths. Among the most fundamental applications of HITs are quotient types, which are ubiquitous in mathematics for identifying elements under an equivalence relation. In HoTT, quotient types are not merely sets of equivalence classes; their properties are deeply intertwined with the univalence axiom and the homotopy interpretation of types.

A quotient type A / R, where R is an equivalence relation on A, is typically defined as a HIT with:

  • A constructor [a] : A / R for each element a : A, representing the canonical projection.
  • A constructor glue : [a] = [b] for each pair (a, b) : A × A such that a R b, representing the identification of equivalent elements.
  • Higher constructors to ensure that glue respects the reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of R, and that all paths in A / R arise from these identifications.

The universal property of a quotient type in HoTT states that to define a function f : A / R → B, it suffices to define a function g : A → B such that for any a, b : A with a R b, there is a path g(a) = g(b) in B. This is the standard "mapping out" property of quotients, but crucially, the condition is about paths (equalities in the homotopy sense), not strict definitional equality.

The interaction with the univalence axiom is particularly significant. Univalence implies that if two types are equivalent, they are identical. This has profound consequences for quotients:

  1. Quotients of Sets are Sets: If A is a set (i.e., all its parallel paths are trivial, meaning 0-truncated), and R is an equivalence relation on A, then the quotient A / R is also a set. This means that any two elements x, y : A / R are either equal or not, and if they are equal, there is a unique path between them. This aligns with the classical understanding of quotient sets.
  2. Quotients of Higher Types can be Higher Types: If A is a higher type (e.g., a 1-type or an ∞-groupoid), then its quotient A / R can also be a higher type. For example, the circle S¹ can be constructed as the quotient of the integers ℤ by the relation n R m if n = m (mod k), where k is some integer. More commonly, S¹ is defined as the quotient of the interval I by identifying its endpoints 0 and 1. This results in a type with non-trivial higher paths (the fundamental loop of S¹).
  3. Univalent Quotients: The "glue" constructors in a quotient HIT are not just arbitrary paths; they are often chosen to be "univalent" in the sense that they represent the canonical identification. This ensures that the quotient construction behaves well with respect to equivalences. For instance, if we quotient a type A by the kernel of a function f : A → B, the resulting quotient type A / ker(f) is univalently equivalent to the image of f.

A particularly important application is the construction of homotopy quotients. For a group G acting on a type X, the "naive" quotient X / G (where x ~ gx for g ∈ G) often loses information about the group action. The homotopy orbit type X // G (also known as the classifying space BG if X is a point, or the Borel construction E G ×_G X) is a more sophisticated quotient that captures the homotopy-theoretic information of the action. It is typically defined as a HIT with points [x] : X // G for x : X, and paths [x] = [g x] for g : G and x : X, along with higher paths for the group laws. This construction is crucial for defining classifying spaces, bundles, and other structures in synthetic homotopy theory.

The robustness of quotient types in HoTT, supported by HITs and univalence, allows for a faithful and computationally meaningful representation of quotient constructions across all levels of the homotopy hierarchy, from simple sets to complex higher groupoids.

The Constructive Foundations of HoTT and the Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov Interpretation

Homotopy Type Theory is fundamentally a constructive system, meaning it adheres to intuitionistic logic rather than classical logic. This has deep philosophical and practical implications for how mathematics is done and understood within HoTT. The constructive nature is rooted in the Curry-Howard correspondence, which identifies propositions with types and proofs with terms (or programs).

The Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov (BHK) interpretation provides a concrete way to understand the meaning of logical connectives in constructive mathematics:

  • Proof of A and B (A ∧ B): A proof of A ∧ B is a pair consisting of a proof of A and a proof of B. In HoTT, this corresponds to the product type A × B.
  • Proof of A or B (A ∨ B): A proof of A ∨ B is either a proof of A (with an indication that it's a proof of A) or a proof of B (with an indication that it's a proof of B). In HoTT, this corresponds to the sum type A + B (or disjoint union).
  • Proof of A implies B (A → B): A proof of A → B is a function that transforms any proof of A into a proof of B. In HoTT, this corresponds to the function type A → B.
  • Proof of Falsehood (⊥): There is no proof of falsehood. The empty type 0 (or ⊥) has no terms.
  • Proof of Negation (¬A): A proof of ¬A is a function that transforms any proof of A into a proof of falsehood (A → ⊥). In HoTT, this is A → 0.
  • Proof of Existential Quantification (∃x:A. P(x)): A proof of ∃x:A. P(x) is a pair consisting of an element x : A and a proof of P(x). In HoTT, this corresponds to the dependent sum type Σ (x : A) P(x).
  • Proof of Universal Quantification (∀x:A. P(x)): A proof of ∀x:A. P(x) is a function that transforms any element x : A into a proof of P(x). In HoTT, this corresponds to the dependent product type Π (x : A) P(x).

Crucially, the BHK interpretation means that proofs are constructive algorithms. To prove existence (∃), one must actually exhibit an element. To prove disjunction (∨), one must specify which disjunct holds. This contrasts sharply with classical logic, where the Law of Excluded Middle (A ∨ ¬A) and the Axiom of Choice are accepted, allowing for non-constructive proofs of existence (e.g., proof by contradiction without providing an example) and choice functions without explicit construction.

In HoTT, the Law of Excluded Middle (LEM) does not hold generally. While it might hold for specific "set-like" types (0-truncated types), it does not hold for higher types. For example, for a general type A, the type A + (A → 0) is not necessarily inhabited. Similarly, the Axiom of Choice, in its classical form, is not provable in HoTT. However, certain constructive versions of choice principles, such as the dependent choice for sets, may hold.

The constructive nature of HoTT has several benefits:

  • Computational Content: Every proof in HoTT is a program. This means that formalizing mathematics in HoTT automatically yields executable algorithms, which is invaluable for formal verification and computer science applications.
  • Stronger Foundations: Constructive proofs are often considered more robust and informative because they explicitly demonstrate how to obtain the desired objects or properties.
  • Compatibility with Computer Proof Assistants: The constructive nature makes HoTT highly suitable for implementation in proof assistants like Agda or Coq, which are based on type theory and extract computational content from proofs.

While HoTT is constructive, it is not "too" restrictive. The univalence axiom, for instance, allows for a rich and expressive mathematics that often mirrors classical results, but with a constructive interpretation. For example, while real numbers can be constructed in various ways (Cauchy reals, Dedekind reals), their equivalence in HoTT is a constructive equivalence, not just a classical isomorphism. This blend of constructive rigor with the expressiveness of homotopy theory makes HoTT a unique and powerful foundational system.

The Role of Universes and Universe Polymorphism in Defining Mathematical Structures

In Homotopy Type Theory, as in Martin-Löf Type Theory, the concept of a "universe" is fundamental. A universe is a type whose terms are themselves types. This allows us to speak about types within the type theory itself, creating a reflective system where mathematical structures can be defined and reasoned about at different levels of abstraction. Without universes, we could not, for example, define a "category of types" or a "type of groups."

HoTT typically employs a hierarchy of universes: U₀ : U₁, U₁ : U₂, and so on, often denoted as Type₀ : Type₁, Type₁ : Type₂, etc. This hierarchy is necessary to avoid paradoxes like Russell's paradox (a type of all types that do not contain themselves). Each universe U_i is a type, and its elements are precisely the types "smaller" than U_i. This means that U_i itself is an element of Ui+1, but not an element of U_i.

Key aspects of universes in HoTT:

  • Cumulativity: If A : U_i, then A : Ui+1. This means that types in a smaller universe are also considered types in any larger universe. This property simplifies reasoning and allows for more flexible definitions.
  • Univalence for Universes: The univalence axiom extends to universes. This means that if two types A and B in a universe U_i are equivalent (A ≃ B), then they are identical as elements of U_i (A =U_i B). This is crucial for ensuring that the universe itself behaves like an ∞-groupoid, where equivalent types are treated as the same.
  • Universe Polymorphism: This is a powerful feature implemented in proof assistants like Agda. It allows functions and definitions to be written in a way that works for any universe level. Instead of writing separate definitions for a "list of types in U₀" and a "list of types in U₁," one can write a single polymorphic definition that takes a universe level ℓ as a parameter, e.g., List (A : Type ℓ). This significantly reduces code duplication and improves the generality of formalizations.

The ability to quantify over types (using universes) and to write polymorphic definitions is essential for building complex mathematical structures in HoTT:

  1. Defining Categories and Higher Categories: A "category" can be defined as a type whose elements are objects, and for any two objects, there is a type of morphisms between them, satisfying certain coherence conditions. To define a "category of categories," we need to quantify over categories themselves, which requires universes. For example, a "category of types" would be a category whose objects are types from some universe U_i.
  2. Generic Proofs: Universe polymorphism enables the construction of proofs that hold for any type, regardless of its universe level. This is particularly useful for foundational results that apply uniformly across the type hierarchy. For instance, a proof that "all sets are 0-truncated" can be written polymorphically for any type in any universe.
  3. Consistency and Stratification: The universe hierarchy is a standard technique to ensure the consistency of type theory by preventing self-referential paradoxes. While the consistency of HoTT (with univalence) relative to ZFC has been established via models, the internal stratification provided by universes is a key aspect of its design.
  4. Constructing Universes as HITs: In advanced settings, it's possible to construct new universes as higher inductive-recursive types. This allows for the creation of universes with specific properties, such as a universe of "small types" or a universe of "truncated types," further extending the expressive power of HoTT.

In essence, universes provide the necessary scaffolding for HoTT to be a truly foundational system, capable of internalizing and reasoning about its own structures, and universe polymorphism makes this process practical and efficient for formalization efforts.

Common Traps

  • Confusing Constructive Existence with Classical Existence: Assuming that an existence proof in HoTT (∃x:A. P(x)) implies only classical existence. It always implies constructive existence, meaning an actual term (x, p) can be exhibited.
  • Applying Law of Excluded Middle Universally: Incorrectly assuming that A ∨ ¬A holds for all types in HoTT. It only holds for specific types, typically those that are 0-truncated (sets).
  • Treating Universes as Sets: Misinterpreting universes (Type₀, Type₁, etc.) as simple sets of types. They are types themselves, with their own internal structure and subject to univalence, and they form a cumulative hierarchy to prevent paradoxes.
  • Ignoring Higher Paths in Quotient Types: Believing that quotient types in HoTT only identify elements up to strict equality. The "glue" constructors introduce paths, and the resulting quotient can be a higher type with non-trivial higher paths, especially if the original type was not a set.
  • Overlooking the Implicit Coherence: Trying to explicitly write out coherence diagrams for higher categorical structures in HoTT. The identity types and univalence axiom implicitly handle these, making the synthetic approach much simpler.
  • Assuming Strict Associativity of Path Composition: Forgetting that path composition in HoTT is associative only up to a higher path (a 2-identity), not strictly. This "up to" aspect is fundamental to the homotopy interpretation.
  • Misunderstanding the Internal Language Analogy: Thinking that "HoTT is the internal language of an (∞,1)-topos" is merely a philosophical statement. It's a precise mathematical correspondence where HoTT's syntax directly models the categorical structures.

The Synthetic Eilenberg-Moore Spectral Sequence and Its Convergence in HoTT

The Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence (EMSS) computes the homology of the homotopy pullback of a cospan of spaces X → Z ← Y in terms of the homology of X, Y, and Z and the action of the homology of the loop space ΩZ. In classical algebraic topology, the EMSS takes the form TorH_*(ΩZ)(H_*(X), H_*(Y)) ⇒ H_*(X ×_Z Y) under suitable connectivity and finiteness hypotheses. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the homotopy pullback is directly interpreted as the Σ-type Σ (x : X) Σ (y : Y) (f x = g y), where f : X → Z and g : Y → Z. The synthetic EMSS arises from filtering this total space by the skeletal filtration of the identity type f x = g y, which is equivalent to the path space of Z. The E²-page is constructed internally as the derived tensor product (Tor) over the Pontryagin ring H_*(ΩZ) of the H_*(ΩZ)-comodule structures on H_*(X) and H_*(Y) induced by the maps f and g. The convergence proof in HoTT leverages the fact that the identity type is a higher inductive type generated by reflexivity and path constructors, allowing an inductive argument on the truncation level of the path space. A critical synthetic insight is that the EMSS degenerates at E² when Z is simply connected and the homology is taken with coefficients in a field, a result formalized by constructing a splitting of the filtration using the group-like structure of ΩZ. The main technical obstacle in formalization is the construction of the Pontryagin ring structure on H_*(ΩZ) internally, which requires the synthetic Eckmann-Hilton argument to show that the two loop concatenations agree up to coherent higher homotopies. This has been achieved in the Agda HoTT library for specific cases like the path-loop fibration ΩZ → PZ → Z, where the EMSS collapses to the Serre spectral sequence. The synthetic approach clarifies that the EMSS is fundamentally a statement about the homology of a homotopy fiber product, avoiding the technical overhead of simplicial resolutions or differential graded coalgebras required in classical treatments.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Topological Hochschild Homology and the Cyclotomic Trace Map

Topological Hochschild homology (THH) of a ring spectrum R is the geometric realization of the cyclic bar construction B^cy(R) = |R ⊗ R⊗• ⊗ R|, which carries a natural circle action. In HoTT, a ring spectrum is represented by a connective spectrum object in the ∞-topos of types, or more concretely by an E_∞-algebra in the symmetric monoidal ∞-category of spectra. The synthetic construction of THH(R) proceeds by defining the cyclic bar construction as a higher inductive type generated by points corresponding to tensors r₀ ⊗ r₁ ⊗ … ⊗ r_n and paths encoding the cyclic symmetry and face/degeneracy maps. The circle action S¹ → Aut(THH(R)) is synthesized by the rotation of the cyclic index, which is a path in the type of automorphisms of the HIT. The cyclotomic trace map K(R) → TC(R) factors through THH(R)hS¹, the homotopy fixed points of the circle action. In HoTT, homotopy fixed points of a G-action on a type X are defined as the type of sections of the associated fibration XhG → BG, i.e., Σ (x : XhG) (p : π(x) = base). For G = S¹, this is the type of maps from BS¹ to XhS¹ over BS¹. The synthetic cyclotomic structure maps φ_p : THH(R) → THH(R)tC_p (Tate fixed points) are constructed using the Frobenius endomorphism on the cyclic bar construction, which in HoTT corresponds to a map on the HIT induced by the p-th power map on the circle S¹ → S¹. The key computational advantage of the synthetic approach is that the S¹-action on THH(R) is strict at the level of the HIT definition, whereas classically it is only homotopy coherent. This strictness simplifies the construction of the Tate spectral sequence converging to π_*(THH(R)tC_p), whose E²-page is the Tate cohomology of C_p with coefficients in π_*(THH(R)). The formalization of the Dundas-Goodwillie-McCarthy theorem — that the relative K-theory of a nilpotent extension of ring spectra agrees with relative TC — has been a major driver for developing synthetic spectra in HoTT, as it requires a robust theory of excisive functors and the Goodwillie calculus, both of which are natively expressed using higher inductive types and modalities.

Worked Example: Constructing the Circle Action on Synthetic THH
Define the synthetic cyclic bar construction B^cy(A) for an E_∞-algebra A in HoTT as a HIT. Specify the constructors for the circle action rot : S¹ → (B^cy(A) ≃ B^cy(A)) and prove that rot(base) = id.
  1. HIT Definition of B^cy(A): Define B^cy(A) with constructors:
    • tensor : A → A → B^cy(A) (binary tensor, generalized to n-ary via associativity paths).
    • cycle : Π (a₀ a₁ ... a_n : A), tensor a₀ (tensor a₁ ... a_n) = tensor a₁ (tensor ... (tensor a_n a₀)) (cyclic symmetry).
    • assoc : Π (a b c : A), tensor a (tensor b c) = tensor (tensor a b) c (associativity up to path).
    • Higher coherence paths for the simplicial/cyclic identities.
  2. Circle Action: Define rot : S¹ → (B^cy(A) ≃ B^cy(A)) by circle induction.
    • rot base := id_equiv (the identity equivalence).
    • rot loop := ua (λ x ↦ cycle_path x), where cycle_path is the path constructor cycle applied to the components of x (using the fact that every element of the HIT is generated by tensors). The univalence axiom ua turns the automorphism (given by cyclic rotation) into a path in the universe, hence a loop in the type of equivalences.
  3. Verification: By definition of circle induction, rot base is judgmentally id_equiv. The action of loop is the equivalence induced by the cyclic permutation constructor.
Exam Strategy: Spectral Sequences in HoTT
When asked about convergence of synthetic spectral sequences (Serre, Eilenberg-Moore, Adams), focus on the filtration of a type by truncation levels. The E¹-page is the homology of the associated graded (fibers of the filtration), and the differential arises from the boundary map in the long exact sequence of the filtration. Convergence is equivalent to the statement that the filtration is exhaustive and complete (Hausdorff), which in HoTT translates to the type being the sequential colimit of its truncations. Examiners often test the distinction between conditional convergence (requires connectivity assumptions) and strong convergence (holds for finite Postnikov towers).

The Synthetic Lubin-Tate Theory and Deformation Rings in the Adams-Novikov Spectral Sequence

The Adams-Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) has E²-page ExtBP_*BP(BP_*, BP_*X), where BP is the Brown-Peterson spectrum at a prime p. By the Landweber exact functor theorem and the work of Lubin and Tate, this Ext group is isomorphic to the continuous cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group S_n with coefficients in the Morava module E_n_*X, where E_n is the Lubin-Tate spectrum. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the Lubin-Tate spectrum E_n is constructed as the global sections of a sheaf of E_∞-ring spectra on the moduli stack of formal groups M_fg, specifically on the Lubin-Tate deformation space Spf W(k)[[u₁, ..., un-1]]. The synthetic approach defines the moduli stack of formal groups as a higher inductive-inductive type: a type of formal group laws over commutative rings, with paths given by strict isomorphisms, and higher paths given by homotopies of isomorphisms. The Lubin-Tate deformation space is then the formal neighborhood of a height n formal group law over a perfect field k, which in HoTT is the type of formal group laws equipped with a specified isomorphism to the Honda formal group law modulo (p, u₁, ..., un-1)^∞. The Morava stabilizer group S_n = Aut(Γ_n) is the automorphism ∞-group of the universal deformation, which in HoTT is simply the loop space Ω(M_fg, Γ_n) at the point corresponding to the height n formal group. The E²-page of the ANSS is then synthetically the group cohomology H^*(S_n; E_n_*X), computed as the cohomology of the classifying type BS_n with coefficients in the local system induced by the S_n-action on E_n_*X. The synthetic advantage appears in the construction of the chromatic tower: the Bousfield localization LK(n)X is the fiber of the map X → Ln-1X, where Ln-1 is localization with respect to the Johnson-Wilson theory E(n). In HoTT, this localization is a modality (a reflective subuniverse), and the chromatic fracture square is a pullback square of modalities. The formalization of the Hopkins-Miller theorem (that E_n is an E_∞-ring spectrum) in HoTT reduces to showing that the Goerss-Hopkins obstruction theory for E_∞-structures vanishes, which is a statement about the vanishing of certain André-Quillen cohomology groups in the ∞-topos of types. This has been partially formalized in Cubical Agda using the synthetic obstruction theory framework.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Brown-Comenetz Dual and Anderson Self-Duality of the Sphere Spectrum

The Brown-Comenetz dual of a spectrum X, denoted I_X, is defined by the property that π-k(I_X) ≅ Hom(π_k(X), ℚ/ℤ) for all k. The Anderson dual is a variant using ℝ/ℤ. The sphere spectrum S is not self-dual under Spanier-Whitehead duality, but it is closely related to its Anderson dual I_ℤ S. In synthetic homotopy type theory, spectra are represented as sequential types (ℕ → Type) with structure maps Σ X_n → Xn+1. The Brown-Comenetz dual is constructed internally as the mapping spectrum F(X, I), where I is the injective spectrum representing ℚ/ℤ. The synthetic definition of I uses the fact that ℚ/ℤ is the colimit of ℤ/p^∞, which in HoTT is a higher inductive type generated by a base point and paths corresponding to the Prüfer group structure. The Anderson self-duality of the sphere spectrum at a prime p is the statement that the p-complete sphere S_p^∧ is equivalent to a shift of its Anderson dual: S_p^∧ ≃ Σ-n I_ℤ S_p^∧ for some n (related to the image of J). In HoTT, p-completion is the modality _p (Bousfield localization at the Moore spectrum M(p)). The equivalence is constructed by analyzing the synthetic Adams-Novikov spectral sequence for the sphere. The key synthetic lemma is that the E_∞-page of the ANSS for S_p^∧ computes the homotopy groups of the p-complete sphere, and the Anderson dual corresponds to a shift in the filtration degree. The Gross-Hopkins duality for the Morava E-theory spectrum E_n states that the Gross-Hopkins dual of E_n is Σn²-n E_n. In HoTT, this is a statement about the dualizing module for the Morava stabilizer group S_n acting on the Lubin-Tate space. The synthetic proof uses the fact that the Lubin-Tate space is a formal disk of dimension n²-n, and the dualizing sheaf is the canonical bundle, which is trivializable because the Lubin-Tate space is a formal group. This trivialization is constructed explicitly in HoTT by exhibiting a non-vanishing top differential form on the universal deformation, which corresponds to a generator of the determinant of the Lie algebra of the formal group. The formalization of these dualities in Cubical Agda requires a synthetic theory of determinants and orientations for ∞-group actions, which is developed using the synthetic version of the J-homomorphism and the Pontryagin-Thom construction.

The Synthetic Grothendieck Construction for (∞,1)-Categories and Cartesian Fibrations

The classical Grothendieck construction establishes an equivalence between functors C^op → Cat and Cartesian fibrations over C. In (∞,1)-category theory, this becomes an equivalence between (∞,1)-functors C^op → Cat_∞ and Cartesian fibrations of (∞,1)-categories. In HoTT, (∞,1)-categories are represented as complete Segal types (Rezk types) or as categories in the sense of the Rezk completion. A functor F : C^op → Type (where Type is the ∞-topos of types) corresponds to a type family P : C → Type. The total space of this family is the Σ-type Σ (c : C) P(c). The projection π : Σ (c : C) P(c) → C is a Cartesian fibration in the synthetic sense: for every morphism f : c → d in C and every x : P(d), there exists a Cartesian lift f̃ : (c, f^*(x)) → (d, x) such that any morphism into (d, x) factors uniquely through f̃ up to a contractible space of choices. In HoTT, the Cartesian lift is constructed using the transport operation: f^*(x) := transport^P(f, x). The universal property of the Cartesian lift follows directly from the path induction principle for the identity type of the base category C. The synthetic straightening and unstraightening equivalences are then functions between the type of functors C^op → Type and the type of Cartesian fibrations over C. Straightening takes a Cartesian fibration E → C and produces the functor c ↦ Fiber_E(c). Unstraightening takes a functor F : C^op → Type and produces the projection Σ F → C. The proof that these are inverses relies on the univalence axiom for the universe Type, which identifies equivalences of fibers with paths in the base. A critical advanced application is the synthetic construction of the (∞,1)-category of (∞,1)-categories Cat_∞ as the Rezk completion of the type of small categories. The universal Cartesian fibration over Cat_∞ is the projection from the type of pointed categories (C, c₀) to Cat_∞. This allows the internalization of (∞,1)-category theory within HoTT, including the definition of limits and colimits as right and left adjoints to the diagonal functor, which are constructed using the synthetic adjoint functor theorem (which holds in any ∞-topos). The formalization of the (∞,1)-Yoneda lemma in this setting states that for any C : Cat_∞ and F : C^op → Type, the type of natural transformations from the representable functor y(c) to F is equivalent to F(c), a direct consequence of the univalence of the universe and the definition of natural transformations as sections of a Cartesian fibration.

  • Confusing the Eilenberg-Moore SS with the Serre SS: The EMSS computes homology of a pullback (Tor over loop space homology), while the Serre SS computes homology of a fibration (Tor over base homology). In HoTT, the Serre SS filters the total space by the base; the EMSS filters the pullback by the path space of the base.
  • Assuming THH is just HH topologically: THH has a genuine S¹-action (cyclic symmetry), not just an action up to homotopy. The synthetic HIT definition makes this action strict, which is essential for defining the cyclotomic structure maps φ_p.
  • Treating Lubin-Tate space as a scheme, not a formal moduli problem: In HoTT, the Lubin-Tate deformation space is a higher inductive type representing the functor of Artinian rings. It is not a scheme in the classical sense but a formal ∞-groupoid. Its tangent complex is the Lie algebra of the formal group.
  • Misidentifying Brown-Comenetz dual with Spanier-Whitehead dual: I_X = F(X, I_ℚ/ℤ) vs DX = F(X, S). The sphere is not self-dual under DW duality (DX ≄ X), but S_p^∧ ≃ Σ-n I_ℤ S_p^∧. The shift n depends on the image of J.
  • Thinking Cartesian fibrations require explicit coherence data: In HoTT, a type family P : C → Type is a Cartesian fibration. The transport operation provides the lifts, and path induction proves the universal property. No explicit "Cartesian morphism" data needs to be added.
  • Overlooking the role of Rezk completion in Cat_∞: The type of precategories is not univalent. Cat_∞ is the Rezk completion (a HIT). The universal fibration lives over Cat_∞, not the type of precategories.
  • Assuming the ANSS E²-page is always group cohomology: ExtBP_*BP(BP_*, BP_*X) ≅ H^*(S_n; E_n_*X) only after K(n)-localization and for X of type n. Globally, the ANSS is a spectral sequence of comodules over the Hopf algebroid (BP_*, BP_*BP).
The synthetic approach to these advanced topics reveals that the computational content of stable homotopy theory is natively expressed in the language of higher inductive types and modalities.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Tate Construction and Cyclotomic Structure on THH

The Tate construction is a fundamental operation in equivariant stable homotopy theory that, for a genuine G-spectrum X, produces a spectrum XtG interpolating between homotopy orbits XhG and homotopy fixed points XhG. In synthetic HoTT, the circle group S¹ is represented as the higher inductive type generated by a basepoint and a loop. A cyclotomic spectrum is a sequence of spectra X_n with S¹-actions and structure maps X_n → (Xn+1)tC_p compatible with the cyclotomic Frobenius. Topological Hochschild homology THH(R) of a ring spectrum R carries a canonical S¹-action and cyclotomic structure. In HoTT, THH(R) is constructed as a higher inductive type: the geometric realization of the cyclic bar construction Bcy(R). The S¹-action arises from the cyclic symmetry of the simplicial circle, which is strict in the cubical model. The Tate construction XtS¹ is defined as the fiber of the norm map N : XhS¹ → XhS¹. The norm map itself is constructed using the transfer map in the synthetic stable homotopy category. The cyclotomic Frobenius φ_p : THH(R) → THH(R)tC_p is induced by the p-fold covering map S¹ → S¹ on the cyclic bar construction. A critical synthetic result is that the cyclotomic structure on THH(R) is equivalent to a genuine S¹-action on the associated topological cyclic homology TC(R) := holim_n THH(R)hCp^n. The synthetic proof uses the fact that the Tate construction for finite subgroups C_p ⊂ S¹ commutes with the homotopy limit over n. This allows the internalization of the Bökstedt-Hsiang-Madsen theorem: the cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) factors through THH(R)hS¹. The computational power of this synthetic approach is evident in the calculation of TC(𝔽_p) and TC(ℤ), where the Tate spectral sequence for C_p acting on THH(𝔽_p) collapses synthetically due to the vanishing of negative homotopy groups of THH(𝔽_p), a fact provable by induction on the simplicial degree of the cyclic bar construction using the synthetic Steenrod operations.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Six-Functor Formalism and Étale Descent in Motivic HoTT

Motivic homotopy theory in HoTT is developed by enriching the ∞-topos of types with an interval object 𝔸¹ (the affine line) and a Tate twist 𝔾_m (the multiplicative group). The six-functor formalism (f_*, f_!, f^*, f^!, ⊗, Hom) for a morphism f : X → Y of smooth schemes (represented as higher inductive types satisfying Nisnevich descent) is constructed synthetically using the internal language of the ∞-topos of motivic spaces. The exceptional pushforward f_! is defined as the left adjoint to f^*, existing because f^* preserves limits and the ∞-topos is locally presentable. For an open immersion j : U → X, j_! is the extension by zero, constructed as a pushout of the initial object along the complement. For a proper morphism, f_! ≃ f_*. The exceptional pullback f^! is the right adjoint to f_!, constructed via the Wirthmüller isomorphism in the stable motivic homotopy category SH(S). Étale descent is internalized by requiring that the motivic ∞-topos satisfies descent for étale covers: a type X is étale-local if for every étale cover U → X, the map X → lim (U^•) is an equivalence. The synthetic purity theorem states that for a closed immersion i : Z → X of codimension c with normal bundle N, there is an equivalence i^! Σ^∞_T X_+ ≃ Σ2c,c Th(N), where Th(N) is the Thom space of N. This is proved by reducing to the case of a vector bundle using the deformation to the normal cone, which is a higher inductive type gluing X × 𝔸¹ and the normal bundle along the complement. The six-functor formalism enables the synthetic construction of the motivic cohomology groups Hp,q(X, ℤ) as maps in SH(S) from Σ^∞_T X_+ to the motivic Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum Hℤ(p)[q]. The Beilinson-Lichtenbaum conjecture (now a theorem of Voevodsky-Rost) is expressed synthetically as the statement that the map from motivic cohomology to étale cohomology is an isomorphism in weights p ≤ q and injective for p = q+1, which follows from the synthetic construction of the slice filtration and the identification of the slices of Hℤ.

Technique: Distinguishing Tate Construction from Homotopy Fixed Points in Cyclotomic Spectra
In the synthetic construction of TC(R) from THH(R), why is the Tate construction THH(R)tC_p used in the cyclotomic Frobenius φ_p rather than the homotopy fixed points THH(R)hC_p? Explain the role of the norm map and the connectivity of THH(R) in ensuring the equivalence of the two approaches for the limit defining TC(R).
The cyclotomic Frobenius φ_p : THH(R) → THH(R)tC_p uses the Tate construction because it captures the genuine C_p-equivariant structure required for the cyclotomic category. The norm map N : THH(R)hC_p → THH(R)hC_p has fiber THH(R)tC_p. For connective ring spectra R, THH(R) is connective (π_k = 0 for k < 0). The Tate spectral sequence for a finite group G acting on a connective spectrum has E²s,t = H-s(G; π_t X) ⇒ πs+t XtG. Since π_t X = 0 for t < 0, the spectral sequence is concentrated in t ≥ 0. For the homotopy limit defining TC(R) = holim_n THH(R)hCp^n, the map from homotopy fixed points to Tate construction THH(R)hC_p → THH(R)tC_p is an equivalence in non-negative degrees when THH(R) is connective and the group is finite. This is because the Tate construction vanishes on bounded-below spectra with trivial G-action up to a shift, but here the action is non-trivial. However, the connectivity of THH(R) ensures that the map from the homotopy limit of fixed points to the homotopy limit of Tate constructions is an equivalence on connective covers. The synthetic proof uses the fiber sequence XhG → XhG → XtG and the fact that for connective X, the map XhG → XhG is an isomorphism on π0 and surjective on π1, making XtG connective. Thus the limit over n of THH(R)tCp^n computes the same connective cover as the limit of fixed points, which is TC(R).
Exam Strategy: Synthetic Equivariance and Connectivity
When asked about the Tate construction in HoTT, always check the connectivity hypotheses. The synthetic definition XtG := fib(XhG → XhG) is valid for any G-action, but its computational utility (e.g., vanishing of negative homotopy groups, collapse of spectral sequences) relies on X being connective or bounded below. For cyclotomic spectra, the key lemma is that if X is connective, the map XhG → XtG is an equivalence in degrees ≥ 0 for finite G. This justifies using the Tate construction in the cyclotomic Frobenius without losing connective information. Remember that in cubical type theory, the S¹-action on THH is strict, so the restriction to C_p is a genuine action, not just a homotopy action, which is essential for defining the norm map synthetically.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Surgery Exact Sequence and the Classification of High-Dimensional Manifolds

The surgery exact sequence classifies manifolds up to homotopy equivalence within a given homotopy type. In synthetic HoTT, a smooth manifold M of dimension n is represented as a higher inductive type equipped with a tangent bundle τ_M : M → BO(n), where BO(n) is the classifying space of the orthogonal group O(n) constructed as a HIT. A degree-one normal map (f, b) : M → X consists of a map f : M → X between Poincaré duality spaces (types with a fundamental class [M] : H_n(M) and Poincaré duality isomorphism) and a bundle map b : τ_M → ξ covering f, where ξ : X → BO is a stable spherical fibration. The surgery obstruction θ(f, b) lives in the L-group L_n(π₁(X)), which is defined synthetically as the homotopy groups of the quadratic L-theory spectrum L(ℤ[π₁(X)]). The L-theory spectrum is constructed as a higher inductive type using the Ranicki symmetric construction on the ∞-category of finitely generated free ℤ[π₁(X)]-modules with a duality involution. The surgery exact sequence is a fiber sequence of types: 𝒮(X) → [X, G/O] → L_*(ℤ[π₁(X)]), where 𝒮(X) is the structure set of manifolds homotopy equivalent to X, and G/O is the homotopy fiber of BO → BG (the classifying space for stable spherical fibrations). The map [X, G/O] → L_* is the surgery obstruction map. The synthetic proof of exactness uses the fact that the space of normal invariants [X, G/O] classifies normal maps up to normal bordism, and the surgery obstruction vanishes if and only if the normal map is normally bordant to a homotopy equivalence. The s-cobordism theorem, which identifies the structure set with the set of h-cobordism classes, is proved synthetically using the handlebody decomposition of h-cobordisms, encoded as a higher inductive type with cells corresponding to handles. The Whitehead torsion τ(W) ∈ Wh(π₁(X)) is defined as the class of the chain complex of the universal cover in the projective class group. The synthetic classification of exotic spheres (e.g., Milnor's 7-spheres) follows by computing the surgery obstruction map for X = S^n and identifying the kernel with the group of homotopy spheres Θ_n, which fits into the exact sequence 0 → bPn+1 → Θ_n → Coker J_n → 0, where bPn+1 is the subgroup of spheres bounding parallelizable manifolds and J_n is the image of the J-homomorphism π_n(O) → π_n^S.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Brown Representability Theorem and the Classification of Generalized Cohomology Theories

The Brown representability theorem states that any contravariant functor F : Ho(Spaces)op → Sets that sends coproducts to products and satisfies the Mayer-Vietoris axiom is representable by a spectrum. In synthetic HoTT, the ∞-category of spaces is the ∞-topos of types, and spectra are sequential spectra (or symmetric spectra) internal to the ∞-topos. A generalized cohomology theory is a sequence of functors E^n : Typeop → AbGrp satisfying the Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms (homotopy invariance, exactness for cofiber sequences, additivity for coproducts). The synthetic Brown representability theorem constructs a spectrum E representing a given cohomology theory by defining E_n := F(S^n) for n ≥ 0 and extending to negative n using the suspension isomorphism. The structure maps Σ E_n → En+1 are the adjoints of the suspension isomorphisms E^n(X) ≅ En+1(Σ X). The key synthetic step is verifying that the resulting spectrum is an Ω-spectrum, i.e., the adjoint maps E_n → Ω En+1 are equivalences. This follows from the exactness axiom applied to the cofiber sequence S^n → * → Sn+1, which gives a fiber sequence of representing objects. The classification of generalized cohomology theories up to equivalence is then equivalent to the classification of spectra up to stable equivalence. The synthetic Adams representability theorem extends this to homology theories: any covariant functor F : Ho(Spaces) → AbGrp preserving coproducts and satisfying the Mayer-Vietoris axiom is representable by a spectrum. The proof uses the duality between the ∞-category of spectra and its opposite via the Spanier-Whitehead dual. A critical application is the classification of multiplicative cohomology theories (ring spectra). A ring structure on a cohomology theory corresponds to an E_∞-ring spectrum structure on the representing spectrum. The synthetic construction of the Lazard ring and the universal formal group law shows that complex-oriented cohomology theories (those with a choice of Thom class for complex vector bundles) are classified by maps from the Lazard ring to the coefficient ring E^*. This recovers Quillen's theorem that the formal group law of complex cobordism MU is universal. In HoTT, MU is constructed as the Thom spectrum of the universal complex vector bundle over BU, which is a higher inductive type. The complex orientation is a map Σ^∞_+ ℂP^∞ → MU, and the formal group law arises from the multiplication ℂP^∞ × ℂP^∞ → ℂP^∞.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Goodwillie Derivatives of the Identity and the Stable Homology of Automorphism Groups

The Goodwillie calculus approximates functors between ∞-categories by polynomial functors. The identity functor Id : Spaces_* → Spaces_* on pointed spaces has a Taylor tower whose layers are the derivatives of the identity ∂_n Id. In synthetic HoTT, the n-th derivative ∂_n Id is a spectrum with an action of the symmetric group Σ_n, constructed as the homotopy fiber of the map from the n-excisive approximation P_n Id to the (n-1)-excisive approximation Pn-1 Id, evaluated on the sphere S0. The synthetic construction uses the cross-effect functor cr_n Id(X1, ..., X_n) defined as the total fiber of the n-cube of functors Id(∨i∈S X_i). The derivative is ∂_n Id := cr_n Id(S0, ..., S0). In HoTT, the partition complex is a higher inductive type whose cells correspond to partitions of the set. The Σ_n-action is strict. The Goodwillie derivatives of the identity enter via the scanning map Emb(D2, Σ_g) → Map_*(Σ_g, S2) and the identification of the layers of the embedding calculus tower with the derivatives of the identity. The synthetic proof constructs the scanning map as a map of higher inductive types and uses the fact that the Taylor tower of the identity converges on the sphere S2 to identify the stable homology with the homology of the infinite loop space of the sphere spectrum.

The Synthetic Brown Representability Theorem and Cohomology Theories in HoTT

In the ∞‑topos of types, a reduced cohomology theory is a functor E from the ∞‑category of pointed types to the ∞‑category of abelian groups that sends wedges to products and cofiber sequences to exact sequences. The synthetic Brown representability theorem asserts that every such theory is represented by a spectrum object: a sequence of pointed types Eₙ equipped with equivalences Eₙ ≃ ΩEₙ₊₁. The proof proceeds by first constructing the representing type for each integer degree. For a fixed n, the functor X ↦ Eⁿ(X) is a homotopy invariant functor that preserves limits; by the ∞‑categorical Yoneda lemma it is corepresented by a type Eₙ. The suspension isomorphism Eⁿ(X) ≃ Eⁿ⁺¹(ΣX) then yields the required equivalences Eₙ ≃ ΩEₙ₊₁. The crucial step is to verify that the resulting prespectrum satisfies the Ω‑spectrum condition, which follows from the exactness axiom applied to the cofiber sequence X → * → ΣX. In HoTT this argument is fully internal: the construction of Eₙ uses higher inductive types to form the classifying space of the cohomology theory, and the equivalences are given by path induction on the suspension. The theorem also yields a classification of multiplicative cohomology theories: a ring structure on E corresponds to an E∞-ring spectrum structure on the representing spectrum, which can be expressed as a sequence of maps Eₘ × Eₙ → Eₘ₊ₙ satisfying associativity and commutativity up to coherent homotopy. This synthetic approach avoids the classical set‑theoretic machinery of model categories and provides a direct computational interpretation: the representing types are built as higher inductive types whose constructors correspond to the operations of the cohomology theory.

The Synthetic Tate Construction, Norm Maps, and Cyclotomic Spectra in HoTT

For a finite group G acting on a type X, the homotopy orbits XₕG and homotopy fixed points XʰG are defined as the colimit and limit of the action diagram. The norm map N : XₕG → XʰG is the canonical map induced by the transfer; its cofiber is the Tate construction XᵗG. In synthetic HoTT, XᵗG is a higher inductive type with constructors for the action of G, a point for each orbit, and a path identifying the norm of the basepoint with the basepoint in the fixed points. This definition makes the fiber sequence XₕG → XʰG → XᵗG a definitional cofiber sequence. When X is a spectrum (a sequence of types with loop equivalences), the Tate construction inherits a spectrum structure. The cyclotomic structure on topological Hochschild homology THH(R) of a ring spectrum R is a family of genuine Cₚ-equivariant maps φₚ : THH(R) → THH(R)ᵗCₚ for each prime p. In HoTT, THH(R) is constructed as a higher inductive type encoding the cyclic bar construction, and the Frobenius φₚ is defined by the universal property of the Tate construction applied to the Cₚ-action coming from the cyclic symmetry. The target THH(R)ᵗCₚ is not a ring spectrum in the naive sense but a cyclotomic spectrum; the ring structure on topological cyclic homology TC(R) arises from the homotopy limit of the diagram … → THH(R)ᵗCₚⁿ → THH(R)ᵗCₚⁿ⁻¹ → …. The synthetic proof that TC(R) is an E∞-ring spectrum uses the fact that the norm maps are compatible with the multiplicative structure on THH(R), which is itself a consequence of the higher inductive definition of the cyclic bar construction. This internal treatment makes the cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) a map of E∞-ring spectra directly in type theory.

Encode‑Decode for the Tate Construction
Let G = C₂ act on the circle S¹ by reflection. Compute the homotopy groups of the Tate construction (S¹)ᵗC₂ in degrees 0 and 1.
The action of C₂ on S¹ has fixed points S⁰ (two points). The homotopy orbits (S¹)ₕC₂ are the Borel construction EC₂ ×C₂ S¹, which is a circle bundle over BC₂ ≃ ℝP∞ with fiber S¹. Its homotopy groups are π₀ = 0, π₁ = ℤ ⋊ C₂ (the semidirect product where the generator of C₂ acts by inversion on ℤ). The homotopy fixed points (S¹)ʰC₂ are the mapping space MapC₂(EC₂, S¹); since EC₂ is contractible, this is equivalent to the fixed points S⁰, so π₀ = ℤ/2, π₁ = 0. The norm map N : (S¹)ₕC₂ → (S¹)ʰC₂ induces on π₀ the map 0 → ℤ/2 (zero) and on π₁ the map ℤ ⋊ C₂ → 0. The Tate construction is the cofiber, so its homotopy groups fit into the long exact sequence … → π₁((S¹)ʰC₂) → π₁((S¹)ᵗC₂) → π₀((S¹)ₕC₂) → π₀((S¹)ʰC₂) → …. Substituting gives 0 → π₁((S¹)ᵗC₂) → 0 → ℤ/2 → π₀((S¹)ᵗC₂) → 0. Hence π₁((S¹)ᵗC₂) = 0 and π₀((S¹)ᵗC₂) = ℤ/2.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the homotopy groups of a Tate construction, first identify the homotopy orbits and homotopy fixed points separately using the Borel construction and fixed‑point subspace. Write down the long exact sequence of the cofiber sequence XₕG → XʰG → XᵗG. The norm map is often zero on low degrees for reflection actions; check the action on the fundamental group. The answer is then read off from the exact sequence without needing to construct the Tate HIT explicitly.

The Synthetic Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy Theorem and Algebraic K‑Theory in HoTT

The Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy theorem states that for a nilpotent extension of ring spectra A → B (i.e., the fiber I satisfies Iⁿ = 0 for some n), the relative algebraic K‑theory fiber K(A) → K(B) is equivalent to the relative topological cyclic homology fiber TC(A) → TC(B). In synthetic HoTT, algebraic K‑theory K(R) is defined as the group completion of the ∞‑category of perfect R-modules, which can be constructed as a higher inductive type whose objects are finite projective modules and whose morphisms are equivalences. The cyclotomic trace K(R) → TC(R) is a map of E∞-ring spectra induced by the universal property of group completion applied to the cyclotomic structure on THH(R). The nilpotence hypothesis ensures that the relative THH and TC are nilpotent extensions as well, and the Goodwillie calculus of the identity functor on spaces identifies the layers of the relative K‑theory and TC towers with the same derivatives of the identity. The synthetic proof proceeds by constructing the Goodwillie tower of the functor R ↦ K(R) and R ↦ TC(R) internally: the n-excisive approximation Pₙ is defined as a higher inductive type that freely adds n-cube colimits. The derivatives ∂ₙK and ∂ₙTC are then computed as the fibers of Pₙ → Pₙ₋₁ evaluated on the sphere spectrum. Because the cyclotomic trace is an equivalence on the derivatives (both are the Spanier–Whitehead dual of the partition complex with symmetric group action), the map of towers is an equivalence on each layer. The nilpotence condition guarantees convergence of both towers, yielding the desired equivalence of fibers. This argument is fully formalizable in cubical type theory because all constructions — perfect modules, group completion, Goodwillie approximations — are higher inductive types with computable path structures.

The Synthetic Six‑Functor Formalism and Purity in Motivic HoTT

In motivic homotopy theory, the six functors f_*, f^*, f_!, f^!, ⊗, Hom for a morphism f : X → Y of motivic types are defined internally in the ∞‑topos of motivic spaces. The functors f_! and f^! are the left and right adjoints of f^* and f_* respectively, and they exist because the ∞‑topos is locally presentable and the morphism f is a geometric morphism. The tensor product ⊗ is the smash product of motivic spectra, and Hom is the internal mapping spectrum. The purity theorem states that for a smooth closed immersion i : Z → X of codimension c, there is a canonical equivalence i^! ≃ i^* ⊗ Th(NZ/X), where Th(NZ/X) is the Thom space of the normal bundle. In synthetic motivic HoTT, the deformation to the normal cone is a higher inductive type DZ/X with constructors for the zero section Z × 𝔸¹ → D, the inclusion of the normal bundle NZ/X → D, and a homotopy between them over 𝔸¹ {0}. This HIT provides a motivic homotopy equivalence between the Thom space of the normal bundle and the cofiber of the inclusion Z → X, which is exactly the purity isomorphism. The proof does not require classical scheme theory; it uses only the internal language of the ∞‑topos and the fact that 𝔸¹-homotopy invariance is enforced by localizing at the projection X × 𝔸¹ → X. The six‑functor formalism then follows from the adjunctions between the slice ∞‑topoi, and the projection formula f_!(A ⊗ f^*B) ≃ f_!A ⊗ B is a direct consequence of the cartesian closed structure. This synthetic approach makes the purity theorem a computable equivalence of higher inductive types, enabling formal verification of motivic cohomology calculations.

The Synthetic Milnor Conjecture and the Norm Residue Isomorphism in HoTT

The Milnor conjecture, proved by Voevodsky, asserts that for a field k of characteristic not 2, the Galois cohomology ring H^*(Gal(k), ℤ/2) is isomorphic to the Milnor K‑theory ring K^M_*(k)/2. In motivic HoTT, this is proved by identifying the motivic cohomology of the point Spec k with Milnor K‑theory. The motivic Steenrod algebra Amot acts on motivic cohomology, and the key computation is that the motivic cohomology of a point is the polynomial algebra ℤ/2[τ, ρ] modulo the relation τ² = 0, where τ corresponds to the class of -1 in K^M1(k)/2 and ρ corresponds to the class of a uniformizer. The norm residue isomorphism generalizes this to higher primes p (the Bloch–Kato conjecture): H^*(Gal(k), μ_p⊗*) ≃ K^M_*(k)/p. In synthetic motivic HoTT, the proof constructs the motivic Adams spectral sequence converging to the motivic stable homotopy groups of spheres, and identifies the E₂-page with the cohomology of the motivic Steenrod algebra. The motivic Steenrod operations are defined as higher inductive types encoding the action of the motivic Dyer–Lashof algebra on the motivic Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum Hℤ/p. The vanishing of certain differentials follows from the weight arguments that are internal to the motivic homotopy category. The final step uses the fact that the motivic cohomology of a point is the Milnor K‑theory, which is proved by constructing an explicit equivalence between the motivic Eilenberg–MacLane space K(ℤ/p, n) and the higher inductive type representing the Milnor K‑group. This equivalence is compatible with the Steenrod operations, yielding the norm residue isomorphism as an equivalence of ring spectra in the motivic stable homotopy category.

The Synthetic Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen Theorem and the Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres

The Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen theorem identifies the stable homotopy groups of spheres with the homology of the infinite symmetric group: πₖˢ(S⁰) ≃ Hₖ(BΣ∞; ℤ) for k ≥ 0. In synthetic HoTT, this equivalence is constructed by exhibiting an equivalence between the sphere spectrum 𝕊 and the suspension spectrum of the classifying space of the ∞‑group Σ∞ = colimₙ Σₙ. The key higher inductive type is the free ∞‑group on one generator, which is equivalent to the integers ℤ as an ∞‑group. Its delooping Bℤ is the circle S¹, and the infinite symmetric group Σ∞ is the free ∞‑group on a 0‑type with two elements, i.e., the free ∞‑group on S⁰. The synthetic proof proceeds by constructing the group completion of the ∞‑monoid of finite sets and bijections, which is a higher inductive type with constructors for the empty set, disjoint union, and the group completion paths. The resulting ∞‑group is Σ∞, and its classifying space BΣ∞ is the colimit of the classifying spaces BΣₙ. The sphere spectrum 𝕊 is defined as the suspension spectrum of S⁰, i.e., the sequential colimit Σ^∞S⁰ = colimₙ ΣⁿS⁰. The equivalence 𝕊 ≃ Σ^∞BΣ∞ is then established by showing that both sides represent the same stable homotopy functor on the ∞‑category of types. The computational content of this equivalence is profound: it reduces the computation of stable homotopy groups of spheres to the homology of symmetric groups, which admits a combinatorial description via the Barratt‑Eccles operad. In Cubical Agda, the group completion HIT has been formalized, and the equivalence with the sphere spectrum has been verified up to low degrees, providing a synthetic proof of the isomorphism π₁ˢ ≃ ℤ/2, π₂ˢ ≃ ℤ/2, π₃ˢ ≃ ℤ/24. The synthetic approach also clarifies the role of the Dyer‑Lashof operations on the homology of Σ∞, which correspond to the Steenrod operations on the sphere spectrum under the equivalence.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of Classifying Spaces for ∞‑Groups and Universal Characteristic Classes

For any ∞‑group G in the ∞‑topos of types, the classifying space BG is defined as the higher inductive type with a single point constructor base : BG and a loop constructor loop : G → Ω(BG, base) that is an equivalence of ∞‑groups. This HIT directly encodes the universal property: maps X → BG correspond to principal G‑bundles over X. The universal principal G‑bundle EG → BG is constructed as the homotopy fiber of the point inclusion base : 1 → BG, yielding a contractible type EG with a free G‑action. Universal characteristic classes are then maps BG → K(A, n) for abelian ∞‑groups A, i.e., elements of Hⁿ(BG; A). In synthetic HoTT, the Chern‑Weil homomorphism is constructed internally by differentiating the ∞‑group G to its Lie algebra 𝔤 (when G is a cohesive ∞‑group), forming the Weil algebra W(𝔤), and using the synthetic de Rham complex to produce characteristic classes in real cohomology. For discrete ∞‑groups, characteristic classes are obtained via the group cohomology Hⁿ(BG; A), which is computed as the cohomology of the classifying space. The synthetic construction of the universal Stiefel‑Whitney classes wᵢ : BO(n) → K(ℤ/2, i) proceeds by identifying BO(n) as the classifying space of the orthogonal ∞‑group O(n), which is the automorphism ∞‑group of the standard inner product space ℝⁿ. The classes wᵢ are then defined as the pullbacks of the universal classes along the map BO(n) → BO induced by the inclusion O(n) → O. The Pontryagin classes pᵢ : BO(n) → K(ℤ, 4i) are constructed similarly using the complexification map BO(n) → BU(n) and the Chern classes c₂ᵢ : BU(n) → K(ℤ, 4i). In Cubical Agda, the classifying space BG for a finite group G has been formalized as a higher inductive type with constructors for the group elements and the group laws, and the universal bundle EG has been shown to be contractible. This synthetic approach makes the characteristic classes computable: for example, the first Chern class c₁ : BU(1) → K(ℤ, 2) is an equivalence, and the second Chern class c₂ : BU(2) → K(ℤ, 4) can be computed on specific bundles via the encode‑decode method.

Encode‑Decode for Classifying Spaces
Let G be a finite group presented as a set with multiplication and inverses. Construct the classifying space BG as a higher inductive type with base : BG and paths corresponding to the group elements. Prove that the loop space Ω(BG, base) is equivalent to G as an ∞‑group.
Define BG by the constructors: base : BG, and for each g : G a path loop(g) : base = base, with higher paths enforcing loop(g·h) = loop(g) ⬝ loop(h), loop(e) = refl, and loop(g⁻¹) = loop(g)⁻¹. The encode‑decode method defines a family Code : BG → Type by Code(base) = G and transporting along loop(g) acts by left multiplication by g. The encode function maps a path p : base = x to transport(p, e) : Code(x). The decode function is defined by induction on BG: at base it is the identity on G, and along loop(g) it uses the path constructor of the identity type. One proves that encode and decode are inverses, establishing Ω(BG, base) ≃ G. The ∞‑group structure on Ω(BG, base) corresponds to the group structure on G via this equivalence.
Exam Strategy: Classifying Spaces in HoTT
When asked to construct BG for an ∞‑group G, always specify the HIT constructors: a base point and a loop for each element of G (or a single loop constructor loop : G → ΩBG if G is a type). The universal property "maps X → BG ≃ principal G‑bundles over X" is the defining feature — use it to derive characteristic classes as maps BG → K(A, n). Remember that for cohesive ∞‑groups, the Chern‑Weil map factors through the de Rham coefficient object ♭dR BG.

The Synthetic Adams Conjecture and the Image of the J‑Homomorphism in HoTT

The Adams conjecture, proved by Quillen and Sullivan, states that the J‑homomorphism J : πₖ(O) → πₖˢ becomes trivial after applying the Adams operations ψ^q − 1 for q coprime to the order of the torsion. In synthetic HoTT, the J‑homomorphism is constructed as the map induced by the inclusion of the orthogonal ∞‑group O = colimₙ O(n) into the stable orthogonal ∞‑group O^st = Ω^∞𝕊, which is the ∞‑group of units of the sphere spectrum. The Adams operations ψ^q are defined on the K‑theory spectrum KU as the maps induced by the q‑th power operations on vector bundles. In the synthetic setting, KU is constructed as the higher inductive type representing the group completion of the ∞‑monoid of finite‑dimensional complex vector spaces, and ψ^q is the map induced by the q‑th tensor power. The Adams conjecture is then the statement that the composite (ψ^q − 1) ∘ J : πₖ(O) → πₖ(KU) is null for q coprime to the torsion order. The synthetic proof uses the Adams spectral sequence for the sphere spectrum, whose E₂‑page is ExtA(𝔽₂, 𝔽₂) where A is the Steenrod algebra. The J‑homomorphism corresponds to the map of Adams spectral sequences induced by the map of ring spectra 𝕊 → KO. The Adams operations act on the E₂‑page, and the conjecture follows from the fact that the image of J lies in the kernel of ψ^q − 1 on the E₂‑page. The image of J is then identified as the cyclic summands of πₖˢ of order the denominator of B2k/4k, where B2k are Bernoulli numbers. In synthetic HoTT, this is computed by analyzing the fiber of the map 𝕊 → KO and using the synthetic Adams‑Novikov spectral sequence with coefficients in the Morava K‑theories. The computational content is that the image of J in πₖˢ is non‑zero exactly when k ≡ 0, 1, 3, 7 mod 8, and its order is given by the denominator of the Bernoulli number. This synthetic approach has been partially formalized in Cubical Agda for low degrees, verifying the image of J in π₁ˢ through π₇ˢ.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Join Construction, the Hopf Invariant, and the Kervaire Invariant One Problem

The join of two types X and Y is the higher inductive type X * Y with constructors inl : X → X * Y, inr : Y → X * Y, and for each x : X, y : Y a path join(x, y) : inl(x) = inr(y). The join is equivalent to the suspension of the smash product: X * Y ≃ Σ(X ∧ Y). The Hopf construction takes a multiplication map μ : X × X → X on a connected type X and produces a map h(μ) : Σ(X ∧ X) → ΣX. When X is an H‑space, this map is the Hopf invariant one map. The Hopf invariant one problem asks for which n the Hopf invariant of a map S²ⁿ⁻¹ → Sⁿ can be 1. Adams proved using the Adams spectral sequence that this happens only for n = 1, 2, 4, 8. In synthetic HoTT, the Hopf invariant is defined for any map f : Σ(X ∧ X) → ΣX by considering the cofiber sequence X ∧ X → ΣX → C_f and the induced map on cohomology. The synthetic proof of the Hopf invariant one theorem uses the synthetic Adams spectral sequence with coefficients in the mod 2 Steenrod algebra. The key step is showing that the Steenrod square Sqⁿ acts non‑trivially on the cohomology of the mapping cone only when n = 1, 2, 4, 8. The Kervaire invariant one problem asks for which dimensions n there exists a framed manifold of Kervaire invariant 1. The solution by Hill, Hopkins, and Ravenel uses the equivariant Adams spectral sequence for the group C₂ acting on the sphere spectrum. In synthetic HoTT, the Kervaire invariant is defined as the Arf invariant of the quadratic refinement of the intersection form on the middle homology of a framed manifold. The synthetic proof constructs the Hill‑Hopkins‑Ravenel spectrum Ω as a higher inductive type with a C₂‑action, and shows that the map 𝕊 → Ω induces an isomorphism on homotopy groups up to a certain range, but the Kervaire invariant element θⱼ ∈ π2j+1−2ˢ maps to zero in π2j+1−2(Ω) for j ≥ 7. This proves that the Kervaire invariant is zero for all dimensions except possibly 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, and 126. The synthetic approach makes the equivariant Adams spectral sequence computable by representing the C₂‑spectrum Ω as a higher inductive type with constructors for the C₂‑action and the norm maps.

The Synthetic Blakers‑Massey Theorem for n‑Cubes and Its Applications to Goodwillie Calculus

The classical Blakers‑Massey theorem gives the connectivity of the map from the homotopy pushout of a square to the homotopy pullback. The higher Blakers‑Massey theorem generalizes this to n‑cubes: for an n‑cube of types that is k‑cartesian (i.e., each face is a homotopy pullback up to connectivity k), the total fiber is (n·k)-connected. In synthetic HoTT, an n‑cube is a functor from the poset of subsets of {1,…,n} to types. The theorem is proved by induction on n using the encode‑decode method on the total fiber. The base case n = 2 is the classical Blakers‑Massey theorem, which has been formalized in the HoTT library. The inductive step uses the fact that an (n+1)‑cube can be viewed as a map of n‑cubes, and the connectivity of the total fiber of the map is the sum of the connectivities of the total fibers of the domain and codomain n‑cubes. This synthetic proof is entirely constructive and yields a computational interpretation: the total fiber of a k‑cartesian n‑cube is an (n·k)-type, meaning its homotopy groups vanish above degree n·k. The application to Goodwillie calculus is immediate: the n‑th layer of the Goodwillie tower of a functor F is the n‑th cross‑effect, which is an n‑cube. The Blakers‑Massey theorem for n‑cubes implies that the n‑th cross‑effect is (n·k)-connected if F is k‑excisive. This gives the convergence of the Goodwillie tower for analytic functors. In synthetic HoTT, the derivative of a functor F at a type X is defined as the spectrum ∂F(X) = colimₙ ΩⁿF(X ∨ Sⁿ), and the Goodwillie tower is the Taylor tower of F. The synthetic Blakers‑Massey theorem for n‑cubes provides the connectivity estimates needed to prove that the Taylor tower converges to F for sufficiently connected types. This has been formalized in Cubical Agda for the identity functor and the suspension functor, verifying the convergence of the Goodwillie tower for these cases.

  • Confusing the Barratt‑Priddy‑Quillen theorem (𝕊 ≃ Σ^∞BΣ∞) with the Kahn‑Priddy theorem (stable splitting of Ω^∞Σ^∞X): the former identifies the sphere spectrum with the group completion of finite sets, the latter splits the infinite loop space of a suspension spectrum.
  • Assuming the classifying space BG for an ∞‑group G is always a 1‑type: BG is an (n+1)‑type if G is an n‑type; for discrete groups it is a 1‑type, but for higher groups it has higher homotopy.
  • Thinking the Adams operations ψ^q act on the sphere spectrum directly: they act on K‑theory (KU, KO), and the Adams conjecture relates the J‑homomorphism to the action on K‑theory.
  • Believing the Hopf invariant one problem is solved by the Hopf fibrations alone: the Hopf fibrations give maps of Hopf invariant 1 for n = 1, 2, 4, 8, but Adams' theorem proves no other dimensions admit such maps.
  • Overlooking the role of the C₂‑action in the Hill‑Hopkins‑Ravenel proof of the Kervaire invariant: the spectrum Ω is a genuine C₂‑spectrum, and the proof uses the equivariant Adams spectral sequence, not the classical one.
  • Treating the higher Blakers‑Massey theorem as a mere generalization of the square case: the n‑cube version is essential for Goodwillie calculus because the n‑th cross‑effect is an n‑cube, not a square.
  • Assuming the synthetic Blakers‑Massey theorem requires classical logic: the proof in HoTT is constructive and uses only the encode‑decode method and the higher inductive types for pushouts and pullbacks.

The Synthetic Brown Representability Theorem in HoTT

The Brown representability theorem states that any reduced cohomology theory on the homotopy category of pointed connected CW‑complexes is representable by a spectrum. In synthetic HoTT the theorem is internalised: a reduced cohomology theory is a functor from the ∞‑category of pointed types to abelian groups that sends homotopy pushouts to pullbacks and respects suspension. The synthetic proof constructs a representing spectrum as a sequential colimit of higher inductive types. One begins with a type E₀ representing the degree‑zero part of the theory; for each n a higher inductive type Eₙ₊₁ is defined as the homotopy fiber of the map Eₙ → ΩEₙ₊₁ induced by the suspension isomorphism. The colimit E = colimₙ Eₙ carries a natural Ω‑spectrum structure, and the Yoneda lemma in the ∞‑topos of types yields a natural equivalence between the given cohomology theory and the mapping spectrum Map(−,E). The proof uses only the encode‑decode method for the identity type, the existence of homotopy pushouts (given by higher inductive types), and the fact that the ∞‑topos of types is presentable. No classical choice principles are required; the construction is fully constructive and computes in Cubical Agda. The representing spectrum is unique up to equivalence, and its homotopy groups are precisely the coefficients of the cohomology theory. This synthetic version has been formalised for ordinary cohomology with coefficients in any set‑level abelian group, and for K‑theory via the higher inductive type of vector bundles.

The Synthetic Milnor Exact Sequence for Homotopy Limits

Given a tower of types ⋯ → X₂ → X₁ → X₀ in HoTT, the homotopy limit holim Xₙ is defined as the type of coherent sequences (x₀,x₁,…) with paths pₙ : fₙ(xₙ₊₁) = xₙ. The Milnor exact sequence relates the homotopy groups of the limit to the derived limits of the homotopy groups of the tower. For each k there is a short exact sequence 0 → lim¹ₙ πₖ₊₁(Xₙ) → πₖ(holim Xₙ) → limₙ πₖ(Xₙ) → 0. In synthetic HoTT the sequence is proved by constructing a fiber sequence holim Xₙ → ∏ₙ Xₙ → ∏ₙ Xₙ where the second map is (xₙ) ↦ (xₙ − fₙ(xₙ₊₁)). Applying the long exact sequence of homotopy groups and identifying the kernel and cokernel with the derived functors lim and lim¹ yields the result. The derived limits are computed internally as the homotopy groups of the total fiber of the map of towers ∏ Xₙ → ∏ Xₙ. Because HoTT works in an ∞‑topos, the derived functors are automatically the correct homotopical ones; no model‑category machinery is needed. The proof is constructive and has been formalised in Cubical Agda for towers of n‑types. An important corollary is that if the tower satisfies the Mittag‑Leffler condition on πₖ₊₁ (i.e. the images of the maps eventually stabilise), then lim¹ₙ πₖ₊₁(Xₙ) = 0 and πₖ(holim Xₙ) ≃ limₙ πₖ(Xₙ). This criterion is used in the synthetic computation of the homotopy groups of the sphere spectrum via the Adams tower.

Encode‑Decode on a Tower
Let Xₙ = S¹ for all n with bonding maps the degree‑2 map z ↦ z². Compute π₁(holim Xₙ) and π₀(holim Xₙ) using the synthetic Milnor exact sequence.
