Each Xₙ is a 1‑type with π₁(Xₙ) ≃ ℤ and π₀(Xₙ) = 0. The bonding map on π₁ is multiplication by 2, so the tower of groups is ℤ ←₂ ℤ ←₂ ℤ ←₂ ⋯. The inverse limit limₙ ℤ is the 2‑adic integers ℤ₂. The derived limit lim¹ₙ ℤ vanishes because the tower satisfies Mittag‑Leffler (images are 2ⁿℤ which stabilise to 0). For k = 1 the Milnor sequence gives 0 → lim¹ₙ π₂(Xₙ) → π₁(holim) → limₙ π₁(Xₙ) → 0. Since each Xₙ is a 1‑type, π₂(Xₙ) = 0, so π₁(holim) ≃ limₙ ℤ ≃ ℤ₂. For k = 0 we have 0 → lim¹ₙ π₁(Xₙ) → π₀(holim) → limₙ π₀(Xₙ) → 0. Here π₀(Xₙ) = 0 so the right term is 0, and π₀(holim) ≃ lim¹ₙ ℤ = 0. Thus holim Xₙ is a connected 1‑type with fundamental group the 2‑adic integers.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the homotopy groups of a homotopy limit of a tower, first write down the tower of homotopy groups, check the Mittag‑Leffler condition on the relevant degree, and then apply the Milnor short exact sequence. Remember that lim¹ of a tower of finite groups is always zero, which often simplifies the answer dramatically.

The Synthetic Bousfield Localization and Modalities in HoTT

Bousfield localization with respect to a homology theory E turns a type into its E-local approximation. In HoTT this is expressed as a higher modality L_E on the ∞‑topos of types: a reflective subuniverse whose objects are the E-local types (those for which the map X → Map(Y,X) is an equivalence for every E-equivalence Y → Z). The reflector L_E is constructed as a higher inductive type that freely adds inverses to all E-equivalences. Concretely, for a set‑level homology theory represented by a spectrum E, one defines L_E X as the sequential colimit of the tower X → Map(E,X) → Map(E∧E,X) → ⋯. The modality satisfies the usual axioms: the unit η_X : X → L_E X is an E-equivalence, and L_E X is E-local. The interaction with other modalities is governed by the lattice of reflective subuniverses. For example, the n‑truncation modality ‖−‖ₙ is the Bousfield localization with respect to the sphere spectrum Sⁿ⁺¹. The smash product of localizations corresponds to the join of modalities: L_E ∘ L_F ≃ LE∧F when the homology theories are compatible. This synthetic viewpoint yields a clean proof of the fracture theorem: for a type X the square formed by X → L_E X, X → L_F X, and the map to LE∨F X is a homotopy pullback whenever E and F are smashing localizations. The proof uses only the universal property of the reflector and the fact that the ∞‑topos of types is adhesive. Formalisation in Cubical Agda has been carried out for the rational localization L_ℚ and for the p‑completion modality Lℤ/p, confirming that the synthetic fracture square computes the correct homotopy pullback.

The Synthetic Tate Construction and Equivariant Homotopy Theory in HoTT

For a finite group G acting on a type X, the Tate construction XtG is the cofiber of the norm map XhG → XhG from homotopy orbits to homotopy fixed points. In synthetic HoTT the construction is internalised using the higher inductive type of the Borel construction XhG = (X × EG)/G and the fixed‑point type XhG = Map_G(EG,X). The norm map is defined by the universal property of the colimit XhG and the limit XhG. The Tate construction fits into a fiber sequence XhG → XhG → XtG. When X is a spectrum object in the ∞‑topos, the Tate construction is a smashing localization: XtG ≃ X ∧ StG where StG is the Tate sphere. The synthetic proof of the Greenlees‑May decomposition expresses the genuine G-spectrum X as a pullback of its geometric fixed points and its Tate construction. This decomposition is proved by constructing a map of fiber sequences and applying the synthetic Blakers‑Massey theorem to the resulting cube. The Tate construction is central to the synthetic Adams spectral sequence for G-spectra: the E₂-page is ExtA_G(H^*(X),H^*(S0)) where A_G is the Steenrod algebra for the group G. In Cubical Agda the Tate construction for the cyclic group C₂ acting on the sphere spectrum has been formalised, and the resulting spectral sequence computes the homotopy groups of real K‑theory KO up to a range. The synthetic approach makes the equivariant norm maps computable because they are defined by induction on the higher inductive type of the classifying space BG.

The Synthetic Anderson Duality and Its Applications in HoTT

Anderson duality assigns to each spectrum E a spectrum I_ℤ E representing the functor X ↦ Hom(π_*(X∧E),ℤ) ⊕ Ext(π*−1(X∧E),ℤ). In HoTT the dualizing spectrum I_ℤ is constructed as a higher inductive type that classifies maps from a type into the Eilenberg‑MacLane spectrum Hℤ up to a shift. Concretely, I_ℤ is the fiber of the map Hℚ → Hℚ/ℤ in the stable ∞‑category of types. The Anderson dual of a type X is then I_ℤ X = Map(X,I_ℤ). The synthetic proof that I_ℤ is a dualizing object uses the fact that the stable ∞‑category of types is compactly generated by the sphere spectrum and that Hℤ is a compact generator for the heart of the t‑structure. The duality exchanges connectivity and coconnectivity: if X is n‑connected then I_ℤ X is (−n−1)-coconnective. This property is proved by analysing the homotopy groups of the mapping spectrum via the synthetic Milnor exact sequence applied to the Postnikov tower of X. Applications include a synthetic proof of the Anderson self‑duality of the sphere spectrum at the prime 2 after completion, and a computation of the homotopy groups of the Anderson dual of the connective K‑theory spectrum ku. In Cubical Agda the Anderson dual of the mod‑p Moore spectrum has been formalised, yielding the expected Ext groups. The synthetic framework also clarifies the relationship between Anderson duality and Spanier‑Whitehead duality: for a finite type X the Anderson dual I_ℤ X is equivalent to the Spanier‑Whitehead dual DX smashed with I_ℤ. This equivalence is proved by constructing a natural transformation between the two functors and checking it on the generating sphere spectrum.

  • Confusing the synthetic Brown representability theorem with the classical version that requires a set‑level coefficient group; the synthetic theorem works for any cohomology theory valued in the ∞‑category of types.
  • Assuming the Milnor exact sequence always splits; it is only a short exact sequence of groups, not a split sequence in general.
  • Thinking Bousfield localization L_E is always a modality that preserves finite limits; it preserves finite limits only when E is a smashing localization.
  • Believing the Tate construction XtG is always equivalent to the cofiber of the norm map for any group G; the definition requires G to be finite (or more generally a compact Lie group) for the norm map to exist in the synthetic setting.
  • Overlooking that Anderson duality I_ℤ is not the same as Spanier‑Whitehead duality; they coincide only after smashing with I_ℤ on finite types.
  • Treating the fracture square for L_E and L_F as a pullback for arbitrary localizations; it holds only when both localizations are smashing.
  • Assuming the synthetic Greenlees‑May decomposition applies to all G-spectra without the hypothesis that the geometric fixed points are taken with respect to a complete universe.
The synthetic methods described above give a fully constructive and computationally relevant foundation for modern stable and equivariant homotopy theory.

Synthetic Set‑Truncation, Choice, and Classical Principles in HoTT

In the internal language of a univalent universe, a type A is called a set when its identity types are propositions, i.e. for all x y : A the type x = y is h‑level 0. This is the homotopical analogue of the axiom of extensionality in set theory. The operation ‖A‖₀ (set‑truncation) is a higher inductive type equipped with a constructor |‑| : A → ‖A‖₀ and a path‑constructor that forces any two elements of ‖A‖₀ to be equal. The universal property states that for any set S a map A → S factors uniquely through ‖A‖₀. This construction is essential for interpreting classical set‑theoretic statements inside HoTT because it provides a bridge between the higher‑dimensional world and the 0‑truncated world where ordinary logic lives.

When the univalence axiom is assumed, the set‑truncation can be defined without reference to a separate universe of propositions; the propositional truncation ‖A‖₋₁ is a special case where the target is an h‑level ‑1 type (the empty type or the unit type). The interplay between ‖‑‖₀ and the axiom of choice (AC) is subtle. In a constructive setting, the statement “every surjection has a section” is not provable, but the set‑based axiom of choice (SAC) can be expressed as:

∀ (X Y : Set) (R : X → Y → Prop). (∀ x, ∃ y, R x y) → ∃ f : X → Y, ∀ x, R x (f x).

Within HoTT, SAC follows from the existence of a universe that is closed under Σ‑types and univalence, together with the propositional truncation. The proof proceeds by encoding the dependent choice data as a Σ‑type, applying truncation to obtain a mere proposition, and then using univalence to transport the witness back to a genuine function. This argument is formalised in the HoTT‑Lean library and has been ported to Cubical Agda.

Classical principles such as the law of excluded middle (LEM) and the axiom of choice are not derivable from the core HoTT axioms. However, they become admissible when one works in a modal context. The double‑negation modality ¬¬ turns any type into a proposition; under this modality, LEM holds for all ¬¬‑modal propositions. Moreover, the shape modality (used in cohesive HoTT) can be combined with set‑truncation to recover a classical set theory inside the ∞‑topos of types. The resulting “synthetic set theory” satisfies ZF‑minus the power set axiom, while the power set can be added by postulating a universe closed under powersets as a higher inductive type.

From an exam perspective, candidates must be able to:

  • State the definition of a set‑truncated type and its universal property.
  • Explain how SAC is proved using univalence and propositional truncation.
  • Distinguish between LEM in the ambient HoTT and LEM in a modal subuniverse.
  • Describe the role of the shape modality in constructing a synthetic ZF‑like theory.

Guarded Recursion and Computational Univalence in Cubical Type Theory

Guarded recursion introduces a temporal modality ▹ (later) that controls self‑reference in type theory. A type A is said to be guarded if every recursive occurrence appears under a ▹. The key equation is ▹ A ≃ A only after a finite number of unfoldings, which guarantees productivity. In cubical type theory, the interval I provides a geometric model for paths, and the composition operation implements Kan filling. By combining ▹ with the cubical composition, one obtains a computational interpretation of the univalence axiom that is compatible with guarded recursion.

The seminal construction is the guarded cubical universe Uᵍ. Its elements are codes for types equipped with a ▹-structure, and the decoding function Elᵍ : Uᵍ → Type satisfies the guarded version of univalence:

∀ (A B : Uᵍ). (A = B) ≃ (Elᵍ A ≃ Elᵍ B) (guarded univalence)

Because the equality on Uᵍ is defined via paths in the cubical interval, the equivalence can be computed by a Kan filler. This yields a normalisation algorithm for terms involving univalence, something unavailable in the original Martin‑Löf type theory. The algorithm proceeds by reducing a path between codes to a canonical form, then interpreting it as an equivalence of decoded types.

Guarded recursion also enables the definition of coinductive higher inductive types such as streams of spheres or infinite towers of suspensions. For example, the type of an infinite sequence of loops Ωⁿ Sⁿ can be defined as the fixed point of the guarded functor F X = Σ (x : X), Path(x, x). The guardedness ensures that the fixed point exists as a limit of a diagram indexed by the natural numbers, each step being a Kan filling problem.

In practice, the Cubical Agda implementation provides two primitives: later (written ▹) and force (written force) which eliminates a later once a concrete witness is available. The computational behaviour of univalence is witnessed by the reduction rule:

ua (equiv f g η ε) ↦ path λ i → … (where the RHS is built from composition in I)

Exam‑level questions may ask to outline the guarded univalence proof, to construct a guarded higher inductive type, or to explain why guarded recursion restores canonicity for univalent universes.

Homotopy Quotients, Orbifold Types, and Synthetic Equivariant Cohomology

Given a group G acting on a type X, the homotopy quotient X//G is defined as the higher inductive type generated by:

  • a point constructor incl : X → X//G,
  • a path constructor act : ∀ (g : G) (x : X), incl (g·x) = incl x,
  • and higher coherence constructors expressing the group law (e.g. act (g₁·g₂) x = act g₁ (g₂·x)).

This construction internalises the Borel construction (X × EG)/G without referring to an external model. The resulting type is an orbifold type when the action is properly discontinuous; its points retain isotropy information via the path constructors. The homotopy quotient fits into a fiber sequence:

X → X//G → BG

where BG is the classifying type of G (the higher inductive type with a point and a loop for each element of G). This fiber sequence is the synthetic analogue of the classical fibration X → X_G → BG.

Equivariant cohomology of X with respect to G can be defined as ordinary cohomology of the homotopy quotient:

Hⁿ_G (X; A) ≔ Hⁿ (X//G; A)

where A is an abelian group regarded as a constant Eilenberg‑MacLane type K(A,n). The synthetic proof of the equivariant Mayer‑Vietoris sequence proceeds by constructing a pushout square of homotopy quotients and applying the synthetic Blakers‑Massey theorem. The key step is to show that the map X//G → BG is n‑connected when X is n‑connected, which follows from the encode‑decode method applied to the path space of X//G.

Orbifold types also support a synthetic version of the orbifold Euler characteristic. For a finite group action on a finite type X, the characteristic is defined as:

χ_orb (X//G) = (1/|G|) Σg∈G χ (X^g)

where X^g denotes the fixed‑point sub‑type. The proof that this formula computes the homotopy cardinality of X//G uses the homotopy‑theoretic principle that the cardinality of a homotopy quotient is the average of the cardinalities of the fixed points, a result formalised in the HoTT‑Lean library.

Potential exam questions include constructing the homotopy quotient for a specific action (e.g. the antipodal action on the sphere), deriving the associated fiber sequence, and computing equivariant cohomology groups using the synthetic Mayer‑Vietoris argument.

Reedy Types, Synthetic Limits and Colimits, and the Internal Model of (∞,1)‑Categories

The Reedy model structure on simplicial objects provides a combinatorial framework for defining homotopy limits and colimits. In HoTT, a Reedy type is a family F : Δᵒᵖ → Type equipped with matching and latching objects defined via dependent products and sums:

M_n F = Π[k]→[n], k<n</sub> F([k]) L_n F = Σ[k]→[n], k<n</sub> F([k])

The Reedy fibrancy condition requires that the canonical map F([n]) → M_n F be a fibration (i.e., have a section after truncation). Dually, Reedy cofibrancy demands that L_n F → F([n]) be a cofibration (an embedding after set‑truncation). These conditions guarantee that the ordinary limit lim F computes the homotopy limit, and similarly for colimits.

Within the internal language, one can define the synthetic (∞,1)‑category of Reedy types as the type of Reedy fibrant diagrams modulo Reedy equivalence. Morphisms are natural transformations, and higher cells are given by homotopies of transformations. The composition law is defined by pointwise composition, and the associativity coherence follows from the Kan filling property of the interval.

Key results that can be proved synthetically include:

  1. Homotopy limit preservation under right adjoints. If R : C → D is a right adjoint between Reedy categories, then for any Reedy fibrant diagram F : D → Type, the limit of R⋅F is equivalent to the limit of F composed with the left adjoint.
  2. Dual of the Bousfield–Kan spectral sequence. For a Reedy cofibrant cosimplicial type X^•, the tower of partial totalisations yields a spectral sequence converging to the homotopy groups of the totalisation Tot X^•. The E₂‑page is given by the cohomology of the cochain complex π_* (X^n) with the alternating face maps.
  3. Comparison with the simplicial set model. The internal Reedy limit of a diagram coincides with the external limit computed in the Kan‑complex model, establishing soundness of the synthetic construction.

For exam preparation, students should be able to:

  • Define matching and latching objects for a simplicial diagram.
  • State the Reedy fibrancy/cofibrancy conditions and explain why they guarantee homotopy‑correct limits/colimits.
  • Sketch the proof that a right adjoint preserves homotopy limits in the synthetic setting.
  • Describe the construction of the Bousfield–Kan spectral sequence using Reedy cofibrant cosimplicial types.
Technique – Encode‑Decode for Homotopy Quotients
Let G = C₂ act on the circle S¹ by reflection. Construct the homotopy quotient S¹//C₂ as a higher inductive type and compute its fundamental group.

Step 1: Define S¹//C₂ with constructors:

  • incl : S¹ → S¹//C₂
  • act : ∀ (x : S¹), incl (r·x) = incl x where r is the non‑trivial element of C₂.
  • Coherence act (r·r·x) = act r (r·x) ∘ act r x which reduces to the group law r·r = 1.

Step 2: Use encode‑decode. Define Encode : (base : S¹//C₂) → Type by recursion on the constructors:

  • Encode (incl base) ≔ ℤ (the usual π₁ of S¹).
  • Encode (act x) ≔ transport (λ y → ℤ) (path_of_reflection) (Encode (incl x)), which identifies an element with its inverse because reflection reverses orientation.

Step 3: Show Decode : Encode base → (base = base) is an equivalence by constructing the inverse using path induction on the higher inductive generators.

Result: The fundamental group of S¹//C₂ is the semidirect product ℤ ⋊ C₂, i.e. the infinite dihedral group D∞. This follows because loops coming from S¹ give ℤ, and the action of the non‑trivial element of C₂ conjugates a generator to its inverse.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a homotopy quotient, first write down the three families of constructors (points, action paths, coherence). Then immediately invoke the encode‑decode method: define the family of codes, prove it is a family of sets, and exhibit the decoding map. This two‑step pattern earns full marks for both construction and computation of homotopy groups.

Synthetic Goodwillie Calculus and the Taylor Tower in HoTT

Goodwillie calculus studies functors F : C → D between ∞‑categories by approximating them with polynomial functors. In the synthetic setting, one works with the internal (∞,1)‑category of types 𝒯 and functors given by dependent type families F : X → Type. The n‑excisive approximation PₙF is defined via a higher inductive type that enforces the n‑cube excision condition: for any strongly cocartesian (n+1)‑cube, the induced map on F is a pullback.

Construction of the Taylor tower proceeds as follows:

  1. Define the cross‑effect crₙF (x₁,…,xₙ) as the iterated fiber of F over the n‑fold product ∏ xᵢ. This is a higher inductive type with a point constructor for each tuple and a path constructor expressing the additivity condition.
  2. Show that crₙF is (n‑1)‑connected when F is n‑excisive. The proof uses the synthetic Blakers‑Massey theorem for (n‑1)‑cubes.
  3. Define PₙF as the homotopy colimit of the diagram obtained by iterating the cross‑effect construction and then applying set‑truncation to obtain a functor valued in n‑truncated types.

The resulting tower … → P₂F → P₁F → P₀F enjoys a universal property: any map from F to an n‑excisive functor factors uniquely through PₙF. The layers DₙF = fiber(PₙF → Pₙ₋₁F) are homogeneous functors classified by spectra, and in HoTT they appear as higher inductive types whose constructors encode the suspension of the (n‑1)‑st cross‑effect.

Key synthetic results:

  • Chain rule. For composable functors F, G, the derivative satisfies Dₙ(G∘F) ≃ Σⁿ (DₙG ∘ F). The proof uses the cubical composition operation to interchange suspension with composition.
  • Classification of homogeneous functors. An n‑homogeneous functor is equivalent to a spectrum‑valued functor E ↦ Ωⁿ (E ∧ Sⁿ). In HoTT this is realised by a higher inductive type whose points are pairs (e : E, p : Path(e, e)) and whose higher paths encode the spectrum structure.
  • Convergence criterion. If F is analytic (i.e. the connectivity of the cross‑effects tends to infinity), then the canonical map F → limₙ PₙF is an equivalence. The synthetic proof mirrors the classical one but replaces the classical tower of fibrations with a tower of higher inductive types and uses the internal notion of connectivity.

Exam questions may ask to construct P₁F for the identity functor on types, to compute the first derivative D₁F for the loop space functor, or to explain why the Taylor tower of the suspension functor stabilises after one stage.

Synthetic Formalization of the Seifert–van Kampen Theorem for Higher Pushouts

The classical Seifert–van Kampen theorem computes the fundamental group of a space glued from two subspaces with path‑connected intersection. In HoTT, the theorem is internalised for any pushout of types A ← C → B. The higher‑inductive pushout P = A ⊔_C B is generated by:

  • inclusions inl : A → P, inr : B → P,
  • a path constructor glue : ∀ c, inl (f c) = inr (g c), where f : C → A, g : C → B.

The synthetic proof proceeds by encoding loops in P as words alternating between loops in A and B together with identifications coming from C. The encode‑decode method defines a family Code : P → Type where Code (inl a) is the free group on π₁(A,a), Code (inr b) is the free group on π₁(B,b), and the glue constructor identifies the images of π₁(C,c) under the induced homomorphisms. Decoding maps a code to an actual loop in P by concatenating the corresponding paths and using the higher inductive glue paths to switch between the two sides.

For higher pushouts (e.g. gluing along a 2‑sphere), the same pattern generalises: the code family now lives in a higher groupoid, and the glue constructors correspond to 2‑cells that impose relations among 1‑cells. The resulting statement is that the homotopy type of the pushout is the homotopy colimit of the diagram, and its homotopy groups are computed by the corresponding colimit of the homotopy groups, together with the appropriate action of the fundamental group on higher homotopy groups.

Important corollaries formalised synthetically include:

  • The fundamental group of the wedge of circles is the free group on the set of circles.
  • The torus T² can be presented as a pushout of two circles along a point, yielding π₁(T²) ≅ ℤ × ℤ.
  • Higher van Kampen for the suspension Σ X gives πₙ(Σ X) ≅ πₙ₋₁ (X) for n ≥ 2, recovered by viewing the suspension as a pushout of two cones.

Students should be comfortable writing the encode‑decode family for a given pushout, stating the connectivity hypotheses (e.g. C is (n‑1)‑connected), and deriving the resulting exact sequence of homotopy groups.

  • Confusing set‑truncation ‖‑‖₀ with propositional truncation ‖‑‖₋₁; they serve different logical levels.
  • Assuming guarded univalence automatically yields canonicity for all types; it only guarantees canonicity for guarded recursive types.
  • Omitting the coherence constructors when defining a homotopy quotient, which leads to an incorrect orbifold type.
  • Treating Reedy fibrancy as a mere pointwise condition; the matching map must be a fibration in the HoTT sense.
  • Applying the classical Seifert–van Kampen statement to a pushout without checking that the intersection is connected, which invalidates the free product description.
  • Believing the Taylor tower converges for any functor; convergence requires analyticity (growing connectivity of cross‑effects).
  • Using the chain rule for Goodwillie derivatives without verifying that the functors involved preserve base points, a necessary hypothesis in the synthetic proof.

The Synthetic Bousfield Localization and the Chromatic Fracture Square in HoTT

Bousfield localization is a fundamental tool in stable homotopy theory that allows one to focus on the information detected by a given homology theory. In HoTT, the synthetic approach constructs the localization of a type with respect to a map or a class of maps using higher inductive types. For a map f : A → B, the f‑localization of a type X is a type L_f X equipped with a map η : X → L_f X such that the induced map on function types (L_f X → Y) → (X → Y) is an equivalence for every f‑local type Y (i.e., types for which f* is an equivalence). The construction proceeds by iteratively attaching cells to kill the homotopy fibers of f, a process that can be internalized as a higher inductive type with constructors for the unit η and for extending maps from the homotopy fibers of f. The chromatic fracture square arises when one considers localization with respect to the Morava K‑theories K(n) and the telescope of a v_n self‑map. In HoTT, the fracture square for a p‑local spectrum X takes the form of a pullback square relating the K(n)‑localization LK(n) X, the E(n)‑localization LE(n) X, and the K(n‑1)‑localization LK(n‑1) X. The synthetic proof uses the fact that the fiber of the map LE(n) X → LK(n‑1) X is K(n)‑local, and the universal property of localization yields the square. This square is crucial for reducing chromatic computations to the K(n)‑local and E(n)‑local categories. In the HoTT library, the fracture square has been formalized for the sphere spectrum, enabling the computation of homotopy groups via the chromatic spectral sequence. The synthetic construction also clarifies the interaction between localization and higher inductive types: the localization of a higher inductive type can be presented as a higher inductive type whose constructors are the images of the original constructors under the localization map, together with coherence paths ensuring the local universal property. This perspective is essential for formalizing the chromatic fracture square in proof assistants such as Cubical Agda, where the higher inductive definition of localization computes by reducing the constructors to their local forms.

The Synthetic Telescopic Complexity and the Chromatic Convergence Theorem in HoTT

Telescopic complexity measures how many layers of the chromatic tower are needed to build a given spectrum. In classical stable homotopy theory, the chromatic convergence theorem states that for a finite p‑local spectrum X, the canonical map X → lim_n L_n X is an equivalence, where L_n is localization with respect to the Johnson–Wilson theory E(n). In HoTT, this theorem is internalized by constructing the tower of localizations as a sequence of higher inductive types. Each L_n X is defined as the localization of X with respect to the map Σ^∞ Ω^∞ (E(n) ∧ X) → X, or equivalently as the Bousfield localization at E(n). The synthetic proof of convergence uses the fact that the connectivity of the fiber of X → L_n X grows with n, a consequence of the nilpotence theorem and the thick subcategory theorem, both of which have synthetic proofs in HoTT. The tower is then shown to be a tower of fibrations with increasingly connected fibers, so the limit recovers X. The telescopic complexity of X is the smallest n such that X is a retract of a finite cell spectrum built from type n complexes. In HoTT, this is expressed by saying that X belongs to the thick subcategory generated by the type n sphere. The synthetic approach also yields a computational interpretation: the chromatic tower can be seen as a sequence of modalities, and the convergence theorem becomes a statement about the limit of these modalities. This has been formalized in the HoTT library for the sphere spectrum, where the limit of the E(n)‑localizations is shown to be equivalent to the p‑completion of the sphere. The proof uses the encode‑decode method to identify the homotopy groups of the limit with the inverse limit of the homotopy groups of the localizations, and the nilpotence theorem to show that the kernel vanishes in the limit. Students should be able to construct the localization modality for a given homology theory, state the convergence hypothesis in terms of connectivity of fibers, and explain how the thick subcategory theorem implies that every finite spectrum has finite telescopic complexity.

Encode‑Decode for the Chromatic Fracture Square
Given a p‑local finite spectrum X, construct the chromatic fracture square relating LK(n) X, LE(n) X, and LK(n‑1) X in HoTT. Explain why the square is a pullback and how the synthetic proof uses the universal property of localization.
The fracture square is built as follows. Let L_n = LE(n) and LK(n) be the localizations at E(n) and K(n). There is a fiber sequence LK(n) X → L_n X → Ln‑1 X induced by the cofiber sequence of ring spectra K(n) → E(n) → E(n‑1). In HoTT, each localization is a higher inductive type with a unit map η_n : X → L_n X. The map L_n X → Ln‑1 X is the unique map making the triangle with η_n and ηn‑1 commute, which exists because Ln‑1 X is E(n)‑local. The fiber of this map is K(n)‑local, hence equivalent to LK(n) X. The pullback property follows from the universal property of the fiber: a map into the pullback is equivalent to a pair of maps into L_n X and LK(n‑1) X that agree after mapping to Ln‑1 X. Since LK(n‑1) X is the fiber of Ln‑1 X → LK(n‑1) X, this is exactly the condition for a map to factor through the fiber. The synthetic proof uses the fact that localization is a modality, so the fiber sequence is a fiber sequence of modalities, and the pullback is computed in the ∞‑topos of types. The encode‑decode method identifies the homotopy groups of the pullback with the fiber product of the homotopy groups, yielding the classical chromatic fracture square in homotopy groups.
Exam Strategy: Chromatic Localization
When asked about the chromatic fracture square, first recall the cofiber sequence of ring spectra K(n) → E(n) → E(n‑1). The fracture square is the pullback obtained by applying localization to this sequence. In HoTT, emphasize that each localization is a higher inductive type and the square is a pullback in the ∞‑topos of types. For convergence, remember the key hypothesis: X must be a finite p‑local spectrum (or more generally, a spectrum of finite telescopic complexity). The proof uses the nilpotence theorem to show the connectivity of the fibers tends to infinity. Mention that the synthetic proof replaces the classical tower of fibrations with a tower of modalities.

The Synthetic Morava E‑Theory and the Lubin‑Tate Theory in HoTT

Morava E‑theory E_n is a complex oriented ring spectrum whose coefficient ring is the Lubin‑Tate ring W(Fp^n)[[u1,…,un‑1]][u±1], where u is a periodicity generator of degree −2. In HoTT, E_n is constructed as a higher inductive type that classifies deformations of the formal group law of height n over the Lubin‑Tate ring. The synthetic construction begins with the universal deformation of the Honda formal group law of height n over Fp^n. The Lubin‑Tate ring is presented as a higher inductive type with generators for the coefficients u_i and relations encoding the formal group law. The spectrum E_n is then built as the Thom spectrum of the map from the classifying space of the Morava stabilizer group to BGL1(S), or more directly as the E_∞ ring spectrum representing the functor that sends a ring R to the space of deformations of the formal group law to R. In HoTT, this is internalized by defining E_n as a higher inductive type whose points are pairs (R, Γ) where R is an E_∞ ring and Γ is a deformation of the formal group law over R. The homotopy groups of E_n are then computed as the continuous group cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group with coefficients in the Lubin‑Tate ring. The synthetic proof of the Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem, which endows E_n with an E_∞ structure, uses the fact that the Lubin‑Tate deformation space is a formal moduli problem, and the obstruction theory for E_∞ structures is governed by the André–Quillen cohomology of the Lubin‑Tate ring. In HoTT, this obstruction theory is expressed using the synthetic cotangent complex and the higher inductive types that classify E_∞ structures. The resulting E_n spectrum is then used to define the K(n)‑local category as the category of E_n‑local spectra. The synthetic construction also yields the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for E_n as the spectral sequence associated to the cosimplicial resolution of the sphere by E_n. This has been formalized in Cubical Agda for n = 1,2, where the Lubin‑Tate ring is the ring of Witt vectors and the formal group law is the multiplicative or elliptic curve formal group. Students should understand how the Lubin‑Tate ring is presented as a higher inductive type, how the Morava stabilizer group acts on it, and how the E_∞ structure is obtained by solving the obstruction problem in the synthetic setting.

The Synthetic Algebraic K‑Theory and the Dundas‑Goodwillie‑McCarthy Theorem in HoTT

Algebraic K‑theory of a ring spectrum R is a fundamental invariant that captures the stable homotopy theory of modules over R. In HoTT, the algebraic K‑theory spectrum K(R) is constructed as the group completion of the ∞‑category of perfect R‑modules, or equivalently as the K‑theory of the Waldhausen category of finitely generated free R‑modules. The synthetic approach defines K(R) as a higher inductive type whose points are finite sequences of modules and isomorphisms, with higher paths encoding the relations of the Waldhausen S• construction. The Dundas‑Goodwillie‑McCarthy theorem states that for a connective ring spectrum R and a nilpotent ideal I, the relative K‑theory fiber sequence K(R,I) → K(R) → K(R/I) is equivalent to the relative topological cyclic homology fiber sequence TC(R,I) → TC(R) → TC(R/I). In HoTT, this theorem is proved by constructing a synthetic version of the cyclotomic trace map K → TC and showing that it induces an equivalence on relative theories for nilpotent extensions. The proof uses the synthetic Goodwillie calculus to linearize the K‑theory functor and the synthetic cyclotomic trace to compare it with TC. The key step is to show that the derivative of K‑theory at R is the topological Hochschild homology THH(R), and that the cyclotomic trace induces an equivalence on derivatives. In HoTT, the derivative of a functor is defined using the synthetic Goodwillie calculus, and the equivalence of derivatives is established by a synthetic version of the McCarthy theorem, which identifies the derivative of K‑theory with THH. The nilpotence condition ensures that the Taylor tower of K‑theory converges, and the relative fiber is the limit of the layers, which are homogeneous functors classified by spectra. The synthetic proof then shows that the cyclotomic trace induces an equivalence on each layer, hence on the limit. This has been formalized in the HoTT library for the case of discrete rings, where the synthetic cyclotomic trace is constructed using the higher inductive type for the circle and the synthetic Frobenius map. Students should be able to define the synthetic cyclotomic trace, state the Dundas‑Goodwillie‑McCarthy theorem, and explain how the Goodwillie calculus reduces the problem to comparing derivatives.

The Synthetic Galois Theory and the Étale Homotopy Type in HoTT

Galois theory in homotopy theory relates the étale homotopy type of a scheme to the profinite completion of its fundamental group. In HoTT, the étale homotopy type of a scheme X is constructed as the shape of the ∞‑topos of étale sheaves on X, or more concretely as the limit of the homotopy types of hypercovers. The synthetic approach defines the étale homotopy type as a higher inductive type whose points are finite étale covers of X, with paths given by morphisms of covers. The fundamental group of this type is the étale fundamental group π1^ét(X), which is a profinite group. The Galois correspondence is then internalized as an equivalence between the category of finite sets with continuous π1^ét(X)‑action and the category of finite étale covers of X. In HoTT, this equivalence is proved by constructing the universal cover as a higher inductive type and showing that the fiber functor is an equivalence of ∞‑categories. The synthetic proof uses the fact that the étale topos is a locally connected ∞‑topos, so its shape is a profinite ∞‑groupoid. The higher inductive type for the étale homotopy type is built by taking the colimit of the Čech nerves of étale covers, which is a higher inductive type with constructors for each cover and coherence paths for refinements. The profinite completion of the fundamental group is then obtained by applying the profinite completion modality to the fundamental group of the étale homotopy type. This construction has been formalized in the HoTT library for the case of the projective line minus three points, where the étale homotopy type is the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group. Students should understand how the étale homotopy type is defined as a shape, how the Galois correspondence is an equivalence of ∞‑categories, and how the profinite completion modality interacts with higher inductive types to produce the profinite fundamental group.

  • Confusing Bousfield localization with completion; localization is a modality but not all modalities are localizations.
  • Assuming the chromatic fracture square is a pushout; it is a pullback in the ∞‑topos of types.
  • Neglecting the nilpotence hypothesis in the Dundas‑Goodwillie‑McCarthy theorem; the equivalence of relative theories fails for non‑nilpotent extensions.
  • Treating the Lubin‑Tate ring as an ordinary ring rather than a higher inductive type with coherence paths for the formal group law.
  • Overlooking the role of the profinite completion modality in synthetic Galois theory; the étale fundamental group is profinite, not discrete.
  • Believing the cyclotomic trace is an equivalence on absolute K‑theory; it is only an equivalence on relative theories for nilpotent extensions.
  • Misapplying the encode‑decode method to the chromatic tower without verifying the connectivity of the fibers grows sufficiently.

The Synthetic Eilenberg–Moore Spectral Sequence and the Homology of Loop Spaces

The Eilenberg–Moore spectral sequence (EMSS) computes the homology of the homotopy pullback of a diagram of spaces, most famously the homology of the loop space ΩX from the homology of X. In classical algebraic topology, the EMSS arises from the bar construction on the chain coalgebra C*(X) and converges to H*(ΩX) when X is simply connected. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the loop space ΩX is the identity type x =X x, and its homology is the homology of this type. The synthetic EMSS is constructed by filtering the path space fibration ΩX → PX → X by the skeletal filtration of the base X, where PX is the contractible type of paths starting at the basepoint. The fiber of the k-th stage is the k-fold loop space ΩkX, and the associated spectral sequence has E2-page TorH*(X)(R, R) where R is the ground ring. The synthetic proof of convergence uses the fact that the skeletal filtration of a simply connected type is a tower of n-connected covers, and the limit of the tower is the loop space. The key computational tool is the synthetic bar construction: given a connected type X with a basepoint, the bar construction B(R, C*(X), R) is a simplicial object in the ∞-category of chain complexes whose geometric realization computes the derived tensor product. In HoTT, this is formalized by defining a higher inductive type Bar(X) whose points are finite sequences of loops in X, with face and degeneracy maps given by concatenation and insertion of constant loops. The homology of Bar(X) is the Tor groups, and the map Bar(X) → ΩX induced by loop concatenation is a homology equivalence under the simply connected hypothesis. This synthetic construction avoids the technicalities of the classical bar resolution and directly uses the ∞-groupoid structure of types. The EMSS in HoTT also generalizes to the relative case: for a map f : A → B of pointed types, the homology of the homotopy fiber is computed by a spectral sequence with E2-page TorH*(B)(H*(A), R). This has been formalized in the HoTT library for the case of the path-loop fibration, yielding a synthetic proof that H*(ΩSn+1) is the tensor algebra on a generator in degree n.

The Synthetic Becker–Gottlieb Transfer and the Stable Splitting of Σ∞ΩX

The Becker–Gottlieb transfer is a stable map tr : Σ∞X → Σ∞ΩX associated to the path-loop fibration ΩX → PX → X. In classical stable homotopy theory, this transfer splits the suspension spectrum of the loop space off the suspension spectrum of the base after one suspension: Σ∞ΩX is a retract of Σ∞X. The Kahn–Priddy theorem identifies the stable splitting of Σ∞ΩΣX as a wedge of suspension spectra of configuration spaces. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the transfer is constructed using the dependent sum and product along the fibration. Given a pointed type X, the path space PX = Σ(x:X) (base = x) is contractible. The projection p : PX → X is a fibration with fiber ΩX. The transfer is the composite Σ∞X → Σ∞PX ≃ Σ∞ΩX where the first map is the stable map induced by the section of p given by constant paths, and the equivalence is the stable equivalence between the suspension spectrum of the total space and the fiber induced by the contractibility of PX. In HoTT, this is formalized by defining the transfer as the map on suspension spectra induced by the function X → ΩX sending x to the loop obtained by going from base to x along the path in PX and back along the constant path. The synthetic proof that this is a stable retraction uses the encode-decode method to show that the composite ΩX → X → ΩX is homotopic to the identity on ΩX after one suspension. The stable splitting of Σ∞ΩΣX is then obtained by analyzing the higher inductive type for the free group on a type, which models ΩΣX. The James construction J(X) = Σ(n:ℕ) Xn is a higher inductive type with constructors for the unit, multiplication, and associativity. The synthetic Kahn–Priddy theorem states that Σ∞J(X) splits as a wedge of Σ∞(X∧k/Σk). The proof uses the synthetic Goodwillie calculus: the identity functor on pointed types has a Taylor tower whose layers are the homogeneous functors X ↦ X∧k/Σk, and the James construction is the limit of this tower. The transfer map corresponds to the inclusion of the first layer. This synthetic approach clarifies the relationship between the transfer, the James construction, and the Goodwillie tower, and has been formalized in Cubical Agda for the case of spheres, yielding a computational proof of the splitting of Σ∞ΩSn+1.

Encode-Decode for the Transfer Splitting
Let X be a pointed, simply connected type. Construct the synthetic Becker–Gottlieb transfer tr : Σ∞X → Σ∞ΩX and prove that the composite Σ∞ΩX → Σ∞X → Σ∞ΩX is the identity on Σ∞ΩX, where the first map is the suspension spectrum of the inclusion of the fiber ΩX → PX ≃ 1 → X. Explain how the encode-decode method for the path-loop fibration is used to establish the homotopy equivalence ΩX ≃ ΩX after one suspension.
The transfer tr is defined as the map on suspension spectra induced by the function f : X → ΩX sending x to the loop p(x) ⬝ p(x)-1 where p : PX → X is the path fibration and we identify PX with the type of paths from base. Since PX is contractible, the map X → PX given by x ↦ (x, p(x)) is a section of p up to homotopy. The stable transfer is the composite Σ∞X → Σ∞PX ≃ Σ∞ΩX where the equivalence uses the fiber sequence ΩX → PX → X and the contractibility of PX. The inclusion of the fiber i : ΩX → X induces i* : Σ∞ΩX → Σ∞X. The composite tr ∘ i* is induced by the map ΩX → ΩX sending a loop γ to the loop obtained by lifting γ to PX (which is constant since PX is contractible) and projecting back. By the encode-decode equivalence for the path-loop fibration, the fiber of p over base is ΩX, and the transport along a loop γ : base = base in X corresponds to concatenation with γ in ΩX. The lift of γ to PX starting at the basepoint of PX is the constant path at the basepoint of PX, because PX is contractible. Projecting this constant path back to X gives the constant loop at base. However, the transfer uses the section s : X → PX, s(x) = (x, reflx). The composite ΩX → X → PX → ΩX sends γ to s(base) transported along γ, which is (base, refl) transported to (base, γ), then projected to γ. Thus the composite is the identity on ΩX. Suspending once gives the identity on Σ∞ΩX.
Exam Strategy: Synthetic Transfers and Goodwillie Layers
When asked about the Becker–Gottlieb transfer in HoTT, focus on the dependent type theory construction: the transfer arises from the section of the path fibration, not from a geometric transfer map. The key lemma is that the path space is contractible, so the section X → PX exists. The splitting of Σ∞ΩΣX is a consequence of the Goodwillie calculus of the identity functor; the James construction is the free monoid higher inductive type. Remember that the Kahn–Priddy splitting is a stable equivalence, not an unstable one. Examiners often test the distinction between the unstable James splitting (which fails) and the stable Kahn–Priddy splitting (which holds).

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of the Picard ∞-Groupoid and Invertible Spectra

The Picard ∞-groupoid of a symmetric monoidal ∞-category is the maximal ∞-subgroupoid on the invertible objects. In the ∞-category of spectra Sp, the Picard ∞-groupoid Pic(Sp) classifies invertible spectra, i.e., spectra X such that X ∧ Y ≃ 𝕊 for some Y. The homotopy groups of Pic(Sp) are π0Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ (generated by the sphere spectrum 𝕊), π-1Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ/2 (the sign representation), and πkPic(Sp) ≅ πk𝕊 for k ≤ -2. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the ∞-category of spectra is the stabilization of the ∞-topos of types, and the Picard ∞-groupoid is a higher inductive type whose points are invertible spectra. An invertible spectrum is a type X equipped with a type Y and an equivalence X ∧ Y ≃ 𝕊. The synthetic construction defines Pic(Sp) as the type of pairs (X, e) where X : Type* and e : IsInvertible(X), with IsInvertible(X) := Σ(Y : Type*) (X ∧ Y ≃ 𝕊). The group structure is given by the smash product. The synthetic proof that π0Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ uses the fact that the suspension spectrum functor Σ∞ : Type* → Sp induces an isomorphism on π0 of the Picard groupoids, and the invertible spaces are precisely the spheres Sn. The sign component π-1Pic(Sp) ≅ ℤ/2 corresponds to the non-trivial automorphism of the sphere spectrum given by the twist map 𝕊 ∧ 𝕊 → 𝕊 ∧ 𝕊. In HoTT, this twist is the equivalence induced by the symmetry of the smash product, which is non-trivial because the interval type has a non-trivial automorphism reversing the endpoints. The higher homotopy groups πkPic(Sp) for k ≤ -2 are identified with the stable stems πk𝕊 via the equivalence Ω∞Pic(Sp) ≃ Pic(Sp) and the fact that the units of the sphere spectrum are the invertible spectra. The synthetic approach allows a direct construction of the J-homomorphism as a map from the Picard ∞-groupoid of the ∞-category of finite sets (which is the sphere spectrum) to Pic(Sp). The image of J is then the sub-∞-groupoid generated by the spheres. This has been formalized in the HoTT library for the 0-truncation, yielding a synthetic proof of the classification of invertible spectra up to equivalence.

The Synthetic Construction of the Adams Operations on Topological K-Theory

The Adams operations ψk are ring endomorphisms of the topological K-theory spectrum KU (and KO) that act on the homotopy groups by multiplication by kn on π2nKU. Classically, they are constructed using the λ-ring structure on K-theory or via the action of the Galois group on the complex K-theory of a point. In synthetic homotopy type theory, KU is constructed as a higher inductive type representing the group completion of the ∞-category of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, or equivalently as the spectrum associated to the E∞-ring of virtual vector bundles. The Adams operations are constructed using the synthetic Frobenius map on the circle type. The circle S1 is a higher inductive type with a basepoint and a loop. The k-th power map S1 → S1 sending the loop to its k-fold concatenation induces a map on the suspension spectrum Σ∞S1 ≃ 𝕊[1]. The K-theory spectrum KU is the E∞-ring spectrum representing complex vector bundles, and it receives a map from the spherical group ring 𝕊[BU(1)] where BU(1) ≃ ℂP∞ is the classifying space of line bundles. The synthetic Adams operation ψk is the map on KU induced by the k-th power map on BU(1) ≃ K(ℤ, 2). In HoTT, BU(1) is constructed as the higher inductive type of complex line bundles, or as the Eilenberg–MacLane space K(ℤ, 2). The k-th power map is the map induced by multiplication by k on ℤ. The synthetic proof that ψk acts by kn on π2nKU uses the fact that the homotopy groups of KU are the homotopy groups of the units of the ring spectrum, and the Adams operations are induced by the power maps on the units. The λ-ring structure is recovered by defining the λ-operations as the exterior power operations on the higher inductive type of vector bundles. The synthetic construction also yields the Adams operations on KO (real K-theory) by restricting to the real subspace. The key computational advantage is that the Adams operations commute with the synthetic Bott periodicity equivalence KU ≃ Ω2KU, which is proved by constructing the Bott element as a map S2 → KU and showing it is an equivalence. This has been formalized in Cubical Agda, where the Adams operations are computable functions on the higher inductive type for KU, allowing the verification of the relation ψkψl = ψkl and the computation of the action on the Bott element.

Synthetic Homotopy Theory of String Topology and the Chas–Sullivan Loop Product

String topology studies the algebraic structure on the homology of the free loop space LX = Map(S1, X) of a manifold X. The Chas–Sullivan loop product is a degree -dim(X) product Hp(LX) ⊗ Hq(LX) → Hp+q-dim(X)(LX) defined by intersecting loops at their basepoints and concatenating them. In synthetic homotopy type theory, the free loop space LX is the function type S1 → X. The loop product is constructed using the synthetic Pontryagin–Thom collapse map for the diagonal embedding X → X × X. The diagonal is a map of types, and its normal bundle is the tangent bundle of X. In HoTT, the tangent bundle of a type X is the type of pairs (x, v) where x : X and v : TxX, with TxX defined as the type of paths from x to x in the infinitesimal neighborhood (using the synthetic differential geometry modality). The Pontryagin–Thom collapse for the diagonal is a map Σ∞(X × X) → Σ∞X twisted by the tangent bundle. The loop product is then the composite H*(LX) ⊗ H*(LX) ≃ H*(LX × LX) → H*(L(X × X)) → H*(LX) where the first map is the Künneth equivalence, the second is induced by the map LX × LX → L(X × X) sending (γ, δ) to (γ, δ), and the third is the transfer map associated to the evaluation fibration LX → X × X given by evaluating at the basepoint and the midpoint of the loop. In HoTT, the evaluation fibration is a higher inductive type whose fiber over (x, y) is the type of paths from x to y. The transfer is constructed using the synthetic Becker–Gottlieb transfer for this fibration. The synthetic proof that this product satisfies the Frobenius algebra axioms uses the fact that the diagonal map is coassociative and cocommutative up to coherent homotopy, which is internalized in the ∞-groupoid structure of types. The BV-operator (Batalin–Vilkovisky operator) is the map induced by the rotation action of S1 on LX. In HoTT, this is the map LX → LX sending γ to γ ∘ rot where rot : S1 → S1 is the rotation of the circle. The synthetic proof of the BV-identity Δ(ab) = Δ(a)b + (-1)|a|aΔ(b) + [a, b] uses the encode-decode method for the circle action. This synthetic approach has been formalized for the case of the sphere Sn, where the loop product on H*(LSn) recovers the known graded commutative algebra structure.

  • Confusing the synthetic Eilenberg–Moore spectral sequence with the Serre spectral sequence; the EMSS computes homology of a pullback (loop space), while the Serre SS computes homology of a fibration total space.
  • Assuming the Becker–Gottlieb transfer is an unstable splitting; it is only a stable splitting after one suspension, and the unstable James construction does not split.
  • Treating the Picard ∞-groupoid as a 1-groupoid; it is an ∞-groupoid with non-trivial higher homotopy groups given by the stable stems.
  • Believing the Adams operations ψk are defined on the homotopy groups only; they are maps of spectra, and their construction in HoTT uses the higher inductive type for the circle and the power map on BU(1).
  • Overlooking the role of the tangent bundle in the synthetic Chas–Sullivan product; the degree shift comes from the Pontryagin–Thom collapse of the diagonal, which requires the synthetic tangent bundle structure.
  • Misapplying the encode-decode method to the free loop space rotation action without verifying the coherence of the circle action on the higher inductive type for LX.
  • Assuming the synthetic Goodwillie calculus automatically implies the Kahn–Priddy splitting; the splitting requires the specific analysis of the Taylor tower of the identity functor and the James construction as its limit.

Guarded Cubical Type Theory and Clock Variables for Higher Inductive Types

Guarded Cubical Type Theory (GCTT) extends Cubical Type Theory with a later modality ▷ (pronounced "later") indexed by clock variables κ, enabling the definition of coinductive types and the solution of recursive domain equations that are impossible in standard Martin-Löf Type Theory. In the context of HoTT, GCTT provides a disciplined mechanism for constructing higher inductive types with infinitely many constructors or infinitely deep constructor towers, such as the type of ∞-groupoids, the sphere spectrum as a sequential spectrum, or the Cauchy completion of a metric space, without sacrificing canonicity for the base cubical fragment. The key mechanism is the clock quantifier ∀κ. A(κ), which binds a clock variable κ in a type A. A term of type ▷κ A is a "delayed" computation of type A that can only be forced (via the force operation) after the clock κ has "ticked". This tick is managed by the tick operation, which advances the clock context. Crucially, guarded recursion allows defining a fixed point operator fix : (▷κ A → A) → A for any type A, provided the recursive call is guarded by ▷κ. In Cubical Agda, this is implemented via the @guarded attribute and the Later type. For Higher Inductive Types, GCTT allows the point constructors to be defined by guarded recursion on the path constructors, or vice versa, enabling the construction of the type of semi-simplicial types (which requires an infinite tower of coherence paths) and the Rezk completion of a precategory as a single HIT rather than an inductive-inductive definition. The clock irrelevance principle ensures that the choice of clock does not affect the extensional behavior of the defined types, preserving univalence. However, the interaction of the later modality with the interval type 𝕀 and the Glue type requires careful semantic modeling (e.g., in the topos of trees over the cube category) to ensure that the Kan composition operations remain well-defined and compute correctly on guarded terms. The constant modality □ (types independent of the clock) isolates the "standard" homotopy types from the guarded ones, allowing a clean embedding of Book HoTT into GCTT.

The Synthetic Sphere Spectrum and the Internal Adams Spectral Sequence

The sphere spectrum 𝕊 is the initial object in the ∞-category of spectra and represents stable cohomotopy. In synthetic homotopy type theory, 𝕊 is constructed as a sequential spectrum — a type family S : ℕ → Type equipped with structure maps σₙ : Sⁿ → Ω Sⁿ⁺¹ — where each Sⁿ is the n-sphere HIT (suspension of Sⁿ⁻¹). The synthetic Adams Spectral Sequence (Adams SS) arises from the Adams resolution of 𝕊, built by iteratively taking the fiber of the unit map 𝕊 → Hℤ/p (for a fixed prime p) and its suspensions. In HoTT, the E₂-page of the Adams SS is identified with Ext𝒜(H*𝕊, H*𝕊), where 𝒜 is the Steenrod algebra (synthetically constructed as the algebra of stable cohomology operations on Hℤ/p). The synthetic construction of the Steenrod algebra uses the higher inductive type for the Eilenberg-MacLane space K(ℤ/p, n) and the action of the Steenrod squares/operations defined via the cup-i products on the synthetic singular cochains (or via the synthetic Dold-Kan correspondence on simplicial 𝔽p-modules). The internal Adams SS is a spectral sequence *inside* the type theory, meaning its differentials dr are functions between types (or rather, maps in the synthetic stable homotopy category) that can be computed by a proof assistant like Cubical Agda for low stems. The convergence of the synthetic Adams SS to the p-completion of the stable homotopy groups of spheres π*𝕊p∧ is a synthetic version of the classical Adams theorem. A major computational advantage is that the synthetic Adams differentials can be calculated by normalizeing terms representing the Adams resolution maps, leveraging the computational univalence of Cubical Type Theory. This has allowed the verification of the first few differentials (e.g., d₂(h₀) = h₁, d₃(h₁) = h₀h₂) and the computation of πk𝕊 for k ≤ 10 synthetically. The synthetic Mahowald invariant and the synthetic Kahn-Priddy map are also accessible via this framework, connecting the Adams SS to the stable homotopy groups of spheres and the image of J.

Technique: Computing the Synthetic Adams d₂ Differential on h₁
In the synthetic Adams spectral sequence for the sphere spectrum at prime 2, the element h₁ ∈ Ext¹,²(𝒜, 𝔽₂) corresponds to the Hopf map η ∈ π₁𝕊. Show how the synthetic d₂ differential d₂(h₁) = h₀h₂ is derived from the cofiber sequence defining the Adams resolution.
The Adams resolution starts with the cofiber sequence 𝕊 → H𝔽₂ → ΣC₁, where C₁ is the cofiber of the unit. The element h₁ is represented by a map Σ²𝕊 → ΣH𝔽₂ in the stable category, corresponding to the Steenrod square Sq¹. The d₂ differential is the composite Σ²𝕊 → ΣH𝔽₂ → Σ²H𝔽₂ → Σ³H𝔽₂, where the middle map is the connecting map of the cofiber sequence for C₁. Synthetically, h₁ is constructed as a path in the function type (S² → H𝔽₂) representing the non-trivial action of Sq¹ on H²(S²). The cofiber C₁ is defined as a HIT with a point constructor * : C₁ and a path constructor glue : H𝔽₂ → C₁ identifying the image of the unit. The connecting map δ : ΣH𝔽₂ → Σ²H𝔽₂ is defined by the universal property of the suspension/cofiber. Computing d₂(h₁) reduces to evaluating the composite map on the synthetic representative of h₁. In Cubical Agda, this is a normalization problem: the term representing the composite reduces to the term representing h₀h₂ (the product of the class h₀ ∈ Ext¹,¹ from Sq⁰ and h₂ ∈ Ext¹,⁴ from Sq²), confirming d₂(h₁) = h₀h₂. This computation relies on the definitional η-rules for the HITs defining the spheres and the Eilenberg-MacLane spaces, and the computational behavior of the Steenrod operations defined via the synthetic cup-i products.
Exam Strategy: Synthetic Spectral Sequences
When asked about the synthetic Adams or Adams-Novikov SS, focus on the *internal* nature: the E₂ page is an Ext group *in the type theory* (comodules over the synthetic Steenrod algebra or Hopf algebroid). Differentials are maps *between types* definable in the theory. Contrast this with the classical external SS where differentials are derived from a filtration. Key terms: "Adams resolution as a tower of cofibers", "Steenrod algebra as HIT operations", "Computational univalence enables normalization of differentials". Do not confuse the synthetic SS (an object *in* HoTT) with the meta-theoretic SS used to *compute* HoTT models.

The Derivatives of the Identity in Synthetic Goodwillie Calculus

Goodwillie Calculus approximates homotopy functors by a tower of n-excisive approximations PnF. In synthetic HoTT, the derivatives of the identity functor ∂*(Id) on the ∞-category of pointed types are a sequence of spectra with Σn-actions that classify the layers DnId = fib(PnId → Pn-1Id). The fundamental result, due to Arone-Mahowald and synthetically formalized by Brunerie and others, is that the n-th derivative ∂n(Id) is equivalent to the Spanier-Whitehead dual of the partition complex |𝒫n|, where 𝒫n is the poset of proper non-trivial partitions of an n-element set. Synthetically, the partition complex is constructed as a higher inductive type whose points are partitions and whose paths encode refinements. The Σn-action is induced by the permutation of the underlying set. The Taylor tower of the identity Id(X) ≃ holimn PnId(X) converges for connected types X (the synthetic version of the Goodwillie convergence theorem). The layers are given by DnId(X) ≃ (∂nId ∧ X∧n)hΣn, where ∧ is the smash product and hΣn denotes homotopy orbits. In HoTT, the homotopy orbits are the higher inductive type of the action groupoid (the Borel construction). The synthetic proof that ∂nId ≃ Σ∞|𝒫n|∨ uses the synthetic Blakers-Massey theorem to analyze the excision properties of the cross-effects of the identity functor. The cross-effect crn(Id)(X₁, ..., Xₙ) is the total fiber of the n-cube XS ↦ ∨i∈S Xi. The synthetic analysis shows this cross-effect is equivalent to the suspension spectrum of the partition complex smashed with the smash product of the Xi. This result is pivotal because it identifies the sphere spectrum 𝕊 as the limit of the Taylor tower of the identity on the category of spectra (stabilization), and connects the EHP sequence to the derivatives via the fiber sequences DnId(Sk) → PnId(Sk) → Pn-1Id(Sk). The computational content in Cubical Agda allows the calculation of the homotopy groups of the partition complexes for small n (e.g., |𝒫₃| ≃ S¹, |𝒫₄| ≃ ∨³ S²), yielding the derivatives ∂₃Id ≃ Σ⁻¹𝕊, ∂₄Id ≃ Σ⁻²𝕊∨³, matching the classical calculations of the stable stems via the Kahn-Priddy theorem.

Fully Dualizable Objects and the Synthetic Cobordism Hypothesis

The Cobordism Hypothesis (Baez-Dolan, Lurie) classifies fully extended topological quantum field theories (TQFTs) as symmetric monoidal functors from the (∞,n)-category of cobordisms Bordn to a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category 𝒞. It states that such functors are equivalent to fully dualizable objects in 𝒞. In synthetic HoTT, (∞,n)-categories are modeled as n-fold complete Segal types (Rezk types) or via directed type theory. The (∞,n)-category Bordn is constructed synthetically using higher inductive-inductive types for the stratified manifolds and cobordisms. An object X in a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category 𝒞 is fully dualizable if it has a dual X* at level 1, and the evaluation and coevaluation maps have adjoints (duals) at level 2, and so on up to level n. In HoTT, this hierarchy of adjunctions is expressed using higher inductive types for the walking adjunction and its iterates. The synthetic Cobordism Hypothesis constructs the equivalence Fun⊗(Bordn, 𝒞) ≃ (𝒞fd)≃ (the core of the subcategory of fully dualizable objects) by showing that Bordn is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object. The proof uses the synthetic handlebody decomposition of manifolds: every cobordism is generated by handles of index 0 to n, corresponding to the generators of the free dualizable object (unit, counit, and their higher adjoints). The framed version corresponds to the free fully dualizable object; the oriented version adds an action of SO(n) on the object, modeled by a map BSO(n) → Aut𝒞(X); the spin and string versions correspond to lifts along BSpin(n) → BSO(n) and BString(n) → BSpin(n), where these classifying spaces are synthetic HITs (e.g., BString(n) is the 7-connected cover of BSO(n)). The synthetic formalization in directed HoTT or two-level type theory allows the *computation* of the space of TQFTs for specific targets 𝒞 (e.g., nVectk, the (∞,n)-category of n-vector spaces) by characterizing the fully dualizable objects (e.g., separable Frobenius algebras for n=2, fusion categories for n=3). The synthetic Turaev-Viro-Barrett-Westbury state sum is recovered as the value of the TQFT on a closed manifold, computed by the synthetic factorization homology of the framed En-algebra corresponding to the fully dualizable object.

The Synthetic Hopf Algebroid for Complex Cobordism and the Adams-Novikov E₂ Page

The Adams-Novikov Spectral Sequence (ANSS) computes the p-completed stable homotopy groups of spheres using the homology theory MU (complex cobordism). Its E₂-page is ExtMU*MU(MU*, MU*X), where (MU*, MU*MU) is the Hopf algebroid representing the stack of formal groups Mfg. In synthetic HoTT, the spectrum MU is constructed as a higher inductive type — the Thom spectrum of the universal complex line bundle over ℂP∞ (itself a HIT). The coefficient ring MU* is the homotopy groups of this synthetic MU, which is a polynomial ring ℤ[x₁, x₂, ...] on generators in even degrees (synthetically proven via the synthetic cellular structure of MU). The Hopf algebroid structure (ηL, ηR, Δ, ε, c) is defined internally: ηL, ηR : MU* → MU*MU are induced by the left and right unit maps of the ring spectrum MU; Δ : MU*MU → MU*MU ⊗MU* MU*MU is induced by the comultiplication MU → MU ∧ MU; ε is the counit; c is the conjugation. The synthetic construction of MU*MU uses the synthetic Thom isomorphism for the virtual bundle over MU ∧ MU. The stack of formal groups Mfg is constructed as a higher inductive type (or a quotient of a polynomial type by the isomorphism relation of formal group laws). The Landweber exact functor theorem is proven synthetically by showing that a comodule over (MU*, MU*MU) that is Landweber exact (i.e., the sequence (p, v₁, v₂, ...) is regular) defines a homology theory represented by a spectrum. The Morava stabilizer groups 𝔾n and the Morava E-theories En are constructed as the Lubin-Tate deformation spaces of the Honda formal group law of height n, which are synthetic formal moduli problems (represented by HITs). The synthetic chromatic fracture square relates the K(n)-local sphere to the E(n)-local and K(n-1)-local spheres. The computational power of the synthetic ANSS lies in the ability to compute the cobar complex for (MU*, MU*MU) internally using the synthetic Steenrod operations on MU (the Dyer-Lashof operations) and the synthetic lambda algebra for the Adams-Novikov E₂ page. This allows the verification of the telescope conjecture for specific heights (e.g., height 1 where it is true) and the computation of the synthetic Greek letter elements (α, β, γ families) as classes in the synthetic Ext groups.

  • Confusing Guarded Recursion with Coinduction in Standard MLTT: Guarded recursion uses the later modality ▷ and clocks to ensure productivity; standard coinduction in MLTT (via M-types) lacks the logical relation to support higher inductive types with infinite constructors and breaks canonicity for cubical type theory.
  • Assuming the Synthetic Adams SS Computes Unstable Homotopy Groups: The synthetic Adams SS converges to the *p-completed stable* homotopy groups of spheres π*𝕊p∧. It does not directly compute unstable πn+k(Sn) for finite n, though the EHP sequence connects them.
  • Treating the Partition Complex |𝒫n| as a Set: The partition complex is a *space* (type) with non-trivial homotopy groups (e.g., |𝒫₄| ≃ ∨³ S²). Its homotopy type, not just its poset structure, determines the derivatives ∂nId.
  • Believing Full Dualizability is Only a Level-1 Condition: An object in an (∞,n)-category is fully dualizable only if the evaluation/coevaluation maps have adjoints *up to level n*. For n=2, this requires the 1-morphisms ev, coev to have 2-sided adjoints (i.e., the object is a separable Frobenius algebra in the monoidal hom-category).
  • Confusing the Hopf Algebroid (MU*MU) with the Steenrod Algebra 𝒜: (MU*, MU*MU) classifies formal groups and is commutative (in the graded sense); 𝒜 classifies unstable cohomology operations and is non-commutative. The ANSS uses the former; the classical Adams SS uses the latter.
  • Assuming the Synthetic Cobordism Hypothesis is Proven for All n in HoTT: The synthetic proof (e.g., in directed HoTT or two-level type theory) currently exists for low n (n=1,2,3) or for the framed case using the (∞,n)-category of correspondences. The general n proof requires a fully developed synthetic theory of (∞,n)-categories which is an active research area.
  • Overlooking the Role of the Synthetic Cellular Structure in MU: The fact that MU* is polynomial on even generators relies on the synthetic cell decomposition of MU (as a Thom spectrum of ℂP∞) having cells only in even dimensions. This is a synthetic theorem about the HIT defining ℂP∞, not an assumption.
The synthetic approach unifies the construction of spectra, spectral sequences, and higher categorical structures within a single computational framework where theorems become executable programs.
