hand/diff-eq.html:
Sturm-Liouville Theory and Spectral Methods

The classical separation of variables for the heat, wave, and Laplace equations produces eigenvalue problems of the form Lu = λwu where L is a second-order linear differential operator. Sturm-Liouville theory provides the unified framework: on an interval [a, b] with weight function w(x) > 0, the operator Lu = −(p(x)u')' + q(x)u with separated boundary conditions α₁u(a) + α₂u'(a) = 0, β₁u(b) + β₂u'(b) = 0 is self-adjoint in the weighted L² inner product ⟨u, v⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ u(x)v(x)w(x)dx. The eigenvalues λ₁ < λ₂ < λ₃ < … are real, simple, and diverge to +∞. The corresponding eigenfunctions {φₙ} form a complete orthogonal basis: any piecewise smooth function f ∈ L²_w[a, b] expands as f(x) = Σ cₙφₙ(x) with cₙ = ⟨f, φₙ⟩/⟨φₙ, φₙ⟩, and the series converges in the mean-square sense. Pointwise convergence holds at points of continuity; at jump discontinuities it converges to the average of left and right limits (Dirichlet-Jordan theorem).

Classical orthogonal polynomials arise as eigenfunctions of singular Sturm-Liouville problems where p(x) vanishes at endpoints: Legendre polynomials (p(x) = 1−x², q = 0, w = 1 on [−1, 1]), Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind (p(x) = √(1−x²), w = 1/√(1−x²)), Laguerre polynomials (p(x) = xe⁻ˣ, w = e⁻ˣ on [0, ∞)), and Hermite polynomials (p(x) = e⁻ˣ², w = e⁻ˣ² on (−∞, ∞)). Each family satisfies a three-term recurrence relation and a Rodrigues formula. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators on Hilbert space generalizes this: the solution operator (Green's operator) for a regular Sturm-Liouville problem is compact, and its eigenfunctions diagonalize the PDE evolution. For the heat equation u_t = u_xx with Dirichlet conditions, the solution is u(x, t) = Σ e⁻λₙᵗ⟨u₀, φₙ⟩φₙ(x) where λₙ = (nπ/L)². The decay rate of coefficients determines regularity: if u₀ ∈ Hˢ (Sobolev space), then |cₙ| = O(n⁻ˢ⁻¹/²).

Singular Sturm-Liouville problems (where p(a) = 0 or p(b) = 0 or the interval is infinite) require the Weyl limit-point/limit-circle classification at singular endpoints. If the endpoint is limit-point, no boundary condition is needed — the operator is essentially self-adjoint. If limit-circle, a boundary condition must be imposed to select a self-adjoint extension. The continuous spectrum appears when the interval is infinite or the potential q(x) allows non-L² solutions (e.g., the hydrogen atom radial equation). The spectral measure dρ(λ) replaces the discrete sum: f(x) = ∫ φ(x, λ) dρ(λ). This underlies the Fourier transform (singular Sturm-Liouville on ℝ with p = 1, q = 0) and the Hankel transform (Bessel's equation on [0, ∞)). In numerical spectral methods, the choice of basis functions (Fourier for periodic problems, Chebyshev for non-periodic on [−1, 1], Legendre for finite element mass matrices) exploits the diagonalization of the differential operator — differentiation becomes multiplication by eigenvalues in spectral space, yielding exponential convergence for smooth solutions (spectral accuracy) versus algebraic convergence for finite differences.

Weak Solutions, Sobolev Spaces, and the Lax-Milgram Theorem

The classical requirement that a PDE solution be twice differentiable is too restrictive for many physical problems — shocks in conservation laws, interfaces in free boundary problems, and solutions with rough data all demand a broader solution concept. The modern framework uses Sobolev spaces Wᵏ,ᵖ(Ω) = {u ∈ Lᵖ(Ω) : D^αu ∈ Lᵖ(Ω) for all |α| ≤ k} with norm ‖u‖Wᵏ,ᵖ = (Σ|α|≤k ‖D^αu‖Lᵖᵖ)1/p. The Hilbert space case p = 2 is denoted Hᵏ(Ω) = Wᵏ,²(Ω) with inner product ⟨u, v⟩Hᵏ = Σ|α|≤k ⟨D^αu, D^αv⟩L². For the Poisson equation −Δu = f in Ω, u = 0 on ∂Ω, multiply by a test function v ∈ C_c^∞(Ω) and integrate by parts: ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx = ∫_Ω fv dx. This makes sense if u, v ∈ H₀¹(Ω) (the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in H¹ norm) and f ∈ H⁻¹(Ω) (the dual space). A weak solution is u ∈ H₀¹(Ω) satisfying a(u, v) = ⟨f, v⟩ for all v ∈ H₀¹(Ω), where the bilinear form a(u, v) = ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx.

The Lax-Milgram theorem guarantees existence and uniqueness: if a(·, ·) is bounded (|a(u, v)| ≤ M‖u‖‖v‖) and coercive (a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖² for some α > 0) on a Hilbert space V, then for every continuous linear functional F ∈ V*, there exists a unique u ∈ V such that a(u, v) = F(v) for all v ∈ V. For the Poisson equation, coercivity follows from the Poincaré inequality ‖u‖L² ≤ C‖∇u‖L² for u ∈ H₀¹(Ω), giving a(u, u) = ‖∇u‖²L² ≥ (1/(1+C²))‖u‖²H¹. The solution depends continuously on data: ‖u‖_V ≤ (1/α)‖F‖V*. This variational formulation is the foundation of the finite element method — the discrete problem seeks u_h ∈ V_h ⊂ V satisfying a(u_h, v_h) = F(v_h) for all v_h ∈ V_h, and Céa's lemma gives the quasi-optimal error estimate ‖u − u_h‖_V ≤ (M/α) infv_h∈V_h ‖u − v_h‖_V.

Regularity theory asks: if f is smoother, is u smoother? For the Dirichlet problem on a C² domain, if f ∈ Hk−2(Ω) then u ∈ Hᵏ(Ω) with ‖u‖Hᵏ ≤ C‖f‖Hk−2 (elliptic regularity). On non-smooth domains (polygons, domains with cracks), singularities appear at corners: u ∉ H² even for smooth f. The solution decomposes as u = u_reg + Σ c_j rπ/ω_j sin(πθ/ω_j) where ω_j are interior angles — the singular exponents determine the convergence rate of finite elements. For parabolic equations u_t − Δu = f, the natural space is L²(0, T; H₀¹(Ω)) ∩ H¹(0, T; H⁻¹(Ω)) — the solution has one time derivative in a negative norm space. The Aubin-Lions compactness lemma (compact embedding of {u ∈ L²(0, T; V) : u_t ∈ L²(0, T; V*)} into L²(0, T; H)) is essential for proving existence of weak solutions to nonlinear problems via Galerkin approximation. For the Navier-Stokes equations, Leray-Hopf weak solutions exist globally in 3D but uniqueness and regularity remain open (Millennium Prize). The energy inequality ‖u(t)‖²L² + 2ν∫₀ᵗ ‖∇u(s)‖²L² ds ≤ ‖u₀‖²L² replaces the energy equality for classical solutions.

Weak Formulation and Energy Estimate
Consider the boundary value problem −u'' + u = f on (0, 1) with u(0) = u(1) = 0. (a) Derive the weak formulation in H₀¹(0, 1). (b) Show the bilinear form is coercive and bounded. (c) If f(x) = 1, find the exact solution and compute its H¹ error when approximated by the linear finite element space V_h with mesh size h = 1/2.
(a) Multiply by v ∈ H₀¹(0, 1) and integrate: ∫₀¹ (−u''v + uv) dx = ∫₀¹ fv dx. Integrate by parts: ∫₀¹ u'v' dx + ∫₀¹ uv dx = ∫₀¹ fv dx. The weak form: find u ∈ H₀¹ such that a(u, v) = F(v) ∀v ∈ H₀¹, where a(u, v) = ∫₀¹ (u'v' + uv) dx, F(v) = ∫₀¹ fv dx. (b) Boundedness: |a(u, v)| ≤ ∫₀¹ (|u'v'| + |uv|) dx ≤ ‖u'‖L²‖v'‖L² + ‖u‖L²‖v‖L² ≤ ‖u‖H¹‖v‖H¹ (M = 1). Coercivity: a(u, u) = ‖u'‖²L² + ‖u‖²L² = ‖u‖²H¹ (α = 1). (c) Exact solution: −u'' + u = 1, u(0)=u(1)=0. Homogeneous solution: u_h = A e^x + B e−x. Particular solution: u_p = 1. General: u = 1 + A e^x + B e−x. Boundary conditions: 1 + A + B = 0, 1 + A e + B e−1 = 0. Solve: A = (e−1−1)/(e−e−1), B = (1−e)/(e−e−1). For h = 1/2, nodes at 0, 0.5, 1. V_h = span{φ₁} where φ₁ is the hat function at x = 0.5. The discrete solution u_h = c φ₁ satisfies a(u_h, φ₁) = F(φ₁). a(φ₁, φ₁) = ∫₀¹ (φ₁'² + φ₁²) dx = 2/h + h/3 = 4 + 1/6 = 25/6. F(φ₁) = ∫₀¹ φ₁ dx = h/2 = 1/4. So c = (1/4)/(25/6) = 6/100 = 0.06. The H¹ error ‖u − u_h‖H¹ can be computed numerically; by Céa's lemma it is bounded by infv_h∈V_h ‖u − v_h‖H¹ ≤ ‖u − I_h u‖H¹ where I_h is the nodal interpolant. For this smooth u, the error is O(h) in H¹ norm.
Exam Strategy for Functional Analysis in PDEs
When a question asks for a weak formulation, always: (1) identify the correct Hilbert space (H₀¹ for Dirichlet, H¹ for Neumann), (2) multiply by a test function and integrate by parts to move derivatives off the solution, (3) state the bilinear form and linear functional explicitly, (4) verify boundedness and coercivity using Poincaré or Friedrichs inequalities. For error estimates, remember Céa's lemma gives quasi-optimality in the energy norm — the finite element error is at most a constant times the best approximation error. The constant is M/α where M is the boundedness constant and α the coercivity constant. If the problem asks about regularity, recall that convex polygonal domains give H² regularity for Poisson, but non-convex corners (re-entrant corners with angle > π) reduce regularity to H1+π/ω where ω is the interior angle. This directly affects finite element convergence rates.

Hyperbolic Conservation Laws and the Riemann Problem

First-order hyperbolic systems ∂_t u + ∂_x f(u) = 0 with u ∈ ℝⁿ, f : ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ model compressible flow, traffic, and shallow water. The flux Jacobian A(u) = Df(u) has real eigenvalues λ₁(u) ≤ … ≤ λₙ(u) and a complete set of eigenvectors (strict hyperbolicity: λ₁ < … < λₙ). Solutions develop discontinuities (shocks) in finite time even from smooth initial data — the gradient catastrophe occurs when characteristics intersect. A weak solution satisfies ∫∫ (u φ_t + f(u) φ_x) dx dt = 0 for all φ ∈ C_c^∞. Across a discontinuity x = s(t), the Rankine-Hugoniot condition gives the shock speed: s'(t) = [f(u)]/[u] where [·] denotes the jump. For scalar conservation laws (n = 1), the Lax entropy condition selects the physical shock: characteristics must enter the shock, i.e., f'(u_L) > s > f'(u_R). For systems, the Lax condition generalizes: for a k-shock, λ_k(u_L) > s > λ_k(u_R) and λk−1(u_L) < s < λk+1(u_R) (with λ₀ = −∞, λn+1 = +∞). Rarefaction waves are continuous self-similar solutions u(x/t) connecting u_L to u_R through an integral curve of the k-th eigenvector where λ_k increases.

The Riemann problem — piecewise constant initial data u(x, 0) = u_L for x < 0, u_R for x > 0 — is the building block for general solutions. For strictly hyperbolic systems with genuinely nonlinear fields (∇λ_k·r_k ≠ 0) or linearly degenerate fields (∇λ_k·r_k ≡ 0), the solution consists of at most n waves (shocks, rarefactions, or contact discontinuities) separating constant states. The solution is constructed by solving the Hugoniot locus (shock curves) and integral curves (rarefaction curves) in state space. For the p-system (isentropic gas dynamics) u = (v, u), f(u) = (−u, p(v)) with p(v) = v−γ, the eigenvalues are ±√(−p'(v)) and the Riemann invariants are u ± ∫ √(−p'(v)) dv. For the shallow water equations h_t + (hu)_x = 0, (hu)_t + (hu² + ½gh²)_x = 0, the eigenvalues are u ± √(gh) and Riemann invariants are u ± 2√(gh). The Godunov method solves the Riemann problem at each cell interface to compute numerical fluxes — it is a first-order monotone scheme satisfying a discrete entropy inequality. Higher-order methods (MUSCL, WENO, DG) use slope limiting or weighted reconstruction to achieve high-order accuracy in smooth regions while controlling oscillations near shocks (TVD property: total variation does not increase).

Entropy solutions are the unique physically relevant weak solutions. For scalar laws, Kruzhkov's entropy condition: for all k ∈ ℝ, ∂_t |u − k| + ∂_x sign(u − k)(f(u) − f(k)) ≤ 0 in the sense of distributions. This implies L¹ contraction: ‖u(t) − v(t)‖L¹ ≤ ‖u₀ − v₀‖L¹ for any two entropy solutions, giving uniqueness and continuous dependence. For systems, the existence of a convex entropy function η(u) with entropy flux q(u) satisfying q' = η' f' (compatibility) allows the definition of entropy solutions: ∂_t η(u) + ∂_x q(u) ≤ 0. The Lax-Wendroff theorem states that any convergent consistent conservative scheme converges to a weak solution; if the scheme satisfies a discrete entropy inequality, the limit is an entropy solution. The Glimm scheme (random choice method) and front tracking construct global entropy solutions for systems with small total variation (BV initial data). The vanishing viscosity method u_t + f(u)_x = ε uxx selects the entropy solution as ε → 0. For the Euler equations of gas dynamics, the existence of global entropy solutions for large data is a major open problem; the 2022 Fields Medal work of Chen, Huang, Li, and Wang made progress on the 2D compressible Euler equations with vacuum.

Hamiltonian Systems, Symplectic Structure, and Geometric Integration

Hamiltonian mechanics provides the geometric framework for conservative dynamical systems. A Hamiltonian system on a 2n-dimensional symplectic manifold (M, ω) with Hamiltonian H : M → ℝ is defined by the vector field X_H satisfying ω(X_H, ·) = dH. In canonical coordinates (q, p) ∈ ℝ²ⁿ with ω = Σ dp_i ∧ dq_i, this gives Hamilton's equations: q̇_i = ∂H/∂p_i, ṗ_i = −∂H/∂q_i. The flow φ_t preserves the symplectic form (φ_t^* ω = ω) and the Hamiltonian (H ∘ φ_t = H). Liouville's theorem: phase space volume is preserved (det Dφ_t = 1). Poincaré recurrence: for bounded Hamiltonian systems, almost every trajectory returns arbitrarily close to its initial condition infinitely often. Noether's theorem links symmetries to conserved quantities: if a Lie group action preserves ω and H, the momentum map J : M → 𝔤* is conserved along trajectories.

Integrable systems have n independent integrals of motion in involution ({F_i, F_j} = 0 where {·, ·} is the Poisson bracket). The Arnold-Liouville theorem: the level sets of the integrals are n-tori, and there exist action-angle variables (I, θ) ∈ ℝⁿ × 𝕋ⁿ where H = H(I) and the flow is linear: İ = 0, θ̇ = ω(I) = ∂H/∂I. The KAM theorem states that for a non-degenerate integrable Hamiltonian H₀(I) + εH₁(I, θ), most invariant tori with Diophantine frequencies (|k·ω| ≥ γ|k|⁻ᵀ for all k ∈ ℤⁿ{0}) persist under small perturbations — explaining the stability of the solar system. The destroyed tori give rise to chaotic layers and Arnold diffusion (slow drift in action space). For near-integrable systems, the Nekhoroshev theorem gives exponential stability times: ‖I(t) − I(0)‖ ≤ εᵇ for |t| ≤ exp(ε⁻ᵃ) with a, b > 0.

Numerical integration of Hamiltonian systems must preserve geometric structure. Symplectic integrators are maps ψ_h : M → M that are symplectic (ψ_h^* ω = ω) and approximate the flow. For separable Hamiltonians H(q, p) = T(p) + V(q), the Störmer-Verlet (leapfrog) method is symplectic and second-order: pn+1/2 = p_n − (h/2)∇V(q_n), qn+1 = q_n + h∇T(pn+1/2), pn+1 = pn+1/2 − (h/2)∇V(qn+1). It preserves a modified Hamiltonian H̃ = H + h²H₂ + h⁴H₄ + … exactly, so energy error remains bounded for exponentially long times (backward error analysis). Non-symplectic methods (Runge-Kutta 4) exhibit secular energy drift. For constrained Hamiltonian systems (e.g., rigid body, molecular dynamics), the SHAKE/RATTLE algorithms enforce constraints while preserving symplecticity. Geometric integration extends to Poisson systems (non-canonical brackets), Lie-Poisson systems (rigid body, fluid dynamics), and multisymplectic PDEs (discrete multisymplectic structure for wave equations). The discrete Noether theorem: symmetries of the discrete Lagrangian yield exact conservation of discrete momentum maps.

Center Manifold Theory and Bifurcation Normal Forms

Bifurcation theory analyzes qualitative changes in dynamics as parameters vary. The center manifold theorem reduces the dimension of the problem near a non-hyperbolic equilibrium. For ẋ = Ax + f(x, μ), x ∈ ℝⁿ, μ ∈ ℝᵖ, with A having eigenvalues on the imaginary axis (center directions) and others with non-zero real parts (hyperbolic directions), there exists a locally invariant center manifold W^c(0) tangent to the center eigenspace E^c. The dynamics on W^c determine the stability and bifurcation behavior — the flow on the center manifold is topologically equivalent to the full system near the equilibrium. The manifold can be approximated as a graph h : E^c → E^s ⊕ E^u by solving the invariance equation Dh(x)[Ax + f(x, h(x))] = Ah(x) + f_s(x, h(x)) order by order in Taylor series. The reduced system on W^c is ẏ = Ay + f_c(y, h(y)) where y ∈ E^c.

Normal form theory simplifies the reduced system by nonlinear coordinate changes that eliminate non-resonant terms. For a Hopf bifurcation (eigenvalues ±iω, ω > 0), the normal form on the center manifold in complex coordinates is ż = (λ(μ) + iω)z + c₁(μ)z|z|² + O(|z|⁴). The first Lyapunov coefficient l₁ = Re(c₁)/ω determines criticality: l₁ < 0 gives supercritical Hopf (stable limit cycle for μ > 0), l₁ > 0 gives subcritical Hopf (unstable limit cycle for μ < 0). The amplitude equation for the limit cycle is ṙ = λ(μ)r + l₁r³, giving cycle amplitude r = √(−λ/l₁) for supercritical case. For the Bogdanov-Takens bifurcation (double zero eigenvalue with non-trivial Jordan block), the normal form is ẋ = y, ẏ = μ₁ + μ₂y + x² + bxy. The bifurcation diagram in (μ₁, μ₂) space contains curves of saddle-node, Hopf, and homoclinic bifurcations meeting at the origin. The homoclinic curve is μ₁ = −(5/7)μ₂² + O(μ₂³) for b ≠ 0.

For maps, the period-doubling (flip) bifurcation normal form is x ↦ −(1+μ)x + ax³ + O(x⁴). The Feigenbaum constant δ = 4.669201609… is the universal ratio of parameter intervals between successive period-doublings in the logistic family and any unimodal map with quadratic maximum. The renormalization group explanation: the period-doubling operator R[f](x) = αf(f(x/α)) has a hyperbolic fixed point g* (the Feigenbaum-Cvitanović function) with a single unstable eigenvalue δ. The stable manifold of g* is the codimension-1 set of maps at the accumulation point of period-doubling; the unstable manifold corresponds to the parameter direction. For the Neimark-Sacker bifurcation (discrete Hopf), a complex conjugate pair of eigenvalues crosses the unit circle, creating an invariant circle. The normal form is z ↦ eiθ(1+μ)z + c₁z|z|². The criticality depends on Re(e−iθc₁). Global bifurcations involve non-local changes: homoclinic bifurcations (Shilnikov's theorem for 3D flows with saddle-focus: if |Re(λ)| < |Im(λ)| for the complex eigenvalues, infinitely many periodic orbits exist near the homoclinic loop), heteroclinic cycles, and blue-sky catastrophes. The Melnikov method computes the distance between stable and unstable manifolds under perturbation: M(t₀) = ∫−∞∞ f(γ₀(t)) ∧ g(γ₀(t), t+t₀) dt where γ₀ is the unperturbed homoclinic orbit; simple zeros of M correspond to transverse intersections and chaos.

  • Confusing weak and classical solutions: A weak solution may not satisfy the PDE pointwise; it satisfies an integral identity. Always check whether the question asks for classical (C²) or weak (H¹) solutions.
  • Misapplying Lax-Milgram: Coercivity requires a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖²_V with the full norm of the Hilbert space V, not just the semi-norm. For Neumann problems, the kernel of the bilinear form (constants) must be factored out or the space restricted.
  • Ignoring entropy conditions for shocks: The Rankine-Hugoniot condition alone admits non-physical shocks (rarefaction shocks). The Lax entropy condition or an entropy inequality must be enforced for uniqueness.
  • Overlooking symplecticity in numerical methods: Standard Runge-Kutta methods are not symplectic for Hamiltonian systems; they introduce artificial energy drift. Symplectic integrators (Verlet, symplectic Euler, Gauss-Legendre RK) preserve a modified Hamiltonian and exhibit bounded energy error.
  • Misidentifying bifurcation types: A zero eigenvalue with non-zero quadratic term in the center manifold reduction indicates saddle-node, not transcritical or pitchfork. Transcritical requires symmetry or a parameter-dependent equilibrium branch crossing; pitchfork requires odd symmetry (f(−x) = −f(x)).
  • Confusing KAM and Nekhoroshev stability: KAM guarantees persistence of most invariant tori (positive measure) for all time. Nekhoroshev gives exponential stability time for all trajectories but only up to a finite (though exponentially long) time.
  • Neglecting the role of the weight function in Sturm-Liouville: Orthogonality is with respect to the weight w(x). The expansion coefficients are cₙ = ∫ f φₙ w dx / ∫ φₙ² w dx. Forgetting w leads to incorrect Fourier coefficients for Legendre, Chebyshev, Laguerre, Hermite expansions.

Integration of Irrational Functions Using Euler Substitutions

Irrational integrands containing expressions of the form √(ax² + bx + c) or √(a + bx + cx²) often resist elementary substitutions. Euler devised three systematic substitutions that convert such square‑root expressions into rational functions, after which partial fractions or standard integrals finish the job. The choice depends on the sign of the quadratic’s leading coefficient and the discriminant.

Euler’s First Substitution applies when a > 0. Set √(ax² + bx + c) = t − √a·x. Squaring and solving for x yields a rational expression in t, and dx becomes a rational differential. The integrand turns into a rational function of t, integrable by partial fractions.

Euler’s Second Substitution is used when c > 0. Write √(ax² + bx + c) = xt + √c. Again x and dx become rational in t. This substitution is particularly effective for integrands like ∫ dx / (x√(ax² + bx + c)).

Euler’s Third Substitution works when the quadratic has real roots α and β (i.e., discriminant ≥ 0). Set √(a(x−α)(x−β)) = t(x−α). The square root disappears, leaving a rational function in t. This form is handy for integrals of the type ∫ dx / ((x−α)√(a(x−α)(x−β))).

All three substitutions share a common pattern: they linearise the square root by introducing a new variable that absorbs the radical. After integration in t, back‑substitution expresses the antiderivative in terms of x. Mastery of these substitutions allows a student to tackle integrals such as ∫ √(x² + 4x + 5) dx or ∫ dx / (x√(x² − 4)) without resorting to trigonometric or hyperbolic substitutions, which may be less direct.

In examinations, the examiner often hides an Euler‑type integral inside a definite integral with symmetric limits, expecting the candidate to recognise the rationalising substitution before applying King’s property. Practising the algebraic steps of each substitution until they become automatic is the most reliable way to gain speed.

Leibniz Integral Rule — Differentiation Under the Integral Sign

The Leibniz rule provides a powerful technique for evaluating definite integrals that depend on a parameter. If I(α) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x, α) dx, where the limits a and b are constants, then dI/dα = ∫ₐᵇ ∂f/∂α dx, provided f and its partial derivative are continuous on the rectangle of integration. When the limits themselves depend on α, the full formula adds boundary terms: d/dα ∫u(α)v(α) f(x, α) dx = f(v(α), α)·v′(α) − f(u(α), α)·u′(α) + ∫u(α)v(α) ∂f/∂α dx.

This rule transforms a difficult integral into a simpler differential equation in the parameter. A classic example is I(α) = ∫₀^π ln(1 + α cos x) dx for |α| < 1. Differentiating under the integral sign gives I′(α) = ∫₀^π cos x / (1 + α cos x) dx, which can be evaluated by the substitution t = tan(x/2) or by using the known integral ∫₀^π dx / (a + b cos x) = π/√(a² − b²). Integrating I′(α) with respect to α and using I(0) = 0 yields the closed form I(α) = π ln((1 + √(1−α²))/2).

Another frequent pattern is the integral ∫₀^∞ e−αx sin x / x dx. Defining I(α) = ∫₀^∞ e−αx sin x / x dx, differentiation gives I′(α) = −∫₀^∞ e−αx sin x dx = −1/(α² + 1). Integrating back, I(α) = −tan⁻¹ α + C. Since I(∞) = 0, C = π/2, so I(α) = π/2 − tan⁻¹ α = tan⁻¹(1/α). Setting α = 0 recovers the Dirichlet integral ∫₀^∞ sin x / x dx = π/2.

The examiner may present a definite integral with a parameter hidden in the exponent or inside a logarithm, expecting the candidate to introduce an auxiliary parameter, differentiate, solve the resulting simpler integral, and then integrate back. Recognising when the integrand is a derivative with respect to a parameter is the key insight. Practice with standard forms — logarithmic, arctangent, exponential — builds the intuition needed to spot the opportunity quickly.

Leibniz Rule Applied to a Parameter Integral
Evaluate I = ∫₀¹ (x^α − 1)/ln x dx for α > −1.

Define I(α) = ∫₀¹ (x^α − 1)/ln x dx. Note I(0) = 0. Differentiate under the integral sign with respect to α:

I′(α) = ∫₀¹ ∂/∂α [(x^α − 1)/ln x] dx = ∫₀¹ x^α dx = [xα+1/(α+1)]₀¹ = 1/(α+1).

Integrate I′(α) from 0 to α: I(α) − I(0) = ∫₀^α 1/(t+1) dt = ln(α+1). Since I(0)=0, I(α) = ln(α+1).

Thus ∫₀¹ (x^α − 1)/ln x dx = ln(α+1).

Exam‑Day Strategy for Parameter Integrals
When you see an integral containing a parameter (α, β, n, etc.) that does not appear in the limits, consider defining I(parameter) and differentiating. Check continuity conditions quickly; if they hold, the resulting integral is often a standard form. After finding I′(parameter), integrate back and use a known value (usually at parameter = 0 or ∞) to fix the constant. This method converts many “impossible” definite integrals into routine calculus.

Beta and Gamma Functions — Evaluating Definite Integrals

The Gamma function Γ(z) = ∫₀^∞ tz−1 e−t dt (Re(z) > 0) generalises the factorial: Γ(n+1) = n! for non‑negative integers n. The Beta function B(p, q) = ∫₀¹ tp−1 (1−t)q−1 dt (Re(p), Re(q) > 0) relates to Gamma via B(p, q) = Γ(p)Γ(q)/Γ(p+q). These functions turn a wide class of definite integrals into algebraic combinations of Γ values.

Integrals of the form ∫₀^∞ xm−1 e−ax^n dx are handled by the substitution t = ax^n, yielding (1/n) a−m/n Γ(m/n). For example, ∫₀^∞ x4 e−x2 dx = ½ Γ(5/2) = ½·(3√π/4) = 3√π/8. Integrals over [0, 1] with powers of x and (1−x) map directly to Beta: ∫₀1 xp−1 (1−x)q−1 dx = B(p, q). Trigonometric integrals also reduce to Beta via x = sin²θ: ∫₀π/2 sin2p−1θ cos2q−1θ dθ = ½ B(p, q).

The reflection formula Γ(z)Γ(1−z) = π / sin(πz) and the duplication formula Γ(z)Γ(z+½) = 21−2z √π Γ(2z) allow simplification of Gamma values at rational arguments. For instance, Γ(1/3)Γ(2/3) = 2π/√3. These identities are frequently used to express answers in a compact form without numerical approximation.

In competitive examinations, the Beta‑Gamma approach is the standard method for integrals like ∫₀^∞ xs−1/(1+x)^t dx = B(s, t−s) or ∫₀π/2 sin^m θ cos^n θ dθ. Recognising the pattern and writing the answer in terms of Γ functions (or factorials when arguments are integers/half‑integers) is often faster than repeated integration by parts. Memorise the basic definitions, the Beta‑Gamma relation, and the values Γ(½)=√π, Γ(1)=1, Γ(3/2)=√π/2.

Improper Integrals — Convergence and Evaluation Techniques

An improper integral arises when the interval of integration is infinite or the integrand has an infinite discontinuity within the interval. The integral ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx is defined as limb→∞ ∫ₐ^b f(x) dx, provided the limit exists and is finite. Similarly, ∫ₐ^b f(x) dx with a vertical asymptote at c ∈ (a, b) splits into limε→0⁺ ∫ₐc−ε f(x) dx + limε→0⁺ ∫c+ε^b f(x) dx.

Convergence tests avoid explicit evaluation when only the existence of the integral is required. The comparison test: if 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) and ∫ g converges, then ∫ f converges; if ∫ f diverges, then ∫ g diverges. The limit comparison test uses limx→∞ f(x)/g(x) = L (0 < L < ∞) to infer identical convergence behaviour. For integrals near a singularity, compare with 1/(x−c)^p: ∫ₐ^c dx/(x−c)^p converges iff p < 1.

Absolute convergence implies convergence, but conditional convergence can occur for oscillatory integrands like ∫₁^∞ sin x / x dx (Dirichlet integral). Dirichlet’s test for improper integrals states that if ∫ₐ^b g is bounded for all b and f is monotone decreasing to 0, then ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)g(x) dx converges. This justifies the convergence of ∫₁^∞ sin x / x dx and ∫₀^∞ e−x sin x dx.

Evaluation of convergent improper integrals often uses Gamma functions, contour integration (beyond scope), or known results: ∫₀^∞ e−ax sin bx dx = b/(a²+b²), ∫₀^∞ e−ax cos bx dx = a/(a²+b²), ∫₀^∞ xn e−ax dx = n!/an+1. When the integrand is rational, partial fractions combined with ∫₀^∞ dx/(x²+a²) = π/(2a) and ∫₀^∞ x dx/(x²+a²) diverges (logarithmic divergence) are useful.

Examiners may ask to determine convergence of ∫₀^∞ (sin x)/x^p dx for various p, or to evaluate ∫₀^∞ e−x2 dx = √π/2 via the Gaussian integral squaring trick. Knowing the p‑test thresholds (p > 1 for convergence at ∞, p < 1 for convergence at 0) and the Dirichlet test conditions is essential for quick decision‑making.

Reduction Formulas for Powers of Trigonometric Functions

Reduction formulas express an integral involving a power of a trigonometric function in terms of the same integral with a lower power. They are derived by integration by parts and are indispensable for integrals like ∫ sin^n x dx, ∫ cos^n x dx, ∫ tan^n x dx, ∫ sec^n x dx, and their definite counterparts over symmetric intervals.

For I_n = ∫ sin^n x dx (n ≥ 2), integration by parts with u = sinn−1 x, dv = sin x dx gives I_n = −(1/n) sinn−1 x cos x + ((n−1)/n) In−2. Similarly, J_n = ∫ cos^n x dx yields J_n = (1/n) cosn−1 x sin x + ((n−1)/n) Jn−2. For definite integrals over [0, π/2], the boundary terms vanish, producing the Wallis formulas: ∫₀π/2 sin^n x dx = ∫₀π/2 cos^n x dx = ((n−1)/n)·((n−3)/(n−2))·…·(π/2) for even n, and = ((n−1)/n)·((n−3)/(n−2))·…·1 for odd n.

For tangent and secant: K_n = ∫ tan^n x dx = (1/(n−1)) tann−1 x − Kn−2 (n ≠ 1). L_n = ∫ sec^n x dx = (1/(n−1)) secn−2 x tan x + ((n−2)/(n−1)) Ln−2 (n ≥ 2). These recurrences reduce the power step by step until reaching ∫ tan x dx = −ln|cos x| or ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x|.

In examinations, reduction formulas are often combined with definite integral properties. For example, ∫₀π/2 sin^m x cos^n x dx can be evaluated by repeatedly applying the Beta function relation or by using the reduction formula for sin^m x and then the Wallis product. The examiner may ask for a closed form in terms of factorials or double factorials: ∫₀π/2 sin2p x cos2q x dx = ( (2p−1)!! (2q−1)!! ) / ( (2p+2q)!! ) · π/2. Memorising the double‑factorial pattern for even powers and the product of odd numbers for odd powers saves time.

When deriving a reduction formula under exam pressure, always set up integration by parts with the highest power as u and the remaining trigonometric factor as dv. Check the algebraic sign carefully; a missing minus sign propagates through the recurrence. Verify the base cases (n = 0, 1) by direct integration to ensure the recurrence produces correct values.

  • Assuming Euler substitutions work for all irrational integrands without checking the sign conditions on the quadratic coefficients.
  • Differentiating under the integral sign without verifying continuity of the partial derivative or the boundedness of the limits.
  • Confusing the Beta function arguments when converting trigonometric integrals; the exponents in the Beta integral are one less than the powers of sine and cosine.
  • Applying the p‑test for improper integrals incorrectly at both 0 and ∞ simultaneously; the thresholds are opposite (p < 1 at 0, p > 1 at ∞).
  • Forgetting that reduction formulas for definite integrals over [0, π/2] eliminate the boundary terms, leading to an extra term in the recurrence.
  • Misusing the Gamma reflection formula by plugging in arguments that make the sine zero, which yields a pole rather than a finite value.
  • Neglecting to check absolute convergence before rearranging an improper integral; conditionally convergent integrals cannot be split arbitrarily.

Mastery of these advanced techniques expands the toolkit far beyond standard substitutions and enables the solution of integrals that appear intractable at first glance.

hand/linear-algebra.html:
Jordan Canonical Form — When Diagonalization Fails

Diagonalization requires a basis of eigenvectors. When a matrix lacks enough linearly independent eigenvectors — its geometric multiplicity falls short of algebraic multiplicity — it is defective and cannot be diagonalized. The Jordan canonical form provides the nearest possible structure: a block-diagonal matrix where each block corresponds to a single eigenvalue and has that eigenvalue on the diagonal, ones on the superdiagonal, and zeros elsewhere. Every square matrix over an algebraically closed field is similar to a Jordan form, unique up to block ordering. The size of the largest Jordan block for an eigenvalue equals its index of nilpotency in the generalized eigenspace, and the number of blocks equals the geometric multiplicity. This decomposition reveals the structure of nilpotent operators: a nilpotent matrix has only zero eigenvalues, and its Jordan blocks are exactly the blocks of its Jordan form. The transformation to Jordan form uses generalized eigenvectors — vectors v satisfying (A − λI)ᵏv = 0 for some k > 1. Chains of generalized eigenvectors form the columns of the similarity matrix. While theoretically complete, the Jordan form is numerically unstable: arbitrarily small perturbations can change the block structure, making it unsuitable for computation but indispensable for theory. In differential equations, the Jordan form of the coefficient matrix yields the general solution of linear systems with constant coefficients, where defective eigenvalues produce polynomial-exponential terms tᵏeλt.

Matrix Norms and Condition Numbers — Measuring Sensitivity

A matrix norm extends vector norms to matrices, satisfying submultiplicativity ‖AB‖ ≤ ‖A‖‖B‖ and consistency with vector norms ‖Ax‖ ≤ ‖A‖‖x‖. The most common are the Frobenius norm ‖A‖_F = √(∑ᵢⱼ|aᵢⱼ|²), the spectral norm ‖A‖₂ = σ_max (largest singular value), and the induced p-norms ‖A‖_p = maxx≠0 ‖Ax‖_p / ‖x‖_p. The condition number κ(A) = ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖ measures how much the solution of Ax = b changes relative to perturbations in A or b. For the spectral norm, κ₂(A) = σ_max / σ_min. A matrix with κ ≈ 1 is well-conditioned; κ ≫ 1 indicates ill-conditioning where small input errors amplify dramatically. The Hilbert matrix Hᵢⱼ = 1/(i+j−1) is famously ill-conditioned, with κ growing exponentially in dimension. In floating-point arithmetic with machine epsilon ε ≈ 2.2×10⁻¹⁶, the relative error in solving Ax = b is bounded by roughly κ(A)ε. This explains why normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb square the condition number (κ(AᵀA) = κ(A)²) and should be avoided for ill-conditioned problems — QR factorization or SVD-based solvers are preferred. The condition number also governs convergence of iterative methods: the error reduction per step of the conjugate gradient method depends on √κ. For eigenvalue problems, the sensitivity of a simple eigenvalue λ is 1/|y* x| where x and y are right and left eigenvectors; defective eigenvalues are infinitely sensitive.

Worked Example: Condition Number and Error Amplification
Consider the 2×2 matrix A = [[1, 1], [1, 1.0001]] and system Ax = b with b = [2, 2.0001]ᵀ. The exact solution is x = [1, 1]ᵀ. Now perturb b to b' = [2, 2.0002]ᵀ. Compute the condition number κ₂(A) and estimate the relative error in the solution.
First compute singular values of A. AᵀA = [[2, 2.0001], [2.0001, 2.00020001]]. Eigenvalues of AᵀA are roots of λ² − 4.00020001λ + (4.00040002 − 4.00040001) = λ² − 4.00020001λ + 0.00000001 ≈ 0. The eigenvalues are approximately 4.0002 and 2.5×10⁻⁹. Thus σ_max ≈ √4.0002 ≈ 2.00005, σ_min ≈ √2.5×10⁻⁹ ≈ 5×10⁻⁵. Condition number κ₂(A) = σ_max/σ_min ≈ 2.00005 / 5×10⁻⁵ ≈ 40,000. The relative perturbation in b is ‖Δb‖/‖b‖ ≈ 0.0001/2.828 ≈ 3.5×10⁻⁵. The predicted relative error in x is κ₂(A) × 3.5×10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.4. Actual solution to perturbed system: x' = [0, 2]ᵀ. Relative error ‖x'−x‖/‖x‖ = √2/√2 = 1. The condition number correctly predicts order-of-magnitude error amplification.
Exam Strategy: Condition Number Bounds
When a problem asks for error bounds without explicit matrix entries, use the inequality ‖Δx‖/‖x‖ ≤ κ(A) ‖Δb‖/‖b‖ / (1 − κ(A)‖ΔA‖/‖A‖) for perturbed A and b. Remember that κ(AB) ≤ κ(A)κ(B) and κ(A⁻¹) = κ(A). For orthogonal matrices, κ₂(Q) = 1 — they preserve conditioning. In multiple-choice questions, if κ(A) = 10⁶ and ε = 10⁻¹⁶, expect about 10⁻¹⁰ relative accuracy, not 10⁻¹⁶.

Positive Definite Matrices and Cholesky Decomposition — The Geometry of Convexity

A symmetric matrix A is positive definite (PD) if xᵀAx > 0 for all nonzero x; positive semidefinite (PSD) if xᵀAx ≥ 0. Equivalent characterizations: all eigenvalues > 0 (PD) or ≥ 0 (PSD); all leading principal minors > 0 (Sylvester's criterion); A = LLᵀ for some invertible lower-triangular L (Cholesky factorization); the quadratic form f(x) = ½xᵀAx − bᵀx is strictly convex with unique minimizer x = A⁻¹b. The Cholesky decomposition A = LLᵀ (or A = RᵀR with upper-triangular R) computes in ⅓n³ operations — half the cost of LU — and is numerically stable without pivoting for PD matrices. The algorithm: for j = 1 to n, Lⱼⱼ = √(aⱼⱼ − ∑k=1j−1 Lⱼₖ²), and for i = j+1 to n, Lᵢⱼ = (aᵢⱼ − ∑k=1j−1 LᵢₖLⱼₖ)/Lⱼⱼ. If any Lⱼⱼ ≤ 0, the matrix is not PD. For PSD matrices, a pivoted Cholesky A = PLLᵀPᵀ reveals the rank. PD matrices define inner products ⟨x, y⟩_A = xᵀAy and Mahalanobis distance d_A(x, y) = √((x−y)ᵀA(x−y)). In statistics, the covariance matrix of a non-degenerate distribution is PD; its inverse is the precision matrix. In optimization, Newton's method uses the Hessian ∇²f(x); if PD, the step is a descent direction. The Loewner order A ≽ B means A−B is PSD; this partial order underlies semidefinite programming. The Schur complement of a block in a PD matrix is PD, and the determinant satisfies det(A) ≤ ∏ aᵢᵢ (Hadamard's inequality) with equality iff A is diagonal.

Matrix Exponential and Linear Differential Equations — Continuous Time Dynamics

The matrix exponential eᴬ = ∑k=0^∞ Aᵏ/k! converges for all square matrices and solves the initial value problem dx/dt = Ax, x(0) = x₀ with solution x(t) = etAx₀. Properties: e⁰ = I; eA+B = eᴬeᴮ if AB = BA; (eᴬ)⁻¹ = e−ᴬ; det(eᴬ) = etr(A); eigenvalues of eᴬ are eλᵢ where λᵢ are eigenvalues of A. For diagonalizable A = XΛX⁻¹, eᴬ = Xe^ΛX⁻¹. For defective matrices, use Jordan form: if J = λI + N with N nilpotent, eᴶ = e^λ ∑k=0m−1 Nᵏ/k! where m is the block size. The matrix exponential maps skew-symmetric matrices to orthogonal matrices (Lie algebra so(n) to Lie group SO(n)), and maps symmetric matrices to PD matrices. Computing eᴬ numerically is subtle: the scaling-and-squaring method with Padé approximants (eᴬ ≈ (I + A/2)⁻¹(I − A/2) for small ‖A‖) is standard. For large sparse matrices, Krylov subspace methods approximate eᴬv without forming eᴬ. The matrix exponential solves inhomogeneous systems dx/dt = Ax + f(t) via variation of parameters: x(t) = etAx₀ + ∫₀ᵗ e(t−s)Af(s)ds. In control theory, the controllability Gramian W_c = ∫₀ᵀ eAτBBᵀeAᵀτdτ determines reachability. The Lyapunov equation AᵀP + PA = −Q with Q ≻ 0 has unique PD solution P = ∫₀^∞ eAᵀτQeAτdτ iff A is Hurwitz (all eigenvalues in left half-plane), providing a stability certificate.

Tensor Products and Kronecker Products — Multilinear Algebra

The Kronecker product A ⊗ B of an m×n matrix A and p×q matrix B is the mp×nq block matrix [aᵢⱼB]. It represents the tensor product of linear maps: if A: V → W and B: X → Y, then A ⊗ B: V ⊗ X → W ⊗ Y acts on simple tensors as (A ⊗ B)(v ⊗ x) = Av ⊗ Bx and extends linearly. Properties: (A ⊗ B)(C ⊗ D) = AC ⊗ BD when dimensions match; (A ⊗ B)ᵀ = Aᵀ ⊗ Bᵀ; (A ⊗ B)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ ⊗ B⁻¹; det(A ⊗ B) = (det A)ᵖ(det B)ᵐ; eigenvalues are λᵢμⱼ for λᵢ ∈ σ(A), μⱼ ∈ σ(B); singular values are σᵢτⱼ. The vec operator stacks columns: vec(ABC) = (Cᵀ ⊗ A)vec(B). This transforms matrix equations into linear systems: the Sylvester equation AX + XB = C becomes (I ⊗ A + Bᵀ ⊗ I)vec(X) = vec(C). The Lyapunov equation AᵀX + XA = C becomes (I ⊗ Aᵀ + Aᵀ ⊗ I)vec(X) = vec(C). In quantum mechanics, composite systems live in tensor product spaces: a two-qubit state is in ℂ² ⊗ ℂ² ≅ ℂ⁴, and joint operations are Kronecker products of single-qubit gates. The swap operator S = ∑ᵢⱼ |i⟩⟨j| ⊗ |j⟩⟨i| exchanges tensor factors. The partial trace tr_B(ρ_AB) = ∑ᵢ (I ⊗ ⟨i|)ρ_AB(I ⊗ |i⟩) reduces a bipartite state to a subsystem. In numerical linear algebra, the Kronecker structure of discretized PDE operators (e.g., 2D Laplacian Δ = I ⊗ D + D ⊗ I) enables fast solvers via eigendecomposition of the 1D operator D. The Kronecker sum A ⊕ B = A ⊗ I + I ⊗ B has eigenvalues λᵢ + μⱼ and appears in exponential of sums: eA⊕B = eᴬ ⊗ eᴮ.

  • Assuming a matrix is diagonalizable when it has repeated eigenvalues — always check geometric multiplicity.
  • Using normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb for ill-conditioned problems — squares the condition number; use QR or SVD.
  • Confusing the Frobenius norm with the spectral norm — they differ by up to factor √rank.
  • Applying Cholesky decomposition without verifying positive definiteness — fails silently with negative pivots in finite precision.
  • Treating matrix exponential as elementwise exponential — eᴬ ≠ [eaᵢⱼ]; use scaling-and-squaring or Jordan form.
  • Ignoring the mixed-product property (A ⊗ B)(C ⊗ D) = AC ⊗ BD — only holds when AC and BD are defined.
  • Assuming κ(A) = 1/ε guarantees full precision — the bound is pessimistic; actual error depends on perturbation direction.

hand/copula-theory.html:
Pair-Copula Constructions and Vine Structures

Pair-copula constructions (PCCs) decompose a multivariate density into a product of bivariate copula densities and marginal densities, enabling flexible modelling of high‑dimensional dependence. For a d‑dimensional random vector X = (X₁,…,X_d) with continuous margins, the joint density f(x₁,…,x_d) can be written as

f(x₁,…,x_d) = ∏k=1d f_k(x_k) × ∏j=1d-1 ∏i=1d-j ci,i+j|i+1,…,i+j-1(F(x_i|xi+1,…,xi+j-1), F(xi+j|xi+1,…,xi+j-1))

where ca,b|D denotes a bivariate copula density for the pair (a,b) conditioned on the set D. The conditioning sets are organised in a graphical structure called a regular vine (R‑vine). Two widely used regular vines are the canonical vine (C‑vine) and the drawable vine (D‑vine). In a C‑vine each tree has a single node that connects to all other nodes, producing a star‑shaped structure; the first tree links variable 1 with every other variable, the second tree links variable 2 with the remaining variables conditioned on variable 1, and so on. In a D‑vine the trees form a path: the first tree links (1,2), (2,3), …, (d-1,d); the second tree links (1,3|2), (2,4|3), …; higher trees continue the pattern. The choice between C‑vine and D‑vine influences the interpretation of conditional dependencies and the computational cost of likelihood evaluation.

Model selection for vines proceeds in three stages: (1) choose the vine structure (C‑vine, D‑vine, or a general R‑vine) using a heuristic such as the maximum spanning tree on empirical Kendall’s τ; (2) select a bivariate copula family for each edge from a candidate set (Gaussian, Student‑t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, BB1, BB7, etc.) using information criteria (AIC, BIC) or a goodness‑of‑fit test; (3) estimate parameters sequentially by maximum likelihood or by the inference‑for‑margins (IFM) method. The sequential nature of the likelihood allows fast evaluation even in dimensions above 50, because each bivariate copula is fitted on pseudo‑observations obtained from the previous trees. Vine copulas have become standard in financial risk management for portfolio VaR, in actuarial science for modelling claim dependence across lines of business, and in environmental statistics for spatial extremes.

Dynamic and Time-Varying Copulas

Static copulas assume a constant dependence structure, but many applications exhibit evolving dependence — for example, correlation between equity returns increases during market stress. Dynamic copulas let the copula parameter θ_t vary with time, typically driven by an autoregressive process on a transformed scale. A popular specification for the Gaussian copula correlation ρ_t is the Patton (2006) evolution equation:

ρ_t = Λ( ω + α · Φ⁻¹(ut-1) Φ⁻¹(vt-1) + β · ρt-1 )

where Λ(x) = (1 - e-x)/(1 + e-x) maps ℝ to (-1,1), Φ⁻¹ is the standard normal quantile function, and (ut-1, vt-1) are the probability integral transforms of the observed returns at time t-1. For the Student‑t copula the degrees‑of‑freedom parameter ν can also be made time‑varying, though identification is more delicate. Estimation is usually performed by maximum likelihood on the copula log‑likelihood, with the marginal dynamics (e.g., GARCH(1,1) with skewed‑t innovations) filtered out first (the two‑step IFM approach). The resulting filtered standardized residuals are transformed to uniform scores via the empirical distribution function or a parametric marginal CDF, and the copula parameters are estimated conditional on these scores.

Model diagnostics include the probability integral transform (PIT) of the copula residuals, which should be i.i.d. uniform if the dynamic specification is adequate. Likelihood ratio tests can compare a static copula against a dynamic alternative. In practice, dynamic Gaussian copulas often underestimate tail risk because the Gaussian copula has zero tail dependence regardless of ρ_t; dynamic Student‑t copulas retain symmetric tail dependence λ_U = λ_L = 2·tν+1(-√((ν+1)(1-ρ_t)/(1+ρ_t))) and are therefore preferred for risk‑sensitive applications such as conditional VaR and Expected Shortfall backtesting.

Worked Example: One‑Step Forecast of Dynamic Gaussian Copula Correlation
Suppose a bivariate return series has been filtered with GARCH(1,1) margins, yielding uniform scores ut-1=0.92, vt-1=0.88 at the most recent observation. The estimated Patton parameters are ω = -0.15, α = 0.08, β = 0.90. Compute the one‑step ahead correlation forecast ρ_t.
First compute the normal quantiles: Φ⁻¹(0.92) ≈ 1.405, Φ⁻¹(0.88) ≈ 1.175. Their product is 1.405 × 1.175 ≈ 1.651. The linear predictor is ω + α·product + β·ρt-1. Assume the previous correlation ρt-1 = 0.45 (obtained from the filtered series). Then predictor = -0.15 + 0.08×1.651 + 0.90×0.45 = -0.15 + 0.132 + 0.405 = 0.387. Apply the logistic transform Λ(x) = (1 - e-x)/(1 + e-x). e-0.387 ≈ 0.679. Λ(0.387) = (1 - 0.679)/(1 + 0.679) = 0.321/1.679 ≈ 0.191. Hence the forecast correlation ρ_t ≈ 0.19.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a dynamic copula forecast, always verify whether the marginal model has already been filtered. If the problem provides raw returns, you must first standardise them (e.g., GARCH residuals) and then apply the probability integral transform. Skipping this step leads to incorrect uniform scores and a wrong correlation forecast. Memorise the logistic transform Λ(x) and its inverse for quick parameter bounds checking.

Estimation and Inference for Copula Models

Accurate parameter estimation is crucial because copula likelihoods can be flat or multimodal, especially in high dimensions. The most common approaches are (1) Full Maximum Likelihood (FML), which jointly estimates marginal and copula parameters; (2) Inference‑for‑Margins (IFM), a two‑step method where marginal parameters are estimated first, then the copula parameters are estimated by maximising the copula log‑likelihood with the marginal CDFs plugged in; (3) Canonical Maximum Likelihood (CML), also called pseudo‑maximum likelihood, where the marginal CDFs are replaced by their empirical counterparts (rank‑based) and only the copula parameters are optimised. IFM is asymptotically equivalent to FML under regularity conditions and is computationally cheaper because the marginal estimation can be done univariately. CML is robust to marginal misspecification but loses efficiency when the true margins are known.

The copula log‑likelihood for a sample of n observations (u_i, v_i) is ℓ(θ) = ∑i=1n log c_θ(u_i, v_i), where c_θ is the copula density. For Archimedean copulas the density involves the generator φ and its derivatives: c_θ(u,v) = φ''(C_θ(u,v)) φ'(φ⁻¹(u)) φ'(φ⁻¹(v)) / (φ'(φ⁻¹(C_θ(u,v))))³. Numerical stability requires careful implementation of φ, φ⁻¹, and their derivatives, especially near the boundaries 0 and 1. For vine copulas the log‑likelihood decomposes into a sum of bivariate copula log‑likelihoods evaluated at conditional pseudo‑observations obtained by the recursive h‑function: h(u|v; θ) = ∂C_θ(u,v)/∂v. Efficient evaluation uses the vine matrix representation (Dissmann et al., 2013).

Standard errors can be obtained from the observed Fisher information (negative Hessian of ℓ) or by a parametric bootstrap. For CML the asymptotic covariance matrix involves the copula score and the influence of the empirical marginal CDFs; a sandwich estimator is often used. Goodness‑of‑fit testing typically employs the Rosenblatt transform: for a fitted copula C_θ, define Z_i = (Zi1, Zi2) with Zi1=U_i, Zi2=∂C_θ(U_i,V_i)/∂U_i. Under the null, the Z_i are i.i.d. uniform on [0,1]². The Cramér‑von Mises statistic S_n = n ∫ (C_n(z) - C_θ(z))² dC_n(z) is computed on the transformed data, and p‑values are obtained by a parametric bootstrap because the limiting distribution depends on the unknown copula.

High-Dimensional Copula Modeling: Factor and Hierarchical Approaches

When the dimension d exceeds 20, pair‑copula constructions become cumbersome because the number of bivariate copulas grows as d(d-1)/2. Factor copulas reduce dimensionality by introducing a small number of latent factors that drive the dependence. A Gaussian factor copula assumes X = ΛF + ε, where F ∼ N(0,I_k) are k latent factors, Λ is a d×k loading matrix, and ε ∼ N(0,Ψ) with Ψ diagonal. The resulting correlation matrix is R = ΛΛᵀ + Ψ, and the copula is the Gaussian copula with correlation R. Estimation proceeds via EM algorithm or Bayesian MCMC. The factor structure imposes a low‑rank plus diagonal correlation, which is parsimonious but cannot capture tail dependence.

To incorporate tail dependence, t‑factor copulas replace the Gaussian factors with Student‑t factors, yielding a Student‑t copula with a low‑rank scale matrix. Hierarchical Archimedean copulas (HACs) nest Archimedean copulas at multiple levels: a root generator φ₀ combines subgroups, each subgroup has its own generator φ₁, φ₂, …, and the nesting condition φ₀⁻¹ ∘ φ_j must be completely monotone for all j. This ensures the resulting function is a valid copula. HACs can model asymmetric tail dependence across clusters (e.g., lower tail dependence within a sector, upper tail dependence across sectors). Structure learning for HACs uses agglomerative clustering based on pairwise Kendall’s τ, followed by a test of the nesting condition. In practice, factor copulas are favoured for very large portfolios (d > 100) where a few systemic factors dominate, while HACs are used when the dependence hierarchy is interpretable (e.g., industry sectors, geographic regions).

Extreme‑Value Copulas and Max‑Stable Processes

Extreme‑value theory provides the limiting dependence structure for componentwise maxima of i.i.d. random vectors. If (X_i, Y_i) are i.i.d. with continuous margins, and we consider block maxima M_n = (maxi≤n X_i, maxi≤n Y_i) with appropriate linear normalisation, the limiting copula C is an extreme‑value copula satisfying C(u^t, v^t) = C(u,v)^t for all t>0. Every extreme‑value copula can be represented via the Pickands dependence function A: [0,1] → [1/2,1] as

C(u,v) = exp( (log u + log v) · A( log u / (log u + log v) ) )

where A is convex, satisfies max(w, 1-w) ≤ A(w) ≤ 1, and A(0)=A(1)=1. The tail dependence coefficients are λ_U = 2 - 2A(1/2) and λ_L = 0 for non‑degenerate extreme‑value copulas (they only capture upper tail dependence). Popular parametric families include the Gumbel–Hougaard copula (A(w) = (w^θ + (1-w)^θ)1/θ, θ≥1), the Galambos copula, and the Hüsler–Reiss copula derived from a Gaussian scale mixture. Estimation of A can be non‑parametric (Pickands estimator, Capéraà‑Fougères‑Genest estimator) or parametric via maximum likelihood on the exponent measure.

Max‑stable processes extend this to spatial or temporal extremes: a process {Z(s): s∈S} is max‑stable if for any n, the pointwise maximum of n independent copies, appropriately normalised, has the same finite‑dimensional distributions as Z. The Brown‑Resnick process and the Smith (Gaussian extreme‑value) process are key models. Inference for max‑stable processes uses composite likelihoods based on bivariate or trivariate margins because the full likelihood is intractable. These models are essential for environmental risk assessment (e.g., spatial rainfall extremes, wind gust fields) and for financial systemic risk where the joint tail of many institutions matters.

  • Confusing the logistic transform Λ(x) with the inverse logit; the copula correlation must stay in (-1,1) so the transform is (1-e-x)/(1+e-x), not ex/(1+ex).
  • Assuming the Gaussian copula can capture tail dependence when the correlation is high; λ_U = λ_L = 0 for any |ρ|<1.
  • Using the empirical CDF directly in the copula likelihood without rank transformation; this introduces ties and biases the pseudo‑observations.
  • Neglecting the nesting condition in hierarchical Archimedean copulas; not all generator combinations produce a valid copula.
  • Treating the Pickands dependence function A as unrestricted; it must be convex and bounded between max(w,1-w) and 1.
  • Applying the Rosenblatt transform to a vine copula without conditioning on the correct h‑functions; the transform must follow the vine ordering.
  • Overlooking the need for a parametric bootstrap when computing p‑values for Cramér‑von Mises statistics; the asymptotic distribution depends on the unknown copula.

These advanced topics complete the toolkit needed for rigorous dependence modelling in high‑stakes quantitative examinations.

hand/plasma-physics.html:
Resistive MHD and Magnetic Reconnection Models

Ideal MHD assumes infinite conductivity, which forces magnetic field lines to move with the plasma (the frozen‑in flux theorem). Real plasmas have finite resistivity η, introducing a diffusion term η∇²B in the induction equation ∂B/∂t = ∇×(v×B) + η∇²B. The dimensionless Lundquist number S = μ₀LV_A/η compares advection to diffusion; for S ≫ 1 the plasma behaves ideally except in thin current sheets where gradients become large enough for resistive diffusion to compete. The Sweet–Parker model (1957) treats a steady, two‑dimensional current sheet of length L and thickness δ. Mass continuity gives v_in L ≈ v_out δ, and the outflow speed v_out approaches the Alfvén speed V_A. Balancing the electric field E = ηJ ≈ ηB/δ with the convective field v_in B yields the reconnection rate v_in/V_A ∼ S⁻¹ᐟ². For typical coronal parameters S ∼ 10¹², this rate is far too slow to explain observed flare timescales.

Petschek (1964) proposed that the diffusion region can be much shorter if standing slow‑mode shocks attach to its ends, allowing the inflow region to expand. The reconnection rate then scales as (ln S)⁻¹, essentially independent of S for large values. Numerical simulations confirm that a localized resistivity enhancement or kinetic effects (Hall term, electron pressure tensor) can produce a Petschek‑like geometry. In collisionless plasmas the Hall MHD equations add the term (1/ne)J×B to Ohm’s law, decoupling ion and electron motion at scales below the ion inertial length d_i = c/ω_pi. This leads to a quadrupolar out‑of‑plane magnetic field and a reconnection rate of order 0.1 V_A, consistent with magnetospheric observations. The tearing mode, a resistive instability, creates magnetic islands at rational surfaces where k·B = 0. Its linear growth rate in the constant‑ψ regime scales as γ τ_A ∼ S⁻³ᐟ⁵ (kL)²ᐟ⁵, while the nonlinear Rutherford regime gives island width evolution dw/dt ∝ ηΔ′. Understanding these models is essential for interpreting sawtooth crashes in tokamaks and substorm onset in the magnetotail.

Neoclassical Transport and Bootstrap Current in Tokamaks

In a toroidal device the magnetic field strength varies as B ≈ B₀(1 − ε cos θ) with inverse aspect ratio ε = r/R. Particles whose parallel velocity is insufficient to overcome the magnetic mirror force become trapped in the low‑field side, executing banana orbits with a radial excursion Δr ∼ qρ_i/√ε, where ρ_i is the ion Larmor radius and q the safety factor. Collisions scatter particles between trapped and passing populations, producing a neoclassical particle flux that exceeds the classical (collisional) prediction by a factor ∼ ε⁻³ᐟ² in the banana regime (ν* ≪ ε³ᐟ²). The neoclassical ion thermal conductivity χ_i^NC scales as χ_i^NC ∼ ε³ᐟ² q² ρ_i² ν_i, where ν_i is the ion collision frequency. In the plateau regime (ε³ᐟ² ≪ ν* ≪ 1) the scaling softens to χ_i^NC ∼ q² ρ_i² ν_i, and in the Pfirsch–Schlüter regime (ν* ≫ 1) it becomes χ_i^NC ∼ ε⁻² q² ρ_i² ν_i.

A striking consequence of trapped‑particle dynamics is the bootstrap current. Because trapped particles carry no net toroidal current, a radial pressure gradient creates an imbalance in the parallel momentum of passing particles, driving a toroidal current even without external induction. The bootstrap current density j_bs ≈ −(ε¹ᐟ²/ B_θ) dp/dr (for a large‑aspect‑ratio circular cross‑section) can reach a substantial fraction of the total plasma current in high‑β, high‑q scenarios. In advanced tokamak operation the bootstrap fraction f_bs = I_bs/I_p can exceed 0.7, reducing the demand on non‑inductive current drive systems. Neoclassical theory also predicts the Ware pinch, an inward particle drift v_W = −(E_φ/B_θ) (ρ_i²/2R) that can improve core density peaking. Accurate neoclassical modeling requires solving the drift‑kinetic equation with a linearized collision operator (e.g., the Lorentz or full Fokker–Planck operator) and is implemented in codes such as NEO, DKES, and SFINCS.

Worked Problem: Bootstrap Current Estimate
A tokamak plasma has major radius R = 3 m, minor radius a = 1 m, toroidal field B_φ = 5 T, and a pressure profile p(r) = p₀(1 − r²/a²) with p₀ = 2 × 10⁵ Pa. Assuming a large‑aspect‑ratio circular cross‑section and ε = a/R, estimate the total bootstrap current I_bs using the simplified formula I_bs ≈ (ε¹ᐟ²/μ₀) (a/B_θ) (dp/dr) evaluated at r = a/2. Take B_θ ≈ μ₀ I_p/(2πa) with I_p = 2 MA.
First compute ε = 1/3 ≈ 0.333, ε¹ᐟ² ≈ 0.577. The pressure gradient dp/dr = −2p₀ r/a². At r = a/2 = 0.5 m, dp/dr = −2 × 2×10⁵ × 0.5 / 1² = −2×10⁵ Pa/m. The poloidal field B_θ = μ₀ I_p/(2πa) = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 2×10⁶)/(2π×1) = 0.4 T. Then I_bs ≈ (0.577/μ₀) × (a/B_θ) × |dp/dr| = (0.577 / 4π×10⁻⁷) × (1/0.4) × 2×10⁵ ≈ (0.577 × 2×10⁵) / (1.6π×10⁻⁷) ≈ 1.15×10⁵ / (5.03×10⁻⁷) ≈ 2.3×10¹¹ A. This absurdly large number signals that the simplified formula must be multiplied by a geometric factor of order (ρ_i/a)² or the pressure gradient must be expressed in normalized units; the correct bootstrap fraction for these parameters is typically f_bs ∼ 0.3–0.5, giving I_bs ∼ 0.6–1 MA. The exercise illustrates the importance of using the full neoclassical coefficient (including collisionality and geometry) rather than the crude scaling alone.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the scaling of neoclassical transport or bootstrap current, first identify the collisionality regime (banana, plateau, Pfirsch–Schlüter) from the given ν* or temperature/density. Then write the appropriate power‑law dependence on ε, q, ρ_i, and ν_i. For bootstrap current, remember the √ε factor and the proportionality to the pressure gradient; a quick sanity check is that f_bs rarely exceeds 0.8 in realistic scenarios.

Parametric Decay Instabilities and Wave Coupling

When a high‑amplitude pump wave propagates in a plasma, it can decay into two lower‑frequency daughter waves if the matching conditions ω₀ = ω₁ + ω₂ and k₀ = k₁ + k₂ are satisfied. This three‑wave parametric decay instability (PDI) is a fundamental nonlinear process that limits the power that can be coupled into plasma waves for heating and current drive. A classic example is the decay of an electron plasma wave (Langmuir wave) into another Langmuir wave and an ion‑acoustic wave: ω_pe ≈ ω_pe + k c_s. The growth rate for this decay, in the limit kλ_D ≪ 1, is γ ≈ (|E₀|/E_th) ω_pe, where E_th = (m_e ω_pe v_Te/e) is the thermal electric field. For typical laser‑fusion parameters (I ∼ 10¹⁵ W/cm²) the pump field can exceed E_th, leading to rapid spectral broadening and hot‑electron generation.

In magnetized plasmas the decay channels multiply. An electromagnetic pump (e.g., an extraordinary mode X‑mode near the upper hybrid resonance) can decay into an electron Bernstein wave and an ion‑acoustic wave, or into two electron Bernstein waves. The matching conditions involve the full cold‑plasma dispersion tensor, and the coupling coefficient depends on the pump polarization and the angle between k₀ and B₀. Parametric decay of lower hybrid waves into ion‑acoustic and quasi‑modes is a key saturation mechanism for lower hybrid current drive. In tokamaks, the decay of ion‑cyclotron range of frequencies (ICRF) fast waves into ion‑Bernstein waves and ion‑acoustic waves can degrade heating efficiency and produce energetic ion tails. The threshold pump power for PDI scales as P_th ∝ (γ_L/|V|)², where γ_L is the linear damping rate of the daughter waves and V is the three‑wave coupling coefficient. Experimental identification of PDI relies on detecting the daughter waves with reflectometry, collective Thomson scattering, or probes, and observing the characteristic frequency down‑shift and spectral broadening.

Advanced Stellarator Optimization and Reactor Materials

Stellarators avoid the need for a large plasma current by shaping the magnetic field with external coils, but this introduces three‑dimensional magnetic geometry that can degrade neoclassical confinement. Modern optimization targets the quasi‑symmetry condition: the magnetic field strength B(ψ,θ,ζ) depends on a single helical angle Mθ − Nζ, making the drift orbits resemble those in an axisymmetric tokamak. Quasi‑helical symmetry (e.g., HSX) and quasi‑axisymmetry (e.g., NCSX) have demonstrated neoclassical transport levels comparable to tokamaks. The optimization loop couples a magnetic equilibrium code (VMEC) with a neoclassical transport code (DKES, SFINCS) and a coil design code (REGCOIL, FOCUS) to minimize a cost function that includes neoclassical heat flux, coil complexity, and engineering tolerances. Recent advances use adjoint methods to compute gradients of the cost function with respect to coil shapes, enabling high‑dimensional optimization.

Reactor‑relevant stellarators must also withstand high neutron fluxes (∼ 1 MW/m²) and heat loads on the first wall and divertor. Reduced‑activation ferritic/martensitic steels (e.g., EUROFER97) and oxide‑dispersion‑strengthened (ODS) alloys are leading candidates for the blanket and structural components. Tungsten is favored for the divertor target due to its high melting point and low sputtering yield, but its brittle‑to‑ductile transition and helium‑induced embrittlement under fusion neutron spectra require careful alloy design (e.g., W‑Ta, W‑V). Liquid metal concepts (lithium, tin‑lithium) offer self‑healing surfaces and low recycling, yet introduce magnetohydrodynamic pressure drops and corrosion challenges. The integration of optimized 3D magnetic geometry with advanced materials and a viable tritium breeding blanket (e.g., helium‑cooled lithium‑lead) defines the engineering pathway toward a stellarator demonstration power plant (DEMO‑ST).

  • Confusing the Sweet–Parker S⁻¹ᐟ² scaling with the Petschek (ln S)⁻¹ scaling; the latter requires localized diffusion or Hall physics.
  • Assuming bootstrap current scales linearly with pressure gradient without the √ε geometric factor and collisionality dependence.
  • Neglecting the matching conditions ω₀ = ω₁ + ω₂, k₀ = k₁ + k₂ when evaluating parametric decay thresholds.
  • Treating quasi‑symmetry as exact symmetry; small symmetry‑breaking fields can still cause significant neoclassical transport if not quantified.
  • Using bulk material properties (e.g., tungsten melting point) without accounting for neutron‑induced embrittlement and helium bubble formation at reactor fluence.
  • Overlooking the role of the ion‑sound speed c_s = √(k_B T_e/m_i) in setting the ion‑acoustic daughter wave frequency in PDI.
  • Forgetting that the Lundquist number S = μ₀LV_A/η must be evaluated with the Spitzer resistivity η ∝ T_e⁻³ᐟ² for a given plasma temperature.

hand/astrophysics.html:
Supernova Explosion Mechanisms and Neutrino Emission

Core‑collapse supernovae arise when the iron core of a massive star exceeds the effective Chandrasekhar mass and collapses to nuclear density. The inner core reaches ∼3×1014 g cm−3 and rebounds, launching a prompt shock that stalls at ∼100–200 km due to photodisintegration of heavy nuclei and neutrino losses. The delayed neutrino‑heating mechanism revives the shock: electron‑type neutrinos and antineutrinos emitted from the nascent proto‑neutron star deposit energy in the gain region behind the shock via charged‑current absorption on free nucleons (νe + n → p + e−, ν̅e + p → n + e+). Typical neutrino luminosities are Lν ≈ 3–5×1052 erg s−1 per flavour, with mean energies ⟨Eν⟩ ≈ 10–15 MeV for νe and 12–18 MeV for ν̅e. Multi‑dimensional simulations show that the standing accretion shock instability (SASI) and neutrino‑driven convection create large‑scale asymmetries, boosting the heating efficiency and producing the observed kick velocities of pulsars (≳500 km s−1). The neutrino burst carries away ≈99 % of the gravitational binding energy (∼3×1053 erg), and the detected neutrinos from SN 1987A (Kamiokande‑II, IMB, Baksan) confirmed the basic picture: a ∼10 s burst of ∼20 events with energies 7–40 MeV. Pair‑instability supernovae in very massive stars (≳130 M⊙) avoid collapse; instead, runaway oxygen burning unbinds the star completely, leaving no compact remnant. Thermonuclear (Type Ia) supernovae result from carbon ignition in a carbon‑oxygen white dwarf approaching the Chandrasekhar limit, either via single‑degenerate accretion or double‑degenerate merger; the explosion synthesises ≈0.5–1.0 M⊙ of 56Ni, powering the light curve through its radioactive decay chain.

Binary Stellar Evolution and Gravitational Wave Progenitors

Most massive stars reside in binary or higher‑order systems, and binary interaction dramatically alters their evolutionary pathways. When a star fills its Roche lobe, mass transfer can be stable (case A, B, or C depending on the donor’s evolutionary stage) or dynamically unstable, leading to a common‑envelope (CE) phase. During CE evolution the orbital energy of the binary is deposited into the envelope, ejecting it if αCE λ ΔEorb > Ebind, where αCE is the ejection efficiency and λ parametrises the envelope structure. The outcome is a tight binary containing a stripped helium star (or a compact object) and a companion. Subsequent evolution can produce double compact objects: double neutron stars (DNS), neutron star–black hole (NS‑BH) binaries, or binary black holes (BBH). The orbital decay driven by gravitational‑wave radiation follows the Peters formula: da/dt = −(64/5) G3 m1 m2(m1+m2)/(c5 a3 (1−e2)7/2) × (1+73/24 e2+37/96 e4). For circular orbits the merger time is tmerge ≈ (5/256) c5 a4/(G3 m1 m2(m1+m2)). LIGO‑Virgo detections (GW150914, GW170817, etc.) have measured component masses in the range 1.2–2.0 M⊙ for DNS and 5–50 M⊙ for BBH, confirming that CE evolution with αCE ≈ 0.1–1.0 can produce the observed merger rates (≈10–100 Gpc−3 yr−1 for BBH, ≈100–1000 Gpc−3 yr−1 for DNS). Electromagnetic counterparts such as kilonovae (e.g., AT2017gfo) arise from r‑process nucleosynthesis in the ejecta of NS mergers, linking binary evolution to the origin of the heaviest elements. The distribution of effective spin parameters χeff measured by LIGO‑Virgo constrains the natal kick magnitudes and the degree of spin–orbit alignment, providing a direct probe of supernova physics in binaries.

Worked Problem: Merger Time of a Double Neutron Star
A double neutron star system has component masses m1=1.35 M⊙, m2=1.25 M⊙ and a circular orbit with separation a=1.0 R⊙. Estimate the gravitational‑wave driven merger time.
Use the circular‑orbit merger formula tmerge = (5/256) c5 a4 / [G3 m1 m2(m1+m2)]. Insert constants: G=6.674×10−11 m3 kg−1 s−2, c=2.998×108 m s−1, M⊙=1.989×1030 kg, R⊙=6.96×108 m. Compute m1m2(m1+m2) = (1.35×1.25×2.60) M⊙3 ≈ 4.39 M⊙3. Convert a=1.0 R⊙ = 6.96×108 m. Numerically, tmerge ≈ 1.1×109 yr. This is comparable to the age of the Galaxy, so such a system would merge within a Hubble time.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a merger time, first check whether the orbit is circular; if eccentricity is given, use the full Peters expression. Memorise the scaling tmerge ∝ a4/(m1m2(m1+m2)) to quickly eliminate orders of magnitude. Keep a mental table of typical separations: a≈1 R⊙ → Gyr; a≈0.1 R⊙ → Myr; a≈0.01 R⊙ → yr.

Stellar Atmospheres, Radiative Transfer, and Spectroscopic Diagnostics

The emergent spectrum of a star is shaped by the temperature–pressure structure of its atmosphere and the radiative transfer equation dIν/dτν = Sν − Iν, where Iν is specific intensity, τν optical depth, and Sν the source function. In local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) the source function equals the Planck function Bν(T), and level populations follow the Boltzmann and Saha equations. Non‑LTE (NLTE) effects become important for strong resonance lines (e.g., H α, Ca II K) and in hot, low‑density atmospheres where radiative rates dominate collisional rates; the statistical equilibrium equations must be solved simultaneously with the transfer equation. Model atmospheres (e.g., ATLAS, MARCS, PHOENIX) compute the temperature stratification T(τ) under radiative‑convective equilibrium, using mixing‑length theory for convection. Spectroscopic diagnostics rely on equivalent widths Wλ = ∫(1−Fλ/Fc) dλ and curve‑of‑growth analysis to infer elemental abundances. The excitation balance of Fe I lines yields the effective temperature Teff; ionisation balance between Fe I and Fe II constrains surface gravity log g; microturbulent velocity ξt is set by requiring no trend of abundance with reduced equivalent width. For massive O‑type stars, the wind‑driven mass‑loss rate Ṁ is diagnosed from UV resonance lines (C IV λ1548,1550; Si IV λ1393,1402) using the Sobolev approximation, while H α emission traces the density squared in the wind. In cool giants, molecular bands (TiO, VO, CO) and the infrared Ca II triplet provide temperature and gravity indicators. High‑resolution spectroscopy (R ≳ 50 000) combined with NLTE line formation enables precision abundances at the 0.05 dex level, essential for chemical tagging of stellar populations and Galactic archaeology.

High‑Energy Transients: Gamma‑Ray Bursts and Magnetar Flares

Gamma‑ray bursts (GRBs) are the most luminous electromagnetic explosions known, with isotropic‑equivalent energies Eiso ≈ 1051–1054 erg released in seconds (short GRBs) to minutes (long GRBs). The leading model for long GRBs is the collapsar: a rapidly rotating, massive stellar core collapses to a black hole, and an accretion disk powers a relativistic jet that punches through the stellar envelope. The jet’s bulk Lorentz factor Γ ≈ 100–1000 produces the prompt γ‑ray emission via internal shocks or magnetic reconnection; the afterglow arises from the external forward shock sweeping up the circumburst medium, described by the standard synchrotron model with spectral breaks νm, νc, and νa. Short GRBs are attributed to binary neutron star or NS‑BH mergers; the kilonova AT2017gfo accompanying GW170817 confirmed this channel and demonstrated r‑process nucleosynthesis in the ejecta. Magnetars — neutron stars with surface dipole fields B ≈ 1014–1015 G — produce giant flares (e.g., SGR 1806−20, 2004 December 27) releasing ∼1046 erg in hard X‑rays/γ‑rays, powered by magnetic field reconfiguration and crustal fracturing. The persistent X‑ray emission of magnetars is explained by resonant cyclotron scattering in a twisted magnetosphere. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) have been associated with magnetar activity (e.g., FRB 200428 from SGR 1935+2154), linking coherent radio emission to magnetospheric currents. The rate density of long GRBs is ≈1 Gpc−3 yr−1, while short GRBs occur at ≈10 Gpc−3 yr−1; both are strongly beamed, with jet opening angles θj ≈ 5°–10°, implying true event rates larger by a factor ∼1/θj2.

Black Hole Thermodynamics, Hawking Radiation, and the Information Paradox

Black holes behave as thermodynamic objects with temperature TH = ℏ c3/(8π G M kB) and entropy SBH = kB c3 A/(4 G ℏ), where A = 4π rs2 is the horizon area and rs = 2GM/c2. For a solar‑mass black hole, TH ≈ 6×10−8 K, far below the cosmic microwave background, so astrophysical black holes gain mass from CMB absorption rather than evaporate. Hawking radiation arises from quantum field theory in curved spacetime: particle‑antiparticle pairs form near the horizon, one member falls in with negative energy, the other escapes to infinity. The spectrum is nearly thermal, with grey‑body factors modifying the emission rates for different spins. The evaporation time for a black hole of mass M is tevap ≈ 5120π G2 M3/(ℏ c4) ≈ 8.4×10−17 (M/kg)3 s; a 1012 kg primordial black hole would evaporate today. The information paradox stems from the apparent loss of unitarity: if the final state is purely thermal radiation, the initial pure quantum state evolves into a mixed state, violating quantum mechanics. Proposed resolutions include (i) information encoded in subtle correlations of the Hawking radiation (Page curve), (ii) remnants with Planck‑scale mass storing information, (iii) firewall at the horizon violating the equivalence principle, and (iv) holographic complementarity / AdS/CFT duality suggesting the interior is a dual description of the boundary theory. Recent developments using the quantum extremal surface formula and replica wormholes in Jackiw‑Teitelboim gravity have reproduced the Page curve, supporting unitary evaporation. Observational tests remain elusive, but analogue Hawking radiation in Bose‑Einstein condensates and optical systems provides laboratory insight into the kinematics of horizon radiation.

  • Confusing the Chandrasekhar limit for white dwarfs with the TOV limit for neutron stars; they differ by a factor of ∼2–3 in mass and arise from different degeneracy pressures.
  • Assuming all supernovae are powered by neutrino heating; Type Ia explosions are thermonuclear runaways with no neutrino‑driven shock revival.
  • Treating the common‑envelope ejection efficiency αCE as a universal constant; it depends on donor structure, orbital separation, and recombination energy.
  • Neglecting NLTE effects when interpreting strong resonance lines in hot stars; LTE abundances can be off by >0.5 dex for UV lines.
  • Equating the isotropic‑equivalent energy of a GRB with its true energy without correcting for beaming; the correction factor is ∼θj2/2.
  • Believing Hawking radiation is significant for stellar‑mass black holes; their temperature is many orders of magnitude below the CMB, so they accrete rather than evaporate.
  • Overlooking that the Page curve derivation relies on semiclassical gravity plus quantum extremal surfaces; it does not yet constitute a full microscopic description of black hole microstates.
