hand/mean-curvature-flow.html:
White's Local Regularity Theorem and the ε-Regularity Criterion

Brian White proved in 2000 that a mean curvature flow which is sufficiently close to a multiplicity‑one plane in a parabolic cylinder must be smooth and graphical on a smaller cylinder. The precise statement: there exists a universal constant ε > 0 such that if a Brakke flow V_t satisfies the Gaussian density ratio Θ(V_t, (x0, t0), r) ≤ 1 + ε for all r ≤ r0, then the flow is a smooth graph over the tangent plane in the parabolic cylinder P(x0, t0, r0/2). The Gaussian density ratio is defined by Θ(V, (x0, t0), r) = (4πr²)-n/2 ∫ exp(−|x−x0|²/(4r²)) dμVt0−r²(x). This ε‑regularity theorem is the parabolic analogue of Allard's regularity theorem for stationary varifolds and provides the main tool for proving that singular sets have parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n−1. The proof uses a blow‑up argument combined with Huisken's monotonicity formula: if the density ratio is close to 1, the rescaled flow converges to a static plane, and the graphical excess decays geometrically. A key corollary is that any point where the Gaussian density equals 1 is a regular point; conversely, singular points have density strictly greater than 1. The theorem also yields a quantitative estimate: the C1,α norm of the graphical representation is controlled by the excess. In applications, one often checks the ε‑regularity condition by estimating the L² norm of the second fundamental form on a parabolic ball; if ∫P_r |A|² ≤ ε, then the flow is smooth on Pr/2. This criterion underlies many partial regularity results for Brakke flows and for the level‑set flow after the work of Evans‑Spruck and Chen‑Giga‑Goto.

Ilmanen's Elliptic Regularization and the Construction of Brakke Flows

Tom Ilmanen introduced elliptic regularization in 1994 as a method to construct Brakke flows for arbitrary initial rectifiable varifolds with locally bounded first variation. The idea is to approximate the parabolic problem by a family of elliptic problems in one higher dimension. For a given time step τ > 0, one considers the functional E_τ(V) = ∫ (1 + |xn+2|²/τ) dμ_V on varifolds in ℝn+2 and minimizes it among varifolds that project to the given initial varifold at time 0. The minimizer is a stationary varifold in ℝn+2 with a weight that encodes the time direction. Slicing this stationary varifold by the hyperplanes xn+2 = const yields a discrete‑in‑time family of varifolds in ℝn+1. As τ → 0, a subsequence converges to a Brakke flow. The elliptic regularization has several advantages: it works for any integer rectifiable varifold without any curvature assumptions, it automatically produces a flow that satisfies the Brakke inequality, and it provides a natural framework for proving existence of flows with prescribed boundary conditions. Ilmanen also showed that if the initial varifold is smooth and mean convex, the elliptic regularization coincides with the classical smooth flow for a short time. The construction was later refined by Kasai‑Tonegawa and others to obtain uniqueness for mean convex initial data. A crucial technical ingredient is the compactness theorem for integral varifolds with bounded first variation in the higher‑dimensional space, which follows from Allard's compactness theorem. The elliptic regularization also yields a natural notion of “generalized mean curvature” for the limiting Brakke flow, defined as the first variation of the limiting varifold. This approach has become the standard existence theory for weak mean curvature flow in geometric measure theory.

Identifying the ε‑regularity scale in a blow‑up argument
Suppose a Brakke flow V_t in ℝ³ has a singular point at (0,0) with Gaussian density Θ = 1.2. Explain why the ε‑regularity theorem does not guarantee smoothness at (0,0) and describe how one would use a blow‑up sequence to analyse the tangent flow at this point.
The ε‑regularity theorem requires the Gaussian density ratio to be ≤ 1 + ε for some universal ε (typically ε ≈ 10⁻³). Since Θ = 1.2 > 1 + ε, the hypothesis fails, so the theorem gives no regularity conclusion. To analyse the singularity, choose a sequence of scales r_k → 0 and consider the rescaled flows V(k)_t defined by V(k)_t = (1/r_k) (Vr_k² t − 0). By Huisken's monotonicity formula, the Gaussian densities of the rescaled flows at (0,0) are all equal to 1.2. The compactness theorem for Brakke flows yields a subsequential limit V^∞_t, which is a tangent flow at (0,0). This limit is a self‑similar Brakke flow (a cone or a self‑shrinker) with density 1.2. Classification of low‑density self‑shrinkers in ℝ³ shows that the only possibilities with density < 2 are the round shrinking sphere (density ≈ 1.57) and the shrinking cylinder S¹×ℝ (density ≈ 1.77). Since 1.2 is below both, the tangent flow must be a static plane with multiplicity 1.2, which is impossible for an integer rectifiable varifold. Hence the assumption that a singular point has density 1.2 leads to a contradiction; in reality any singular point in ℝ³ has density at least the density of the cylinder, ≈ 1.77. This illustrates how ε‑regularity and blow‑up analysis combine to restrict possible singularity models.
Exam‑day strategy for regularity questions
When a question asks whether a point is regular, first compute or estimate the Gaussian density ratio. If the ratio is ≤ 1 + ε, cite White's ε‑regularity theorem directly. If the ratio is larger, set up a blow‑up sequence, invoke compactness of Brakke flows, and identify the tangent flow using known classification of self‑shrinkers (sphere, cylinder, plane). Remember that integer multiplicity forces the density of a tangent flow to be an integer multiple of the density of a smooth self‑shrinker; this often yields a quick contradiction.

Colding-Minicozzi Theory of Generic Singularities and the Multiplicity One Conjecture

Tobias Colding and William Minicozzi developed a comprehensive theory of generic singularities for mean curvature flow in a series of papers from 2012 onward. They proved that for a generic smooth initial hypersurface, the first singularity is modeled on a multiplicity‑one self‑shrinker, and that the only stable self‑shrinkers are the round sphere, the generalized cylinders S^k×ℝn−k, and the plane. The multiplicity one conjecture, now a theorem in many cases, asserts that the Gaussian density of any tangent flow at a singular point equals the multiplicity of the limiting varifold, which for generic flows is one. Colding‑Minicozzi introduced the notion of “generic singularities” as those that persist under small perturbations of the initial data. They showed that the set of initial hypersurfaces producing non‑generic singularities is of infinite codimension in the C^∞ topology. A key tool is the Lojasiewicz‑Simon gradient inequality for the F‑functional, which gives a rate of convergence of the rescaled flow to a self‑shrinker. The theory also provides a description of the singular set: it is a countable union of smooth manifolds of dimension at most n−1, and at almost every singular point the tangent flow is a cylinder Sn−1×ℝ. The multiplicity one result was extended by Bernstein‑Wang and by Hershkovits‑White to all integral Brakke flows with a mean convex assumption. These results have profound implications for the structure of singularities and for the validity of surgery procedures, because they guarantee that neck regions are asymptotically cylindrical with multiplicity one, allowing precise surgical cuts.

Mean Curvature Flow with Boundary and the Neumann Problem

When a hypersurface evolves by mean curvature flow while its boundary is constrained to lie on a fixed supporting hypersurface Σ ⊂ ℝn+1, the natural boundary condition is that the evolving surface meets Σ orthogonally (the Neumann condition). The short‑time existence for smooth initial data with orthogonal intersection was proved by Stahl (1996) and later by Ecker‑Huisken for graphical hypersurfaces. The flow preserves the orthogonal intersection angle if the supporting hypersurface is convex; if Σ is not convex, the angle may change and the flow can develop boundary singularities. A major result by Buckland (2005) shows that for a mean convex initial hypersurface with boundary on a convex Σ, the flow exists until the interior becomes singular or the boundary hits a non‑convex part of Σ. The monotonicity formula adapts to the boundary setting by adding a boundary term involving the second fundamental form of Σ. Huisken's monotonicity formula with boundary yields a Gaussian density that is monotone non‑increasing, and the ε‑regularity theorem extends to boundary points provided the density is close to 1/2 (the density of a half‑plane). Recent work by Edelen‑Huisken and by Hershkovits‑White establishes a boundary regularity theory: if the Gaussian density at a boundary point is < 1, the flow is smooth up to the boundary. The classification of boundary singularities is more subtle; self‑shrinkers with boundary on a plane correspond to half‑spheres and half‑cylinders. The Neumann problem also arises naturally in the study of capillary surfaces and in the level‑set method for flows with obstacles.

Network Flows and the Evolution of Triple Junctions

Network flow generalizes mean curvature flow to unions of curves (or hypersurfaces) meeting at junctions with prescribed angles. The classical case is the motion of three curves in the plane meeting at 120° angles (triple junctions). The flow is defined by the condition that each curve moves by its curvature vector, and at the junction the sum of unit tangent vectors is zero (Herring's condition). Short‑time existence for regular networks was proved by Bronsard‑Reitich (1993) and by Mantegazza‑Novaga‑Tortorelli (2004). The flow preserves the 120° condition if the initial network satisfies it. Singularities can occur when a curve shrinks to zero length (a “type‑I” singularity) or when a junction becomes degenerate. The classification of self‑similar network shrinkers by Ilmanen‑Neves‑Schulze (2014) shows that the only embedded self‑shrinkers with triple junctions are the standard triod (three half‑lines meeting at 120°) and the “lens” shaped networks. A major open problem is the global existence of network flow past singularities; Brakke‑type varifold solutions for networks have been constructed by Kim‑Tonegawa (2017) using a discrete‑time minimizing movements scheme. The network flow appears in materials science (grain boundaries) and in the study of foam evolution. The level‑set method for networks was developed by Giga‑Goto‑Ishii‑Sato (1998) using a system of viscosity equations. Recent work by Lira‑Mazzeo‑Pluda (2020) analyzes the asymptotic behavior of network flow on surfaces, showing convergence to a geodesic network under certain curvature conditions.

  • Confusing the ε‑regularity constant ε with the Gaussian density value; the theorem requires density ≤ 1+ε, not density ≤ ε.
  • Assuming that every tangent flow is a smooth self‑shrinker; tangent flows can be stationary cones or multiplicities of smooth shrinkers.
  • Neglecting the integer multiplicity condition when applying the multiplicity one conjecture; a density of 1.5 cannot arise from an integer rectifiable varifold.
  • Overlooking the boundary term in Huisken's monotonicity formula for flows with Neumann conditions; the density at a boundary regular point is 1/2, not 1.
  • Treating network flow as a simple extension of curve shortening flow without accounting for the junction conditions; the 120° angle is essential for the variational structure.
  • Believing that Brakke flow uniqueness holds for all initial data; uniqueness fails in general and is known only for mean convex or graphical initial conditions.
  • Misapplying the level‑set fattening criterion; fattening occurs when the zero level set develops interior, which signals non‑uniqueness of the geometric evolution, not a failure of the viscosity solution.

These advanced topics complete the picture of mean curvature flow beyond the foundational theorems and prepare the aspirant for research‑level questions on regularity, weak solutions, and singularity analysis.

hand/info-theory.html:
Channel Coding Theorem — Achievability and Converse

The channel coding theorem, proved by Shannon in 1948, establishes that for any discrete memoryless channel with capacity C, reliable communication at rates R < C is possible, while rates R > C are impossible. The achievability part uses random coding: generate a codebook of 2nR codewords independently according to the input distribution that maximizes mutual information. By the law of large numbers, the joint typicality decoder succeeds with high probability as blocklength n grows, provided R < I(X;Y). The converse follows from Fano's inequality: if a sequence of codes achieves vanishing error probability, then nR ≤ I(X^n;Y^n) + nε_n, and because the channel is memoryless, I(X^n;Y^n) ≤ nC. Dividing by n and letting n → ∞ yields R ≤ C. The theorem also extends to channels with memory under appropriate ergodicity assumptions, where the capacity is given by the limit of (1/n) max I(X^n;Y^n).

Key steps in the achievability proof include the definition of jointly typical sets, the packing lemma, and the use of the union bound over error events. The converse relies on the data‑processing inequality and the fact that conditioning reduces entropy. Modern refinements, such as the strong converse, show that for many channels the error probability tends to one exponentially fast when R > C. The exponent is given by the sphere‑packing bound or the reliability function E(R). Understanding both directions is essential for evaluating the fundamental limits of any communication system.

Network Information Theory — Multiple Access, Broadcast, and Relay Channels

Network information theory generalizes point‑to‑point results to multi‑user scenarios. The multiple‑access channel (MAC) models several transmitters sending to a single receiver. Its capacity region is the set of rate tuples (R1,…,R_K) satisfying Σi∈S R_i ≤ I(X_S;Y|XS^c) for all subsets S ⊆ {1,…,K}, where the mutual information is evaluated under a product input distribution. The region is a polymatroid, and successive decoding achieves all corner points. The broadcast channel (BC) has one transmitter and multiple receivers. For the degraded BC, the capacity region is known and achieved by superposition coding and successive cancellation. For general BCs, the capacity region remains open; the best known inner bound is the Marton region with a common message, and the outer bound is the UVW bound. Relay channels introduce a node that assists communication. The decode‑and‑forward and compress‑and‑forward strategies give achievable rates, while the cut‑set bound provides a universal outer bound. These models underpin modern cellular, satellite, and ad‑hoc networks, and their study reveals how cooperation and interference management shape fundamental limits.

Worked Example: MAC Sum‑Rate Bound
Consider a two‑user binary additive MAC: Y = X1 ⊕ X2 ⊕ Z, where X1, X2 ∈ {0,1} are independent Bernoulli(½) and Z ∼ Bernoulli(p) independent of the inputs. Compute the maximum sum rate R1 + R2 achievable with vanishing error probability.
The sum‑rate bound for the MAC is R1 + R2 ≤ I(X1,X2;Y). Since X1 and X2 are independent uniform bits, X1 ⊕ X2 is also uniform. The channel reduces to a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p. Its capacity is 1 − H(p), where H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1−p) log₂(1−p). Therefore the maximum sum rate is 1 − H(p) bits per channel use. This bound is tight because the MAC region for this symmetric channel is a pentagon whose sum‑rate vertex equals the point‑to‑point capacity of the equivalent BSC.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a capacity region, first identify the channel model (MAC, BC, relay). Write down the standard single‑letter mutual‑information expressions. For MAC, list all subset bounds; for degraded BC, write the superposition‑coding region. If the model is not degraded, state the best known inner and outer bounds. Always check whether the input distribution is specified or must be optimized; if unspecified, assume the capacity‑achieving distribution (often uniform for symmetric channels).

Information-Theoretic Security — Wiretap Channel and Secret Key Agreement

Information‑theoretic security guarantees secrecy without computational assumptions. The wiretap channel, introduced by Wyner (1975), consists of a main channel to the legitimate receiver and a degraded eavesdropper channel. The secrecy capacity is C_s = maxp(x) [I(X;Y) − I(X;Z)], where the maximum is over input distributions. If the eavesdropper's channel is not degraded, the Csiszár‑Körner formula gives the secrecy capacity as maxp(u,x) [I(U;Y) − I(U;Z)] with an auxiliary random variable U. Secret key agreement over a public channel with correlated observations uses the source model: Alice, Bob, and Eve observe i.i.d. triples (X,Y,Z). The secret key capacity equals the conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) when public discussion is unlimited. The achievability uses privacy amplification (hashing) and information reconciliation (error correction). These results form the basis of quantum key distribution proofs and modern physical‑layer security in wireless networks.

Algorithmic Information Theory — Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy

Algorithmic information theory defines the information content of an individual object as the length of the shortest program that outputs it on a universal Turing machine. The Kolmogorov complexity K(x) of a binary string x is the minimal description length. It is uncomputable but satisfies fundamental inequalities: K(x) ≤ |x| + O(1), and for any computable probability distribution P, the expected Kolmogorov complexity satisfies E_P[K(X)] = H(P) + O(1), where H(P) is the Shannon entropy. The coding theorem of Levin and Chaitin states that −log m(x) = K(x) + O(1), where m(x) is the universal a priori probability. This links algorithmic randomness to Martin‑Löf randomness: a sequence is algorithmically random iff its prefixes have maximal Kolmogorov complexity. In practice, Kolmogorov complexity motivates the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle for model selection and provides a theoretical foundation for lossless compression limits beyond stationary ergodic sources.

Finite Blocklength Analysis — Dispersion and Second‑Order Asymptotics

Shannon's theorem is asymptotic in blocklength n. Real systems operate at finite n, where the maximal achievable rate R*(n,ε) for error probability ε admits a second‑order expansion: R*(n,ε) = C − √(V/n) Q-1(ε) + O(log n / n). Here C is the channel capacity, V is the channel dispersion (the variance of the information density), and Q-1 is the inverse Gaussian tail function. For a binary symmetric channel with crossover p, V = p(1−p) [log₂((1−p)/p)]². The normal approximation provides accurate predictions for moderate n (e.g., n ≈ 100–1000) and is used in 5G URLLC link‑budget calculations. The achievability proof uses random coding with a threshold decoder and the Berry‑Esseen theorem; the converse uses the meta‑converse and the Neyman‑Pearson lemma. Extensions to channels with state, feedback, and multi‑user settings are active research areas. Understanding dispersion is crucial for designing ultra‑reliable low‑latency communication systems.

  • Confusing the MAC sum‑rate bound with the individual user bounds; the sum bound is often the tightest constraint.
  • Assuming the broadcast channel capacity region is known for all cases; only degraded and a few special classes have exact characterizations.
  • Neglecting the auxiliary random variable U in the Csiszár‑Körner secrecy capacity formula for non‑degraded wiretap channels.
  • Treating Kolmogorov complexity as computable; it is only approximable up to an additive constant.
  • Applying the asymptotic capacity formula to short packets without the dispersion correction, leading to overly optimistic rate estimates.
  • Overlooking that the normal approximation requires the channel dispersion V > 0; for zero‑dispersion channels (e.g., noiseless) the second‑order term vanishes and a different scaling applies.
  • Misidentifying the cut‑set bound as the capacity of a relay channel; it is only an outer bound, and the true capacity remains unknown in general.

These advanced topics deepen the toolkit needed to analyse modern communication and security systems beyond the classical point‑to‑point framework.

hand/electrochemistry.html:
Electrochemical Kinetics: Overpotential, Tafel Equation, and Reaction Mechanisms

Thermodynamics tells whether a reaction can occur; kinetics tells how fast it proceeds at an electrode surface. The difference between the applied electrode potential and the equilibrium potential is the overpotential (η). Three contributions are usually distinguished: activation overpotential (ηact) arising from the energy barrier of the charge‑transfer step, concentration overpotential (ηconc) caused by depletion or accumulation of reactants near the interface, and ohmic overpotential (ηohm) due to solution resistance and contact resistances. The total overpotential is the sum η = ηact + ηconc + ηohm.

The fundamental relationship between current density (i) and activation overpotential is the Butler‑Volmer equation: i = i₀ [exp(αₐ nF ηact/RT) − exp(−α_c nF ηact/RT)], where i₀ is the exchange current density, αₐ and α_c are the anodic and cathodic transfer coefficients (αₐ + α_c = 1 for a single‑step electron transfer), n is the number of electrons, F the Faraday constant, R the gas constant and T the absolute temperature. At high overpotentials (|η| > 0.1 V) one exponential dominates, giving the Tafel equation: ηact = a + b log|i|, with Tafel slope b = 2.303 RT/(α nF). A plot of η versus log|i| (Tafel plot) yields i₀ from the intercept and α from the slope.

Mechanistic insight comes from identifying the rate‑determining step (RDS). For the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic media, two classic pathways exist: the Volmer‑Heyrovsky mechanism (Volmer step: H⁺ + e⁻ → Hads; Heyrovsky step: Hads + H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂) and the Volmer‑Tafel mechanism (Volmer step followed by Tafel recombination: 2 Hads → H₂). The observed Tafel slope distinguishes them: ~120 mV/dec for Volmer RDS, ~40 mV/dec for Heyrovsky RDS, and ~30 mV/dec for Tafel RDS (at 298 K). Similar analysis applies to oxygen evolution, chlorine evolution, and CO₂ reduction, where multi‑electron pathways and adsorbed intermediates (e.g., *OOH, *CO) dictate the kinetic parameters.

Exchange current density i₀ is a powerful descriptor of intrinsic catalytic activity. For Pt in 0.5 M H₂SO₄, i₀ ≈ 10⁻³ A cm⁻² for HER, whereas for Hg it is ~10⁻¹² A cm⁻², explaining the huge overpotential on mercury. Surface structure, alloying, and adsorbates modify i₀ and α, which is why nanostructured catalysts and single‑atom sites are active research areas. In practical electrolyzers, the total cell voltage is Ecell = E°cell + ηanode + ηcathode + iRΩ; minimizing each term is the central engineering challenge.

Concentration Cells, Liquid Junction Potentials, and the Nernst‑Planck Equation

A concentration cell generates an emf solely from differences in chemical potential of the same species in two half‑cells. For a simple metal‑ion electrode M|Mz+(c₁)||Mz+(c₂)|M, the Nernst equation gives E = (RT/zF) ln(c₂/c₁). When the two electrolytes are in direct contact, a liquid junction potential (Elj) develops because ions diffuse at different rates. The Henderson equation provides an approximate value: Elj = (RT/F) Σ (uᵢ − uⱼ) / Σ (uᵢ + uⱼ) ln(aᵢ/aⱼ), where u are ionic mobilities and a activities. In practice a salt bridge with a high‑mobility, equitransferent electrolyte (e.g., KCl) minimizes Elj because K⁺ and Cl⁻ have nearly equal mobilities.

The rigorous description of ion transport in solution is the Nernst‑Planck equation: Jᵢ = −Dᵢ ∇cᵢ − (zᵢ F Dᵢ/RT) cᵢ ∇φ + cᵢ v, where Jᵢ is the flux of species i, Dᵢ its diffusion coefficient, φ the electric potential, and v the hydrodynamic velocity. The first term is Fickian diffusion, the second migration in the electric field, the third convection. In a concentration cell without forced convection, the steady‑state condition ∇·Jᵢ = 0 leads to the diffusion‑migration coupling that underlies the liquid junction potential. For a binary electrolyte with equal diffusion coefficients (D₊ = D₋), the migration term cancels and Elj = 0; this is the principle behind the use of KCl salt bridges.

Concentration cells find analytical use in ion‑selective electrodes (ISEs). A glass pH electrode is essentially a H⁺ concentration cell: the internal reference solution (fixed aH⁺) and the test solution (variable aH⁺) are separated by a thin glass membrane that develops a potential E = E° + (RT/F) ln(aH⁺,test/aH⁺,int). The Nernstian slope at 298 K is 59.16 mV per pH unit. Deviations from ideality (non‑Nernstian slopes, asymmetry potentials) are traced to non‑ideal membrane permselectivity and surface hydration layers, which can be modeled by extending the Nernst‑Planck framework to include site‑binding equilibria.

In electrochemical synthesis, concentration polarization limits current density. The limiting current ilim = zF D cb/δ (δ = diffusion layer thickness) marks the onset of severe concentration overpotential. Rotating disk electrodes (RDE) control δ via the Levich equation: ilim = 0.62 zF D2/3 ω1/2 ν−1/6 cb, where ω is angular rotation rate and ν kinematic viscosity. This hydrodynamic control enables precise kinetic measurements free from mass‑transport distortion.

Worked Example: Tafel Analysis of HER on Nickel
A nickel cathode in 1 M KOH shows the following steady‑state data for the hydrogen evolution reaction (cathodic current density i in mA cm⁻², overpotential η in mV): (10, 120), (30, 150), (100, 190), (300, 230). Assuming the high‑overpotential Tafel region applies, determine the exchange current density i₀ and the cathodic transfer coefficient α_c.
Convert i to A cm⁻²: 0.01, 0.03, 0.10, 0.30. Plot η versus log₁₀|i|. The points lie on a straight line; linear regression gives slope b ≈ 120 mV/decade and intercept a ≈ −120 mV (extrapolated to log|i| = 0). The Tafel slope b = 2.303 RT/(α_c F). At 298 K, 2.303 RT/F = 0.05916 V. Hence α_c = 0.05916 / b = 0.05916 / 0.120 ≈ 0.49. The intercept a = −b log i₀, so log i₀ = −a/b = 120/120 = 1, giving i₀ = 10¹ mA cm⁻² = 0.01 A cm⁻². The result α_c ≈ 0.5 and i₀ ≈ 10 mA cm⁻² is consistent with literature values for Ni in alkaline HER.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Tafel slope or exchange current density, first verify that the data are in the high‑overpotential region (|η| > 0.1 V). Use the 0.05916 V constant at 298 K for base‑10 logs; if temperature differs, compute 2.303 RT/F explicitly. Remember that the Butler‑Volmer equation reduces to the Tafel form only when one exponential term is negligible. For concentration cells, always check whether a liquid junction potential is mentioned; if a salt bridge of KCl is used, you may set Elj ≈ 0. In Nernst‑Planck problems, identify which flux terms are zero (e.g., no convection in a stagnant cell) before integrating.

Corrosion Thermodynamics: Pourbaix Diagrams and Cathodic Protection

Corrosion is the spontaneous electrochemical degradation of a metal in its environment. The thermodynamic driving force is captured by the Pourbaix diagram (potential–pH diagram), which maps the stable phases of a metal–water system at equilibrium. For iron, the diagram shows three principal domains: immunity (Fe(s) stable), corrosion (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ aqueous ions stable), and passivation (Fe₂O₃/Fe₃O₄ solid oxide film stable). The boundaries are derived from the Nernst equation for each half‑reaction, e.g., Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe(s) gives E = E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) − (0.05916/2) log(1/[Fe²⁺]), and Fe₂O₃ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻ ⇌ 2Fe(s) + 3H₂O gives a line with slope −0.05916 V/pH. Water stability lines (H₂/H⁺ and O₂/H₂O) envelope the diagram; potentials above the oxygen line oxidize water, below the hydrogen line reduce water.

Kinetic factors often dominate: a metal may be thermodynamically in the corrosion region but exhibit negligible corrosion rate due to a protective passive film (e.g., Cr₂O₃ on stainless steel). The pitting potential (Epit) marks the breakdown of passivity in the presence of aggressive anions (Cl⁻). Below Epit the passive current density ipass is low (µA cm⁻²); above it, localized attack initiates. The repassivation potential (Erp) is the potential to which the metal must be lowered to heal pits.

Cathodic protection forces the metal potential into the immunity region by making it the cathode of an external circuit. Two modes exist: sacrificial anode (Zn, Al, Mg alloys) where the anode corrodes preferentially, and impressed current where a DC power supply drives current from inert anodes (mixed metal oxide, platinized Ti). The protection criterion for steel in seawater is typically E ≤ −0.80 V vs. Ag/AgCl (seawater). The required current density iprot depends on the environment; for bare steel in seawater iprot ≈ 100–200 mA m⁻², while a coated pipeline may need only 10–20 mA m⁻². Overprotection (excessively negative potentials) can cause hydrogen embrittlement or coating disbondment.

Corrosion rate can be quantified from the corrosion current icorr using Faraday’s law: penetration rate (mm yr⁻¹) = (K icorr EW)/ρ, where K = 3.27 × 10⁻³ (mm g µA⁻¹ cm yr⁻¹), EW is equivalent weight (M/z), and ρ density. Electrochemical techniques such as linear polarization resistance (LPR) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) provide icorr non‑destructively. The Stern‑Geary equation icorr = B/Rp (B = βₐβ_c/[2.303(βₐ+β_c)]) links polarization resistance Rp to icorr using anodic and cathodic Tafel slopes β.

Battery Chemistry: Primary, Secondary, and Flow Cells – Thermodynamic Limits and Practical Voltage

A battery converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy through spontaneous redox reactions. The open‑circuit voltage (OCV) of a cell is given by ΔG° = −nF E°cell. For the Leclanché cell (Zn|NH₄Cl|MnO₂), the overall reaction Zn + 2MnO₂ + 2NH₄⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Mn₂O₃ + 2NH₃ + H₂O yields E° ≈ 1.5 V. Alkaline MnO₂/Zn cells replace NH₄Cl with KOH, raising the OCV to ~1.55 V and improving low‑temperature performance. Primary lithium cells (Li|organic electrolyte|MnO₂, SOCl₂, FeS₂) achieve 3.0–3.6 V because of lithium’s very negative standard potential (−3.04 V vs. SHE) and high specific capacity (3860 mAh g⁻¹).

Secondary (rechargeable) cells must sustain reversible intercalation or conversion reactions. The lead‑acid battery (Pb|H₂SO₄|PbO₂) operates via Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O, E° = 2.05 V per cell; practical voltage 2.0–2.1 V on charge, 1.8–2.0 V on discharge. Nickel‑cadmium (NiCd) uses Cd + 2NiO(OH) + 2H₂O ⇌ Cd(OH)₂ + 2Ni(OH)₂, E° = 1.20 V. Nickel‑metal‑hydride (NiMH) replaces Cd with a hydrogen‑absorbing alloy (AB₅ or AB₂ type), giving higher specific energy (~80 Wh kg⁻¹) and no toxic Cd. Lithium‑ion cells (graphite|LiPF₆ in EC/DMC|LiCoO₂, LiFePO₄, NMC) deliver 3.6–3.8 V nominal, with specific energies 150–250 Wh kg⁻¹. The voltage window is limited by electrolyte stability (≈4.3 V vs. Li/Li⁺ for carbonate electrolytes) and structural stability of the cathode.

Flow batteries decouple power and energy by storing active species in external tanks. The vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) uses V²⁺/V³⁺ (negative) and VO²⁺/VO₂⁺ (positive) in sulfuric acid, with cell voltage ~1.26 V. Because the same element appears in both half‑cells, cross‑contamination does not cause permanent capacity loss. Energy capacity scales with tank volume; power scales with stack size. Other chemistries include Zn‑Br₂, Fe‑Cr, and organic redox‑active molecules (quinones, viologens) aiming for lower cost and higher solubility.

Practical cell voltage under load is V = E°cell − ηact − ηconc − iRΩ. Internal resistance RΩ includes electrolyte resistance, separator resistance, and contact resistances. At high rates, concentration overpotential dominates, leading to voltage sag and reduced usable capacity. Ragone plots (specific energy vs. specific power) illustrate the trade‑off: supercapacitors deliver high power but low energy; Li‑ion occupies a middle ground; flow batteries offer high energy at moderate power. Temperature strongly affects kinetics and conductivity; low‑temperature performance is a key differentiator for automotive applications.

Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy: Equivalent Circuits and Parameter Extraction

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) probes the frequency response of an electrochemical system by applying a small sinusoidal perturbation (typically 10 mV rms) over a range of frequencies (10⁵–10⁻³ Hz) and measuring the resulting current. The impedance Z(ω) = V(ω)/I(ω) is a complex quantity represented as Nyquist plots (−Z'' vs. Z') or Bode plots (|Z| and phase vs. frequency). The data are interpreted by fitting to an equivalent circuit composed of resistors, capacitors, constant‑phase elements (CPE), and Warburg diffusion elements.

The simplest model for a corroding electrode or a battery interface is the Randles circuit: solution resistance Rs in series with a parallel combination of charge‑transfer resistance Rct and double‑layer capacitance Cdl, followed by a Warburg impedance ZW = σ ω−1/2 (1−j) representing semi‑infinite linear diffusion. In the Nyquist plot, Rs is the high‑frequency intercept on the real axis; the diameter of the semicircle equals Rct; the 45° line at low frequencies corresponds to Warburg diffusion. The CPE (ZCPE = 1/[Q (jω)ⁿ]) replaces an ideal capacitor when surface roughness or heterogeneity depresses the semicircle (n < 1).

For lithium‑ion electrodes, additional elements appear: a solid‑electrolyte interphase (SEI) resistance RSEI and capacitance CSEI in series with Rct, and a finite‑length Warburg (or Gerischer) element for solid‑state diffusion in the active particles. The diffusion coefficient D can be extracted from the Warburg coefficient σ using σ = RT/(n²F²A√2D c) for a planar electrode, or from the finite‑diffusion time constant τ = L²/D for a particle of thickness L.

Parameter extraction relies on non‑linear least‑squares fitting (e.g., Levenberg‑Marquardt algorithm). Goodness‑of‑fit is assessed by χ², residual plots, and Kramers‑Kronig validation (linearity, causality, stability). Common pitfalls include: using an overly simple circuit that masks multiple time constants, ignoring inductance at high frequencies (lead inductance), and fitting data outside the linear response regime (perturbation too large). Properly executed EIS yields Rs, Rct, Cdl, D, and kinetic parameters (i₀ via Rct = RT/(nF i₀)), making it indispensable for battery diagnostics, corrosion monitoring, and fuel‑cell catalyst evaluation.

  • Confusing the sign convention for overpotential: η = Eapplied − Eeq for cathodic polarization (negative η) and positive for anodic; many candidates reverse the sign in Tafel calculations.
  • Assuming the Nernst equation applies directly to concentration cells with a liquid junction without correcting for the junction potential; the measured emf includes Elj unless a salt bridge of equitransferent electrolyte is used.
  • Treating the Pourbaix diagram as a kinetic map; it only shows thermodynamic stability, not corrosion rates. A metal in the corrosion region may be practically passive.
  • Using the standard cell voltage E° as the operating voltage of a battery under load; the practical voltage is always lower due to activation, concentration, and ohmic overpotentials.
  • Fitting EIS data with an ideal capacitor when the Nyquist semicircle is depressed; a constant‑phase element (CPE) is required, and the exponent n must be reported.
  • Neglecting the temperature dependence of the Tafel slope (b = 2.303 RT/αF) and the Nernstian factor (0.05916 V at 298 K); using 0.059 V at other temperatures introduces systematic error.
  • Review these traps before the exam.

hand/cryptography.html:
Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) and Modern Modes

Authenticated encryption (AE) simultaneously provides confidentiality and integrity. AEAD extends AE by allowing additional authenticated data (AAD) that is authenticated but not encrypted — typical uses include packet headers, version fields, or metadata that must be integrity‑protected while remaining readable. The security goal is IND‑CCA2 for confidentiality and INT‑CTXT for integrity; a single forgery attempt must have negligible probability.

The most widely deployed AEAD constructions are AES‑GCM, ChaCha20‑Poly1305, AES‑CCM, and OCB. AES‑GCM combines counter‑mode encryption with a polynomial‑based MAC (GHASH) computed in the Galois field GF(2¹²⁸). It requires a unique 96‑bit nonce for each encryption under the same key; nonce reuse collapses both confidentiality and authenticity because the keystream repeats and the GHASH key becomes recoverable. ChaCha20‑Poly1305 avoids hardware‑dependent AES instructions, using a 256‑bit key, a 96‑bit nonce, and a 128‑bit Poly1305 authenticator; it is the default in TLS 1.3 for non‑AES platforms. AES‑CCM (Counter with CBC‑MAC) is used in constrained environments (e.g., IEEE 802.15.4) but imposes a two‑pass structure and a maximum message length of 2⁶⁴‑1 bytes. OCB (Offset Codebook) achieves full parallelism and a single pass but is encumbered by patents in some jurisdictions, limiting adoption.

Implementation pitfalls dominate real‑world failures. Reusing a nonce, truncating the authentication tag, or processing AAD after ciphertext verification are common errors. The TLS 1.3 record layer mandates a 128‑bit tag for AES‑GCM and ChaCha20‑Poly1305, and it binds the sequence number into the nonce to guarantee uniqueness. In protocols that allow variable‑length AAD (e.g., QUIC), the AAD must be canonically encoded before authentication to avoid length‑extension ambiguities. Formal verification tools such as ProVerif and EasyCrypt have been used to prove the security of AEAD compositions under the random‑oracle model for the underlying hash or PRF.

Side‑Channel Countermeasures and Constant‑Time Implementation

Side‑channel attacks exploit physical leakage — timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emanations, cache‑access patterns, or branch‑predictor state — to recover secret keys without breaking the underlying mathematics. A classic timing attack on RSA uses the variation in modular exponentiation time caused by the sliding‑window algorithm; a cache‑timing attack on AES exploits the data‑dependent lookup of S‑box tables. Countermeasures fall into three categories: algorithmic masking, constant‑time coding, and hardware‑level hardening.

Masking splits each sensitive variable into random shares (e.g., Boolean masking: x = x₁ ⊕ x₂) and performs all operations on shares independently. First‑order masking defeats simple power analysis; higher‑order masking (e.g., ISW scheme) resists attacks that combine multiple leakage points but incurs quadratic overhead. Constant‑time programming eliminates data‑dependent branches and memory accesses: all loops run for a fixed number of iterations, table lookups are replaced by bit‑sliced or vectorized operations, and conditional moves (CMOV) replace if‑else constructs. For AES, bitsliced implementations compute eight S‑boxes in parallel using only logical instructions, removing cache‑based leakage entirely. For elliptic‑curve scalar multiplication, the Montgomery ladder or fixed‑window scalar multiplication with precomputed tables accessed in a constant‑time pattern prevents timing leakage.

Hardware countermeasures include random clock jitter, dual‑rail precharge logic, and on‑chip noise generators. However, software mitigations must assume a worst‑case microarchitectural model: speculative execution (Spectre/Meltdown) can transiently execute secret‑dependent paths, leaving microarchitectural footprints. Mitigations such as retpoline, LFENCE serialization, and compiler‑injected speculation barriers are required in high‑assurance libraries (e.g., OpenSSL 3.0, BoringSSL, libsodium). Formal verification of constant‑time properties is now feasible with tools like ct‑verif and Vale, which prove that the compiled binary exhibits no secret‑dependent control flow or memory access.

Worked Example: Detecting a Nonce‑Reuse Vulnerability in AES‑GCM
A developer encrypts two distinct messages M₁ and M₂ under the same AES‑GCM key K using the same 96‑bit nonce N. The ciphertexts are C₁ = Enc(K, N, M₁, AAD₁) and C₂ = Enc(K, N, M₂, AAD₂). Show how an attacker who obtains (C₁, tag₁) and (C₂, tag₂) can recover the XOR of the plaintexts and forge a valid tag for a chosen plaintext.
In AES‑GCM the keystream block S = AES‑CTR(K, N) is identical for both encryptions because the nonce and key are identical. The ciphertexts are C₁ = M₁ ⊕ S and C₂ = M₂ ⊕ S. XORing the ciphertexts yields C₁ ⊕ C₂ = M₁ ⊕ M₂, revealing the plaintext XOR without any key knowledge. The authentication tag is computed as tag = GHASH(H, AAD, C) ⊕ E(K, J₀) where H = E(K, 0) and J₀ = N || 0³¹ || 1. Since H and the final encryption of J₀ are identical for both messages, the attacker can compute Δ = tag₁ ⊕ tag₂ = GHASH(H, AAD₁, C₁) ⊕ GHASH(H, AAD₂, C₂). Because GHASH is linear over GF(2¹²⁸), the attacker can construct a new ciphertext C* = C₁ ⊕ ΔC and a corresponding tag* = tag₁ ⊕ Δtag that will verify under the same key and nonce, achieving a forgery. The root cause is nonce reuse; the fix is to enforce a strict nonce construction (e.g., 96‑bit random with a 32‑bit counter) or switch to a nonce‑misuse‑resistant scheme such as AES‑GCM‑SIV.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the security impact of nonce reuse in an AEAD mode, immediately write: “Keystream reuse ⇒ plaintext XOR recovery; GHASH linearity ⇒ tag forgery.” Cite the two independent consequences (confidentiality loss and integrity loss) and name a nonce‑misuse‑resistant alternative (AES‑GCM‑SIV or ChaCha20‑Poly1305 with a deterministic nonce derived from a message counter). This two‑point answer captures the full mark scheme.

Threshold Cryptography and Distributed Key Generation

Threshold cryptography splits a secret key into n shares such that any t shares (t ≤ n) can reconstruct the key or jointly perform a cryptographic operation, while fewer than t shares reveal nothing. The foundational primitive is Shamir secret sharing over a finite field: a dealer picks a random polynomial f(x) of degree t‑1 with f(0) = secret, and distributes shares (i, f(i)) to participants. Verifiable secret sharing (VSS) adds commitments (e.g., Feldman’s gf(i) or Pedersen’s gf(i)hr(i)) so that participants can verify consistency without learning the secret.

Distributed key generation (DKG) removes the trusted dealer. In the Pedersen DKG, each participant acts as a dealer for a Shamir sharing of their own random value, broadcasts commitments, and all participants verify received shares. The final secret key is the sum of all participants’ secrets; the public key is the product of the corresponding commitment generators. This protocol tolerates up to t‑1 malicious parties under the assumption of a synchronous broadcast channel. The resulting key pair can be used for threshold signatures (e.g., BLS threshold signatures, where each party produces a partial signature σ_i = H(m)sk_i and the combiner aggregates via Lagrange interpolation) or threshold decryption (e.g., ElGamal threshold decryption where each party computes a partial decryption share).

Practical deployments include the Internet Computer’s threshold BLS signatures for chain‑key cryptography, the drand network’s DKG for public randomness beacons, and threshold ECDSA wallets (e.g., GG20, Lindell‑Nof) used by custodial services. Security proofs rely on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem in the underlying group and the robustness of the VSS against adaptive corruptions. Recent advances (e.g., FROST, a Schnorr‑based threshold signature) reduce communication rounds to two and eliminate the need for a trusted setup, making threshold schemes viable for high‑throughput blockchain validators and secure multiparty computation pre‑processing.

Homomorphic Encryption: From Theory to Practical Schemes

Homomorphic encryption (HE) allows computation on ciphertexts, producing an encryption of the result without ever decrypting. The first fully homomorphic scheme (Gentry, 2009) used ideal lattices and bootstrapping — a procedure that refreshes a noisy ciphertext by evaluating the decryption circuit homomorphically. Modern HE families are categorized by the algebraic structure they exploit: integer‑based (DGHV), LWE‑based (BFV, BGV, CKKS), and TFHE (fast bootstrapping over the torus).

BFV and BGV operate on the ring R_q = ℤ_q[x]/(xⁿ+1) with plaintext modulus t and ciphertext modulus q. They support exact integer arithmetic (addition and multiplication) with a noise budget that grows multiplicatively; after a bounded multiplicative depth the ciphertext must be bootstrapped or the modulus switched (modulus‑switching) to reduce noise. CKKS (Cheon‑Kim‑Kim‑Song) encodes approximate real numbers via a scaling factor Δ, enabling efficient evaluation of polynomial approximations (e.g., neural‑network inference) with controlled precision loss. TFHE (Chillotti‑Gama‑Georgiev‑Izabachène) represents bits as LWE samples over the torus 𝕋 = ℝ/ℤ and achieves sub‑millisecond bootstrapping per gate, making it suitable for low‑latency private queries.

Performance trade‑offs: BFV/BGV ciphertexts are ~1–2 KB per slot (SIMD packing via the Chinese Remainder Theorem), CKKS ciphertexts are similar but require careful scaling management, and TFHE ciphertexts are larger (~10 KB) but bootstrapping is constant‑time. Libraries such as Microsoft SEAL (BFV/CKKS), PALISADE (BGV/BFV/CKKS), and Concrete (TFHE) provide production‑grade implementations with SIMD batching, automatic modulus‑switching, and hybrid key‑switching for rotation operations. Standardization efforts (ISO/IEC 18033‑5, ETSI HE) are converging on API definitions and parameter sets for 128‑bit post‑quantum security.

Cryptographic Agility, Protocol Negotiation, and Standardization

Cryptographic agility is the ability of a protocol to negotiate and switch algorithms without breaking existing deployments. TLS 1.3 exemplifies modern agility: the ClientHello offers a list of supported cipher suites (e.g., TLS_AES128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256) and key‑exchange groups (X25519, X448, secp256r1, ffdhe2048). The server selects the most preferred mutually supported suite, and the handshake authenticates the chosen parameters via the transcript hash. Downgrade protection is achieved by binding the negotiated group and suite into the finished messages; a man‑in‑the‑middle cannot force a weaker suite without detection.

Hybrid key exchange combines a classical algorithm (e.g., X25519) with a post‑quantum KEM (e.g., Kyber‑768) so that the session key is derived from both shared secrets (K = KDF(classical_secret || pq_secret)). This provides immediate quantum‑resistant security while retaining compatibility with legacy endpoints. The IETF TLS Working Group has standardized hybrid key‑exchange extensions (draft‑ietf‑tls‑hybrid‑design) and the NIST PQC standardization process (2024) selected CRYSTALS‑Kyber (KEM) and CRYSTALS‑Dilithium (signatures) as primary algorithms, with Falcon and SPHINCS+ as alternatives. Algorithm identifiers (OIDs) are registered in the IANA registry; implementations must reject unknown OIDs to avoid algorithm‑confusion attacks.

Agility introduces risks: algorithm‑confusion (e.g., using an RSA signature verification key as an ECDSA key), cross‑protocol attacks (reusing a key pair across TLS and SSH), and implementation complexity that expands the trusted code base. Best practice mandates algorithm‑specific key derivation (HKDF with distinct labels), explicit domain separation, and a policy engine that disables deprecated suites (e.g., RSA key transport, CBC‑mode ciphers) by default. Automated testing frameworks (Project Wycheproof, TLS‑Attacker) verify correct handling of edge cases such as empty extensions, duplicate extensions, and malformed group parameters.

  • Assuming AEAD security holds when the nonce is generated by a low‑entropy source — nonce reuse is the single most common cause of catastrophic failure.
  • Believing that constant‑time source code guarantees constant‑time execution — compiler optimizations, micro‑architectural speculation, and data‑dependent cache effects can re‑introduce leakage.
  • Treating threshold signatures as a drop‑in replacement for single‑party signatures without verifying the underlying DKG’s robustness against adaptive corruptions.
  • Using CKKS for exact integer arithmetic — its approximate nature introduces rounding errors that accumulate and can break correctness in financial or cryptographic protocols.
  • Neglecting domain separation in hybrid key exchange — concatenating raw shared secrets without a KDF label enables cross‑protocol key‑reuse attacks.
  • Assuming that algorithm agility alone prevents downgrade attacks — the transcript must cryptographically bind the negotiated parameters, otherwise a middlebox can strip extensions.
  • Overlooking the need for post‑quantum key‑size planning — lattice‑based KEMs require larger public keys and ciphertexts, impacting MTU and handshake latency in constrained networks.

hand/surface-chemistry.html:
Adsorption Isotherm Models Beyond Langmuir and Freundlich

The Langmuir and Freundlich equations are the first isotherms taught, but real surfaces often deviate from their assumptions. The BET (Brunauer–Emmett–Teller) model extends Langmuir to multilayer adsorption by assuming that the first layer follows Langmuir kinetics while subsequent layers condense with a heat of adsorption equal to the heat of liquefaction. Its linear form, (P/[V(P₀−P)]) = 1/(VₘC) + (C−1)P/(VₘC P₀), yields the monolayer capacity Vₘ and the constant C, which reflects the strength of adsorbate–surface interaction. The Temkin isotherm accounts for a linear decrease in adsorption energy with coverage, giving θ = (RT/ΔH) ln(K₀P), where ΔH is the heat of adsorption at zero coverage. The Dubinin–Radushkevich (D‑R) equation, ln V = ln V₀ − (RT/E)² (ln(P₀/P))², is derived from a pore‑filling mechanism and provides the characteristic energy E, useful for microporous carbons. The Sips (Langmuir–Freundlich) model combines both: θ = (K P)ⁿ / (1 + (K P)ⁿ), reducing to Langmuir when n = 1 and to Freundlich at low pressures. Selecting the appropriate isotherm requires examining the linearized plots, the physical nature of the adsorbent (microporous vs. mesoporous), and the temperature range; misapplication leads to erroneous surface area or pore‑size estimates.

Kinetics of Heterogeneous Catalysis: Rate‑Determining Steps and Surface Coverage

In heterogeneous catalysis the overall rate is governed by the slowest elementary step. The Langmuir–Hinshelwood (L‑H) mechanism assumes both reactants adsorb on adjacent sites before reacting; the rate law becomes r = k θ_A θ_B = k K_A K_B P_A P_B / (1 + K_A P_A + K_B P_B)² when surface reaction is rate‑determining. The Eley–Rideal (E‑R) mechanism involves reaction between an adsorbed species and a gas‑phase molecule, giving r = k θ_A P_B = k K_A P_A P_B / (1 + K_A P_A). The Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) cycle, common in oxidation catalysis, proceeds via lattice oxygen participation: the catalyst is reduced by the reactant and re‑oxidized by gas‑phase O₂, so the rate depends on the redox properties of the solid. Surface coverage θ is central; at low pressures θ ≈ K P (linear), while at high pressures θ → 1 (saturation). Promoters such as K₂O in the Haber‑Bosch Fe catalyst increase K_N₂, enhancing N₂ dissociation, whereas poisons like S block active sites, decreasing the number of available sites Nₛ. Temperature‑programmed desorption (TPD) and in‑situ spectroscopy (DRIFTS, XPS) are used to identify the rate‑determining step and to quantify surface intermediates under reaction conditions.

Technique
A catalytic reaction follows the Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism with both reactants A and B adsorbing on the same type of site. Derive the rate expression when the surface reaction between adsorbed A* and B* is the rate‑determining step, assuming ideal adsorption and no dissociation.
For L‑H with surface reaction as RDS, the rate r = k θ_A θ_B. Using Langmuir adsorption for each species on identical sites: θ_A = K_A P_A / (1 + K_A P_A + K_B P_B) and θ_B = K_B P_B / (1 + K_A P_A + K_B P_B). Substituting gives r = k K_A K_B P_A P_B / (1 + K_A P_A + K_B P_B)². This expression predicts a maximum rate at intermediate pressures and a decrease at high pressures due to site blocking.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the rate law of a heterogeneous catalytic reaction, first identify the proposed mechanism (L‑H, E‑R, or MvK) and the rate‑determining step. Write the surface coverages using Langmuir isotherms, then substitute into the elementary rate expression. Simplify only after substitution; premature simplification often leads to missing denominator terms that examiners test.

Stability of Colloidal Systems: DLVO Theory and Steric Stabilization

The Derjaguin–Landau–Verwey–Overbeek (DLVO) theory quantifies the balance between electrostatic repulsion and van der Waals attraction between colloidal particles. The total interaction energy V_T = V_R + V_A, where V_R = (π ε ε₀ a ζ²) ln[1 + exp(−κh)] for two spheres of radius a at surface‑to‑surface distance h, ζ is the zeta potential, κ⁻¹ the Debye length, and ε the dielectric constant. The attractive term V_A = −A_H a / (12 h) for h ≪ a, with A_H the Hamaker constant. A primary minimum at very small h leads to irreversible coagulation; a secondary minimum at larger h can cause reversible flocculation. The critical coagulation concentration (CCC) follows the Schulze–Hardy rule: CCC ∝ z⁻⁶ for counter‑ions of valence z. Steric stabilization adds a polymer layer that generates an osmotic repulsion V_S ≈ (π a Γ² / δ) (1 − h/2δ)² for h < 2δ, where Γ is the adsorbed amount and δ the layer thickness. Combined electrostatic‑steric (electrosteric) stabilization is exploited in paints, inks, and drug‑delivery nanocarriers. The zeta potential, measured by electrophoresis, indicates the sign and magnitude of surface charge; values above ±30 mV generally confer kinetic stability. pH, ionic strength, and specific ion adsorption shift the zeta potential and thus the position of the energy barrier.

Advanced Emulsion Formulation: Phase Inversion Temperature and Microemulsions

Emulsion type (oil‑in‑water vs. water‑in‑oil) is governed by the hydrophilic‑lipophilic balance (HLB) of the surfactant and the phase inversion temperature (PIT). For non‑ionic surfactants such as polyoxyethylene alkyl ethers, the HLB decreases with temperature because dehydration of the ethylene oxide chains reduces hydrophilicity. At the PIT the surfactant’s affinity for oil and water becomes equal, the interfacial tension reaches a minimum, and the emulsion inverts. Formulating at a temperature slightly below the PIT yields stable O/W emulsions; slightly above gives W/O. The PIT can be tuned by blending surfactants of different chain lengths or by adding co‑surfactants (e.g., medium‑chain alcohols). Microemulsions are thermodynamically stable, single‑phase systems with droplet radii 10–100 nm, formed when the surfactant film curvature is near zero and the interfacial tension is ultra‑low (≤10⁻³ mN m⁻¹). They require a precise surfactant/co‑surfactant ratio and often a cosolvent. The Winsor classification (I, II, III, IV) describes the phase behavior: Winsor III (middle‑phase microemulsion in equilibrium with excess oil and water) is the region of lowest tension and is exploited in enhanced oil recovery. Nanoemulsions, kinetically stable with droplets 50–200 nm, are produced by high‑pressure homogenization or microfluidization and find use in parenteral drug delivery and food fortification.

Applications of Surface Chemistry in Nanotechnology and Environmental Remediation

Surface chemistry underpins the synthesis, functionalization, and deployment of nanomaterials. In the sol‑gel process, hydrolysis and condensation of metal alkoxides (e.g., tetraethyl orthosilicate) are controlled by pH, water‑to‑precursor ratio, and catalysts to produce silica nanoparticles with tailored porosity. Surface silanol groups are subsequently modified with organosilanes (e.g., aminopropyltriethoxysilane) to impart specific reactivity for biomolecule attachment. In catalysis, shape‑selective zeolites such as ZSM‑5 (MFI topology, pore diameter ~0.55 nm) direct hydrocarbon cracking and isomerization by restricting transition‑state geometry. Photocatalytic TiO₂ (anatase) generates electron‑hole pairs under UV light; surface adsorption of pollutants (dyes, phenols) precedes oxidative degradation. For water treatment, activated carbon’s microporous structure provides high adsorption capacity for organic contaminants; its performance is described by the Freundlich or D‑R isotherms. Magnetic nanoparticles (Fe₃O₄) coated with silica or polymers enable magnetic separation after adsorption of heavy metals (Pb²⁺, Hg²⁺) or radionuclides. In sensors, self‑assembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold create ordered surfaces for immobilizing antibodies or DNA probes; the surface plasmon resonance shift upon binding provides label‑free detection. These applications illustrate how control of interfacial phenomena — adsorption, charge, wettability, and reactivity — translates into functional materials for energy, health, and environment.

  • Assuming the Langmuir isotherm applies to multilayer adsorption on microporous solids.
  • Confusing the rate‑determining step in L‑H with that in E‑R, leading to an incorrect denominator power.
  • Neglecting the contribution of the secondary minimum in DLVO when predicting reversible flocculation.
  • Using the HLB value alone to predict emulsion type without considering temperature‑dependent PIT for non‑ionic surfactants.
  • Treating microemulsions and nanoemulsions as interchangeable, ignoring the thermodynamic stability of the former.
  • Overlooking the role of specific ion adsorption in shifting the zeta potential and thus the CCC.
  • Forgetting that promoter effects in heterogeneous catalysis are often quantified by changes in adsorption equilibrium constants rather than activation energy alone.

hand/logarithmic-geometry.html:
Logarithmic Hodge Theory: Log Hodge Filtration and the Kato–Nakayama Realization

The classical Hodge decomposition for smooth projective varieties extends to log smooth fs log schemes via the Kato–Nakayama space Xlog. For a log smooth morphism f: X → S with S a log point, the log de Rham complex Ω•X/S(log) carries a decreasing filtration F• defined by the order of logarithmic poles. The associated graded pieces are the log differential forms ΩpX/S(log) which are locally free on the log smooth locus. The hypercohomology ℍn(X, Ω•X/S(log)) computes the log de Rham cohomology HndR,log(X/S). Kato proved that the filtration F• on HndR,log is strictly compatible with the weight filtration on log étale cohomology under the comparison isomorphism HndR,log(X/S) ⊗ ℚp ≅ Hnét,log(X, ℚp) ⊗ BdR for p-adic fields. The Kato–Nakayama space provides a topological realization: its singular cohomology with ℚ coefficients is canonically isomorphic to log étale cohomology with ℚ coefficients, and the mixed Hodge structure on Hn(Xlog, ℚ) is the one induced by the log Hodge filtration and the weight filtration coming from the log étale side. In particular, for a semistable degeneration over a DVR, the limit mixed Hodge structure on the nearby fiber coincides with the log mixed Hodge structure on the special fiber equipped with its canonical log structure. The log Hodge numbers hp,qlog = dim GrFp GrWp+q Hp+qdR,log satisfy the symmetry hp,qlog = hq,plog and the Hodge–Riemann bilinear relations, as shown by Kato–Usui and later by Niziol using log syntomic cohomology. These invariants are stable under log blow‑ups and form the basis for the logarithmic version of the Hodge conjecture, which remains open in general but is known for log abelian varieties and log K3 surfaces.

Logarithmic Derived Geometry: Cotangent Complex and Deformation Theory

In derived algebraic geometry a log structure is encoded by a sheaf of monoids M on a derived scheme X together with a map M → OX of E∞-monoids. The log cotangent complex LX/Slog is defined as the fiber of the map LX/S → LM/OS induced by the log structure morphism. When X → S is log smooth, LX/Slog is perfect of Tor-amplitude [0,1] and its H0 is the sheaf of log differentials Ω1X/S(log). The derived deformation theory of log schemes is controlled by the log tangent complex TX/Slog = RHom(LX/Slog, OX). For a log smooth morphism, the obstruction space for lifting a log morphism along a square‑zero extension is Ext2(LX/Slog, I) and the space of infinitesimal automorphisms is Ext1(LX/Slog, I). Olsson and others have shown that the log cotangent complex satisfies base‑change and transitivity triangles compatible with the classical ones, and that the log de Rham complex Ω•X/S(log) is the derived de Rham complex of the log structure. In the p-adic setting, the log prismatic complex ΔX/Slog constructed by Bhatt–Lurie–Mathew recovers log crystalline cohomology after derived completion, and the log Nygaard filtration on ΔX/Slog induces the log Hodge filtration on log de Rham cohomology. These derived tools are essential for the construction of log motivic cohomology and for the proof of the log weight–monodromy conjecture via perfectoid methods.

Worked Example: Log Cotangent Complex of a Normal Crossing Divisor
Let X = Spec k[x,y]/(xy) with the log structure given by the divisor D = {xy = 0}. Compute the log cotangent complex LX/klog and identify its cohomology sheaves.
The log structure is the chart ℕ2 → k[x,y]/(xy) sending (1,0) ↦ x, (0,1) ↦ y. The classical cotangent complex LX/k is the two‑term complex [I/I2 → Ω1k[x,y]/k ⊗ OX] with I = (xy). The log cotangent complex fits into a distinguished triangle LM/Ok → LX/k → LX/klog →. Here LM/Ok is the complex [ℕ2 → OX] placed in degrees −1,0. Taking cohomology yields H−1(LX/klog) = 0, H0(LX/klog) = Ω1X/k(log) which is locally free of rank 2 generated by dlog x, dlog y, and H1(LX/klog) = 0 because the log structure is fs and the morphism is log smooth. Thus LX/klog ≅ Ω1X/k(log) in degree 0.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the log cotangent complex of a toric or normal crossing log scheme, first write the chart monoid, then use the distinguished triangle relating the classical cotangent complex, the log structure map, and the log cotangent complex. Remember that for log smooth fs morphisms the log cotangent complex is concentrated in degree 0 and equals the sheaf of log differentials.

Logarithmic Gromov–Witten Theory and Tropical Correspondence

Logarithmic stable maps were introduced by Abramovich–Chen–Gross–Siebert to compactify the moduli of maps to a log smooth target X with a divisorial log structure. A log stable map consists of a prestable log curve C → S and a morphism f: C → X of log schemes satisfying a stability condition. The moduli stack Mlog(X, β) carries a virtual fundamental class constructed via the log perfect obstruction theory of the log cotangent complex. The resulting log Gromov–Witten invariants Nβlog are rational numbers that coincide with the usual Gromov–Witten invariants when X is proper and the log structure is trivial. The tropicalization of a log stable map is a balanced weighted graph in the tropicalization Σ(X) of the target, and the tropical multiplicity of a tropical curve equals the log Gromov–Witten invariant of the corresponding log map. The correspondence theorem of Gross–Siebert and Abramovich–Chen states that for a toric degeneration of a Calabi–Yau variety, the log Gromov–Witten invariants of the central fiber equal the tropical curve counts in the base of the degeneration. This provides a combinatorial algorithm for computing Gromov–Witten invariants of mirror pairs and underlies the Gross–Siebert program for mirror symmetry. In the logarithmic setting, the quantum cohomology ring of X is defined using log invariants and satisfies the same associativity and divisor equations as the classical quantum cohomology, but with additional structure coming from the log tangent bundle.

Logarithmic Mirror Symmetry: The Gross–Siebert Program

The Gross–Siebert program constructs mirror Calabi–Yau varieties from a toric degeneration whose central fiber is a union of toric varieties glued along toric strata. The input data is a polarized tropical manifold (B, P) where B is an integral affine manifold with singularities and P is a polyhedral decomposition. From this data one builds a log Calabi–Yau variety X0 over Spec k[ℕ] with a log structure encoding the gluing. The mirror family is obtained by a dual construction on the dual intersection complex B∨. The key technical tool is the scattering diagram on B, a collection of walls with attached automorphisms of the torus algebra k[Λ] that encode the corrections needed to make the gluing consistent. The consistency of the scattering diagram is equivalent to the Maurer–Cartan equation in the log deformation theory of X0. The log Gromov–Witten invariants of X0 are computed by counting tropical curves in B, and the generating function of these invariants satisfies the tropical vertex equations. The mirror symmetry conjecture predicts an isomorphism between the log quantum cohomology of X0 and the log period integrals on the mirror family, which has been proved in many cases by Gross–Siebert–Ruddat using log Hodge theory and the log SYZ fibration. The program extends to non‑Calabi–Yau log Fano varieties, where the scattering diagram lives on the tropicalization of the anticanonical divisor and the mirror is a Landau–Ginzburg model with a log superpotential.

Logarithmic p‑adic Hodge Theory: Log Fontaine Rings and Comparison Isomorphisms

For a log smooth fs log scheme X over a p‑adic field K with ring of integers OK and log structure given by the valuation, the log Fontaine rings Ainflog, BdRlog, Bstlog are constructed by adjoining log structures to the classical period rings. The log de Rham cohomology H•dR,log(X/OK) carries a log Hodge filtration and a log Galois action. The log de Rham comparison isomorphism of Niziol states that for a proper log smooth X there is a canonical Galois‑equivariant isomorphism H•ét,log(XK̄, ℚp) ⊗ BdRlog ≅ H•dR,log(X/OK) ⊗ BdRlog compatible with filtrations. The log crystalline comparison of Tsuji and Faltings identifies log crystalline cohomology H•crys,log(Xk/W(k)) with log étale cohomology after tensoring with Bstlog, and the log monodromy operator N on the log crystalline side matches the log Galois monodromy on the étale side. The log Hyodo–Kato isomorphism is recovered as the specialization of the log crystalline comparison to the semistable case. These comparison theorems are the p‑adic backbone of the log weight–monodromy conjecture and of the log p‑adic Langlands correspondence for GL2 over Qp, where the log Fontaine rings appear in the construction of the log (φ, Γ)-modules attached to log Galois representations.

  • Confusing the log cotangent complex with the classical cotangent complex; the former is concentrated in degree 0 for log smooth fs morphisms, the latter may have higher Tor terms.
  • Assuming log Hodge numbers satisfy the same symmetry as classical Hodge numbers without checking the log smoothness and fs hypotheses.
  • Mixing up the Kato–Nakayama space (a topological space) with the log analytic space; the former provides Betti realization, the latter is the analytic log scheme.
  • Neglecting the role of the log structure on the base in the semistable reduction theorem; the base must carry the standard log structure associated to the uniformizer.
  • Treating log Gromov–Witten invariants as ordinary Gromov–Witten invariants of the underlying scheme; they differ by contributions from the log structure on the target.
  • Overlooking the necessity of the Kummer flat topology for log étale cohomology; the usual étale topology does not see the log structure.
  • Believing the log weight–monodromy conjecture is proved in full generality; it is known for semistable varieties (Saito, Scholze) but remains open for arbitrary log smooth families.
