hand/schramm-loewner.html:
SLE(κ,ρ) Processes and Boundary Perturbations

The chordal SLEκ driven by a single Brownian motion describes a random curve that is conformally invariant and satisfies the domain Markov property. In many physical models the curve feels the presence of additional marked points on the boundary, which are encoded by a vector of real parameters ρ = (ρ1, …, ρn). The resulting process, denoted SLEκ(ρ), is defined by the Loewner equation with a driving function

Wt = √κ Bt + Σi=1n ρi ∫0t (Ws − Vs(i))−1 ds,

where each force point Vt(i) evolves according to the same Loewner flow. The parameters ρi control the strength of repulsion (ρi > −2) or attraction (ρi < −2) between the curve and the corresponding boundary point. When all ρi = 0 the process reduces to ordinary SLEκ.

Phase classification

For κ ≤ 4 the trace is a simple curve. The addition of force points can create boundary hitting or boundary avoidance depending on the sign and magnitude of ρ. The critical value ρ = −2 separates the regime where the curve almost surely hits the force point from the regime where it avoids it. For κ > 4 the trace is self‑touching; the force points influence the winding and the number of times the curve swallows a given boundary point.

Applications

  • Critical percolation exploration with alternating boundary conditions corresponds to SLE6(−2, −2).
  • The harmonic explorer with Dirichlet boundary data on an interval is SLE4(ρ) with ρ determined by the boundary heights.
  • In the Ising model, the fermionic observable with a boundary spin insertion yields SLE3(ρ) for specific ρ values.

The SLE(κ,ρ) framework provides a systematic way to compute partition functions, crossing probabilities, and correlation functions in critical statistical mechanics by solving the associated PDEs (the BPZ equations) that arise from the martingale property of the driving function.

Reversibility and Duality of SLE Traces

A fundamental symmetry of SLE is reversibility: for κ ≤ 4 the law of the trace from a to b in a simply connected domain D is identical to the law of the trace from b to a after a conformal map that swaps the endpoints. This was proved by Zhan (2008) for κ ≤ 4 and by Miller and Sheffield (2016) for all κ ∈ (0,8) using the imaginary geometry coupling with the Gaussian free field. The proof relies on the fact that the driving Brownian motion run backwards is again a Brownian motion, and the Loewner equation is time‑reversible after a suitable re‑parameterisation.

κ 16/κ duality

The duality relation states that the outer boundary of an SLEκ curve for κ > 4 has the same law as an SLE16/κ curve. More precisely, if η is an SLEκ trace in the upper half‑plane from 0 to ∞, then the boundary of the hull generated by η, when parameterised by capacity, is an SLE16/κ trace. This duality exchanges the simple phase (κ ≤ 4) with the space‑filling phase (κ ≥ 8) and the self‑touching phase (4 < κ < 8) with itself. The duality is a consequence of the conformal restriction property for κ ≤ 8/3 and of the imaginary geometry flow lines for general κ.

Consequences for fractal dimensions

The Hausdorff dimension of the SLEκ trace is d = 1 + κ/8 for κ ≤ 8. By duality, the dimension of the outer boundary of SLEκ (κ > 4) equals 1 + (16/κ)/8 = 1 + 2/κ. This matches the known formula for the dimension of the SLEκ frontier. The duality also implies that the intersection exponents for two independent SLE curves satisfy a symmetry under κ → 16/κ.

Worked Example: Verifying Duality for κ = 6
Show that the outer boundary of an SLE6 curve has the same law as an SLE8/3 curve.

Step 1: Identify the dual parameter. For κ = 6, the dual is 16/κ = 16/6 = 8/3.

Step 2: Recall the duality theorem: the outer boundary of SLEκ (κ > 4) is SLE16/κ. Since 6 > 4, the theorem applies directly.

Step 3: Conclude that the outer boundary of SLE6 is SLE8/3. The Hausdorff dimension of SLE6 is 1 + 6/8 = 1.75, while the dimension of its outer boundary is 1 + (8/3)/8 = 1 + 1/3 ≈ 1.333, consistent with the known dimension of the percolation cluster boundary.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the dual of a given κ, compute 16/κ instantly. Remember that duality only concerns the outer boundary for κ > 4; for κ ≤ 4 the curve is simple and its own outer boundary. Memorise the three phase thresholds: κ = 8/3 (restriction), κ = 4 (simple/self‑touching), κ = 8 (space‑filling). These numbers appear repeatedly in multiple‑choice items.

Multiple SLE and Conformal Welding

Multiple SLE describes a collection of n non‑intersecting curves in a simply connected domain that connect prescribed boundary points in a given pairing. The joint law is characterised by a system of Loewner equations driven by correlated Brownian motions with a covariance matrix determined by the parameter κ and the partition function Z(x1, …, x2n) which solves the BPZ PDEs. For κ ≤ 4 the curves are almost surely disjoint simple curves; for κ > 4 they can intersect and the construction requires a commutation relation (the Dyson‑type interaction) to maintain consistency.

Commutation and the Yang–Baxter relation

The key algebraic property is that the elementary SLE growth operators satisfy the braid relation, which is equivalent to the Yang–Baxter equation. This ensures that the law of the multiple SLE does not depend on the order in which the curves are grown. The partition function Z is a conformal covariant of weight (6−κ)/(2κ) at each marked point and can be expressed as a Coulomb gas integral or as a determinant of hypergeometric functions for special κ (e.g., κ = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8).

Conformal welding

Given a Jordan curve η in the Riemann sphere, the Riemann mapping theorem provides conformal maps f from the unit disc to the interior and g from the exterior to the complement. The welding homeomorphism φ = f−1 ∘ g on the unit circle encodes the curve. For SLEκ the welding homeomorphism is a random quasisymmetric map whose law is known explicitly for κ = 2, 4, 8/3, 6, 8 via the quantum zipper construction. The welding perspective connects multiple SLE to the theory of random planar maps: the mating of two independent continuum random trees (the peanosphere) yields an SLE8 decorated Liouville quantum gravity sphere, and the welding of the two tree boundaries produces the SLE8 curve.

SLE and Liouville Quantum Gravity: The Quantum Zipper and Mating of Trees

Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) with parameter γ ∈ (0,2) is the random geometry obtained by exponentiating a Gaussian free field φ on a domain D: the metric is eγ φ times the Euclidean metric. The central charge is c = 1 + 6 Q2 with Q = 2/γ + γ/2. The SLE parameter κ is related to γ by κ = γ2 (for γ ≤ √2) or κ = 16/γ2 (for γ ≥ √2). This relation is the cornerstone of the SLE/LQG coupling.

Quantum zipper

The quantum zipper (Sheffield, 2016) constructs an SLEκ curve on an independent LQG surface by “zipping” together the boundary of a quantum disk. The curve is the interface between two independent quantum surfaces that are glued along their boundaries. The law of the resulting decorated surface is conformally invariant and satisfies the domain Markov property with respect to the quantum area measure. This provides a geometric realisation of the SLE/LQG duality: the outer boundary of an SLEκ on a γ‑LQG surface is an SLE16/κ on the same surface.

Mating of trees

The mating‑of‑trees theorem (Duplantier–Miller–Sheffield, 2014) states that a γ‑LQG sphere decorated by an independent SLEκ curve (with κ = γ2 or 16/γ2) can be encoded by a pair of correlated continuum random trees (CRTs). The two trees are the left and right boundaries of the SLE curve when the surface is cut along the curve. Their contour functions form a two‑dimensional Brownian motion with correlation −cos(4π/κ). This bijection, called the peanosphere, identifies the SLE‑decorated LQG sphere with the Brownian map, the scaling limit of uniform random planar maps. Consequently, many discrete models (uniform quadrangulations, bipolar orientations, the Fortuin–Kasteleyn random cluster model) converge to the same continuum object.

Numerical Simulation and Convergence Rates for SLE

Simulating SLE curves is essential for testing conjectures and for applications in image analysis and turbulence modelling. The standard algorithm discretises the Loewner equation by a time step Δt and updates the conformal maps via the slit map gt+Δt(z) = gt(z) + Δt / (gt(z) − Wt). The driving function Wt is sampled as √κ times a Gaussian increment. For chordal SLE in the upper half‑plane the map can be represented by a composition of elementary slit maps, which is numerically stable for moderate capacities.

Convergence analysis

Kennedy (2009) proved that the simple Euler scheme converges weakly with order 1/2 in the capacity parameter: the expected Hausdorff distance between the discrete trace and the true SLE trace is O(Δt1/2). Higher‑order schemes (Milstein, Runge–Kutta) improve the strong convergence to order 1 for κ ≤ 4, but for κ > 4 the non‑smoothness of the trace limits the strong order to 1/2. Adaptive time‑stepping based on the local derivative of the map reduces the number of steps needed to reach a given capacity.

Practical considerations

  • Use the zipper algorithm (Marshall–Rohde) for whole‑plane and radial SLE: it builds the curve by iteratively adding small slits and updating the conformal map via the Schwarz–Christoffel transformation.
  • For multiple SLE, simulate the system of driving functions with the correct covariance matrix; the Cholesky decomposition of the covariance yields independent Brownian increments.
  • Validate simulations by checking conformal invariance: map the generated curve to a different domain and compare statistics (e.g., hitting distributions) with theoretical predictions.

Recent work (Johansson‑Viklund, 2022) shows that the discrete exploration path of critical percolation on a triangular lattice of mesh size a converges to SLE6 in the strong topology with rate a1/3+o(1), providing a quantitative benchmark for numerical experiments.

  • Confusing the duality parameter: the dual of κ is 16/κ, not 8/κ or κ/2.
  • Assuming reversibility holds for all κ without the imaginary geometry coupling; it fails for κ > 4 without the GFF framework.
  • Treating SLE(κ,ρ) as ordinary SLE when any ρi ≠ 0; the force points change the hitting probabilities and the partition function.
  • Misidentifying the phase thresholds: κ = 8/3 is the restriction threshold, κ = 4 separates simple from self‑touching, κ = 8 is the space‑filling threshold.
  • Neglecting the covariance structure in multiple SLE simulations; independent Brownian drivers produce intersecting curves that do not have the correct law.
  • Using a fixed time step for large capacities; adaptive stepping is required to control the numerical error near the tip of the curve.
  • Forgetting that the quantum zipper constructs SLE on an independent LQG surface, not on a deterministic Euclidean domain.
The advanced topics above complete the next level of the SLE lesson.

hand/optimal-transport.html:
Entropic Regularization and the Sinkhorn Algorithm

Entropic regularization adds a strictly convex penalty to the Kantorovich problem, turning the linear program into a strictly convex optimization that can be solved by iterative scaling. For two discrete probability vectors a, b in the simplex and a cost matrix C, the regularized problem reads

minπ ≥ 0 ⟨π, C⟩ + ε ∑i,j πij (log πij − 1) subject to π 1 = a, πᵀ 1 = b.

The parameter ε > 0 controls the trade‑off between fidelity to the original transport cost and the entropy of the coupling. As ε → 0 the solution converges to a solution of the unregularized Kantorovich problem; as ε → ∞ the coupling approaches the independent product a ⊗ b. The optimality conditions yield the scaling form π = diag(u) K diag(v) with K = exp(−C/ε). The vectors u, v are found by the Sinkhorn iterations

u ← a ⊘ (K v), v ← b ⊘ (Kᵀ u)

where ⊘ denotes element‑wise division. These iterations converge linearly to the unique scaling vectors, and each step costs O(n²) for dense matrices. The algorithm is trivially parallelizable on GPUs and has become the workhorse for large‑scale optimal transport in machine learning, computer vision, and computational biology.

Beyond the discrete setting, entropic regularization admits a continuous formulation: the Schrödinger bridge problem. For absolutely continuous marginals μ₀, μ₁ on ℝⁿ with densities ρ₀, ρ₁, the regularized problem minimizes ∫ ρ log(ρ/ρ₀ρ₁) dx + (1/ε) ∫ c(x,y) dπ(x,y) over couplings π with marginals μ₀, μ₁. The solution is a Markov diffusion whose drift is the gradient of a time‑dependent potential solving a pair of Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations. This connection links optimal transport to stochastic control and provides a probabilistic interpretation of the Sinkhorn algorithm as an iterative proportional fitting procedure for path measures.

From a numerical analysis perspective, the regularized problem is well‑posed for any ε > 0, and the error in Wasserstein distance between the regularized and unregularized solutions is O(ε log(1/ε)) under mild assumptions. Adaptive schemes that decrease ε during the iterations (ε‑scaling) accelerate convergence while preserving stability. Recent work also explores Anderson acceleration and Newton‑type methods for the dual formulation, achieving superlinear convergence for moderate ε.

In practice, the choice of ε is problem‑dependent: too large ε oversmooths the transport plan, too small ε leads to numerical underflow in the kernel K. A common heuristic sets ε proportional to the median of the cost matrix entries. For image processing tasks, ε is often chosen so that the resulting transport plan captures the desired geometric features without excessive diffusion.

The JKO Scheme and Gradient Flows in Wasserstein Space

The Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) scheme provides a variational time‑discretization of gradient flows in the Wasserstein space (P₂(ℝⁿ), W₂). Given a functional F : P₂ → ℝ ∪ {+∞} that is lower semicontinuous and λ‑convex along geodesics, the implicit Euler step reads

ρk+1 ∈ argminρ ∈ P₂ { F(ρ) + (1/2τ) W₂²(ρ, ρk) }

where τ > 0 is the time step. The sequence {ρk} defines a piecewise constant interpolation ρτ(t) = ρk for t ∈ ((k−1)τ, kτ]. As τ → 0, ρτ converges narrowly to a curve ρ(t) that satisfies the Evolution Variational Inequality (EVI)

½ d/dt W₂²(ρ(t), ν) + F(ρ(t)) ≤ F(ν) − (λ/2) W₂²(ρ(t), ν) for all ν ∈ P₂.

This EVI characterizes the gradient flow of F in the sense of metric spaces. The JKO scheme thus recovers classical PDEs as gradient flows of natural energies: the heat equation is the gradient flow of the Boltzmann–Shannon entropy H(ρ) = ∫ ρ log ρ dx; the porous medium equation ∂tρ = Δρm (m > 1) is the gradient flow of the internal energy Um(ρ) = (1/(m−1)) ∫ ρm dx; the Fokker–Planck equation ∂tρ = ∇·(ρ ∇V) + Δρ is the gradient flow of the free energy F(ρ) = ∫ ρ V dx + H(ρ).

The scheme also applies to non‑local energies, e.g., the aggregation equation ∂tρ = ∇·(ρ ∇(W * ρ)) with interaction potential W, which is the gradient flow of the interaction energy (1/2) ∫∫ W(x−y) dρ(x) dρ(y). The λ‑convexity of the energy along Wasserstein geodesics is the key structural property guaranteeing existence, uniqueness, and stability of the flow. For the entropy on ℝⁿ, λ = 0; on a manifold with Ric ≥ K, λ = K.

Numerically, the JKO step is a convex optimization problem over probability measures. For discrete measures it reduces to a regularized optimal transport problem, often solved via the Sinkhorn algorithm described above. For continuous densities, particle methods (blob methods, variational particle schemes) approximate the minimization by evolving a finite set of particles with weights. The convergence of these particle approximations to the true gradient flow has been established under appropriate regularity assumptions.

The JKO framework has become a unifying language for dissipative PDEs, linking functional inequalities (log‑Sobolev, Talagrand, HWI) to the geometry of the underlying space. It also provides a natural setting for splitting schemes: if F = F₁ + F₂ with each Fi having a tractable proximal map, one can alternate the JKO steps for F₁ and F₂, yielding operator‑splitting algorithms with provable convergence.

Worked Example: JKO Step for the Heat Equation
Let ρ⁰ be a smooth probability density on ℝ. Perform one JKO step with time step τ for the entropy functional H(ρ) = ∫ ρ log ρ dx. Show that the minimizer ρ¹ satisfies ρ¹ = ρ⁰ * Gτ, where Gτ is the Gaussian kernel with variance 2τ.
The JKO step minimizes H(ρ) + (1/2τ) W₂²(ρ, ρ⁰). By the Benamou–Brenier formula, W₂²(ρ, ρ⁰) = inf ∫₀¹ ∫ |vt|² ρt dx dt over curves (ρt, vt) solving ∂tρt + ∇·(ρt vt) = 0 with ρ₀ = ρ⁰, ρ₁ = ρ. The optimality condition for the joint minimization yields vt = ∇φt with φ solving the Hamilton–Jacobi equation ∂tφ + ½|∇φ|² = 0. The first variation of H gives δH/δρ = log ρ + 1. The Euler–Lagrange equation for the JKO functional reads log ρ¹ + 1 + (1/τ) φ₁ = constant, where φ₁ is the Kantorovich potential from ρ⁰ to ρ¹. For quadratic cost on ℝ, the optimal map is T(x) = x − τ ∇ log ρ¹(T(x)). Linearizing for small τ gives T(x) ≈ x − τ ∇ log ρ⁰(x). The pushforward of ρ⁰ by this map is the solution of the heat equation at time τ, which is exactly the convolution with the Gaussian kernel Gτ(x) = (4πτ)−1/2 exp(−x²/(4τ)). Hence ρ¹ = ρ⁰ * Gτ.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to identify the gradient flow of a given energy in Wasserstein space, first check λ‑convexity of the energy along geodesics. Write down the JKO minimization, compute the first variation of the energy, and match the resulting Euler–Lagrange equation to a known PDE. Remember that the heat equation corresponds to entropy, porous medium to power‑law internal energy, and Fokker–Planck to free energy. For discrete settings, recall that the JKO step becomes an entropic optimal transport problem solvable by Sinkhorn iterations.

Multi‑Marginal Optimal Transport and Its Applications

Multi‑marginal optimal transport (MMOT) generalizes the two‑marginal Kantorovich problem to an arbitrary number of marginals. Given probability measures μ₁, …, μk on spaces X₁, …, Xk and a cost function c : X₁ × … × Xk → ℝ, the problem is

infπ ∈ Π(μ₁,…,μk) ∫ c(x₁,…,xk) dπ(x₁,…,xk)

where Π(μ₁,…,μk) denotes the set of couplings with the prescribed marginals. The dual formulation involves k potentials φi satisfying ∑ φi(xi) ≤ c(x₁,…,xk) and maximizing ∑ ∫ φi dμi. When the cost is of the form c(x₁,…,xk) = ∑i<j</sub> cij(xi, xj) (pairwise interactions), the problem is equivalent to a two‑marginal problem on a product space, but the general case is fundamentally different.

A prominent application is the strong‑interaction limit of density functional theory (DFT) in quantum chemistry. The exact electron‑electron interaction energy can be expressed as a multi‑marginal optimal transport problem with Coulomb cost c(x₁,…,xN) = ∑i<j</sub> 1/|xi − xj| and identical marginals given by the electron density ρ. The optimal plan is supported on a graph of a cyclical monotone map, leading to the concept of co‑motion functions. This formulation provides a rigorous lower bound for the exchange‑correlation energy and has inspired new density functionals.

In economics, MMOT models matching markets with multiple types of agents (e.g., workers, firms, tasks). The cost function encodes the total surplus of a match, and the optimal plan describes the equilibrium assignment. The Shapley–Shubik assignment game is a discrete MMOT with a supermodular cost, guaranteeing the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium that coincides with the optimal transport plan.

Computationally, MMOT suffers from the curse of dimensionality: the coupling π lives on a product space of dimension ∑ dim Xi. For discrete marginals with n points each, the number of variables is nk. Entropic regularization extends naturally, yielding a multi‑marginal Sinkhorn algorithm that iteratively scales a k‑dimensional tensor. The iterations converge linearly, but the memory cost remains exponential. Low‑rank tensor formats (Tensor Train, Hierarchical Tucker) and stochastic gradient methods on the dual potentials are active research directions to mitigate this bottleneck.

Recent theoretical advances include the characterization of optimality via c‑cyclical monotonicity for general costs, the equivalence between MMOT and martingale optimal transport when one marginal is a martingale, and the development of a Wasserstein‑type distance for tuples of measures (the multi‑marginal Wasserstein distance). These tools are now used in generative modeling (multi‑domain translation), Bayesian inference (fusion of posterior samples), and the study of mean‑field games with common noise.

Regularity Theory for the Monge–Ampère Equation

The Monge–Ampère equation det D²u = f arises as the Jacobian equation for the optimal transport map T = ∇u pushing forward a density ρ₀ to ρ₁ = f ρ₀ on a convex domain Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ. The regularity of u is central to the smoothness of the transport map and to the geometry of the Wasserstein space. The classical theory, developed by Caffarelli, establishes interior C¹,α regularity for convex solutions when f is bounded away from zero and infinity, and the target domain is convex. The key steps are:

  1. Strict convexity of u follows from the Aleksandrov maximum principle and the assumption that f ≥ λ > 0.
  2. C¹,α regularity is proved via a blow‑up argument and the Harnack inequality for the linearized Monge–Ampère operator Lu v = trace(adj(D²u) D²v).
  3. If f is Ck,α and the domains are Ck+2,α, then u ∈ Ck+2,α up to the boundary (global regularity) provided the boundary data satisfy a compatibility condition (the second boundary value problem ∇u(Ω) = Ω*).

Counterexamples show that convexity of the target domain is necessary: if Ω* is not convex, singularities can form even for smooth positive densities. The regularity theory extends to the cost c(x,y) = |x−y|²/2 on Riemannian manifolds, where the equation becomes det(D²u − D²xc(x, ∇u(x))) = f(x)/g(∇u(x)) with g the target density. Ma–Trudinger–Wang introduced the MTW tensor (cost‑sectional curvature) as the curvature condition ensuring regularity for general costs. For the quadratic cost on a manifold, the MTW tensor coincides with the sectional curvature of the manifold.

In the context of optimal transport, the regularity of the potential u implies that the optimal map is a diffeomorphism, the displacement interpolation is smooth, and the Wasserstein geodesics are unique. This underpins the Otto calculus: the tangent space at a smooth density consists of gradients of smooth functions, and the Riemannian metric is well defined. When densities are merely bounded and bounded away from zero, the optimal map is still a homeomorphism (Caffarelli’s global W²,p estimates), which is sufficient for many analytic arguments.

Recent work addresses degenerate densities (f vanishing on sets) and non‑convex domains using the notion of Alexandrov solutions and the theory of viscosity solutions. The partial regularity theory (Caffarelli, 1990s) shows that the singular set of a convex Alexandrov solution has Hausdorff dimension at most n−1. For the optimal transport problem with quadratic cost on ℝⁿ, this implies that the transport map is smooth outside a negligible set, a fact used in the proof of the Brenier theorem for general marginals.

Wasserstein Barycenters and Their Computation

Given probability measures μ₁, …, μm in P₂(ℝⁿ) and weights λ₁, …, λm > 0 with ∑ λi = 1, the Wasserstein barycenter (or Fréchet mean) is defined as

ν* ∈ argminν ∈ P₂ ∑i=1m λi W₂²(ν, μi).

Existence and uniqueness follow from the strict convexity of the squared Wasserstein distance along geodesics in P₂(ℝⁿ). The barycenter inherits regularity properties: if all μi are absolutely continuous with densities bounded away from zero and infinity on convex domains, then ν* is also absolutely continuous with a density enjoying the same bounds. Moreover, the optimal transport maps Ti from ν* to μi satisfy ∑ λi Ti = Id ν*-a.e., a characterization that generalizes the Euclidean barycenter condition.

Computationally, the barycenter problem is a multi‑marginal optimal transport problem with a specific cost structure. For discrete measures supported on a common grid of size N, the problem can be written as a linear program with mN variables and N constraints. Entropic regularization yields a convex problem solvable by a multi‑marginal Sinkhorn algorithm that iteratively updates scaling vectors for each marginal. The algorithm converges to the regularized barycenter, and as ε → 0 the solution approaches the true barycenter. For continuous measures, particle methods represent each μi by a weighted point cloud and optimize the particle positions and weights of ν* using gradient descent on the Wasserstein space (the JKO scheme applied to the barycenter functional).

Applications abound: in image processing, the barycenter of a set of images provides a meaningful average that respects geometric features (e.g., shape interpolation). In Bayesian statistics, the Wasserstein barycenter of posterior distributions from distributed data subsets yields a consensus posterior that captures the geometry of the parameter space. In generative modeling, barycenters in the latent space of a Wasserstein autoencoder produce interpolations that follow the data manifold.

Theoretical extensions include barycenters on metric measure spaces satisfying CD(K,N) conditions, where the barycenter inherits the same curvature‑dimension bounds. The stability of barycenters under perturbations of the input measures is quantified by the Lipschitz continuity of the barycenter map with respect to the Wasserstein distance. For Gaussian measures, the barycenter has a closed form: if μi = N(mi, Σi), then ν* = N(∑ λi mi, Σ*) where Σ* is the unique positive definite solution of Σ* = ∑ λi (Σ*1/2 Σi Σ*1/2)1/2. This formula is used in covariance estimation and in the analysis of Gaussian processes.

  • Confusing the unregularized Kantorovich problem with its entropic regularization; the latter yields a strictly convex problem with a unique solution for any ε > 0, while the former may have multiple optimal plans.
  • Assuming the Sinkhorn algorithm converges for any cost matrix without checking that the kernel K = exp(−C/ε) has full support; zero entries in K can break convergence.
  • Neglecting the λ‑convexity requirement in the JKO scheme; without it the implicit Euler step may not define a unique minimizer, and the EVI characterization fails.
  • Overlooking the necessity of convex target domains in the Monge–Ampère regularity theory; non‑convex targets can produce singular optimal maps even for smooth densities.
  • Treating the multi‑marginal Sinkhorn iterations as a simple extension of the two‑marginal case without accounting for the exponential growth of tensor size; practical implementations require low‑rank approximations.
  • Believing that the Wasserstein barycenter of discrete measures is always supported on the union of the input supports; the barycenter can have support outside this union due to the geometry of optimal transport.
  • Forgetting that the MTW tensor condition is both necessary and sufficient for regularity of optimal maps for general costs; on manifolds it reduces to non‑negative sectional curvature for the quadratic cost.

hand/noncommutative-geometry.html:
Real Spectral Triples and KO‑Dimension

A real spectral triple (A, H, D, J, γ) adds two operators to the basic data: an antilinear isometry J (the real structure) and a grading γ (present only in even KO‑dimension). The operator J implements charge conjugation and satisfies J² = ε, JD = ε' DJ, Jγ = ε'' γJ with signs ε, ε', ε'' ∈ {±1} that depend only on the KO‑dimension n mod 8. The KO‑dimension table is a cornerstone of the classification: for n = 0 one has ε = 1, ε' = 1, ε'' = 1; for n = 1 ε = 1, ε' = -1, ε'' = 1; for n = 2 ε = -1, ε' = -1, ε'' = 1; for n = 3 ε = -1, ε' = -1, ε'' = -1; for n = 4 ε = -1, ε' = 1, ε'' = -1; for n = 5 ε = -1, ε' = 1, ε'' = 1; for n = 6 ε = 1, ε' = 1, ε'' = 1; for n = 7 ε = 1, ε' = -1, ε'' = 1. The product of a 4‑dimensional spin manifold (KO‑dimension 4) with a finite space of KO‑dimension 6 yields total KO‑dimension 10 ≡ 2 (mod 8), which is the value required for the Standard Model spectral triple. The real structure also enforces the order‑one condition [[D, a], Jb*J⁻¹] = 0 for all a, b ∈ A, guaranteeing that the Dirac operator behaves as a first‑order differential operator on the bimodule defined by J. This condition is essential for the derivation of the gauge field kinetic terms from the spectral action.

Finite Spectral Triples and the Classification of Particle Representations

The finite part F = (A_F, H_F, D_F, J_F, γ_F) of the Standard Model spectral triple is completely determined by the representation theory of the algebra A_F = ℂ ⊕ ℍ ⊕ M₃(ℂ). The Hilbert space H_F decomposes into left‑handed and right‑handed fermions, each carrying a representation of A_F. The left‑handed quarks transform as (2, 3)1/6 under SU(2)_L × SU(3)_c with hypercharge 1/6, the left‑handed leptons as (2, 1)-1/2, the right‑handed up‑type quarks as (1, 3)2/3, the right‑handed down‑type quarks as (1, 3)-1/3, and the right‑handed charged leptons as (1, 1)-1. The neutrino sector is extended by right‑handed neutrinos (1, 1)0 to allow Majorana masses. The finite Dirac operator D_F is a matrix of Yukawa couplings that mixes generations and couples the Higgs field to fermions. Its block structure respects the grading γ_F and the real structure J_F, which implements charge conjugation on the finite Hilbert space. The order‑one condition forces the off‑diagonal blocks of D_F to be linear in the Higgs field, reproducing the Standard Model Yukawa Lagrangian. The KO‑dimension of the finite triple is 6, which together with the 4‑dimensional manifold gives total KO‑dimension 2, the value that yields the correct fermion doubling and the correct sign for the Einstein–Hilbert term in the spectral action.

Dimensional Reduction of the Spectral Action
Given the product geometry M × F with total Dirac operator D = D_M ⊗ 1 + γ⁵ ⊗ D_F, compute the leading term of the bosonic spectral action Tr(f(D/Λ)) in the heat‑kernel expansion and identify the coefficient of the Einstein–Hilbert term.
The heat‑kernel expansion of Tr(f(D/Λ)) reads ∑k≥0 f2k Λ4-2k a2k(D²). For a 4‑dimensional manifold the Seeley–DeWitt coefficient a0(D²) = (4π)-2 ∫_M tr(1) dvol gives the cosmological constant term. The coefficient a2(D²) contains the scalar curvature: a2(D²) = (4π)-2 (1/6) ∫_M tr(R) dvol where R is the scalar curvature of M. The trace over the finite Hilbert space yields a factor dim H_F = 96. Thus the Einstein–Hilbert term appears as f2 Λ² (1/6)(4π)-2 96 ∫_M R dvol = (f2 Λ² / 24π²) 96 ∫_M R dvol = (4 f2 Λ² / π²) ∫_M R dvol. Identifying (1/16πG) = (4 f2 Λ² / π²) gives the Newton constant in terms of the cutoff and the moment f2.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Einstein–Hilbert term from the spectral action, remember that only the a2 Seeley–DeWitt coefficient contributes at order Λ². Write down the universal factor (4π)-2 (1/6) tr(R) and then multiply by the trace over the finite Hilbert space. The moment f2 is defined as ∫0^∞ f(u) u du; you do not need its explicit value unless the problem supplies it.

Heat Kernel Asymptotics and Seeley–DeWitt Coefficients

The spectral action relies on the asymptotic expansion of the heat kernel Tr(e-t D²) ∼ ∑k≥0 t(k-4)/2 a_k(D²) as t → 0. The coefficients a_k are integrals over the manifold of local invariants built from the curvature of the Levi‑Civita connection, the gauge field strength, and the Higgs field. For a product geometry M × F the total Dirac operator squares to D² = D_M² ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_F² + γ⁵ ⊗ [D_M, D_F]. Because D_M acts only on the manifold factor and D_F only on the finite factor, the mixed commutator vanishes, and the heat kernel factorises: Tr(e-t D²) = Tr_M(e-t D_M²) Tr_F(e-t D_F²). The Seeley–DeWitt coefficients for the manifold part are well known: a0 = (4π)-2 ∫ tr(1), a2 = (4π)-2 (1/6) ∫ tr(R), a4 contains the Yang–Mills term tr(FμνFμν), the Higgs kinetic term tr((D_μ φ)† D^μ φ), and the quartic Higgs potential tr(φ† φ φ† φ). The finite part contributes only to the overall multiplicities because D_F is a matrix; its heat kernel is Tr_F(e-t D_F²) = ∑_i e-t λ_i² where λ_i are the eigenvalues of D_F. In the limit t → 0 this trace tends to dim H_F, providing the factor 96 that appears in all coefficients. The moment integrals f2k = ∫0^∞ f(u) u2k-1 du weight each coefficient in the spectral action. The positivity of f guarantees that the cosmological constant term (proportional to f0 Λ⁴) and the Einstein–Hilbert term (proportional to f2 Λ²) have the correct signs for a physically viable model.

Renormalization Group Flow of the Spectral Action

The spectral action is defined at a unification cutoff Λ. To connect with low‑energy physics one must run the couplings down to the electroweak scale using the renormalization group equations (RGEs) derived from the Standard Model Lagrangian that emerges from the heat‑kernel expansion. The gauge couplings g1, g2, g3 of U(1)_Y, SU(2)_L, SU(3)_c satisfy the one‑loop beta functions β_i = (b_i/16π²) g_i³ with coefficients b = (41/10, -19/6, -7) for the Standard Model particle content. The Higgs quartic coupling λ and the top Yukawa coupling y_t have beta functions that depend on the gauge couplings and on each other. The spectral action predicts specific boundary conditions at Λ: the gauge couplings unify to a single value g_* determined by the moment f2, the Higgs quartic coupling is related to the gauge couplings by λ = (1/2) g_*² (up to group‑theoretic factors), and the top Yukawa coupling is fixed by the eigenvalue of D_F corresponding to the top quark. Solving the coupled RGEs yields a prediction for the Higgs pole mass around 170 GeV at the unification scale, which runs to approximately 125 GeV at the electroweak scale, in agreement with the measured value. The top quark mass prediction is similarly sensitive to the initial Yukawa coupling and the gauge couplings; the spectral action typically gives a top mass in the range 170–180 GeV, compatible with experiment. Higher‑loop corrections and threshold effects at the unification scale can shift these numbers, but the qualitative agreement is a strong test of the noncommutative geometry framework.

Noncommutative Geometry and Quantum Gravity: Fuzzy Spaces and Asymptotic Safety

Beyond the Standard Model, noncommutative geometry offers a concrete route to quantum gravity. A fuzzy sphere S²_N is defined by the matrix algebra MN+1(ℂ) with a Dirac operator built from the generators of SU(2). Its spectrum approximates that of the ordinary sphere as N → ∞, while for finite N the space has a finite number of degrees of freedom, implementing a minimal length scale. The spectral triple of the fuzzy sphere satisfies all axioms except the smoothness condition, making it a genuine noncommutative manifold. In the context of the spectral action, replacing the continuous manifold M by a fuzzy approximation yields a finite‑dimensional matrix model whose partition function can be studied non‑perturbatively. The renormalization group flow of such matrix models has been investigated using functional renormalization group techniques; evidence suggests the existence of an ultraviolet fixed point (asymptotic safety) where the dimensionless couplings become scale‑invariant. If the full spectral triple of quantum spacetime admits a similar fixed point, the theory would be ultraviolet complete without the need for a separate quantum gravity framework. Moreover, the commutator [D, a] encodes the differential structure; deforming this commutator leads to a generalized uncertainty principle Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2 (1 + β (Δp)²), a hallmark of quantum gravity phenomenology. The interplay between the finite spectral triple of the Standard Model and a fuzzy or otherwise noncommutative spacetime manifold is an active research direction that may eventually explain the origin of the algebra A_F from deeper geometric principles.

  • Confusing the KO‑dimension of the finite triple (6) with the total KO‑dimension (2) and misapplying the sign table for J and γ.
  • Forgetting that the order‑one condition forces the Yukawa couplings to be linear in the Higgs field, leading to incorrect gauge‑invariant operators.
  • Using the wrong Seeley–DeWitt coefficient for the Einstein–Hilbert term; the relevant coefficient is a2, not a4.
  • Neglecting the trace over the finite Hilbert space (factor 96) when extracting the gravitational constant from the spectral action.
  • Assuming the gauge couplings unify exactly at one loop without accounting for the spectral action boundary conditions that relate g_* to the moment f2.
  • Treating the fuzzy sphere as a smooth manifold and applying the reconstruction theorem, which requires smoothness and fails for finite‑dimensional algebras.
  • Overlooking that the asymptotic safety scenario in noncommutative geometry depends on the existence of a fixed point for the dimensionless couplings of the spectral action, not merely on the finiteness of the matrix model.

hand/optics.html:
Fourier Optics and Spatial Frequency Filtering

Fourier optics treats the propagation of light through an optical system as a linear shift‑invariant process in the spatial‑frequency domain. The complex amplitude at the exit pupil is the Fourier transform of the object transparency, multiplied by the pupil function P(ξ,η) that encodes aperture shape and aberrations. The intensity in the image plane is the squared modulus of the inverse transform of this product. The optical transfer function (OTF) is the autocorrelation of the pupil function; its modulus, the modulation transfer function (MTF), quantifies contrast loss at each spatial frequency. For a circular aperture of diameter D, the cutoff frequency is ν_c = D/(λf), where f is the focal length. The Abbe diffraction limit follows directly: the smallest resolvable period is λ/(2 NA), with numerical aperture NA = n sin θ_max.

A classic 4f correlator implements spatial filtering by placing a mask at the Fourier plane between two lenses of equal focal length f. The first lens produces the Fourier spectrum; the mask transmits selected spatial frequencies; the second lens performs the inverse transform, yielding a filtered image. Low‑pass filtering removes high‑frequency noise, while high‑pass filtering enhances edges. Phase‑only filters (e.g., a π phase step) enable phase‑contrast imaging without amplitude loss. The Wiener filter, H_W(ν) = H*(ν) / (|H(ν)|² + K), provides optimal restoration in the presence of additive noise, where K is the noise‑to‑signal power ratio.

Practical limits arise from finite detector pixel size, which imposes a Nyquist frequency ν_N = 1/(2Δx). Aliasing occurs when object frequencies exceed ν_N; anti‑aliasing filters are therefore essential in digital holography and computational imaging. The space‑bandwidth product (SBP) of an imaging system, SBP = (field‑of‑view) × (cutoff frequency)², determines the number of resolvable spots and is a key figure of merit for microscope objectives and lithography lenses.

Coherence Theory and Interferometric Techniques

Coherence quantifies the correlation between field values at different points in space or time. Temporal coherence is described by the complex degree of coherence γ(τ) = ⟨E*(t)E(t+τ)⟩ / ⟨|E(t)|²⟩; its Fourier transform yields the spectral power density S(ν) (Wiener‑Khinchin theorem). The coherence length ℓ_c = c τ_c, where τ_c is the coherence time, determines the maximum path‑difference for observable fringes. For a source with Gaussian spectrum of width Δν, ℓ_c ≈ 0.44 c/Δν. Spatial coherence follows the Van Cittert‑Zernike theorem: the mutual intensity at two points in a far‑field plane equals the Fourier transform of the source intensity distribution. A spatially incoherent extended source therefore produces a coherence area inversely proportional to its angular size.

Interferometers convert phase differences into intensity variations. The Michelson interferometer splits a beam with a 50/50 beamsplitter, reflects the arms, and recombines them; the detected intensity I(Δ) = I₀[1 + |γ(Δ)| cos(2πΔ/λ + φ)] reveals the coherence function. The Mach‑Zehnder interferometer uses two separate beamsplitters, allowing independent access to both output ports for balanced detection. In Fourier‑transform spectroscopy, a Michelson interferometer records the interferogram I(Δ) versus optical path difference Δ; the spectrum is obtained by cosine Fourier transform. Phase‑shifting interferometry acquires several frames with known phase steps (e.g., 0, π/2, π, 3π/2) to compute the wrapped phase φ = atan2(I₃−I₁, I₀−I₂). Unwrapping algorithms then retrieve continuous wavefront maps.

Modern applications include optical coherence tomography (OCT), where low‑coherence interferometry provides axial resolution Δz ≈ 0.44 λ₀²/Δλ, and gravitational‑wave detectors (LIGO), which employ Fabry‑Pérot arm cavities to enhance effective arm length and use homodyne readout to reach strain sensitivities below 10⁻²³/√Hz. The Hanbury Brown‑Twiss intensity interferometer measures the second‑order correlation g⁽²⁾(τ) to infer stellar angular diameters, demonstrating that intensity correlations survive even when first‑order coherence vanishes.

Worked Example: Coherence Length of a Spectral Line
A spectral line centred at λ₀ = 600 nm has a full width at half maximum Δλ = 0.02 nm. Assuming a Gaussian profile, calculate the coherence length ℓ_c in millimetres.
For a Gaussian spectrum, the coherence time τ_c = (2√(ln 2)/π) · (λ₀²/(c Δλ)). Using λ₀ = 600 × 10⁻⁹ m, Δλ = 0.02 × 10⁻⁹ m, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s: τ_c ≈ 0.44 · (600² × 10⁻¹⁸)/(3 × 10⁸ · 0.02 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 0.44 · (3.6 × 10⁻¹³)/(6 × 10⁻³) ≈ 0.44 · 6 × 10⁻¹¹ s ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻¹¹ s. The coherence length ℓ_c = c τ_c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ · 2.6 × 10⁻¹¹ ≈ 7.8 mm. Rounded to two significant figures, ℓ_c ≈ 7.8 mm.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question gives a spectral width Δλ or Δν, first identify whether the profile is Gaussian or Lorentzian; the numerical prefactor for ℓ_c differs (0.44 for Gaussian, 0.66 for Lorentzian). Write the formula symbolically, substitute units consistently (convert nm to m), and keep track of powers of ten. A quick sanity check: visible light with Δλ ≈ 1 nm yields ℓ_c of order 100 µm; narrower lines give millimetre‑scale coherence.

Optical Aberrations, Wavefront Error, and Adaptive Optics

Aberrations are deviations of the actual wavefront from an ideal reference sphere. The Seidel (third‑order) aberrations — spherical, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, and distortion — are expressed as polynomial terms in pupil coordinates (ρ,θ) and field angle. Zernike polynomials provide an orthogonal basis over the unit circle; each term Z_n^m corresponds to a specific aberration mode (e.g., Z40 = defocus, Z3^±1 = coma, Z2^±2 = astigmatism). The root‑mean‑square (RMS) wavefront error σ_W relates to the Strehl ratio S ≈ exp[−(2πσ_W/λ)²] (Maréchal approximation). Diffraction‑limited performance requires σ_W ≤ λ/14 (≈ λ/14 RMS), corresponding to S ≥ 0.8.

Adaptive optics (AO) corrects dynamic aberrations in real time. A wavefront sensor (Shack‑Hartmann or pyramid) measures local slopes; a reconstructor computes the modal coefficients; a deformable mirror (DM) with N actuators applies the conjugate shape. The Greenwood frequency f_G ≈ 0.43 v/r₀ (v = wind speed, r₀ = Fried parameter) sets the required control bandwidth. For astronomical telescopes, r₀ ≈ 10–20 cm at 500 nm; f_G is typically 50–100 Hz, demanding DM update rates > 1 kHz. Laser guide stars (Rayleigh or sodium resonance at 589 nm) provide reference beacons when natural guide stars are unavailable. In retinal imaging, AO corrects ocular aberrations (dominated by defocus and astigmatism) to achieve cellular‑resolution fundus photographs.

Segmented primary mirrors (e.g., Keck, JWST) introduce phasing errors; edge sensors and piston‑tip‑tilt actuators maintain co‑phasing to a fraction of λ. The optical path difference (OPD) budget allocates tolerances among manufacturing, alignment, thermal, and dynamic contributions. Modern lithography tools (EUV, λ = 13.5 nm) employ projection optics with < 0.5 nm RMS wavefront error, achieved through ion‑beam figuring and interferometric metrology.

Nonlinear Optical Processes and Frequency Conversion

In media with non‑centrosymmetric structure, the polarization expands as P = ε₀(χ⁽¹⁾E + χ⁽²⁾E² + χ⁽³⁾E³ + …). The second‑order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾ enables three‑wave mixing: second‑harmonic generation (SHG, ω+ω→2ω), sum‑frequency generation (SFG), and difference‑frequency generation (DFG). Phase matching requires Δk = k(2ω) − 2k(ω) = 0. Birefringent phase matching uses angle tuning in uniaxial crystals (e.g., KDP, BBO) to equalise ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices. Quasi‑phase matching (QPM) periodically poling the crystal (period Λ = 2π/Δk) reverses the sign of χ⁽²⁾, allowing first‑order QPM with effective nonlinearity d_eff = (2/π)d₃₃.

Third‑order effects (χ⁽³⁾) include third‑harmonic generation, Kerr effect (intensity‑dependent refractive index n = n₀ + n₂I), self‑phase modulation, four‑wave mixing, and Raman gain. The nonlinear Schrödinger equation governs pulse propagation in fibers: ∂A/∂z + (iβ₂/2)∂²A/∂t² = iγ|A|²A, where γ = n₂ω₀/(cA_eff). Soliton formation occurs when anomalous dispersion (β₂ < 0) balances self‑phase modulation (N = √(γP₀T₀²/|β₂|) = 1). Supercontinuum generation in photonic‑crystal fibers exploits higher‑order dispersion and Raman scattering to produce octave‑spanning spectra.

Optical parametric amplifiers (OPAs) and oscillators (OPOs) use χ⁽²⁾ to amplify a signal wave while generating an idler; the gain bandwidth can exceed 100 nm, enabling few‑cycle pulse synthesis. High‑harmonic generation (HHG) in noble gases driven by intense femtosecond lasers produces coherent extreme‑ultraviolet (XUV) radiation up to keV photon energies; the cutoff energy follows E_cutoff = I_p + 3.17 U_p, where I_p is ionisation potential and U_p ∝ Iλ² is the ponderomotive potential. Attosecond pulse trains and isolated attosecond pulses are derived by spectral filtering of HHG spectra.

Quantum Optics: Photon Statistics and Entanglement

Quantum optics describes light in terms of field operators. The Glauber‑Sudarshan P‑representation classifies states: coherent states |α⟩ have Poissonian photon statistics (g⁽²⁾(0)=1), thermal states exhibit bunching (g⁽²⁾(0)=2), and Fock states |n⟩ show antibunching (g⁽²⁾(0)=0). The Hong‑Ou‑Mandel interferometer sends two identical photons into a 50/50 beamsplitter; coincidence detection drops to zero when temporal overlap is perfect, demonstrating two‑photon interference and the bosonic nature of photons.

Squeezed states reduce quantum noise in one quadrature below the vacuum level at the expense of increased noise in the conjugate quadrature. The squeezing parameter r yields variance V_θ = (1/4)e^(−2r) for the squeezed quadrature. Squeezed vacuum injected into the dark port of a Michelson interferometer improves gravitational‑wave detector sensitivity beyond the shot‑noise limit. Entangled photon pairs generated by spontaneous parametric down‑conversion (SPDC) obey energy and momentum conservation: ω_p = ω_s + ω_i, k_p = k_s + k_i. Polarisation entanglement (|H⟩|V⟩ + |V⟩|H⟩)/√2 violates Bell’s CHSH inequality (S ≤ 2 for local realism, quantum prediction S = 2√2).

Quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols such as BB84 encode bits in non‑orthogonal polarisation bases; security follows from the no‑cloning theorem and disturbance‑detection principle. Continuous‑variable QKD uses Gaussian‑modulated coherent states and homodyne detection, achieving key rates of several Mbps over metropolitan fibres. Quantum imaging exploits spatial entanglement to achieve sub‑shot‑noise resolution (quantum illumination) and ghost imaging, where an object is imaged using photons that never interacted with it, correlated with a reference beam.

  • Confusing the Rayleigh criterion (1.22 λ/D) with the Abbe limit (λ/2 NA) — they apply to different imaging geometries (circular aperture vs. coherent illumination).
  • Assuming temporal coherence length ℓ_c = λ²/Δλ without the numerical prefactor; the factor depends on spectral line shape (0.44 for Gaussian, 0.66 for Lorentzian).
  • Treating the Strehl ratio as exactly exp[−(2πσ/λ)²] for large aberrations; the Maréchal approximation holds only for σ ≲ λ/14.
  • Neglecting the difference between phase matching and quasi‑phase matching in χ⁽²⁾ processes; QPM requires periodic poling and yields a reduced effective nonlinearity (2/π factor).
  • Misidentifying photon bunching (g⁽²⁾(0)>1) as a signature of entanglement; bunching occurs for thermal light, while entanglement is revealed by Bell‑inequality violation or sub‑Poissonian statistics.
  • Overlooking that adaptive‑optics bandwidth must exceed the Greenwood frequency, not just the atmospheric coherence time τ₀ = 0.314 r₀/v.
  • Using the thin‑lens Fourier transform formula without accounting for the quadratic phase factor exp[ik(x²+y²)/2f] that appears when the input plane is not at the front focal plane.

These advanced topics extend the foundational optics curriculum into the regimes where modern research, precision metrology, and quantum technologies operate.

hand/cluster-algebras.html:
Cluster Algebras from Surfaces and Tagged Arcs

Cluster algebras admit a geometric realisation via marked surfaces, a construction due to Fomin, Shapiro and Thurston (2008). A marked surface (S, M) consists of an oriented surface S with boundary together with a finite set M of marked points on the boundary and possibly in the interior (punctures). Tagged arcs are curves connecting marked points, considered up to isotopy, with a tagging at each endpoint that records whether the arc approaches the marked point from the left or the right side of the boundary. The set of all tagged arcs forms the cluster variables of a cluster algebra whose initial seed is given by an ideal triangulation of the surface. Mutations correspond to flips of diagonals in the triangulation: replacing one arc by the unique other arc that together with the remaining arcs forms a new ideal triangulation. The exchange matrix is the signed adjacency matrix of the quiver associated to the triangulation; its entries count intersections of arcs with a sign determined by orientation. This surface model explains many combinatorial properties: the Laurent phenomenon follows from the fact that each arc can be expressed as a Laurent polynomial in the arcs of any triangulation, with coefficients given by counts of perfect matchings of associated snake graphs (Musiker, Schiffler, Williams, 2011). Moreover, the cluster complex is isomorphic to the simplicial complex of non‑crossing tagged arcs, and the cluster modular group coincides with the mapping class group of the surface. The construction also yields a natural parametrisation of the cluster variables by laminations on the surface, linking cluster algebras to Thurston’s theory of measured foliations.

Fock–Goncharov Coordinates and Higher Teichmüller Theory

Fock and Goncharov (2006) introduced a cluster‑theoretic coordinate system on the moduli space XG,S of framed G-local systems on a marked surface S, where G is a split semisimple algebraic group. For G = SL_m these coordinates generalise the classical Penner coordinates on the decorated Teichmüller space (the case m=2). The construction assigns to each ideal triangulation a seed whose cluster variables are certain cross‑ratio functions on the space of local systems. Mutations of the seed correspond to changes of triangulation and are realised by explicit rational transformations — the cluster X-mutations. The resulting cluster atlas provides a positive structure: the totally positive part XG,S(R>0) is identified with the space of positive representations of the fundamental group of S into G(R). This positivity underlies the definition of the higher Teichmüller spaces and yields a canonical basis of the coordinate ring via the tropicalisation of the cluster X-coordinates. The tropical points are integral laminations on the surface, and the cluster modular group acts by piecewise‑linear transformations preserving the tropical semifield structure. The Fock–Goncharov framework also produces a cluster ensemble (A,X) with a natural pairing, leading to a quantisation where the quantum dilogarithm implements the mutation automorphisms. These quantum cluster varieties have been used to construct invariants of 3‑manifolds and to formulate the spectral networks of Gaiotto–Moore–Neitzke.

Worked Example: Flip of a Tagged Arc
Consider a once‑punctured quadrilateral with vertices labelled 1,2,3,4 in cyclic order and a puncture p. The initial triangulation uses the diagonal (1,3) and the two boundary arcs (1,p) and (3,p). Perform the mutation at the cluster variable corresponding to the diagonal (1,3). Write the exchange relation for the new cluster variable and identify the resulting tagged arc.
In the surface model the exchange relation for a flip of an internal arc γ in a quadrilateral with sides a,b,c,d (in cyclic order) is γ γ' = a c + b d. Here the sides are the boundary arcs (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,1) and the two arcs incident to the puncture are (1,p) and (3,p). The diagonal (1,3) is γ. The two opposite sides of the quadrilateral are (1,2) and (3,4) — call them a and c — and the other pair are (2,3) and (4,1) — call them b and d. The exchange relation becomes (1,3) · (2,4) = (1,2)(3,4) + (2,3)(4,1). The new arc γ' is the other diagonal (2,4). Because the puncture lies inside the quadrilateral, the flipped arc (2,4) is a plain (untagged) arc; no tagging change occurs. Thus the mutated cluster variable corresponds to the tagged arc (2,4) with the same tagging at the endpoints as the original diagonal.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the exchange relation of a surface cluster algebra, first draw the quadrilateral formed by the two triangles adjacent to the mutable arc. Identify the four boundary arcs of that quadrilateral; the exchange relation is always the sum of the products of opposite sides. Remember that tagged arcs at punctures may acquire a tag change only when the flipped arc is incident to a puncture and the quadrilateral has a puncture on its boundary — in that case the new arc receives the opposite tag at that puncture.

Categorification via 2‑Calabi–Yau Categories and Cluster Characters

The additive categorification of cluster algebras was achieved by Buan, Marsh, Reineke, Reiten and Todorov (2006) who introduced cluster categories. For a quiver Q without oriented cycles, the cluster category C_Q is the orbit category D^b(mod kQ)/τ-1[1], where τ is the Auslander–Reiten translation and [1] the shift functor. This category is triangulated, 2‑Calabi–Yau (i.e. Hom(X,Y) ≅ Hom(Y,X[2])^* functorially), and its indecomposable objects correspond bijectively to cluster variables of the associated cluster algebra. Cluster‑tilting objects in C_Q correspond to clusters, and mutation of cluster‑tilting objects realises the cluster mutation. The cluster character (or Caldero–Chapoton map) sends an object X to a Laurent polynomial X_X in the initial cluster variables; for rigid objects this polynomial coincides with the corresponding cluster variable. The categorification explains the Laurent phenomenon and positivity: the coefficients count Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians Gr_e(X). For acyclic quivers the cluster category is equivalent to the module category of the preprojective algebra of the associated Dynkin diagram, linking cluster algebras to the representation theory of preprojective algebras and to the geometry of Nakajima quiver varieties.

Quantum Dilogarithm and Wall‑Crossing in BPS Spectra

In the physics of N=2 supersymmetric gauge theories, the spectrum of BPS states is encoded by a quiver with potential. Kontsevich and Soibelman (2008) showed that the wall‑crossing formula for the BPS indices is governed by the quantum dilogarithm Φ_q(x) = Πn=0^∞ (1+q2n+1x)-1. The product of quantum dilogarithms ordered by the phase of the central charge is invariant under mutations of the quiver, which correspond to changes of stability condition. This invariance is precisely the quantum cluster mutation relation in the quantum torus algebra generated by the variables X_γ satisfying X_γ Xγ' = q⟨ γ,γ'⟩ Xγ' X_γ. The quantum dilogarithm identity Φ_q(X_γ) Φ_q(Xγ') = Φ_q(Xγ') Φ_q(Xγ+γ') Φ_q(X_γ) reproduces the pentagon identity for the quantum cluster X-transformation. Gaiotto, Moore and Neitzke (2010) used this structure to construct the hyperkähler metric on the moduli space of vacua via spectral networks, where the cluster coordinates provide Darboux coordinates on the twistor space. The same quantum dilogarithm appears in the quantisation of the Fock–Goncharov X-variety, linking the mathematical theory of quantum cluster algebras to the physical wall‑crossing phenomenon.

Positivity, Greedy Basis and the Laurent Phenomenon Algebras

The positivity conjecture, proved by Gross, Hacking, Keel and Kontsevich (2018) using the theory of scattering diagrams, asserts that every cluster variable expands as a Laurent polynomial with positive integer coefficients in any cluster. An alternative combinatorial proof was given by Lee, Li and Zelevinsky (2012) who introduced the greedy basis: for an acyclic cluster algebra, the greedy basis elements are indexed by the integer lattice Z^n and are constructed by a greedy algorithm that picks the minimal degree monomial not yet in the span of previously chosen elements. The greedy basis coincides with the dual canonical basis when the cluster algebra is of finite type, and it provides a canonical positive basis for all acyclic cluster algebras. The construction extends to the broader class of Laurent phenomenon algebras (Lam and Pylyavskyy, 2016), where the exchange relations are allowed to be arbitrary Laurent polynomials satisfying a coprimeness condition. In this setting the Laurent phenomenon still holds, and a version of the greedy basis can be defined using the tropicalisation of the exchange relations. The positivity of the greedy basis elements implies the positivity of all cluster variables, and the tropical points of the associated A-variety parametrise the basis. This combinatorial approach has been instrumental in proving the periodicity conjecture for cluster algebras from surfaces and in establishing the existence of theta bases for general cluster varieties.

  • Confusing the cluster A-variables with the X-variables; they live on dual tori and mutate by different formulas.
  • Assuming every quiver mutation corresponds to a flip of an ideal triangulation — this holds only for cluster algebras from surfaces, not for arbitrary quivers.
  • Neglecting the tagging at punctures when writing exchange relations for tagged arcs; the tag can change under mutation.
  • Treating the quantum dilogarithm identity as a formal power series identity without the correct ordering of factors dictated by the central charge phases.
  • Believing the greedy basis exists for all cluster algebras; it is currently constructed only for acyclic (or more generally, injective‑reachable) cases.
  • Overlooking that the cluster category is 2‑Calabi–Yau only for quivers without oriented cycles; for quivers with cycles one must use the generalised cluster category of Amiot.
  • Misidentifying the tropicalisation of the X-variety with the set of integral laminations without specifying the choice of seed.
The advanced sections above complete the required material for this lesson.

hand/cosmology.html:
Primordial Nucleosynthesis and Light Element Abundances

Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) occurs when the universe cools to temperatures of order 0.1–1 MeV, roughly 1–200 seconds after the initial singularity. At these energies the weak interactions that interconvert neutrons and protons freeze out, fixing the neutron‑to‑proton ratio at about 1:6. The subsequent nuclear reactions are governed by the baryon‑to‑photon ratio η = n_b / n_γ, which is directly related to the present‑day baryon density Ω_b h². The deuterium bottleneck — the high photon‑to‑baryon ratio that photodisintegrates D until T ≈ 0.07 MeV — delays the onset of heavier element synthesis. Once deuterium survives, rapid two‑body reactions produce 4He, 3He, D, and 7Li. The primordial 4He mass fraction Y_p is relatively insensitive to η but depends strongly on the expansion rate, which is set by the effective number of relativistic neutrino species N_eff. Standard BBN with N_eff = 3.046 predicts Y_p ≈ 0.247, D/H ≈ 2.5×10⁻⁵, 3He/H ≈ 1.0×10⁻⁵, and 7Li/H ≈ 5×10⁻¹⁰. Observations of metal‑poor H II regions give Y_p = 0.245 ± 0.003, while quasar absorption systems yield D/H = (2.53 ± 0.04)×10⁻⁵. The lithium abundance remains a long‑standing discrepancy: the Spite plateau in metal‑poor stars shows 7Li/H ≈ 1.6×10⁻¹⁰, a factor of three below the BBN prediction. This “lithium problem” may signal physics beyond the standard model (e.g., particle decay, varying fundamental constants) or systematic stellar depletion. Precise BBN predictions combined with CMB‑determined η provide a powerful cross‑check of the ΛCDM model and constrain exotic energy components during the first minutes.

Recombination Physics and the Last Scattering Surface

Recombination is the process by which free electrons and protons combine to form neutral hydrogen, rendering the universe transparent to photons. The standard treatment uses the Peebles effective three‑level atom model, which accounts for the bottleneck at the n=2 level: direct recombinations to the ground state produce Lyman‑α photons that immediately re‑ionize neighboring atoms, so the net recombination rate is set by the slower two‑photon decay from 2s and the cosmological redshifting of Lyman‑α photons out of resonance. The Saha equation gives a good approximation at high redshift (z ≳ 1300), but the full rate equation must be integrated to obtain the free‑electron fraction x_e(z). The visibility function g(z) = e-τ dτ/dz, where τ is the Thomson optical depth, peaks at z_* ≈ 1089 with a full width at half maximum Δz ≈ 80. This finite thickness of the last scattering surface damps anisotropies on angular scales smaller than the Silk scale (ℓ ≳ 1000) because photons random‑walk out of overdense regions before decoupling. The same scattering generates linear polarization: quadrupole temperature anisotropies at the last scattering surface produce E‑mode polarization, while primordial gravitational waves would generate B‑modes. The acoustic peaks in the temperature power spectrum arise from sound waves in the photon‑baryon fluid; their angular positions are set by the sound horizon at recombination r_s(z_*) and the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface. Accurate recombination codes (e.g., RECFAST, CosmoRec) are essential for percent‑level CMB parameter estimation.

Examiner's trap
A question states: “The redshift of recombination is z ≈ 1100, while the redshift of photon decoupling is z ≈ 1089. Explain the difference.” Many candidates answer that they are the same event.
Recombination refers to the epoch when the ionisation fraction drops below 50 %, which occurs slightly earlier (z ≈ 1100) because the Saha equilibrium still holds. Photon decoupling is defined by the peak of the visibility function, where the probability of a photon last scattering is maximal; this happens when the Thomson optical depth falls to unity, at z ≈ 1089. The two redshifts differ by Δz ≈ 10–15 because the universe remains partially ionised for a short period after recombination, and the finite thickness of the last scattering surface shifts the peak of g(z) to lower redshift.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the key numbers: z_* ≈ 1089, Δz ≈ 80, sound horizon r_s ≈ 144 Mpc, and the Silk damping multipole ℓ_Silk ≈ 1300. When a question asks for the angular scale of the first acoustic peak, use θ_* = r_s / D_A(z_*) ≈ 0.6°, which corresponds to ℓ ≈ 200. This shortcut avoids recomputing the full integral under time pressure.

Structure Formation: From Linear Perturbations to Nonlinear Collapse

The growth of cosmic structure is described by the evolution of the matter density contrast δ(k, a) = δρ_m / ρ_m. In the linear regime (δ ≪ 1) each Fourier mode grows independently with the growth factor D(a), which in a ΛCDM universe satisfies the differential equation D'' + (3/a + H'/H) D' - (3/2) Ω_m(a) D / a² = 0. During radiation domination the Meszaros effect suppresses growth on sub‑horizon scales, imprinting a turnover in the transfer function T(k) at the matter‑radiation equality scale k_eq ≈ 0.01 Mpc⁻¹. The linear matter power spectrum today is P_lin(k) = A_s (k/k_*)n_s-1 T²(k) D²(a=1). Nonlinear evolution is commonly modelled with the spherical collapse model: a top‑hat overdensity evolves as a closed Friedmann universe, reaching turnaround at δ_lin ≈ 1.06 and virialisation at δ_lin ≈ 1.686. The Press‑Schechter formalism uses this critical linear overdensity to derive the halo mass function dn/dM ∝ (ρ_m/M) |d ln σ⁻¹/dM| exp(-δ_c²/2σ²), where σ(M) is the variance of the linear density field smoothed on mass scale M. Modern N‑body simulations calibrate the Sheth‑Tormen and Tinker mass functions, which improve the high‑mass tail. Halo bias b(M) relates the halo overdensity to the matter overdensity; on large scales b(M) ≈ 1 + (ν²-1)/δ_c with ν = δ_c/σ(M). The nonlinear matter power spectrum P_nl(k) is obtained from perturbation theory (e.g., standard perturbation theory, effective field theory) or from fitting functions such as HALOFIT. Baryon acoustic oscillations survive as a ∼5 % modulation in P_nl(k) and provide a standard ruler for distance measurements.

Observational Probes of Dark Energy: Supernovae, BAO, and Weak Lensing

Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) serve as standardisable candles: after correcting for light‑curve shape (stretch) and colour, their peak absolute magnitude has an intrinsic scatter of ≈0.1 mag. The distance modulus μ = m - M = 5 log₁₀(D_L/10 pc) yields the luminosity distance D_L(z). In a flat universe D_L(z) = (1+z) ∫₀^z dz'/H(z'), so SNe Ia constrain the expansion history H(z) and the dark‑energy equation of state w(z). Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) provide a complementary standard ruler: the comoving sound horizon at the drag epoch r_d ≈ 147 Mpc appears as a peak in the galaxy two‑point correlation function at a separation s = r_d. Measuring the angular scale θ_BAO = r_d / D_M(z) and the radial scale Δz_BAO = r_d H(z) / c gives both the comoving angular diameter distance D_M(z) and H(z) independently. Weak gravitational lensing measures the coherent distortion (shear) of background galaxy shapes by foreground large‑scale structure. The shear two‑point correlation functions ξ_±(θ) or their Fourier counterparts, the convergence power spectra C_ℓκκ, probe the combination of geometry and growth. Tomographic binning of source galaxies by photometric redshift yields a 3D map of the matter distribution and breaks degeneracies between Ω_m, σ₈, and w. Joint analyses of SNe Ia, BAO, and weak lensing (e.g., from DES, KiDS, HSC, and future LSST, Euclid, Roman) achieve percent‑level constraints on w₀ and w_a, testing whether dark energy is a cosmological constant (w = -1) or a dynamical field.

The Hubble Tension and Possible Resolutions

The Hubble tension refers to the ≈5–6 σ discrepancy between the local measurement of the Hubble constant H₀ from the distance ladder (Cepheid‑calibrated SNe Ia) and the value inferred from the CMB under the ΛCDM model. The SH0ES collaboration reports H₀ = 73.04 ± 1.04 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, while Planck 2018 gives H₀ = 67.4 ± 0.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. The tension persists after extensive checks for systematic errors in Cepheid photometry, metallicity corrections, and SN Ia standardisation. Independent geometric distance anchors (masers, tip of the red giant branch, surface brightness fluctuations) yield intermediate values, but none fully bridge the gap. Early‑universe solutions modify the sound horizon r_s at recombination, which rescales the CMB‑inferred H₀. Proposals include early dark energy (a scalar field that contributes ≈10 % of the energy density around matter‑radiation equality), additional relativistic species (ΔN_eff > 0), or a primordial magnetic field. Late‑universe solutions alter the expansion history at z < 1, e.g., a phantom dark energy component (w < -1) or modified gravity that enhances the effective gravitational constant. However, most late‑time models worsen the fit to BAO and supernova data. The tension may also indicate unaccounted systematics in the distance ladder, such as Cepheid crowding or SN Ia host‑galaxy correlations. Upcoming high‑precision measurements from JWST Cepheids, Gaia parallaxes, and the Roman Space Telescope will decisively test whether the tension signals new physics or residual measurement bias.

  • Confusing the redshift of recombination (z ≈ 1100) with the peak of the visibility function (z ≈ 1089) leads to incorrect angular‑scale calculations.
  • Assuming the primordial lithium abundance matches BBN predictions ignores the well‑documented factor‑of‑three discrepancy known as the lithium problem.
  • Treating the linear growth factor D(a) as scale‑independent on all scales neglects the Meszaros suppression and the scale‑dependent growth induced by massive neutrinos.
  • Using the Press‑Schechter mass function without the Sheth‑Tormen correction overestimates the abundance of massive clusters at high redshift.
  • Equating the BAO scale measured in the transverse direction with the radial BAO scale without accounting for the Alcock‑Paczynski effect biases constraints on H(z) and D_A(z).
  • Attributing the Hubble tension solely to early‑dark‑energy models without checking consistency with BAO and weak‑lensing data is a common oversimplification.
  • Remember that the sound horizon at the drag epoch r_d is the fundamental ruler for BAO, while the sound horizon at recombination r_s sets the CMB acoustic scale; they differ by ≈3 % and must not be interchanged.
