hand/algebraic-geometry.html:
Derived Categories and Fourier–Mukai Transforms

The derived category Db(Coh X) of bounded complexes of coherent sheaves on a smooth projective variety X provides a natural setting for functors only partially defined on Coh X. Objects are complexes up to quasi‑isomorphism; morphisms are roofs of quasi‑isomorphisms. The triangulated structure encodes exact triangles from short exact sequences, allowing uniform treatment of cones, shifts, and mapping cones.

A Fourier–Mukai transform is an exact functor Φ𝒦 : Db(Coh X) → Db(Coh Y) of the form Φ𝒦(−) = RπY*(πX*(−) ⊗L 𝒦), where 𝒦 ∈ Db(Coh (X × Y)) is the kernel, πX, πY are projections, and ⊗L is the derived tensor product. When X = Y is an abelian variety and 𝒦 is the Poincaré line bundle on X × X̂, Φ𝒦 is an equivalence — the classical Mukai duality. Orlov’s representability theorem shows that any exact functor between derived categories of smooth projective varieties admitting left and right adjoints is isomorphic to a Fourier–Mukai functor, making kernels the universal language for equivalences, autoequivalences, and stability conditions.

Applications include the derived McKay correspondence, where the derived category of a crepant resolution of a quotient singularity is equivalent to the derived category of equivariant sheaves on the covering space, and homological mirror symmetry, where the derived Fukaya category of a Calabi–Yau manifold is conjecturally equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on its mirror. A full exceptional collection in Db(Coh X) yields a semi‑orthogonal decomposition into copies of Db(k), a powerful tool for K‑theory and Hochschild homology.

Higher Direct Images and the Grothendieck Spectral Sequence

For a morphism f : X → Y of schemes, the higher direct image sheaves Rif*ℱ are the right derived functors of f* on quasi‑coherent sheaves. When f is proper and ℱ coherent, the theorem on formal functions identifies the completion of (Rif*ℱ)y with the inverse limit of Hi(Xn, ℱ|Xn), where Xn are infinitesimal neighbourhoods of the fibre Xy — the algebraic analogue of Grauert’s theorem.

The Grothendieck spectral sequence arises from composing two left exact functors. For f = g ∘ h with h : X → Z and g : Z → Y, there is a spectral sequence E2p,q = Rpg*(Rqh*ℱ) ⇒ Rp+qf*ℱ. Taking h as a closed immersion and g proper gives a spectral sequence relating pushforwards along the inclusion of a divisor. Degeneration criteria (e.g., fibres of cohomological dimension ≤ 1) control pushforwards of canonical sheaves, essential for the canonical bundle formula in the minimal model program.

Base change theorems compare (Rif*ℱ)y with Hi(Xy, ℱ|Xy). Grothendieck’s cohomology and base change theorem states that if y ↦ dim Hi(Xy, ℱ|Xy) is locally constant, then (Rif*ℱ)y ⊗ k(y) → Hi(Xy, ℱ|Xy) is an isomorphism and Rif*ℱ is locally free. This underpins moduli space constructions via the determinant of cohomology and the semicontinuity theorem.

Worked Example: Leray Spectral Sequence for a Blow‑up
Let π : X̃ → X be the blow‑up of a smooth variety X along a smooth centre Z of codimension c ≥ 2, with exceptional divisor E ≅ ℙ(NZ/X). Compute Riπ*𝒪X̃ for all i.
The fibres of π are points outside E and projective spaces ℙc−1 over Z. For i = 0, π*𝒪X̃ = 𝒪X because π is birational and X is normal. For 0 < i < c−1, cohomology of ℙc−1 with coefficients in 𝒪 vanishes, so Riπ*𝒪X̃ = 0. For i = c−1, Hc−1(ℙc−1, 𝒪) = 0 as well, hence Rc−1π*𝒪X̃ = 0. All higher direct images vanish because fibres have dimension c−1. Thus Riπ*𝒪X̃ = 0 for i > 0, and the Leray spectral sequence degenerates at E2, giving Hi(X̃, 𝒪X̃) ≅ Hi(X, 𝒪X).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for higher direct images of a blow‑up, first identify fibre dimensions and use vanishing of cohomology of 𝒪 on projective space. Normality of the target forces π*𝒪 = 𝒪, and Grauert–Riemenschneider vanishing often kills higher direct images of the relative canonical sheaf.

Étale Cohomology and the Weil Conjectures

Étale cohomology provides a Weil cohomology theory for varieties over finite fields, replacing singular cohomology unavailable in characteristic p. For a scheme X of finite type over a separably closed field, the étale site Xét has objects étale morphisms U → X and coverings by jointly surjective families. Sheaves of ℤ/ℓℤ‑modules (ℓ ≠ p) yield cohomology groups Hiét(X, ℤ/ℓℤ) satisfying Poincaré duality, the Künneth formula, and the Lefschetz trace formula.

The Weil conjectures, proved by Deligne using ℓ‑adic cohomology, assert that for a smooth projective variety X over 𝔽q the zeta function Z(X, t) = exp(∑n≥1 |X(𝔽qn)| tn/n) is rational, satisfies a functional equation, and its zeros and poles have absolute value q−i/2 (the Riemann hypothesis). The proof constructs the Frobenius endomorphism on Hiét(X̄, ℚℓ) and shows its eigenvalues are algebraic integers with the required absolute values, using the hard Lefschetz theorem and the Hodge index theorem in the ℓ‑adic setting.

Applications extend to the Langlands programme: ℓ‑adic cohomology of Shimura varieties carries actions of Galois and reductive groups, realizing local Langlands correspondences. The weight‑monodromy conjecture predicts that the weight filtration on the cohomology of a degeneration matches the monodromy filtration; this remains open in general but is known for curves and abelian varieties.

Birational Geometry and the Minimal Model Program in Higher Dimension

The Minimal Model Program (MMP) classifies projective varieties up to birational equivalence via divisorial contractions and flips. For a ℚ‑factorial variety X with terminal singularities and nef KX, the cone theorem describes the Mori cone NE(X) as the nef cone plus countably many extremal rays generated by rational curves with negative intersection against KX. The contraction theorem associates to each extremal ray a morphism contracting exactly those curves.

When the contraction is small (exceptional locus of codimension ≥ 2), a flip replaces the contracted locus with another variety having opposite normal bundle, preserving ℚ‑factoriality and terminal singularities. The existence of flips in dimension ≥ 4 was established by Birkar, Cascini, Hacon, and McKernan (2010) via finite generation of the canonical ring. The abundance conjecture predicts that if KX is nef then some multiple is base‑point‑free, yielding a morphism to the canonical model; this is known for varieties of general type up to dimension three and for log canonical pairs in all dimensions under additional hypotheses.

The geography of models is encoded in the movable cone and the Cox ring. For a Fano variety, the Mori dream space property (finite generation of the Cox ring) guarantees MMP termination with a Mori fibre space. Boundedness of Fano varieties of fixed dimension and ε‑log canonical threshold, proved by Birkar (2016), implies such varieties form a bounded family, a cornerstone for moduli spaces of K‑stable Fano varieties.

Arithmetic Geometry: Schemes over Spec ℤ and Arakelov Theory

Viewing Spec ℤ as the base scheme places number fields on the same footing as function fields. A regular, projective, flat scheme X → Spec ℤ of relative dimension d is an arithmetic variety. Fibres over primes p are varieties over 𝔽p; the generic fibre is a variety over ℚ. Arakelov theory equips X(ℂ) with a Kähler metric, defining intersection numbers of arithmetic divisors (a divisor on X plus a Green current on X(ℂ)). The arithmetic intersection pairing satisfies a Hodge index theorem and a Riemann–Roch formula due to Gillet and Soulé.

The arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem expresses the arithmetic degree of the determinant of cohomology of a hermitian vector bundle via the arithmetic Chern character, Todd form, and an analytic torsion term. This yields explicit height formulas, e.g., the Faltings height of an abelian variety. Faltings’ theorem (the Mordell conjecture) on finiteness of rational points on curves of genus ≥ 2 follows by comparing the Arakelov degree of the Hodge bundle with the self‑intersection of the relative dualizing sheaf.

Recent developments include the arithmetic Kodaira vanishing theorem (Yuan–Zhang) and arithmetic intersection numbers for cycles on Shimura varieties, used in the proof of the Colmez conjecture on Faltings heights of CM abelian varieties. Perfectoid spaces, introduced by Scholze, provide a new framework for p‑adic Hodge theory and comparison of étale and de Rham cohomology, advancing the Langlands programme and cohomology of locally symmetric spaces.

  • Confusing derived functors on the abelian category with functors on the derived category — they agree only after taking cohomology.
  • Assuming every Fourier–Mukai kernel gives an equivalence; the kernel must satisfy Orlov’s spanning and orthogonality conditions.
  • Neglecting the ℓ ≠ p condition in étale cohomology; ℓ = p requires crystalline or de Rham theories.
  • Applying the cone theorem without verifying ℚ‑factoriality and terminal singularities; the statement fails otherwise.
  • Treating Arakelov divisors as ordinary divisors on the generic fibre; the Green current is essential for the arithmetic intersection product.
  • Overlooking the need for a proper flat model over Spec ℤ in arithmetic intersection theory; non‑flat models give incorrect fibre contributions.
  • Misidentifying the weight filtration with the monodromy filtration without checking the semistable reduction hypothesis.

These advanced topics form the backbone of modern research in algebraic geometry and are essential for high‑level examination problems.

hand/chemical-equilibrium.html:
Temperature Dependence of Equilibrium Constants: The van't Hoff Equation

The equilibrium constant varies with temperature because the standard Gibbs free energy change ΔG° = −RT ln K depends on T. For a reaction with a constant standard enthalpy change ΔH° over a modest temperature range, the integrated van't Hoff equation gives ln(K₂/K₁) = −ΔH°/R (1/T₂ − 1/T₁). This relation shows that for an exothermic reaction (ΔH° < 0) K decreases as temperature rises, while for an endothermic reaction (ΔH° > 0) K increases. The differential form d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²) is useful for estimating the shift in K per kelvin. In practice, ΔH° itself can be temperature‑dependent; the Kirchhoff equation ΔH°(T₂) = ΔH°(T₁) + ∫ΔCₚ dT accounts for heat‑capacity differences between products and reactants. When high precision is required, one fits experimental K values at several temperatures to a polynomial in 1/T or uses the full thermodynamic cycle ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° with temperature‑dependent ΔH° and ΔS°. A typical problem provides K at two temperatures and asks for ΔH° assuming it is constant; the student must correctly apply the integrated form and watch the sign of ΔH°. Another common problem: given ΔH° and ΔS° at 298 K, calculate K at 500 K, requiring conversion of ΔS° to J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and careful unit handling (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). The van't Hoff plot (ln K versus 1/T) yields a straight line of slope −ΔH°/R only when ΔH° is constant; curvature signals a significant ΔCₚ.

Ionic Strength, Activity Coefficients, and Real Solution Equilibria

Textbook equilibrium expressions use concentrations, but rigorous thermodynamics requires activities aᵢ = γᵢ cᵢ (or γᵢ mᵢ for molality). The activity coefficient γᵢ approaches 1 only at infinite dilution. In solutions of appreciable ionic strength I = ½ Σ cᵢ zᵢ², electrostatic interactions lower the effective concentration of ions. The Debye–Hückel limiting law log₁₀ γᵢ = −A zᵢ² √I (A ≈ 0.509 for water at 25 °C) works for I < 0.01 M. For higher ionic strengths the extended Debye–Hückel equation log₁₀ γᵢ = −A zᵢ² √I / (1 + B a √I) (B ≈ 0.328 Å⁻¹ M⁻¹ᐟ², a = ion‑size parameter) or the Davies equation log₁₀ γᵢ = −A zᵢ² (√I/(1+√I) − 0.3 I) are used. In equilibrium calculations, the thermodynamic constant K° = Π aᵢ^νᵢ is constant, while the concentration‑based quotient Kc = Π cᵢ^νᵢ varies with I. For example, the solubility product of AgCl (Ksp = 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C) expressed in activities is invariant; the apparent solubility in 0.1 M NaNO₃ is higher because γ_Ag⁺ and γ_Cl⁻ < 1. Problems often ask for the molar solubility of a salt like BaSO₄ in a background electrolyte using the Davies equation. The steps: (1) write Ksp = a_Ba²⁺ a_SO₄²⁻ = γ_Ba [Ba²⁺] γ_SO₄ [SO₄²⁻]; (2) estimate I from all ions present; (3) compute γ for each ion; (4) solve for [Ba²⁺]. Neglecting activity coefficients leads to a systematic under‑prediction of solubility in ionic media. Another common error: using the limiting law beyond its validity range, which over‑estimates the deviation.

Worked Example: Activity‑Corrected Solubility
Calculate the molar solubility of CaF₂ (Ksp = 3.9×10⁻¹¹) in a 0.05 M NaCl solution at 25 °C using the Davies equation. Assume the ion‑size parameter a = 4 Å for both Ca²⁺ and F⁻.
  1. Write the dissolution equilibrium: CaF₂(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2 F⁻. Let s = molar solubility. Then [Ca²⁺] = s, [F⁻] = 2s.
  2. Ionic strength I = ½ Σ cᵢ zᵢ². I = ½(0.05×1² + 0.05×1² + s×2² + 2s×1²) ≈ 0.05 + 3s. Since s ≪ 0.05, I ≈ 0.05 M.
  3. Davies equation: log₁₀ γ = −A z² (√I/(1+√I) − 0.3 I). With A = 0.509, √I = 0.2236. For Ca²⁺ (z=2): log₁₀ γ_Ca = −0.509×4×(0.2236/1.2236 − 0.015) = −2.036×(0.1827 − 0.015) = −2.036×0.1677 = −0.341 → γ_Ca = 0.456. For F⁻ (z=1): log₁₀ γ_F = −0.509×1×0.1677 = −0.0853 → γ_F = 0.822.
  4. Thermodynamic Ksp = a_Ca a_F² = (γ_Ca s)(γ_F 2s)² = γ_Ca γ_F² 4 s³.
  5. Solve for s: s³ = Ksp / (4 γ_Ca γ_F²) = 3.9×10⁻¹¹ / (4 × 0.456 × 0.822²) = 3.9×10⁻¹¹ / (4 × 0.456 × 0.676) = 3.9×10⁻¹¹ / 1.233 = 3.16×10⁻¹¹. s = (3.16×10⁻¹¹)¹ᐟ³ = 3.17×10⁻⁴ M.
  6. Check assumption: 3s = 9.5×10⁻⁴ ≪ 0.05, valid.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem gives an ionic strength or a background electrolyte, always compute activities before applying Ksp or Ka. The Davies equation is widely used for I up to ~0.5 M in competitive‑exam chemistry. Memorise A = 0.509 and the form √I/(1+√I) − 0.3I. Typical ion‑size parameters are ≈4 Å for most monovalent ions and ≈6 Å for divalent ions; use these if not provided. If the question only asks for a qualitative trend, state that increasing ionic strength decreases activity coefficients and thus increases apparent solubility or dissociation.

Polyprotic Acid Equilibria: Stepwise Dissociation and Overlapping Buffer Regions

Polyprotic acids (HₙA) lose protons sequentially: HₙA ⇌ H⁺ + Hₙ₋₁A⁻ (Ka₁), Hₙ₋₁A⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + Hₙ₋₂A²⁻ (Ka₂), … Each step has its own Ka, typically decreasing by 10³–10⁵. For phosphoric acid, Ka₁ = 7.5×10⁻³ (pKa₁ = 2.12), Ka₂ = 6.2×10⁻⁸ (pKa₂ = 7.21), Ka₃ = 4.8×10⁻¹³ (pKa₃ = 12.32). Because the pKa values are well separated, each proton generates a distinct buffer region centered at pH = pKaᵢ. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation applies to each step: pH = pKa₁ + log([H₂PO₄⁻]/[H₃PO₄]) for the first buffer, pH = pKa₂ + log([HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻]) for the second, etc. When pKa values are close (ΔpKa < 2), the buffer regions overlap and the simple stepwise treatment fails; one must solve the full set of mass‑balance, charge‑balance, and equilibrium equations simultaneously. For carbonic acid (pKa₁ = 6.35, pKa₂ = 10.33) the separation is sufficient for separate buffers, but the first dissociation is complicated by CO₂ hydration equilibrium (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃, Kh = 1.7×10⁻³). In titration of a diprotic acid with strong base, the first equivalence point occurs at pH ≈ (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2 only if the acid is not too weak and concentrations are moderate. The exact pH at the first equivalence point is given by [H⁺] = √(Ka₁ Ka₂ + Ka₁ Kw / C) where C is the formal concentration of the acid salt. Problems frequently test the concept of “amphiprotic salt” pH (e.g., NaHCO₃, Na₂HPO₄) using the approximation pH = ½(pKa₁ + pKa₂) and ask when this approximation breaks down (very dilute solutions or when Ka₁ ≈ Ka₂). Another common task: calculating the fraction of each species (α₀, α₁, α₂) as a function of pH using α₀ = [H⁺]²/D, α₁ = Ka₁[H⁺]/D, α₂ = Ka₁Ka₂/D with D = [H⁺]² + Ka₁[H⁺] + Ka₁Ka₂.

Solubility Product, Common Ion Effect, and Precipitation Criteria

The solubility product Ksp governs the equilibrium between a sparingly soluble solid and its ions: MₓAᵧ(s) ⇌ x Mʸ⁺ + y Aˣ⁻, Ksp = a_Mˣ a_Aʸ. In dilute solutions activities ≈ concentrations, so Ksp ≈ [Mʸ⁺]ˣ [Aˣ⁻]ʸ. The common ion effect states that adding a soluble salt sharing an ion shifts the equilibrium left, reducing solubility. For example, the solubility of AgCl in pure water is s = √Ksp = 1.33×10⁻⁵ M; in 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.1 M, so s = Ksp / 0.1 = 1.77×10⁻⁹ M. Precipitation occurs when the ion product Q = [Mʸ⁺]ˣ [Aˣ⁻]ʸ exceeds Ksp. In mixed‑ion solutions, selective precipitation is possible if the Ksp values differ sufficiently. For a mixture of Ba²⁺ and Sr²⁺ with (NH₄)₂SO₄, BaSO₄ (Ksp = 1.1×10⁻¹⁰) precipitates first because its Ksp is lower; SrSO₄ (Ksp = 3.2×10⁻⁷) remains in solution until [SO₄²⁻] reaches ~3×10⁻⁶ M. The fraction of the first ion precipitated before the second begins can be calculated by equating the ion product of the second salt to its Ksp while the first is still precipitating. Complex ion formation (e.g., Ag⁺ + 2 NH₃ ⇌ Ag(NH₃)₂⁺, Kf = 1.6×10⁷) dramatically increases apparent solubility; the conditional solubility product Ksp' = Ksp / (1 + Kf[NH₃]²) is used. Problems often combine common ion, pH (for salts of weak acids like CaCO₃), and complexation: “Will CaC₂O₄ precipitate when 0.01 M Ca²⁺ is mixed with 0.01 M oxalic acid at pH 4.0? (Ka₁ = 5.6×10⁻², Ka₂ = 5.4×10⁻⁵, Ksp = 2.3×10⁻⁹).” The solution requires computing [C₂O₄²⁻] from the diprotic acid equilibria at the given pH, then comparing Q = [Ca²⁺][C₂O₄²⁻] with Ksp.

Electrochemical Equilibria: The Nernst Equation and Its Applications

Electrochemical cells provide a direct experimental handle on equilibrium constants. For a redox half‑reaction Ox + ne⁻ ⇌ Red, the electrode potential E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(a_Red/a_Ox). At 25 °C, E = E° − (0.05916/n) log₁₀(a_Red/a_Ox). For a full cell, Ecell = E°cell − (0.05916/n) log₁₀ Q, where Q is the reaction quotient written with activities. At equilibrium Ecell = 0, so log₁₀ K = nE°cell/0.05916, linking the standard cell potential to the thermodynamic equilibrium constant. This relationship is exact and does not assume ideal solutions; activities must be used for rigorous work. In concentration cells (identical electrodes, different ion activities), Ecell = (0.05916/n) log₁₀(a₂/a₁), allowing direct measurement of activity ratios. The Nernst equation also underpins pH measurement with the glass electrode: E = E° − 0.05916 pH (at 25 °C). In potentiometric titrations, the equivalence point corresponds to the steepest potential change; the Gran plot linearises the titration curve for precise endpoint determination. A typical problem: “Calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction Fe³⁺ + Cu ⇌ Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺ given E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.771 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.340 V.” The cell potential E°cell = 0.771 − 0.340 = 0.431 V, n = 1, so log₁₀ K = 0.431/0.05916 = 7.28 → K = 1.9×10⁷. Another common variation: temperature dependence of E° via ΔG° = −nFE° = ΔH° − TΔS°, leading to dE°/dT = ΔS°/nF. Students must remember that the Nernst equation uses natural log in its fundamental form (RT/nF) ln Q; the base‑10 version is a convenience at 25 °C only.

  • Assuming K is temperature‑independent when ΔH° is large; always check if van't Hoff correction is needed.
  • Using concentrations instead of activities in Ksp or Ka calculations for solutions with I > 0.01 M.
  • Applying the simple pH = ½(pKa₁ + pKa₂) formula for amphiprotic salts at very low concentrations where water autoprotolysis matters.
  • Neglecting the common ion effect when a background electrolyte shares an ion with the sparingly soluble salt.
  • Forgetting that the Nernst equation’s 0.05916 factor is valid only at 25 °C; at other temperatures use (RT/nF) ln 10.
  • Treating stepwise Ka values of polyprotic acids as independent when ΔpKa < 2, leading to erroneous buffer‑capacity estimates.
  • Confusing the reaction quotient Q with the equilibrium constant K in precipitation predictions; precipitation occurs only when Q > Ksp.

These advanced topics complete the equilibrium toolkit needed for high‑level problem solving.

hand/math-logic.html:
Proof Theory and Ordinal Analysis

Proof theory investigates the structure of formal proofs and assigns ordinal measures to the strength of theories. Gentzen’s 1936 consistency proof for Peano arithmetic (PA) introduced transfinite induction up to the ordinal ε₀, establishing that PA proves the well‑foundedness of every ordinal < ε₀ but not of ε₀ itself. The proof‑theoretic ordinal of a theory T is the supremum of ordinals α for which T proves the well‑ordering of a primitive recursive notation system for α. For PA this ordinal is exactly ε₀; for stronger systems such as Π¹₁‑CA₀ it reaches the Feferman–Schütte ordinal Γ₀. Ordinal analysis yields conservation results: if a theory T has proof‑theoretic ordinal α, then any Π⁰₂ sentence provable in T is already provable in a weak base theory plus transfinite induction up to α. This technique underlies the classification of subsystems in reverse mathematics and provides a calibrated hierarchy of mathematical theorems by the ordinal strength required for their proofs.

Modern ordinal analysis extends to impredicative systems using collapsing functions and ordinal diagrams. The Bachmann–Howard ordinal measures the strength of Kripke–Platek set theory with infinity, while the Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal corresponds to Π¹₁‑comprehension. These ordinals are not merely abstract benchmarks; they appear in the termination proofs of rewrite systems, in the analysis of Kruskal’s tree theorem, and in the verification of programs via well‑founded recursion. The method of “proof‑theoretic reduction” shows that a stronger theory can be interpreted in a weaker one plus a well‑ordering principle, making explicit the exact non‑constructive content of classical theorems.

Reverse Mathematics and Subsystems of Second‑Order Arithmetic

Reverse mathematics, initiated by Friedman and developed by Simpson, calibrates the logical strength of ordinary mathematical theorems by identifying the weakest subsystem of second‑order arithmetic that proves them. The base system RCA₀ (Recursive Comprehension Axiom) includes Δ⁰₁ comprehension and Σ⁰₁ induction; it captures computable mathematics. Over RCA₀, many classical theorems are equivalent to one of five principal subsystems (including RCA₀): WKL₀ (Weak König’s Lemma), ACA₀ (Arithmetical Comprehension), ATR₀ (Arithmetical Transfinite Recursion), and Π¹₁‑CA₀ (Π¹₁ Comprehension). For example, the Heine–Borel covering theorem for [0,1] is equivalent to WKL₀, the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem for sequences in [0,1] is equivalent to ACA₀, and the statement “every countable abelian group is a direct sum of a divisible group and a reduced group” is equivalent to ATR₀.

The equivalence proofs proceed in two directions: a forward direction showing the theorem proves the comprehension or induction scheme of the subsystem, and a reversal constructing a model of the base theory where the theorem fails if the subsystem’s principle is omitted. This methodology reveals that many theorems of analysis, algebra, and combinatorics align with these five levels, though some natural statements (like RT²₂) sit strictly between them. The program also extends to higher‑order arithmetic and to the study of combinatorial principles such as Ramsey’s theorem for pairs (RT²₂), which lies strictly between WKL₀ and ACA₀.

Worked Example
Which subsystem of second‑order arithmetic is equivalent over RCA₀ to the statement “Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence” (the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem)?
Over RCA₀ the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem for sequences in [0,1] is equivalent to ACA₀. The forward direction uses the theorem to compute the limit superior of a Σ⁰₁‑definable set, yielding arithmetical comprehension. The reversal builds a model of RCA₀ + ¬ACA₀ in which a bounded sequence without a convergent subsequence exists, typically by diagonalising against all potential limits. Hence the correct answer is ACA₀.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the reverse‑mathematical strength of a theorem, first recall the “big five” subsystems and their hallmark equivalences. If the theorem involves compactness of Cantor space or the existence of paths in infinite binary trees, think WKL₀. If it requires forming the range of a function or the limit of a Cauchy sequence, think ACA₀. For transfinite constructions up to countable well‑orderings, think ATR₀. For statements quantifying over all analytic sets, think Π¹₁‑CA₀. Mapping the theorem to the nearest known equivalence saves time and avoids over‑reaching.

Higher Recursion Theory and the Analytical Hierarchy

Higher recursion theory lifts classical recursion‑theoretic notions from ω to the Baire space ω^ω and to the analytical hierarchy of formulas with quantifiers over reals. A set A ⊆ ω^ω is Σ¹₁ (analytic) if it is the projection of a Borel set; it is Π¹₁ (co‑analytic) if its complement is Σ¹₁. The Suslin theorem states that a set is Borel iff it is both Σ¹₁ and Π¹₁. The analytical hierarchy continues with Σ¹n+1 = ∃X Σ¹_n and Π¹n+1 = ∀X Π¹_n, where X ranges over reals. Kleene’s normal form theorem provides universal Σ¹₁ and Π¹₁ sets, and the Spector–Gandy theorem characterises Σ¹₁ as the class of sets 1‑reducible to a Σ¹₁‑complete set.

The hyperarithmetical hierarchy, built by iterating the Turing jump along recursive well‑orderings, coincides with Δ¹₁ (the sets both Σ¹₁ and Π¹₁). The least non‑recursive ordinal ω₁^CK (Church–Kleene) is the supremum of recursive well‑orderings; the hyperarithmetical sets are exactly those recursive in ∅(α) for some α < ω₁^CK. Higher recursion theory also studies the degrees of unsolvability of Σ¹₁ sets, the structure of the Σ¹₁‑degrees, and the basis theorems: every non‑empty Σ¹₁ set contains a hyperarithmetical member (Kleene basis), and every non‑empty Π¹₁ set contains a member of minimal degree (a basis theorem). These results underpin the analysis of definability in second‑order arithmetic and the calibration of comprehension schemes.

Forcing, Independence, and the Continuum Hypothesis

Cohen’s forcing method, introduced in 1963, constructs models of ZFC in which the continuum hypothesis (CH) fails. A forcing notion ℙ is a partially ordered set; a filter G ⊆ ℙ generic over a ground model M meets every dense subset of ℙ belonging to M. The generic extension M[G] satisfies ZFC and adds a new subset of ω (a Cohen real) without collapsing cardinals. By iterating forcing with finite support, Cohen produced a model where 2ℵ₀ = ℵ₂, establishing the independence of CH from ZFC. Later, Solovay and Tennenbaum developed iterated forcing with countable support to obtain Martin’s axiom (MA) plus ¬CH, while Easton’s theorem characterised the possible values of the continuum function on regular cardinals.

Forcing also yields independence results for combinatorial statements such as the Suslin hypothesis, the Whitehead problem for abelian groups, and the existence of Kurepa trees. The method of Boolean‑valued models provides an algebraic reformulation: a complete Boolean algebra B gives a Boolean‑valued universe V^B where each sentence receives a truth value in B; generic filters correspond to ultrafilters on B. Proper forcing, introduced by Shelah, preserves ω₁ and enables the construction of models where the proper forcing axiom (PFA) holds, implying 2ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and many structural consequences for the real line. The consistency strength of large cardinal axioms is calibrated by their ability to produce generic embeddings, linking forcing to inner model theory.

Descriptive Set Theory and Determinacy

Descriptive set theory studies the structure of definable subsets of Polish spaces, especially the real line. The Borel hierarchy Σ⁰_α, Π⁰_α, Δ⁰_α (α < ω₁) classifies sets by countable unions and intersections of open sets. The projective hierarchy Σ¹_n, Π¹_n, Δ¹_n (n ≥ 1) extends this by projections and complements of Borel sets. Classical regularity properties — Lebesgue measurability, the Baire property, the perfect set property — hold for all Borel sets and, under large cardinal assumptions, for all projective sets. The axiom of determinacy (AD) asserts that every two‑player infinite game of perfect information on ω is determined; AD contradicts the full axiom of choice but holds in L(ℝ) assuming infinitely many Woodin cardinals.

Martin’s theorem (1975) proves that all Borel games are determined in ZFC. The projective determinacy (PD) hierarchy, established by Martin and Steel (1989) using large cardinals, shows that Σ¹n+1 determinacy follows from the existence of n Woodin cardinals. Under PD, every projective set is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property, and either is countable or contains a perfect subset. The Wadge hierarchy refines the projective hierarchy by continuous reducibility, yielding a well‑ordering of the Wadge degrees of Borel sets (of length θ₀ under AD). These results connect the logical complexity of definitions with the topological regularity of the defined sets, and they provide the semantic backbone for the analysis of second‑order arithmetic subsystems.

  • Confusing the proof‑theoretic ordinal of PA (ε₀) with the Church–Kleene ordinal ω₁^CK.
  • Assuming every theorem of analysis is equivalent to one of the big five subsystems; some natural statements (e.g., RT²₂) sit strictly between them.
  • Treating Σ¹₁ and Π¹₁ as complements of each other in the analytical hierarchy without recalling that Δ¹₁ = Σ¹₁ ∩ Π¹₁ is the hyperarithmetical class.
  • Believing forcing adds only Cohen reals; proper forcing, random forcing, and Sacks forcing add reals with distinct preservation properties.
  • Thinking AD is compatible with the full axiom of choice; AD implies the failure of AC for sets of reals.
  • Equating the continuum hypothesis with the statement “2ℵ₀ = ℵ₁” without noting that Easton’s theorem allows many other values for the continuum on regular cardinals.
  • Overlooking that the Wadge hierarchy provides a well‑ordering of Borel Wadge degrees, but the projective Wadge hierarchy is not well‑ordered in ZFC alone.

The advanced topics above give a calibrated map of logical strength, definability, and independence that examiners expect candidates to navigate precisely.

hand/nuclear-chemistry.html:
Nuclear Decay Modes Beyond Alpha Beta Gamma

While alpha, beta‑minus, beta‑plus and gamma emission dominate introductory textbooks, several additional decay pathways are essential for a complete description of nuclear stability. Electron capture (EC) competes with positron emission when the Q‑value is insufficient to create a positron‑electron pair; the nucleus captures an inner‑shell electron, converting a proton to a neutron and emitting a neutrino. The resulting atomic vacancy produces characteristic X‑rays or Auger electrons, which are exploited in electron‑capture spectroscopy. Internal conversion (IC) provides an alternative to gamma emission: the excitation energy is transferred directly to an orbital electron, ejecting it with kinetic energy equal to the transition energy minus the binding energy. The IC coefficient, α = λ_IC / λ_γ, varies strongly with atomic number and multipolarity, and must be accounted for when measuring absolute gamma intensities. Double beta decay (2νββ) occurs in even‑even nuclei where single beta decay is energetically forbidden; two neutrons simultaneously transform into two protons, emitting two electrons and two antineutrinos. The neutrinoless variant (0νββ), if observed, would demonstrate lepton‑number violation and a Majorana nature of the neutrino. Proton emission and neutron emission are observed far from stability, typically in very proton‑rich or neutron‑rich isotopes produced in accelerator facilities. Cluster decay, such as the emission of 14C from 223Ra, represents a rare tunnelling process intermediate between alpha decay and spontaneous fission. Each of these modes follows selection rules governed by angular‑momentum and parity conservation, and their partial half‑lives can be calculated using the Weisskopf estimates or more sophisticated shell‑model calculations. Mastery of these channels is required for interpreting decay‑scheme diagrams, designing radiochemical separations, and evaluating the radiotoxicity of exotic isotopes.

Neutron Capture Cross Sections and Activation Analysis

Neutron capture, denoted (n,γ), is the principal mechanism for producing radioisotopes in reactors and for analytical techniques such as neutron activation analysis (NAA). The microscopic capture cross section σ(E) varies with neutron energy; for many nuclei it follows a 1/v law in the thermal region (E ≈ 0.025 eV) and exhibits resonances at higher energies described by the Breit‑Wigner formula. The macroscopic cross section Σ = Nσ, where N is the number density of target atoms, determines the reaction rate R = ΦΣ, with Φ the neutron flux. In a typical thermal reactor, Φ ≈ 1014 n cm⁻² s⁻¹, giving production rates of order 106 atoms s⁻¹ per µg of target for isotopes with σ ≈ 100 barn. The activity A(t) of the product nuclide during irradiation follows the Bateman equation: A(t) = N₀σΦ(1 − e−λt), where λ is the decay constant of the product. After irradiation, the activity decays as A(t) = A₀e−λt. NAA exploits the characteristic gamma‑ray energies and half‑lives of the induced radionuclides to quantify trace elements at sub‑ppb levels. The method is non‑destructive, multi‑elemental, and matrix‑independent when using comparator standards or the k₀‑standardization method. Important corrections include neutron self‑shielding (reduction of flux inside a thick sample), gamma‑ray self‑absorption, and coincidence summing in close‑geometry detectors. The k₀‑method uses pre‑determined nuclear constants (k₀, Q₀, σ₀) to calculate concentrations without individual standards, relying on a well‑characterised neutron spectrum (thermal, epithermal, fast). Applications range from archaeological provenance studies (e.g., obsidian sourcing) to certification of high‑purity materials for semiconductor manufacturing. Understanding the energy dependence of σ(E) and the neutron spectrum in the irradiation position is crucial for accurate quantification.

Worked Example: Activity After Neutron Irradiation
A 10 mg sample of natural gold (100 % 197Au) is irradiated in a thermal neutron flux of 5 × 1013 n cm⁻² s⁻¹ for 2 hours. The thermal capture cross section for 197Au(n,γ)198Au is 98.7 barn. 198Au decays with a half‑life of 2.695 days. Calculate the activity of 198Au at the end of irradiation.
Number of 197Au atoms: N = (10 mg / 197 g mol⁻¹) × 6.022 × 1023 mol⁻¹ = 3.06 × 1019 atoms. Capture rate R = NσΦ = 3.06 × 1019 × 98.7 × 10⁻²⁴ cm² × 5 × 1013 cm⁻² s⁻¹ = 1.51 × 1010 s⁻¹. Decay constant λ = ln 2 / (2.695 days × 86400 s day⁻¹) = 2.98 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. Irradiation time t = 7200 s. Saturation factor (1 − e−λt) ≈ λt = 2.98 × 10⁻⁶ × 7200 = 0.0215. Activity A = R × (1 − e−λt) = 1.51 × 1010 × 0.0215 = 3.25 × 108 Bq ≈ 8.8 mCi.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem gives flux, cross section, mass, and half‑life, first compute the number of target atoms, then the production rate R = NσΦ. Use the exact saturation factor (1 − e−λt) rather than the λt approximation unless λt < 0.01. Keep units consistent: cross section in cm² (1 barn = 10⁻²⁴ cm²), flux in n cm⁻² s⁻¹, time in seconds. The final activity is in becquerels; convert to curies only if the question asks (1 Ci = 3.7 × 1010 Bq).

Reactor Neutron Economy: Multiplication Factor, Burnup, and Fuel Cycle

The sustainability of a chain reaction is quantified by the effective multiplication factor k_eff, defined as the ratio of neutrons in one generation to the preceding generation. For a steady‑state reactor k_eff = 1; k_eff > 1 indicates a supercritical excursion, while k_eff < 1 leads to shutdown. The four‑factor formula for an infinite homogeneous thermal reactor expresses k_∞ = η f p ε, where η = νσ_f/σ_a is the reproduction factor (ν ≈ 2.43 for 235U), f = Σ_a^F / Σ_a^total is the thermal utilisation factor, p is the resonance escape probability, and ε is the fast‑fission factor. In a finite reactor, leakage reduces k_eff = k_∞ P_NL P_TL, where P_NL and P_TL are non‑leakage probabilities for fast and thermal neutrons respectively. Burnup, measured in GWd t⁻¹ HM (gigawatt‑days per tonne of heavy metal), tracks the energy extracted per unit fuel mass. As burnup increases, fissile 235U depletes while fertile 238U captures neutrons to breed 239Pu, partially compensating reactivity loss. The buildup of fission products such as 135Xe (σ_a ≈ 2.6 × 106 barn) and 149Sm introduces strong parasitic absorption, causing the xenon transient after power changes. Fuel management strategies — batch refuelling, shuffling, and the use of burnable poisons (e.g., Gd₂O₃, B₄C) — flatten the reactivity swing over a cycle. The once‑through fuel cycle discharges spent fuel after ~45–60 GWd t⁻¹ HM, while closed cycles reprocess to recover Pu and U for mixed‑oxide (MOX) fuel, extending resource utilisation. Advanced concepts such as thorium‑based fuels (232Th → 233U) and fast‑spectrum reactors (where η for 239Pu exceeds 2.5) aim to improve breeding ratios and reduce long‑lived actinide inventories. Mastery of the neutron balance equations, the impact of temperature feedback (Doppler broadening, moderator density), and the time‑dependent behaviour of poisons is essential for reactor physics examinations.

Radiation Detection Principles: Scintillation, Semiconductor, and Gas Detectors

Accurate measurement of radiation type, energy, and intensity underpins all nuclear applications. Scintillation detectors convert ionising radiation into visible photons via a scintillator crystal (NaI(Tl), CsI(Tl), LaBr₃(Ce), or plastic). The light yield is proportional to deposited energy; a photomultiplier tube (PMT) or silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) amplifies the signal. Energy resolution (FWHM/E) for NaI(Tl) at 662 keV is ~7 %, while LaBr₃(Ce) achieves ~3 %. Pulse‑shape discrimination (PSD) in organic scintillators separates neutrons from gamma rays by exploiting different decay time constants. Semiconductor detectors (HPGe, Si(Li), CdZnTe) collect electron‑hole pairs directly; the required energy per pair is ~2.96 eV in Si and ~2.96 eV in Ge, yielding superior resolution (HPGe ~0.2 % at 1.33 MeV). HPGe detectors require liquid‑nitrogen cooling to suppress thermal noise; room‑temperature CdZnTe offers moderate resolution (~2 % at 662 keV) with portability. Gas‑filled detectors operate on ionisation (ion chambers), proportional multiplication (proportional counters), or avalanche (Geiger‑Müller tubes). The proportional region provides energy spectroscopy for alpha and low‑energy beta particles; the gas gain depends on the Townsend coefficient and applied voltage. Multi‑wire proportional chambers (MWPC) and drift chambers extend this principle to position‑sensitive tracking. Neutron detection commonly employs 3He proportional counters (high thermal cross section 5330 barn) or 6Li‑loaded scintillators (glass or plastic). Fast neutrons are moderated before detection or measured via recoil protons in organic scintillators. Calibration uses standard sources (137Cs, 60Co, 241Am) and efficiency curves derived from Monte Carlo simulations (MCNP, GEANT4). Understanding detector response functions, dead‑time corrections (paralyzable vs non‑paralyzable), and minimum detectable activity (MDA) calculations is critical for quantitative radiometry.

Long‑Lived Nuclear Waste: Transmutation Strategies and Geological Disposal

Spent nuclear fuel contains fission products (half‑lives up to 105 years for 99Tc, 129I, 135Cs) and minor actinides (Np, Am, Cm) with half‑lives of 103–106 years, dominating long‑term radiotoxicity. Partitioning and transmutation (P&T) aims to separate these nuclides and convert them into shorter‑lived or stable isotopes via neutron capture or fission. In fast‑spectrum reactors or accelerator‑driven systems (ADS), the high neutron flux and hard spectrum increase the fission‑to‑capture ratio for minor actinides, enabling their destruction. For example, 241Am (t₁/₂ = 432 years) captures a neutron to become 242Am, which quickly β⁻ decays to 242Cm (t₁/₂ = 163 days) and then fissions or decays further. The transmutation rate λ_t = σΦ must exceed the natural decay rate λ_d for effective reduction; typical ADS designs target Φ ≈ 1015 n cm⁻² s⁻¹. However, the process generates additional heat and radiation, requiring robust fuel matrices (e.g., inert‑matrix fuels, ceramic‑ceramic composites). Geological disposal remains the internationally accepted endpoint. The multiple‑barrier concept combines engineered barriers (waste form, canister, buffer material such as bentonite clay) with the natural geological barrier (low‑permeability host rock: granite, claystone, salt, or tuff). Performance assessment models couple thermal‑hydrological‑mechanical‑chemical (THMC) processes over 105–106 years, evaluating radionuclide release, transport, and dose to a hypothetical future human. Key safety functions include containment (preventing water contact), retardation (sorption and diffusion in buffer), and isolation (geological stability). Regulatory criteria often specify a dose limit of 0.1 mSv yr⁻¹ for the maximally exposed individual. International projects such as Onkalo (Finland), Yucca Mountain (USA, now inactive), and the Swedish KBS‑3 concept illustrate different host‑rock choices and repository designs. Understanding the interplay between waste form chemistry (e.g., borosilicate glass dissolution rates), near‑field geochemistry (redox conditions, complexation), and far‑field transport is essential for evaluating long‑term safety cases.

  • Confusing electron capture with positron emission when the Q‑value is below 1.022 MeV; EC dominates for low‑energy transitions.
  • Neglecting the internal conversion coefficient when calculating absolute gamma‑ray intensities, leading to systematic underestimation of transition probabilities.
  • Using the 1/v approximation for neutron capture cross sections in the epithermal region where resonances dominate.
  • Forgetting to apply the saturation factor (1 − e−λt) in activation calculations, especially for long‑lived products where λt ≪ 1.
  • Assuming k_eff = k_∞ for a finite reactor and ignoring leakage probabilities, which can shift criticality by several percent.
  • Overlooking xenon‑135 poisoning dynamics after a power reduction, causing misprediction of reactivity worth and startup margins.
  • Treating detector dead time as purely non‑paralyzable when the counting rate approaches the inverse of the resolving time, resulting in underestimated true count rates.

These advanced topics provide the depth required for competitive examinations and professional practice in nuclear chemistry.

hand/derived-algebraic-geometry.html:
Derived Artin Stacks and the Geometry of Derived Mapping Stacks

Derived Artin stacks extend the classical notion of Artin stacks to the derived setting by requiring a smooth atlas from a derived scheme and a diagonal representable by derived schemes. In the ∞‑categorical framework developed by Lurie and Toën‑Vezzosi, a derived Artin stack is a functor from the ∞‑category of simplicial commutative rings to spaces that satisfies étale descent and admits a smooth surjection from a derived scheme. The cotangent complex of a derived Artin stack is defined as the derived pullback of the cotangent complex of its atlas, and it controls the deformation theory of the stack analogously to the case of derived schemes. A central example is the derived mapping stack Map(X, Y) for derived schemes X and Y; when X is proper and Y is a derived Artin stack locally of finite presentation, Map(X, Y) is itself a derived Artin stack whose tangent complex at a map f is given by the derived global sections of the pullback of the tangent complex of Y along f. This construction underlies the derived moduli of perfect complexes, the derived stack of G‑bundles, and the derived critical loci appearing in shifted symplectic geometry. The derived Artin property also guarantees the existence of a good truncation functor to classical Artin stacks, allowing comparison of derived and underived intersection theories via the virtual fundamental class.

One of the key technical tools is the representability theorem for derived mapping stacks, which uses the fact that the functor of points of a derived Artin stack is a hypersheaf for the étale topology on simplicial rings. The proof proceeds by showing that the diagonal is relatively representable and that the stack admits a smooth cover by a derived scheme, often constructed via a derived version of the Hilbert scheme or Quot scheme. The derived Artin stack structure on the moduli of perfect complexes ℝM_P, for instance, is established using the fact that the derived Quot scheme parametrizing quotients of a fixed perfect complex is a derived scheme smooth over the base. The cotangent complex of ℝM_P at a point E is ℝHom(E, E)[1], and the obstruction theory is perfect because the trace map yields a symmetric perfect obstruction theory. This perfectness is essential for constructing the virtual fundamental class via the Behrend‑Fantechi machinery in the derived setting.

Derived Artin stacks also provide the natural home for derived Lagrangian correspondences. A derived Lagrangian in a derived symplectic stack of degree k is a morphism from a derived Artin stack L to X equipped with an isotropic structure and a non‑degeneracy condition on the relative cotangent complex. The derived intersection of two Lagrangians carries a (−1)‑shifted symplectic structure, a result that generalizes classical symplectic reduction. In the context of the derived geometric Langlands program, the derived stack of G‑local systems on a curve is expected to be a derived Artin stack with a 1‑shifted symplectic structure, and Hecke modifications are conjectured to correspond to derived Lagrangian correspondences. These structures are believed to encode the categorified geometric Satake equivalence and the construction of Hecke eigensheaves via derived methods.

Derived Intersection Theory and the Virtual Fundamental Class via Perfect Obstruction Theories

Derived intersection theory replaces the classical Tor‑formula for the intersection product with a derived tensor product of structure sheaves. Given a Cartesian square of derived schemes where one map is a regular immersion, the derived fiber product computes the correct intersection multiplicity without the need for moving lemmas. The virtual fundamental class of a derived scheme X equipped with a perfect obstruction theory E → L_X is defined as the refined Gysin pullback of the fundamental class of the intrinsic normal cone C_X along the zero section of the vector bundle stack h¹/h⁰(E∨). In the derived setting, the intrinsic normal cone is naturally represented by the derived scheme Spec(Sym(L_X[1])) and the obstruction theory is a morphism of perfect complexes that is an isomorphism on h⁰ and a surjection on h⁻¹. The virtual dimension is the rank of E, and the virtual class lives in the Chow group of the classical truncation t₀X with rational coefficients.

The Behrend‑Fantechi construction of the virtual fundamental class is recovered when the derived scheme is the classical truncation of a derived scheme with a symmetric perfect obstruction theory. In particular, for the derived moduli stack ℝM of stable maps or perfect complexes, the tangent complex T_ℝM = ℝπ_*ℝℋom(E, E)[1] provides a symmetric perfect obstruction theory, and the associated virtual class coincides with those constructed by Li‑Tian in symplectic geometry and by Behrend‑Fantechi in algebraic geometry. The derived language simplifies the proof of functoriality: a morphism of derived schemes with compatible obstruction theories induces a pullback on virtual classes satisfying the expected projection formula. Moreover, the derived intersection product of two virtual cycles is computed by the derived tensor product of the corresponding perfect obstruction theories, yielding a virtual class on the derived fiber product that matches the classical excess intersection formula after truncation.

Applications to enumerative geometry include the definition of Donaldson‑Thomas invariants for Calabi‑Yau threefolds via integration over the derived moduli of sheaves. The derived moduli stack carries a (−1)‑shifted symplectic structure, and the virtual fundamental class can be identified with the fundamental class of the derived critical locus of a Chern‑Simons‑type functional. The Kontsevich‑Soibelman wall‑crossing formula admits an interpretation as an identity in the motivic Hall algebra of the derived category of coherent sheaves, where the product is given by derived extension of objects. The categorified DT theory of Joyce‑Song produces integer‑valued invariants by integrating the Behrend function against the virtual class, and the derived framework makes the wall‑crossing transformations manifest as mutations in the derived category. These results suggest that derived intersection theory provides an essential language for the modern theory of virtual fundamental classes.

Derived Intersection Product Computation
Let X be a smooth projective variety and i: Z → X, j: W → X be regular immersions of codimensions c and d. Describe the derived intersection Z ×^h_X W and explain how its virtual fundamental class relates to the classical intersection product [Z] · [W] in the Chow group of X.
The derived fiber product Z ×^h_X W is the derived scheme whose structure sheaf is the derived tensor product O_Z ⊗^LO_X O_W. Because i and j are regular immersions, the Tor‑amplitude of this derived tensor product is concentrated in degrees [−min(c,d), 0]. The classical truncation t₀(Z ×^h_X W) is the scheme‑theoretic intersection Z ∩ W, and the higher homotopy groups encode the excess intersection bundle. The virtual fundamental class of the derived intersection is defined using the perfect obstruction theory given by the relative cotangent complex LZ ×^h_X W / X ≅ i*LZ/X ⊕ j*LW/X. Since LZ/X ≅ NZ/X[−1] and similarly for W, the obstruction theory is symmetric of virtual dimension dim X − c − d. The virtual class [Z ×^h_X W]^vir ∈ Adim X−c−d(Z ∩ W) coincides with the refined Gysin pullback i^![W] = j^![Z] in the Chow group, which is exactly the classical intersection product [Z] · [W] when the intersection is proper. If the intersection is not proper, the derived intersection still carries a virtual class of the expected dimension, and its pushforward to X equals the Fulton‑MacPherson intersection product defined via the normal cone. Thus the derived intersection product simultaneously generalizes the proper intersection product and the excess intersection formula.
Exam Strategy for Derived Intersection Theory
When a question asks for the virtual fundamental class of a derived intersection, first identify the perfect obstruction theory (usually the relative cotangent complex). Compute its virtual dimension as the rank of the obstruction theory. Then recall that the virtual class is the refined Gysin pullback of the fundamental class of the intrinsic normal cone. In practice, for regular immersions the answer reduces to the classical intersection product or the excess intersection formula; state both and note that the derived construction unifies them.

The Derived Loop Space, Hochschild Homology, and the Cyclic Bar Construction

The derived loop space LX of a derived scheme X is the derived mapping stack Map(S¹, X), where S¹ is the simplicial circle. Its functor of points sends a simplicial ring A to the space of maps from the constant simplicial scheme Spec A × S¹ to X. The derived loop space carries a natural S¹‑action by rotation of the circle, and its cotangent complex is given by the derived pullback of the cotangent complex of X along the evaluation map. The Hochschild homology HH_*(X) of X is defined as the derived global sections of the structure sheaf of LX, i.e., HH_*(X) = Γ(LX, OLX). When X is a smooth classical scheme, the Hochschild‑Kostant‑Rosenberg isomorphism identifies HH_*(X) with the algebraic de Rham complex Ω^*_X, and the S¹‑action corresponds to the de Rham differential. In the derived setting, the HKR isomorphism generalizes to a filtration on HH_*(X) whose associated graded pieces are the derived exterior powers of the cotangent complex L_X.

The cyclic bar construction provides a concrete simplicial model for the derived loop space. For a simplicial commutative ring A, the cyclic bar construction B^cyc(A) is a cyclic object in simplicial rings whose geometric realization computes the derived loop space of Spec A. The Hochschild homology of A is then the homotopy groups of the realization of B^cyc(A). This construction is functorial and compatible with base change, making it a powerful tool for explicit calculations. For example, if A = k[x]/(x²) is the dual numbers, the derived loop space of Spec A is the derived scheme whose ring of functions is the derived tensor product A ⊗^LA⊗A A, which can be computed via the cyclic bar complex and yields a non‑trivial S¹‑action reflecting the non‑smoothness of Spec A. The derived loop space also appears in the derived version of the Atiyah class: the Atiyah class of a perfect complex E on X is a map E → E ⊗ L_X[1] in the derived category, and its trace gives a class in HH¹(X) that classifies the derived deformation of E.

In the context of shifted symplectic geometry, the derived loop space of a derived symplectic stack of degree k carries a (k−1)‑shifted symplectic structure. When k = 1, LX has a 0‑shifted symplectic structure, i.e., an ordinary symplectic structure, which is the derived analogue of the fact that the loop space of a symplectic manifold is symplectic. This observation informs the construction of the derived Fukaya category and the relationship between derived loop spaces and topological field theories. The cyclic bar construction also computes the factorization homology of X on the circle, linking derived algebraic geometry to the cobordism hypothesis. These connections illustrate that the derived loop space is a central object bridging derived deformation theory, Hochschild homology, and extended topological quantum field theory.

Derived Deformation Theory of Morphisms and the Relative Cotangent Complex

The deformation theory of a morphism f: X → Y of derived schemes is controlled by the relative cotangent complex LX/Y, which fits into a fiber sequence f*L_Y → L_X → LX/Y. The tangent complex of the derived mapping stack Map(Y, X) at f is the derived global sections of the pullback of the tangent complex of X along f, and the obstruction theory for deforming f is given by the Ext groups of LX/Y. When f is a closed immersion defined by a derived ideal I, the relative cotangent complex is I/I²[1], and its derived symmetric algebra computes the derived normal cone. The derived deformation functor Def_f sends a derived Artin ring A to the space of lifts of f to X × Spec A. Schlessinger's conditions in the derived setting require that Def_f preserves homotopy pullbacks along small extensions, and they are satisfied precisely when LX/Y is perfect and of Tor‑amplitude in [−1, 0]. In that case, the deformation functor is pro‑representable by a derived formal moduli problem, i.e., a formal derived scheme Spf R where R is a complete derived local ring.

The relative cotangent complex also governs the derived version of the Kodaira‑Spencer map. For a family π: X → S of derived schemes, the Kodaira‑Spencer class lives in Ext¹_S(LX/S, O_X) and classifies the derived deformation of the fibers. When the family is a derived Lagrangian fibration in a shifted symplectic stack, the relative cotangent complex is self‑dual up to a shift, and the Kodaira‑Spencer map becomes an isomorphism identifying the tangent complex of the base with the derived global sections of the relative cotangent complex. This duality is the derived analogue of the classical symplectic geometry of Lagrangian fibrations. In the derived geometric Langlands program, the relative cotangent complex of the map from the derived stack of G‑bundles to the derived stack of local systems is expected to encode the Hecke operators, and its derived symmetric algebra is conjectured to produce the categorical Whittaker sheaves.

Applications to virtual fundamental classes arise when one considers a morphism f: X → Y that is a derived local complete intersection. Then LX/Y is perfect of amplitude [−1, 0], and the intrinsic normal cone of X over Y is a derived vector bundle stack. The virtual fundamental class of X relative to Y is defined by the refined Gysin pullback along the zero section of this vector bundle stack. This relative virtual class satisfies a functoriality property: for a Cartesian square of derived schemes with compatible obstruction theories, the virtual class of the fiber product is the derived pullback of the virtual classes. This formalism underlies the definition of relative Donaldson‑Thomas invariants and the wall‑crossing formulas for relative stability conditions. The derived deformation theory of morphisms thus provides the technical foundation for the relative virtual cycle machinery essential in modern enumerative geometry.

  • Confusing the derived loop space with the classical loop space; the derived version retains higher homotopical information lost in the classical truncation.
  • Assuming the cotangent complex of a derived Artin stack is always perfect; it is perfect only when the stack is locally of finite presentation.
  • Neglecting the S¹‑action on the derived loop space when computing Hochschild homology; the cyclic structure is essential for the Connes differential and the HKR filtration.
  • Treating the virtual fundamental class of a derived intersection as an ordinary cycle without reference to the perfect obstruction theory; the virtual class lives in the Chow group of the classical truncation but depends on the derived structure.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the absolute and relative cotangent complexes in deformation problems; the relative complex controls deformations of a morphism while the absolute complex controls deformations of the source.
  • Misapplying the Behrend‑Fantechi construction to a derived scheme without a symmetric perfect obstruction theory; symmetry is required for the virtual class to be independent of choices.
  • Forgetting that the derived mapping stack Map(X, Y) is a derived Artin stack only when X is proper and Y is locally of finite presentation; otherwise it may fail to be an Artin stack.

hand/string-theory.html:
Worldsheet Conformal Anomaly and Critical Dimension

The Polyakov action has a classical Weyl symmetry broken quantum mechanically by the conformal anomaly. The anomaly arises from the non‑invariance of the functional measure under Weyl rescalings and is proportional to the central charge of the worldsheet CFT. Each free bosonic coordinate contributes +1 to the central charge; the reparametrization ghosts (b,c) contribute −26. Vanishing total central charge gives the critical dimension D = 26 for the bosonic string. In the superstring, fermionic coordinates contribute +1/2 each and super‑ghosts (β,γ) contribute +11. The combined matter‑ghost central charge cancels only for D = 10. Vanishing Weyl anomaly is equivalent to BRST nilpotency and, after GSO projection, to the absence of a tachyonic ground state. Light‑cone quantization also requires D = 26 (bosonic) or D = 10 (superstring) for Lorentz algebra closure. This interplay is a cornerstone of string consistency.

Central Charge Contributions

  • Bosonic coordinate X^μ : c = 1 per dimension
  • Fermionic coordinate ψ^μ (NSR) : c = 1/2 per dimension
  • Reparametrization ghosts (b,c) : c = −26
  • Super‑ghosts (β,γ) : c = +11

The total central charge c_total = D·c_matter + c_ghosts must be zero. For the bosonic string c_total = D·1 − 26 = 0 ⇒ D = 26. For the superstring c_total = D·(1 + 1/2) − 26 + 11 = 0 ⇒ D = 10.

BRST Quantization and Physical State Conditions

BRST quantization covariantly imposes the Virasoro constraints on the Hilbert space. The BRST charge Q is constructed from the matter Virasoro generators L_m and the ghost oscillators b_m, c_m as Q = Σ_m c−m L_m − ½ Σm,n (m−n) :c−m c−n bm+n:. Nilpotency Q² = 0 holds exactly when the total central charge vanishes, i.e., in the critical dimension. Physical states are the cohomology of Q at ghost number one: Q|ψ⟩ = 0 with |ψ⟩ not BRST‑exact. This reproduces the Virasoro constraints L_n|ψ⟩ = 0 (n>0) and (L0−a)|ψ⟩ = 0, with a=1 (bosonic) or a=0 (superstring after GSO). Spurious states are BRST‑exact and decouple from amplitudes. The superstring BRST charge also includes super‑Virasoro generators G_r and super‑ghosts β,γ. Cohomology at picture number −1 (or −½) gives the physical NS and R spectra. BRST is essential for proving perturbative unitarity and constructing off‑shell string field theory.

BRST Cohomology Problem
Show that the BRST charge Q for the bosonic string is nilpotent only when the spacetime dimension D = 26.
Compute Q² using the operator product expansions of the ghost fields and the Virasoro algebra. The term proportional to the central charge c appears as Q² ∼ (c−26) ∫ c ∂c. Setting Q² = 0 forces c = 26. Since each free boson contributes 1 to c, the number of bosonic coordinates must be 26. Hence D = 26.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the critical dimension, write the central‑charge cancellation equation explicitly. Examiners award marks for showing the ghost contribution (−26) and the matter contribution (D). Do not merely quote the result.

D‑Brane Boundary Conformal Field Theory and Open String Spectrum

D‑branes are described by boundary conditions mixing left‑ and right‑moving fields. For a Dp‑brane, Neumann directions (0,…,p) have ∂_σ X^a = 0 at the boundary; Dirichlet directions (p+1,…,9) have X^i = constant. These conditions are encoded in a boundary state |B⟩ implementing the gluing conditions on the oscillators: (α_n^a + ᾱ−n^a)|B⟩ = 0 and (α_n^i − ᾱ−n^i)|B⟩ = 0. The overlap of two boundary states gives the annulus amplitude, which modular transformation relates to the open‑string one‑loop partition function. The Cardy condition requires integer multiplicities of chiral algebra irreps in the open‑string spectrum between two D‑branes. For N coincident Dp‑branes, Chan‑Paton factors enlarge the endpoint symmetry from U(1) to U(N). Massless open‑string modes then comprise a U(N) gauge field A_a (a=0,…,p) and 9−p scalars Φ^i for transverse fluctuations. The low‑energy effective action is the Dirac‑Born‑Infeld action plus a Chern‑Simons term coupling to R‑R potentials. Boundary CFT also computes disk amplitudes with closed‑string vertex operators, determining D‑brane tension and R‑R charge.

Boundary State for a Dp‑Brane

|B_p⟩ = T_p δ9−p(x^i − y^i) exp[− Σn=1^∞ (1/n) α−n·S·ᾱ−n] |0⟩_α |0⟩_ᾱ ⊗ |B_ghost⟩, where Sμν = diag(−1,…,−1, +1,…,+1) with −1 for Neumann and +1 for Dirichlet directions.

Flux Compactifications and Moduli Stabilization

In type IIB, background three‑form fluxes H3 (NS‑NS) and F3 (R‑R) generate a superpotential for complex structure moduli and the axio‑dilaton τ = C0 + i/g_s. The Gukov‑Vafa‑Witten superpotential is W = ∫_M (F3 − τ H3) ∧ Ω, where Ω is the holomorphic three‑form of the Calabi‑Yau threefold M. It fixes complex structure moduli and τ at supersymmetric minima D_i W = 0. Kähler moduli (controlling four‑cycle sizes) remain unfixed since W is independent of them. Non‑perturbative effects (Euclidean D3‑brane instantons, gaugino condensation on D7‑branes) generate a Kähler‑dependent term W_np = A e−aρ. The combined superpotential W = W_flux + W_np with Kähler potential K = −2 ln(𝒱) − ln(−i∫ Ω∧Ω̄) − ln(−i(τ−τ̄)) yields a scalar potential stabilizing all moduli in an AdS vacuum (KKLT). Adding an anti‑D3‑brane in a warped throat uplifts to a de Sitter vacuum, breaking supersymmetry and adding a positive potential term. The flux landscape is often estimated to contain ~10500 distinct vacua, each corresponding to quantized flux choices ∫ H3, ∫ F3 ∈ ℤ. Moduli stabilization is essential for connecting string theory to low‑energy physics and cosmology.

Holographic Renormalization and the AdS/CFT Dictionary

AdS/CFT equates the partition function of type IIB string theory on AdS5×S5 with N=4 super‑Yang‑Mills on the 4D boundary. The radial coordinate r in AdS5 maps to the boundary energy scale: r→∞ is UV, r→0 is IR. Holographic renormalization renders the on‑shell bulk action finite by adding local counterterms on a cutoff surface at large r. The renormalized action S_ren generates connected CFT correlators: ⟨O(x1)…O(x_n)⟩ = δ^n S_ren / δφ0(x1)…δφ0(x_n), with φ0 the boundary value of the bulk field dual to O. The mass m of a bulk scalar field is related to the scaling dimension Δ of the dual operator by m2 L2 = Δ(Δ−4). For gauge fields, the boundary value sources the conserved current; bulk equations reproduce boundary Ward identities. The dictionary extends to fermions, p‑forms, and metric fluctuations, enabling computation of transport coefficients like η = s/(4π) at strong coupling. Holographic renormalization also shows how RG flow emerges from bulk geometry; domain‑wall solutions interpolating between AdS vacua correspond to RG flows between fixed points.

  • Confusing the critical dimension of the bosonic string (26) with that of the superstring (10) in BRST nilpotency arguments.
  • Neglecting the ghost contribution (−26) when writing the central‑charge cancellation condition.
  • Assuming the BRST charge is nilpotent in any dimension; it fails off the critical dimension.
  • Misidentifying the boundary state gluing matrix S for mixed Neumann/Dirichlet directions.
  • Overlooking that flux superpotentials do not depend on Kähler moduli, requiring non‑perturbative effects for full stabilization.
  • Treating the radial coordinate in AdS as a mere geometric parameter rather than the RG scale of the boundary theory.
  • Forgetting that holographic renormalization counterterms are local functionals of the induced metric and boundary fields.

hand/schubert-calculus.html:
Equivariant Schubert Calculus and Localization

Equivariant Schubert calculus refines ordinary intersection theory by incorporating the action of a torus T ≅ (ℂ×)n on the Grassmannian Gr(k,n). The equivariant cohomology ring HT*(Gr(k,n)) is a module over the polynomial ring ℤ[t1,…,tn] where the ti are the Chern roots of the standard representation. Schubert classes σλT form a basis over this polynomial ring, and their product expands as σλT·σμT = Σν cλμν(t) σνT with structure constants cλμν(t) that are polynomials in the equivariant parameters. The Atiyah‑Bott–Berline‑Vergne localization theorem reduces the computation of these polynomials to a sum over the T‑fixed points, which are indexed by k‑element subsets I ⊂ {1,…,n}. At a fixed point pI, the restriction σλT|pI is a product of linear forms (tj−ti) determined by the boxes of λ that lie inside the diagram of I. This yields explicit positive formulas: cλμν(t) are polynomials with non‑negative integer coefficients when expressed in the basis of factorial Schur polynomials. The equivariant Pieri rule adds a horizontal strip with weight given by the sum of the corresponding t‑differences, and the equivariant Littlewood‑Richardson rule can be stated in terms of Knutson‑Tao puzzles with edge labels. Applications include the proof of the positivity conjecture for ordinary Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients (by setting all ti=0) and the derivation of quantum equivariant Pieri rules where the quantum parameter q carries equivariant weight. The localization approach also provides an algorithmic way to evaluate Gromov‑Witten invariants on Grassmannians by reducing them to integrals over the fixed‑point locus in the moduli space of stable maps.

K‑Theoretic Schubert Calculus and Grothendieck Polynomials

In K‑theory the role of Schubert classes is played by the classes of structure sheaves 𝒪Xλ of Schubert varieties. The K‑theory ring K(Gr(k,n)) has a ℤ‑basis given by the (dual) Grothendieck polynomials Gλ(x) (or their stable limits, the symmetric Grothendieck polynomials). Multiplication follows the rule Gλ·Gμ = Σν (−1)|ν|−|λ|−|μ| cλμν Gν, where the integers cλμν are the K‑theoretic Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients. These coefficients count set‑valued tableaux of shape ν/λ with weight μ satisfying a lattice‑word condition, a generalization of the ordinary Littlewood‑Richardson tableaux. The K‑theoretic Pieri rule adds a horizontal strip but allows multiple boxes in a column, producing alternating signs that reflect the Euler characteristic of the intersection. The dual basis, given by the stable Grothendieck polynomials gλ, satisfies a simpler positive multiplication: gλ·gμ = Σν dλμν gν with dλμν ≥ 0. The geometric Satake correspondence identifies these structure constants with tensor product multiplicities for the Langlands dual group GLn(ℂ). In the equivariant K‑theory KT(Gr(k,n)) the classes are represented by factorial Grothendieck polynomials, and localization again reduces products to evaluations at fixed points. The quantum K‑theory ring QK(Gr(k,n)) incorporates Gromov‑Witten invariants in K‑theory; its product is governed by the quantum K‑theoretic Pieri rule of Buch‑Mihalcea, where the quantum parameter q appears with a shift in the factorial parameters. These structures have found applications in the study of Macdonald polynomials at t=0 and in the combinatorics of non‑symmetric Macdonald polynomials via the Demazure‑Lusztig operators.

Worked Example: Equivariant Pieri Computation
Compute the equivariant product σ(1)T·σ(2,1)T in HT*(Gr(2,4)) where the torus weights are t1,t2,t3,t4.

Step 1: Identify the fixed points. For Gr(2,4) the T‑fixed points correspond to 2‑element subsets I ⊂ {1,2,3,4}: 12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34.

Step 2: Write the restriction of each Schubert class at a fixed point pI. For a partition λ, σλT|pI = ∏(i,j)∈λ (tI(j) − tI(i)) where I(i) is the i‑th element of I in increasing order. For λ=(1) (a single box in row 1) the restriction is tI(2)−tI(1). For λ=(2,1) the diagram has boxes (1,1),(1,2),(2,1); the restriction is (tI(2)−tI(1))·(tI(3)−tI(1))·(tI(2)−tI(2)) = 0 because the third factor vanishes. Hence σ(2,1)T restricts to zero at every fixed point, so the product is zero in equivariant cohomology.

Step 3: Conclude σ(1)T·σ(2,1)T = 0. This matches the ordinary Pieri rule where adding a box to (2,1) would exceed the 2×2 rectangle, giving zero.

Exam Strategy
When a question asks for an equivariant product, first list the fixed points and compute restrictions using the box‑weight formula. If any factor vanishes identically, the whole product is zero — this shortcut avoids expanding large determinant formulas. Remember that setting all ti=0 recovers the ordinary Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients, so you can check your answer by comparing with the classical Pieri rule.

Schubert Calculus on Orthogonal and Symplectic Grassmannians

The isotropic Grassmannians OG(n,2n+1) (type B) and SG(n,2n) (type C) parametrize maximal isotropic subspaces for a non‑degenerate symmetric or skew‑symmetric form. Their Schubert varieties are indexed by strict partitions λ ⊂ (n,n−1,…,1) for type B and by partitions λ ⊂ (n,n−1,…,1) with no restriction on strictness for type C. The cohomology rings H*(OG) and H*(SG) are quotients of the polynomial ring ℤ[p1,…,pn] by the ideal generated by the relations coming from the Chern classes of the universal isotropic bundle. The Schubert classes σλ satisfy Pieri‑type rules: multiplying by the special class σ(1) adds a box to λ in all possible ways that keep the diagram a valid strict (or ordinary) partition, with the additional rule that adding a box to the first row may also remove a box from the last row when the diagram hits the boundary of the staircase. The Giambelli formula expresses an arbitrary σλ as a Pfaffian (type B) or a determinant (type C) of special classes. The Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients for these varieties are given by the combinatorics of shifted tableaux (type B) and of ordinary tableaux with a symmetry condition (type C). They are known to be non‑negative and satisfy the same positivity properties as in type A. Quantum cohomology of isotropic Grassmannians has been developed by Buch‑Kresch‑Tamvakis; the quantum Pieri rule includes a term with the quantum parameter q that corresponds to removing a rim hook of length 2n+1 (type B) or 2n (type C). These quantum rules have been used to compute Gromov‑Witten invariants for lines on orthogonal and symplectic Grassmannians, yielding enumerative results such as the number of lines meeting 2n−2 Schubert varieties of codimension one in OG(n,2n+1). The equivariant and K‑theoretic analogues follow the same pattern, with factorial Schur P‑ and Q‑functions playing the role of the equivariant Schubert classes.

Positivity, Geometric Implications, and Algorithmic Computation

A central theme in modern Schubert calculus is the positivity of structure constants. For ordinary cohomology of Grassmannians, the Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients cλμν are non‑negative integers; this was proved geometrically by Kleiman’s transversality theorem and combinatorially by the Knutson‑Tao honeycomb model. In equivariant cohomology, the polynomials cλμν(t) have non‑negative coefficients when expanded in the basis of factorial monomials, a result of Graham and of Knutson‑Tao‑Woodward. In K‑theory, the alternating signs in the product of Grothendieck polynomials are explained by the fact that the dual basis gλ has positive structure constants dλμν. These positivity phenomena have deep geometric consequences: they imply that Schubert varieties intersect transversely for generic translates, that the cone of effective curves is generated by Schubert curves, and that the quantum product preserves the positive cone. Algorithmically, the Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients can be computed in polynomial time using the hive model or the Berenstein‑Zelevinsky polytope; the equivariant coefficients can be obtained by evaluating the hive integrals with linear weights. Software packages such as SageMath (schubert module), Macaulay2 (Schubert2), and the Python library lrcalc implement these algorithms and are standard tools for researchers. For quantum coefficients, the rim‑hook algorithm of Bertram‑Ciocan‑Fontanine‑Fulton reduces the computation to a finite number of classical Littlewood‑Richardson products. In the isotropic cases, the shifted Littlewood‑Richardson rule of Worley and the Pfaffian formula of Ikeda‑Naruse provide effective computation. Mastery of these algorithms is essential for solving enumerative problems that appear in advanced examinations, where a single coefficient may be requested for a specific triple of partitions.

Applications to Mirror Symmetry and Gromov‑Witten Theory

Schubert calculus provides the mathematical foundation for many predictions of mirror symmetry. The small quantum cohomology ring QH*(Gr(k,n)) is isomorphic to the Jacobian ring of the Landau‑Ginzburg superpotential W = x1+…+xk + q/(x1⋯xk) under the identification of the quantum parameter q with the exponentiated Kähler parameter. The three‑point genus‑zero Gromov‑Witten invariants ⟨σλ,σμ,σν⟩d are exactly the quantum Littlewood‑Richardson coefficients cλμν(d) appearing in the quantum product. For the quintic threefold in ℙ4, the number of degree‑d rational curves is obtained by evaluating the appropriate Gromov‑Witten invariants on the Grassmannian Gr(2,5) via the localization formula of Graber‑Pandharipande. The famous prediction of 2875 lines (d=1) and 609250 conics (d=2) on the quintic were first verified by Schubert calculus on the space of stable maps to Gr(2,5). Higher‑genus invariants are governed by the topological recursion relations and the holomorphic anomaly equations, which can be expressed in terms of intersection numbers on the moduli space of stable maps to Grassmannians. The equivariant quantum cohomology, where the torus action on the Grassmannian lifts to the moduli space, yields the equivariant Gromov‑Witten invariants that satisfy the quantum differential equations of the mirror Landau‑Ginzburg model. These connections have led to the development of the quantum Satake correspondence, relating the quantum cohomology of Grassmannians to the representation theory of quantum groups at roots of unity. In examinations, a typical question may ask to compute a specific genus‑zero invariant using the quantum Pieri rule or to verify the associativity of the quantum product for a given triple of partitions, which reduces to checking the WDVV equations in the Grassmannian setting.

  • Confusing the ordinary Littlewood‑Richardson rule with its equivariant or K‑theoretic variants — the latter involve polynomials or alternating signs.
  • Forgetting that the quantum parameter q carries degree and may appear with a sign in the quantum Pieri rule for isotropic Grassmannians.
  • Applying the type A Giambelli determinant to orthogonal or symplectic Grassmannians where a Pfaffian or a different determinant is required.
  • Assuming all structure constants are positive in K‑theory; only the dual Grothendieck basis has positive coefficients.
  • Misidentifying the fixed‑point set in equivariant localization — for Gr(k,n) it is k‑subsets, but for flag varieties it is permutations.
  • Neglecting the rim‑hook removal condition when using the quantum Giambelli formula; the determinant includes q‑terms that correspond to removing rim hooks of length n.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the small quantum cohomology (only three‑point invariants) and the big quantum cohomology (all higher‑point invariants) in mirror symmetry computations.
