hand/coding-theory.html:
List Decoding and the Johnson Bound

Classical unique decoding corrects up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors, where d is the minimum Hamming distance. List decoding relaxes this requirement: given a received word y, the decoder outputs a list of all codewords within radius τn (τ a fraction of the block length n). The Johnson bound gives a universal guarantee for any code of relative distance δ = d/n: if τ ≤ 1 − √(1−δ), the list size is bounded by a polynomial in n. For binary codes this simplifies to τ ≤ ½(1−√(1−2δ)). The bound is tight for certain families; for example, Reed–Solomon codes achieve list-decoding radius 1−√R (where R = k/n) via the Guruswami–Sudan algorithm, which interpolates a bivariate polynomial and factors it to recover all candidate messages. The algorithm runs in O(n³) field operations and was later improved to quasi‑linear time by Alekhnovich and by Koetter–Vardy soft‑decision variants. List decoding is essential in modern applications such as cryptography (hardness of decoding random linear codes), complexity theory (hardness amplification), and concatenated coding schemes where an outer list decoder feeds an inner unique decoder. The trade‑off between list size and decoding radius is captured by the list‑decoding capacity theorem: for any rate R and error fraction τ < 1−R, there exist codes with list size L = O(1/ε) where ε = 1−R−τ, and no code can exceed τ = 1−R. This mirrors the Shannon capacity but with a list output instead of a unique decision.

Algebraic Geometry Codes — Goppa and Beyond

Algebraic geometry (AG) codes generalize Reed–Solomon codes by evaluating functions from the Riemann–Roch space L(D) of a smooth projective curve X over GF(q) at n rational points P₁,…,Pₙ. The divisor G (with support disjoint from the evaluation points) defines the code C = {(f(P₁),…,f(Pₙ)) : f ∈ L(G)}. Its length is n, dimension k = ℓ(G) − ℓ(G−D) (where D = Σ Pᵢ), and minimum distance d ≥ n − deg(G). By choosing curves with many rational points relative to their genus g (i.e., curves attaining the Drinfeld–Vladut bound), one obtains families of codes that beat the Gilbert–Varshamov bound for sufficiently large q (q ≥ 49). The classic example is the Hermitian curve yq+y = xq+1 over GF(q²), which has q³+1 rational points and genus g = q(q−1)/2. From it one constructs codes with parameters approaching the Tsfasman–Vladut–Zink (TVZ) bound: R + δ ≥ 1 − 1/(√q−1). Decoding AG codes up to half the designed distance can be done by the Sakata–Feng–Rao majority‑vote algorithm, which uses the Weierstrass semigroup at a point to order basis functions and perform syndrome‑based error location. List decoding of AG codes follows the Guruswami–Sudan paradigm, with interpolation on the curve and factorization in the function field. Recent work on folded AG codes and multiplicity codes further pushes the list‑decoding radius toward 1−R. AG codes are used in high‑rate storage systems and in the construction of locally recoverable codes with optimal locality.

Worked Example: Minimum Distance of a Hermitian Code
Consider the Hermitian curve over GF(4) defined by y² + y = x³. Let G = 5P∞ where P∞ is the point at infinity, and evaluate at the 9 affine rational points. Compute the designed minimum distance of the resulting AG code.
The curve has genus g = 1. The divisor G has degree deg(G) = 5. The number of evaluation points n = 9. By the AG bound, d ≥ n − deg(G) = 9 − 5 = 4. Since ℓ(G) = deg(G) − g + 1 = 5 − 1 + 1 = 5 (Riemann–Roch, as deg(G) > 2g−2), the dimension k = 5. Thus the code is a [9,5,≥4] code over GF(4). The designed distance is 4; the true minimum distance equals 4 because the bound is tight for this parameter set.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the designed distance of an AG code, always compute n − deg(G) first; then verify that deg(G) > 2g−2 to apply the simple Riemann–Roch dimension formula k = deg(G) − g + 1. If deg(G) ≤ 2g−2, you must compute ℓ(G) directly from the Weierstrass semigroup.

Network Coding and Rank‑Metric Codes

Network coding allows intermediate nodes to transmit linear combinations of incoming packets, increasing throughput in multicast scenarios. The algebraic model represents each packet as a vector over GF(q) and each node’s operation as multiplication by a matrix. Errors and erasures in the network correspond to additive perturbations of the transmitted matrix, leading to the rank metric: the distance between two matrices A, B ∈ GF(q)m×n is rank(A−B). Rank‑metric codes, notably Gabidulin codes, are the q‑analogue of Reed–Solomon codes. A Gabidulin code of length n ≤ m and dimension k is defined by evaluating linearized polynomials f(x) = Σi=0k−1 a_i xq^i at n linearly independent points α₁,…,α_n ∈ GF(q^m). The codewords are the m×n matrices whose columns are the evaluations. The minimum rank distance is d = n−k+1, achieving the Singleton bound for the rank metric. Decoding up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ rank errors uses a rank‑metric Berlekamp–Massey algorithm that finds the minimal linearized polynomial annihilating the syndrome matrix. Applications include error correction in random linear network coding (RLNC), cryptography (McEliece‑type systems based on Gabidulin codes), and distributed storage with optimal repair bandwidth. Recent constructions of twisted Gabidulin codes avoid known structural attacks while preserving efficient decoding.

Finite‑Length Bounds and Normal Approximation

Shannon’s capacity theorem is asymptotic; practical systems operate at finite blocklength n. The maximal achievable rate R*(n,ε) for blocklength n and error probability ε satisfies the normal approximation (Polyanskiy–Poor–Verdú, 2010): R*(n,ε) = C − √(V/n) Q⁻¹(ε) + O(log n / n), where C is the channel capacity, V is the channel dispersion, and Q⁻¹ is the inverse Gaussian Q‑function. For the binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p, C = 1−H(p) and V = p(1−p) [log((1−p)/p)]². For the AWGN channel with SNR ρ, C = ½ log₂(1+ρ) and V = ½ ρ(ρ+2)/(ρ+1)² (log₂ e)². The dispersion term quantifies the back‑off from capacity required at finite n. Converse bounds (meta‑converse, dependence‑testing bound) and achievability bounds (random coding union bound, RCU) sandwich R*(n,ε) tightly. These bounds guide the design of short‑packet communications in 5G URLLC and IoT, where n may be as low as 100–200 symbols. The normal approximation also informs the choice of code rate for a target latency: given n and ε, one can compute the maximum rate without resorting to exhaustive simulation.

Density Evolution and Threshold Analysis for LDPC Codes

Density evolution (DE) tracks the probability density of log‑likelihood ratios (LLRs) passed along edges of the Tanner graph under belief‑propagation decoding, assuming the all‑zero codeword and an infinite blocklength (cycle‑free) limit. For a regular (d_v, d_c) LDPC ensemble on the binary erasure channel (BEC) with erasure probability ε, DE reduces to the scalar recursion xℓ+1 = ε (1 − (1 − x_ℓ)d_c−1)d_v−1, where x_ℓ is the erasure probability of messages from variable to check nodes at iteration ℓ. The BP threshold ε* is the supremum ε for which x_ℓ → 0. For the AWGN channel, DE operates on Gaussian densities parameterized by their mean (or variance) due to symmetry; the recursion updates the mean via the function φ(μ) = 1 − E[tanh(L/2)] where L ∼ N(μ, 2μ). The threshold is the largest channel parameter (e.g., σ²) for which the mean diverges to infinity. Irregular degree distributions λ(x), ρ(x) are optimized by linear programming (for BEC) or differential evolution (for AWGN) to maximize the threshold, often approaching within 0.0045 dB of capacity. Finite‑length scaling laws (e.g., the error floor due to trapping sets) are analyzed via the scaling law α n−2/3 Q((ε*−ε) n1/3) for the BEC. DE also underpins the design of spatially coupled LDPC ensembles, whose threshold saturates to the MAP threshold of the underlying ensemble, achieving capacity on a wide class of channels.

  • Confusing the Johnson bound for unique decoding with the list‑decoding radius; the former is ⌊(d−1)/2⌋, the latter can exceed it up to 1−√(1−δ).
  • Assuming all AG codes meet the TVZ bound; only curves with many rational points relative to genus do, and the bound holds asymptotically for q ≥ 49.
  • Treating rank‑metric distance as Hamming distance; rank metric counts the rank of the difference matrix, not the number of non‑zero entries.
  • Using the asymptotic capacity formula C for short packets without the √(V/n) back‑off term; this overestimates achievable rates at n ≤ 200.
  • Believing density evolution thresholds apply directly to finite‑length codes; DE predicts the infinite‑length BP threshold, while finite‑length performance suffers from cycles and trapping sets.
  • Mixing up the Berlekamp–Massey algorithm for Reed–Solomon (scalar syndromes) with the rank‑metric BM algorithm (matrix syndromes); they operate on different algebraic structures.
  • Thinking that list decoding always outputs a small list; for radii beyond the Johnson bound the list size can become exponential, and no efficient algorithm is known.
The advanced topics above extend the core coding theory curriculum into areas that frequently appear in higher‑level examinations and research‑oriented problem sets.
